# About this Manual

This technical reference manual is designed to help customers deploy the Qualcomm® Snapdragon™ 410E processors into commercial embedded computing and IoT products.

Designed to meet the demanding requirements of embedded computing applications with its high performance, energy efficiency, multimedia features, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, the Snapdragon 410E processor is ideal for a broad mix of use cases, such as connected homes, building automation, industrial control, digital signage, smart surveillance and other IoT devices.
<!-- page 52 -->

# 1 APQ8016E Overview

This chapter provides high-level description of the integrated in the SoC modules and their main features.

## 1.1 APQ8016E device

Qualcomm® Snapdragon™ 410E processor (model APQ8016E) for embedded computing and internet of things (IoT) products offers state-of-the-art feature set and processor performance. Combined with high-level of concurrency, low power consumption, multimedia features, integrated connectivity, support for Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity it provides powerful solutions and superior user experience for every platform. With its integrated peripherals and high processing capabilities APQ8016E can be used in many different applications. Some examples are shown in Table 1-1.

### Table 1-1 Applications examples

| Category | Examples |
| :--- | :--- |
| Embedded computing | Robotics (drones, robots, droids)<br>Medical devices<br>Digital signage |
| IoT | Smart homes (smart appliances, intelligent lighting, security, whole-home audio and video)<br>Smart cities (smart transportation, smart meters, smart infrastructure, smart lighting)<br>Wearables (digital eyewear, smartwatches, wearable cameras) |
| Gaming and graphics | 3D mobile gaming<br>Graphics and compute applications |
| Wireless products | Music player-enabled devices and applications<br>Cameras |

The following list summarizes the distinctive features of the APQ8016E device:

* Quad-core ARM® Cortex® A53 processor up to 1.2 GHz per core
* Single Hexagon™ QDSP6 v5 core at up to 691 MHz DSP for ultra-low power audio
* Integrated Wi-Fi/BT/FM connectivity
* Qualcomm® Adreno™ A306 3D graphics module (up to 400 MHz)
<!-- page 53 -->

* GNSS Gen8CF-Lite GPS
* Display support: Mobile display processor, up to two concurrent displays: up to 1.5 Gbps 4-lane MIPI DSI, and wireless display (WFD) up to 1920x1080 at 30fps
* Camera support: 6 Gbit/sec raw data dump and dual ISP up to 13 MP/5 MP 1x 2-lane CSI, 1x (4 and 2) lane CSI with JPEG encode
* Interfaces: USB2.0, MIPI-CSI, MIPI-DSI, SD3.0, eMMC v4.5 with DDR support

## 1.2 APQ8016E block diagram

Figure 1-1 shows a high-level overview of the integrated modules in the SoC.

#### Figure 1-1: APQ8016E device block diagram
*Description:* High-level system architecture block diagram of the APQ8016E SoC. The central backbone is the **System NoC** (Network on Chip), which connects major subsystems:
- **Memory Interfaces**: LPDDR2/LPDDR3 (32-bit, 533MHz) connected via EBI (External Bus Interface consisting of DDR PHY and BIMC) and managed by an SMMU.
- **GPU**: Connected to the System NoC via a System Bus Interface, with a Control Bus Interface from the PCNOC, and 128KB GMEM.
- **CAMSS (Camera Subsystem)**: Contains MIPI CSID 1 and 2, VFE 4ULT (8MP 30fps), CCI (I2C), MICRO, CPP, and JPEG encoder. Connects to System NoC via System Bus IF / VBIF.
- **MDSS (Mobile Display Subsystem)**: Supports MIPI D-PHY 4-lane, containing MIPI DSI and MDP 520 (1080p 40fps). Connects to System NoC via System Bus IF / VBIF.
- **Video Codec (VENCODEC)**: Supports 720p@30fps and 1080p@30fps.
- **IMEM**: 16KB internal memory connected to System NoC.
- **APSS (Application Processor Subsystem)**: Contains Quad-core ARM Cortex A53 CPU with 512KB L2 cache, QGIC 2, SR2PLL, QTimers, WDOG, and CFG_REGS.
- **QDSP6**: Hexagon DSP connected to the System NoC with control from PCNOC.
- **GNSS**: Gen8B-Lite GPS with ADC GNSS.
- **WCSS (Wireless Connectivity Subsystem)**: Contains cCPU, Decode, cMEM, IRQ, DM Lite, BT, FM, WLAN, and DAC/ADC.
- **Peripheral and System Configuration NoC**: A vertical bus connecting USB 2.0 HS (via BAM), SPDM, SDCC (24-bit and 18-bit), Boot ROM, PMIC_ARB, BLSP (6x QUP, 2x UART, BAM-L), MPM, TLMM, TCSR, PWC, GCC, TSENS, and PRNG. It also links to the Debug SS (with DAP), DEHR, MMU, RPM, and the **ULT Audio** subsystem (containing Digital CODEC, LPA IF, CSR, AV Timer, VFR, and 4KB Audio Memory).

Some of the hardware features integrated in the APQ8016E must be enabled by software. See the latest version of the applicable software release notes to identify enabled APQ8016E features. Enabling some features will require additional licensing fees.
<!-- page 54 -->

## 1.3 APQ8016E features overview

### 1.3.1 Processors

#### 1.3.1.1 ARM Cortex A53 subsystem (APSS)

Integrated quad-core ARM Cortex 64-bit processor is running at up to 1.2 GHz. It is used as an application processor for running high level operating system (HLOS), user interface and executing application tasks. The main features of this subsystem are:

* Compliant to ARMv8-A architecture with support of AArch32 and AArch64 modes
* 512 KB L2 unified cache
* TrustZone support
* Support for 32-bit and 64-bit A53 operation modes
* Serves as primary boot processor
* Interfaces:
  * AXI master port to connect A53 CPU(s) to system memory
  * AXI slave port as accelerated coherency port (ACP) for external agents (GPU/SMMU) to access APSS L2 cache
  * AHB slave interface for connection to a system peripheral interconnect (PCNoC)
  * APB slave port interface for connections to a system debug access port (DAP)
  * ATB interface for connections to a system CoreSight™ trace component
  * Standard JTAG interface
  * RPM (resource power manager) interface for each A53 core used during power shutdown and restore
  * PMIC voltage control (PVC) interface for communication with PMIC arbiter

#### 1.3.1.2 QDSP6 processor

The Qualcomm Hexagon™ processor is a general-purpose digital signal processor (QDSP6) designed for high performance and low power across a variety of applications. It is a 32-bit byte-vector operations and both fixed and floating-point multi-threaded processor.

The QDSP6 supports the following main features:

* Runs on up to 691 MHz
* Instructions set architecture:
  * Supports parallel execution with instructions grouped into very long instruction word (VLIW) packets each containing from one to four instructions
  * Little-endian single 32-bit virtual address space for program code and data
  * Full featured memory management unit
<!-- page 55 -->

    * Thirty-two 32-bit general registers for pointer, scalar and packed vector data
    * Supports single instruction, multiple data (SIMD)
  * Multi-threading:
    * Supports dynamic multi-threading (DMT) on L2 cache misses or when in wait-for-interrupt or off mode
    * 32 KB data cache
    * 768 KB level-2 (L2) cache

### 1.3.2 Multimedia

#### 1.3.2.1 Multimedia display subsystem (MDSS)

The MDSS provides the following main features:

* Support for up to two concurrent displays:
  * MIPI DSI: Up to 1200×800 at 60fps
  * Wireless display (WFD): Up to 1920×1080 at 30fps
* One MIPI DSI controller with the following main features:

    * De-noising (artifacts/noise removal)

  * Surface support:
    * Single video surface in packed, pseudo-planar, or planar format
    * Up to two graphics surfaces in ARGB (16bpp, 24bpp, 32bpp) format
    * Single DMA surface in packed, pseudo-planar, or planar format used for rotation
  * Shared memory pool (SMP) for latency buffer
  * Writeback (WB) and rotation support
  * Core clock at 266.67 MHz in normal mode and 320 MHz in turbo mode

Device has one camera subsystem (CAMSS) which encompasses the following sub-modules:

#### 1.3.2.3 Graphic processor unit (GPU)

Integrated in the device Qualcomm® Adreno™ A306 3D low power, fully programmable graphics unit provides comprehensive support for advanced graphics APIs:

* OpenGL ES 1.x, 2.0, and 3.0
* OpenCL 1.0, 1.1 Embedded Profile
* DirectX 9.3 (Windows 10 only)

GPU module is fully controlled through the provided QUALCOMM API.

#### 1.3.2.4 Video encoder/decoder (VENCDEC)

Integrated in the device one digital video encoder/decoder (VENCDEC) module has the following main features:

* Time-multiplexed multi-stream encoding and decoding up to eight channels
* Encode:
  * 720p @ 30 fps (H.264 base/main/high)
  * 720x576 @ 30 fps (MPEG-4 ASP/H.263)
  * 1080p @ 30 fps (MPEG-4/H.264/VP8)
  * WFD 720p @ 30 fps

* Video conference – 15 fps at QCIF (MPEG4, H.263)

VENCDEC module is fully controlled through the provided QUALCOMM API.

#### 1.3.2.5 Virtualizing bus interface (VBIF)

Virtualizing bus interface (VBIF) performs common functions for the device multimedia modules, such as aggregation of data streams, address virtualization, transaction formatting, protocol conversions.

VBIF has the following main features:

* Compliance to ARMv7 virtual to physical address translation
* VBIF client:
  * Support for addressing resolution equal to the client data bus width (64-bit, 128-bit, and 256-bit addressing data buses)
  * Support for a heterogeneous mix of client configurations with different data bus
  * Ability to re-initialize individual client ports without affecting the other VBIF clients
  * Supports separate clocking for each client interface
  * Ability to reorder transaction responses to the clients
  * Write data timeout feature to avoid hanging the master port if the client does not provide data
  * Ability to limit the maximum number of beats in a transaction under software control.
<!-- page 59 -->

* VBIF master:
  * Supports multiple arbitration schemes such as fixed priority, longest time waiting, round robin, and a modified round robin for QoS.
  * Support of independent clocks for the DDR and OCMEM paths
  * Software controlled transaction limits to limit the number of outstanding transactions separately for reads and writes.

#### 1.3.2.6 Ultra-low power audio (ULT Audio)

Designed to support various audio data flows the ULT Audio subsystem provides efficient hardware interfaces for audio, voice, and other applications. ULT Audio has the following main features:

* Provides low-latency audio DMA to and from local RAM (LPM) or DRAM for audio interfaces
* Provides timer and synchronization hardware to support:
  * Concurrent voice/audio ratematching
  * Audio/video (AV) synchronization between local audio clocks and network interfaces, such as Bluetooth, and broadcast audio
* Provides configuration access bridge to integrated analog audio codec
  * Routes audio/voice from various audio/voice interfaces and provides synchronization services for the following interfaces:
    * Integrated audio codec (DMA and synchronization)
    * Third-party I2S devices, such as external speaker drivers and audio codecs (DMA and synchronization)
    * Integrated wireless connectivity networking (WCSS) FM and Bluetooth (synchronization only)
* Supports two AHB buses:
  * AHBI bus for internal transfers
  * AHBX bus for LPA_IF (audio interface) to PCNoC (peripheral-configuration NoC) transfers
* ULT Audio hardware works with audio voice firmware that runs on QDSP6 outside ULT Audio to provide:
  * Meeting of real time voice and audio processing requirements
  * Support of CS voice processing with low round-trip latency
  * Support of QoS for high-level operating system (HLOS) VoIP and multimedia (MM) audio comparable to traditional CS voice:
    * Access to integrated analog audio codec for ULT Audio
    * Low-power audio rendition (tunneled and non-tunneled for HLOS power collapse)
    * Audio calibration and tuning services for HLOS
<!-- page 60 -->

    * Hardware acceleration for MIPS-intensive or low-power audio/voice
    * Support of real time device concurrency, control, routing, mixing, and synchronization
    * Protection of proprietary code algorithms and data from HLOS
    * Support of non-real time audio encode, decode, and processing requirements offloaded from HLOS
    * Support of emerging use cases like low-power microphone activity detection

### 1.3.3 Air interfaces

#### 1.3.3.1 Wireless connectivity subsystem (WCSS)

Device wireless connectivity subsystem (WCSS) integrates three wireless technologies: Bluetooth (BT), FM, and WLAN, which can operate concurrently.

* WLAN baseline features:
  * 802.11 standard compliance
  * Support of Wi-Fi direct and Wi-Fi positioning and optimization for Wi-Fi display
  * Support of simultaneous STA/AP (station/access point) mode
  * Support of up to 16 stations and up to 4 multiple BSSIDs (basic service set ID)
  * Multi-user MU-MIMO for receiver mode (multiple-input and multiple-output)
  * 300 Mbps over 80 MHz channel
  * Fast channel switching
* FM stereo with no radio data system (RDS) in both TX and RX, providing support to navigation system and traffic updates
* Bluetooth fully compliant to BT 4.0

WCSS module is fully controlled through the provided QUALCOMM API.

#### 1.3.3.2 Global Navigation Subsystem (GNSS)

Integrated in the device location engine GNSS provides the required hardware signal processing of navigation signals. The main features of the subsystem include:

* 6-bit SAR (successive-approximation-register) ADC
* 3 Baseband processors (BP)
  * BP1 supports L1/L2 narrow GPS, GALILEO E1, L1 QZSS
  * BP2 supports L1 BEIDOU
  * BP3 supports L1/L2 GLONASS
* Correlation processor (CP) compatible with GPS L2C and GALILEO E1 signals


<!-- page 61 -->

* Support of time transfer (clock comparison) trigger mechanism to bound the time-uncertainty at the receiver
  * Six blanking signals
* GNSS module is fully controlled through the provided QUALCOMM API.

### 1.3.4 General Connectivity

#### 1.3.4.1 BAM-enabled low speed peripherals (BLSP)

Device has integrated bus access manager (BAM) low-speed peripherals (BLSP) module. BLSP gathers slow peripheral cores, specifically QUP and UART, and provides them with BAM capability. BLSP is based on a BAM-lite version of the BAM module. Device BLSP supports:
* Two UART modules
* Six QUP modules (I2C or SPI interfaces to peripherals)

##### 1.3.4.1.1 Qualcomm universal peripherals engine (QUP)

The QUP engine is an advanced high-performance slave port that provides a common data path (an output and an input FIFO) for the device inter-integrated circuit (I2C) and serial peripheral interface (SPI) interfaces. Integrated in the device are six identical instances of QUP with the following main features:
* **I2C:**
  * Compliant to Phillips Semiconductors I2C specification, version 5.0
  * Support of 7-bit addressing mode
  * Support of standard-mode up to 100 Kbps
  * Support of fast-mode up to 400 Kbps
  * Support of fast-mode plus up to 1 Mbps (up to 1 MHz)
* **SPI:**
  * Supports only SPI master mode up to 50 MHz
  * Supports up to three chip-select lines
  * Support of programmable data path from 4 bits to 32 bits
  * Support of numerous protocol variants
<!-- page 62 -->

##### 1.3.4.1.2 Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter (UART)

The UART module is used for transmitting and receiving data through a serial UART/SIM/IrDA interface. It is used for communication with other UART protocol-compliant devices. Integrated in the device two UART modules support the following main features:
* Baud rates from 75 to up to 115200 bps, and 4 Mbps
* 5-8 bits character size, 0.5-2 bits stop bit, no/even/odd/space parity
* Support of single-character mode
* Utilizes BAM to transfer data between its Rx/Tx buffers and system memory
* Integration with internal UIM controller

#### 1.3.4.2 Top level device multiplexer (TLMM)

The TLMM module provides software-controlled mechanism for sharing multiple internal functional interfaces onto a much smaller set of general purpose input/output (GPIO) pads. Main features of the module include:
* Multiplexing different interfaces on the GPIO pads
* Channeling the interrupts from the I/Os to the respective processors
* Supports daisy chaining of various test access port (TAP) controllers on the chip

#### 1.3.4.3 HS universal serial bus core and PHY (HS USB and PHY)

The device supports one high speed universal serial bus (HS USB) port with physical layer (PHY) blocks, compatible with USB 2.0. Main supported features are:
* USB 2.0 specification-compliant as a peripheral or embedded host
* Supports USB host mode and USB peripheral mode features
* **HS USB 2.0 controller:**
  * Supports USB peripheral (device) mode at high speed (HS) 480 Mbps, full speed (FS) 12Mbps, and low speed (LS) 1.5 Mbps
  * Supports USB host mode at speeds HS, FS, and LS (1.5 Mbps)
* **USB-2.0 PHY supports:**
  * USB 2.0 functions, drivers, and receivers for correct D+/D– signaling
<!-- page 63 -->

#### 1.3.4.4 Secure digital card controller (SDCC)

Secure digital card controller (SDCC) is a simple, high-performance, serial interface. The SDCC provides bidirectional data transfer between the system memory and the storage device (eMMC, MMC, SD card, and SDIO device). Integrated in the device two dual voltage SDCC ports have the following main features:
* Configurable width of SD data bus: up to 8 data lines for SDCC1 and up to 4 data lines for SDCC2
* Support for the following standards:
  * SD version 3.0 and earlier
  * eMMC version 4.5 and earlier
  * SDIO version 3.00 and earlier
* Support of standard host controller interface (SDHCI)
* Support of different bus speed modes (SD):
  * DS (default speed)
  * HS (high speed)
  * SDR12, SDR25, SDR50, SDR104 - ultra-high speed (UHS-I): single data rate (SDR)
  * DDR50 - ultra-high speed (UHS-I): double data rate (DDR)
* Support of different bus speed modes (eMMC):
  * DS
  * HS
  * DDR
  * HS200
* Support of dynamic bus clock scaling
* Support of SD/eMMC boot capabilities

#### 1.3.4.5 Peripheral web core (PWC)

Peripheral web core (PWC) serves as pulse coded modulation interface. It is used for generating density modulated signals that, after passing through a filter, become analog signals and can produce fixed densities or alternate between densities to create variations in the analog signal. Device has integrated three PWC modules. Each of the modules can be used independently. Main features include:
* Three configurable pulse-density output signals with base frequency set at 4.8 MHz
* One general purpose clock divider output with frequency and duty-cycle controlled by dedicated control registers
<!-- page 64 -->

#### 1.3.4.6 Memory support

Device uses a single embedded multi chip package (eMCP) dual function LPDDR3/eMMC memory solution or discrete eMMC and LPDDR parts. The LPDDR3 is a 32bit width bus implementation interfacing directly to the APQ8016 build-in LPDDR controller. The maximum DDR clock is 533Mhz. The eMMC is an 8bit implementation interfacing with APQ8016 SDCC1 interface supporting eMMC 4.5 specifications.

Device memory subsystem also encapsulates several different modules under external bus interface (EBI) module:
* Bus integrated memory controller (BIMC)
* On chip internal memory controller (OCIMEM)
* DMA engine for hardware retention (DEHR)

EBI module also encapsulates all DDR PHYs and comprises of 32-bit data channels:
* AHB2PHY: provides AHB configurable bridge (connected to PCNoC) and programmable registers to control and configure the DDR_PHYs
* One command address (CA) PHY block, and four data bytes (DQ) PHY blocks;

The EBI supports the following main features:
* Single channel 32-bit SDRAM interface
* Two chip selects
* Up to 2 GB for both chip selects (maximum total density supported is 2 GB)
* Single AHB2PHY interface
* Supports frequencies:
  * 200 MHz – switch voltage sequence (SVS) mode
  * 400 MHz – mission mode
  * 533 MHz – turbo mode

Bus integrated memory controller (BIMC) comprises multiple subcomponents with specific functionalities:
* **Front-end AXI interface portion** serves as a front-end interface to the rest of the chip and performs operations such as slave address mapping, DDR memory density configuration, MPU configuration, arbitration settings, and performance monitoring. It comprises:
  * AXI interconnect through reusable bus & interconnect components (BRIC)
  * SDRAM controller and memory organizer (SCMO) with the following main features:
    * Converts read and write transaction addresses into DRAM addressing (into rank, bank, row, and column)
    * Orders transactions to maximize hits to open rows, to minimize row pre-charges and activities
    * Buffers writes, to coalesce and delay the writes to allow for critical transactions to take precedence
<!-- page 65 -->

* **Back-end portion** (also called DRAM controller or memory controller MC) handles all aspects of dealing with the critical part of the interface to LPDDR2, LPDDR3, and PCDDR3 DRAMs such as initialization, selfrefresh, frequency scaling, and so on. It comprises:
  * DDR protocol engine module (DPE):
    * Transacts with DRAM for all commands and maintains signaling and signal timing requirements of DRAM.
  * SDRAM housekeeping engine module (SHKE)
    * Initializes DRAM
    * Maintains periodicity of periodic commands to DRAM, for example, refresh, calibration, status register read, activity-based self-refresh, and power down modes
* DDR test engine module (DTE)

On chip internal memory controller (OCIMEM) provides internal memory resources to clients over a synchronous AXI interface. It contains two slave interfaces ports:
* 64-bit AXI port connected to the SNoC allows access to the internal memory resources.
* 32-bit AHB port connected to the PCNoC allows programming of OCIMEM internal registers.

DMA engine for hardware retention (DEHR) is a DMA engine, which is used to save and restore configuration data during power collapse. It has the following main features:
* Supports security protection mechanisms to safely transfer data.
* Saves and restores BIMC configuration data during BIMC power collapse

### 1.3.5 Device resources

Device has implemented many system level resources. Several of those resources are common and shared amongst the autonomous subsystems in the chip.

#### 1.3.5.1 Power and resource management (RPM)

RPM is a dedicated engine for managing SoC common resources, such as buses, clocks, core, and memory power rails, to attain the lowest dynamic and static power profile of that SoC. The engine operates with low latency and low-power. The RPM directly communicates with the processors in each subsystem to process and coordinate shared power/resource requests. Main features of the subsystem are:
* Cortex-M3® ARMv7-M architecture processor at 150 MHz with nested vectored interrupt controller (NVIC) and support of suspend and wait for interrupt (SWFI) instruction
* RPM interrupt controller for priority queuing of interrupts and support of both edge-sensitive and level-sensitive interrupts
* Multibank code RAM
* 64 KB multibank data RAM
* Synchronous to the RPM processor AMBA high-performance bus (AHB)
<!-- page 66 -->

RPM is fully controlled through the provided QUALCOMM API. It is software driven so is flexible in adapting to the most optimum algorithms for efficiently managing power of the rest of the chip.

#### 1.3.5.2 PMIC arbiter (PMIC_ARB)

Device PMIC arbiter serves to provide various hardware and software masters with concurrent and autonomous access to the off-chip PMIC via a single MIPI system power management interface (SPMI). The PMIC arbiter contains the SPMI controller and provides security for its configuration port. The PMIC arbiter prioritizes multiple clients that are attempting to access the PMIC. Main features include:
* Provides a mechanism for software and hardware masters to access off-chip PMIC peripherals in a concurrent and autonomous manner
* Supports 4KB boundaries in the memory map to support SMMU register access control security
* Supports the full set of SPMI opcodes supported by the SPMI master
* Supports SPMI reads and writes from one to eight bytes in length
* Supports 6 SW masters
* Supports clock gating
* Supports programmable priority based on the arbiter port

#### 1.3.5.3 Global clock controller (GCC)

Device clock generation and propagation is based on one global clock controller (GCC) and many clock controllers (CC) distributed into subsystems. GCC provides clock sources to:
* Three independent clock blocks:
  * Global clock block (accessible by all processors on the chip)
  * Applications processor A53 subsystem (APSS)
  * Wireless connectivity subsystem (WCSS)
* ULT Audio and multimedia
* Resource and power management subsystem (RPM)
* System, configuration and peripheral interconnects
* Memory and bus integrated memory controller (BIMC)
* Qualcomm debug subsystem (QDSS)
* All the peripherals on the SoC
* Various other subsystems and clock interfaces

Main features of the GCC are:
* Provides on-chip generation of high-speed clock sources relative to reference inputs
* Distributes single-phase clock sources to all cores and blocks
<!-- page 67 -->

* Supports clock gating to reduce power consumption
* Programmable divide ratios, clocks source selection and switching (where applicable)
* Uses 19.2 MHz crystal oscillator (CXO) as master clock input

#### 1.3.5.4 Interconnect (NoC)

Device network on chip (NoC) is implemented to provide a high-performance, low-latency interconnect. The main purpose of the NoC is to connect masters and slaves, following standard protocols, and to allow them to communicate with each other. NoC has independent clock domains for each slave port, each master port, and an arbitration logic on per a slave basis. This allows only necessary to process any given master’s request and slave’s response pieces of NoC to be clocked as required. Device has integrated two interconnects:
* Main top-level interconnect or system network on chip (SNoC)
* Peripheral and configuration interconnect (PCNoC).

Device network on chip supports:
* AMBA 2.0 AXI bus standard
* Quality of service (QoS) features
* Bus performance monitoring

#### 1.3.5.5 Interrupts

Device interrupt system is based on a Qualcomm generic interrupt controller (QGIC2). QGIC2 is a fully programmable interrupt controller designed to be paired with an ARM-compliant CPU core. It is integrated within the APSS and performs the following functions:
* Receives interrupts from the system or from private CPU peripherals
* Processes the interrupts with priority information set by software
* Directs the interrupts to their host CPU core(s)

Main features of the QGIC controller are:
* Compatible to ARM GIC 2.0 specification
* Compatible to ARM TrustZone architecture
* 16 software generated interrupts (SGIs)
* 16 private peripheral interrupts (PPIs)
* 256 shared peripheral interrupts (SPIs)
* 32 priority levels
<!-- page 68 -->

#### 1.3.5.6 Qualcomm timer (QTMR)

Qualcomm timer (QTMR) implements the ARM generic timer specification. QTMR is used to generate timer triggered events based on an equal-to or greater than comparison with a SoC global counter. QTMR module has the following main features:
* Support of AHB-lite slave port interface
* 32-bit data width accesses
* Synchronized with SoC global counter, which has:
  * Fine granularity (19.2 MHz) for measuring time and calculating very short delays
  * 56-bit wide counter
  * Continual incrementing even when a processor is power collapsed

#### 1.3.5.7 Bus access manager (BAM)

Bus access manager (BAM) is a component inserted between a peripheral module and the subsystem bus to act like DMA engine. Device supports three versions of BAM module:
* **BAM:** full performance version
* **BAM-NDP:** non-data path version which enables peripherals with fast fabric connectivity to access the data directly
* **BAM-Lite:** an optimized version which gathers slow peripherals and provides them with BAM capability

BAM module supports the following main features:
* Directs data exchange between two peripherals - BAM to BAM mode
* Serves as system producer to BAM connection - data blocks of any size and at any address are gathered by hardware from memory
* Serves as BAM to system consumer connection - data is scattered by hardware into data blocks of any size at any address boundary in memory
* Supports multiple pipe connections with other BAMs (consumer/producer) or system memory for transferring and receiving data
* Supports secured BAMs - protected by an integrated APU from malicious accesses
* Supports power save mode
<!-- page 69 -->

#### 1.3.5.8 System memory management unit (SMMU)

Device system memory management units (SMMU) performs translation of virtual memory addresses (VA), used by the processors, to physical memory addresses (PA) for the physical memory system. The SMMU subsystem also handles memory protection, cache control, and bus arbitration. Based on ARM® CoreLink™ MMU-500 device SMMU subsystem has the following main features:
* Two SMMU instances:
  * APPS SMMU - consists of 9 TBU (translation buffer units) and 1 TCU (translation control unit)
  * GPU SMMU - consists of 1 TBU and 1 TCU
* Support of 32-bit VA and 32-bit PA
* Support of 32 configurable contexts
* Supports 4 KB, 64 KB, 2 MB page sizes
* Support of interrupt aggregation logic for APPS TCU context bank interrupts
* Provides address virtualization to processors and other masters in the device
* Protects memory access by controlling access permissions
* Supports clock gating

#### 1.3.5.9 Pseudo-random number generator (PRNG)

Pseudo random number generator (PRNG) generates cryptographic random numbers. The two primary PRNG uses are in cryptographic key exchange algorithms or in gaming applications.

#### 1.3.5.10 Top control and status registers (TCSR)

Core top control and status registers (TCSR) block provides variety of control and status registers protected by xPU configured as APU (address protection unit), as well as 4KB resource group partitioning. It also provides mutex registers for software to pass control among different CPUs and collections of miscellaneous registers for top level control. TCSR block generates summary security violation interrupts, AHB slave timed out interrupts and serial interface interrupts (UART and QUP).

#### 1.3.5.11 Temperature sensors (TSENS)

Temperature sensor (TSENS) module is a digital controller which provides software interface and control to key functionalities for monitoring of the die temperature. Main features of the module are:
* Supports periodic temperature measurement
* Supports hardware shutdown capability at extreme temperatures, to avoid permanent damage due to extreme temperature condition
* Supports up to eleven (one main and ten remote) temperature sensors
<!-- page 70 -->

* Provides dedicated programmable temperature thresholds and a control for each individual sensor
* Provides two programmable temperature limits
* Internal oscillator for ADC
* Low-power operation during continuous mode
* Software reset capability
* Support of aggregated interrupt for thermal mitigation management

#### 1.3.5.12 Qualcomm debug subsystem (QDSS)

Qualcomm debug subsystem (QDSS) provides a system level debug, trace, and monitoring. QDSS supports:
* CoreSight trace standards
* APB-AP debug port interface
* Cross-triggering functionality
* QDSS main subsystems are:
  * **Debug access port (DAP) subsystem** with main features:
    * Read/write the system address map via AHB/AXI-AP access
    * Access the entirety of the QDSS control plane (debug APB bus)
    * Provides JTAG-AP accesses to all JTAG debugged CPU/DSPs in the system
  * **System trace macrocell (STM) subsystem**
  * **Cross triggering subsystem** responsible for sourcing and sinking of all cross triggers generated/received in the system
  * **Timestamp subsystem** responsible for generating and transporting a master 64-bit CoreSight timestamp synchronously to multiple timestamp capable trace source receivers in the device

QDSS main features include:
* 512KB configuration space, accessible to both an externally attached debugger as well as to any other software driver running on any system CPU/DSP
* Support for acceptance of ATB trace streams from all system ATB trace sources
* Support for sinking ATB trace data to:
  * QDSS TPIU (Trace port interface unit)
  * Trace data to system memory via embedded trace router (ETR)
  * Trace data over USB - USB3.0 (or USB2.0) via ETR and NDP BAM
  * Dynamic reading via embedded trace FIFO
* Support of cross-triggering
* Support of STM interface to QDSS trace path


<!-- page 71 -->
### 1.3.6 APQ8016E chipset

Complementary ICs within the APQ8016E chipset include:
* **Power management IC**: PM8916 with battery charger SMB1360 (see Power management PM8916 IC)
* **Wireless connectivity IC**: WCN3620 A/B (see Wireless connectivity WCN3620 A/B IC)
* **GNSS RF receiver IC**: WGR7640 (see GNSS RF receiver WGR7640)

Figure 1-2 shows a high-level overview of the APQ8016E chipset.

#### Figure 1-2: APQ8016E chipset block diagram
*Description:* Block diagram showing the APQ8016E main chip and its connections to WGR7640, WCN3620 A/B, and PM8916.
- **APQ8016E** contains:
  - **Processors**: ARM Quad Cortex-A53 uP.
  - **Chipset and RFFE I/Fs**: Serial buses, Discrete stat and ctrl, GNSS ADC (connected to WGR7640 GNSS receiver), BB t/r switch with WCSS DACs/ADCs (connected to WCN3620 A/B WLAN/BT/FM).
  - **Air interfaces**: GNSS Gen 8C (GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, Beidou), WCN processing (WLAN/BT/FM).
  - **Memory support**: EBI (connected to LPDDR2/LPDDR3), Connectivity SDCC1 (connected to eMMC), Internal memory.
  - **Connectivity**: BLSP (x6) (UART, I2C, SPI), SDCC2, WCSS (connected to WCN3620 A/B WLAN), HS USB w/ PHY.
  - **Multimedia**: MDP (with 4-lane MIPI_DSI connected to Display), CAMIF timing, 4-lane MIPI_CSI, 2-lane MIPI_CSI, Video/VFE, codecs, GPU, Audio/codec digital, Ultra low power audio (ULP Audio).
  - **Internal functions**: Thermal sensors, Resources and power management, Mode/config/resets, GP clock and PDM outs, JTAG/QDSS/ENET (connected to debug), Clock generation.
  - **GPIOs / PWR and GND**.
- **WGR7640** (GNSS RF receiver IC) contains: Status and control, RxLO circuits, GNSS receiver.
- **WCN3620 A/B** (Wireless connectivity IC) contains: WLAN/BT front-end, Bluetooth RF and BB, WLAN RF, FM RF and BB, Support and I/Os.
- **PM8916** (Power management IC) contains: Input power management (connected to System power), Output power management (provides Supply voltages to APQ8016E), User interface, Audio codec, IC-level interface, General housekeeping (connected to APQ8016E GP clock and PDM outs, and providing clocks back).
<!-- page 72 -->
#### 1.3.6.1 Power management PM8916 IC

The PM8916 device integrates all wireless handset power management, general housekeeping, and user interface support functions into a one mixed-signal IC. PM8916 has the following major functional blocks:
* Input power management
* Output power management
* User interfaces
* Audio codec
* IC-level interfaces
* General housekeeping

PM8916 main features include:
* Single charger source – USB
* Linear battery charger
  * USB source with built-in 16 V over-voltage protection (OVP)
  * Integrated OVP FET transistor
* Bidirectional battery UICC alarm (BUA) for graceful UICC (universal integrated circuit card) shutdown upon battery or UICC removal
* System-clock and sleep-clock sources for entire chipset
* Four GPIOs of which two can output high-speed clocks
* Pulse width modulator (PWM) for dimming control of external white light-emitting diode (WLED) IC driver
* Plug-and-play support
* Programmable reset control
* Audio codec (ADCs and DACs), stereo head phone, ear and speaker amplifiers with digital decimator and interpolator chains

PM8916/PM8916-1 specification can be found on Qualcomm developer network:
PM8916/PM8916-1 Power Management IC Device Specification

#### 1.3.6.2 Wireless connectivity WCN3620 A/B IC

The wireless connectivity WCN3620 IC integrates top-level support circuits and three different wireless connectivity technologies into a single device suitable for handsets and other mobile devices:
* Wireless local area network (WLAN) compliant with the IEEE 802.11 a/b/g/n specification
* Bluetooth (BT) compliant with the BT specification version 4.x (BR/EDR+BLE)
* Worldwide FM radio, with Rx modes supporting the radio data system (RDS) for Europe and the radio broadcast data system (RBDS) for the USA
<!-- page 73 -->
WCN3620 main features include:
* WLAN supports 2.4 GHz
* Bluetooth (BT) shares the WLAN 2.4 GHz front-end
* FM Rx-only uses headset wiring as an antenna
* All RF transceiver circuits are integrated into the WCN3620

WCN3620 specification can be found on Qualcomm developer network:
WCN3620 Wireless Connectivity IC Device Specification

#### 1.3.6.3 GNSS RF receiver WGR7640

The WGR7640 IC is a dedicated global navigation satellite services (GNSS) radio frequency (RF) receiver.

WGR7640 main features include:
* GNSS receiver input for GPS, GLONASS, and COMPASS operation
* GNSS RF-to-baseband quadrature down-converter
* An analog GNSS baseband interface to the baseband device
* GNSS Rx local oscillator (LO) source
* Voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) and phase lock loop (PLL) circuits that support GNSS operating bands
* Option to support an external low-noise amplifier (LNA)
* Low operating voltages save battery current and allows the WLP GPS receiver (WGR) IC power to be supplied by the PMIC’s switched-mode power supply (SMPS) circuits
* Single-wire serial bus interface (SSBI) for efficient initialization, status, and control

WGR7640 specification can be found on Qualcomm developer network:
WGR7640 GNSS RF Receiver IC Device Specification

## 2.2 Applications and baseband processors

The device consists of the following processors:
* Quad-core ARM Cortex v53 processors
* ARM9 wireless connectivity processor (WCSS)
* ARM9 video encoder/decoder (VENCDEC) processor
* M3 resource and power manager (RPM) processor

## 2.3 Bus Architecture

The network on chip (NoC) is implemented in this device to provide a high-performance, low-latency interconnect. It is used for the main top-level interconnect (system NoC) and the peripheral and configuration bus (PCNoC). For more information about PCNoC, see Table 2-4.

# 3 Processors

## 3.1 ARM Cortex – A53 subsystems (APSS)

This chapter describes the application processor subsystem (APSS).

### 3.1.1 APSS overview

The APSS consists of quad ARM A53 CPU cores and related cache memories, along with a number of functional support blocks. These functions comprise a subsystem, suitable for running a high-level operating system (HLOS) and user interface, and executing application tasks.

Table 3-1 lists the APSS supported features.

#### Table 3-1: APSS features

| Module name | Features |
|---|---|
| APSS | <ul><li>Quad A53 CPU block</li><li>Compliance to ARMv8 architecture</li><li>Support for 32-bit and 64-bit A53 operation mode</li><li>L1 caches</li><ul><li>32 KB Icache</li><li>32 KB Dcache</li></ul><li>512 KB L2 cache; runs at 1/2 of core frequency</li><li>Accesses to L2 from other masters through ACP slave ports compliant to AXI3 spec</li><li>Qualcomm generic interrupt controller (QGIC2)</li><li>Memory mapped QTimer</li><li>Watchdog timer</li><li>Single dedicated PLL for both CPU and L2 clock</li><li>Dedicated SPM for each A53 CPU and L2 power management</li><li>Independent RBCPR controller for dynamic voltage fine-tuning of VDD_APC_GDS</li><li>Voting logic for TZ, hypervisor, and HLOS to vote for core/L2/cluster power collapse</li><li>Boot address remapper, configurable by software</li><ul><li>128 KB address range and 128 KB granularity</li><li>Separate CSR for secure or nonsecure address remapping</li></ul><li>Interfaces</li><ul><li>One AXI3 master port to connect A53 CPUs to system memory</li><li>One AXI3 ACP slave port to access L2 from other masters</li><li>One AHB slave port from a system-level bus to connect other authorized chip masters to subsystem-local peripherals</li><li>Hardware interrupt input sources to interrupt controller; software programmable interrupt outputs to interrupt controllers in other subsystems</li><li>RPM interface</li><li>PMIC arbiter interface to support the SPM + RBCPR</li></ul></ul> |

#### 3.1.2 APSS internal connectivity

Figure 3-1 shows the APSS internal interface signals.

#### Figure 3-1: APSS internal connectivity
*Description:* A block diagram illustrating the interface signals between the APSS (Application Processor Subsystem) and other subsystem blocks (WCSS, Q6SS, RPM, GCC) as well as internal interrupts and peripheral connections.
- **WCSS (Wireless Connectivity Subsystem):** Receives 4 inter-processor communication (IPC) interrupt signals from APSS: `APCS_WCNIPCINTERRUPT_0` through `APCS_WCNIPCINTERRUPT_3`.
- **Q6SS (Hexagon DSP Subsystem):** Receives 4 IPC interrupt signals from APSS: `APCS_MSSIPCINTERRUPT_0` through `APCS_MSSIPCINTERRUPT_3`.
- **RPM (Resource Power Manager):** Exchange signals with APSS, receiving:
  - Core-specific shutdown and bring-up requests (`APC0_SYSSHUTDOWNREQ`, `APC0_SYSBRINGUPREQ` up to `APC3_*`).
  - RPM HLOS (High-Level OS) IPC interrupts (`APCS_RPMHLOSIPCINTERRUPT_0` to `_2`).
  - RPM TrustZone (TZ) IPC interrupts (`APCS_RPMTZIPCINTERRUPT_0` to `_2`).
  - L2 cache shutdown and bring-up requests (`APCS_SYSL2SHUTDOWNREQ`, `APCS_SYSL2BRINGUPREQ`).
  - Debug core power-up interrupt (`APCS_DBGCOREPWRUPINT`).
  - RPM VMM (Virtual Machine Manager) IPC interrupts (`APCS_RPMVMMIPCINTERRUPT_0` to `_3`).
- **GCC (Global Clock Controller):** Sends 6 clock and reset signals to APSS:
  - Resets: `GCC_APSS_ARES`, `APSS_ALT_ARES`.
  - Clocks: `GCC_APSS_AUX_CLK`, `GCC_SYS_NOC_APSS_AHB_CLK`, `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`, `GCC_APSS_AXI_CLK`.
- **APSS Internal Components:**
  - **Internal Interrupts block:** Outputs 6 signals to **QGIC2** (Qualcomm Generic Interrupt Controller v2):
    - Wakeup synchronization signals: `QGICWAKEUPSYNC_0` through `QGICWAKEUPSYNC_3`.
    - Watchdog timer interrupts: `WDT_BARKINT` and `WDT_BITEEXPIRED`.
  - **AHB slave bus:** Bidirectional connection at the bottom of the APSS block interfaces with the **Peripheral and System Configuration NoC**.
<!-- page 83 -->

#### 3.1.3 APSS functional description

##### 3.1.3.1 APSS architecture

The APSS includes functional blocks as listed in Table 3-1. Figure 3-2 shows a high-level block diagram of the APSS.

#### Figure 3-2: APSS functional block diagram
*Description:* A detailed block diagram showing the internal architecture of the APSS, including the A53 complex, peripheral controllers, and interfaces to external SoC buses (BIMC and SNOC).

- **A53 Complex:**
  - Consists of four **Cortex-A53 cores (CPU0 to CPU3)**.
  - Each core contains a **32 KB Instruction Cache (2-way, 64B line)** and a **32 KB Data Cache (4-way, 64B line)**.
  - Cores connect to the **Integrated L2 controller** via an ACE interface (128-bit read, 256-bit write).
  - The **Integrated L2 controller** contains SCU memory and L1tag copy logic.
  - The controller connects to a **512 KB L2 Cache (16-way, 64B line)** through a multiplexer (MUX).
  - The controller connects via AXI to the **TCM redirect (+ aliasing logic)** block, which also interfaces with a **TCM controller**.
  - The TCM redirect block interfaces with a **Boot remapper** via AXI, which in turn connects to the external **BIMC (AXI3, 64-bit)** bus.
  - An **Accelerator Coherency Port (ACP)** provides a bidirectional path from the external **BIMC** to the L2 controller's SCU.

- **Peripheral & Control Blocks (connected to the internal AHB Bus):**
  - **SR2PLL**: Phase-Locked Loop.
  - **QGIC2**: Interrupt Controller.
  - **QTimer**: System Timer.
  - **RBCPR controller**: Rapid Bridge Core Power Reduction.
  - **SPM0** (4 stacked blocks): Subsystem Power Manager.
  - **L2 SAW2**: SPM and AVS block for L2 cache.
  - **ACSR0** (4 stacked blocks): APSS Control and Status Registers.
  - **GCSR**: Global Control and Status Registers.
  - **WDOG**: Watchdog timer.
  - **Power up state m/c**: Power-up state machine.
  - These blocks communicate via a vertical **AHB bus**, which interfaces with the external **SNOC** at the bottom, and provides **RPM i/f** and **PMIC i/f** external signals.

- **Other Components:**
  - **Temp sensor**: Thermal sensor inside the APSS with an external indicator signal.
<!-- page 86 -->

The A53 CPU is an ARM® architecture application processor. Quad A53 CPU block and shared logic have common supply and can dynamically change this supply voltage and clock frequency to save power. Note that:
- Both the A53 CPUs and A53 L2 controller are powered by a shared voltage rail, VDD_APC_GDS.
- A53 CPUs and A53 L2 controller are GDHS to minimize leakage.
- The L2 memory is powered by the VDD_MX voltage rail. The L2 cache is a split rail custom macro with head switch control.

The power of each A53 CPU and shared logic (L2 memory, L2 controller) is managed by the respective SPM and SAW2.

##### 3.1.3.2 APSS boot

There are two types of boot supported by the APSS: cold boot, and warm (watchdog) boot.

As per the SoC boot architecture, APSS CPU0 is the first processor to come out of reset on a cold boot or a watchdog reset, and start executing APSS PBL from ROM. PBL is responsible for SBL authentication and loading. Since PBL is a small piece of code, it does not have a DDR driver and, in addition, for performance reasons, the next boot stage SBL has to run out of internal memory. For optimizing cost, L2 of APSS CPU doubles as a TCM during the SBL stage of boot.

The SoC boot architecture provides support for switching from a 32-bit HLOS (AArch32) to a 64-bit HLOS (AArch64). Switching to 64-bit mode could be made using A53 RMR register and warm reset functionality as per ARMv8 architecture exception model. Since RMR functionality and switching can happen only at highest exception level - EL3 if there is A53, the boot stage at which switching can happen to be either PBL, SBL or TZ. The SoC boot architecture uses switch between SBL to TZ as the point of 32->64-bit switch. Rest of the boot stages and their functionality do not have any significant impact on the architecture of the APSS.

###### 3.1.3.2.1 Cold boot

**Boot master (APSS CPU0)**

The following applies in order for APSS CPU0 to be the first processor to boot:
- APSS CPU0 comes out of reset with its default XO clock enabled upon hardware reset (`RESIN_N`) de-assertion.
- All other processors (that is, RPM, QDSP6, and so on) remain in reset state on hardware reset de-assertion.
- Application processor has access to all processors’ reset and clock enable. AP takes these processors out of reset during cold boot.
- Hardware reset is asserted for at least 32 cycles for the AP’s internal registers to initialize.
- APSS provides hardware logic (APSS boot FSM) to release APSS CPU0 out of reset while meeting AP reset sequence, such as unclamp AP L2 cache, and so on.
- APSS PBL increases operating point to max nominal clock, so that boot performance is consistent with expectation.
<!-- page 87 -->

- The default value of the boot-remapper is set to `0x00100000` and the `VINITHI` bit in the `APCS_BOOT_START_ADDR_SEC` register is `0x0`.

**APSS boot FSM**

As mentioned, APSS CPU0 is the first processor to come out of reset. A special piece of hardware, referred to as APSS boot FSM, is responsible for APSS CPU0, L2 SCU, and L2 memory bringup at XO frequency. The various delays involved in power-up sequence of application processor CPU0 are controlled via fuses.

APSS boot FSM is on `VDD_CX` rail. It operates on XO clock (19.2 MHz), so the entire bringup sequence for L2 and CPU0 operates on this clock. APSS boot FSM is triggered upon:
1. Cold boot
2. Watchdog first pass
3. Watchdog second pass

After primary core has booted, it boots the secondary core using the init boot sequence shown in Table 3-7.

**Table 3-7 A53 CPU[1,2,3] init boot sequence**

| Register | Value | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00000033` | Assert reset |
| `APCS_ALIASn_APC_PWR_GATE_CTL` | `0x10000001` | Program skew to 16 XO clk cycles, close core logic GDHS |
| *Wait 2us (delay loop)* | | |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00000031` | De-assert core mem clamp. (Clamp coremem is asserted by default) |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00000039` | Close core mem array GDHS |
| *Wait 1.2us (delay loop)* | | |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00020038` | De-assert clamp |
| *Wait 1.2us (delay loop)* | | |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00020008` | De-assert core 0 reset |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x00020088` | Assert PWRDUP |

**Watchdog debug mode boot sequence**

In watchdog debug mode (first pass), APSS boot FSM asserts the `DBGL1RSTDISBLE` and `L2RSTDISABLE` to stop the automatic clean and invalidate of memories by hardware and release the reset for CPU0.

In this case, the power will be maintained for APSS, so the boot FSM will only execute the reset sequence for L2-SCU and CPU0.

After primary core has booted, it boots the secondary cores for debug using the boot sequence as shown in Table 3-8.
<!-- page 88 -->

**Table 3-8 A53 CPU[1,2,3] watchdog debug mode boot sequence**

| Register | Value | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x0000001D` | Assert warm core reset |
| `APCS_ALIASn_APC_PWR_GATE_CTL` | `0x10000001` | Program skew to 16 XO clk cycles, close core logic GDHS |
| *Wait 2 us (Delay Loop)* | | |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x0002001C` | De-assert clamp |
| *Wait 1.2 us (Delay Loop)* | | |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x0002000C` | De-assert core 0 reset |
| `APCS_ALIASn_CPU_PWR_CTL` | `0x0002008C` | Assert PWRDUP |

> [!NOTE]
> Watchdog second pass falls under cold boot category.

**Setting L2 as TCM**

The APSS allows setting L2 as 512 K contiguous physically addressed TCM. The following sequence is executed by boot to set up L2 as TCM:
1. Power up the A53 core 0 and release it from reset (APSS PBL).
2. Enable TCM redirection by setting `TCM_REDIRECT_EN_0` bit in `APCS_TCM_START_ADDR` register. (Currently code execution must not be from the TCM physical address region).
3. Set up the redirect address range for A53 from APSS PBL by programming the `TCM_START_ADDR` bit field in the `APCS_TCM_START_ADDR` register. This address is 512 K aligned.
4. Execute `DMB`.
5. Fetch the boot code from flash and copy it to L2 in TCM mode (TCM redirection bit set). The A53 transactions should be noncacheable in TCM mode. Since A53 MMU is disabled by default, the booting happens in noncacheable mode.
6. Proceed with secure boot flow, ensuring that the accesses are still noncacheable in A53, and L2 is in TCM mode. Exclusive accesses are not supported in the TCM mode.
7. After executing the secure boot flow, disable L2 TCM mode by clearing the `TCM_REDIRECT_EN_0` bit in the `APCS_TCM_START_ADDR` register.
8. Execute `DMB`.
9. Enable L1 and L2 caches for A53 by setting bit [2] in A53 system control register (`SCTRL`) to `0x1`, and proceed normally.
<!-- page 89 -->

##### 3.1.3.3 APSS IPC interrupts

A53 CPU interacts with other CPUs within the SoC using interprocessor communication (IPC) interrupts. These are edge-triggered interrupts. A software writes to `APCS_IPC_INTERRUPT` or `APCS_TZ_IPC_INTERRUPT` register generates an IPC interrupt.

APSS has two execution environments (EE). The EE is independent of the number of CPUs present in the A53 complex. The two EE are:
- An HLOS running on A53 CPU. This is counted as one EE even if there are four CPUs in the A53 complex. HLOS uses `APCS_IPC_INTERRUPT` register to generate software interrupt.
- A TZ image running on A53 CPU. TZ uses `APCS_TZ_IPC_INTERRUPT` register to generate software interrupt.

##### 3.1.3.4 APSS power and clock management

APSS manages power of A53 complex resources. They are:
- Individual A53 CPU power. This includes A53 core and some related debug logic.
- L2SCU power. This includes L2, L2 controller, and qsb i/f logic.

##### 3.1.3.4.2 A53 CPU low-power management

Each CPU can execute a wait for interrupt (WFI) instruction to enter wait state, in which that CPU is quiesced and consumes a minimum of power, while waiting for an interrupt to wake it from wait state. Each CPU can enter a particular sleep mode by programming the associated `SAW2_SPM_CTL` register to act for the CPU after the CPU enters wait state. The code example for three possible sleep modes is shown in Table 3-14.

##### 3.1.3.4.3 A53 CPU active power management (WFE, SEV)

The ARMv8 architecture implements the wait for event (WFE) mechanism that permits a processor in a multiprocessor system to request entry to a low-power state, and, if the request succeeds, to remain in that state until it receives an event generated by a send event (SEV) operation on another processor in the system.

For example, a multiprocessor operating system requires locking mechanisms to protect data structures from being accessed simultaneously by multiple processors. These mechanisms prevent the data structures becoming inconsistent or corrupted if different processors try to make conflicting changes. If a lock is busy, because a data structure is being used by one processor, it might not be practical for another processor to do anything except wait for the lock to be released. For example, if a processor is handling an interrupt from a device it might need to add data received from the device to a queue. If another processor is removing data from the queue, it will have locked the memory area that holds the queue. The first processor cannot add the new data until the queue is in a consistent state and the lock has been released. It cannot return from the interrupt handler until the data has been added to the queue, so it must wait.

A spin-lock mechanism is not ideal for all situations:
- In a low-power system, the tight read loop is undesirable because it uses energy to no effect.
- In a multi-threaded processor, the execution of spin-locks by waiting threads can significantly degrade overall performance.

Using the WFE and SEV mechanism can improve the energy efficiency of a spinlock. In this situation, a processor that fails to obtain a lock can execute a WFE instruction to request entry to a low-power state. When a processor releases a lock, it must execute an SEV instruction, causing any waiting processors to wake up. Then, these processors can attempt to gain the lock again.


<!-- page 91 -->

> **NOTE:** Using WFE may not always be better than normal semaphore value polling. Scenarios with higher polling duration will certainly benefit. APSS only clock gates on WFE so that high exit latency does not comes in way of its use for spin-lock efficiency.

##### 3.1.3.4.4 A53 L2SCU power management

L2SCU power management can be controlled by SAW2. L2SCU asserts APCC_SYSL2SLEEPREQ to enter low-power state. APCC_SYSL2SLEEPREQ signal is asserted when following condition is true:
* No L2 activity
* All CPUs are in WFI state or clamp

L2SCU can enter a particular sleep mode by programming the APCS_L2_SAW2_SPM_CTL register. The code example for possible sleep mode is shown in Table 3-15.

#### 3.1.3.5 APSS watchdog timer

The APSS has a single watchdog (WDOG) timer instance. The WDOG has a 20-bit counter, which increments on the sleep clock (32 kHz). Once enabled by writing to the APCS_WDOG_CTL register, the WDOG counter starts counting. When the WDOG counter value reaches the value programmed in the APCS_WDOG_BARK_TIME register, the bark interrupt (WDT_BARKINT) is asserted. This is a level interrupt. It is connected to the APSS_QGIC2_SPI[3] input.

As part of the interrupt handler, CPU must reset the WDOG by writing to the APCS_WDOG_RESET register. Failing to do so will allow the WDOG counter to reach a value programmed in the APCS_WDOG_BITE_TIME register. The bite interrupt (WDT_BITEEXPIRED) is asserted when the WDOG counter is greater than or equal to the APCS_WDOG_BITE_TIME register value. This is a level interrupt. It is connected to A53SS QGIC2 SPI[4] interrupt.

#### 3.1.3.6 APSS generic timers

The APSS has four CP15 timer frames per core and one QTMR block configured for seven timer frames. All frames are configured for physical timers. Frame 0 of CP15 and frame 0 of QTMR are configured for virtual timers as well. Refer to the QTMR chapter for details.

#### 3.1.3.7 APSS interrupt controller

The APSS has an internal Qualcomm generic interrupt controller (QGIC2) responsible for handling system or A53 private peripheral interrupts and presenting them to the A53 CPU cores. Refer to the QGIC2 chapter for details.
<!-- page 92 -->

<!-- page 94 -->

* It is the responsibility of the SW and/or ACP master to ensure that ACP writes are disabled before scheduling a shared power collapse. Predicting ACP writes during power collapse and handling it is out of scope for APSS power controller logic.

| Modes | SPM_SYS_PC_MODE | SPM_START_ADR | ISAR | WAKEUP_CONFIG | SPM_EN |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| APCS_STANDBY | 0x0 | 0x0 | 0x0 | 0x3 | 0x1 |
| APCS_GDHS_OFF_L2RAM_ON | 0x1(1) | 0xC | 0x0 OR 0x1 | 0x3 | 0x1 |

The SPM_SYS_PC_MODE bit needs to be programmed to indicate the ACP/L2 PM logic if the current low-power mode is clock gating or power collapse. This information is used for early exit from clock gating mode when a request comes over ACP bus. This is mandatory to be programmed 0x1 for all the power collapse modes, as otherwise it may lead to race conditions.

If woken up due to ACP request, SW can choose in advance next L2 low-power mode between current mode and clock gating mode. If the ISAR bit it set to 0x1, it is software responsibility to reset the APCS_L2_SAW2_SPM_CTL register on wake-up path and also on the fall-through path, well in advance of next WFI for clock gating mode.
<!-- page 95 -->

#### 3.1.4.6 L1/L2 cache initialization during low-power modes

After cold reset sequence in APSS PBL, L1RSTDISABLE for each core is set to 0. L2RSTDISABLE for L2 is also set to 0. This is the reset value of the following registers:
* L2_RST_DIS bit in APCS_L2_PWR_CTL register
* L1_RST_DIS bit in APCS_BANKED_CPU_PWR_CTL register

Software at any stage (SBL, sysini, TZ, HLOS) must maintain these settings.

During per core collapse, L1 is always collapsed so on exit, L1 is initialized in hardware (L1_RST_DIS register bit being set to zero).

During shared collapse APCS_*_L2RAM_OFF, L2 is initialized in hardware (L2_RST_DIS register bit being set to zero).

During shared collapse APCS_*_L2RAM_ON, L2 is not initialized in hardware (SPM_SYS_PC_MODE bit in APCS_L2_SAW2_SPM_CTL register).

#### 3.1.4.7 Shared power collapse sequence with L2 flush

As a part of shared collapse sequence, L2 needs to be cleaned and invalidated before triggering SPM. L2 cleans and invalidate (also referred to as L2 flush) can be achieved in ways as described below.

Before starting L2 flush in SW, it is customary to stall transactions coming over ACP bus. This is to ensure that while L2 flush is going on, transactions over ACP bus do not allocate new entries to L2 cache. L2 redirect in BIMC can be disabled only after L2 flush has completed, so that DDR has updated data before receiving any ACP requests.

SW steps for performing L2 flush:
1. Request for stalling ACP transfers to L2 (set the ACP_STALL_REQ bit in the APCS_MISC_PWR_CTL register)
2. Poll for the acknowledgment from hardware that ACP transfers are stalled (poll for the ACP_STALL_ACK bit in the APCS_MISC_PWR_STS register)

   > **NOTE:** This handshake is required to ensure that ACP bus is stalled at the transaction boundary.

3. L2 flushes in SW
4. Disable L2 redirect in BIMC
5. Clear the request for stalling ACP transfers to L2 (clear the ACP_STALL_REQ bit in the APCS_MISC_PWR_CTL register)

   > **NOTE:** This makes the ACP_STALL_ACK bit in the APCS_MISC_PWR_STS register go low and also remove the stall from the ACP bus.

6. Perform other power-down steps as mentioned in TRM, execute WFI.
<!-- page 96 -->

#### 3.1.4.8 Interrupt slip through window

There exists an interrupt slip through the window between assertion of STANDBYWFI and start of CPU power collapse sequence. This window is for around 4-6 XO cycles during which if an interrupt occurs, the CPU starts executing while SPM does its power collapse. This if not handled, can lead to system instability as CPU may start a transaction with BIMC and go down without completing it.

The recommended way to handle this is by masking the QGIC2 CPU interface before executing WFI. Following is the recommended pseudocode to be run in TZ.
1. Program APCS_BANKED_SPM_VOTE_TZ to enable votes for all power control operation. (For L2 low-power mode enable votes by programming APCS_L2_SPM_VOTE_TZ)
2. Check if there is any contention in the voting registers
3. XOR (APCS_BANKED_SPM_VOTE_TZ, APCS_BANKED_SPM_VOTE_HYP, APCS_BANKED_SPM_VOTE_HLOS) =?
   a. For L2 low-power mode: XOR (APCS_L2_SPM_VOTE_TZ, APCS_L2_SPM_VOTE_HYP, APCS_L2_SPM_VOTE_HLOS) =?
4. If XOR output is nonzero, jump to fall through path without executing the power collapse sequence. If the XOR output is zero, then go to next step
5. Perform all the sequence as mentioned in A53 TRM for entry into power collapse before executing WFI
6. Check if HPPI QGIC2 register is set. If yes, jump to fall through path. If no, go to next step
7. Disable QGIC2 CPU interface by programming corresponding QGIC2 register
8. Execute WFI

   > **NOTE:** To reduce the interrupt slip through window to four XO cycles, following register needs to be programmed: APCS_XO_CBCR = 0x1

### 3.1.5.3 APCS_BANKED_ACS register definitions

#### 3.1.5.3.1 0x8000 APCS_BANKED_APC_SECURE

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x0000000F
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

The APCS_BANKED_APC_SECURE register is used to enable or disable nonsecure bus transactions. When reading this register, nonsecure agents will always read '0'. Secure agents see the actual value of the register.

##### Table 3-18 APCS_BANKED_APC_SECURE

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 | **VOTE** | **0x1:** NSEC<br>**0x0:** SEC<br>Controls security treatment for SPM vote registers: APCS_BANKED_SPM_VOTE_HLOS |
| 2 | **RESERVED** | Reserved |
| 1 | **CLK_CTL** | **0x1:** NSEC<br>**0x0:** SEC<br>Controls security treatment for sleep control registers: APCS_BANKED_APC_PWR_STATUS, APCS_BANKED_APC_PWR_GATE_STATUS |
| 0 | **SLP_CTL** | **0x1:** NSEC<br>**0x0:** SEC<br>Controls security treatment for clock control registers: APCS_BANKED_CPU_PWR_CTL, APCS_BANKED_APC_PWR_GATE_CTL, APCS_BANKED_APC_A53_CFG_STS |

#### 3.1.5.3.2 0x8004 APCS_BANKED_CPU_PWR_CTL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000088
* **Security Treatment:** Controlled by the SLP_CTL bit of APCS_BANKED_APC_SECURE

This register is used to control the clamps, reset, and array head switches.

##### Table 3-19 APCS_BANKED_CPU_PWR_CTL (continued on next page)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | **CLK_EN** | Clock enables for CORE clock. This is only to work around hardware dynamic clock gating problems.<br>**0x1:** ALWAYS_ENABLED<br>**0x0:** DYNAMICALLY_ENABLED_BY_HARDWARE |
<!-- page 105 -->

##### Table 3-19 APCS_BANKED_CPU_PWR_CTL (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 | **CORE_SLEEP_STATE** | Report that the CPU is in sleep state |
| 7 | **CORE_PWRD_UP** | Report that the CPU is powered up |
| 6 | **GATE_CLK** | When set, this bit forces the CPU clock to be gated off. This control is intended to permit external masters such as the RPM to gate off the CPU clock during sleep modes, when power control is being done by an external master instead of the SPM.<br>The output of this register bit is OR’ed with a clock gating control output from the SPM, so that if either the SPM asserts the control, or the RPM sets this bit, the CPU clock will be gated off.<br>When set, this bit gate the CPU clock that must be asserted during sleep state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 5 | **COREPOR_RST** | When set, this bit asserts cold reset to the CPU core |
| 4 | **CORE_RST** | When set, this bit asserts warm reset to the COPU core |
| 3 | **CORE_MEM_HS** | When cleared, this bit opens a head switch to put the core memories into a low-leakage, non-data-retaining state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 2 | **L1_RST_DIS** | When set, this bit disables L1 initialization during low-power mode exit |
| 1 | **CORE_MEM_CLAMP** | When set this bit clamps the output from the headswitch core memories. This bit is OR'ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the core memories |
| 0 | **CLAMP** | When set, this bit asserts the clamp signal that must be asserted prior to collapsing CPU voltage, VDD_APC_GDS. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |

## 3.1.5.6 APCS_GLB register definitions

### 3.1.5.6.1 0x11000 APCS_GLB_SECURE

Type: RW

Clock: SYS_AHB_CLK

Reset State: 0x0000001F

Security Treatment: Restricted

The APCS_GLB_SECURE register is used to enable or disable nonsecure bus transactions. When reading this register, nonsecure agents will always read '0'. Secure agents see the actual value of the register.

#### Table 3-44 APCS_GLB_SECURE
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4 | VOTE | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for SPM vote registers:<br>APCS_L2_SPM_VOTE_HLOS |
| 3 | ACP | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for ACP-related registers:<br>APCS_AINACTS_CNT,<br>APCS_MISC_PWR_CTL,<br>APCS_MISC_PWR_STS |
| 2 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 1 | PWR | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for the global sleep control registers:<br>APCS_L2_PWR_CTL,<br>APCS_L2_PWR_STATUS |
| 0 | STS | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for the global clock control registers:<br>APCS_PWR_CTL_OVERRIDE,<br>APCS_GLB_CLK_STATUS,<br>APCS_AUX_CLK_ON |

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 22 | PRESETDBG | When set, this bit drives PRESETDBGn signal low |
| 21:18 | L1_RAM_COLLAPSE_DIS | When set, this bit overrides the L1 RAM collapse operation by SPM. Instead the L1 RAMs will be retained in the case where APC voltage is retained |
| 17 | SCU_RAM_COLLAPSE_DIS | When set, this bit overrides the SCU RAM collapse operation by SPM. Instead the SCU RAMs will be retained in the case where APC voltage is retained |

|---|---|---|

| 13 | L2_RET_SLP | – |
| 12 | SYS_RESET | Setting this bit asserts the SYS_APCCSYS_ARESET_N input to the APSS CPU, causing a warm system reset (all powered non- debug logic will be reset) to the CPU core without resetting subsystem functions such as timers, clock control, etc. |

| 8 | L2_HS_CLAMP | When set, this bit clamps the outputs from the head switched L2 logic into the unswitched domain. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the CPU (resets to 1) |

| 1 | SCU_ARRAY_HS | – |
| 0 | L2_ARRAY_HS | When set, these bits close the array head switches for 512 KB sections of the L2 cache array. When clear (default reset value), array head switch is open, resulting a lower cache array leakage when data does not need to be retained in the array. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the CPU |

## 3.1.5.9 APCS_WDT register definitions

### 3.1.5.9.1 0x17000 APCS_WDOG_SECURE

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000001

**Security Treatment:** Restricted

The APCS_WDOG_SECURE register is used to enable or disable nonsecure bus transactions. When reading this register, nonsecure agents will always read '0'. Secure agents see the actual value of the register.

#### Table 3-93 APCS_WDOG_SECURE
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | WDT | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for the WDOG registers:<br>- APCS_WDOG_RESET<br>- APCS_WDOG_CTL<br>- APCS_WDOG_STATUS<br>- APCS_WDOG_BARK_TIME<br>- APCS_WDOG_BITE_TIME |

### 3.1.5.9.2 0x17004 APCS_WDOG_RESET

**Type:** W

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the WDT bit of APCS_WDOG_SECURE

The APCS_WDOG_RESET register resets the watchdog counter. In normal operation, the microprocessor should periodically write this command register to reset the watchdog counter. This command register also disables the watchdog freeze.

#### Table 3-94 APCS_WDOG_RESET
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | RESET | This bit generates the WDT_STB during the nonsleep mode. A pulse is generated on WDT_STB when this bit is written with a ‘1’ |
<!-- page 145 -->

### 3.1.5.9.3 0x17008 APCS_WDOG_CTL

**Type:** W

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the WDT bit of APCS_WDOG_SECURE

This register controls when the watchdog timer is enabled.

#### Table 3-95 APCS_WDOG_CTL
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | UNMASKED_INT_ENABLE | Enable unmasked interrupt (IRQ or FIQ) to wake up the WDOG timer:<br>0x1: ENABLE<br>0x0: DISABLE |
| 0 | ENABLE | Enable WDOG timer:<br>0x1: ENABLE<br>0x0: DISABLE |

### 3.1.5.9.4 0x1700C APCS_WDOG_STATUS

**Type:** R

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the WDT bit of APCS_WDOG_SECURE

This is the watchdog status register.

#### Table 3-96 APCS_WDOG_STATUS
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | FROZEN | This bit indicates whether the or not WDOG timer is frozen at count 0.<br>0x1: YES (frozen)<br>0x0: NO (not frozen) |
| 20:1 | COUNT | Counter value [19:0] of the watchdog counter.<br>Note: The sleep counter value is sampled using the AHB clk. Multiple reads are required to determine the value (assuming AHB clk is much faster than sleep clock). |
| 0 | EXPIRED_STATUS | This bit indicates that WDOG expire status<br>0x1: YES (wdog timer has expired)<br>0x0: NO (wdog timer has not expired) |
<!-- page 146 -->

### 3.1.5.9.5 0x17010 APCS_WDOG_BARK_TIME

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x0007FFFF

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the WDT bit of APCS_WDOG_SECURE

The APCS_WDOG_BARK_TIME register defines the time in SLEEP_CLK when to assert the watchdog bark interrupts. The value can be between 0 and 12787 (the time when the watchdog times out). The default value is 0x3FFF, but this reset value is not readable through the AHB interface. This value is larger than the watchdog timeout of 0x31F3, effectively disabling the watchdog bark interrupt.

#### Table 3-97 APCS_WDOG_BARK_TIME
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 19:0 | DATA | The WDOG counter value on which to trigger the bark interrupt. |

### 3.1.5.9.6 0x17014 APCS_WDOG_BITE_TIME

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x000FFFFF

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the WDT bit of APCS_WDOG_SECURE

The WDOG_BITE_TIME register defines the time in SLEEP_CLK when to assert the watchdog bite interrupts. The value can be between 0 and 12787 (the time when the watchdog times out). The default value is 0x3FFF, but this reset value is not readable through the AHB interface. This value is larger than the watchdog timeout of 0x31F3, effectively disabling the watchdog bite interrupt.

#### Table 3-98 APCS_WDOG_BITE_TIME
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 19:0 | DATA | The WDOG bite expiration time |
<!-- page 147 -->

## 3.1.5.11 APCS_ALIAS0_ACS register definitions

### 3.1.5.11.1 0x88000 APCS_ALIAS0_APC_SECURE

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x0000000F

**Security Treatment:** Restricted

The APCS_ALIAS0_APC_SECURE register is used to enable or disable nonsecure bus transactions. When reading this register, nonsecure agents will always read '0'. Secure agents see the actual value of the register.

#### Table 3-106 APCS_ALIAS0_APC_SECURE
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 | VOTE | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for SPM vote registers:<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_SPM_VOTE_HLOS |
| 2 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 1 | CLK_CTL | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for sleep control registers:<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_APC_PWR_STATUS<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_APC_PWR_GATE_STATUS |
| 0 | SLP_CTL | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for clock control registers:<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_CPU_PWR_CTL<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_APC_PWR_GATE_CTL<br>- APCS_ALIAS0_APC_A53_CFG_STS |

### 3.1.5.11.2 0x88004 APCS_ALIAS0_CPU_PWR_CTL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000088

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by the SLP_CTL bit of APCS_ALIAS0_APC_SECURE

This register is used to control the clamps, reset, and array head switches.


<!-- page 151 -->

### Table 3-107 APCS_ALIAS0_CPU_PWR_CTL

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | CLK_EN | Clock enables for CORE clock. This is only to work around hardware dynamic clock gating problems.<br>0x1: ALWAYS_ENABLED<br>0x0: DYNAMICALLY_ENABLED_BY_HARDWARE |
| 10 | CORE_SLEEP_STATE | Report that the CPU is in sleep state |
| 7 | CORE_PWRD_UP | Report that the CPU is powered up |
| 6 | GATE_CLK | When set, this bit forces the CPU clock to be gated off. This control is intended to permit external masters such as the RPM to gate off the CPU clock during sleep modes, when power control is being done by an external master instead of the SPM.<br>The output of this register bit is OR’ed with a clock gating control output from the SPM, so that if either the SPM asserts the control, or the RPM sets this bit, the CPU clock will be gated off.<br>When set, this bit gate the CPU clock that must be asserted during sleep state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 5 | COREPOR_RST | When set, this bit asserts cold reset to the CPU core |
| 4 | CORE_RST | When set, this bit asserts warm reset to the COPU core |
| 3 | CORE_MEM_HS | When cleared, this bit opens a head switch to put the core memories into a low-leakage, non-data-retaining state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 2 | L1_RST_DIS | When set, this bit disables L1 initialization during low-power mode exit |
| 1 | CORE_MEM_CLAMP | When set this bit clamps the output from the headswitch core memories. This bit is OR'ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the core memories |
| 0 | CLAMP | When set, this bit asserts the clamp signal that must be asserted prior to collapsing CPU voltage, VDD_APC_GDS. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |

##### Table 3-128 APCS_ALIAS1_CPU_PWR_CTL
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | CLK_EN | Clock enables for CORE clock. This is only to work around hardware dynamic clock gating problems.<br>0x1: ALWAYS_ENABLED<br>0x0: DYNAMICALLY_ENABLED_BY_HARDWARE |
| 10 | CORE_SLEEP_STATE | Report that the CPU is in sleep state |
| 7 | CORE_PWRD_UP | Report that the CPU is powered up |
<!-- page 163 -->

##### Table 3-128 APCS_ALIAS1_CPU_PWR_CTL (Continued)
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6 | GATE_CLK | When set, this bit forces the CPU clock to be gated off. This control is intended to permit external masters such as the RPM to gate off the CPU clock during sleep modes, when power control is being done by an external master instead of the SPM.<br>The output of this register bit is OR’ed with a clock gating control output from the SPM, so that if either the SPM asserts the control, or the RPM sets this bit, the CPU clock will be gated off.<br>When set, this bit gate the CPU clock that must be asserted during sleep state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 5 | COREPOR_RST | When set, this bit asserts cold reset to the CPU core |
| 4 | CORE_RST | When set, this bit asserts warm reset to the COPU core |
| 3 | CORE_MEM_HS | When cleared, this bit opens a head switch to put the core memories into a low-leakage, non-data-retaining state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 2 | L1_RST_DIS | When set, this bit disables L1 initialization during low-power mode exit |
| 1 | CORE_MEM_CLAMP | When set this bit clamps the output from the headswitch core memories. This bit is OR'ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the core memories |
| 0 | CLAMP | When set, this bit asserts the clamp signal that must be asserted prior to collapsing CPU voltage, VDD_APC_GDS. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |

| 1 | CLK_CTL | 0x1: NSEC<br>0x0: SEC<br>Controls security treatment for sleep control registers:<br>APCS_ALIAS3_APC_PWR_STATUS,<br>APCS_ALIAS3_APC_PWR_GATE_STATUS |

### 3.1.5.17.2 0xB8004 APCS_ALIAS3_CPU_PWR_CTL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** SYS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000088
* **Security Treatment:** Controlled by the SLP_CTL bit of APCS_ALIAS3_APC_SECURE

This register is used to control the clamps, reset, and array head switches.

### Table 3-170 APCS_ALIAS3_CPU_PWR_CTL

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | CLK_EN | Clock enables for CORE clock. This is only to work around hardware dynamic clock gating problems.<br>0x1: ALWAYS_ENABLED<br>0x0: DYNAMICALLY_ENABLED_BY_HARDWARE |
| 10 | CORE_SLEEP_STATE | Report that the CPU is in sleep state |
| 7 | CORE_PWRD_UP | Report that the CPU is powered up |
| 6 | GATE_CLK | When set, this bit forces the CPU clock to be gated off. This control is intended to permit external masters such as the RPM to gate off the CPU clock during sleep modes, when power control is being done by an external master instead of the SPM. The output of this register bit is OR’ed with a clock gating control output from the SPM, so that if either the SPM asserts the control, or the RPM sets this bit, the CPU clock will be gated off.<br>When set, this bit gate the CPU clock that must be asserted during sleep state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 5 | COREPOR_RST | When set, this bit asserts cold reset to the CPU core |
| 4 | CORE_RST | When set, this bit asserts warm reset to the COPU core |
| 3 | CORE_MEM_HS | When cleared, this bit opens a head switch to put the core memories into a low-leakage, non-data-retaining state. This bit is OR’ed with a SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
| 2 | L1_RST_DIS | When set, this bit disables L1 initialization during low-power mode exit |
| 1 | CORE_MEM_CLAMP | When set this bit clamps the output from the headswitch core memories. This bit is OR'ed with SAW2 outputs before passing to the core memories |
| 0 | CLAMP | When set, this bit asserts the clamp signal that must be asserted prior to collapsing CPU voltage, VDD_APC_GDS. This bit is OR’ed with SAW2 output before passing to the CPU core. |
<!-- page 187 -->

## 3.2 Qualcomm DSP subsystem (QDSP6)

This section describes the QDSP6 subsystem integrated in the SoC.

### 3.2.1 QDSP6 overview

The QDSP6, integrated within the device is a low-power processor, used for ultra low-power audio subsystem applications (ULT Audio). The QDSP6 subsystem can operate under a number of specific use cases. For example, the QDSP6 is used as a ULT processor for audio, sensor, and open DSP.

Figure 3-3 shows a high-level overview of the QDSP6 integrated in the SoC.

#### Figure 3-3 QDSP6 overview

*Description:* A block diagram showing the interfaces between the QDSP6 and other system components:
- **QDSP6**: The main processor block (large rectangle).
- **GCC** (Global Clock Controller): A block on the left that connects to the QDSP6 via two unidirectional arrows:
  - **Clocks**
  - **Resets**
- **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem): A block on the left that receives interrupts from the QDSP6 via a bus line (marked with a slash) labeled **Interrupts**.
- **System NoC** (System Network on Chip): A horizontal bidirectional bus at the bottom connected to the QDSP6 via a bidirectional arrow.
