#### 4.1.1.3.3 MDP reset options

There are two types of reset available: hard reset and soft reset.

The difference between a soft reset and a hard reset is that the soft reset only resets the control logic but not the configuration registers. Following a hard reset, software must reprogram everything and set up the entire MDSS, DSI PHY included, because individual blocks cannot be reset using the hard reset. The hard reset resembles a power-on reset.

The reset state of MDP is idle and in the lowest power state after a power-on reset.

There are no blocks that are active unless explicitly enabled by software. All functionality is triggered by software by either enabling the timing engine by writing to the `MDP_INTF_1_`...
<!-- page 230 -->
`TIMING_ENGINE_EN` register, or by kick starting the operation through writing 0x1 to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` register (n = 0 to 4).

A software reset exists per data path and is triggered by writing to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register.

#### Hard reset

The hard reset of the MDSS is within the reset control register (`GCC_MDSS_BCR`) in the SoC GCC module. The `GCC_MDSS_BCR` register resets all the blocks and registers in MDP and DSI modules.

The reset from the GCC module is an asynchronous reset. The clocks to the MDSS must be off while the reset is in progress.

Individual blocks cannot be reset using the hard reset. The asynchronous reset from the GCC module resets the entire MDSS.

#### Soft reset

MDP and DSI support a soft reset. If initiated during an active transfer, the filling of the ping pong FIFOs continues for that frame. Because pixels are still pulled from the FIFO on the pixel clock domain, underflow is possible. To avoid underflow, software must wait until after the transfer is complete (if possible) before issuing a soft reset.

For DSI command mode transfers, both MDP and DSI controllers are required to be soft reset. Because the interface involves handshaking, both controllers require soft reset because they must remain in sync.

Soft reset must wait for memory transactions to complete so that the system is not left in an indeterminate state. Hardware automatically handles this functionality, but software must wait until the soft reset is complete before moving on and reconfiguring.

##### Table 4-12 MDP soft reset sequence

| Step | Action |
| :---: | :--- |
| 1 | Write 1 to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register. |
| 2 | Wait for the `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register to read back 0. |

#### Soft reset - command mode panel

For a soft reset of a command mode panel, the order is as follows:
1.  Program the pipeline control registers and all configuration registers (SSPP, layer mixer, DSPP, and so on)
2.  Write `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` (with 0x1)
3.  Something has gone wrong and a soft reset is issued by writing to `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register
4.  Wait for soft reset to complete


<!-- page 231 -->

5. Write `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` (with 0x1) to trigger again. No reconfiguration is required.

Software can only have one soft reset pending at a time. Initiate the reset of a data path when there are no other soft resets pending.

Therefore, the following sequence, for example, is illegal:
1. Write to `MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET` register
2. Write to `MDP_CTL_1_SW_RESET` register
3. Wait for `MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET` to complete
4. Wait for `MDP_CTL_1_SW_RESET` to complete

The proper sequence is as follows:
1. Write to `MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET` register
2. Wait for `MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET` to complete
3. Write to `MDP_CTL_1_SW_RESET` register
4. Wait for `MDP_CTL_1_SW_RESET` to complete

### Soft reset - active panel

For a soft reset of an active panel, the order is as follows:
1. Program the pipeline control registers and all configuration registers (SSPP, layer mixer, DSPP, timing engine registers, and so on)
2. `MDP_INTF_1_TIMING_ENGINE_EN` to enable the timing engine
3. Something has gone wrong and a soft reset is issued by writing to `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register
4. Wait for the soft reset to complete
5. Do nothing else as the timing engine is still running and continues to process on the next VSync.

> [!NOTE]
> If a soft reset is initiated before or during the active region of the frame, the current frame underflows and sends out underflow color (which can appear as a blink on the panel). To avoid underflow, initiate a soft reset after the active region and during the vertical front porch.

### 4.1.1.3.4 MDP interrupts

The MDSS issues a single unified interrupt signal (`MDSS_IRQ`) to system level, which is the combination of the MDP module interrupt (`MDP_IRQ`) and the MIPI DSI module interrupt (`DSI0_IRQ`).

The `MDSS_HW_INTR_STATUS` register indicates which module (MDP or DSI) has a pending interrupt.

There are a few types of events that can trigger the MDP interrupt:
<!-- page 232 -->

#### Status interrupts

To clear all MDP interrupts, write 1 to the appropriate field in the `MDP_INTR_CLEAR` register.
To enable the interrupt controller, write 1 to the appropriate field in the `MDP_INTR_EN` register.

All interrupts are generated on the MDP core clock domain but logged for software read-back on the AHB clock domain (through the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register).

##### Table 4-13 MDP interrupts

| Interrupt | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `WB_0_DONE` | Memory Block Writeback path 0 is complete |
| `WB_2_DONE` | Memory Line Writeback path 2 is complete |
| `PING_PONG_0_DONE` | Ping-pong buffer 0 frame is done |
| `PING_PONG_0_RD_PTR` | Tear check read pointer for ping-pong buffer 0 has reached programmed count. |
| `PING_PONG_0_WR_PTR` | Tear check write pointer for ping-pong buffer 0 has reached programmed count. |
| `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` | Interface 1 has underrun |
| `INTF_1_VSYNC` | Interface 1 VSync signal. Used to indicate frame boundaries for the panel |
| `PING_PONG_0_TEAR_DETECTED` | Enable interrupt when Tearing (TE signal) detected for the tear check block connected to ping-pong 0 |

The interrupt signal out of the MDSS is a level signal and is a gate of the enable and status registers. Therefore, in the interrupt subroutine, if an interrupt source is cleared but a different interrupt is still pending, then the interrupt line is not lowered; it remains high.

#### Interface interrupt

The programmable line (`PROG_LINE`) interrupt is used to generate an interrupt at a particular line or pixel within a line. It is controlled via `MDP_INTF_1_INTF_INTR_EN`, `MDP_INTF_1_INTF_INTR_CLEAR` and `MDP_INTF_1_INTF_INTR_STATUS` registers.

To configure the interrupt, the driver must program the `INTR_CORD` field in the `MDP_INTF_1_PROG_LINE_INTR_CONF` register to a particular pixel within the total region (active & blanking) of the display, then enable the interrupt bit in `MDP_INTF_1_INTF_INTR_EN` register.

This interrupt is double buffered and can at most be triggered once per frame. For command mode this interrupt cannot be used. Instead, the `PING_PONG_0_WR_PTR` interrupt can be used for command mode.

#### Error interrupts

The MDSS VBIF module provides error interrupts for failed memory accesses. For more information, see Chapter Virtualizing Bus Interface (VBIF). The only MDP detected error is the panel underrun. If a panel underrun occurs, it is noted in the `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` field of the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register.
<!-- page 233 -->

Panel underrun is a hard error. It results in display artifacts or a constant color displayed on the panel. A panel underrun is either a programming error or a system inefficiency such that the fill rate does not meet the drain rate.

Once detected, hardware stops fetching data for the current frame and tries to recover on the next frame. Because the panel expects data, the MDP sends a programmable constant color to the panel. To clear the status bit, write 1 to the `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` field in the `MDP_INTR_CLEAR` register.

The underrun error does not apply to command mode panels. A command mode panel is not a pulling interface. The only error that occurs is a programming error that results in a hang. To recover, perform a soft data path reset.

To detect a hardware hang requires watchdog timers, which are described in Section Timeouts and watchdog timers.

#### Timeouts and watchdog timers

There are no timeout functions within MDP, but to help software detect a hardware hang, dedicated display watchdog timers (`WD_TIMER_0` and `WD_TIMER_1`) are included in the MDP module.

The key features of the MDP watchdog timers are:
* Run independently of each other
* Runs off VSync clock
* 32-bit MAIN counter starts at 0 (when timer cleared)
  * Increments counter up to maximum count value (32 bits), stops and flags interrupt or
  * Free running (if maximum count value set to 0), and counter-wraps
* Programmable 4-bit decode granularity that configures how many clock ticks to count before the MAIN 32-bit counter increments. See the `WD_TIMER_x_GRANULARITY` register field description within `MDP_WD_TIMER_x_CTL2` register (x = 0 or 1), for details and mapping.
* Effective MAIN counter granularity ranges between 30 mins (for 8 clock ticks setting) to 8 hours (for 128 clock ticks setting)
* Current value of MAIN counter is readable from register
* Counter-clear/start/stop capabilities

The typical register programming sequence for the `WD_TIMER_0` is as follows:
1. Ensure `MDSS_VSYNC_CLK` clock is active
2. Ensure `MDSS_ARES` reset is deasserted
3. Set `MDP_INTR_EN [WD_TIMER_0_DONE]` = 1 (interrupt enable)
4. Set `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_LOAD_VALUE[31:0]` with timer count up to value (if desired; if not programmed, default is 0 and timer is free running)
5. Set `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_CTL [WD_TIMER_0_CLEAR]` = 1 (this resets the timer counter and IRQ)
<!-- page 234 -->

6. Set `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_CTL2 [WD_TIMER_0_ENABLE]` = 1 (this starts the counter to count up)
7. Once Timer counts to programmed `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_LOAD_VALUE[31:0]` value
8. MDP/MDSS interrupt is triggered
9. Check `MDP_INTR_STATUS [WD_TIMER_0_DONE]` (Once Timer counts to programmed `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_LOAD_VALUE[31:0]` value, interrupt is triggered here.)
10. Check `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_STATUS_VALUE` (to see current timer counter value; can check at anytime including free running timer mode)
11. Set `MDP_INTR_CLEAR [WD_TIMER_0_DONE]` = 1 (write 1 to clear interrupt)
12. Set `MDP_WD_TIMER_0_CTL [WD_TIMER_0_CLEAR]` = 1 (this resets the timer counter and IRQ)

### 4.1.1.3.5 MDP data flow operations

#### Data flows

Table 4-14 lists the major types of data flows that the MDP in MDSS processes.

##### Table 4-14 MDP data flows

| Data | Operating mode |
| :--- | :--- |
| Panel | Active or command |
| Memory write back | Line |
| Memory write back | Block (specifically, rotation) |

Regardless of the ultimate destination, the data path is controlled and programmed the same way for all modes.

The MDP blends graphic images stored in the frame buffer and sends the composite image to a single display (a DSI panel). The data flows from memory to the single display as shown in Figure 4-7.

#### Figure 4-7: MDP back-end composition of a single display, DSI panel

*Description:* A block diagram illustrating the data flow from system memory to a DSI display panel through the Mobile Display Subsystem (MDSS).
The diagram contains the following components from left to right:
1. **Memory** (External)
2. An outer block containing:
   * **Memory Controller**
   * **NOC/Fabric**
   * **MDSS** (dashed box enclosing **VBIF** and **MDP**)
   * **MIPI DSI**
   * **MIPI D-PHY** (dashed box)
3. **DSI panel** (External)

Bi-directional communication links exist between Memory <-> Memory Controller <-> NOC/Fabric <-> VBIF <-> MDP.
Data flows from MDP to MIPI DSI (labeled 4), which then communicates bi-directionally with MIPI D-PHY (labeled 5), which finally outputs to the DSI panel (labeled 6).

Three colored data flow paths are highlighted:
* **Path 1 (Red):** Represents a layer read from Memory, passing through the Memory Controller, NOC/Fabric, and VBIF, into the MDP.
* **Path 2 (Green):** Represents another layer read from Memory, following the same path into the MDP.
* **Path 3 (Blue):** Represents the blended output from the MDP, flowing through MIPI DSI and MIPI D-PHY to the DSI panel.

The following steps describe the data flow from memory to the single display:
1. One of the layers that must be displayed is stored in memory outside of the MDP. MDP reads the frame buffer line-by-line until the frame is complete.
<!-- page 235 -->

2. The other layer that displays is stored in memory outside of the MDP. MDP reads the frame buffer line-by-line until the frame is complete.
3. Within the MDP core, these two frame buffers are composed and blended, line-by-line.
4. The composite, blended data is then sent to the DSI controller over a standard RGB interface (8 bits per component, VSync, HSYNC, data enable).
5. The DSI controller transfers the data to the MIPI PHY.
6. The MIPI PHY takes the data from the DSI controller and serializes it to display it on the panel.

The MDSS can also send a rotated data to a single display panel, as shown in Figure 4-8.

#### Figure 4-8: MDP display of a rotated image to a DSI panel

*Description:* A block diagram showing the data flow for displaying a rotated image. The components are the same as in Figure 4-7 (Memory, Memory Controller, NOC/Fabric, MDSS with VBIF and MDP, MIPI DSI, MIPI D-PHY, and DSI panel).
The data flow sequence is as follows:
* **Path 1 (Green) & Path 2 (Red):** Data is read from Memory into MDP.
* **Path 3 (Blue, returning):** The composed/rotated image is written back from MDP to Memory (arrow pointing to Memory, labeled 3).
* **Path 4 (Blue, proceeding):** The final image is read from Memory (labeled 4), passes through MDP (blended), and flows through MIPI DSI (labeled 5), MIPI D-PHY (labeled 6), to the DSI panel (labeled 7).

The following steps describe the display of a rotated image to a DSI panel:
1. Data is read from memory for composition. The image orientation might not match the orientation of the panel. The data is fetched block-by-block using a source pipe that supports block mode fetching.
2. The rotated image is not sent to the panel, but rather backed out to memory, block-by-block.
3. The blended image is fetched from memory, line-by-line.
4. The data is sent to the DSI controller over a standard RGB interface (8 bits per component, VSync, HSYNC, data enable).
5. The DSI controller transfers the data to the MIPI PHY.
6. The MIPI PHY serializes the data, over the link, to display it on the panel.
<!-- page 236 -->

#### Datapath configuration

The top-level register programming describes the complete data path for a specific data path ID (`MDP_CTL_<id>_*` registers, where id = 0 to 4).

MDP supports three hardware concurrent datapaths: a single datapath to the display panel, one writeback datapath for wireless display, and one writeback rotation datapath. MDP has five sets of control datapath registers: `MDP_CTL_<id>_*`, where id = 0 to 4. That is, `MDP_CTL_0_*` to `MDP_CTL_4_*` registers.

Each control path is self-contained. Any control path can be routed to any of the hardware datapaths. These sets of registers per datapath (see Table 4-15), can each be triggered, flushed, and controlled independently.

##### Table 4-15 MDP datapath control registers

| Register | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_CTL_<id>_TOP` | Establishes general control flow for the given datapath |
| `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` | Flushes the double buffered registers to control synchronized updates for all registers at a common VSync boundary for this datapath |
| `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` | Triggers software to start datapath (for datapaths that must be pushed by software) |
| `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>`, where m=0, 1, 2, 3, 4 | Describes the connection to the layer mixer `<m>` path, if used |

Depending on the selected datapath, the corresponding source and destination registers require further programming. However, these control registers provide the basis for describing the path taken.

Software can partition the various datapaths by doing one of the following:
* Use `MDP_CTL_0` to control layer mixer 0 and its path through DSPP0 and to ping-pong0.
* Use `MDP_CTL_1` to control layer mixer 3 and its path through WB2, and so on.

This mapping provides software the flexibility to assign datapaths and hardware resources as necessary. Hardware does not mandate it.

#### MDP control top register

The `MDP_CTL_<id>_TOP` register configures the operating mode for the pipeline. It defines the complete datapath all the way to the interfaces (DSI).

##### Table 4-16 MDP memory output connection

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MEM_SEL` | Memory output | 0x0: NO memory output selected<br>0x1: Memory BLOCK mode output selected for rotation 0<br>0x2: Memory BLOCK mode output selected for rotation 1<br>0x3: Memory LINE mode output selected for rotation 0<br>0x4: Memory LINE mode output selected for rotation 1<br>0x5: Memory LINE mode output selected for linear memory writeback |
<!-- page 237 -->

To define the writeback port and its mode, select the appropriate memory output via the `MEM_SEL` field of the `MDP_CTL_<id>_TOP` register. MDP has two writeback ports: Writeback 0 (WB0) and Writeback 2 (WB2).

##### Table 4-17 MDP writeback ports and modes

| Writeback port | Writeback port mode | MEM_SEL value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| wb0 | Block (sourced by DMA0) | 0x1: Memory BLOCK mode output selected for rotation 0 |
| wb2 | Line only (sourced by Layer mixer3) | 0x5: Memory LINE mode output selected for linear memory writeback |
| -none- | For datapaths that go to display panels (with no memory writeback requirements), set the memory output to none | 0x0: NO memory output selected |

Because writeback programming can be enabled on any of the control datapaths, there are five sets of writeback registers - one per datapath.

`MDP_WB_0_<*>` refers to the writeback registers for control datapath 0. `MDP_WB_1_<*>` refers to the writeback registers for control datapath 1. `MDP_WB_4_<*>` refers to the writeback registers for control datapath 4. `MDP_WB_0_<*>` does not necessarily refer to writeback 0, unless writeback 0 is connected on control datapath 0. If WB2 is connected on datapath 0, `MDP_WB_0_<*>` would refer to the configuration rather than `MDP_WB_2_<*>`.

##### Table 4-18 MDP output interface connection

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `OUT_SEL` | Output ping-pong interface connection to external display interface | 0x0: No connection from Ping-Pong buffers to output interfaces<br>0x2: Interface 1 (DSI0) |

There is no implied dependency in the hardware that a particular datapath, such as Layermixer0, can only drive interface 0. This field indicates to which interface (if applicable) the datapath routes.

If the datapath destination is memory only, set this field to 0x0 (no connection).

##### Table 4-19 MDP stream identification

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `STREAM_SEL` | Command streams for interleaving | This field is don’t care for video mode streams<br>0x0: Stream 0<br>0x1: Stream 1<br>0x2: Stream 2 |

This field allows multiple command mode streams to be routed to a single DSI interface. The display interface uses the stream identification (`STREAM_SEL`) to identify different streams to interleave.
<!-- page 238 -->

##### Table 4-20 MDP interface mode

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MODE_SEL` | Mode of the destination interface | Needed to distinguish interfaces such as DSI that can be either mode. DSI can also interleave streams of different types (command and video) to a single core<br>0x0: Video Mode<br>0x1: Command Mode |

This field indicates the mode of the destination interface: video or command.

#### MDP control layer register

The `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_m` registers, where m=0, 1, 2, 3, 4, define the layer mixer input connections for the blending operation. Any of the SSPPs can be routed to any of the layer mixers.

The layer mixer blends a number of layers (up to 5). The cursor layer is always the top layer. There are five possible locations for the pipeline outputs.

##### MDP layer mixer configuration

| Position | Layer | Description | Blending? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Top | Cursor | Can be smaller than base layer and offset from (0,0). Because the hardware does not perform cropping, the offset plus size cannot be larger than the base layer. | Y |
| Middle | Stage 0 fg<br>Stage 1 fg<br>Stage 2 fg<br>Stage 3 fg | Can be smaller than base layer and offset from (0,0). Because the hardware does not perform cropping, the offset plus size cannot be larger than the base layer. | Y |
| Bottom | Base | Bottom layer. Must be at offset (0,0). Same size as the layer mixer output. | N |

If a source pipe does not contribute to the layer mixer output, set the field to 0x0.

Hardware uses these settings to initiate fetch and blending functions. Connecting an incorrectly configured source pipe leads to hardware hangs.

##### Table 4-21 MDP border color connection

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BORDER_OUT` | Border color connection | Border color is always the base layer.<br>0x0: Border color not used<br>0x1: Border color enabled |

This field enables border color. No data is fetched from memory and a programmable color is inserted as the base layer.
<!-- page 239 -->

##### Table 4-22 MDP cursor connection

| Register Field | Function | Selection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `CURSOR_OUT` | Cursor connection | Cursor layer is always the top layer. Cursor is only applicable in line mode operation and cannot be used in block mode processing.<br>0x0: Cursor is not used<br>0x1: Cursor is enabled |

This field enables the cursor. The offset plus the size of the cursor must not be larger than the base layer.

> [!NOTE]
> No cursor is available for layer mixer3. The cursor only applies for datapaths that ultimately reach the display interface, that is, layer mixer0.

#### MDP control flush register

The `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register allows for synchronized updates of the double-buffered registers. It indicates that the registers of a pipe/layer mixer are all programmed and are safe to update to the back copy of the double buffered registers.

To allow for independent control and updates, each part of the MDP pipeline (VIG_0, RGB_0, RGB_1, and so on) is a separate field. However, the flush bits reside within a single register access. If multiple flush bits are set (for example, VIG_0 and LAYER_MIXER_0), they update simultaneously.

Once the flush register is written, the double-buffer registers are updated on the next VSync. If the VSync has not arrived, the register field returns a 1. Before the register values update, the flush bit must be written (with 0x1) and the VSync must have arrived (see Figure 4-9).

#### Figure 4-9: MDP flush operation

*Description:* A schematic diagram showing the double-buffer synchronization logic.
It consists of:
* A register block on the left: **Software programs these values**.
* A MUX (multiplexer) in the center with inputs 0 and 1. The software-programmed register connects to MUX input 1.
* A register block on the right: **Hardware operates on these values**. The MUX output connects to this register's input. The output of this register loops back to MUX input 0.
* Control logic: An AND gate with inputs `FLUSH.<field>` and `vsync`. The output of this AND gate controls the MUX selection.
When both `FLUSH.<field>` and `vsync` are active (1), the MUX selects input 1, loading the software-programmed values into the hardware register. Otherwise, the MUX selects input 0 (loopback), retaining the current hardware values.

> [!NOTE]
> Flush registers are required for active timing panels (such as DSI video mode), to ensure coherent updates. For software-initiated command mode panels, this register is still required.

To ensure complete synchronization for a datapath, for example, ViG0 + RGB0 connected through the layer mixer0, through DSPP0, complete the following programming:
* Program all of the appropriate VIG0 registers.
* Program all of the appropriate RGB0 registers.
<!-- page 240 -->

* Program all of the appropriate layer mixer0 registers.
* Program all of the appropriate DSPP0 registers.
* Set the following bits in a single register write to ensure that they update at the same time:
  * `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH.VIG_0`
  * `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH.RGB_0`
  * `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH.LAYER_MIXER_0`
  * `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH.DSPP_0`

On the next VSync, the updates occur for all these blocks.

> [!NOTE]
> Registers within a source pipe cannot be flushed separately. Flush all of the RGB pipe registers or none. There is no way to flush the source buffer addresses.

#### Configuring active panels

Complete the following steps to configure active panels:
1. Configure the pipeline datapath.
2. Write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register.
3. Program the timing registers to match the panel specification.
4. Enable the timing engine.

Do not enable the timing engine before completing all programming. The hardware begins driving the control signals immediately after the timing engine is enabled. Fetching source data is initiated based on the VSync sent out. All programming must be written before initiation. Because the panel is an active display, there is no need to push frames to the panel. The hardware automatically manages the fetching of the new data on every VSync.

To signal the hardware to pick up a new image, software can write a new source address, including any changes, and write to the flush register. Following the write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register, the hardware picks up the new settings on the next VSync (see Figure 4-10).

#### Figure 4-10: MDP active panel timing diagram

*Description:* A timing diagram illustrating when register updates take effect relative to VSYNC pulses.
The timeline shows six VSYNC pulses: VSYNC #1 through VSYNC #6.
* **VSYNC #1 to VSYNC #3:** Software programs all double-buffered registers. During this time, the hardware continues to use the "Previous register settings".
* **Between VSYNC #3 and VSYNC #4:** Software writes to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register (indicated by a dashed vertical arrow).
* **VSYNC #4 onwards:** The "Updated register settings" are used by the hardware.

Software can program all the double-buffered registers, but the changes do not go into effect until the following VSync (VSync #4 in Figure 4-10).


<!-- page 241 -->

> [!NOTE]
> Registers that are not double-buffered take effect immediately.

### Configuring the timing engine
The timing engines send out 24-bit RGB888 on the output interface to the DSI controller. All timing parameters shown in Figure 4-11 come directly from the panel specifications.

#### Figure 4-11 MDP timing engine parameters
*Description:* A 2D diagram illustrating the layout of the display and active regions relative to horizontal and vertical blanking periods (porches). The diagram consists of three nested rectangular regions with a coordinate system defined by Hsync and Vsync signals:
- **Active region** (teal, innermost): The actual image content area. Its horizontal span is defined from `active_h_start` to `active_h_end`. Its vertical span is defined from `active_v_start` to `active_v_end`.
- **Display region (border fill)** (light blue, middle): The region surrounding the active region, which can be filled with a border color. Its horizontal span is defined from `display_h_start` to `display_h_end`. Its vertical span is defined from `display_v_start` to `display_v_end`.
- **Porch** (grid pattern, outermost): The blanking overhead region.
  - **Horizontal**: The area before the display region is the `hori. back porch`, and the area after is the `hori. front porch`.
  - **Vertical**: The area above the display region is the `vertical back porch`, and the area below is the `vertical front porch`.

For the two registers that control the timing engine size (`MDP_INTF_1_HSYNC_CTL` and `MDP_INTF_1_VSYNC_PERIOD_F0`), the value for both the `HSYNC_PERIOD` and `VSYNC_PERIOD` are expressed in pixel clocks. The maximum values for both are large enough to support any available panel (see Table 4-23).
<!-- page 242 -->

#### Table 4-23 MDP timing engine control registers

| Register | Bits | Bit name | Description | Max |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_INTF_1_HSYNC_CTL` | 28:16 | `HSYNC_PERIOD` | HSYNC Period in pixel clocks, the time between start of HSYNC pulse and the start of the next HSYNC pulse.<br>`hsync_period = width + h_porch`, where `width` = output image width, `h_porch = (h_back_porch + h_front_porch)`. `h_back_porch` starts at the beginning of HSYNC pulse. | 4095 pixels (12 bits) |
| | 11:0 | `PULSE_WIDTH` | HSYNC pulse width in pixel clocks | |
| `MDP_INTF_1_VSYNC_PERIOD_F0` | 23:0 | `VSYNC_PERIOD` | VSync Period in pixel clocks, the time between start of VSync pulse and the start of the next VSync pulse.<br>`vsync_period = height + v_porch`, where `height` = output_image_height, `v_porch = (v_back_porch + v_front_porch)`. `v_back_porch` starts at the beginning of VSync pulse. | 16777215 pixels (24 bits) |

For accurate parameters, see the VESA Display Stream Compression Standard.

The timing engines have a line count value to indicate to software which line of the interface they are currently on. The MDP line counter also includes blanking lines.

### Active panel line count
MDP provides the current line of the panel to software to see how close it is to the upcoming VSync, for example. Software knows the exact location of the current frame processing (see Figure 4-12).

#### Figure 4-12 MDP active line count
*Description:* A vertical layout diagram of a display frame showing how the line count corresponds to different phases of the frame transmission:
- The top-left corner of the frame represents the trigger point for `INTF_1_VSYNC interrupt`.
- The total height of the frame (including vertical porches and the active display area) is tracked by the `MDP_INTF_1_LINE_COUNT` register, as indicated by a double-headed arrow spanning the entire height on the left.
- Within the frame, the vertical sequence is:
  - `vertical back porch` (top region, above the active area).
  - Active region (the striped block in the center).
  - `vertical front porch` (bottom region, below the active area).
- The bottom-right corner of the active region triggers the `PING_PONG_0_DONE interrupt`.
<!-- page 243 -->

The line count present in MDP provides a clear version of the current panel location.

### Active panel timing engine interrupts
When an active panel timing engine is running, MDP generates the following interrupts:
* `INTF_1_VSYNC`
* `PING_PONG_0_DONE`
* `INTF_1_UNDERRUN`

All interrupts are logged in the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register. To clear them, write 1 to the corresponding field in the `MDP_INTR_CLEAR` register.

#### Figure 4-13 MDP active panel timing diagram
*Description:* A timing diagram showcasing the relation between panel interface signals and interrupts across a single frame:
- **Signals**:
  - `vsync`: Active-low vertical sync signal.
  - `hsync`: Horizontal sync pulses occurring regularly.
  - `data_enable`: Active-high data enable signal that transitions high during active pixels.
  - `data(RGB)`: RGB data blocks sent during the active period of `data_enable`.
- **Interrupts and Events**:
  - `INTF_0_VSYNC INTERRUPT` (red arrow): Triggered at the falling edge of the `vsync` signal, marking the start of a frame.
  - `t_vbp` (vertical back porch): The duration from the `vsync` falling edge until the first active line (start of `data_enable` pulses).
  - `t_dh` (data height): The active vertical display duration containing `data_enable` and active `data(RGB)`.
  - `PING_PONG_0_DONE` (red arrow): Triggered at the end of the last active pixel line in `data(RGB)`.
  - `t_vfp` (vertical front porch): The duration from the end of the last active line until the next falling edge of `vsync`.
  - `SW free to program registers for frame 2 here` (bracket): Spans from the start of the first frame's active data sequence until the start of the next frame's VSync.

Figure 4-13 shows one frame. The `INTF_1_VSYNC` interrupt (similarly to `INTF_0_VSYNC` shown in Figure 4-13) is generated and logged on the initial VSync sent to the panel signaling start of frame. At the end of the frame, another `INTF_1_VSYNC` interrupt is generated, signaling end of frame. If the timing engine was disabled in the middle of the frame, the last frame is still produced and sent to the panel. A final `INTF_1_VSYNC` interrupt is generated, but a VSync signal is not sent to the panel.

The `PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt is generated when the last pixel is sent from the MDP ping pong buffer. However, the frame is not complete because there is vertical blanking time before the VSync is sent to the panel. The panel updates refresh at 60 fps so the register programming (including flush) must complete within a frame to receive continuous panel updates.

Software must wait until the initial `INTF_1_VSYNC` interrupt is generated before disabling the timing engine. Because multiple clock domains are involved (AHB register clock, pixel clock), a subsequent register write to disable the timing engine could occur before the initial register write enabling the timing engine. Therefore, software must wait until the timing engine is active before disabling it.
<!-- page 244 -->

### Changing timing engine parameters
MDP implements a feature, where double buffer updates to the timing engine parameters (blanking parameters) allow for changes to the active panel refresh rate.

To establish a new refresh rate (normally lower for power saving), software can reprogram the `MDP_INTF_1` timing parameters and write the timing flush register bit for the display interface. Hardware uses the new refresh rate on the next VSync following the write to the register (see Figure 4-14).

#### Figure 4-14 MDP variable rate refresh timing diagram
*Description:* A timeline showing the effect of double-buffered parameter changes relative to VSYNC signals:
- Six sequential VSYNC pulses are shown, numbered VSYNC #1 through #6.
- A horizontal arrow at the top shows:
  - "Previous parameter settings used" for the duration containing VSYNC #1, #2, and #3.
  - "Updated parameter settings used" for the duration containing VSYNC #4, #5, and #6.
- A label pointing to the period before VSYNC #3 says: "Program all double-buffered registers including timing parameters".
- A vertical dashed arrow between VSYNC #3 and VSYNC #4 represents the action: "Write to `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register and `MDP_INTF_1_TIMING_ENGINE_EN` flush bit". This action triggers the transition to the updated parameters, which take effect starting at VSYNC #4.

Table 4-24 lists the programming sequence to update the timing engine parameters within MDP and DSI.

#### Table 4-24 MDP variable rate refresh programming sequence

| Sequence | Notes |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Startup Condition** | 1. Initialize DSI controller for video mode operation.<br>2. Set `DSI_TIMING_DB_MODE` to `0x1` (see Chapter MIPI DSI for DSI register descriptions).<br>3. Configure the MDP datapath.<br>4. Program the MDP timing registers to match the panel specification.<br>5. Write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register and set `TIMING_1` bit to flush timing engine parameters.<br>6. Enable the timing engine. |
| **Change Refresh Rate** | 1. Update video mode programming in DSI.<br>2. Enable double buffering by setting `DSI_TIMING_DB_MODE` to 1 (see Chapter MIPI DSI for DSI register descriptions).<br>3. Program updated set of DSI video mode registers to match the required new refresh rate for the panel:<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- `VIDEO_MODE_TOTAL`<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- `VIDEO_MODE_HSYNC`<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- `VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC`<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- `VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC_VPOS`<br>4. Flush the DSI change by writing a 1 to `DSI_TIMING_FLUSH`. When `DSI_TIMING_DB_MODE` is set, write this flush bit to make the change effective.<br><br>5. Update timing engine programming in MDP.<br>6. Program updated set of MDP timing registers to match the required new refresh rate.<br>7. Write to the `MDP_INTF_1_FLUSH` register bit and set the `TIMING_1` bit to update the timing engine parameters. |
<!-- page 245 -->

Software does not change the number of layers that are blended while the refresh rates are changing. If software is required to change from 1 to 3 layers at the same time, then software does one of the following:
* Change to three layers and then change timing engine parameters on the next frame.
* Change timing engine parameters first and then change to three layers.

Any changes to the existing configuration can be made at the same time as the timing engine parameter changes (updating buffer addresses). Adding/removing layers must not occur at the same time as timing engine parameter changes.

### Underrun
Underrun indicates that the MDP core was unable to supply the panel with the requisite data on time. It is an interrupt signaled by the `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` status bit.

If the MDP controller cannot supply the pixels on time, it feeds a software programmable color, defined in the `MDP_INTF_1_UNDERFLOW_COLOR` register. When the underflow color appears on the display, it appears as a fatal error to the end user.

The `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` interrupt can be generated at any point in the active region of the display. Once the underrun is generated, no more pixels are processed for the remainder of the frame.

To prevent underflow, ensure that the fill rate is greater than the drain rate.

The drain rate occurs on the pixel clock domain and is sent to the panel. For the fill rate, data is fetched from memory on the AXI clock domain and processed by the MDP pipeline on the MDP core clock domain (see Figure 4-15).

Preventing underrun (for all supported use cases) and ensuring that the display gets sufficient bandwidth requires careful programming across the entire chip.

#### Figure 4-15 MDP active display clocks
*Description:* A block diagram showing the flow of display data across three distinct clock domains:
- **Memory**: The source of image data at the top of the diagram.
- **AXI clock domain**: The interface for fetching data from memory.
- **MDP core clock domain**: The central area of processing, bounded by horizontal dashed lines. It contains the **MDP processing pipeline** block. Data is processed here after being fetched from memory.
- **Pixel clock domain**: The final stage before output, bounded by the lower dashed line.
- **Panel**: The physical display panel at the bottom (represented by a dashed border box) which receives the serialized display data from the pixel clock domain.
<!-- page 246 -->

### Minimum vertical blanking considerations
MDP needs sufficient time to prefill its pipeline so that it can provide pixels during the active region. The implication is that the vertical blanking time needs to be sufficiently large to accommodate the fill up time. If programmable fetch is not enabled, then all the fetch and prefill needs to complete during the vertical back porch (VBP). If the VBP is too small then programmable fetch can be enabled to use some of the vertical front porch (VFP) and start processing earlier. However, the total blanking time needs to be large enough so that all features can be enabled.

The following table illustrates the different features and their effect on latency through the pipeline. The latency directly translates into a need for large enough vertical blanking so that MDP pipeline can fill up and be ready for steady state processing.

The recommendation is that OEMs have enough vertical blanking in the panel configuration for the given chipset. Since the resulting value can be quite large, the table allows for feature trade-off decisions if there’s no way to accommodate the blanking parameters.

#### Table 4-25 MDP pipeline latencies

| MDP block | Number of lines |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Scaling** | |
| - Disabled | 0 |
| - PCMN | 1 |
| - Bilinear/nearest neighbor | 2 |
| - CAF | 4 |
| **Horizontal Flip** | |
| - Disabled | 0 |
| - Enabled | 1 |
| **CMD mode** | 1 |
| **SoC overhead** | See the note below. |
| **MIN config** | Linear, no scale, no hflip |
| **MAX config** | Linear, CAF, hflip |
| **TOTAL Active Panels** | 1-6 |
| **TOTAL Command Mode Panels** | 2-7 |

> [!NOTE]
> The System On Chip (SoC) overhead adds additional requirement to account for prefill bandwidth and prefill time. This doesn’t necessarily need to be added to worst case vertical blanking but mandates a minimum amount.

### Configuring command mode panels
Unlike active panels, command mode panels have no timing information that pulls data from the MDP design. Command mode panel data is pushed, and initiated by software.

Hardware ensures that a complete line is ready and waiting in the ping-pong buffer before sending a line to the display interface. This line is transferred uninterrupted (with no bubbles) from MDP to DSI.

Complete the following steps to configure command mode panels:
<!-- page 247 -->

1. Configure the pipeline datapath.
2. Write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH` register to enable the update of the desired SW registers.
3. Write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` register (with `0x1`) to trigger the data frame. MDP generates one frame of data (see Figure 1-16).

#### Figure 1-16 MDP command mode panel data frame
*Description:* A timeline showing the sequence of software triggers and interrupts for command mode panel transmission over two consecutive frames:
- **Frame 1**:
  - Initiated by writing `0x1` to the `MDP_CTL_0_CTL_START` register (red arrow at the start of `data(RGB)`).
  - Active data block (consisting of multiple horizontal line transmissions) lasts for "1 frame".
  - During this frame, software is free to program registers for the upcoming Frame 2, as indicated by a bracket labeled "SW free to program registers for frame 2 here".
  - Once the last pixel is sent, the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt is triggered (red arrow at the end of `data(RGB)`).
- **Frame 2**:
  - Similarly initiated by a write to `MDP_CTL_0_CTL_START` for frame 2.
  - Bracket indicates: "SW free to program registers for frame 3 here".
  - Concludes with the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt.

Upon completion of the frame, the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` status bit is set in the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register field. This bit indicates that the data was sent out of the MDP core. The data has not been completely sent to the panel because there is more delay in traversing the DSI controller, and the DSI PHY before reaching the panel. However, once the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` status bit is set, software can push more frames.

To achieve a high frame rate, software can issue another write to the `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` register (with `0x1`) shortly after receiving the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt. While hardware pushes out the frame, software can program the next frame settings so that it kicks off as soon as the previous frame is complete. The target is to achieve 60 fps on command mode panels.

### Tear check
Tearing occurs when the write time for data and the display time for the written data get out of sync. Tearing occurs when data is written out faster or slower than the scan rate.

Tear check applies only to command mode panels, which have their own timing generator and local frame buffers for display refresh.

To convey timing information, a tearing effect (TE) signal is provided from the panel to the host processor. This TE signal is also referred to as a VSync input. MDP uses this input to synthesize an internal version of the panel’s write and read pointers. This synthesis allows the MDP to ensure the write pointer is always behind the read pointer.

When frame buffer content is written too fast, tearing appears as shown in Figure 4-16.
<!-- page 248 -->

#### Figure 4-16 MDP tearing (too fast)
*Description:* A chart and visualization depicting tearing when writing to the frame buffer is faster than the panel refresh rate:
- **Sawtooth Chart (Top)**: Plots line numbers over time. The black sawtooth line represents the frame buffer read pointer (panel refresh). The red line represents the frame buffer write pointer. The red line has a steeper slope (faster write speed) and starts after the first read cycle. It crosses the black read pointer line during the second cycle before Time B.
- **Visual Representation (Bottom)**:
  - **Time A**: The frame buffer contains a yellow smiley face, which matches the image displayed on the screen.
  - **Time B**: The frame buffer is updated to a red face with crossed eyes (dead face). However, because the write pointer overtook the read pointer mid-frame, the display screen shows a torn image: the top half is the yellow smiley face, and the bottom half is the red dead face.
  - **Time C**: The write is complete, and both the frame buffer and the display correctly show the red dead face.

When frame buffer content is written too slowly, tearing appears as shown in Figure 4-17.

#### Figure 4-17 MDP tearing (too slow)
*Description:* A chart and visualization depicting tearing when writing to the frame buffer is slower than the panel refresh rate:
- **Sawtooth Chart (Top)**: Plots line numbers over time. The black sawtooth line represents the frame buffer read pointer. The red line represents the frame buffer write pointer. The red line has a gentler slope (slower write speed) and starts during the first read cycle. The black read pointer line overtakes the red write pointer line during the second cycle before Time B.
- **Visual Representation (Bottom)**:
  - **Time A**: The frame buffer and display correctly show a yellow smiley face.
  - **Time B**: The frame buffer update to a red dead face is in progress but incomplete, showing a red face on top and a sliver of yellow smiley on the bottom. The display screen is torn, showing the newly written red dead face on the top half and the old yellow smiley face on the bottom half.
  - **Time C**: The write is finally complete, and both the frame buffer and display show the red dead face.

To prevent tearing, limit the data that is written out to the exact refresh rate of the display by using the TE signal from the display and the tear check logic of the SoC. When tear checking is enabled, data written from the SoC to command mode panels synchronizes to the panel scan.

Tear check logic estimates the line number of the display scan using a counter, the value of which is called the read pointer. The incoming TE signal from the panel resets the read pointer. Configure the rate at which the read pointer increments through the MDP synchronization registers.
<!-- page 249 -->

The tear check logic compares the read pointer with the write pointer (line number of the output). If the read and write pointers satisfy certain conditions, the output goes out to the panel. Otherwise it is held until the conditions are satisfied.

The start of a frame can be sent out when the read pointer is within a window—the start position and width of the window is configurable through the register. Each line of the frame can be sent out when the write pointer is not too close to the read pointer; the distance between read and write pointer is configured through register. The goal is to keep the write pointer behind the read pointer (see Figure 4-18).

#### Figure 4-18 MDP tear check
*Description:* A line number vs. time graph demonstrating how the tear check logic regulates the write pointer based on the read pointer position:
- **Pointers**:
  - `Read pointer` (black diagonal line): Represents the linear scan of the panel.
  - `Write pointer` (red stepped line): Represents the data written by the SoC. The stepped pattern indicates burst transfers of block data.
- **Configurable Parameters**:
  - `Start pos` and `Start pos + start threshold` (horizontal dashed lines): Define the window during which the start of a frame (SOF) can be triggered.
  - `SOF can start within this window` (horizontal double-headed arrow at the bottom): The time interval corresponding to the start threshold.
  - `Continue threshold` (vertical double-headed arrow): The minimum line distance that must be maintained between the read pointer and write pointer. If the write pointer gets too close to the read pointer (i.e. distance is less than the threshold), writing is suspended until the read pointer advances.
- **Events**:
  - `Dma Done interrupt, Sw may trigger a new frame` (vertical dashed lines at the end of Frame 1 and Frame 2): Signaled when the DMA transfer completes, prompting the software to trigger the next frame's scan.

During the start window, if data is not ready, the entire frame output is delayed until the next frame for any of the following reasons:
* Software triggers too late.
* Software misses the start window because it is too narrow.
* Output data rate is so slow that there is not enough time for software to set up and trigger.

### Tear check - SoC writes faster than panel read
If the start window is set early in a frame, the output data rate might be slowed down because the panel scan rate limits the output data rate. The read pointer limits the slope of the write pointer. The goal of tear check is to avoid the write pointer crossing the read pointer. In this scenario, the output might intermittently become once every two frames (see Figure 4-19).
<!-- page 250 -->

#### Figure 4-19 MDP slow output data rate
*Description:* A line number vs. time graph showing a scenario where the update rate drops to 30 Hz (once every two frames) because the start window is set too early:
- **Pointers**: `Read pointer` (black diagonal line) and `Write pointer` (red stepped line).
- **Setup**: `Start pos` and `Start pos + start threshold` are set low (early in the frame).
- **Issue**: The write for Frame 2 completes at the end of the first read cycle, triggering a DMA Done interrupt. Software has a narrow window (indicated by "Sw has this much time to setup and trigger a new frame") to trigger the next frame before the read pointer exits the start window.
- **Result**: The software trigger arrives too late, missing the start window for the second read cycle. The write for Frame 3 is held at 0 (flat red line) until the third read cycle enters the start window. This causes the panel to update only once every two frame refreshes.

To take advantage of a fast output rate, set the start window near the end of the frame to maximize the output data rate. The update occurs once per frame, but there is more bandwidth for software to set up and trigger the next frame (see Figure 4-20).

#### Figure 4-20 MDP fast output data rate
*Description:* A line number vs. time graph showing how setting the start window near the end of the frame allows for a continuous 60 Hz update rate:
- **Pointers**: `Read pointer` (black diagonal line) and `Write pointer` (red line).
- **Setup**: `Start pos` and `Start pos + start threshold` are set high (near the end of the frame, close to the maximum line number).
- **Effect**: By shifting the start window to the end of the read cycle, the time available for software setup is greatly extended. The double-headed arrow "Sw has this much time to setup and trigger a new frame" spans almost the entire frame duration.
- **Result**: Software easily triggers the subsequent frames (Frame 2, Frame 3, Frame 4) within their respective start windows, allowing for continuous frame updates on every read cycle.

### Tear check - SoC writes slower than panel read
If the maximum output rate is slower than the panel scan, the panel updates once every two frames. For example, the panel updates at 30 Hz while the panel refresh rate is 60 Hz. To avoid tearing, set the start window closer to the beginning of a frame (see Figure 4-21).


<!-- page 251 -->

#### Figure 1-22: MDP output rate slower than panel scan
*Description:* A line graph showing "Line number" (Y-axis) vs "Time" (X-axis). The graph contains black lines representing the "Read pointer" (panel scan) and red lines representing the "Write pointer" (MDP output). The slope of the read pointer is steeper than the write pointer, indicating that the MDP output rate is slower than the panel scan rate. Horizontal dashed lines mark "Star pos" and "Start pos + start threshold". A time window between the read pointer crossing "Star pos" and "Start pos + start threshold" is labeled "SOF can start within this window". Because the write pointer finishes before the next frame's start threshold, there is a time period labeled "Sw has this much time to setup and trigger a new frame" before the next frame needs to start, avoiding tearing.

Tearing cannot be avoided if the start window is too far from the beginning of the frame (Figure 4-22).

#### Figure 1-23: MDP tearing: start too far from frame beginning
*Description:* A line graph showing "Line number" (Y-axis) vs "Time" (X-axis), with the same axes and markings as Figure 1-22. In this case, the write pointer for Frame 2 starts too late, well after the read pointer has crossed the "Start pos + start threshold" line. The steeper read pointer line intersects the shallower write pointer line. At the intersection, the read pointer overtakes the write pointer. An annotation explains: "Panel shows first half from Frame 2, second half is still content of Frame 1", demonstrating tearing because the start window was missed.

To match the connection path to the DSI interface, each ping-pong output has a tear check module. Even if the command mode streams are interleaved to a single interface, the tear check logic applies to each stream individually. As a result, there are up to three incoming VSync signals.

### Enabling tear check
To enable the tear check module, write (1) to the EN bit of the `MDP_PP_0_TEAR_CHECK_EN` register. Configure how the read pointer (rptr) and the write pointer (wptr) increment, by configuring the following registers:
1. Select the source of TE signals in `MDP_MDP_VSYNC_SEL` register.
2. Set the number of vsync_clk cycles in 1 line in the `VSYNC_COUNT` field of the `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC` register.
3. Set `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_HEIGHT` register to `0x7FFF`.
4. Set the tear check read pointer initial value to `MDP_PP_0_VSYNC_INIT_VAL` register. When a TE is detected, the read pointer will be reset to this initial value.
<!-- page 252 -->

5. Optional: set the line number to `MDP_PP_0_RD_PTR_IRQ` register. When the tear check read pointer reach this value, a tear check read pointer interrupt will be generated.
6. Optional: override the tear check read pointer to a value by setting the value in `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_WRCOUNT` register.
7. In Ping-pong split mode, set the `SMART_PANEL_FREE_RUN` field to 1 in the `MDP_SPLIT_DISPLAY_LOWER_PIPE_CTRL` register.
8. Enable TE input by setting the `VSYNC_IN_EN` field to 1 in `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC` register.
9. Enable the Tear Check read pointer counter by setting `VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` field to 1 in the `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC` register.
10. Configure the Tear check start window and threshold in `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_THRESH` and `MDP_PP_0_START_POS` registers.
11. Optional: set the line number to `MDP_PP_0_WR_PTR_IRQ` register. When the tear check write pointer reach this value, a tear check write pointer interrupt will be generated.
12. Enable Tear check by setting `MDP_PP_0_TEAR_CHECK_EN` register to 1.
13. Optional: set the Y offset of the ROI in `MDP_PP_0_OUT_LINE_COUNT` register.
14. Flush and start frame update.
15. Repeat steps 13 and 14 for each frame update. Note that the tear check read pointer has to stay in sync with the panel. No matter if there is a full frame update, partial update or even with no frame update at all, the tear check read pointer should not be disabled, that is: `VSYNC_IN_EN` or `VSYNC_COUNT_EN` should remain 1.

### Detecting tearing
When the internal read pointer reaches the value programmed in the `MDP_PP_0_RD_PTR_IRQ` register or when the internal write pointer reaches the value programmed in the `MDP_PP_0_WR_PTR_IRQ` register, then MDP generates an interrupt. These interrupts are set in the appropriate `PING_PONG_0_RD_PTR` and `PING_PONG_0_WR_PTR` interrupt bits within the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register. They can perform much more accurate triggering of frames as described in the various scenarios (see Section Tear check - SoC writes faster than panel read and Section Tear check - SoC writes slower than panel read).

### Autorefresh with external TE
Autorefresh is a feature to automatically and periodically send a frame update to a DSI command mode panel. Autorefresh can be done every N number of TE (external TE or SW TE).
1. Enable autorefresh:
   a. Enable auto-refresh:
      ```
      MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG.ENABLE=1
      MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG.FRAME_COUNT= autorefresh_frame_cnt
      ```
   b. Wait for `MDP_INTR_STATUS` `PING_PONG_0_AUTOREFRESH_DONE` interrupt (To make sure that transfer is on-going and prevent race conditions with the panel Vsync)
2. Disable auto-refresh with external TE:
<!-- page 253 -->

   a. Disable syncing with the external TE (that is, `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_IN_EN` = 0)
   b. Check if MDP fetch is active or not:
      Read the line_count (`MDP_PP_0_PP_LINE_COUNT`)
      `IF (line_count < active_height)` /* MDP fetch is active */
   c. If active, wait for `MDP_INTR_STATUS.PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt
   d. Disable autorefresh (`MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG` = 0)
   e. Enable syncing to the external TE (`MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_IN_EN` = 1)
3. Kickoff (configuration update) when autorefresh is enabled with external TE:
   a. Disable syncing with the external TE (that is, `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_IN_EN` = 0)
   b. Registers programming for this in-coming frame N.
   c. Wait for Ping Pong done interrupt for any previous frame N-1.
   d. Program the flush registers.
   e. Write to the `MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG` register. Here, the option could be re-writing the same configuration or modifying the `FRAME_COUNT`.
   f. Enable syncing to the external TE (`MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_IN_EN` = 1)
   g. Wait for `MDP_INTR_STATUS.PING_PONG_0_AUTOREFRESH_DONE` interrupt.

### Autorefresh with software TE
1. Set Up and Start Autorefresh
   a. Configure frame rate in `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC` (same way as setting panel vsync rate for tear check)
   b. `vsync_count = vsync_clk frequency / (vsync_frame_rate * height)`
   c. Configure autorefresh rate: once per N frames in `MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG.FRAME_COUNT`
   d. `FRAME_COUNT = vsync_frame_rate / autorefresh rate`
   e. Enable autorefresh in `MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG.ENABLE`
   f. Initialize the line and frame counter in `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_WRCOUNT` (and a write to this register will make the synchronization counter to start counting)
2. Pause Autorefresh
   To pause autorefresh, just disable the synchronization counters, that is: set `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` to 0.
3. Resume/restart Autorefresh
<!-- page 254 -->

To restart autorefresh after pause, just re-enable the synchronization counters, that is: set `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` to 1.

To resume autorefresh after pause:
   a. Write `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` to 1.
   b. Read the value of `MDP_PP_0_INT_CNT_VAL` register.
   c. Write `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_WRCOUNT` to the value of `MDP_PP_0_INT_CNT_VAL` (the write will trigger the counting).
4. To restart autorefresh after stop:
   a. Write `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` to 1.
   b. Write `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_WRCOUNT` to 0 (the write will trigger the counting).
5. Stop Autorefresh:
   To stop autorefresh, just disable the synchronization counters and reset the counters:
   a. Set `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_WRCOUNT` to 0.
   b. Set `MDP_PP_0_SYNC_CONFIG_VSYNC.VSYNC_COUNTER_EN` to 0.
   c. If a frame is started by autorefresh, wait until it is done.
   d. Set `MDP_PP_0_AUTOREFRESH_CONFIG.ENABLE` to 0.

### Memory writeback line mode
In line mode, memory writeback data comes from these sources (see Table 4-17):
* WB2: layer mixer 3

The four output formats are as follows:
* YUV420 pseudo planar (NV12)
* RGB565
* RGB888
* xRGB8888

The "x" component is a software programmable value. For WB2, the generated alpha character is not written back from the layer mixer. It is dropped after the layer mixer and it is not stored in a ping-pong FIFOs. The packer can be instructed to insert a software programmable value, when the output frame format is xRGB8888.

The A/R/G/B components can bypass the CSC/Chroma down/dither blocks (when the blocks are disabled), and the packer will write out frames in ARGB8888 format. Also, the packer can be instructed to insert a software programmable value, when the output frame format is xRGB8888.

See Section Output formats for programming restrictions and memory layout formats.

In the writeback path, dither and CSC/Chroma down paths are mutually exclusive. Software cannot dither YUV formats. Dither is only available for RGB formats where the CSC/Chroma down modules are disabled. The `WB_2_DONE` interrupt status bit in `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register signals that a writeback operation is complete.
<!-- page 255 -->

### Memory writeback block mode
In block mode, memory writeback implies a rotation path.

The block mode supports a n*90 degree rotation (where n=0, 1, 2, or 3).

> [!NOTE]
> All combinations are handled by a joint effort between fetch and writeback modules. The fetch implements the horizontal and vertical flips whereas the writeback module implements 0 or 90 degree rotation.

To enable the memory writeback, set the `MEM_SEL` field within the appropriate `MDP_CTL_<id>_TOP` register.

One writeback path implements a block mode writeback (see Table 4-17 for more details):
* DMA0 - WB0

The block mode writeback processing is performed in 128 × 128 blocks. No other operations aside from rotation are performed (no scaling or blending on the datapath).

All input formats can be rotated. The output formats for block mode are the same as the input formats.

The `WB_0_DONE` interrupt status bit in `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register signals that a writeback operation is complete.

## 4.1.1.3.6 MDP shared memory pool (SMP)

### SMP overview
The shared memory pool (SMP) provides more efficient and versatile use of the line buffer memory.

Before the shared memory pool, the fetch engines line buffers were sized for the largest supported resolution. If the product called for a smaller resolution, the area was wasted and not reused.

With the introduction of the shared memory pool, the line buffers are consolidated into a central location that is allocated per use case. This added flexibility requires software developers to allocate the required amount of memory to each shared memory pool client.

### SMP sizing
Shared memory pool memory elements and client ports vary by target.

##### Table 4-26 MDP SMP sizing
| SMP MMBs | Client ports | Size of MMB | Total memory |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 8 | 7 | 8 KB | 64 KB |
<!-- page 256 -->

### SMP port allocations
The SMP ports are allocated from 0 to n-1.

##### Table 4-27 MDP SMP port allocations
| Description | Definition | Port |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| IDLE | Unconnected | 0 |
| ViG 0 pipe fetch Y-component | `VIG_0_FETCH_Y_W` | 1 |
| ViG 0 pipe fetch Q-component | `VIG_0_FETCH_CR_W` | 2 |
| ViG 0 pipe fetch Cb-component | `VIG_0_FETCH_CB_W` | 3 |
| DMA 0 pipe fetch Y-component | `DMA_0_FETCH_Y_W` | 4 |
| DMA 0 pipe fetch Cr-component | `DMA_0_FETCH_CR_W` | 5 |
| DMA 0 pipe fetch Cb-component | `DMA_0_FETCH_CB_W` | 6 |
| RGB 0 fetch ARGB | `RGB_0_FETCH_W` | 7 |
| RGB 1 fetch ARGB | `RGB_1_FETCH_W` | 8 |

### SMP programming
While the MDP pipeline is active and accessing the shared memory pool (SMP), software must not alter the SMP configuration.

The allocation of memory to a particular client is static and remains unchanged while the use case is running. Memory can be allocated and added to a new datapath while a completely separate datapath is running, but the datapath configuration remains unchanged.

The SMP is structured in subpools of memory, memory macro blocks (MMB). The write channel connections for these subpools are programmed through the `MDP_SMP_ALLOC_W_<n>` register (n = 0 to 10) while the read channel connections are programmed through the `MDP_SMP_ALLOC_R_<n>` register. The number of subpools available varies by target.

The only fields in the `MDP_SMP_ALLOC_W_<n>` and `MDP_SMP_ALLOC_R_<n>` registers that are needed are the `MMB_<m>_MUX_W` and `MMB_<m>_MUX_R` fields (m = 0 to 32).

Setting the `MMB_0_MUX_W` field to 0x1 assigns the memory macro block 0 to `VIG_0_FETCH_Y`.

Setting `MMB_0_MUX_W` field to 0x2 assigns the memory macro block 0 to `VIG_0_FETCH_CR`.

Although there are different `MMB_<n>_MUX_W` and `MMB_<n>_MUX_R` registers, always program them to the same value (client).
<!-- page 257 -->

### SMP granularity
All latency values must be rounded up to the nearest SMP MMB.

Each latency line must equal at least two lines.

For example, ARGB8888 or line width requires 15360 bytes (1920 pixels × 4 bytes/pixel × 2 lines), which requires 3.75 MMBs, so 4 MMBs are allocated.

If it is the RGB0 port (ID 7), the allocation is as follows:
```
MMB_0_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_1_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_2_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_3_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
```

4 MMBs (0-3) are allocated to RGB0 port.

For example, the YUV format for the 1920 width NV12 format has two planes. The first plane requires 3840 bytes (1920 pixels × 1 byte/pixel × 2 lines) which is 1 MMB. The Chroma plane (consisting of Cr and Cb components) requires 1 MMB as well.

Assuming ViG0, the allocation is as follows:
```
MMB_4_MUX_W = 1 // VIG_0_FETCH_Y
MMB_5_MUX_W = 2 // VIG_0_FETCH_CR
```

Software must know the total allocation required per read/write client. This total depends on the size and format of the data stored in the SMP.

The SMP MMB does not need be contiguous. The following allocation is also acceptable to provide 4 MMBs to RGB0:
```
MMB_0_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_2_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_4_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
MMB_6_MUX_W = 7 // RGB0
```

For a given use case, unused MMBs can be allocated to other clients to provide more latency buffer. Unused SMP blocks consume less power.

### SMP macro block limitations
For YUV formats, the fetch implementation uses a 16-bit counter to maintain the number of bytes per socket. So, the total bytes that can be allocated is 65535 bytes.

For the 8-KB MMBs on MDP, this allocation limit creates the following restrictions per socket:
* RGB formats (non-BWC): Any number of MMBs up to 31 ([1, 31])
* YUV formats (non-BWC): Any number of MMBs up to 7 per socket ([1, 7] for Y, and [1, 7] for UV)

> [!NOTE]
> The upper limit is more than the SMP MMBs mandated by that use case.
<!-- page 258 -->

## 4.1.1.3.7 MDP source surface processing pipes (SSPP)
The MDP includes the following source surface processing pipelines (SSPPs): ViG0, RGB0, RGB1, and DMA0. A CURSOR0 pipeline is also supported.

### SSPP configuration
Complete the following steps to program a source surface processing pipe (SSPP) to fetch an image from memory:
1. Configure the height and width of the region of interest (ROI).
2. Configure decimation.
3. Configure the base addresses.
4. Configure the address sync modes.
5. Configure stride.
6. Configure source formats.
7. Configure Chroma site sampling.
8. Configure interleaving.
9. Configure pseudo planar formatting.
10. Configure operation mode.
11. Configure ViG operation modes: QSEED: phase step, initial phase, and CAF.
12. Configure QSEED.

### SSPP height and width
Hardware uses the settings in Figure 4-21 to fetch data from external memory.

#### Figure 4-21: MDP SSPP height and width
*Description:* A diagram illustrating the coordinate system and parameters for selecting a Region of Interest (ROI) from a source image. The full source image is depicted as a large light-gray rectangle with a total width of `SRC_IMG_SIZE.SRC_W` and a total height of `SRC_IMG_SIZE.SRC_H`. Inside the source image, a smaller yellow rectangle represents the "ROI". The top-left corner of the ROI is offset from the top-left corner of the source image by `SRC_XY.SRC_X` horizontally and `SRC_XY.SRC_Y` vertically. The size of the ROI itself is specified by `SRC_SIZE.ROI_W` for its width and `SRC_SIZE.ROI_H` for its height.
<!-- page 259 -->

The information in Figure 4-21 is also used for scaling. Hardware must know if it can over-fetch the boundaries and by how much.

> [!NOTE]
> If the following rules are violated, MDSS cannot operate correctly.

If the `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_IMG_SIZE` = `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_SIZE`, then there are no allowable pixels to fetch on any of the edges. Hardware repeats the end pixels.

Hardware expects the following configurations for a `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_*` register (where `*` = `SRC_SIZE`, `SRC_XY` or `SRC_IMG_SIZE`):

`SRC_SIZE.ROI_H + SRC_XY.SRC_Y ≤ SRC_IMG_SIZE.SRC_H`

`SRC_SIZE.ROI_W + SRC_XY.SRC_X ≤ SRC_IMG_SIZE.SRC_W`

For the minimum and maximum size in the pipeline, see Section Output formats.

> [!NOTE]
> To fetch larger resolutions than the source pipe supports, software can enable decimation or source split the image across two source pipes.

The width values are the exact width and height values rather than the "n-1" value. The default value of 0x0 must change before starting a region of interest (ROI) because a width or height of 0x0 is not supported.

All of these registers are double-buffered with flush.

### SSPP base address
MDP has four sets of address registers that are 23 bits wide and byte-aligned. Each register refers to the separate plane where the surface is stored. Depending on the layout of the source data in memory, MDP can use any or all of the registers.

The hardware and software interface define the color components based on the datatype: graphics or video (see Table 4-28).

##### Table 4-28 MDP SSPP color mapping for YUV and RGB formats
| Component | YUV mapping | RGB mapping |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| Color0 | Luma (Y) | Green |
| Color1 | Chroma (CB) | Blue |
| Color2 | Chroma (CR) | Red |
| Color3 | Alpha | Alpha |
<!-- page 260 -->

##### Table 4-29 MDP SSPP base address definitions
| Register | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC0_ADDR` | <ul><li>Interleaved format base address</li><li>Color0 (Green) component base address in planar format</li><li>Luma component base address in non-interleaved format</li></ul> |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC1_ADDR` | <ul><li>Not used in Interleaved format – "don't care"</li><li>Color1 (Blue) component base address in planar format</li><li>Chroma component base address in pseudo-planar format</li><li>CB component in planar YUV format</li></ul> |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC2_ADDR` | <ul><li>Not used in Interleaved format – "don't care"</li><li>Color2 (Red) component base address in planar format</li><li>Not used in pseudo-planar format – "don't care"</li><li>CR component in planar YUV format</li></ul> |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC3_ADDR` | <ul><li>Not used in Interleaved format – "don't care"</li><li>Color3 (Alpha) component base address in planar format</li><li>Alpha address in pseudo-planar format</li><li>Alpha component in planar YUV format</li></ul> |

These registers are double-buffered with flush when in frame sync mode.

### SSPP address sync modes
Address synchronization sets the boundary on which the fetch address synchronizes.

There are two types of address buffering defined in the `ADDR_SYNC_MODE` field of the `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_FETCH_CONFIG` register:
* Frame (default)
* Line

The function of the `ADDR_SYNC_MODE` field is to define the boundary on which fetch address synchronizes. Setting this field to line forces the address updates on the next line, which performs the software requested feature of updating on HSYNC. Updating on line boundaries likely results in tearing on the panel because hardware is fetching from new memory buffer.

When the `ADDR_SYNC_MODE` field is set to 0x1 (line boundary), the current base address is sent to the fetch engine and is used on the next line fetch.

> [!NOTE]
> Because the fetch buffer changed in the middle of processing, this creates tearing.

Source surface pipes have software readable registers that return the source address values hardware is processing, not the software-programmed values.


<!-- page 261 -->

Software uses these registers to know when a surface has been flushed and can free the buffers from the VBIF MMU.
* `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_CURRENT_SRC0_ADDR`
* `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_CURRENT_SRC1_ADDR`
* `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_CURRENT_SRC2_ADDR`
* `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_CURRENT_SRC3_ADDR`

### SSPP stride

Stride (or pitch) refers to the width (in bytes) of the image surface in memory.

Each plane base address has an associated independent stride value. These stride values are set by two stride registers.

#### Table 4-30 MDP SSPP stride registers

| Register | Bit field | Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE0` | SRCP1_YSTRIDE | Plane 1 Y stride in bytes |
| | SRCP0_YSTRIDE | Plane 0 Y stride in bytes |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE1` | SRCP3_YSTRIDE | Plane 3 Y stride in bytes |
| | SRCP2_YSTRIDE | Plane 2 Y stride in bytes |

The values are defined in number of bytes and independent of the source widths.

These registers are double-buffered with flush.

### SSPP source formats

Two registers define the source format. Supported formats are listed in sections Interleaved formats, Pseudo planar formats, and Planar formats.

#### Table 4-31 MDP SSPP source format registers

| Register | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_UNPACK_PATTERN` | Unpacking pattern, maximum of four pattern elements starting from LSB to MSB (0 – 4) |
| `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` | Source format configuration for each pipeline. |

### Chroma site sampling

The `SRC_CHROMA_SAMP` field of the `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` register defines the sampling of the source format.

There are four valid settings that indicate the subsampling of the source format.
<!-- page 262 -->

#### Table 4-32 MDP SSPP chroma subsampling

| Setting | Source subsampling | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `0x0` | RGB/YUV444 | Fully sampled in both directions |
| `0x1` | YUV422 H2V1 | Subsampled horizontally |
| `0x2` | YUV422 H1V2 | Subsampled vertically |
| `0x3` | YUV420 | Subsampled horizontally and vertically |

> [!NOTE]
> Subsampling refers to subsampling by two. Uncommon formats such as subsampling by 4/8/16 (in either direction) are not supported.

### Source format programming

The `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` register programming for different formats is listed in Table 4-33 below. Note that 10-bit formats are identified by setting the `UNPACK_DX_FORMAT` field to `0x1` in the `SRC_FORMAT` register.

| Format | SRC_FORMAT Register Value | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `ARGB_8888` | `0x0002_37FF` | Linear single plane 32bpp fetch<br>DX_FORMAT=0<br>TIGHT=1<br>FRAME_FORMAT=0x0 |
| `ARGB_1010102` | `0x0002_77FF` | Only bit-14 changes to indicate 10-bit<br>DX_FORMAT=1<br>TIGHT=1<br>FRAME_FORMAT=0x0 |
| `PSDO_YUV_420 (NV12)` | `0x0192_923F` | Linear 2 plane NV12 setting<br>DX_FORMAT=0<br>TIGHT=1<br>FRAME_FORMAT=0x0 |

> Note that the hardware does not handle fractional UV components so odd values are not supported; consistent with all existing YUV formats.
