### Pseudo planar formats

For pseudo planar formats, luma is in its own plane and the Chroma components (CrCb) are packed in separate interleaved planes.

The unpack count and pattern apply to the interleaved Chroma plane only. There are two applicable settings that are supported; a separate alpha plane is also possible.

#### Table 4-35 MDP SSPP pseudo planar formats

| Format | Unpack pattern | SRC0 (G/Y) | SRC1 (B/Cb) | SRC2 (R/Cr) | SRC3 (A) | Unpack count | BPP |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| YCrCb | 0x0000_0201 | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | NO | 2 | 2 |
| YCbCr | 0x0000_0102 | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | NO | 2 | 2 |
| YCrCbA | 0x0000_0201 | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | 2 | 2 |
| YCbCrA | 0x0000_0102 | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | 8 bits | 2 | 2 |

### Planar formats

Planar formats are 8-bit color components for YCbCr with each plane stored linearly. There is no requirement for an unpack pattern or unpack count because each plane is fetched separately.

### SSPP basic operation mode

The `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE` register defines the operation mode for each SSPP pipeline.

#### MDP SSPP basic operation mode selection

| Register field | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `IGC_LUT_EN` | Enable Inverse Gamma Correction LUT at the end of the SSPP to translate data from 8 bits to 12 bits for blending. If disabled, data is replicated to produce a 12-bit value.<br>0x0: Disabled (mapped Linearly from 8-bit to 12-bit)<br>0x1: Enabled |
| `FLIP_MODE` | Flip Operation: indicates whether left-right and/or up-down flip is required. Setting this field impacts the fetch order and/or the unpacking order from the SMP.<br>Lower Bit: Left/Right flip<br>Upper Bit: Up/Down flip |

### SSPP ViG operation mode

The ViG0 pipeline includes the following sub-modules:
* Unpack module, which is responsible for sending data downstream the pipe in lenear mode.
* QSEED2 module, which is responsible for scaling (up/down), as well as chroma upsampling. At the output of QSEED2, every color component is fully sampled (that is, YUV444 for YUV formats, or ARGB8888 for RGB formats).
<!-- page 265 -->

* Color Space Conversion (CSC) module, which is used to translate YUV formats to the RGB format.
* Picture adjustment (SPA/CE) module.
* Inverse gamma correction/look-up table (IGC_LUT) module.

The maximum performance of the ViG pipeline is 1 pixel/clock at the output. For downscaling cases, the input to QSEED2 can be up to 4 pixels/clock.

The `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE` register defines the additional enables for ViG-specific functions, picture adjustment, histogram, and color space conversion (CSC).

### ViG scaler (QSEED2)

The QSEED2 scaler, located in the ViG pipe, is used to scale and up-sample Chroma components to fully sampled values.

#### Table 4-36 MDP QSEED2 configuration

| Format | Chroma component | Luma component |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| YUV420 | Upscale by 2 both vertically and horizontally | Unity scale |
| YUV422 H2V1 | Subsampled horizontally:<br>Upscale by 2 horizontally and unity scale vertically | Unity scale |
| YUV422 H1V2 | Subsampled vertically:<br>Upscale by 2 vertically and unity scale horizontally | Unity scale |

Each color component can have a different scaling method.

#### Table 4-37 MDP QSEED2 color component configuration

| Color component | Upscale/unity scale | Downscale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Color 0 | Content Adaptive OR Bilinear OR Pixel Repeat | PCMN |
| Color 1 | Bilinear OR Pixel Repeat | PCMN |
| Color 2 | Bilinear OR Pixel Repeat | PCMN |
| Color 3 | Bilinear OR Pixel Repeat | PCMN |

> [!NOTE]
> Any other setting can hang the MDP hardware (for example, setting to bilinear for downscaling settings).

The QSEED always receives an alpha (color3) value from the unpack logic. If the format does not have an alpha component, hardware forces it to 0x0. The correct filter selection must be programmed for alpha even if an alpha plane does not exist. For example, if the format is YUV420 pseudo-planar and the Y component is set to PCMN (because it is downscaling), the alpha channel must be set to PCMN as well. The alpha component mimics the fully sampled Y plane.

Content Adaptive Filtering (CAF) is valid for pseudo-planar or planar YUV formats only. It is illegal to use CAF for RGB formats and leads to undetermined behavior (including possible system hangs).
<!-- page 266 -->

CAF can only be enabled when both directions (vertical and horizontal) are upscaling. CAF cannot be enabled for only one direction.

When one direction is upscaling and another direction is downscaling, the downscaling method must be PCMN while the other direction can only be repeat or bilinear. CAF is not allowed.

#### Table 4-38 MDP QSEED2 scaling cases

| Scaling cases | Color planes | Available scaling methods |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Up or unity scale | Luma (Y) | Content-adaptive, bilinear, pixel repeat |
| | Chroma (U/V), R, G, or B | Bilinear, pixel repeat |
| | Alpha | Bilinear, pixel repeat |
| Downscale | Luma (Y) | PCMN |
| | Chroma (U/V), R, G, or B | PCMN |
| | Alpha | PCMN |

Edge filter coefficients are updated for every frame. The new value of the `SMOOTH_SHARPENING_STRENGTH` register takes effect at the beginning of each frame.

The MDP core can process up to four pixels per clock when downscaling, allowing the pipeline to have the same frequency requirements for a downscale up to and including ¼. Because higher downscale ratios require an increase in core clock processing, there is no hardware support for larger downscale ratios.

> [!NOTE]
> The maximum upscale ratio is 20x and requires no additional clock frequencies.

### Scaler phase step

For a scaling case with input dimensions, *inwidth* and *inheight*, and output dimensions, *out width* and *outheight*, calculate the phase step X and Y according to the following equations:

$$step_x = \frac{in_{width} \cdot 2^{21}}{out_{width}}$$

and

$$step_y = \frac{in_{height} \cdot 2^{21}}{out_{height}}$$

respectively, where $2^{21}$ represents the unity “1” in fixed-point hardware design.

The phase step size of each color component must be calculated using the input-output dimension information of its own component.

For all the supported input data formats, Components 0 and 3 have the same dimensions. Components 1 and 2 also have the same dimensions. So, components 0 and 3 have the same phase step sizes, as do Components 1 and 2.
<!-- page 267 -->

### Scaler initial phase

This initial phase class includes the following registers:
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_COMP0_3_INIT_PHASE_X`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_COMP0_3_INIT_PHASE_Y`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_COMP1_2_INIT_PHASE_X`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_COMP1_2_INIT_PHASE_Y`

To achieve in-phase output data, program initial phases in MDP. The QSEED2 supports various input data formats, including YUV420 and YUV422. Formats with Chroma subsampling have phase differences between Luma and Chroma samples. The phase differences are represented as various Chroma sites in video coding (see Figure 4-22). These phase differences allow QSEED2 initial phases to compensate for the phase difference and achieve in-phase output data.

#### Figure 4-22: MDP QSEED2 chroma and luma components not co-sited
*Description:* Layout diagram showing relationship between Luma samples (represented by blue circles) and Chroma samples (represented by yellow 'X's) before and after QSEED2 processing.
Before QSEED2 (left side, four examples):
* Example 1 (top-left): Chroma sample is co-sited with the top-left Luma sample.
* Example 2 (top-right): Chroma sample is centered between four Luma samples (2x2 grid).
* Example 3 (bottom-left): Chroma sample is vertically centered between two Luma samples on the left.
* Example 4 (bottom-right): Chroma sample is horizontally centered between two Luma samples on the top row.

After QSEED2 (right side):
* The output shows all four Luma samples co-sited with Chroma samples, representing a fully sampled (YUV 4:4:4) output.

> [!NOTE]
> The hardware supports a maximum pixel extension value of 5 on either side.

Thus practical use cases need to limit initial phase value to the following range:

$$-4 \le \text{initial\_phase} < 3$$

In addition to multiple Chroma sites, several factors can change the phase difference between Luma and Chroma samples before the QSEED2 module in the ViG pipe.
* Decimation downscaler
* 90 degree rotation
* Horizontal flip
* Vertical flip (see Figure 4-23)

#### Figure 4-23: MDP ViG pipe: phase differences (luma and chroma)
*Description:* Block diagram showing the pipeline of operations in the MDP ViG pipe that affect the phase differences between luma and chroma samples before they reach the QSEED2 module.
The pipeline consists of the following sequential stages:
1. Input phase difference: $(\Delta p_{0x}, \Delta p_{0y})$
2. **Decimation** block, which outputs intermediate phase difference $(\Delta p_{1x}, \Delta p_{1y})$.
3. **90 degree rotation** block.
4. **Horizontal flip** block.
5. **Vertical flip** block, which outputs intermediate phase difference $(\Delta p_{2x}, \Delta p_{2y})$.
6. **QSEED2** block, which performs the final scaling and upsampling.

Table 4-39 shows the QSEED2 API input parameters. The API includes functions to calculate the initial phases for regular scaling cases and for dual-pipe mode. These functions track the change of
<!-- page 268 -->

the phase difference pair $(\Delta P_x, \Delta P_y)$ in the ViG pipe to the QSEED2 input. Then the initial phase is calculated to offset these phase differences.

The following function definition is the interface for regular scaling cases:

```c
int32 cal_init_phase_for_qseed2(uint32 num_comps,
                               uint32 chroma_subsample_x_flg,
                               uint32 chroma_subsample_y_flg,
                               MDP_Chroma_Sample_Site chroma_site_io,
                               MDP_RotateMode rot90ed_io,
                               uint32 vertical_fliped,
                               uint32 horizontal_flip,
                               MDP_Interlaced interlace_io,
                               MDP_Interlaced_Field even_field_io,
                               uint16 *line_skip,
                               uint16 *pixel_skip,
                               uint32 *comp_filter_method_x,
                               uint32 *comp_filter_method_y,
                               uint32 *comp_phase_step_x,
                               uint32 *comp_phase_step_y,
                               int32 *comp_init_phase_x,
                               int32 *comp_init_phase_y);
```

#### Table 4-39 MDP QSEED2 API parameters

| Parameter | Description |

### Scaler content adaptive filtering (CAF)

The content adaptive filtering (CAF) class registers include:
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_SMOOTH_STRENGTH`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_EDGE`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_SMOOTH`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_NOISE`
<!-- page 270 -->

* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_EDGE_FILTER_COEFF_START`

Among them, parameters `SHARP_THRESHOLD_EDGE`, `SHARP_THRESHOLD_SMOOTH` and `SHARP_THRESHOLD_NOISE` are threshold values used in the 4-tap content-adaptive filtering process. `SHARP_THRESHOLD_EDGE` and `SHARP_THRESHOLD_SMOOTH` classify the computed Sobel result (see Figure 4-24).

#### Figure 4-24: MDP CAF interpolation filter selection (high level)
*Description:* Flowchart showing the high-level logic for MDP Content Adaptive Filtering (CAF) interpolation filter selection based on the Sobel operator result.
* **Source Data** is processed by the **Sobel Operator** to produce a **Sobel Result**.
* The **Sobel Result** is evaluated against two thresholds:
  * If the result is greater than `sharp_threshold_edge` (Yes path), the **Edge filter for interpolation** is selected.
  * If the result is less than `threshold_smooth` (Yes path), the **denoising filter for interpolation** is selected. This filter also uses the `threshold_noise` parameter.
  * If neither condition is met (No paths from both decision blocks, labeled "else"), the **normal filter for interpolation** is selected.

The value for the `SHARP_THRESHOLD_EDGE` parameter cannot be smaller than that of the `THRESHOLD_SMOOTH` parameter.

The `THRESHOLD_NOISE` parameter establishes threshold value for denoising filtering (see Figure 4-25).

#### Figure 4-25: MDP CAF threshold noise
*Description:* Block diagram illustrating the logic for applying `THRESHOLD_NOISE` to determine the value of $P_{avgk}$ (for $k = -2, -1, 0, 1$ in both horizontal and vertical directions).
* Inputs are $P_k$ (source data) and $P'$ (pre-interpolated result).
* The difference $P_k - P'$ is calculated, and its absolute value is taken via the **ABS** block.
* This absolute difference is subtracted from `THRESHOLD_NOISE`.
* The result of this subtraction determines the output $P_{avgk}$:
  * If the result is greater than or equal to 0 (meaning the absolute difference is within the threshold), then $P_{avgk} = P'$.
  * If the result is less than 0 (meaning the absolute difference exceeds the threshold), then $P_{avgk} = P_k$.

In Figure 4-25, P’ represents a pre-interpolated result of the sample to be interpolated. The final interpolation result is represented by Q. Pk in the figure represents source data that are used for the interpolation of pixel Q. One can see the threshold value `THRESHOLD_NOISE` is used to determine $P_{avgk}$, $k = -2, -1, 0$ and $1$, values, which are used in the outer-smoothing process shown in Figure 4-26.


<!-- page 271 -->

#### Figure 4-26 MDP CAF outer-smoothing

*Description:* Block diagram showing the MDP CAF outer-smoothing process that generates the final output interpolation result $Q$.
- There are two multipliers (labeled with green circles containing 'X').
  - The first multiplier takes $P_{avg-2}$ and $32 - \text{phase}(s)$ as inputs.
  - The second multiplier takes $P_{avg1}$ and $\text{phase}(s)$ as inputs.
- The outputs of these two multipliers are summed together (green circle containing '+').
- This sum is then right-shifted by 5 bits ($>>5$).
- The shifted value is added to $P'$, $P_{avg-1}$, and $P_{avg0}$ in a four-input adder (green circle containing '+').
- The output of this adder is right-shifted by 1 bit ($>>1$).
- A constant value of $0\text{x}1$ is added to the result of the shift (green circle containing '+').
- The result of this addition is right-shifted by 1 bit ($>>1$).
- Finally, the value is clamped to the range $[0, 255]$ to produce the output $Q$.

The outer-smoothing process generates the final output interpolation result Q. This is a bilateral filtering result. It can perform smoothing while preserving structures.

If there are no denoising and sharpening requests, use the following settings can be used as the default setting.

| MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_EDGE_FILTER_COEFF_START | 0, it is set to 1 only when sharp_smooth_strength is updated to a different value. |
| MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_EDGE | 112 |
| MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_SMOOTH | 8 |
| MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SHARP_THRESHOLD_NOISE | 2 |

Content-adaptive sharpening is recommended because in this setting tiny noise is not amplified. However, for some content, sharpening the whole image provides a more vivid effect.

#### Scaler denoising/image blurring

Denoising (blurring background) is also completed by CAF setting. For general denoising applications, set the parameters THRESHOLD_SMOOTH and THRESHOLD_NOISE based on Table 4-40 setting. This process does not blur out the structural features in an image.

Some applications require strong smoothing/blurring. This can be completed by programming the parameter SHARP_SMOOTH_STRENGTH to be values in range of [-1, -256]. Changing the parameter value from -1 to -256 creates a stronger smoothing effect. The settings to blur everything are listed in Table 4-43.

#### Scaler filter coefficients

This class includes registers `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_NORMAL_FILTER_COEFF_N` and `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_QSEED2_SMOOTH_FILTER_COEFF_N`.

In the current MDP hardware implementation, the filter coefficients have been pre-programmed. They are not allowed to be programmed through software interface yet.

#### Scaler pixel extension programming

The pixel extension refers to the extra pixels fed to the QSEED2 scaler in order to produce an output image. There are a number of factors that influence the value programmed on the top/bottom/left/right such as:
- Scaling type (PCMN/bilinear/repeat/CAF)
- Initial phase
- Phase step

The output size is completely dictated by register programming so the extra pixels are required to be fed on the input side such that the appropriate number of output pixels are generated. The number of pixels/lines to be extended are programmed within fetch_unpack module to either overfetch or repeat the pixels/lines. QSEED2 is delivered with the appropriate number of pixels according to the following equations:

$$\text{scale\_in\_width} = \text{src\_width} + \text{pixel\_extension\_left} + \text{pixel\_extension\_right}$$

$$\text{scale\_in\_height} = \text{src\_height} + \text{pixel\_extension\_top} + \text{pixel\_extension\_bottom}$$

Initially, pixel extensions were completely handled and calculated by hardware. However, in order to provide flexibility and reduce hardware cost, the pixel extension units have been completed transferred to software programming.

> [!NOTE]
> The recommendation is that software always uses SW pixel extension registers even though hardware calculation units are present in MDP.

The exact calculation is outside the scope of this document. A software API is provided for MDP that can be integrated into the SW driver code. Below is a snippet of the code illustrating the calculations involved.

#### ViG color space conversion (CSC)

In the ViG pipe, the `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.CSC_1_EN` register field enables the CSC.

The act of enabling the color space conversion through `CSC_1_EN` is doubled buffered. However, before CSC is enabled, the following CSC configuration must be programmed.

CSC is configurable to convert from YUV $\rightarrow$ RGB, or RGB $\rightarrow$ YUV.

This is controlled by the `CSC_DST_DATA_FORMAT` and `CSC_SRC_DATA_FORMAT` fields in `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE` register to indicate the destination and source formats respectively.
<!-- page 274 -->

Typically CSC in ViG is used to convert YUV $\rightarrow$ RGB.

The register default is already set for this typical scenario in ViG.

The sequence of operations in CSC is:
- Pre-clamp
- Pre-bias
- Matrix multiplication
- Post-bias
- Post-clamp

#### Figure 4-27 MDP CSC sequence

*Description:* Detailed block diagram of the "MDP CSC Matrix" pipeline showing data width and types at each stage:
- **Input**: 3 channels of unsigned 8-bit data (`3 x U8`).
- **Pre-clamp**: Clamps the input data. Output remains `3 x U8`.
- **Pre-bias**: Adds pre-bias. Output becomes 3 channels of signed 10-bit data (`3 x S10 (10b)`).
- **Reg1 (MDP_pipe_stage)**: Pipeline register (flip-flop). Output is `3 x S10`.
- **3x3 matrix**: Performs matrix multiplication. Output is 9 channels of signed 14-bit data with 9 fractional bits (`9 x S14.9`).
- **Reg2 (MDP_pipe_stage)**: Pipeline register (flip-flop). Output is `9 x S14.9`.
- **Adder (+)**: Sums the matrix terms. Output is 3 channels of signed 16-bit data with 1 fractional bit (`3 x S16.1`).
- **Post-bias**: Adds post-bias. Output is 3 channels of signed 17-bit data with 1 fractional bit (`3 x S17.1`).
- **Round**: Performs rounding. Output remains `3 x S17.1`.
- **Post-clamp**: Clamps the output. Final output is 3 channels of unsigned 8-bit data (`3 x U8`).

None of the registers related to programming of the datapath are double buffered. The not double buffered registers are as follows:
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_CSC_1_COMP_[0…2]_PRE_CLAMP`
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_CSC_1_COMP_[0…2]_PRE_BIAS`
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_CSC_1_MATRIX_COEFF_[0…4]`
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_CSC_1_COMP_[0…2]_POST_BIAS`
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_CSC_1_COMP_[0…2]_POST_CLAMP`

#### Color space conversion usage

The color space conversion block is not used for hue, saturation, and value adjustment. These operations are performed in the picture adjustment blocks in the ViG and DSPP pipes. Thus, the CSC block only needs to be programmed to provide the standard conversions from YUV to sRGB color spaces. The inverse function, sRGB to YUV is performed by the CSC block in the writeback (WB2) pipe.

The following values can be used to convert from YUV to sRGB color space:

#### ViG picture adjustments (PA)

#### Figure 4-28 MDP general PA diagram

*Description:* Block diagram of the "PA / Histogram" module.
- The main pipeline is inside the "MDP Picture Adjustment" sub-module:
  - **Input** enters the **RGB to HSV** conversion block.
  - The HSV signal then passes sequentially through:
    - **Skin, Sky & Foliage Adj** (Memory Color Adjustment)
    - **Six-Zone Adj**
    - **HSV Adj**
  - After the **HSV Adj** block, the signal splits:
    - The main path continues to a **LUT** (Look-Up Table) block, and then to the **HSV to RGB** block, which generates the final output.
    - A secondary path branches off to a **Hist** (Histogram) block located outside the "MDP Picture Adjustment" block but within the main "PA / Histogram" block.
- A **Config** input is shown entering the main "PA / Histogram" block from the bottom left.

To enable global picture adjustment, set these bits:

```
MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_EN = 1
MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_<HUE/SAT/VAL/CONT>_MASK = 1
```

| $H_{adj}$ | Notes |
| :--- | :--- |
| $H_{adj} = H_{in} + \delta_h$ | $\delta_h$ is specified in `SPA_HUE_ADJUST` |

##### Table 4-46 MDP PA adjusted saturation

| Mode | $S_{adj}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| GAIN* | $S_{adj} = S_{in} \cdot (1 + \delta_s)$ |

#### Figure 4-30 MDP PA $\delta_s$ (y-axis) with K at different levels, $S_{in}$ (x-axis)

*Description:* A graph showing curves for $\delta_s$ (y-axis, ranging from 0.00 to 0.35) versus $S_{in}$ (x-axis, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0).
- The graph contains nine symmetric, bell-shaped curves labeled L1 to L9 in the legend.
- All curves start at 0.0 at $S_{in} = 0.0$, peak at $S_{in} = 0.5$, and return to 0.0 at $S_{in} = 1.0$.
- The peak value increases from L1 (approx 0.03) to L9 (approx 0.31).
<!-- page 278 -->

The curve keeps low-end dark unchanged, high-end from saturation, and mid-range incr/decr smoothly.

The base curve for $\delta_s$ ($M=1$) is saved into a 256 entry ROM $\text{LUT}_{sv}$, each entry in U10 format. $S_{in}$ is used to index $\text{LUT}_{sv}$ and this formula becomes:

$$S_{adj} = S_{in} \cdot (1 + K \cdot \text{LUT}_{sv}[S_{in}])$$

$K$ is specified in the `VALUE` field of `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_SPA_SAT_ADJUST` register.
The following are some special cases:
- If the $S_{in} < \text{MDP\_VP\_0\_VIG\_0\_SPA\_SAT\_ADJUST.THRSHLD}$, then $\delta_s = 0$. This means no saturation adjustment, $S_{adj} = S_{in}$.
- If $K \le 32$, $S_{adj} = 0$

The first part of the Value adjustment is the same as Saturation:

##### Table 4-47 MDP PA saturation value adjustment (value adjustment 1)

| Mode | $V_{adj}$ | Calculation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Offset | $V_{in} + \delta_v$ | $\delta_v = N \cdot 2 \cdot V_{in}^2 \cdot (1 - V_{in})^2$ |
| Gain* | $V_{in} \cdot (1 + \delta_v)$ | |

\*For better performance, use only Gain mode.

It uses the exact same base curve as $\delta_s$ (ROM content is the same as $\text{LUT}_{sv}$). $N$ is specified in `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_SPA_VAL_ADJUST` register. Unlike Saturation, there is no threshold.

The second part of Value adjustment is contrast adjustment.

##### Table 4-48 MDP PA contrast adjustment (value adjustment 2)

| $C_{adj}$ | Calculation |
| :--- | :--- |
| $V_{adj} + \delta_c$ | $\delta_c = -M \cdot 0.1 \cdot \sin(2 \pi V_{adj}) \cdot (1 - e^{-V_{adj}/0.1})$ |

[Figure/Graph] shows $\delta_c$ (y-axis) with $M$ at different levels, $V_{adj}$ (x-axis).
<!-- page 279 -->

#### Figure 4-31 MDP PA $\delta_c$ (y-axis) with M at different levels, $V_{adj}$ (x-axis)

*Description:* A graph showing the contrast adjustment delta $\delta_c$ (y-axis, ranging from -0.20 to 0.20) versus $V_{adj}$ (x-axis, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0).
- The graph contains 10 curves labeled L1 to L10.
- For $V_{adj}$ from 0.0 to 0.5, the delta is negative, forming a dip. The minimum of the dip is around $V_{adj} = 0.27$. The dip is shallower near 0 due to exponential damping.
- For $V_{adj}$ from 0.5 to 1.0, the delta is positive, forming a peak. The maximum of the peak is at $V_{adj} = 0.75$.
- The amplitude of the curves increases from L1 to L10, with L10 having a minimum of approx -0.16 and a maximum of approx 0.16.

The base curve is stored in a 256 entry ROM $\text{LUT}_c$, each entry in S10 format.

$V_{adj}$ is used to index $\text{LUT}_c$ and this formula becomes:

$$C_{adj} = V_{adj} + M \cdot \text{LUT}_c[V_{adj}]$$

$M$ is specified in the `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_SPA_CONT_ADJUST` register.

#### Figure: Contrast Adjustment Transfer Function

*Description:* A graph showing the final contrast-adjusted value $C_{adj}$ (y-axis, 0.0 to 1.0) versus $V_{adj}$ (x-axis, 0.0 to 1.0).
- It shows three curves:
  - **$M = 0.00$**: A straight diagonal line representing no change ($C_{adj} = V_{adj}$).
  - **$M = 1.65$**: An S-shaped curve (below the diagonal for $V_{adj} < 0.5$, above for $V_{adj} > 0.5$) that increases contrast by darkening darks and lightening lights.
  - **$M = -1.65$**: An inverse S-shaped curve (above the diagonal for $V_{adj} < 0.5$, below for $V_{adj} > 0.5$) that decreases contrast.

Figure 1-35 (likely a misreference to another figure, possibly Figure 4-32 on the next page) shows the operation for Hue, Value (Brightness), and Contrast adjustment. Saturation adjust is similar to Value adjust with the additional special cases not depicted.
<!-- page 280 -->

#### Figure 4-32 MDP PA hue, value, and contrast adjustment summary

*Description:* Block diagram illustrating the processing flow for Hue, Brightness (Value), and Contrast adjustments:
- **Hue Adjust**:
  - The input hue $iH$ and `hue_adjust` control signal are added together (circle with `+`).
  - The result passes through a **Circular clip** block to produce the adjusted hue.
- **Brightness**:
  - The input value $iV$ is fed into a **ROM 256x16 Interpolation** block and also passes to a yellow combiner block (labeled with `X`).
  - The output of the ROM is multiplied by the `rf_level` control signal in a multiplier (grey circle with `X`).
  - The output of this multiplier is combined with the original $iV$ in the yellow combiner block (labeled with `X`).
  - The result is clamped/clipped to produce the brightness-adjusted value, which is then passed to the Contrast stage.
- **Contrast**:
  - The brightness-adjusted value (input to Contrast stage) is fed into another **ROM 256x16 Interpolation** block and also passes to a yellow combiner block (labeled with `X`).
  - The output of this ROM is multiplied by the `rf_contrast` control signal in a multiplier (grey circle with `X`).
  - The output of this multiplier is combined with the input value in the yellow combiner block (labeled with `X`).
  - The result is clamped/clipped to produce the final output.
  - *Note:* The yellow combiner blocks in both Brightness and Contrast stages are labeled with `X` (multiplication), although mathematical descriptions suggest addition for the contrast stage.

#### Picture adjustment usage

The default register values (0x00) for the hue, saturation, and value adjust cause unity affect (hue, saturation, and value are unchanged).

If the Histogram LUT is enabled, the default ROM contents (0x00) cause the output to clamp to black.

To enable the histogram LUT with a unity (no effect) setting, $\text{HIST\_LUT}_n = n$, for $n = 0\text{-}255$.

##### Table 4-49 MDP PA picture adjustments

| Adjustment | Bit value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hue adjust | Signed 12-bit | Represents the range of -180 to +180 degrees. Typically, do not program more than $\pm$10 degrees for picture adjustment. |
| Sat adjust | Signed 8-bit | Represents $\pm$100%.<br>-128 provides 0 saturation (black and white).<br>+127 represents a 100% saturation increase.<br>The saturation threshold is an unsigned 8-bit value. If the actual saturation for a pixel is below this threshold, no adjustment is done. This causes almost neutral colors to stay neutral. |
| Val adjust | Signed 8-bit | -128 represents the maximum darkening.<br>+127 represents the maximum brightening. |

Programming values are subjective. They depend on the context of the adjustment.

#### Picture adjustment LUTv

To enable LUTv adjustment, set the following register fields:
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_EN = 1`
- `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_LUTV_EN = 1`


<!-- page 281 -->

The LUTv processing order is as shown in Figure 4-33. The LUTv is the last picture adjustment, thus the `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_LUTV_FIRST_EN = 0` (default value set in HW, cannot be modified by SW).

#### Figure 4-33 MDP PA LUTv processing order
*Description:* A block diagram showing the Picture Adjustment (PA) and Histogram data flow. The outer block is labeled "PA / Histogram". There is an input from the left and a "Config" input at the bottom left. The main input feeds into a block labeled "MDP Picture Adjustment" which contains a sequential processing chain:
1. "RGB to HSV"
2. "Skin, Sky & Foliage Adj"
3. "Six-Zone Adj"
4. "HSV Adj"
After "HSV Adj", the path splits: one path goes to "LUT" (inside "MDP Picture Adjustment"), and another path branches off to a block labeled "Hist" (inside the main "PA / Histogram" box, but outside the "MDP Picture Adjustment" box).
The path from "LUT" feeds into "HSV to RGB" (still inside "MDP Picture Adjustment").
The output of "HSV to RGB" is the final output to the right.

For projects that support LUTv access with auto-increment, to fully program one LUTv table, software writes 256 times to `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV` register.

```c
for (i=0; i<256; i++) {
  PA_LUTV = "color0 value";
}
```

For projects that support LUTv access with direct register mapping, to program the entire LUTv, write to `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV_IDX_i`, [i = 0…127] registers.

There are 128 registers total. Each register accesses two consecutive LUTv locations.

For projects with 8b-V component with direct register mapping:
* `PA_LUTV_IDX_0[7:0]` provides access to `LUTV[0]` content
* `PA_LUTV_IDX_0[23:16]` provides access to `LUTV[1]` content.

There are two sets of LUTv. Upon completion of the LUTv programming, software issues `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV_SWAP = 1`.
At any time, software has sole write access on one LUTv while hardware has sole read access on another LUTv. Once a LUTv is fully programmed, software writes to `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV_SWAP` to switch the hardware-software access. The `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV_SWAP` register is double-buffered. The actual switch occurs on the next double buffer update event.
The `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_HIST_SEL.PA_LUTV_SEL` register field shows the LUTv number that the software can currently access. After the swap, hardware uses the newly software-programmed LUTv.

For auto-increment LUTv access, upon swap the LUTv write pointer automatically points to entry 0. The `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_PA_LUTV.INDEX` register field indicates the current write pointer position of the LUT currently available for software.
<!-- page 282 -->

### Skin, sky, and foliage color adjustment

For a simplified block diagram of skin, sky and foliage adjustment, see Figure 4-34.

#### Figure 4-34 MDP PA skin, sky, and foliage color adjustment
*Description:* A block diagram showing the flow of memory color adjustment. 
Inputs:
* `rf_[H/S/V]min` and `rf_[H/S/V]max`: inputs to the "Color Detect" block.
* `enable`: input to the "Color Detect" block.
* `HSV(11, 8, 8)`: input data. It is routed to:
  * "Color Detect"
  * "Normalization" (specifically the `h` component)
  * The `+/x Clamp` block
  * The bypass input of the output multiplexer (`mux`)
* `rf_mid`: input to "Normalization".
* `rf_h_gain`, `rf_s_gain`, `rf_v_gain`: control inputs to the three stacked "PWL" (Piece-Wise Linear) blocks.

Processing flow:
1. The `h` component of the input `HSV` is normalized in the "Normalization" block using `rf_mid`.
2. The normalized values are passed to the "PWL" blocks, which also take the gain inputs (`rf_h_gain`, `rf_s_gain`, `rf_v_gain`).
3. The "PWL" blocks output adjustment factors `Hf`, `Sf`, and `Vf`.
4. The `+/x Clamp` block applies these adjustment factors to the original `HSV(11, 8, 8)` values and clamps the result.
5. The "Color Detect" block determines if the input color matches the target region based on the min/max thresholds. It outputs a select signal to the `mux`.
6. The `mux` selects between the adjusted HSV values (from `+/x Clamp`) and the original HSV values (bypass) based on the detection result.
7. The output is `HSV(11, 8, 8)`. There is also an auxiliary status output from the "Color Detect" block that exits to the right.

To enable memory color adjustment, set the following `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE` register fields:
* `PA_EN = 1`
* `PA_MEM_COL_<SKY/SKIN/FOL>_MASK = 1`

The three types of memory color processing are identical. But, each memory color has independent color qualifier and adjustment parameters.

Color qualifier is set in `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_REGION_<HUE/SAT/VAL>` registers.

Color detection determines if the pixel falls within the skin/sky/foliage zone according to the following comparison:

$$\text{HUE\_MIN} \le H_i \le \text{HUE\_MAX}$$

$$\text{SAT\_MIN} \le S_i \le \text{SAT\_MAX}$$

$$\text{VAL\_MIN} \le V_i \le \text{VAL\_MAX}$$

The pixel is qualified for a memory color adjustment only if all three conditions are satisfied.

The amount of adjustment is approximated by a piece-wise linear curve.
<!-- page 283 -->

#### Figure 4-35 MDP PA skin, sky, foliage gain adjustment
*Description:* A graph illustrating the piece-wise linear (trapezoidal) gain adjustments for Hue, Saturation, and Value based on the input Hue ($H_{in}$).
* The horizontal axis represents the input Hue ($H_{in}$), with markers for $H_{min}$, $H_{mid}$, and $H_{max}$. The maximum value on the axis is labeled $0x5FF$ (equivalent to 360 degrees).
* The vertical axis represents the adjustment values ($H_{adj}$, $V_{adj}$, $S_{adj}$), centered around 0.
* The adjustments are symmetrical trapezoids centered between $H_{min}$ and $H_{max}$.
* The orange curve represents a positive adjustment (e.g., Hue adjustment) with a rising slope defined by $H_{gain}$ and a flat top.
* The green curve represents a smaller positive adjustment (e.g., Saturation adjustment) with a rising slope defined by $S_{gain}$.
* The magenta curve represents a negative adjustment (e.g., Value adjustment) with a falling slope defined by $V_{gain}$.
* The distance from $H_{min}$ to the start of the flat top is defined by $H_{mid}$ (indicated by a horizontal double-headed arrow labeled "Hmid" starting from $H_{min}$).

The H, S, V adjustment values are added or multiplied to the input H, S, V, and clamped for the final adjusted value.

This hardware block operates in 10b mode. The data input to the block has two LSB tied to 0. The output goes directly to 6-ZONE, which also operates in 10b.

When `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_EN = 1` and 1 memory color MASK is set, the latency through the block (without backpressure) is 4 pipe stages. When `PA_EN = 0` or all of the MASK are 0, the latency is 1 pipe stage.

The adjusted H:

$$H_{adj} = H_i + \delta H \text{ followed by clamping.}$$

The adjusted S:

$$S_{adj} = S_i (1 + \delta S) \text{ followed by clamping.}$$

The adjusted V:

$$V_{adj} = V_i (1 + \delta V) \text{ followed by clamping.}$$

The following parameters describe the PWL for Hue, Sat, and Val adjustment in memory color.

The base of the trapezoid is identical for Hue, Sat, and Val and is defined by the following register fields:
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_REGION_HUE.MIN`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_REGION_HUE.MAX`

The slope of the trapezoid is independent for Hue, Sat, and Val and is defined by the following register fields:
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_ADJUST_PWL0.HUE_GAIN`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_ADJUST_PWL1.SAT_GAIN`
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_ADJUST_PWL1.VAL_GAIN`
<!-- page 284 -->

The horizontal width from $HUE_{MIN}$ to the point where the trapezoid plateaus is common among the HUE, SAT, VAL adjustment and is defined by the following register field:
* `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_<SKIN/SKY/FOLIAGE>_ADJUST_PWL0.HUE_MID`

#### Figure 1-39 MDP PA order precedence
*Description:* A flow chart illustrating the precedence of Picture Adjustment (PA) blocks. 
* The input is `10b RGB` which is converted to HSV by `RGB2HSV`.
* There are three multiplexers controlled by the signal `LUTV_FIRST_EN`. A note states: "Note: LUTV_FIRST_EN is always set to 0, and cannot be controlled by SW".
* **Default Path (`LUTV_FIRST_EN = 0`):**
  1. The output of `RGB2HSV` is routed through the top-right multiplexer (input 0) to the memory color and six-zone adjustment decision tree.
  2. The pixel is checked sequentially:
     * `Skin_mask?` $\rightarrow$ if yes and it's a `Skin pixel?` $\rightarrow$ `Skin adjust`.
     * `Sky_mask?` $\rightarrow$ if yes and it's a `Sky pixel?` $\rightarrow$ `Sky adjust`.
     * `Foliage_mask?` $\rightarrow$ if yes and it's a `Foliage pixel?` $\rightarrow$ `Foliage adjust`.
     * `Six zone *_mask?` $\rightarrow$ if yes $\rightarrow$ `Six zone adj`.
  3. If a pixel is adjusted by any of the above, it bypasses the subsequent checks in this tree.
  4. The output of these adjustments (or bypass) goes to a check for `PA_*_MASK`.
     * If `PA_*_MASK` is enabled, the pixel goes to `Global HSIC adj`.
     * If not, it bypasses it.
  5. The output of the global adjustment (or bypass) is routed back to the top-left multiplexer (input 0).
  6. From the top-left multiplexer, the data goes to the `ACE` block (which contains `HIST` and `LUTV`). If `LUTV_EN?` is true, it is processed by `LUTV`.
  7. The output of `LUTV` (or bypass) is routed to the bottom multiplexer (input 0).
  8. Finally, the data is converted back to RGB by `HSV2RGB` to produce `10b RGB` output.
* **Alternative Path (`LUTV_FIRST_EN = 1`, Unsupported):**
  * The flow is reversed: data goes to `ACE` (`LUTV`/`HIST`) first, and then to the memory color/six-zone/global HSIC adjustment tree, before going to `HSV2RGB`.

If a pixel has been adjusted for memory color or 6-zone, it falls through subsequent blocks and cannot be adjusted again.

To enable global pixel adjustments, set the `PA_MEM_PROTECT_ENABLE` field in the `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE` register using Table 53.
<!-- page 285 -->

### MDP PA global pixel adjustment settings

| PA_MEM_PROTECT_ENABLE setting | Function |
| :---: | :--- |
| 0 | Allows global pixel adjustment whether the pixel was previously processed by memory color or 6-zone |
| 1 | Allows global pixel adjustment only if the pixel was not previously processed by memory color or 6-zone |

### Six-zone color adjustment

Figure 4-36 is a simplified diagram of the six-zone color adjustment block (only supported for the DSPP0 pipeline).

#### Figure 4-36 MDP PA six-zone color adjustment diagram
*Description:* A block diagram of the six-zone color adjustment block.
Inputs:
* `rf_six_[H/S/V]_en`: control inputs that enable adjustment for each component, routed to the select lines of the stacked output multiplexers (`mux`).
* `HSV(11, 8, 8)`: input data. It is routed to:
  * "Index" block (specifically the `h` component)
  * The bypass input of the output multiplexers (`mux`)
  * The `+/x` adjustment block
Processing flow:
1. The `h` component of the HSV input is used by the "Index" block to generate an index.
2. The index is used to look up values in the "LUT Interpolation 2x180x(12x3)" block.
3. The LUT interpolation block outputs adjustment factors `Hf`, `Sf`, and `Vf`.
4. The `+/x` block applies these adjustment factors to the input `HSV(11, 8, 8)` data.
5. The stacked `mux` selects either the adjusted HSV values or the original bypass HSV values based on the `rf_six_[H/S/V]_en` signals.
6. The output is `HSV(11, 8, 8)`.

The LUT provides 360 degree H/S/V adjustment.

To translate Hue with one degree precision, truncate the 4 LSB of Hue (range 0 to $256 \times 24 = 6144$? No, the text says: `range 0 to × 180 = 384 dec`. Wait, `0 to 24 * 16 = 384`?
Let's read text: `range 0 to × 180 = 384 dec`. There might be a typo in the text.
Actually, if it's 384 entries: `360 / 384 = 0.9375` degree.
`0.9375 * 384 = 360` degrees.
So the LUT has 384 entries.
To index a 384-entry LUT with a hue value:
If hue is 10-bit?
If the range of Hue is `0 to 0x1800` (which is 6144).
If we truncate 4 LSB of Hue: `6144 >> 4 = 384`.
So the range of `hue >> 4` is `0 to 384`. That matches!
So the text `range 0 to × 180 = 384 dec` might have been `range 0 to 0x1800 >> 4 = 384 dec` or similar.
Let's write what is logical: "range 0 to 0x1800 (truncated by 4 LSBs gives 0 to 384 dec)".

The LUTs contain the final adjustment curve: `LUT_Hc`, `LUT_Sc`, `LUT_Vc` in S2.10 format.

#### Table 4-50 MDP PA six-zone hue equivalents

| Hue | 8-bit mode | 10-bit mode (6-zone block) | Degree |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 to 0x1800 | 0x600 | 0x600 << 2 | 0 – 360 |

Because the access to the hue, sat, and val LUTs share index, to save area, the three LUTs are combined into one physical RAM. Each entry holds a piece of the H, S, and V curve. The 384 entry LUT is split into two: one with all the odd and the other with all the even entries. Physically there are two RAMs, each 192 entry × 36-bit. Two consecutive entries, one from each LUT, are accessed for each valid pixel to be used for interpolation for the fractional step. The final adjustment is calculated as:

$$LUT_{final} = \frac{LUT_{upper} - LUT_{lower}}{16} \times hue[3:0] + LUT_{lower}$$

where $LUT_{lower} = LUT[hue \gg 4]$, $LUT_{upper} = LUT[(hue \gg 4) + 1]$.

The H, S, V adjustment values are added or multiplied to the input H, S, V, and clamped for the final adjusted value.

This block operates in 10-bit. Only the 8 MSBs of output go to the HSCI adjustment block. The 2 LSBs are unconnected.

When `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_OP_MODE.PA_EN = 1` and one of the 6-zone color component’s MASK is set (to 0x1), the latency through the block (without backpressure) is 4 pipe stages. When `PA_EN = 0` or all the MASK are 0, the latency is 1 pipe stage.
<!-- page 288 -->

The 6-zone LUT is accessed by auto-increment. To program the entire LUT:
1. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1.VALUE` and `SAT` register fields.
2. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0.HUE` register field (keep the rest of the fields at hardware default).
3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 for 383 times.

The write to `VALUE` and `SAT` register fields must occur before the write to `HUE` because the `HUE` write triggers the increment to the LUT write pointer.

For debug, 6-zone LUT supports software read:
1. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0` register fields:
   `VALUE_UPDATEn = 1`, `INDEX_UPDATE = 1`, `INDEX = <location to start reading>`.
2. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1` register.
3. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0` register.
4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 for 383 times.
5. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1` register.
6. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0` register.

The `VALUE` and `SAT` (`MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1` register) values must be read before `HUE` (`MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0` register) because the `HUE` read triggers the increment to the LUT read pointer. To avoid an undetermined read result, a write transaction specifying the starting read location must precede the read sequence.

To write, a similar sequence is followed:
1. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0` register fields:
   `VALUE_UPDATEn = 1`, `INDEX_UPDATE = 1`, `INDEX = <location to start writing>`.
2. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1.VALUE` and `SAT` register fields.
3. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0.HUE` register fields (return to hardware default).
4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 for 383 times.
5. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P1.VALUE` and `SAT` register fields.
6. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0.HUE` register field.
<!-- page 289 -->

#### Table 4-51 MDP PA six-zone adjustment registers

| Adjustment register | Field name | Bits | Description | Bit format/value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_SIX_ZONE_ADJ_CURVE_P0** | INDEX_UPDATE | 26 | Set this to 1 to point current LUT location to INDEX. The LUT location is auto-incremented on every value write or read, when there is no INDEX_UPDATE. Before every series of read, there must be an INDEX_UPDATE. | |
| | VALUE_UPDATEN | 25 | Set this to 0 to enable VALUE to be written to the current location of the LUT. | |

| | SAT_MIN | 7:0 | Saturation must be greater than or equal to this threshold to qualify for 6-zone adjustment. | U8 |

### HSCI block

When `MDP_VP_0_VIG_0_OP_MODE.PA_EN = 1` and at least one of the HSCI component’s MASK is set (1), latency in this block is six pipe stages without back pressure. When `PA_EN = 0` or all HSCI components’ MASK are 0, latency is one pipe stage without backpressure.
<!-- page 290 -->

Figure 4-37 is a simplified diagram of the HSCI block.

#### Figure 4-37 MDP PA HSCI diagram
*Description:* A simplified block diagram of the Hue, Saturation, Contrast, and Intensity (HSCI) adjustment blocks, showing Hue Adjust, Brightness (Intensity), and Contrast processing.
* **Hue Adjust:**
  * Inputs: `hue_adjust` and `iH` (input Hue).
  * The input Hue `iH` and the adjustment value `hue_adjust` are added together.
  * The result passes through a "Circular clip" block to produce the adjusted Hue output.
* **Brightness:**
  * Inputs: `rf_level` (brightness level control) and `iV` (input Value).
  * The input `iV` is routed to a "ROM 256x16 Interpolation" block and also bypassed to a multiplier.
  * The output of the interpolation block is multiplied by `rf_level`.
  * The result of this multiplication is then multiplied by the bypassed input `iV`.
  * The final result is clamped to produce the brightness-adjusted Value.
* **Contrast:**
  * Inputs: `rf_contrast` (contrast control) and the output from the Brightness block.
  * The input from the Brightness block is routed to a "ROM 256x16 Interpolation" block and also bypassed to a multiplier.
  * The output of the interpolation block is multiplied by `rf_contrast`.
  * The result of this multiplication is then multiplied by the bypassed input.
  * The final result is clamped to produce the contrast-adjusted Value output.

There is `HUE/SAT/VAL/CONT_MASK` to independently enable each component adjustment.

### Histogram

The MDP histogram in DSPP0 pipe provides histogram collection functionality for ACE (adaptive contrast enhancement) and/or CABL (Content Adaptive Back Light) applications.

The MDP histogram provides two 256 bins of V of HSV color (or maximum RGB). Both auto-increment access and direct access are supported.

Histogram is collected on the unadjust V component from the PA and is enabled by setting the `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_OP_MODE.HIST_EN` register bit to 1.

This histogram is a RAM of $2 \times 256 \text{ bins} \times 24\text{bits/bin}$.

Each bin number corresponds to the matching V value.

Histogram can be collected over a specified number for frames as specified in the `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_FRAME_COLLECTED` register.

The histogram block in the PA of the DSPP is shown in Figure 4-38.


<!-- page 291 -->

#### Figure 4-38: MDP PA histogram block
*Description:* A block diagram showing the "PA / Histogram" module. The module receives standard data input and a "Config" input. Inside, there is an "MDP Picture Adjustment" block and a "Hist" (Histogram) block. The input data enters the "MDP Picture Adjustment" block, where it undergoes sequential processing: "RGB to HSV", "Skin, Sky & Foliage Adj", "Six-Zone Adj", and "HSV Adj". After "HSV Adj", the data path splits: one path goes down to the "Hist" block (highlighted in yellow), and the other path continues through a "LUT" block followed by an "HSV to RGB" block to produce the final output.

#### Figure 4-39: MDP PA histogram control timing
*Description:* A timing diagram illustrating the interaction between hardware histogram collection and software read operations over successive frames (internal Frame Count 0 to 6).
- **START**: Initiates at the beginning of frame 0.
- **HW activity**: Alternates between using "table-0" (during frames 0, 2, 4) and "table-1" (during frames 1, 3). In frame 5, because the software has acquired a lock, the hardware cannot swap tables and continues to collect data using "table-0" (marked "Swap is not done, so HW continue to use 'current' table"). In frame 6, it resumes alternating and collects using "table-1".
- **DONE**: An interrupt occurs at each frame boundary.
- **SW read**: The software locks, reads, and unlocks the inactive table during frames.
  - Frame 1: Reads Table 0 (FCNT=0).
  - Frame 2: Reads Table 1 (FCNT=1).
  - Frame 3: Reads Table 0 (FCNT=2).
  - Frame 5: Reads Table 1 (FCNT=3) while holding the Lock. This active lock blocks the hardware swap ("HW swap is disabled").
  - Frame 6: Reads Table 0 (FCNT=5).

The programming sequence from the Histogram block includes the following steps:
1. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_OP_MODE.HIST_EN = 1`
2. Wait for `DSPP_0_DONE` interrupt in the `MDP_HIST_INTR_STATUS` register
3. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_COLLECT_CTL.LOCK = 1`
4. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_V_DATAn_BIN_i` register 256 times to read out all bins, optionally:
   a. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_SUM` register
   b. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_MIN_MAX` register
   c. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_FRAME_COLLECTED` register
   d. Read `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HSIT_SEL.HIST_SEL` register
5. Write `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_COLLECT_CTL.LOCK = 0` (release lock only after software is finished reading to prevent hardware from swapping the table in the middle of software read)
<!-- page 292 -->

Wait for another `DSPP_0_DONE` interrupt and repeat steps 3 to 6. If software fails to release the LOCK before the next two frame start (second SOF after the `DSPP_0_DONE`) following a `DSPP_0_DONE`, it misses the read of some frames and signals a non-contiguous `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_HIST_FRAME_COLLECTED.FRAME_NUM` register field value. As depicted in Figure 4-40, all the cases `rd0` read result of DB0. In case 1 to 3, `rd1` reads the DB1 result. Case 4 `rd1` skips DB1 result, and reads the DB2 result.

#### Figure 4-40: MDP PA histogram timing diagram
*Description:* This timing diagram illustrates four cases of software locking behavior relative to the Start of Frame (SOF) signal, the `HIST_DONE` interrupt, and double-buffer frames (DB0, DB1, DB2) and their blanking periods.
- **Signals**:
  - **SOF**: Pulse at the start of each active frame (DB0, DB1, DB2).
  - **HIST_DONE**: Arrow indicating the interrupt when hardware completes histogram collection at the end of each active frame (transition to blank).
  - **LOCK case1**: Lock is set during DB0 blank for `rd0`, released before DB1. Set during DB1 blank for `rd1`, released before DB2. `rd1` reads DB1.
  - **LOCK case2**: Lock is set during DB0 blank for `rd0`, held into DB1, and released before DB1 ends. Lock is set during DB1 blank for `rd1`. `rd1` reads DB1.
  - **LOCK case3**: Lock is set during DB0 blank for `rd0`, held through DB1 and DB1 blank, and released just as DB2 starts. Lock is set shortly after in DB2 for `rd1`. `rd1` reads DB1.
  - **LOCK case4**: Lock is set during DB0 blank for `rd0`, held through DB1, DB1 blank, and DB2, and only released during DB2 blank. Lock is set again in DB2 blank for `rd1`. `rd1` skips the DB1 result and reads DB2.

### SSPP RGB operation mode

The RGB0 and RGB1 pipelines include the following sub-modules:
* **Unpack module**: Responsible for sending data downstream the pipes in linear mode. The RGB pipelines support interleaved RGB formats only.
* **Inverse gamma correction/look-up table (IGC_LUT) module**.

The maximum performance of each RGB pipeline is 1 pixel/clock at the output.

The RGB pipeline functions are specified in the subset of SSPP operation mode registers, as described in sections *SSPP height and width* through *SSPP basic operation mode*. There are no additional functionalities for RGB pipelines.
<!-- page 293 -->

### SSPP DMA operation mode

The DMA0 pipeline includes the following sub-modules:
* **Unpack module**: Can operate in either block mode (when DMA0 is connected to the WB0 pipe for rotation) or in line mode (when DMA0 is connected to layer mixer 3).
* **Inverse gamma correction/look-up table (IGC_LUT) module**.

The maximum performance of the DMA pipeline is:
* 1 pixel/clock at the output to the layer mixer.
* 4 pixels/clock at the output to the WB0 pipe.

In line mode, the DMA pipe can only support RGB formats that do not require scaling, since there is no QSEED2 to scale or chroma up-sample.

In block mode, all formats are supported.

#### DMA line mode

In line mode the DMA has limited functionality. Line mode cannot YUV formats because it has neither the QSEED2 module (to perform Chroma upsampling) nor the CSC (to convert it to RGB format). DMA has no scaling capabilities. The source size fetched from memory must match the destination size fed to the layer mixer.

#### DMA block mode

In block mode the DMA0 output connects directly to the WB0 input.

The rotation function must be specified in two places:
* **Rotation write module**
* **Fetch module** (the rotation/flip parameters determine the fetch order)

To perform rotation in a DMA block mode, the rotation mode specified in the `ROT90` field of the `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` register must match the rotation mode specified in the `ROT_MODE` field of the `MDP_WB_0_DST_OP_MODE` register:

##### Table 4-52: MDP rotation register programming

| Register | Field | Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` | `ROT90` | Source image is to be rotated 90 degrees |
| `MDP_WB_0_DST_OP_MODE` | `ROT_MODE` | `0x0`: Rotate 0<br>`0x1`: Rotate 90 |

Because the writes occur in raster scan order, the fetch pattern differs and must be programmed using the `ROT90`-bit field.
<!-- page 294 -->

### SSPP inverse gamma correction (IGC) RAMs

During initialization, several RAMs must be programmed for correct translation from 8-bit to 12-bit space. The RAMs must be programmed before enabling the inverse gamma correction functionality through `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<n>_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE.IGC_LUT_EN` register field (where, pipe = ViG, RGB, or DMA, and n = 0 or 1).

The programming of RAMs is straightforward in that software just continually writes to one register space and hardware automatically increments the address to the RAM. So, to program the IGC RAMs for the ViG pipeline, software writes to each color component entry 256 times (depth of the RAM) to complete programming.

```c
for (i = 0; i <= IGC_LUT_RAM_DEPTH; i++) {
  MDP_VIG_IGC_COLOR0_RAM_LUTn = "color0 value";
  MDP_VIG_IGC_COLOR1_RAM_LUTn = "color1 value";
  MDP_VIG_IGC_COLOR2_RAM_LUTn = "color2 value";
}
```

The initialization programming is required for all RAMs used in the MDP hardware.

These RAMs are used as look-up tables by the hardware. Therefore, if MDP is power collapsed then these RAMs must be placed in memory retention state. The datapath RAMs are controlled differently than configuration RAMs to save power and prevent software from repeating a lengthy initialization routine each time MDP wakes up from a power collapsed state.

The `IGC_LUT_EN` register field is unique for every instance of IGC. The `IGC_COLORx_RAM_LUTn` register is shared across instances of the same type of source / DSPP pipe. For example, there are two instances of type RGB pipe. Both IGC instances among the two RGB pipes are controlled by the same `MPD_RGB_IGC_COLORx_RAM_LUTn` registers. There are independent registers for each color0, 1, 2. Alpha (color3) has no IGC table, it is passed straight through as an 8-bit value.

To completely program the IGC RAM of a particular color, software can write to `MPD_VIG_IGC_COLORx_RAM_LUTn.VALUE` register field 256 times (Note: text says 265, but loop says `IGC_LUT_RAM_DEPTH` which is likely 256) as illustrated above. Every bit of the `MPD_VIG_IGC_COLORx_RAM_LUTn.VIG_MASK` register field controls a particular ViG instance. If the `VIG_MASK` bit is set, the IGC RAM of that ViG instance is not updated. By default, all the `MASK` bits are unset, so that RAM update is broadcast to every instance of ViG. This is to save software time from having to update each RAM instance individually if all of the RAMs of the same color are to have the same value. The IGC RAM for each color must still be programmed individually.

The `INDEX` field in the same register allows for the update to a specific location of the RAM. The `INDEX_UPDATE` register field must be set to allow for the `INDEX` to be updated to the RAM. The `VALUE_UPDATEn` field must be kept at 0 to allow `VALUE` to be updated to the RAM. Value and index can be updated at the same time if `VALUE_UPDATEn=0` and `INDEX_UPDATE=1`.

> [!NOTE]
> The index update feature is not fully verified for MDP. Software relies only on auto-increment method for the IGC LUT update.

Software must not attempt to read the IGC LUT register as this auto-increments the IGC LUT pointer. This displaces the pointer to the location shown in `INDEX` register field.
<!-- page 295 -->

Any write following it writes from `INDEX+1` location. Software reset restores the IGC LUT pointer back to 0, but the existing IGC LUT content is not cleared.

#### IGC RAMs usage

The IGC block at the end of the source pipes is used to convert sRGB, Rec601, and Rec709 gamma corrected input streams, to linear color space.

> [!NOTE]
> This conversion is sometimes skipped, but it results in poor blending results. The IGC block must be enabled and programmed.

An incorrect guess at the incoming stream gamma results in better blending results than blending in the non-corrected non-linear space. In MDP, there are multiple conversions between linear and non-linear color spaces, and skipping any of these conversions cause significant artifacts downstream.

sRGB, Rec601, and PC/Internet are usually encoded with the sRGB gamma correction, while video is usually encoded with Rec709. If the source of the stream is completely unknown, then sRGB would be the fallback assumption.

Driver provides a mechanism to quickly load either of these tables into the IGC.

### Layer mixer

The layer mixer configuration defines the blending operation for a given datapath. The layer mixer operates in linear color space, so the corresponding IGC must be programmed correctly to linearize (de-gamma) the input surfaces.

The input layer may or may not carry an alpha component. If alpha component is not present for a layer, the blending block assigns a pre-programmed, constant alpha value to every pixel on that layer. This assigned alpha value may or may not be used in the blending process, depending on the alpha blending modes selected.

If a layer mixer is used, the register `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>` (where, id = 0 to 4 is the selected data path, and m = 0 or 3 is the selected layer mixer) must be programmed to non-0 and define the connections to the particular layer mixer. This register fully defines the layer mixer connections for the blending operation of a given layer mixer X. This register must be left with its hardware default, if the given layer mixer is not used. It configures the crossbar at the input of the layer mixer.
* The layer mixer can blend up to 6 layers
* If a cursor is enabled for the given layer mixer, cursor is **ALWAYS** the topmost layer
<!-- page 297 -->

* Although programming of the cursor is allowed at any stage, the hardware crossbar implementation restricts the cursor to topmost layer.
* If border is enabled, border is **ALWAYS** the base layer.
* The rest of the source pipes (RGB, ViG, DMA) can occupy any one of remaining available layers.
* It is strictly prohibited to program more than one source to the same layer unless the source pipes are in source split configuration.
* It is strictly prohibited to connect a source to multiple layer mixers at the same time unless the source pipe is configured in source split configuration.

The layer mixer contains a cascade of $n$ blenders (see Figure 4-41 for an example with 5 blenders).

#### Figure 4-41: MDP layer mixer blenders
*Description:* A block diagram showing the cascaded arrangement of blenders in the layer mixer.
- At the top, a **Crossbar** block routes inputs through a clocked stage containing multiple FIFOs.
- The blender stages are cascaded sequentially:
  - **Blend0** receives background input $B_0$ and foreground input $F_0$, producing an output.
  - **Blend1** receives the output of Blend0 as background and $F_1$ as foreground.
  - **Blend2** receives the output of Blend1 as background and $F_2$ as foreground.
  - **Blend3** receives the output of Blend2 as background and $F_3$ as foreground.
  - **Blend4** receives the output of Blend3 as background and $F_4$ as foreground, producing the final output labeled "to IGC" and "Out".
- Each block is labeled "2 layers blend and color key", has its own internal FIFO, and is clocked by `MDP_CLK`.

Each blender takes in two source surfaces, one being background, one being foreground, and produces one blended output surface. The blending configuration of blend0 to blend3 are described by a set of identical registers.

The color3 output (alpha) of the blender requires no blending.

The output alpha is the unmodified alpha from one of the two sources based on `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_OP_MODE.BLENDn_COLOR3_OUT` setting; either the foreground alpha or the background alpha can be propagated to the next layer.

The derivation for the other color components (color0 to 2) involves a blending equation:
<!-- page 298 -->

The `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_OP` register (where $x = 0$ to $3$) describes the blending operation.

The register field prefixed by "BG" determines how to derive $\alpha_b$; similarly, the field prefixed by "FG" determines $\alpha_f$.

First, the `BG_ALPHA_SEL` field determines the start alpha value, $\alpha_{alpha\_sel}$.

Foreground can pick the background alpha to start and vice versa to achieve per-pixel alpha blending, or a constant value can be chosen to achieve constant alpha blending.

The constant can be selected from one of the `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_FG_ALPHA` or `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_BG_ALPHA` registers.

Taking the foreground $\alpha_f$ as example, the maximum transformation that can be applied hereafter is:

$$\alpha_f = \frac{255 - \text{round}\left[ \frac{(255 - \alpha_{f_{alpha\_sel}}) \times (K + 1)}{256} \right]}{255}$$

(if there is no color keying).

The same transformation process applies to background but using BG configuration settings.
* If `FG_INV_ALPHA_SEL = 1`, $(255 - \alpha_{alpha\_sel})$ is applied. Otherwise, the alpha is kept as $\alpha_{alpha\_sel}$.
* If `FG_MOD_ALPHA = 1`, the multiplication with $(K+1)$ is applied.
* $K$ is the value stored in `BLEND<x>_FG_ALPHA`.
* If `FG_INV_MOD_ALPHA = 1`, the result up to this point is subtracted from 255.

> [!NOTE]
> The operations are in terms of 255 range (for 8-bit $\alpha$ and $K$) first, and are divided by 255 at the end to normalize to 1.

If `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_OP.TRANSP_EN = 1`, the alpha derived from the above equation might be overridden. The decision is based on the pixel color values and the color keying range bounded by the `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_FG_TRANSP_LOW0/1` and `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BLEND<x>_FG_TRANSP_HIGH0/1` registers.

If all three color components of the foreground are within the (inclusive) range, the foreground pixel becomes transparent and background becomes opaque.

Foreground $\alpha_f$ becomes 0 while background $\alpha_b$ automatically becomes 1.

On the contrary, if background has `BLEND_TRANSP_EN` and the background pixel falls within its color keying range, background $\alpha_b$ becomes 0 while foreground $\alpha_f$ becomes 1.
<!-- page 299 -->

If both foreground and background fall within their respective color keying range, it is treated the same as foreground transparent, background opaque; meaning that $\alpha_f$ becomes 0 while background $\alpha_b$ becomes 1.

If neither the foreground nor the background matches their respective color key range, the alpha calculated from the transformation formula is the final alpha for the blending.

The configuration for blend5 (assuming 6 layers blending) is a little more specific than the rest of the blenders. Its foreground alpha configuration is defined by the CURSOR registers. Its background alpha does not have register programmability; instead, its settings are implied by the foreground CURSOR settings in the `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_CURSOR_BLEND_CONFIG` and `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_CURSOR_BLEND_PARAM` registers.

The following is the equation for background and foreground blending alpha:

$$\alpha_b = 1 - \alpha_{alpha\_sel}$$
$$\alpha_f = \alpha_{alpha\_sel}$$

(if there is no color keying).

The only software programmability in the equation is the $\alpha_{alpha\_sel}$.

The `BLEND_ALPHA_SEL` register field determines the $\alpha_{alpha\_sel}$ for both the background and foreground.

If `BLEND_TRANSP_EN = 1`, the alpha derived from the above equation might be overridden. The decision is based on the pixel color values and the color keying range bounded by `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_CURSOR_BLEND_TRANSP_LOW0/1` and `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_CURSOR_BLEND_TRANSP_HIGH0/1` register settings.

If all three color components of the cursor are within the (inclusive) range, the cursor pixel becomes transparent and background becomes opaque. Foreground $\alpha_f$ becomes 0 while background $\alpha_b$ automatically becomes 1. If the cursor pixel does not match the cursor color key range, the alpha calculated from the transformation formula is the final alpha for the blending. The background to blend5 does not go through color keying match. It is either opaque or multiplied by $\alpha_b$.
<!-- page 300 -->

Table 4-53 enumerates the different blending possibilities within the layer mixer.

#### Table 4-53: MDP layer mixer blending equations

Blending formula: $D_{i+1} = K_S \times F + K_D \times B_i$

| Pre-multiplied $\alpha$ | Alpha Value | Inverse Blending | $K_D$ | $K_S$ |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Non pre-multiplied $\alpha$** | Constant $\alpha$ | N | $1-C$ | $C$ |
| | | Y | $C$ | $1-C$ |
| | BG Per Pixel $\alpha$ | N | $1-\alpha_B(i,j)$ | $\alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | | Y | $\alpha_B(i,j)$ | $1-\alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | FG Per Pixel $\alpha$ | N | $1-\alpha_F(i,j)$ | $\alpha_F(i,j)$ |
| | | Y | $\alpha_F(i,j)$ | $1-\alpha_F(i,j)$ |
| | Modulation $\alpha$ (Const * BG Per Pixel $\alpha$) | N | $1-C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ | $C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | | Y | $C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ | $1-C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | Modulation $\alpha$ (Const * FG Per Pixel $\alpha$) | N | $1-C \times \alpha_F(i,j)$ | $C \times \alpha_F(i,j)$ |
| | | Y | $C \times \alpha_F(i,j)$ | $1-C \times \alpha_F(i,j)$ |
| **Pre-multiplied $\alpha$** | Constant $\alpha$ | N | $1-C$ | $1$ |
| | | Y | $1$ | $1-C$ |
| | BG Per Pixel $\alpha$ | N | $1-\alpha_B(i,j)$ | $1$ |
| | | Y | $1$ | $1-\alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | FG Per Pixel $\alpha$ | N | $1-\alpha_F(i,j)$ | $1$ |
| | | Y | $1$ | $1-\alpha_F(i,j)$ |
| | Modulation $\alpha$ (Const * BG Per Pixel $\alpha$) | N | $1-C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ | $1$ |
| | | Y | $1$ | $1-C \times \alpha_B(i,j)$ |
| | Modulation $\alpha$ (Const * FG Per Pixel $\alpha$) | N | $1-C \times \alpha_F(i,j)$ | $1$ |
| | | Y | $1$ | $1-\alpha_F(i,j)$ |

### Layer level connection

> [!NOTE]
> The `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>` registers (where $m = 0$ or $3$) define the input connections for the blending operation for the layer mixer $m$, for the selected data path ($id = 0$ to $4$).

The control value required to describe the level to which a given input source is connected is described in the table below.




<!-- page 301 -->

| Control value | Layer connection |
|---|---|
| 0x0 | No Connection |
| 0x1 | Base Layer |
| 0x2 | Stage 0’s FG |
| 0x3 | Stage 1’s FG |
| 0x4 | Stage 2’s FG |
| 0x5 | Stage 3’s FG |
| 0x6 | Stage 4’s FG |
| 0x7 | Stage 5’s FG |
| 0x8 | Stage 6’s FG |
| 0x9 | Stage 7’s FG |
| 0xa | Stage 8’s FG |
| 0xb | Stage 9’s FG |
| 0xc | Stage 10’s FG |

The fields that must be programmed with the appropriate control value to describe the level to which a particular input pipe is connected are spread across multiple registers in order to maintain backwards compatibility. The required fields are listed in the table below.

| Source pipes | Control register fields |
|---|---|
| ViG_0 | `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>.VIG_0_OUT` |
| RGB_0 | `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>.RGB_0_OUT` |
| RGB_1 | `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>.RGB_1_OUT` |
| DMA_0 | `MDP_CTL_<id>_LAYER_<m>.DMA_0_OUT` |

### Base layer

If the layer mixer is used, the base layer size must be properly defined and all layers above must be confined within the (inclusive) base size, specified by `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_OUT_SIZE` (m = 0 or 3) register.

The hardware cannot support blend out of base layer position or blend any negative coordinate.

If border is not connected, the `OUT_SIZE` must match the destination size of the surface that is being selected as the base.

If border is connected, the `OUT_SIZE` defines the border size with border color defined by the `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BORDER_COLOR_0` and `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_BORDER_COLOR_1` registers.

Except for the `TRANSP_HIGH` and `TRANSP_LOW`, all of the layer mixer blending registers are double-buffered. Because the transparency range is static throughout many frames, it is not
<!-- page 302 -->

double-buffered. For the double-buffered registers, set the `MDP_CTL_<id>_FLUSH.LAYER_MIXER_<m>` register field to allow the double-buffered value to be propagate on the next vsync or the next `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` in the non-active timing display output.

> [!NOTE]
> The requirement, that base layer should be the same size as the output size, is no longer supported. This essentially frees up a layer to blend because the base layer can be any size. Hardware feeds border color anytime the base layer does not occupy the entire output space.

### Flush requirement

When changing layers, there is usually a data path (CTL) flush, as well as a layer mixer (LM) flush, since the layer configuration will need to be updated. There is a requirement to flush the layer mixer and the CTL flush to have the connectivity properly pipelined by hardware.

The table below enumerates the full requirement with the subtle hardware requirement, outlined in the first row.

| Use case | Required flush |
|---|---|
| Layer mixer connectivity | CTL flush: YES<br>LM flush: NO |
| Layer mixer registers only, just changing blending registers | CTL flush: NO<br>LM flush: YES |

### Gamma correction (GC)

The gamma correction parameters must be programmed before enabling the inverse gamma correction for 12 to 8 bit conversions (occurring after the blending in the layer mixer).

#### Gamma correction ARLUT

A linear segment approximation is implemented in the ARLUT.

The parameters are not double buffered. To trade accuracy for area saving, instead of mapping the GC curve to 212 entry x 8bit LUT, the hardware implements a 16 segment, piece-wise linear interpolation of the GC curve. Each segment is defined by programmable start x coordinate, slope and offset for each of the R, G, B components. The 8bit alpha component is simply passed straight through.

Each GC ARLUT instance has a dedicated register programming.

##### Table 4-54 MDP gamma correction ARLUT registers

| Register | Function |
|---|---|
| `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_GC_ARLUT_<RED,GREEN,BLUE>_STARTX_n` | start |
| `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_GC_ARLUT_<RED,GREEN,BLUE>_SLOPE_n` | slope |
| `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_<m>_GC_ARLUT_<RED,GREEN,BLUE>_OFFSET_n` | offset |
<!-- page 303 -->

Hardware has three LUTs (16 entry) to individually store start x, slope and offset.
Software writes 16 times to each of these registers to fully program the 16 segment parameters.
Hardware automatically increment the entry of the LUT for every write trigger to these registers.
Software can read the current position of the write pointer by reading the `SEGMENT` field in the registers in Table 4-54.

> [!NOTE]
> Software can not read the LUT content.

> [!NOTE]
> LUT value is not retained upon power collapse. When coming out of power collapse, the GC LUT must be re-programmed.

## 4.1.1.3.8 MDP destination surface processing pipe (DSPP)

### DSPP configuration

The DSPP0 is the back end processing pipe that is used to process the data destined for the display interface. The output of the DSPP is written into the ping-pong buffers.

The DSPP0 pipeline includes the following sub-modules:
* **Picture adjustment (SPA/CE) module**.
* **Inverse gamma correction/look-up table (IGC_LUT) module**.
* **Polynomial Color Correction (PCC) module**, which has two main functions:
  * To compensate for factors that affect display color accuracy in LCD display panels, such as mismatches between RGB matching functions, mismatches with the target white point, and color cross talk between RGB channels.
  * To compensate for spectral shifts that occur due to the backlight modulation.
* **Dither module**, which implements the image dithering operation to reduce display artifacts when output is in reduced RGB color depth.

The throughput on the input and output of the DSPP pipeline is 1 pixel/clock.

Complete the following steps to program destination surface processing pipes:
1. Configure the picture adjustment and histogram (same as SSPP, see Section ViG picture adjustments (PA)).
2. Configure the inverse gamma correction (same as SSPP, see Section SSPP inverse gamma correction (IGC) RAMs).
3. Configure the polynomial color correction (PCC).
4. Configure the panel correction.
5. Configure dithering.
<!-- page 305 -->

### DSPP polynomial color correction (PCC)

The Polynomial Color Correction (PCC) block compensates for color cross talk on a display.

It is a 3x11 matrix multiplication. The first three terms of this matrix are the same as the standard 3x3 matrix multiplication used in the color space conversion block. The remaining terms allow for adjustments based on the RxR, GxG, BxB, RxG, RxB and RxGxB products.

To maintain unity (output = input), program the R, G and B coefficients to 1 (0x8000) and all other registers to 0. The MDP hardware expects the following Polynomial Color Correction (PCC) coefficients and associated register programming:
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_CONSTANT_COEFF`, where c = <0, 1, 2>
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_R_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_G_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_B_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RR_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RG_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RB_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_GG_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_BG_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_BB_COEFF`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RGB_COEFF_0`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RGB_COEFF_1`

These registers are not double buffered.

Value changes in programming of above registers takes immediate effect in the PCC hardware module synchronous to the input clock to the PCC block.

The hardware and software interface define the color components in terms of 0, 1, 2, and 3. These values are replaced with their corresponding color component (see Table 4-55).

#### Table 4-55 MDP PCC color component conversion

| Component | Graphic Format Meaning | Video Format Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| COLOR 0 | GREEN (G) | LUMA (Y) |
| COLOR 1 | BLUE (B) | Cb |
| COLOR 2 | RED (R) | Cr |
| COLOR 3 | ALPHA (A) | ALPHA (A) |
<!-- page 306 -->

Table 4-56 shows the mapping between plane and color.

#### Table 4-56 MDP PCC plane/color mapping

| Plane | Color |
|---|---|
| Plane0 | Red (R) |
| Plane1 | Green (G) |
| Plane2 | Blue (B) |

These registers can only be changed during startup and/or blanking periods, when no pixel processing is occurring.

The `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_OP_MODE.PCC_EN` register bit enables PCC, which is double buffered. The `PCC_EN` bit can be cleared (disabled) during programming of the PCC coefficients. It can be set (enabled) after PCC coefficients programming is complete.

The following registers must be interpreted as:
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RGB_COEFF_0`:
  * Sign (MSB) + 7 fractional bits of a S1.39 format
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_PCC_PLANEc_RGB_COEFF_1`:
  * Remaining 32 fractional bits of a S1.39 format

### DSPP panel correction (PC)

The panel correction (PC) block is a duplication of the gamma correction block from the SSPP (see Section Gamma correction (GC)).

The PC block has two functions:
* Correct panel behaviors
* Convert the linear output of the gamut PCC block to gamma corrected output

If no panel correction is required, program this block to apply either an sRGB or Rec709 gamma correction, depending on the desired output color space.

For a sRGB gamma programming, see Section Gamma correction use. For programming a Rec709 gamma, use the following values:
