### DSPP dithering

Hardware expects the following dither matrix coefficients and associated register programming:
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_MATRIX_ROW0`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_MATRIX_ROW1`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_MATRIX_ROW2`
* `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_MATRIX_ROW3`

These registers are not double buffered.

Changes to registers takes immediate effect in the dither hardware module synchronous to the input clock to the dither block.

The hardware and software interface define the color components in terms of 0, 1, 2, and 3. These values are replaced with their corresponding color component (see Table 4-57).

#### Table 4-57 MDP dithering color component conversion

| Component | Graphic format | Video format |
|---|---|---|
| COLOR 0 | GREEN (G) | LUMA (Y) |
| COLOR 1 | BLUE (B) | Cb |
| COLOR 2 | RED (R) | Cr |
| COLOR 3 | ALPHA (A) | ALPHA (A) |
<!-- page 308 -->

For the `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_BITDEPTH` register, only components 0, 1, and 2 can be programmed with color mapping as shown in Figure 4-57. Component 3 (Alpha) does not require dithering.

This register is not double buffered.

These registers can only be changed during startup and/or blanking periods, when no pixel processing is occurring.

The `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_OP_MODE.DST_DITHER_EN` register (double buffered) bit enables dithering. The `DST_DITHER_EN` bit can be cleared (disabled) during programming of the dither matrix coefficients. It can be set (enabled) after the dither-matrix-coefficient programming is complete. The effective number of output bits (reduced bits) is defined in the `MDP_VP_0_DSPP_0_DITHER_BITDEPTH` register fields.

### Writeback (WB) pipelines configuration

The writeback (WB) pipelines include the logic needed to interface with DMA RD engine or layer mixer. The received frame is processed by color space transformation modules (color space conversion, chroma down sampling, dithering, and rotation) and sent to the writeback engine. The WB engine packs the data into 128-bits words (beats) and collects them in bursts (up to 8 beats) for each active memory plane. The data bursts are then send to the VBIF to be written into the memory. The MDP includes two writeback modules, WB0 and WB2, each having its own VBIF write client.

WB0 receives data traffic from DMA0 pipeline (block path). The block path color space transformation consists of a Rotator module. This allows data fetched by the DMA read engine to be written back in the memory after being rotated.

WB2 receives data traffic from the layer mixer 3 (line path). The line path allows color space conversion and/or chroma down-sampling to be performed on the received data, before it is written back into memory.
<!-- page 309 -->

#### Figure 4-42: MDP writeback architecture

*Description:* The diagram illustrates two writeback paths, WB2 (Line Path) and WB0 (Block Path), connecting to the VBIF Interface:
* **WB2 (Line Path)**:
  * Input comes from the Layer Mixer Interface (1 pixel/clock, 32-bit width).
  * Passes through the **CSC** (Color Space Conversion) block (32-bit output) and the **Chroma Down** (Chroma Down-sampling) block (32-bit output).
  * Feeds into the **WB 2** block containing **WB Packer** (128-bit output), **WB Buffer** (128-bit output), and **WB DMA WR** (Writeback DMA Write).
  * Finally outputs Address (32-bit) and Data (128-bit) to the **VBIF Interface**.
* **WB0 (Block Path)**:
  * Input comes from the DMA Interface (4 pixel/clock, 128-bit width).
  * Passes through the **Rotator Matrix** block (128-bit output).
  * Feeds into the **WB 0** block containing **WB Packer** (128-bit output), **WB Buffer** (128-bit output), and **WB DMA WR** (Writeback DMA Write).
  * Finally outputs Address (32-bit) and Data (128-bit) to the **VBIF Interface**.

#### Table 4-58 MDP writeback clients, source, and color path transformation

| Writeback client | Traffic source | Color path transformation |
|---|---|---|
| WB0 | DMA interface (Block path) | Rotation |
| WB2 | Layer mixer interface (Line path) | Color space conversion (CSC) and chroma down-sampling |

The writeback pipe collects data into 128-bit words (beats) and consolidates them into bursts (up to 8 beats) for each active memory plane.
<!-- page 310 -->

#### Table 4-59 MDP writeback color formats

| Color format | Output Pixel Depth | Output Format Permutations |
|---|---|---|
| A/RGB interleaved | 16BPP | RGB565, BGR565, ARGB1555, RGBA5551, ABGR5551, BGRA5551, ARGB4444, RGBA4444, ABGR4444, BGRA4444 |
| | 24BPP | RGB888, BGR888 |
| | 32BPP | ARGB8888, RGBA8888, ABGR8888, BGRA8888 |
| YUV interleaved | 32BPP | INTL_YUYV, INTL_YVYU, INTL_UYYV, INTL_VYUY |
| A/YUV pseudo planar | YUV422 | PSDO_YUV_H2V1, PSDO_YVU_H2V1, PSDO_YUV_H1V2, PSDO_YVU_H1V2, PSDO_YUVA_H2V1, PSDO_YVUA_H2V1, PSDO_YUVA_H1V2, PSDO_YVUA_H1V2 |
| | YUV420 | PSDO_YUV_420, PSDO_YVU_420, PSDO_YUVA_420, PSDO_YVUA_420 |
| YUV planar | YUV422 | PLNR_YUV_H2V1, PLNR_YUV_H1V2 |
| | YUV420 | PLNR_YUV_420 |

The MDP DMA write engine operates in two modes: line mode and block mode.

#### Table 4-60 MDP DMA write engine operating modes

| Mode | Start of line address calculation (addr = ) |
|---|---|
| Line | `dstc_addr + line_count × dstc_ystride` |
| Block | `dstc_addr + (128 × block_index_y + line_count) × dstc_ystride + block_index_x × bpp` |
| <all other bursts> | `addr + burst_length` |

Complete the following steps to program the writeback pipes:
1. For the writeback block path (WB0 pipe only), configure the rotator.
2. For the writeback line path (WB2 pipe only), configure the color space conversions.
3. For the writeback line path (WB2 pipe only), configure the chroma down-sampling.

### WB rotator module

Source frames are fetched and partitioned into blocks by DMA read, then send to the rotator module.

#### Table 4-61 MDP WB rotator maximum block input size

| Rotation | Maximum block input (High tier) | Maximum block input (Low tier) |
|---|---|---|
| 0° / 90° | 128x128 | 64x64 |


<!-- page 311 -->
Rotated blocks are reassembled into frames (in the memory) by DMA write.

DMA read is aware of the rotation (0°/90°) and fetches the blocks in the order required by DMA write (writeback writes data in normal scan order).

The rotator module supports multiple color formats:
* ARGB (32bpp)
* ARGB (16bpp)
* RGB (24bpp)
* RGB (16bpp)
* YCrCb (4:2:2)
* YCrCb (4:2:0)

The rotator engine processes 4 pixels/clock, for a maximum bandwidth of 4256 MB/sec (Fclk=266 MHz).

### Table 4-62 MDP WB rotator configuration registers

| Field name | Register | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ROT_EN | MDP_WB_\<id\>_DST_OP_MODE, where \<id\> = 1 to 4 refers to the used control data path. | Rotator Enable.<br>0x0. Rotator disabled.<br>0x1. Rotator enabled. |
| ROT_MODE | MDP_WB_\<id\>_DST_OP_MODE | Rotator Mode.<br>0x0. Rotator executes a rotation with 0°.<br>0x1. Rotator executes a rotation with 90°. |
| ROT_BLOCK_SIZE | MDP_WB_\<id\>_DST_OP_MODE | Block Size.<br>0x0. Maximum block size is 64x64 pixels.<br>0x1. Maximum block size is 128x128 pixels. |
| DST_CHROMA_SAMP | MDP_WB_\<id\>_DST_FORMAT | Destination Chroma Sampling Format.<br>0x0. RGB<br>0x1. YUV422 H2V1<br>0x2. YUV422 H1V2<br>0x3. YUV420<br>0x4 – 0x7. Not used |

* When ROT_EN = 0x0, all traffic is sent to the downstream block (through bypass mux, equivalent to a rotation with 0°). ROT_EN = 0x1 only when a rotation with 0° / 90° is performed.
* When ROT_MODE = 0x0 (rotation with 0°), the dimensions of the input block are unchanged (if the input block is 75x67, the input block has 75 rows and 67 columns, then the output block is 75x67).
* When ROT_MODE = 0x1 (rotation with 90°), the dimensions of the input block are swapped (if the input block is 75x67, then the output block is 67x75).
<!-- page 312 -->
* Source/destination frame sizes (SRC_W/DST_W and SRC_W/DST_H register fields) must be programmed accordingly.
* Also source/destination color format (SRC_CHROMA_SAMP/DST_CHROMA_SAMP register fields) might differ when a 90° rotation is performed (YUV422_H2V1 becomes YUV_H1V2 after a 90° rotation).

### WB color space converter (CSC)

The writeback color space converter (CSC) converts data from RGB to YUV formats or from YUV to RGB, based on programming. The conversion translates fully sampled values between one color space and another.

Write to the following registers to program the CSC matrix coefficients:
* MDP_WB_\<id\>_CSC_MATRIX_COEFF_\<n\>, where n = 0,1,2,3,4, and id = 0 to 4
* MDP_WB_\<id\>_CSC_COMP\<n\>_PRECLAMP, where n = 0,1,2
* MDP_WB_\<id\>_CSC_COMP\<n\>_PREBIAS, where n = 0,1,2
* MDP_WB_\<id\>_CSC_COMP\<n\>_POSTCLAMP, where n = 0,1,2
* MDP_WB_\<id\>_CSC_COMP\<n\>_POSTBIAS, where n = 0,1,2

### WB chroma down-sampling

Chroma down sampling decreases the Chroma sampling in YUV formats only. It is performed after converting RGB data to YUV. A fully sampled YUV of a 16x16 image has 16 Y values and 16 UV components. The Chroma down sample decreases the UV components to 16 Y and 8 UV components.

Reducing UV components slightly degrades the image quality. However, fewer bytes to transfer equates to less bandwidth, lower power use, and higher performance. Chroma down sampling receives YUV444 traffic (fully sampled), subsamples color 1 / 2 planes (CbCr components) to generate YUV422/YUV420 data.

### Table 4-63 MDP WB chroma down-sampling output formats

| Output format | Horizontal Averaging | Horizontal Dropping | Vertical Averaging | Vertical Dropping |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| YUV422 | x | x | | |
| YUV420 | x | x | x | x |

Chroma down sampling supports a maximum line length of 2048 pixels. It can process 1 pixel/clock.

> [!NOTE]
> Chroma down sampling only applies to YUV formats. Enabling Chroma down sampling on other formats will cause the MDP to hang.
<!-- page 313 -->
### WFD writeback engine

The WFD writeback engine is designated as WB2 pipe within the MDP. This is in contrast with the rotator writeback engine, which have a designation of WB0. The difference between WFD (WB2) and WB0, is that WB2 supports raster image write back (line mode write back) only.

The WFD data flow in the display engine is illustrated in Wireless display (WFD) writeback. The MDP compositing engine creates a composed image. The composed image is delivered to the WFD writeback engine to write back to DDR memory. The writeback image is intended for WFD (wireless display).

In concurrent writeback mode, the writeback image is intended to be used by display engine for the subsequent display. It is a power saving feature for static display. Single compositing pass is required for the static image and subsequent display can pick up the image concurrent writeback during the compositing video frame.

### WFD writeback coordinate system

The WFD writeback is a 2D operation. It writes a 2D image into DDR memory. The DDR memory region that store the writeback image is called a surface. A surface is defined by a memory offset and a pitch. A pitch is defined as the maximum width (in bytes) of a 2D image line (subject to memory alignment rules).

The 2D writeback image coordinate system origin is the top left corner. The image write sequence is horizontally from left to right and vertically top to bottom. The unit of the x coordinate is a pixel and unit of y coordinate is a line. The image may not cover the entire surface. The region that image covered in a surface is called ROI (region of interest). The ROI is defined by the origin of the ROI (DST_X, DST_Y) and the width and height. Figure 4-43 shows the writeback coordinate system and its associated parameters.

The translation of image x,y coordinate into DDR memory address depends on pixel format (color depth, packing etc.), as well as if the surface is linear or tiled. For linear surface the memory address is a linear equation of x, y coordinate. Tiled surfaces are not supported by the MDP in this SoC. For writeback surfaces, there could be either single plane write for fully sampled pixels or two plane write for UV sampled pixel format such as NV12. For two plane write, each plane has its own memory offset and pitch but share a single dst_x,dst_y, dst_w and dst_h. Figure 4-43 shows a single plane write back surface parameters. Figure 4-44 shows dual plane write back surface parameters.

### WFD writeback programming sequence

In order to program WFD writeback to write an image to memory, complete the following steps:
* Configure destination formats
* Configure the width/height and offset_x/y of the region of interest (ROI).
* Configure the base addresses and strides
* Configure operation mode (linear)

Table 4-66 shows the write back configuration registers definition.

`MDP_WB_<id>_DST_OP_MODE.ROT_EN = 0`, where id = 0 to 4 is the selected control data path.

### WFD writeback traffic shaper

Traffic shaper is provided in WFD to limit the writeback bandwidth to the targeted bandwidth. The traffic shaper can be enabled by programming the following register field:

`MDP_TRAFFIC_SHAPER_WR_CLIENT_2.EN=1`

The WFD traffic shaper smooths out the WFD DDR write bandwidth during the entire frame. This is suitable for WFD running in non-real time mode, where the writeback bandwidth need to be controlled to a specific target in order to not affect the MDP real time client operation.

### WFD VBIF write client

Each WB pipeline has its own VBIF write client.

In order to ensure there are no gaps in the outgoing data transfer to AXI/VBIF interface, all write data must available before initiating an access.
<!-- page 320 -->
## 4.1.1.3.9 MDP display interface

### Ping-pong logic

The ping-pong module includes the logic to interface directly with the upstream DSPP blocks, and the downstream display interface block through the tear check logic. The input stream to the ping-pong from the DSPP (1 pixel/cycle) is line-based video/graphics data of 8 bits per color component (BPC), that is 24-bit (RGB/YCbCr 888) per cycle. The ping-pong buffer input write module packs the stream data into 128-bit words and into the line buffers. The ping-pong output buffer read module unpacks the line buffer words into 2 pixels (that is, 48 bits) per cycle and generates the output stream. This module serves as the line buffer for the MDP output display interface.

The ping-pong module has its own register settings to specify video (or graphics) width and height, which serve to generate the EOL/EOF associated with each output stream. The ping-pong also pads one pixel to the last cycle of each line, when the input pixel per line is an odd number (as opposed to even number), due to the 2 pixel per cycle output data width.

The ping-pong also generates the frame done interrupt (PING_PONG_0_DONE), when the stream for the whole frame is transferred to the downstream block.

The ping-pong uses internal RAM (6 instances of 256 x 64 bits each), which supports up to a 2048-pixels/line video stream with 2-line capability.

A read and write watermark and control logic is implemented to prevent underflow/overflow.

The ping-pong module supports both a pull and push output modes:
* **Pull mode**: Normally, whenever there is a 128-bit (about 5 input pixels) word accumulated from the input (that is, the write side of the ping-pong buffer), the block is ready to output stream at 2 pixels/cycle to the downstream block. When the line width is equal to or less than 5 pixels, the output stream is ready whenever the input EOL arrives in the line buffer, where the whole line pixels are padded to form one 128-bit word in the line buffer.
* **Push mode**: The push mode differs from the pull mode when the output is ready for the downstream block. For the push mode, the ping-pong is ready and only starts to output the video stream whenever there is one whole line of data accumulated in the ping-pong buffer. This mode of operation guarantees a continuous line stream for the downstream blocks. This is implemented to support certain display interfaces that require a non-stopping line stream.

### Autorefresh and tear check

The autorefresh and tear check functions are associated with smart panels/command mode panels.

Autorefresh allows the hardware to periodically push frames to a smart panel, thus mimicking an active display that does not require the software to explicitly push frames at a certain refresh rate.

Tear check, as its name implies, controls updates to the smart panels so that the read/write pointers do not cross and cause tearing on the panel. Tearing occurs when the data being written out is faster or slower than what the display can support. Tearing can be prevented by limiting the data that is getting written out to the exact refresh rate of the display. This is achieved by synchronizing the output to the Tearing Effect (TE) signal provided by the display.


<!-- page 321 -->
The TE signals may be selected from SoC GPIOs or from the DSI controller. The TE signals from the panel may be directly connected to the SoC pins. The panel may provide a TE signal sequence through the DSI link, and the DSI controller will interpret that signal sequence and generate a TE pulse to the MDP. For more information, see Section “DSI command MDP stream trigger methods” within Chapter “MIPI® Display Serial Interface (DSI) and Physical Layer (DSI PHY)”.

The tear check and autorefresh functions are further described in Section Configuring command mode panels.

#### Display interface

The display interface within the MDP (INTF_1) generates the signals to pass data to the connected MIPI DSI controller, supporting the following features:
* Video mode: progressive timing generation only
* Command mode
* Interleaving video and command mode streams to the DSI controller
* Interleaving multiple command mode streams to the DSI controller

For more information on the display interface configuration, refer to Sections Configuring active panels and Configuring command mode panels.

### 4.1.1.3.10 MDP performance

#### Block level performance features

To provide performance management, each source surface processor has an `MDP_VP_0_<pipe>_<m>_SSPP_FETCH_CONFIG` register to tweak the burst sizes made to the fabric.

By default, the hardware is set for maximum burst size: a burst of 8 on a 128-bit bus (set in the `MAX_BURST_SIZE` field).

Changes to limit the number of outstanding requests must be changed within the VBIF who supplies this register for each client interface.

Do not change these values while the core is processing; only set them when the core is idle.

#### Quality of service (QoS)

Each VBIF client port is responsible for conveying the health of the interface engine onto the memory fabric. This is done by signal two signals on the client interface; namely `cREQPRIORITY` and `cPRIORITYLVL`.

There is a one `cREQPRIORITY` indication per transaction per client port so the health of the current transaction is propagated along with the size, address, and so on.

There are three watermark registers defined per fetch client port that aid in generating an internal `mdpREQPRIORITY` health status. Software is responsible for programming the FIFO watermark levels. The latency buffer levels refer to the amount of space available to be filled. So a value of 0x0 indicates completely full with no space left to fetch.
<!-- page 322 -->
As illustrated in Figure 1-49 (likely referring to Figure 4-45), if the latency buffer level is above all watermark levels, `mdpREQPRIORITY` equals 2’b11, which is the highest priority level. If the latency buffer level is below all watermark levels, then `mdpREQPRIORITY` is equal to 2’b00, which is the lowest priority level.

#### Figure 4-45 MDP latency buffer
*Description:* The diagram illustrates how `mdpREQPRIORITY` is determined based on the available space in the SMP (Shared Memory Pool) relative to three programmed watermark levels. A horizontal rectangle represents the "TOTAL SMP SPACE" (representing the amount of space available to be filled, where 0 is on the left and maximum capacity is on the right). Three vertical dashed lines project upwards from the SMP space to mark the watermark thresholds:
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` (lowest value)
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1` (middle value)
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2` (highest value)

* **Yellow Bar:** Covers the range from `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` to `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1`. Marked as `mdpREQPRIORITY = 2'b01`.

Circle markers at the boundary transitions show a white circle at the upper end of a lower priority range, and a colored circle (yellow, orange, red) at the lower end of the next higher priority range.

Software is required to program the appropriate `REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0`, `REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1`, `REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2` registers with correct values in relation to one another; notably:

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` <= `REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1` <= `REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2`

The recommended values are to set them to ¼, ½, ¾ of the total SMP available space. So if 1 MacroBlock (referred to as 1 MB in text) has been allocated, the 4 KB of space and the settings would be:

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` = 64

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1` = 128

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2` = 192

These values account for whether 4 MacroBlocks (referred to as 4 MBs in text) were allocated:

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` = 256

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1` = 512

`REQPRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2` = 768
<!-- page 323 -->
Hardware keeps track of the current state of the latency buffer and generates the corresponding `mdpREQPRIORITY` status for each transaction. The generation of the status does not take into account outstanding memory reads but rather the actual state of the latency buffer once the memory request was issued. Although not recommended, SW can generate a fixed priority by programming the watermark levels appropriately. For example, setting all watermark levels to 0x0 results in MDP always generating `mdpREQPRIORITY` level 0x3 as shown in Figure 4-46.

A single red bar spans the entire SMP space starting from 0 (marked with a red circle), indicating that the priority is fixed at `mdpREQPRIORITY = 2'b11` (0x3) regardless of the buffer level.

For the writeback clients, there is no way to dynamically generate the priority of the writes. There is no latency buffer to which to associate the data. These signals come directly from a software programmable register per the writeback interface. The `mdpREQPRIORITY` status is then put through a remapper to generate the `cREQPRIORITY` value on the client side. This allows translation of health status to a priority level on the bus.

#### Figure 4-48 MDP mdpREQPRIORITY remapper
*Description:* A simple block diagram showing the signal flow. The input signal `mdpREQPRIORITY` enters a block labeled "re-mapper", and the output is `cREQPRIORITY`. Arrows indicate flow from left to right.
<!-- page 324 -->
There are two remapper registers depending on the class of the request; one for real-time clients and one for rotation clients.

The two remapper registers shared by all clients are `MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_CLASS_0` (for real-time clients) and `MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_CLASS_1` (for rotation clients). This allows software flexibility for use cases where the MDP health status can be reassigned on the system memory fabric. For example, if MDP is internally generating a health value of 2’b01 that could possibly be remapped to 2’b00 for example on the system fabric.

Similarly to the `mdpREQPRIORITY` generation, the same watermark registers generate the `mdpPRIORITYLVL` signal per client port. There is one `cPRIORITYLVL` signal per client port. Compared to `mdpREQPRIORITY`, which is asserted per transaction and reflects the value of the present transaction, `mdpPRIORITYLVL` reflects the status of the client interface and all planes sitting behind that interface (luma client plus Chroma clients when fetching multi plane fetches).

#### Figure 4-49 MDP mdpPRIORITYLVL
*Description:* The diagram illustrates how the `mdpPRIORITYLVL` signal is determined based on the available space in the SMP (Shared Memory Pool) relative to three programmed watermark levels. It is structurally identical to Figure 4-45. A horizontal rectangle represents the "TOTAL SMP SPACE". Three vertical dashed lines mark the watermark thresholds:
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0`
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1`
* `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2`

Above these, four colored bars represent the priority levels:
* **Green Bar (lowest priority):** Covers the range from 0 to `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0`. Labeled `mdpPRIORITYLVL = 2'b00`.
* **Yellow Bar:** Covers the range from `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_0` to `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1`. Labeled `mdpPRIORITYLVL = 2'b01`.
* **Orange Bar:** Covers the range from `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_1` to `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2`. Labeled `mdpPRIORITYLVL = 2'b10`.
* **Red Bar (highest priority):** Covers the range from `REQ_PRIORITY_FIFO_WATERMARK_2` to the maximum SMP space. Labeled `mdpPRIORITYLVL = 2'b11`.

---

VBIF does a simple “max” calculation off ALL VBIF clients and presents this on the bus. Therefore, all inactive clients must be set to 2’b00 (lowest priority level). Hardware automatically sets these values; no additional software actions are required.

The remapper shown in Figure 4-50 is the SAME remapper logic used to generate the `cREQPRIORITY` signaling.

#### Figure 4-50 MDP maxmdpPRIORITYLVL remapper
*Description:* A block diagram showing the signal flow for the priority level remapper. The input signal `maxmdpPRIORITYLVL` enters a block labeled "re-mapper", and the output is `cPRIORITYLVL`. Arrows indicate flow from left to right.

---

For the writeback clients, there is no way to dynamically generate the priority level of the writes. There is no latency buffer to which to associate the data. These signals come directly from a software programmable register per writeback interface.

Software must program the `MDSS_MDP_WB_<n>_DST_WRITE_CONFIG` register appropriately; namely the `REQ_PRIORITY` and `PRIORITY_LEVEL` fields. These registers DO not go through the remapper registers described in Figure 4-50 because this is already completely
<!-- page 325 -->
software programmable. These fields default to 0x0 and therefore must be programmed to the recommended settings from system performance.

MDP has no control over priority elevation by other modules in the SoC. QoS reporting from VBIF might not ensure priority for MDP at the BIMC, if there are large CPU/GPU requests competing at that instant. This can be detrimental to real-time clients like MDP.

#### QoS recommendations

The following is an explanation of particular performance settings for MDP:
* Map real-time clients to priority level 2
* Map non-real time clients to priority level 1
* Because VBIF implements round-robin arbitration based on priority levels, real-time clients receive higher priority than non-real time clients. As a result, all real-time clients are arbitrated round-robin. System simulations have shown that this is good for all simulated use cases. Do not use QoS for real-time clients because the VBIF might “starve” certain clients and not arbitrate fairly.
* To do this, the `MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_CLASS_0` register is used to translate real-time client priority levels. Set this register to 0xAA, which translates all priority levels to 2.
* Similarly, set `MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_CLASS_1` register to 0x55 to translate all non-real time clients to signal priority level 1.
* The other register that is required to be programmed is the round robin QoS arbitration bit (in the MDSS VBIF memory space).
  `VBIF_ROUND_ROBIN_QOS_ARB.RR_QOS_EN` = 0x1
* This requires that the arbitration be set to round robin, which it is by default:
  `VBIF_ARB_CTL.ROUND_ROBIN_ARB_EN_A0` = 0x1
  `VBIF_ARB_CTL.FIXED_ARB_EN_A0` = 0x0

> [!NOTE]
> Writeback clients do not have a concept of QoS because they are not based on FIFO levels. There are software programmable registers if the default values of 0x0 are to be changed.

* The values must be (where id denotes the selected control data path, 0 to 4):
  `MDP_WB_<id>_DST_WRITE_CONFIG.REQ_PRIORITY` = 0x1
  `MDP_WB_<id>_DST_WRITE_CONFIG.PRIORITY_LEVEL` = 0x1

#### QoS HFLIP considerations

The horizontal flip (HFLIP) implementation impacts the QoS priority levels that are generated and sent to the fabric. Because the line is written left-to-right but consumed right-to-left, the priority that is generated always thinks it is full (see Figure 4-51).
<!-- page 326 -->
#### Figure 4-51 MDP QoS HFLIP
*Description:* The diagram compares buffer priority generation scenarios under different HFLIP configurations. It consists of three vertical columns representing buffer fill levels from "FULL" (top) to "EMPTY" (bottom):
1. **NO HFLIP same watermark programming:** A vertical bar divided into four equal sections labeled 0, 1, 2, and 3 from top to bottom. All sections are white (active), representing normal priority generation.
2. **HFLIP same watermark programming:** A vertical bar where the bottom two sections (labeled 2 and 3) are blacked out, representing unavailable buffer space. Only the top two sections (0 and 1) are active (white). This indicates that because HFLIP causes the buffer to appear at least half full, only priority levels 0 and 1 can be generated.
3. **HFLIP modified watermark programming:** A vertical bar where the bottom portion (approximately 2/5ths) is blacked out. The remaining top portion is divided into four smaller sections labeled 0, 1, 2, and 3 (all active/white). This shows that by modifying the watermarks, all four priority levels can still be generated within the reduced active buffer space.

---

The first column shows the priority levels being sent for the entire allocation, based on fill levels.

The second column shows hflip enabled. The blacked out region indicates that the line is being read out in reverse. The buffer assumes that the line is always full; so, the overall fill level always indicates at least ½ full. Only priority levels 0 and 1 are generated.

Because priorities are not generated fast enough to indicate urgency, this condition creates panel underflow and customer-platform problems.

The third column shows alternative watermark programming to ensure that priority levels generate urgent level 2 and 3 transactions. So priority levels are generated correctly, watermark programming occurs on a frame before the hflip switch. The worst case is that non-hflip transactions have elevated priorities for a frame.

This method “removes” one line consumed by the hflip when programming watermark levels.

#### MDP HFLIP sample programming (1080p ARGB8888)

| HFLIP? | Calculation | Watermark 0 | Watermark 1 | Watermark 2 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **No** | 1080 × 4 bytes/pixel × 2 lines = 8640 bytes.<br>8640 bytes / 4096 = 2.1 SMP blocks (rounded up to 3 SMPs required).<br>Total SMP size = (3 × 4096) / 16 = 768 entries (128-bit; 16-byte entries). | 768 × ¼ = 192 | 768 × ½ = 384 | 768 × ¾ = 576 |
| **Yes** | One line consumes:<br>(1080 × 4 bytes/pixel × 1) / 16 = 270 SMP entries.<br>768 – 270 = 498 SMP entries for remaining lines. | 498 × ¼ = 124 | 498 × ½ = 249 | 498 × ¾ = 373 |
<!-- page 327 -->
#### Traffic shaper

The traffic shaper values are needed for writeback rotation clients to ensure that their bandwidth is spread out the entire frame. They are not real time with no instantaneous bandwidth requirements, they only must finish within 16 ms to provide 60 fps updates.

> [!NOTE]
> Traffic shaper settings do not change with MDP clock scaling and therefore must be adjusted accordingly based on the actual MDP clock frequency settings.

To determine the settings, calculate the required bandwidth:

`YUV 420 PP (NV1) = 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 bytes × 60 fps = 187 MB/s` (Wait, "NV1" might be "NV12" or similar, but I will keep "NV1" as in text).

If MDP is running at 266MHz, then 187 / 266 = 0.7 bytes per clock is needed at a minimum.

If MDP is running at 320 MHz, then 187 / 320 = 0.58 bytes per clock is needed at a minimum.

The granularity of the traffic shapers is 0.0625 (1/16), so set the traffic shaper value to a larger step that passes the use case requirements. The calculation assumes ideal bus conditions and must be programmed with what is going on within the rest of the system. A traffic shaper can be programmed with a “fudge” factor to account for these system delays and any additional latency settings that are required. Instead of having the writeback finish exactly on the boundaries, more bandwidth can be allocated to finish earlier but still “shape” it to prevent flooding the bus (if settings of traffic shaper turn out to be say 23, then programming it 25 makes it finish marginally faster).

The traffic shaper buffers are double-buffered. Software must follow the below programming sequence if/when changing formats:

| Bandwidth client | When to adjust settings |
| :--- | :--- |
| Higher | Before transition |
| Lower | After transition to avoid underflow before it changes to lower bandwidth |

#### Hardware underflow recovery control

If an underflow is detected, the hardware enters automatic recovery. This can be controlled in the `MDP_VIDEO_INTF_UNDERFLOW_CTL` register bits.

##### HW auto-recovery enabled

When HW auto-recovery is enabled the following sequence of events is executed:
1. When an underrun is detected the hardware automatically tells all source pipes to stop making new requests to memory. The `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` register bit is set to ‘1’, where id = 0 to 4 is the selected control data path.
2. Once all outstanding read requests have returned each source pipe acknowledges the pipe is IDLE and thus safe to reset the pipe. No new requests are initiated to memory by that source pipe.
<!-- page 328 -->
3. Once all source pipes involved in the use case indicate completion then the hardware asserts reset to put the pipe into a good state.
4. The underrun interrupt is now set and `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` bit clears to ‘0’.

If the underrun recovery doesn’t complete that means hardware is most likely waiting in step 2 for completion.

There are MDSS VBIF registers to confirm this is the case:
1. `VBIF_XIN_HALT_CTRL1` register shows which client(s) is not IDLE (that is, which client(s) has not acknowledged in step 2).
2. `VBIF_AXI_HALT_CTRL1` shows if AXI port(s) is not IDLE (that is, VBIF waiting for AXI(s) OTs to complete).

If the recovery takes a long time to complete, then any new frames that need to be processed are not initiated until we reach the end of the full sequence. The panel starts up new each frame, so if no new frames are started then they will also underrun until the full sequence is completed.

The underrun interrupt is also only asserted upon successful completion of the recovery state. So if a new frame is detected (via the MDP `INTF_1_VSYNC` interrupt) and `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` bit is asserted, then that implies a new frame occurred while the previous frame was in its underrun recovery state.

##### HW auto-recovery disabled

If this feature is disabled, then software is notified of the underflow event immediately and hardware takes no further action. Once notified, software can trigger the `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` bit for that panel to clean up the hardware.

Note that the same sequence is initiated as above with the only difference being SW initiated as opposed to HW transitioning automatically:
* Detect `INTF_1_UNDERRUN` interrupt
* Write to `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` to stop current transactions and initiate cleanup.
* Wait for `MDP_CTL_<id>_SW_RESET` to complete.

No further trigger is required as the pipe begins processing on the next frame.

##### HW auto-recovery continuous underrun

There might be instances when the HW auto-recovery has not completed, due to something outside of MDP that has been reset or power down, that leaves MDP waiting for reads. Note that more often, that is usually what could lead to underrun in the first place.

If a piece of hardware on the path to memory was reset or power collapsed, MDP would be waiting for reads that would never return since they would be lost in flight.
<!-- page 329 -->
If MDP is stuck in this state, then SW reset can never complete since it is waiting on OTs (outstanding transactions) from memory.

Even MDSS VBIF cannot be reset. MDSS VBIF has a `VBIF_XIN_HALT_CTRL0` and `VBIF_AXI_HALT_CTRL0` registers to stop requests. However, MDSS VBIF will also wait for OTs to return before asserting reset, so it follows the same sequencing as MDP.

So, if the transactions got lost, then MDP cannot recover as a whole and needs a complete asynchronous reset sequence and reprogramming.

#### Operation timeline

For MDSS, the displays must be fed with data, when it is required.

For active timing panels, the timing requirements are fixed. If the data feed does not keep up, it results in an underflow: a hard failure.

For command mode panels, when data is not pushed out fast enough and frames per second targets are not met, the performance decreases. Even though there is no visible corruption on the panel, it is considered a hard failure.

For active panels, the fill rate must keep up with drain rate. If there are multiple panels, the fill rate of the MDP engine must be greater than the sum of all drain rates.

Table 4-67 lists the bandwidth requirements for given resolutions.

#### Table 4-67 MDP bandwidth requirements per resolution

| Resolution | Description | Comment | Bandwidth |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| gHD 960x540 | 960 × 540 × 60 Hz × 4 bytes/pixel | Graphics | 119 MB/s |
| gHD 960x540 | 960 × 540 × 60 Hz × 1.5 bytes/pixel | Video | 45 MB/s |
| HD 1920x1080 | 1920 × 1080 × 60 Hz × 4 bytes/pixel | Graphics | 475 MB/s |
| HD 1920x1080 | 1920 × 1080 × 60 Hz × 1.5 bytes/pixel | Video | 178 MB/s |
| WUXGA 1920x1200 | 1920 × 1080 × 60 Hz × 4 bytes/pixel *(sic)* | Graphics | 527 MB/s |
| WUXGA 1920x1200 | 1920 × 1080 × 60 Hz × 4 bytes/pixel *(sic)* | Video Still 1080p | 178 MB/s |

---

For each panel that is active, the required bandwidth is the sum of the input resolution bandwidth.

So that line data is ready to be sent to the display with the panel timing, MDP has latency hiding buffers in each of the fetch engines. Because the data is drained at the panel timing, the total processing time for each active frame is from VSync to the end of active data. The `PING_PONG_0_DONE` interrupt always occurs at the end of the active data for active panels.

For command mode panels, the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` status bit is set in the `MDP_INTR_STATUS` register field when the last piece of data is sent out of MDP to the DSI controller. To achieve maximum frame rate, the time from triggering the engine through a write to `MDP_CTL_<id>_CTL_START` (with 0x1) and until the `PING_PONG_0_DONE` status bit is set must be as short as possible. If tear check is enabled, the incoming VSync (or tearing effect (TE)) signal keeps the updates in line with the panel refresh rate to prevent tearing artifacts from appearing on the panel.

Because data is always expanded to a full 8 bits per component within the hardware pipeline, the following expansion is done before data processing.

#### Figure 4-53 MDP RBG565 expansion *(sic)*
*Description:* The diagram illustrates the bit replication method used to expand RGB565 components to 8-bit components (plus an 8-bit Alpha channel):
* **ALPHA:** 8 bits, all set to `0`.
* **RED:** Expanded from 5 bits (`R4:R0`) to 8 bits by replicating the 3 MSBs: `[R4, R3, R2, R1, R0, R4, R3, R2]`.
* **GREEN:** Expanded from 6 bits (`G5:G0`) to 8 bits by replicating the 2 MSBs: `[G5, G4, G3, G2, G1, G0, G5, G4]`.
* **BLUE:** Expanded from 5 bits (`B4:B0`) to 8 bits by replicating the 3 MSBs: `[B4, B3, B2, B1, B0, B4, B3, B2]`.

- BLUE component (8 bits) replicates the 5-bit B [B4:B0] as: B4, B3, B2, B1, B0, B4, B3, B2 (most significant bits B4, B3, B2 are copied to the three least significant bits).

- Byte at address 0x0 contains Green bits G2, G1, G0 at bits 7-5, and Red bits R4, R3, R2, R1, R0 at bits 4-0.
- Byte at address 0x1 contains Alpha bit A0 at bit 7, Blue bits B4, B3, B2, B1, B0 at bits 6-2, and Green bits G4, G3 at bits 1-0.
<!-- page 339 -->
The data is expanded to 8 bits per component.

#### Figure 4-79: MDP ABGR1555 expansion
*Description:* A bit diagram showing the internal pipeline representation for ABGR1555 after expansion:
- ALPHA component (8 bits) replicates the 1-bit A [A0] to all 8 bits: A0, A0, A0, A0, A0, A0, A0, A0.
- RED component (8 bits) replicates the 5-bit R [R4:R0] as: R4, R3, R2, R1, R0, R4, R3, R2 (most significant bits R4, R3, R2 are copied to the three least significant bits).
- GREEN component (8 bits) replicates the 5-bit G [G4:G0] as: G4, G3, G2, G1, G0, G4, G3, G2 (most significant bits G4, G3, G2 are copied to the three least significant bits).
- BLUE component (8 bits) replicates the 5-bit B [B4:B0] as: B4, B3, B2, B1, B0, B4, B3, B2 (most significant bits B4, B3, B2 are copied to the three least significant bits).

### Constant Color (Solid Fill)

The pipes support a constant color/solid fill mechanism for each layer.
<!-- page 343 -->

> [!NOTE]
> Program the source format registers (`_SRC_FORMAT`), as if it were ARGB8888 (32 bpp) and simply enable the `SOLID_FILL` register bit.

Solid fill does not support:
- Scaling of any kind (upscale or downscale)
- Horizontal/vertical flip

When solid fill is enabled, the fetch engine does not fetch data from memory. And, read bandwidth is not consumed on the memory fabric.

Solid fill is not supported in the VIG SSPPs when QSEED2 (that is, scaling) is enabled.

### Output formats

The output formats match the supported input formats. Because there are two write back modules capable of operating in different mode, there are some differences.

The programming module must be aware of the rotation status of the input formats. For example, if an YUV422-H2V1 format was input and rotated 90 degrees, then the output would be YUV422-H1V2 and programmed as such.

### Rotator downscale

The block mode path includes a downscale module to provide bandwidth savings. This module also provides an offline (non-real time) downscale module to help achieve larger downscales in MDP.

Only power of 2 downscales are supported. The residual amount is downscaled on the second pass in the QSEED/RGB scale module. The rotate downscale only supports source dimensions that are divisible by the downscale factor.

$$src\_width \pmod{downscale\_factor} = 0$$
$$src\_height \pmod{downscale\_factor} = 0$$

(Note: The text reads: `src_width % src_height mod downscale_factor = 0`, which indicates that both width and height must be divisible by the downscale factor).

Instead of having hardware fetch pixels/lines only to drop them, the onus is on the programming to ensure that the dimensions are programmed correctly.

For example, if a 129 × 129 block was downscaled by two then software would have to program 128 × 128 source ROI.
<!-- page 344 -->

### Data Path Size Restrictions

Figure 4-91 shows the minimum and maximum heights and widths through the MDP core pipeline. This diagram illustrates the sizes from memory all the way to the panel.

#### Figure 4-91 MDP data path size restrictions
*Description:* A vertical block diagram showing the flow of display data from memory to the physical display panel, specifying the minimum and maximum size constraints at each pipeline stage.

```mermaid
graph TD
    MEMORY[MEMORY] --> Fetch[Fetch]
    Fetch --> SrcPipe[Source Pipe<br/>VIG/RGB/DMA/CURSOR]
    SrcPipe --> Layermixer[Layermixer]
    Layermixer --> PingPong[Ping Pong]
    PingPong --> Displays[Displays<br/>DSI / WB2 WFD]
```

**Stage Specifications:**

1. **MEMORY**
   - **Minimum Size:**
     - RGB: $1 \times 1$
     - YUV: $2 \times 2$ (420, H2V1, H1V2) with `EVEN` width/height/src_offsets
   - **Maximum Size (16-bit stride/offset/dimensions):**
     - RGB: 16383 wide $\times$ 65535 (@ 32bpp)
     - YUV: $65534 \times 65534$

2. **Fetch**
   - **Minimum Size:**
     - RGB: $1 \times 1$
     - YUV: $2 \times 2$ (420, H2V1, H1V2) with `EVEN` width/height/src_offsets
   - **Maximum Size (must decimate if source is larger than this):**
     - RGB: $2048 \times 2048$
     - YUV: $2048 \times 2048$

3. **Source Pipe (ViG/RGB/DMA/CURSOR)**
   - **Minimum Size:**
     - RGB: $1 \times 1$
     - YUV: $1 \times 1$ (any offset regardless of source format)
   - **Maximum Size:**
     - RGB: $2048 \times 2048$
     - YUV: $2048 \times 2048$

4. **Layermixer**
   - **Minimum Size:** $2 \times 2$
   - **Maximum Size:** $2048 \times 4096$

5. **Ping Pong**
   - **Minimum Size:** $2 \times 2$
   - **Maximum Size:** $4096 \times 4096$

6. **Displays (DSI / WB2 (WFD))**
   - **Minimum Size:** $2 \times 2$
   - **Maximum Size:** $4096 \times 4096$

Programming registers outside of verified values will result in unexpected HW behavior. The width of the source pipes within the MDP is 2048 pixels.
<!-- page 345 -->

### Block Mode Restrictions

In block mode the maximum width is limited to the processing performance required. Because the total size is broken up into $128 \times 128$ blocks, there is no restriction on the size; all registers are 16 bits wide.

Rotating a single surface of $4096 \times 4096$ without breaking it up into two passes is possible. In fact, the largest height and width are 64K pixels.

### Line Mode Writeback Restrictions

The writeback path to memory can be combined to a maximum of 4096. To write back that large a width, the Chroma down memory cannot be used. It is only sized to 2048 pixels width.

The Chroma down memory is required for subsampling with averaging in the vertical direction. If the Chroma down memory is not used (use line drop), then 4096 can be written out. If the memory is used, the width is restricted to 2048 pixels.

The WB0/WB2 paths are at 2048 pixel maximum in all formats.

Write back output paths have no concept of a region of interest. All outputs are relative to the destination base address at destination offset $(0, 0)$. If an offset is required, then SW must adjust the destination address accordingly.
<!-- page 346 -->

#### 4.1.1.3.12 MDP Use Cases

This section provides generic programming examples for various basic MDSS use-case scenarios.

### Active Mode Single Display

The datapath (in red color) in Figure 4-92 describes displaying a graphics surface on a DSI panel.

#### Figure 4-92 MDP active mode single display data flow
*Description:* A detailed block diagram of the Mobile Display Subsystem (MDSS) and Mobile Display Processor (MDP) illustrating the data flow for an active mode single display configuration. The active datapath is highlighted in red, tracing from the Frame Buffer (FB) in memory to the DSI Controller.

```mermaid
graph TD
    FB[Frame Buffer FB] --> VBIF_xin1[VBIF xin1 / Traffic Shaper]
    VBIF_xin1 --> Fetch[Fetch: V Flip, Decimation, Security]
    Fetch --> SMP[Shared Memory Pool SMP]
    SMP --> RGB0[RGB0 SSPP: Unpack H Flip, GC_LUT]
    RGB0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> Crossbar[Crossbar]
    Crossbar --> LM0[Layer Mixer 0: Line mode, GC LUT]
    Cursor --> LM0
    LM0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> DSPP0[DSPP0: Picture Adj, IGC LUT, Color Corr, Panel Corr LUT, Dither]
    DSPP0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> PingPong[Ping Pong]
    PingPong -- "2 pixels / clk" --> TearCheck[Tear Check]
    TearCheck -- "2 pixels / clk" --> INTF_1[INTF_1: Timing Gen, DSICMD]
    INTF_1 -- "Video / CMD" --> DSI_Ctrl0[DSI Controller 0]
```

**Inactive Pipeline Elements (shown in grey in diagram):**
- **VBIF Ports:** `xin0`, `xin5`, `xin2`, `xin7` (Cursor/DSI Arbiter)
- **SSPP Pipes:** 
  - `VIG0` (Unpack, QSEED2, CSC, SPA/CE, IGC_LUT)
  - `RGB1` (Unpack, IGC_LUT)
  - `DMA0` (Unpack, GC_LUT)
- **Layer Mixers:** `Layer Mixer 3` (Line mode)
- **Writeback Paths:**
  - `WB0` (Rotator, Pack) connected to `Memory BLOCK 64x64x4 bytes` (block mode)
  - `WB2` (Line Buffer, CSC, Chroma Down, Pack, Write Back Line) (line mode)
<!-- page 347 -->

For this scenario, the data flow within MDP is:
1. Data fetched from frame buffer stored in memory.
2. The data is fetched through VBIF and stored in the Shared Memory Pool.
3. Data is read from the Shared Memory Pool and flows down the RGB SSPP.
4. Data flows through the layer mixer for blending.
   > [!NOTE]
   > In this example, no blending is performed, but data flows through layer mixer.
5. Data flows through DSPP on the way to the panel.
6. Data is pulled from the ping pong FIFO according to the DSI timing engine.
7. Assuming that MDP has come up from a power-on reset, complete the following steps to program this functionality:
8. Program all the initialization registers:
   a. RGB IGC LUT entries
   b. Layer mixer GC LUT entries
9. Program the Shared Memory Pool for the given use case requirements:
   a. Program and allocate latency buffers. For this example, size the RGB0 pipe to at least two lines of latency.
10. Set up the pipeline datapath (CTL_0 used as an example):
    ```
    MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MEM_SEL = 0x0 (none)
    MDP_CTL_0_TOP.OUT_SEL = 0x2 (Interface 1)
    MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MODE_SEL = 0x0 (video mode)
    MDP_CTL_0_TOP.STREAM_SEL = 0x0 (don't care)
    MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_0.RGB_0_OUT = 0x1 (RGB as base)
    MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_1 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
    MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_2 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
    MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_3 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
    MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_4 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
    ```
11. Set up RGB pipeline:
    ```
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_SIZE = input width, height
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_IMG_SIZE = image width, height
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_XY = offset
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_OUT_SIZE = output width, height
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC0_ADDR = base address
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE0 = stride
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT = pixel format
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_UNPACK_PATTERN = pixel format
    MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE = pipe configuration
    ```
12. Set up Layer Mixer0 pipeline:
    ```
    MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_OP_MODE.GC_LUT_EN = 0x1
    MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_OUT_SIZE = output width, height (must match the base layer output width, height)
    MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_BLEND0_OP.BG_ALPHA_SEL = FG constant
    MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_BLEND0_FG_ALPHA = 0xFF (BG to fully pass through)
    ```
<!-- page 348 -->

13. If necessary, set up DSPP but work from power-on reset in bypass mode.
14. Program primary timing engine values but do not trigger the timing engine yet.
15. Issue a flush command so that programming takes effect on the initial VSync:
    ```
    MDP_CTL_0_FLUSH.RGB_0 = 0x1
    MDP_CTL_0_FLUSH.LAYER_MIXER_0 = 0x1
    MDP_CTL_0_FLUSH.CTL = 0x1
    ```
16. Enable the chosen interrupts.
17. Start the timing engine to start the datapath:
    ```
    MDP_INTF_1_TIMING_ENGINE_EN.EN = 0x1
    ```
18. Wait for frames to complete:
    - `MDP_INTR_STATUS.INTF_1_VSYNC = 1` (Initial VSync indicates timing engine has started)
    - `MDP_INTR_STATUS.PING_PONG_0_DONE = 1` (Indicates that end of active data sent to panel)
    - `MDP_INTR_STATUS.INTF_1_VSYNC = 1` (VSync signal indicates that complete frame sent to the DSI controller)
<!-- page 349 -->

### Command Mode Single Display

The datapath (in red color) in Figure 4-93 describes displaying a graphics surface on a DSI command mode panel.

#### Figure 4-93 MDP command mode single display data flow
*Description:* A block diagram showing the MDSS and MDP data flow for a command mode single display. The active path is highlighted in red, following the same path as Figure 4-92 from the Frame Buffer (FB) through the Shared Memory Pool, RGB0 pipe, Layer Mixer 0, DSPP0, Ping Pong, and Tear Check, but at the interface block (`INTF_1`), the `DSICMD` module is active instead of the `Timing Gen` module, routing the output via the `CMD` signal (red) instead of the `Video` signal (grey) to the `DSI Controller 0`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    FB[Frame Buffer FB] --> VBIF_xin1[VBIF xin1 / Traffic Shaper]
    VBIF_xin1 --> Fetch[Fetch: V Flip, Decimation, Security]
    Fetch --> SMP[Shared Memory Pool SMP]
    SMP --> RGB0[RGB0 SSPP: Unpack H Flip, GC_LUT]
    RGB0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> Crossbar[Crossbar]
    Crossbar --> LM0[Layer Mixer 0: Line mode, GC LUT]
    Cursor --> LM0
    LM0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> DSPP0[DSPP0: Picture Adj, IGC LUT, Color Corr, Panel Corr LUT, Dither]
    DSPP0 -- "1 pixel / clk" --> PingPong[Ping Pong]
    PingPong -- "2 pixels / clk" --> TearCheck[Tear Check]
    TearCheck -- "2 pixels / clk" --> INTF_1[INTF_1: Timing Gen, DSICMD active]
    INTF_1 -- "CMD" --> DSI_Ctrl0[DSI Controller 0]
```

Assuming that MDP has come up from a power-on reset, complete the following steps to program this functionality:
<!-- page 350 -->

1. Program all the initialization registers:
   a. RGB IGC LUT entries
   b. Layer mixer GC LUT entries
2. Program the Shared Memory Pool for the given use case requirements.
   a. Latency buffers must be allocated and programmed. For this example, size the RGB0 pipe to at least two lines of latency.
3. Set up the pipeline datapath.
   ```
   MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MEM_SEL = 0x0 (none)
   MDP_CTL_0_TOP.OUT_SEL = 0x2 (Interface 1)
   MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MODE_SEL = 0x1 (command mode)
   MDP_CTL_0_TOP.STREAM_SEL = 0x0 (command mode stream 0)
   MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_0.RGB_0_OUT = 0x1 (RGB0 as base)
   MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_1 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
   MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_2 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
   MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_3 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
   MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_4 = 0x0 (nothing connected)
   ```
4. Set up RGB pipeline.
   ```
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_SIZE = input width, height
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_IMG_SIZE = image width, height
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_XY = offset
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_OUT_SIZE = output width, height
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC0_ADDR = base address
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE0 = stride
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT = pixel format
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_UNPACK_PATTERN = pixel format
   MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE = pipe configuration
   ```
5. Set up Layer Mixer0 pipeline.
   ```
   MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_OP_MODE.GC_LUT_EN = 0x1
   MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_OUT_SIZE = output width, height (This must match the base layer output width, height)
   MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_BLEND0_OP.BG_ALPHA_SEL = FG constant
   MDP_VP_0_LAYER_0_BLEND0_FG_ALPHA = 0xFF (BG to pass through fully)
   ```
6. If necessary, set up DSPP, but work from power-on reset.
7. Enable the chosen interrupts.
8. Trigger the pipeline.
   ```
   MDP_CTL_0_CTL_0_START = 0x1
   ```
9. Wait for frames to complete:
   - `MDP_INTR_STATUS.PING_PONG_0_DONE = 1` (Indicates that end of active data sent to DSI controller. Not all data sent to the panel yet, but software can trigger another frame.)

# Wireless display (WFD) writeback

The datapath (in red color) in Figure 4-94 describes a wireless display writeback scenario.

#### Figure 4-94 MDP wireless display (WFD) writeback data flow

*Description:* Block diagram of the Mobile Display Subsystem (MDSS) and Mobile Display Processor (MDP) highlighting the data path for wireless display (WFD) writeback in red.

The path starts from the system memory (FB) via VBIF interface `xin1`.
1. The data passes through a traffic shaper and enters the MDP.
2. In MDP, it is fetched by a fetch block (supporting V Flip, Decimation, and Security check).
3. The fetched data is stored in the Shared Memory Pool (SMP).
4. From SMP, the data is routed to the Source Shared Pipe Program (SSPP) block `RGB0`. `RGB0` performs Unpack (with H Flip support) and applies the Inverse Gamma Correction Look-Up Table (IGC_LUT).
5. The output of `RGB0` (at 1 pixel/clock) goes through the Crossbar to `Layer Mixer 3` (operating in line mode).
6. `Layer Mixer 3` applies the Gamma Correction Look-Up Table (GC LUT).
7. The mixed output (at 1 pixel/clock) is routed to the Writeback 2 (`WB2`) block.
8. `WB2` processes the data through a Line Buffer, Color Space Conversion (CSC), Chroma Down-sampler, Packing block, and finally a Write Back Line block.
9. The processed data is written back to system memory (FB) via VBIF interface `wb2 = xin6`, passing through a security block and a traffic shaper.

Assuming that MDP has come up from a power-on reset, complete the following steps to program this functionality:
1. Program all the initialization registers:
   a. RGB IGC LUT entries
   b. Layer mixer GC LUT entries
2. Program the Shared Memory Pool for the given use case requirements.
<!-- page 352 -->

   a. Latency buffers must be allocated and programmed. For this example, size the RGB0 pipe to at least two lines of latency.
3. Set up the pipeline datapath:
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MEM_SEL = 0x5` (linear writeback)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.OUT_SEL = 0x0` (none)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MODE_SEL = 0x0` (don’t care)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.STREAM_SEL = 0x0` (don’t care)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_3.RGB_0_OUT = 0x1` (RGB0 as base)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_0 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_1 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_2 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_4 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
4. Set up RGB pipeline:
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_SIZE` = input width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_IMG_SIZE` = image width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_XY` = offset
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_OUT_SIZE` = output width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC0_ADDR` = base address
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE0` = stride
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` = pixel format
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_UNPACK_PATTERN` = pixel format
   * `MDP_VP_0_RGB_0_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE` = pipe configuration
5. Set up Layer Mixer3 pipeline:
   * `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_3_OP_MODE.GC_LUT_EN = 0x1`
   * `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_3_OUT_SIZE` = output width, height (This must match the base layer output width, height)
   * `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_3_BLEND0_OP.BG_ALPHA_SEL` = FG constant
   * `MDP_VP_0_LAYER_3_BLEND0_FG_ALPHA = 0xFF` (BG to pass through fully)
6. If necessary, set up DSPP, but work from power-on reset.
7. Set up the writeback path:
   There are up to five writeback registers (WB_0 to WB_4) depending on which control datapath (CTL_0 to CTL_4) is used. WB_0 refers to the CTL_0 value.
   * `MDP_WB_0_OUT_SIZE` = output width, height
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_FORMAT` = writeback format
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_PACK_PATTERN` = writeback pattern
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST0_ADDR` = writeback address
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_YSTRIDE0` = stride
8. Enable the chosen interrupts.
9. Trigger the pipeline:
   * `MDP_CTL_0_CTL_0_START = 0x1`
10. Wait for frames to complete:
    * `MDP_INTR_STATUS.WB_2_DONE = 1` (Indicates all the data has been written back to memory)
<!-- page 353 -->

# Rotation writeback

The datapath (in red color) in Figure 4-95 describes a rotation writeback scenario using DMA0.

> [!NOTE]
> Only the DMA0 datapath can be rotated.

#### Figure 4-95 MDP rotation writeback flow

*Description:* Block diagram of the MDSS/MDP data flow highlighting the rotation writeback path in red.
The path starts from system memory (FB) via VBIF `xin2`.
1. The data passes through a traffic shaper and a Fetch block (with V Flip and Security check) into the MDP.
2. It is stored in the Shared Memory Pool (SMP).
3. From SMP, it is routed to the SSPP `DMA0` block. `DMA0` performs Unpack (H Flip) and applies IGC_LUT.
4. The output from `DMA0` bypasses the crossbar and goes directly to the Writeback 0 (`WB0`) block in "Block mode 4 pixels/clk".
5. `WB0` contains `Rotate` and `Pack` blocks and works with a `Memory BLOCK 64x64x4 bytes` to perform rotation.
6. The rotated and packed data is written back to system memory (FB) via VBIF `wb0 = xin3` through security and traffic shaper blocks.

Assuming that MDP has come up from a power-on reset, complete the following steps to program this functionality:
1. Program all the initialization registers:
   a. RGB IGC LUT entries
<!-- page 354 -->

   b. Layer mixer GC LUT entries
2. Program the Shared Memory Pool for the given use case requirements.
   a. Latency buffers must be allocated and programmed. For this example, size the RGB0 pipe to at least two lines of latency.
3. Set up the pipeline datapath:
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MEM_SEL = 0x1` (block mode for rotation 0 writeback)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.OUT_SEL = 0x0` (none)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.MODE_SEL = 0x0` (don’t care)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_TOP.STREAM_SEL = 0x0` (don’t care)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_0 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_1 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_2 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_3 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
   * `MDP_CTL_0_LAYER_4 = 0x0` (nothing connected)
4. Set up DMA pipeline:
   > [!NOTE]
   > Input size must be equal to output size. No scaling is possible.
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_SIZE` = input width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_IMG_SIZE` = image width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_XY` = offset
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_OUT_SIZE` = output width, height
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC0_ADDR` = base address
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_YSTRIDE0` = stride
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_FORMAT` = pixel format
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_UNPACK_PATTERN` = pixel format
   * `MDP_VP_0_DMA_0_SSPP_SRC_OP_MODE` = pipe configuration
5. Set up the Writeback Path.
   There are up to five writeback registers (WB_0 to WB_4) depending on which control datapath (CTL_0 to CTL_4) is used. WB_0 refers to the CTL_0 value.
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_OP_MODE` = parameters including rotation flag
   * `MDP_WB_0_OUT_SIZE` = output width, height
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_FORMAT` = writeback format
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_PACK_PATTERN` = writeback pattern
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST0_ADDR` = writeback address
   * `MDP_WB_0_DST_YSTRIDE0` = stride
6. Enable the chosen interrupts.
7. Trigger the pipeline:
   * `MDP_CTL_0_CTL_0_START = 0x1`
8. Wait for frames to complete:
   * `MDP_INTR_STATUS.WB_0_DONE = 1` (Indicates that all data was written back to memory)

### 4.1.1.4.3 MDSS_HW register definitions

#### MDSS_HW_INTR_STATUS (0x00010)
* **Type:** R
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Description:** MDSS Toplevel Interrupt Collection Status Register. Since there are a number of display IP related interrupt sources, this register indicates which display IP core has an interrupt line asserted to help out the display driver.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4 | DSI0 | 0x0: DSI0 Interrupt line is NOT asserted<br>0x1: DSI0 Interrupt line is asserted |
| 0 | MDP | 0x0: MDP Interrupt line is NOT asserted<br>0x1: MDP Interrupt line is asserted |

### MDP_TRAFFIC_SHAPER_RD_CLIENT_0
* Offset: `0x01030`
* Type: RW
* Reset: `0x00000000`

Traffic Shaper Configuration for read client0. This is mapped to VIG0 read client.

double buffered: YES

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | EN | Traffic Shaper enable |
| 7:0 | BYTES_PER_CLOCK | Determines how many bytes each mdp clock is equivalent to. This is a 4.4 value which allows for up to 1/16 granularity.<br>A value of 0x01 implies 0.0625 (1/16) which is the smallest programmable value.<br>A value of 0xFF implies 15.9375 which is the largest programmable value. |

### 0x011E0 MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_CLASS_0

Type: RW

Reset State: 0x000000E4

QoS remapper to translate health level to priority levels on the bus

Class 0 is used by the real time clients in the system (i.e. ViG/RGB/DMA pipes in line mode) Class 1 is used by the non-real time clients in the system (i.e. DMA pipes in block mode) WB modules are completely SW configurable and dont rely on watermarks.

Therefore they do NOT go through the remapper double buffered: NO

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:6 | REQPRIORITY_3 | Remapping ID for priority 3 onto the client port |
| 5:4 | REQPRIORITY_2 | Remapping ID for priority 0 onto the client port |
| 3:2 | REQPRIORITY_1 | Remapping ID for priority 1 onto the client port |
| 1:0 | REQPRIORITY_0 | Remapping ID for priority 0 onto the client port |

### 0x011EC MDP_UPPER_NEWROI_PRIOR_TO_START

Type: RW

Reset State: 0x00000001

The newroi prior to start is used to flush out incorrect states and such between frames. The newroi is sent prior to the start signals from the PMU's. This field is for the PMU's in the upper pipeline only - there exists a separate register for the lower pipeline (LOWER_NEWROI_PRIOR_TO_START)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | ENABLE | Enable the mode to send out newroi prior to start |

### 0x012E0 MDP_VIDEO_INTF_UNDERFLOW_CTL

- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00001111
- **Description:** VIDEO_INTF_UNDERFLOW_CTRL register controls the auto recovery mechanism on underflow case. Register reprogramming is not allowed when each video interface is running.
- **Double Buffered:** NO

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4 | INTF_1_ERR_RECOVERY_EN | Enable auto recovery during underflow case in interface 1 if NEWROI_PRIOR_TO_START is disabled.<br>0x0 : Disable. SW is required to apply SW reset when underflow interrupt occurs<br>0x1 : Enable. No SW reset is required. Underflow interrupt is generated after auto recovery is finished |

### 0x013E0 MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_LOWER_CLASS_0

**Type:** RW
**Reset State:** 0x000000E4

QoS remapper to translate health level to priority levels on the bus

Class 0 is used by the real time clients in the system (i.e. ViG/RGB/DMA pipes in line mode) Class 1 is used by the non-real time clients in the system (i.e. DMA pipes in block mode) WB modules are completely SW configurable and dont rely on watermarks.

Therefore they do NOT go through the remapper double buffered: NO

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:6 | REQPRIORITY_3 | Remapping ID for priority 3 onto the client port |
| 5:4 | REQPRIORITY_2 | Remapping ID for priority 0 onto the client port |
| 3:2 | REQPRIORITY_1 | Remapping ID for priority 1 onto the client port |
| 1:0 | REQPRIORITY_0 | Remapping ID for priority 0 onto the client port |

### 0x013E4 MDP_QOS_REMAPPER_LOWER_CLASS_1

**Type:** RW
**Reset State:** 0x000000E4

QoS remapper to translate health level to priority levels on the bus

Class 0 is used by the real time clients in the system (i.e. ViG/RGB/DMA pipes in line mode) Class 1 is used by the non-real time clients in the system (i.e. DMA pipes in block mode) WB modules are completely SW configurable and dont rely on watermarks.
<!-- page 426 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:6 | REQPRIORITY_3 | Remapping ID for priority 3 onto the client port |
| 5:4 | REQPRIORITY_2 | Remapping ID for priority 2 onto the client port |
| 3:2 | REQPRIORITY_1 | Remapping ID for priority 1 onto the client port |
| 1:0 | REQPRIORITY_0 | Remapping ID for priority 0 onto the client port |

### 0x013F0 MDP_SPLIT_DISPLAY_LOWER_PIPE_CTRL

**Type:** RW
**Reset State:** 0x00000000

Main configuration of split display in mdp lower pipeline. This register are not double buffered.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | TE_LINE_INTERVAL_WATEMARK | TE interval interrupt is generated if smart panels for split display are not synchronized as many lines as this watermark value. |
| 8 | INTF_2_TIM_GEN_SYNC_MODE | Control synchronization mode for timing generator in interface 2<br>0x0 : No sync mode<br>0x1 : Use INTF_1's enable signal for interface 2 |
| 4 | INTF_1_TIM_GEN_SYNC_MODE | Control synchronization mode for timing generator in interface 1<br>0x0 : No SW trigger change<br>0x1 : Use INTF_2's enable signal for interface 1 |
| 2 | SMART_PANEL_FREE_RUN | Select split display mode for smart panel. This register value should be identical to upper pipe's same name bit before enabling split display.<br>0x1 : Free running mode between panels<br>0x0 : Synchronous mode between panels |
| 1 | SPLIT_DISPLAY_TYPE | Specify panel type. This register value should be identical to upper pipe's same name bit before enabling split display.<br>0x1 : Smart Panel<br>0x0 : Dumb Panel |

### 0x013F8 MDP_LOWER_NEWROI_PRIOR_TO_START

**Type:** RW
**Reset State:** 0x00000001

The newroi prior to start is used to flush out incorrect states and such between frames. The newroi is sent prior to the start signals from the PMU's. This field is for the PMU's in the lower pipeline only - there exists a separate register for the upper pipeline (UPPER_NEWROI_PRIOR_TO_START)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | ENABLE | Enable the mode to send out newroi prior to start |

### Register: MDP_CTL_0_TOP
- **Offset:** 0x02014
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00001F00

**Description:**
Operation Mode Configuration for the Pipeline

The purpose of the register is to define the complete data path of this operation and that includes all the way to the interfaces such as DSI/HDMI/eDP.

Changing of the data path dynamically is NOT supported and requires stopping that data path, reconfiguring the connections, and restarting the datapath.
<!-- page 434 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 17 | MODE_SEL | Interface Mode of the destination interface<br>Needed to distinguish interfaces such as DSI that can be either mode. DSI can also interleave streams of different types (i.e. command and video) to a single core.<br>0x0: Video Mode<br>0x1: Command Mode 1 |
| 16:15 | STREAM_SEL | Stream Identification<br>Used For Interleaving of Command Streams. This field is a don't care for video mode streams.<br>0x0: Stream 0<br>0x1: Stream 1<br>0x2: Stream 2 |
| 7:4 | OUT_SEL | Output Ping-Pong Interface Connection to external display interface<br>0x0: No connection from Ping-Pong buffers to output interfaces<br>0x1: Interface 0<br>0x2: Interface 1<br>0x3: Interface 2<br>0x4: Interface 3 |
| 3:0 | MEM_SEL | Memory Output Connection<br>0x0: NO memory output selected<br>0x1: Memory BLOCK mode output selected for rotation 0<br>0x2: Memory BLOCK mode output selected for rotation 1<br>0x3: Memory LINE mode output selected for rotation 0<br>0x4: Memory LINE mode output selected for rotation 1<br>0x5: Memory LINE mode output selected for linear memory writeback |

### Register: MDP_CTL_0_FLUSH
- **Offset:** 0x02018
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Description:**
Register Flush register

The flush register is used to indicate a pipe/layermixers registers are all programmed, and are safe to update to the back copy of the double buffered registers.

Each pipes/layermixers flush mask bit will be used only when the associated pipe/layermixer is running at active refresh pull mode, e.g., direct out going to LCDC/HDMI/DSI Video.

In such operation mode, the associated pipe/layermixers double buffered registers back copies are updated with the new values at the vsync boundary only when the flush mask bit has already been written a 1.

Each flush mask bit would also returned a 0 once the back copies are updated.

Before the back copies are updated, the associate mask bit would returned a 1 if it has been previously written a 1.
<!-- page 435 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 30 | TIMING_1 | Timing Interface 1 are ready for flush |
| 17 | CTL | Control Pipe register is ready for flush<br>This applies to upper pipe ONLY to change the adding/removal of layers |
| 16 | WB | Write Back registers are ready for flush |
| 15 | DSPP_2 | DSPP2 registers are ready for flush |
| 14 | DSPP_1 | DSPP1 registers are ready for flush |
| 13 | DSPP_0 | DSPP0 registers are ready for flush |
| 12 | DMA_1 | DMA_1 registers are ready for flush |
| 11 | DMA_0 | DMA_0 registers are ready for flush |
| 10 | LAYER_MIXER_4 | Layer Mixer4 registers are ready for flush<br>This includes the cursor registers stored in the layer mixer register space |
| 9 | LAYER_MIXER_3 | Layer Mixer3 registers are ready for flush<br>This includes the cursor registers stored in the layer mixer register space |
| 8 | LAYER_MIXER_2 | Layer Mixer2 registers are ready for flush<br>This includes the cursor registers stored in the layer mixer register space |
| 7 | LAYER_MIXER_1 | Layer Mixer1 registers are ready for flush<br>This includes the cursor registers stored in the layer mixer register space |
| 6 | LAYER_MIXER_0 | Layer Mixer0 registers are ready for flush<br>This includes the cursor registers stored in the layer mixer register space |
| 5 | RGB_2 | RGB2 registers are ready for flush |
| 4 | RGB_1 | RGB1 registers are ready for flush |
| 3 | RGB_0 | RGB0 registers are ready for flush |
| 2 | VIG_2 | VIG2 registers are ready for flush |
| 1 | VIG_1 | VIG1 registers are ready for flush |
| 0 | VIG_0 | VIG0 registers are ready for flush |

### Register: MDP_CTL_0_CTL_START
- **Offset:** 0x0201C
- **Type:** W
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Description:**
Overlay Processor Start Signal for the given Control Operation

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | START | A write to this register will kick off operation for the given operation control and activate all layers |
<!-- page 436 -->

### Register: MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET
- **Offset:** 0x02030
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Description:**
Software Reset of the given control operation

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | RESET | Writing to this bit will trigger a soft reset for the described data path. This register is self-clearing and will return 0x1 if soft reset sequence is not complete. Upon completion, this will return 0x0.<br>Note that this will soft reset the peripheral display interfaces that are described in this path. i.e. if driving intf_0 it will reset the pixel clock domain of intf_0 as well |

### Register: MDP_CTL_0_SW_RESET_OVERRIDE
- **Offset:** 0x02034
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Description:**
Software Reset Override of the given control operation

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | RESET | Writing to this bit will assert reset for the described data path. This value contained in this register will be forced onto the datapath. It will reset the state machines within the scheduler as well for the given datapath.<br>To use this register sequence, SW shall write a value of 0x1 to this register to assert reset. Once SW wants to de-assert reset, SW shall write a value of 0x0. SW will need to ensure the duration of the value 0x1 is long enough to ensure the path is clean and all memory reads are complete. The datapath will not be triggered if this bit is asserted |
