### 4.1.2.7 DSI functional description

The DSI controller receives pixel streams from the mobile display processor (MDP) and panel commands from memory, and then sends the data to a DSI video mode panel or command mode panel via the companion DSI PHY module.

The DSI controller operates in command mode, video mode, or both modes to support different display architectures. It supports all video and command mode pixel requirements per MIPI Alliance Specification v1.01 for Display Serial Interface. The DSI controller also supports up to four peripherals with tagged commands and data using the virtual channel ID field of the header for packets targeted at different peripherals.

The lane management layer in the DSI controller supports up to four datalanes. The controller supports high-speed transmission, and escape-mode transmission and reception. There are set of timers for contention recovery of various types of link activities such as data transmission, bus turnaround (BTA), and reset.

To support peripherals compliant to MIPI Alliance Specification Display Serial Interface v1.01 and earlier, the end of transmission packet (EoTp) generation can be enabled or disabled. For interoperability with earlier versions of DSI peripherals for which error correcting code (ECC) was considered optional, the DSI controller can have ECC verification disabled for the peripheral responses over the bidirectional link. Checksum generation is optional for peripherals, and checksum verification can be enabled or disabled for packets received from the peripheral device.

All serial bus lanes travel from the DSI host to DSI device, except for the first data lane. The first data lane can perform BTA operations that allow it to reverse transmission direction.

The DSI controller includes the following internal interfaces (see JPEG overview):
* Virtualizing bus interface (VBIF) for memory access through MDSS
* DSI video mode and command mode interfaces to MDP
* PHY protocol interface (PPI) to DSI PHY
* AHB interface for registers configuration

### 4.1.2.8 DSI power and clock management

#### 4.1.2.8.1 DSI clock configuration

The DSI controller includes the following internal clock domains:
<!-- page 777 -->

* `CC_DSI0_AHBS_HCLK`: registers configuration clock.
* `CC_DSI0_AHBM_HCLK`: command DMA interface clock (MDP core clock).
* `CC_DSI0_PCLK`: DSI application and protocol layer logic clock; used also for video mode and command mode interface to MDP.
* `CC_DSI0_BYTE_CLK`: lane layer logic clock for high-speed (HS) data transmission. During HS transmission, each byte of data is accompanied by a byte clock. The byte clock must be active while data is transferred.
* `CC_DSI0_ESC_CLK`: lane layer logic clock for non-high-speed (low-power) data transmission, and also for escape mode transmission.

The DSI controller provides also a bit clock (`HR_BITCLK`), which is the clock that goes out from the host to the external LCD driver on the DSI clock lane (see DSI external connectivity). The DSI bit clock is used as the source-synchronous bit clock for capturing the serial data bit in the receiver PHY. This clock must be active while data is transferred.

Table 4-80 lists the clock ratios that require software maintenance.

### Table 4-80 DSI clock ratios

| Video mode | Command MDP mode | Command DMA HS data transmit | Command DMA LP data transmit | PCLK | BYTE_CLK |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| Y | X[^1] | X | X | Set according to video mode stream resolution and frame rate. | `BYTE_CLK = (PCLK * byte_per_pixel) / (num_datalanes * byte_per_data_lane)` |
| N | Y | X | X | Set according to command mode stream resolution and frame rate. If there are two command MDP streams, set for the one with lower pixel depth. | `BYTE_CLK <= (PCLK * byte_per_pixel) / (num_datalanes * byte_per_data_lane)` |
| N | N | Y | N | Set according to desired data rate. | `BYTE_CLK <= (PCLK * 3) / (num_datalanes * byte_per_data_lane)` |
| N | N | N | Y | Set according to desired data rate. For power savings, set this clock to CXO. | Not used. LPDT uses `ESC_CLK`. For power savings, set `DSI0_PHY_PLL` to bypass mode, so that CXO is used directly as byte clock and bit clock. |

[^1]: X = don't care

The following clock setup recommendations is considered:
* `ESC_CLK` must be less than 20 MHz.
* `HR_BITCLK` (bit clock, only used in the DSI PHY) must be four times faster than the `BYTE_CLK`.
<!-- page 778 -->

* Clocks generated by the `DSI0_PHY_PLL` must be stable, so that the clock frequency does not change dynamically during operation.
* Clock rate must be a minimum of 80 Mbits per lane for high-speed data transmission.
* Based on the command mode DMA FIFO watermark settings, the `AHBM_HCLK` clock (that is, MDP core clock) must be faster than PCLK at the factor listed in Section 4.1.2.16.7.

It is safe to turn off clocks to particular block when the DSI controller is idle or has completed the last operation. It is also safe to turn on clocks before triggering any operation.

Table 4-81 lists DSI clock relations for different PHY modes.

### Table 4-81 DSI clock relations for different PHY modes

| Relation | D-PHY with reduced PPI | D-PHY with full PPI |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PCLK to BYTE_CLK** | `PCLK * byte_per_pixel = BYTE_CLK * num_lanes_per_link` | `PCLK * byte_per_pixel = BYTE_CLK * num_lanes_per_link` |
| **BYTE_CLK to BITCLK** | `BYTE_CLK * 8 = BITCLK` | `BYTE_CLK * 8 = BITCLK` |

### 4.1.2.9 DSI block-level power features

When the DSI controller is not in use, it can dynamically turn off some clock branches. To force each dynamic clock branch on, configure the associated bits in `DSI_0_CLK_CTRL` register.

When the entire DSI controller is not in use, wait until it is idle. If the controller was busy in command mode operation, disable the DSI controller after the last operation is done (wait for one of the `DONE_STAT` interrupts, described in Section CCI can be reset in two ways, by using the:)

If the controller was busy in video mode operation, complete the following steps:
1. Turn off the MDP timing engine. See section *Mobile Display Processor (MDP)*, for more information.
<!-- page 779 -->

2. Wait for the last frame to be flushed out of the DSI link (wait for the last `DSI_VIDEO_MODE_DONE_STAT` interrupt).
3. Turn off the DSI video mode engine by clearing the `VIDEO_MODE_EN` bit of the `DSI_0_CTRL` register.

The minimum context save and restore requirement depends on the DSI link state during power gating. If the DSI link is in ULPS, configure the MDSS registers related to ULPS clamps before power is turned off. After power is turned on, restore the DSI controller ultralow power configuration registers. If the link is clamped to the low-power stop state (LP-11) while MDSS is powered off, then re-enable the lanes after power is turned on but before clamps are disabled. For more information, see Section *DSI system-level power management*.

### 4.1.2.10 DSI system-level power management

DSI provides the following low-power modes for the lanes to reduce power consumption:
* **Low-power stop state (LP-11)**: This mode is a functional mode. A DSI lane enters LP-11 mode when the lane is enabled. The `VDD_CX` SoC domain must be kept at least at SVS (see Chapter *Resource Power Manager (RPM)*, for more information).
* **Ultra-low power state (ULPS)**: This mode is a functional mode. The `VDD_CX` SoC domain must be kept at least at SVS.

#### 4.1.2.10.1 DSI ultra-low power state (ULPS)

Once the display enters ULPS, only the DSI PHY must drive '00' to the data lanes. To minimize power consumption, the DSI controller and the rest of MDSS can be power collapsed.

The following steps must be completed to enter and exit the ULPS:
1. Enter ULPS by sending ULPS request on the PPI to the DSI PHY for each lane via a dedicated bit in the `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register. The DSI PHY must then drive '00' to the data lanes. For more information, see the DSI enter ULPS sequence.
2. Clamp/isolate the PPI using secondary clamps and muxes by writing `0x8000` to address `0x0193E020`. After reset, when DSI controller moves to ULPS, these clamps are removed (see step 5 below). The DSI clamps are used to keep the PHY driving the link at a stable state (ULPS or LP-11) while the MDSS is powered up/down. However, when the SoC GCC applies a reset (`GCC_MDSS_ARES`) to MDSS during MDSS power-up, this reset might propagate to the PHY and eventually resets the PHY. This breaks the intention to keep driving the DSI link in stable state. To prevent the DSI PHY from getting reset, write 1 to address `0x0193E024` when DSI clamps are enabled.
3. Power-collapse MDSS by enabling the MDSS power collapse clamps: configure the `CLAMP_IO` bit in the `GCC_MDSS_GDSCR` register (see Chapter *Clock management (GCC)*). The DSI PHY must continue driving '00' to the data lanes. In addition, a DSI PLL and DSI PHY regulator shutdown can be initiated to further lower power consumption. The PHY regulator does not need to be on while the PHY is driving ULPS.
4. Wait until software requests exit from ULPS.
5. Exit ULPS:
   * Disable the MDSS clamps via the `CLAMP_IO` bit in the `GCC_MDSS_GDSCR` register.
<!-- page 780 -->

* Reset the entire MDSS, DSI controller included. As a result the DSI controller enters IDLE state.
* Software must traverse the DSI controller state machine from IDLE to ULPS. The PPI is driven now in ULPS mode, but still clamped/isolated from PHY.
* Disable the PPI clamps and muxes by writing `0x0000` to address `0x0193E020`, so that the PHY can follow DSI controller commands.
* Apply ULPS exit request using the DSI controller to all the lanes in ULPS mode via the dedicated bits in the `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register. For more information, see DSI exit ULPS sequence.
* The DSI PHY would drive each lane to LP Mark-1 state for $t > 1$ ms before moving to idle (LP-11). This is enough time to lock back the PLL, if it was collapsed at PHY level to save power. If the PHY regulator was shut down, it must be turned on and reconfigured.

The explanation of the above steps is as follows: When power is restored to MDSS, the DSI controller (and all of MDSS) is reset and enters the IDLE state. The DSI controller has to be in ULPS state required by the DSI PHY. To keep the DSI controller and DSI PHY synchronized, secondary DSI clamps/muxes exist between the MDSS power collapse clamps and the DSI PHY (see SI clamps). These DSI clamps/muxes drive the DSI PHY with the correct signaling to stay in ULPS until the DSI controller is reset and moves to the ULPS state. From the ULPS state, these DSI clamps/muxes can be disabled.

#### Figure 4-99 SI clamps
*(Note: Figure not extracted)*

#### 4.1.2.10.2 DSI enter ULPS sequence

To enter the ultra-low power state (ULPS), do the following:
1. Ensure a DONE interrupt is received for any DSI operation that has been triggered. For more information, see CCI can be reset in two ways, by using the:.
2. Check `DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS` register and ensure all the `DLN*_FIFO_EMPTY` bits are 1.
3. Check `DSI_0_LANE_STATUS` register and ensure all the lanes are in stop state (`DLN*_STOPSTATE` = 1).
4. Write 1 to the `*_ULPS_REQUEST` fields in `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register.
5. When the lane is in ULPS, the `*_ULPS_ACTIVE_NOT` field in `DSI_0_LANE_STATUS` register is 0.

#### 4.1.2.10.3 DSI exit ULPS sequence

To exit the ultra-low power state (ULPS), perform the following:
1. Ensure `AHB` and `ESC_CLK` clocks are running.
2. Check that the `*_ULPS_ACTIVE_NOT` field in `DSI_0_LANE_STATUS` register is 0 (optional).
3. Write 1 to the `*_ULPS_EXIT` field of `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register.


<!-- page 781 -->

4. Check that the `*_ULPS_ACTIVE_NOT` field of `DSI_0_LANE_STATUS` register is 1 (optional).
5. After wakeup (MIPI D-PHY specification requires at least 1 ms), write 0 to the `*_ULPS_REQUEST` field of `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register.
6. Write 0 to the `*_ULPS_EXIT` field of `DSI_0_LANE_CTRL` register. To avoid metastability do this step after step 4. After ULPS exit, wait for all the lanes to return to stop state (LP-11) before triggering any data transfer.

#### 4.1.2.10.4 DSI low-power state (LP-11)

Once the display enters LP-11, only the DSI PHY must drive ‘11’ to the data lanes. To minimize power consumption, the DSI controller and the rest of MDSS can be power collapsed. This is similar to clamping the PPI interface and having the PHY drive the lanes in a stable ULPS state, as described in Section DSI ultra-low power state (ULPS). However, instead of driving the ULPS state, the lanes must be driven in a stable LP-11 state.

The following steps must be completed to trigger PHY regulator:

1. Enter LP-11 by driving the PPI for ULPS via enabling each of the lanes without performing any data transfer. Each lane can be enabled via a dedicated bit in the `DSI_0_CTRL` register. The DSI PHY must drive ‘11’ to the data lanes.
2. Clamp/isolate the PPI using secondary clamps and muxes by writing 0x8000 to address 0x0193E020. After reset, when DSI controller moves to LP-11, these clamps must be removed (see step 5 below). The DSI clamps are used to keep the PHY driving the link at a stable state (ULPS or LP-11) while the MDSS is powered up/down. However, when the SoC GCC applies a reset (GCC_MDSS_ARES) to MDSS during MDSS power-up, this reset might propagate to the PHY and eventually resets the PHY. This breaks the intention to keep driving the DSI link in stable state. To prevent the DSI PHY from getting reset, write 1 to address 0x0193E024 when DSI clamps are enabled.
3. Power collapse MDSS by enabling the MDSS power collapse clamps: configure the CLAMP_IO bit in the `GCC_MDSS_GDSCR` register (see Chapter Clock management (GCC)). The DSI PHY must continue driving ‘11’ to the data lanes. In addition, a DSI PLL and DSI PHY regulator shutdown can be initiated to further lower power consumption. The PHY regulator does not need to be on while the PHY is driving LP-11.
4. Wait until software requests data transfer through the DSI link.
5. Disable clamps:
   * Disable the MDSS clamps via the CLAMP_IO bit in the `GCC_MDSS_GDSCR` register.
   * Reset the entire MDSS, DSI controller included. As a result the DSI controller enters IDLE state.
   * Enable each lane via a dedicated bit in the `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
   * The PPI is driven now, but still clamped/isolated from PHY.
   * Disable PPI clamps and muxes by writing 0x0000 to address 0x0193E020, so that the PHY can follow DSI controller commands.
<!-- page 782 -->

* The DSI PHY would continue to drive each lane to LP-11. Software can trigger data transfer through DSI now. Software must also lock back the PLL, if it was collapsed at PHY level to save power. If the PHY regulator was shut down, it must be turned on and reconfigured.

### 4.1.2.11 DSI reset options

There are two types of reset available: hard reset and soft reset.

The difference between a soft reset and a hard reset is that the soft reset only resets the control logic but not the configuration registers. Following a hard reset, software must reprogram everything and set up the entire MDSS, DSI PHY included, because individual blocks cannot be reset using the hard reset. The hard reset resembles a power-on reset.

#### 4.1.2.11.1 DSI controller hard reset

The `GCC_MDSS_ARES` signal resets all DSI controller sub-blocks and registers. The `GCC_MDSS_ARES` hard reset can be configured via GCC registers. See section GCC reset controller, in chapter Clock management (GCC), for more information.

The `GCC_MDSS_ARES` is an asynchronous reset. The clocks to DSI controller must be off, while the reset is in progress.

#### 4.1.2.11.2 DSI controller soft reset

The DSI controller supports soft reset via register configuration.

If the soft reset is initiated during an active transfer, the filling of the ping pong FIFOs continues for that frame. Because pixels are still pulled from the FIFO on the PCLK domain, underflow is possible. To avoid underflow, software must wait until after the transfer is complete (if possible) before issuing a soft reset.

For DSI command mode transfers, both MDP and DSI controllers are required to be soft reset. Because the interface involves handshaking, both controllers require soft reset because they must remain in sync. For more information on MDP soft reset, see section MDP interrupts, in section Mobile Display Processor (MDP).

Soft reset must wait for memory transactions to complete, so that the system is not left in an indeterminate state. Hardware automatically handles this functionality, but software must wait until the soft reset is complete before moving on and reconfiguring.

To issue a soft reset to the DSI controller, the following steps must be followed:

1. Disable the controller by setting to 0 the following fields of the `DSI_0_CTRL` register:
   * `DSI_EN`
   * `VIDEO_MODE_EN`
   * `CMD_MODE_EN`
2. Enable all clock branches (clocks must be active when soft reset is applied) by setting to 1 the following fields of the `DSI_0_CLK_CTRL` register:
   * `DSI_FORCE_ON_DYN_AHBM_HCLK`
<!-- page 783 -->

   * `DSI_FORCE_ON_DYN_AHBS_HCLK`
   * `DSI_FORCE_ON_DYN_BYTECLK`
   * `DSI_FORCE_ON_DYN_PCLK`
   * `DSI_ESCCLK_ON`
3. Initialize soft reset by writing 1 to reset register `DSI_0_SOFT_RESET`.
4. Initialize soft reset to MDP. Refer Section MDP reset options, for more information.
5. Wait for a short time (1μs), or poll `DSI_0_STATUS` until it is 0.
6. Remove the soft reset by writing 0 to reset register `DSI_0_SOFT_RESET`.
7. For command mode operation: Enable the controller and command mode by writing 1 to fields `DSI_EN` and `CMD_MODE_EN` in `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
8. For video mode operation: Wait for the MDP timing engine to reach vertical blanking, by polling `MDP_INTF_1_LINE_COUNT` register until it falls into the vertical blanking region. For more information, see section Mobile Display Processor (MDP).

> [!NOTE]
> After bits `DLN0_EN` through `DLN3_EN` of `DSI_0_CTRL` register are set, the number of lanes enabled must not be modified. Otherwise, a reset is required.

> [!NOTE]
> If the controller is disabled while it is busy, a soft reset must be applied.

If the DSI controller is reset while the MDP timing engine is running, the controller must be re-enabled during vertical blanking. The controller can be reset any time when the MDP timing engine is idle.

After the DSI controller is reset, registers that reflect the internal state of the controller are reset. Those registers that reflect an external status (such as PHY lane status or PLL unlock) are not affected.

> [!NOTE]
> The DSI controller can only resume normal operation upon the first VSYNC after the soft reset. Depending on the location of the software reset, an entire frame time can be lost.

#### DSI PHY hard reset

The DSI controller reset interface to the PHY is split into three areas: lanes, PLL, and regulator. Each area can be reset individually. A global reset for all PHY areas is also available. The PHY reset driven by the DSI controller is a hard reset to the PHY.

The following configuration steps for global PHY reset must be followed:

1. Write 1 to the `PHY_SW_RESET` field in `DSI_0_PHY_SW_RESET` register.
2. After a delay, write 0 to the same `DSI_0_PHY_SW_RESET` register field.
3. The following configuration steps for individual PHY areas reset must be followed:
4. Write 1 to the `PHY_PLL_HW_RESET`, `PHY_LN_HW_RESET`, or `PHY_REGULATOR_HW_RESET` field in `DSI_0_PHY_SW_RESET` register.
<!-- page 784 -->

5. After a delay, write 0 to the `DSI_0_PHY_SW_RESET` register.

If a hard reset is applied to MDSS, the hard reset will also propagate to the DSI PHY.

### 4.1.2.12 DSI interrupts

The DSI controller provides a single interrupt signal (DSI0_IRQ) to system level.

There are two types of events that can trigger the DSI interrupt:
* Tasks complete detected
* Error detected

#### 4.1.2.12.1 DSI status interrupts

The status of each interrupt in normal operation can be read from the corresponding `*_STAT` fields in `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register. Table 4-83 lists the interrupts that occur during normal operation.

##### Table 4-83 DSI interrupts in normal operation

| Interrupt status | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `DSI_CMD_MODE_DMA_DONE_STAT` | A burst of command mode DMA packets is sent out of the protocol layer. |
| `DSI_CMD_MDP_STREAM0_DONE_STAT` | A frame of command mode stream0 is sent out of the protocol layer. |
| `DSI_CMD_MDP_STREAM1_DONE_STAT` | A frame of command mode stream1 is sent out of the protocol layer. |
| `DSI_CMD_MDP_STREAM2_DONE_STAT` | A frame of command mode stream2 is sent out of the protocol layer. |
| `DSI_VIDEO_MODE_DONE_STAT` | A frame of video mode stream is sent out of the protocol layer. |
| `DSI_BTA_DONE_STAT` | A bus turnaround (BTA) is completed at lane layer. |
| `DSI_CMD_MDP_DONE_STAT` | A frame of command mode stream, selected by the `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register, is sent out of protocol layer. |

The interrupts generation can be enabled via the corresponding `*_MASK` fields in `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register.

The interrupts can be cleared by writing once to the corresponding acknowledge (`*_AK`) fields in the `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register. Except for `DSI_VIDEO_MODE_DONE` interrupt, ensure that all other interrupts are cleared before triggering the same event. For example, the `DSI_BTA_DONE` interrupt must be cleared before triggering another BTA.

#### 4.1.2.12.2 DSI error interrupts

The `DSI_ERROR_STAT` field in `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register indicates when an error has occurred.
<!-- page 785 -->

##### Table 4-84 DSI controller detected errors

| Error | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `RDBK_DATA_ECC_ERR`[^1] | Single-bit ECC error in the read packet |
| `RDBK_DATA_MULTI_ECC_ERR`[^1] | Multi-bit ECC error in the read packet |
| `RDBK_DATA_CRC_ERR`[^1] | CRC error in the read packet |
| `RDBK_INCOMPLETE_PACKET_ERR`[^1] | Incomplete read packet |
| `ERROR_PACKET`[^1] | Error packet returned from peripheral |
| `LP_RX_TO`[^2] | Low-power reverse transmission timeout |
| `HS_TX_TO`[^2] | High-speed forward transmission timeout |
| `BTA_TO`[^2] | BTA timeout |
| `INTERLEAVE_OP_CONTENTION`[^2] | Interleave operation contention |
| `CMD_DMA_FIFO_UNDERFLOW`[^2] | Command mode DMA FIFO underflow |
| `CMD_MDP_FIFO_UNDERFLOW`[^2] | Command MDP FIFO underflow (failed to receive one complete line from MDP) |
| `DLN0_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW`[^2] | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 0 overflows |
| `DLN1_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW`[^2] | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 1 overflows |
| `DLN2_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW`[^2] | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 2 overflows |
| `DLN3_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW`[^2] | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 3 overflows |
| `DLN0_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW` | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 0 underflows |
| `DLN1_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW` | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane underflows |
| `DLN2_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW` | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 2 underflows |
| `DLN3_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW` | Lane layer high-speed FIFO for datalane 3 underflows |
| `DLN0_ERR_ESC`[^1] | Incorrect LP Rx escape entry |
| `DLN0_ERR_SYNC_ESC`[^1] | LP Rx data that is not byte-aligned |
| `DLN0_ERR_CONTROL`[^1] | Incorrect LP Rx state sequence |
| `DLN0_ERR_CONTENTION_LP0`[^1] | PHY level contention while datalane 0 is driven low |
| `DLN0_ERR_CONTENTION_LP1`[^1] | PHY level contention while datalane 0 is driven high |
| `DPHY_DSIPLL_UNLOCK`[^2] | DSI PLL unlocks |

[^1]: Error from reverse direction operation.
[^2]: Error, which requires DSI controller and PHY reset.

The corresponding `*_MASK` field in `DSI_0_ERR_INT_MASK0` register can be used to turn off any specific type of error generation.

The following status registers can be used to verify the cause of an error:
* `DSI_0_DLN0_PHY_ERR`
* `DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS`
<!-- page 786 -->

* `DSI_0_ACK_ERR_STATUS`
* `DSI_0_TIMEOUT_STATUS`
* `DSI_0_CLK_STATUS`

To recover from an error, the following steps must be completed:
* If the error is marked as an error from reverse direction operation in Table 4-84, then resend the read command to the DSI panel and peripheral.
* If the error is marked as an error which requires DSI controller and PHY reset in Table 4-84, then apply the proper reset, as explained in Section 4.1.2.11. (Note: The extracted text contains an unrelated fragment: "CCI is a small core operating at a low frequency (19.2 MHz). When the core is not in use software disables the CCI clocks from GCC to save the dynamic power.")

### 4.1.2.13 DSI data flow and operation basics

The DSI controller receives pixel data streams from the mobile display processor (MDP) or panel commands from memory, transforms the data into DSI packets, splits the packet data into byte streams, and finally sends each packet to a DSI video mode panel or command mode panel via the companion DSI PHY module.

Data propagates through the DSI application layer, protocol layer, and lane management layer before going out to the DSI PHY, as shown in Figure 4-100. After a DSI operation is triggered, an interrupt is generated when the operation is done (at the end of a frame).

#### Figure 4-100: DSI controller data flow

*Description:* This diagram shows the DSI protocol stack and data flow between the Application Processor (host) and the Peripheral (display panel). The stack contains four layers on both sides:
1. **Application Layer**: Handles "Pixel to Byte Packing Formats" and "Command Generation / Interpretation". Communicates with the Low Level Protocol layer using an 8-bit Data bus and Control lines.
2. **Low Level Protocol**: Handles "Packet Based Protocol" and "ECC and Checksum Generation and Testing". Communicates with the Lane Management layer using an 8-bit Data bus and Control lines.
3. **Lane Management**: Handles "Lane Distribution and Merging". Communicates with the PHY Layer using a `(N+1) x 8 bits` Data bus and Control lines.
4. **PHY Layer**: Handles "Start of Packet / End of Packet", "Serializer / Deserializer", "Clock Management (DDR)", and the "Electrical Layer (SLVS)".
The physical link between the two PHY layers consists of:
* A unidirectional High Speed Clock lane (from Application Processor to Peripheral).
* A bidirectional Data Lane 0 (High Speed Data, optionally Bidirectional in LP Mode).
* Unidirectional Data Lanes 1 to N (High Speed Unidirectional Data from Application Processor to Peripheral).

The DSI controller supports the following modes of operation:
* **Video mode**: The operation in which data transfers from the host to the display module take the form of a real-time pixel data stream.
<!-- page 787 -->

* **Command mode**: The operation in which data transactions primarily take the form of sending commands and data to a display module, which can include local registers and a frame buffer. The host uses the command mode to write and read the display module registers or frame buffer memory or both.
* **Interleaved mode**: When the DSI controller is running a video mode operation, it can perform also various command mode operations.

The general configuration sequence for DSI is as follows:

1. Set the clock frequency by configuring DSI PHY PLL and system clock control (GCC).
2. Configure the DSI PHY.
3. Configure the DSI controller.
4. Configure the modules upstream of the DSI controller (MDP, VBIF).
5. Trigger for DSI operation (panel initialization, pixel streaming, and others).
6. Enable EOT packet generation (optional, for panels that support EOT).

#### 4.1.2.13.1 DSI video mode operation

The DSI video mode operation supports the following features:
* Data formats: RGB565, RGB666 packed, RGB666 loosely packed, RGB888.
* All traffic modes: nonburst mode with sync pulses mode, nonburst mode with sync events mode, burst mode.

The video mode operation must be configured according to the display panel video parameters. The equations that show the relationship between the panel video parameters and the DSI and MDP register settings are provided in Section DSI video parameters and conversion equations. The video mode parameters and their usage are further presented in DSI video parameters.

To configure the video mode operation, follow these general steps:

1. Configure the video parameters:
   * Virtual channel (`VC` field), power mode for blanking regions (`BLLP_PWR_MODE` field), pixel format (`DST_FORMAT` field), and traffic mode (`TRAFFIC_MODE` field) in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_CTRL` register. It is recommended to set to 0 (high-speed mode) the `[HAS][HBP][HFP]_PWR_MODE` fields in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_CTRL` register, due to period length. The periods are potentially short and not long enough for the DSI link to switch back and forth between high-speed mode and low-power stop state.
   * Frame resolution in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_TOTAL` register.
   * Active region in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_ACTIVE_H` and `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_ACTIVE_V` registers.
   * HSync pulse in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_HSYNC` register.
   * VSync pulse in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC` and `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC_VPOS` registers.
   * Bit and channel order of output data in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_DATA_CTRL` register.
<!-- page 788 -->

2. Enable the DSI controller (`DSI_EN` field) and video mode operation (`VIDEO_MODE_EN` field) in `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
3. Configure the MDP to send out pixel streams through the DSI video interface. The `VIDEO_MODE_EN` field in `DSI_0_CTRL` register must be set to 1 before `MDP_INTF_1_TIMING_ENGINE_EN` register.
4. Once the DSI video mode operation is complete, to disable it, disable first the MDP timing engine and wait for the last frame to complete. There is no need to apply a soft reset to the DSI controller, but simply disable it via the `DSI_EN` and `VIDEO_MODE_EN` fields in `DSI_0_CTRL` register.

> [!NOTE]
> Horizontal regions (HSYNC pulse width, horizontal back porch, horizontal front porch, and total horizontal width) must be a certain multiple of pixels regarding lane configuration and pixel format (see Section DSI rules for accurate synchronization timing, for more information).

#### 4.1.2.13.2 DSI video parameters and conversion equations

This section provides information on the display panel video parameters and their conversion to DSI and MDP register settings, which are required for the video mode configuration steps described in Section DSI video mode operation.

Figure 4-101 shows the video mode parameters and their usage.

#### Figure 4-101: DSI video parameters

*Description:* This diagram illustrates how various horizontal and vertical video parameters define the layout of a video frame, including the active display window, horizontal blanking, and vertical blanking regions.
* Horizontal parameters (along the horizontal counter axis):
  - `VS_start`, `VS_end*`: Vertical sync start and end points on the horizontal counter. By default, `HS_start` aligns with `VS_start` (at coordinate 0), but the controller supports skewing.
  - `HS_start`: Start of the Horizontal Sync (HSYNC) pulse.
  - `HS_end`: End of the HSYNC pulse.
  - `Active_h_start`: Start of the active display area.
  - `Active_h_end`: End of the active display area.
  - `Video_h_total`: Total horizontal width including active area and blanking.
* Vertical parameters (along the vertical counter axis):
  - `VS_vpos_start`: Start of the Vertical Sync (VSYNC) signal.
  - `VS_vpos_end`: End of the VSYNC signal.
  - `Active_v_start`: Start of the active display area vertically.
  - `Active_v_end`: End of the active display area vertically.
  - `Video_v_total`: Total vertical height including active lines and blanking.
* Active Display Window:
  - Shaded area defined by horizontal range `[Active_h_start, Active_h_end]` and vertical range `[Active_v_start, Active_v_end]`.
* Coordinates:
  - Top-left corner is marked as `0,0`.
  - A pixel clock wave is shown at the top left.

The following panel video parameters are required when converting to DSI and MDP register settings:
* Display width = active width
<!-- page 789 -->

* Display height = active height
* HSYNC pulse width
* HBP
* HFP
* VSYNC pulse width
* VBP
* VFP
* HS period = (HSYNC pulse width + HBP + active width + HFP) pixels
* VS period = (VSYNC pulse width + VBP + active height + VFP) lines

Table 4-85 lists the equations to convert panel video parameters to DSI register settings.

##### Table 4-85 DSI registers related to video parameters

| Register | Video parameter | Equation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_ACTIVE_H` | Active width | `Active_h_end << 16 + Active_h_start` |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_ACTIVE_V` | Active height | `Active_v_end << 16 + Active_v_start` |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_TOTAL` | Total width and height | `Video_v_total << 16 + Video_h_total` |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_HSYNC` | HSYNC | `HS_end << 16 + HS_start` |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC` | VSYNC | `HS_end << 16 + VS_start` |
| `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_VSYNC_VPOS` | VSYNC | `VS_vpos_end << 16 + VS_vpos_start` |

Where:
* `HS_start = 0`
* `HS_end = HSYNC pulse width`
* `Active_h_start = HSYNC pulse width + HBP`
* `Active_h_end = HSYNC pulse width + HBP + active width`
* `Video_h_total = HS period - 1`
* `VS_start = 0`
* `VS_end = 0`
* `VS_vpos_start = 0`
* `VS_vpos_end = VSync pulse width`
* `Active_v_start = VSync pulse width + VBP`
* `Active_v_end = VSync pulse width + VBP + active height`
* `Video_v_total = VS period - 1`
<!-- page 790 -->

Table 4-86 lists the equations to convert panel video parameters to MDP register settings.

##### Table 4-86 MDP registers related to video parameters

| Register | Video parameter | Equation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `MDP_INTF_1_HSYNC_CTL` | Active width | `HS period << 16 + HSYNC pulse width` |
| `MDP_INTF_1_VSYNC_PERIOD_F0` | Active height | `HS period * VS period` |
| `MDP_INTF_1_VSYNC_PULSE_WIDTH_F0` | Total width and height | `HS period * VSync pulse width` |
| `MDP_INTF_1_DISPLAY_HCTL` | HSYNC | `(HS period - HFP - 1) << 16 + HBP + HS pulse width` |
| `MDP_INTF_1_DISPLAY_V_START_F0` | VSYNC | `HS period * (VBP + VS pulse width)` |
| `MDP_INTF_1_DISPLAY_V_END_F0` | VSYNC | `(VS period - VFP) * HS period - 1` |

### 4.1.2.14 DSI rules for accurate synchronization timing

Video mode peripherals require pixel data delivered in real time. The position of synchronization packets (VSS, VSE, HSS, HSE) in time might not meet the programmed video parameters in the pixel clock due to lane redistribution in the byte clock or word clock. There are recommended rules for video parameter configuration, further shown in Table 4-87 and Table 4-88, that cause the synchronization packets to start on lane 0, regardless of lane redistribution. These rules apply to the HSYNC pulse width, HBP, and H total. Width of the active window and HFP does not need to follow these rules.

##### Table 4-87 DSI minimum duration of HSA, HBP, and HFP

| Power mode | Minimum duration |
| :--- | :--- |
| Highspeed mode | Horizontal period * byte-per-pixel > 12 bytes |
| Lowpower mode | Horizontal period > time for the link to switch from HS mode to LP mode and back to HS mode. This time depends on the PHY timing parameters. |

##### Table 4-88 DSI length requirement of HSA, HBP, and H total

| Format | 1 lane | 2 lanes | 3 lanes | 4 lanes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| RGB565 | Any | Any | Multiple of 3 pixels | Multiple of 2 pixels |
| RGB666 packed | Multiple of 4 pixels | Multiple of 8 pixels | Multiple of 4 pixels | Multiple of 16 pixels |
| RGB666 loosely packed or RGB888 | Any | Multiple of 2 pixels | Any | Multiple of 4 pixels |


<!-- page 791 -->
#### 4.1.2.15 DSI video parameters double buffering (variable refresh)

In video mode, it is possible to change the refresh rate dynamically (by changing the video mode parameters). For example, the refresh rate can be slowed down by increasing the vertical blanking.

It is possible to double buffer the DSI controller video mode parameters, so they take effect on the next VSYNC signal. The configuration sequence is as follows:

1. Enable double buffering by setting the `DSI_0_DSI_TIMING_DB_MODE` register to 1.
2. Change the video parameters in any of the registers from .
3. Flush the register changes by write 1 to the `DSI_0_DSI_TIMING_FLUSH` register.
4. Make equivalent changes to the MDP timing engine registers (see section Mobile Display Processor (MDP), for more information).

##### DSI video mode packet data types override

The data type field for each type of video mode packet can be configured through the following registers:

* `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_SYNC_DATATYPE`
* `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_PIXEL_DATATYPE`
* `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_BLANKING_DATATYPE`

The default values of these registers follow the MIPI Alliance Specification v1.01 for Display Serial Interface. These settings can be changed, if a panel does not follow the specification and requires different values.

#### 4.1.2.16 DSI bus turn-around trigger

During a video mode operation, the `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_BTA_SW_TRIGGER` register can trigger a standalone BTA. The DSI controller issues the BTA in the next BLLP period.

An interrupt can be generated at the end of a BTA, by writing 1 to the `DSI_BTA_DONE_MASK` field of `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register. The status of the interrupt can be read from the `DSI_BTA_DONE_STAT` field. The interrupt status can be cleared by writing once in the `DSI_BTA_DONE_AK` field.

#### 4.1.2.16.1 DSI command mode operation

The DSI controller supports the following operations in command mode:

* Transmitting an image
* Transmitting commands stored in DMA memory
* Setting trigger methods
* TE triggering
* Transmitting a read command followed by a BTA
* Transmitting write commands followed by a BTA
<!-- page 792 -->
* Output pixel byte swap
* Interleaved command mode streams
* LP-11 insertion between lines

#### 4.1.2.16.2 DSI transmitting an image stream

The DSI controller supports the following data types for command mode operation: RGB111, RGB332, RGB444, RGB565, RGB666 (loosely packed), RGB888.

The general programming sequence for transmitting an image stream in command mode is as follows:

1. Configure the transmission:
   * Set pixel format and packing in `DST_FORMAT`, `R_SEL`, `G_SEL`, `B_SEL`, and `RGB_SWAP` fields in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register.
   * Enable the insertion of the DCS command at the first payload byte, if necessary, through the `INSERT_DCS_COMMAND` bit of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_DCS_CMD_CTRL` register.
   * Set the virtual channel for each stream (stream 0, stream 1, and stream 2) in the `*_VC` fields of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM0_CTRL`, `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM1_CTRL`, and `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM2_CTRL` registers.
   * Set the resolution for each stream (stream 0, stream 1, and stream 2) in the `*_V_TOTAL` and `*_H_TOTAL` fields of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM0_TOTAL`, `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM1_TOTAL`, and `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_STREAM2_TOTAL` registers.
   * Set the trigger method as explained in Section DSI command MDP stream trigger methods. In order for MDP to be able to push data to the DSI controller anytime, set the `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field of `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register to ‘none’.
2. Enable the DSI controller in command mode via the `CMD_MODE_EN` and `DSI_EN` bits of `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
3. Configure MDP to send data out of the DSI command mode interface.
4. Trigger the MDP to send out one frame.

> [!NOTE]
> The following sections include additional configuration sequences for command mode operation features, which can be included in the general programming sequence outlined above.
<!-- page 793 -->
#### 4.1.2.16.3 DSI command MDP stream trigger methods

The `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register controls the triggering methods to send a command mode MDP stream frame or a command mode DMA data burst.

Table 4-89 lists the trigger method for a single image stream.

##### Table 4-89 DSI trigger methods

| Step | Configuration | Register |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Free running (recommended)** | | |
| 1 | Start the MDP to send one frame. | See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP). |
| **Software trigger (for debug purpose only)** | | |
| 1 | Select software trigger. | `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 2 | Select the stream to trigger (stream 0, stream 1, or stream 2). | `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 3 | Start the MDP to fetch one frame. | See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP). |
| 4 | Start an MDP trigger. | `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_MDP_SW_TRIGGER` register. |
| **TE trigger (recommended when panel returns TE through the DSI link)** | | |
| 1 | Select TE trigger. | `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 2 | Select the stream to trigger (stream 0, stream 1, or stream 2). | `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 3 | When DSI receives a TE from the panel, it passes the TE to MDP. Configure the MDP tear check logic for frame output synchronization to the TE and start MDP to send one frame. | See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP). |
| **Software plus TE trigger (recommended when panel returns TE through the DSI link)** | | |
| 1 | Select software trigger and TE. | `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 2 | Select the stream to trigger (stream 0, stream 1, or stream 2). | `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 3 | Start the MDP to fetch one frame. | See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP). |
| 4 | Start an MDP trigger. The frame is sent when TE is received and when the link is idle. | `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_MDP_SW_TRIGGER` register. |
<!-- page 794 -->
When the DSI controller is used to drive two or three DSI panels with a DSI hub in between, two or three image streams need to be configured. Each stream must be synchronized with the TE signal of the corresponding panel through the MDP tear check logic (see section Mobile Display Processor (MDP)). If the trigger of any one of the streams needs to be monitored by the DSI controller (non-free-running), then the following sequence must be followed:

1. Select the stream to trigger in non free running mode via the `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. Ensure that the other stream is free-running.
2. Start the MDP to fetch one frame for either stream. See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP).
3. Complete the steps described in for the other stream selected in step 1.

#### 4.1.2.16.4 DSI external TE trigger

When external trigger (TE signal) comes through a GPIO instead of the DSI link, it is generally recommended to use the MDP tear check logic instead of the DSI controller to detect the TE signal. However, the DSI controller can be used to detect whether the TE signal contains both HSYNC and VSync information. Otherwise, use the MDP to detect the external TE signal.

For the cases when DSI controller is used to detect TE, the configuration steps from Table 4-90 must be followed.

##### Table 4-90 DSI external triggers

| Step | Configuration | Register |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Select TE from a dedicated pin. | `TE_SEL` bit in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register. |
| 2 | Select the pin. | `EXT_TE_MUX` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 3 | Select the signal polarity. | `EXT_TE_POL` bit in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 4 | Select when to trigger: | |
| 4a | If the signal contains only VSync, set the register field to 0. | `EXT_TE_MODE` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 4b | If the signal contains VSync and HSYNC, then a trigger is required at VSync. Set the register field to 3. | `EXT_TE_MODE` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 4c | Determine a pulse at VSync or HSYNC by the pulse width. Set the threshold of pulse width detection. | `DSI_0_EXT_TE_PULSE_DETECT_CTRL` register. |
| 4d | If the signal contains VSync and HSYNC and a trigger is required at a particular line, set the register field to 2 (using the edge detection method to detect each line). | `EXT_TE_MODE` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 4e | Set the line to trigger data transmission. | `EXT_TE_HSYNC_TRIG_CNT` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |
| 4f | Set the total number of HSYNC. | `EXT_TE_HSYNC_TOTAL` field in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. |

#### 4.1.2.16.5 DSI TE triggering examples

This section outlines general operation sequences for tearing effect (TE) triggering.

##### Example 1: Software plus TE trigger mode

This is an example for sending one frame by TE through the DSI link.

1. Configure the DSI controller to transmit an image stream, as described in Section 4.1.2.16.2.
2. Initialize the display panel and configures the TE-reporting on the panel side.
3. If the `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register is set to TE+software, the DSI controller performs back-to-back BTA to receive the TE sequence from the panel (when it is triggered).
4. The panel accepts the DCS commands `set_tear_on`, `set_tear_at_line_on`, and `set_tear_off`. See the panel specification (provided by vendor), and MIPI DCS Specification.
5. Select software trigger+TE through the `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register.
6. Enable the DSI controller in command mode via the `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
7. Trigger the MDP for one frame. MDP starts fetching a frame from memory.
8. The frame is sent out to the DSI controller, when MDP receives the TE from the DSI controller.
9. Trigger the DSI so that it issues BTA to the panel and waits for the panel to return a TE sequence through the DSI link. Set to 1 the `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_MDP_SW_TRIGGER` register.
10. Poll for a DONE interrupt. See Section CCI can be reset in two ways, by using the:, for more information.

##### Example 2: TE trigger mode

This is an example for sending continuous frames triggered by TE through the DSI link.

1. Configure the DSI controller to transmit an image stream, as described in Section 4.1.2.16.2.
2. Initialize the display panel and configures the TE-reporting on the panel side.
3. With `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` registers set to TE, the DSI controller automatically performs back-to-back BTA to receive the TE sequence from the panel.
4. The panel accepts the DCS commands `set_tear_on`, `set_tear_at_line_on`, and `set_tear_off`. See the panel specification (provided by vendor), and MIPI DCS Specification.
5. Select TE through the `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register.
6. Enable the DSI controller in command mode via the `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
7. Trigger the MDP for one frame. MDP starts fetching a frame from memory.
8. The frame is sent out to the DSI controller, when MDP receives the TE from the DSI controller.
<!-- page 796 -->
9. Poll for a DONE interrupt. See Section CCI can be reset in two ways, by using the:, for more information.
10. Repeatedly trigger MDP and poll for DMA_P done (see section Mobile Display Processor (MDP)), because the DSI controller automatically polls TE from the panel by issuing BTA after every frame.

##### Example 3: TE signal from external pin

This is an example for using the external TE driven by panel and connected to the external VSYNC pin (`MDP_VSYNC_P`).

A short packet is interleaved with stream 0; with external active high TE trigger signal to trigger both. It is recommended to use MDP to detect the external TE trigger. The external TE trigger is called external VSync in MDP perspective. See section Mobile Display Processor (MDP), for more information.

1. Configure the DSI controller to transmit an image stream, as described in Section 4.1.2.16.2.
2. Configure the commands to be sent from DMA memory, as described in Section 4.1.2.16.7.
3. Configure the external trigger settings in `DSI_0_EXT_MUX` register. Set to 0 for a Vsync edge detection on the rising edge.
4. Trigger the MDP for one frame. MDP starts fetching a frame from memory.
5. The frame is sent out to the DSI controller, when MDP receives the TE from the DSI controller.

#### 4.1.2.16.6 DSI command MDP burst mode

By default, the DSI controller arbitrates the DMA commands (with or without embedded BTA) and the lines of a frame in command mode using a round-robin scheme. If the DMA command is triggered in the middle of a frame, then it is sent at the end of the current line.

If the `BURST_MODE` bit in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL2` register is set to 1, the controller sends out the whole frame in one high-speed burst and sends out the DMA command at the end of frame.

If the `BURST_MODE` bit is set to 0 (default), the DMA command is sent out in the middle of the frame.

As long as the MDP sends a continuous pixel stream to the DSI controller, each frame is sent out in one high-speed burst. Tear check or no memory bandwidth issues are not expected to throttle the MDP while it is sending a continuous pixel stream.
<!-- page 797 -->
Do not use the command MDP burst mode feature in any of the following scenarios:

* Running concurrent video mode and command mode MDP pixel streams.
* Running multiple command mode MDP pixel streams and command DMA trigger mode is set to SOF and EOF.

It is recommended to set the `BURST_MODE` bit to 1 in command mode frame updates. This reduces the LP-11 transitions during a frame transfer.

#### 4.1.2.16.7 DSI transmitting commands from DMA memory

The following general configuration steps must be followed when transmitting commands stored in DMA memory:

1. Configure the DMA control registers:
   * Select embedded mode (`EMBEDDED_MODE` field), set virtual channel (`VC` field), and select power mode (`POWER_MODE` field) in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` register.
   * Set 64-bit aligned base address of command buffer in bytes in `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_OFFSET` register.
   * Set command buffer length in bytes (must be multiple of 4) in `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` register.
   * Select the trigger method via the `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register.
2. Enable the DSI controller in command mode (if not yet enabled) via the `DSI_0_CTRL` register.
3. Trigger command mode DMA operation (if necessary for the selected trigger method).

After the DMA operation is triggered, hardware fetches the commands at the `DSI_DMA_CMD_OFFSET` and loads them into an internal FIFO. It is recommended that:

* The DMA packet payload size must be less than the FIFO size - 4 bytes. The command DMA FIFO size is 512 bytes.
* The number of commands set in `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` register must be below or equal to the FIFO size.
* The `READ_WATERMARK` field in `DSI_0_DMA_FIFO_CTRL` register must be set to the maximum value allowed.
* The DSI controller reads data out from the DMA FIFO when one of the follow condition is met:
  * When the entire DMA packet is loaded in the FIFO, or
  * When the FIFO fill level is above the read watermark

The FIFO must not run out of data in the middle of a DMA packet, otherwise underflow occurs. To avoid underflow, the read watermark should be set to be greater than or equal to the packet size. To send packets that are larger than the FIFO size, there must be sufficient memory bandwidth to fill up the FIFO before underrun.
<!-- page 798 -->
If a command is larger than the size of the internal FIFO, user can control the read-write data flow of the FIFO by configuring FIFO watermarks in the `DSI_0_DMA_FIFO_CTRL` register. Based on the FIFO watermark setting in `WRITE_WATERMARK` field, the MDP core clock must be faster than PCLK at the following factors:

* For `WRITE_WATERMARK` = 0 (default), MDP core clock > 3/32 PCLK
* For `WRITE_WATERMARK` = 1, MDP core clock > 3/16 PCLK
* For `WRITE_WATERMARK` = 2, MDP core clock > 3/8 PCLK
* For `WRITE_WATERMARK` = 3, MDP core clock > 3/4 PCLK

The VBIF priority of the command DMA access can be configured through the `PRIORITY` field in `DSI_0_VBIF_CTRL` register.

The command DMA buffer offset (configurable in `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_OFFSET` register) must be 64-byte aligned.

##### DSI command DMA FIFO for VBIF bypass

In typical operation, the DSI controller fetches DMA commands through the MDP VBIF interface. When software triggers command DMA, the DMA data is fetched from memory.

In some cases, the latency can be long between data fetches. A TPG DMA FIFO in the DSI controller can be used to bypass the VBIF interface. The user can prefill the DMA data in the TPG FIFO through the AHB bus (that is, through direct register writes) before triggering the command DMA operation.

The TPG DMA FIFO size is 64 bytes. The number of valid words (64 bits per word) can be read back from the `WORD_COUNT` field in `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_STATUS` register. To reset the FIFO, write 1 followed by 0 to the `FIFO_RESET` bit of `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_RESET` register.

There are two possible programming modes for writing the TPG DMA FIFO.

##### Mode 0 (default) programming sequence

In mode 0, the TPG DMA FIFO is written through the `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL`, `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL2`, and `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_WRITE_TRIGGER` registers.

1. Enable the TPG DMA FIFO:
   a. Set the `CMD_DMA_TPG_EN` bit in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 1.
   b. Set the `TPG_DMA_FIFO_MODE` field in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 0.
   c. Set the `CMD_DMA_PATTERN_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 3.
2. Preload the DMA command to the TPG DMA FIFO:
   a. Program 64 bits of the DMA command in the `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL`, `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL2` registers.
<!-- page 799 -->
   b. Trigger the FIFO write by writing to the `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_WRITE_TRIGGER` register.
   Software repeats steps 1 and 2 until all DMA commands are written to the FIFO.
3. Configure the command DMA operation as in normal operation:
   a. Program the `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` register.
   b. Program the `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` register.
4. Trigger the command DMA operation as in normal operation.

##### Mode 0 (default) example

Use a software trigger to trigger high-speed transmission of one long packet of datatype 0x39, WC = 5 bytes and payload 0x2A, 0x00, 0x00, 0x04, and 0xFF to virtual channel 0 in HS mode, and using one data lane.

The DSI register settings are as follows:

* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` = 0x00030002
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x40390005
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL2` = 0x0400002A
* `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_WRITE_TRIGGER` = 1
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x000000FF
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL2` = 0x00000000
* `DSI_0_TPG_DMA_FIFO_WRITE_TRIGGER` = 1
* `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` = 0x10000000
* `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` = 0xC
* `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL = 0x4`
* `DSI_0_CTRL` = 0x115
* `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_DMA_SW_TRIGGER` = 1 trigger

##### Mode 1 (recommended) programming sequence

In mode 1, the TPG DMA FIFO is written through the `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` register only.

1. Enable the TPG CMD DMA FIFO:
   a. Set the `CMD_DMA_TPG_EN` bit in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 1.
   b. Set the `TPG_DMA_FIFO_MODE` field in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 1.
   c. Set the `CMD_DMA_PATTERN_SEL` field in `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` register to 3.
2. Preload the DMA command to the TPG DMA FIFO:
<!-- page 800 -->
Program 32 bits of the DMA command in the `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` register. There must be an even number of writes to this register. If the total number of valid commands is an odd number of DWORDs (32 bits), do an extra write to this register with the value of 0.
3. Configure the command DMA operation as in normal operation:
   a. Program the `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` register.
   b. Program the `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` register.
4. Trigger the command DMA operation as in normal operation.

##### Mode 1 (recommended) example

Use a software trigger to trigger high-speed transmission of one long packet of datatype 0x39, WC = 5 bytes and payload 0x2A, 0x00, 0x00, 0x04, and 0xFF to virtual channel 0 in HS mode, and using one data lane.

The DSI register settings are as follows:

* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CTRL` = 0x00030006
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x40390005
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x0400002A
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x000000FF
* `DSI_0_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` = 0x00000000
* `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` = 0x10000000
* `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` = 0xC
* `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` = 0x4
* `DSI_0_CTRL` = 0x115
* `DSI_0_CMD_MODE_DMA_SW_TRIGGER` = 1 trigger

#### 4.1.2.16.8 DSI transmitting commands followed by a BTA

To transmit a read command followed by a BTA, the command must be stored as the last command in the command buffer, with the BTA bit set to 1. The command packing format in memory is listed in Table 4-91.

##### Table 4-91 DSI command packing format in memory

###### Command Header (32-bit DWORD)

| 31 | 30 | 29 | 28 - 24 | 23 - 22 | 21 - 16 | 15 - 0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| QW | S/L | BTA | - | VC | DATA TYPE | WC |

###### Command Payload (Byte Layout)

| Byte 3 | Byte 2 | Byte 1 | Byte 0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DATA3 | DATA2 | DATA1 | DATA0 |
| ... | ... | ... | ... |
| DATA(WC-1) | DATA(WC-2) | DATA(WC-3) | DATA(WC-4) |




<!-- page 801 -->
The following legend applies to:
* **QW (queue-wait)**: When set to 0 indicates not the last packet of the current transfer. When set to 1 indicates the last packet of the current transfer. This bit is legacy mode and must not be used.
* **S/L packet type**: When set to 0 indicates short packet. When set to 1 indicates long packet.
* **BTA**: When set to 0 indicates no BTA request. When set to 1 indicates BTA request after sending the current packet. This bit must be set only for the last packet.

After the command is stored as the last command, the sequence from Section 4.1.2.16.7 can be completed.

The peripheral packets are stored in DSI_0_RDBK_DATA0 to DSI_0_RDBK_DATA3 registers. As they are read, the packets shift from DSI_0_RDBK_DATA0 -> DATA1 -> DATA2 -> DSI_0_RDBK_DATA3.

Similar to read commands, when a write command followed by a BTA must be transmitted, the BTA bit must be set to 1 for the last command in the command buffer.

### 4.1.2.16.9 DSI command DMA trigger methods

The DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL register controls the triggering methods to send a command mode DMA data burst. Refer to Table 4-92.

#### Table 4-92 DSI command DMA trigger methods

| Method | Register configuration | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Software | DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL [COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL] = 4<br>and<br>DSI_0_CMD_MODE_DMA_SW_TRIGGER = 1 | The command mode DMA packet is triggered by software. |
| SOF | DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL [COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL] = 1<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER] = 0<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL] = 0, 1 or 2 | The command mode DMA packet is sent right before the start of the command mode frame update of stream 0, 1, or 2.^(1) |
| EOF | DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL [COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL] = 1<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER] = 1<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL] = 0, 1 or 2 | The command mode DMA packet is sent right after the end of the command mode frame update.^(1) |
| Software + SOF | DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL [COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL] = 5<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER] = 0<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL] = 0, 1 or 2<br>and<br>DSI_0_CMD_MODE_DMA_SW_TRIGGER = 1 | After software trigger, the command mode DMA packet is sent right before the next start of command mode frame update.^(1) |
<!-- page 802 -->
#### Table 4-92 DSI command DMA trigger methods (continued)

| Method | Register configuration | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Software + EOF | DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL [COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL] = 5<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER] = 1<br>[COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL] = 0, 1 or 2<br>and<br>DSI_0_CMD_MODE_DMA_SW_TRIGGER = 1 | After software trigger, the command mode DMA packet is sent right after the next end of command mode frame update.^(1) |

^(1) DMA packet is not sent out, if there is no frame update.

The arbitration between DMA packets and pixel packets is done on a line basis. When a command mode DMA burst is triggered using a software trigger in the middle of a command mode frame transfer (see the software method in Table 4-92), the DMA packets are sent after the end of the current line. When a command mode DMA burst is triggered using a software trigger in the middle of a video mode frame transfer, the DMA packet is sent at the beginning of the next BLLP period (in the vertical blanking region).

When a DMA packet is sent during video mode operation, the transfer time of the packet must fit within one BLLP period (or simply one line time). If the DMA packet contains a read command, which needs to be followed by BTA, the transfer time of the panel read response must be taken into account.

The DMA packet transfer time in HS mode is equal to the $packet\_size\_in\_bits \times bitclk\_period$.

The DMA packet transfer time in LP mode is equal to the $packet\_size\_in\_bits \times 2 \times host\_Tlpx$, where one $Tlpx$ is 1 ESC_CLK period.

The response time from panel to host is equal to the $packet\_size \times 2 \times panel\_Tlpx + panel\_latency\_to\_respond$.

The panel $Tlpx$ can be different from the host $Tlpx$. The ratio between the panel $Tlpx$ and the host $Tlpx$ must be within the following range: [2/3, 3/2].

The transition time between HS and LP is basically the sum of all the HS-related PHY timing parameters.

A DMA trigger exists to control the transfer time of command DMA packets. The `BLOCK_DMA_WITHIN_FRAME` field in `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register enables this feature. Upon a DMA request, the following behavior can be expected:
* If a DMA request occurs in the middle of a frame, it is executed at the end of the frame.
* If a DMA request occurs when there are no frames transferring, it is executed right away.
* If a DMA request and start of frame occur at the same time, then the order of execution depends on the priority set in the `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER` field of `DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL` register.
<!-- page 803 -->
### 4.1.2.16.10 DSI output pixel byte swap

The output pixel byte swap feature flips the output pixel byte order. For example, the pixel packing for RGB565 differs for command mode and video mode. In command mode, to mimic the pixel packing of RGB565 video mode, this feature can be enabled via the `BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP` bit of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register.

In case the byte swap feature is used, it must be included in the sequence in Section 4.1.2.16.2.

### 4.1.2.16.11 DSI interleaved command mode streams

The MDP can send up to three different pixel streams to the DSI controller. Different streams are sent to different command mode panels. Each panel can require different pixel formats, resolutions, and datatypes.

When all three-command mode streams are to be interleaved, the following general configuration steps must be followed:

1. Separate stream 1 settings from stream 0 by setting the `STREAM1_DST_FORMAT_SEL` field in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register to 1.
2. Configure stream 1 parameters:
   a. Pixel format and data packing in `[R][G][B]_SEL1`, `RGB_SWAP1`, `BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP1`, and `DST_FORMAT1` fields of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register.
   b. DCS command insertion via the `INSERT_DCS_COMMAND2` field of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_DCS_CMD_CTRL` register.
3. Configure stream 2 parameters:
   a. Pixel format and data packing in `[R][G][B]_SEL2`, `RGB_SWAP2`, `BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP2`, and `DST_FORMAT2` fields of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL2` register.
   b. DCS command insertion via the `STREAM2_INSERT_DCS_COMMAND` field of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_DCS_CMD_CTRL` register.
4. Program the DSI controller, following the sequence in Section 4.1.2.16.2.
5. Program MDP to send out three command mode streams from display interface 1.
6. Trigger a frame for command mode stream 0 from display interface 1.
7. Trigger a frame for command mode stream 1 from display interface 1.
8. Trigger a frame for command mode stream 2 from display interface 1.
9. Poll for DONE interrupts for stream 0, stream 1, and stream 2. See Section 4.1.2.12, for more details on interrupts.
<!-- page 804 -->
#### DSI LP-11 insertion between lines

> [!NOTE]
> The support of this feature is panel-dependent. For some panels, there could be no sufficient time to transition to LP11 and back to normal state.

Some panels require that the DSI link returns to the low-power stop state (LP-11) after transmission of every line. If a panel requires that the DSI link returns to LP-11, then the LP-11 insertion between lines feature can be enabled. A PCLK timer in the application layer is used to add a delay between lines. To ensure the link returns to LP-11 between lines, the timer must be set to a certain value. The value must be greater than the time required for the link to transition from high-speed mode to the LP-11 state. Typical transition time is less than 2μs. It is recommended to program the timer to be greater than 2μs.

The time required for the link to transition from high-speed mode to LP-11 state equals the sum of delay required by panel + time for PHY to start a new data transmission.

To enable the LP-11 insertion between lines feature, the following steps must be included in the command mode sequence from Section 4.1.2.16.2:

1. Set the timeout in PCLK cycles in the `LENGTH` field of the `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_IDLE_CTRL` register.
2. Set to 1 the `EN` bit in the same register.

### 4.1.2.16.12 DSI large DMA data break-up

This feature enables automatic break-up of DMA command data into multiple smaller packets of equal size. This is added for the use case where a command larger than the DMA FIFO size needs to be sent to the panel. Each packet is sent only when it is loaded in the FIFO, or if it is above the read watermark.

The DSI controller supports this feature for large command, which is divisible by the write-watermark, using non embedded mode (that is, the packet header information is set in register instead of memory).

For example, a 42-KB command can be broken up into 336 packets of 128-bytes payload each, using the following settings:

1. Set to 128 (decimal) the `WC` field in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_DMA_CTRL` register.
2. Set to 1 (for long packet) the `PACKET_TYPE` bit in the same register.
3. Select non-embedded mode by writing 0 in the `EMBEDDED_MODE` bit in the same register.
4. Set to 43008 (for 42KB) the `DSI_0_DMA_CMD_LENGTH` register.
5. Trigger DSI command DMA operation once.

### 4.1.2.16.13 DSI interleaved video and command mode operation

When the DSI controller is running a video mode operation, it can perform command mode operations, such as sending DMA packets, sending pixel packets from a different stream to a command mode panel, or performing BTA. The command mode operations are performed during BLLP periods (BLLP = blanking period during VSA, VBP, and VFP lines):
<!-- page 805 -->
1. Set PCLK to BYTE_CLK ratio according to the video mode pixel format (see Section DSI clock configuration).
2. Start video mode operation (see Section DSI video mode operation).
3. Configure and trigger command mode operation, as required (see Section DSI command mode operation).

The following conditions must be met:
1. The time it takes to transmit the command burst fits into one BLLP period (that is, either A or B from the following list):
   a. A: $active\_width \times video\_mode\_pixel\_depth > command\_DMA\_length\_in\_bytes$.
   b. B: $active\_width \times video\_mode\_pixel\_depth > command\_mode\_pixel\_depth \times command\_mode\_stream\_width \times interleave\_max$, where $interleave\_max$ is the setting of `INTERLEAVE_MAX` field in `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register.
2. Line split mode must be used, if the pixel depth of the command mode pixel stream is lower than the video mode stream. See Section DSI line split mode, for more details.

> [!NOTE]
> Transfer of DMA packet in LP mode following by an embedded BTA in video mode is not supported, if the LP transfer duration is longer than one line time.

> [!NOTE]
> The MDP must be configured to supply two pixel streams to the DSI controller: one stream through the video mode interface, and another stream through the DSI command mode interface.

### 4.1.2.16.14 DSI maximum size of DMA or read packet in video mode

The transfer of command DMA packets or BTA is done during the BLLP period. BLLP is one line worth of blanking in the vertical blanking. The transfer of the DMA packet or BTA starts right after the HSYNC packet and must finish before the next HSYNC. Also, after transfer of the DMA packet or BTA, there must be enough time for the link to transit to LP-11 (stopstate) before the next HSYNC.

> [!NOTE]
> Only one DMA packet is allowed to be sent per trigger and the maximum payload size is 256 bytes.

The maximum DMA/BTA transfer time is the following:

$DMA/BTA\_transfer\_time \le hsync\_period - hsync\_packet\_transfer\_time - LP\_to\_HS\_transition\_time$, where:
* **hsync_packet_transfer_time**:
  * $4\_bytes / (num\_lanes \times byte\_clk\_period)$, if `VIDEO_TRAFFIC_MODE` field in `DSI_0_VIDEO_MODE_CTRL` register = burst mode or nonburst mode with sync events.
  * $hsync\_pulse\_width\_in\_pclk \times pclk\_period$, if `VIDEO_TRAFFIC_MODE` field = nonburst sync pulses mode.
* **LP_to_HS transition time**: (continued on next page)
<!-- page 806 -->
  * $4\mu s$, if DMA power mode is set to HS.
  * $2\mu s$, for all other cases.
* **DMA_transfer_time**:
  * $dma\_packet\_size\_in\_bytes \times byte\_clk\_period$, if DMA packet is sent in HS mode.
  * $(14 + dma\_packet\_size\_in\_bits \times 2) \times esc\_clk\_period$, if DMA packet is sent in LP mode.
* **BTA_transfer_time** = $(24 + panel\_read\_response\_size\_in\_bits \times 2) \times esc\_clk\_period$.
  * **panel_read_response**:
    * $16 \times esc\_clk\_period$, if panel responds with an acknowledge message.
    * $32 \times esc\_clk\_period$, if panel responds with a short packet, which is 32 bits long.
    * $(48 + payload\_in\_bits \times 2) \times esc\_clk\_period$, if panel responds with a long packet with a known size of payload.

### 4.1.2.16.15 DSI line split mode

Line split mode divides a command mode stream line into 64-pixel packets (or less than a 64-pixel packet for the end of a line). This process is useful in the following interleaved video and command mode operation cases:
* When command mode and video mode operations are both enabled, and the command mode pixel depth is smaller than the video mode pixel depth.
* When command mode pixel stream width is wider than the video mode horizontal total.

The line split mode can be enabled by setting to 1 the `LINE_SPLIT` field of `DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL` register. It must be done before the configuration of video and command modes.

## 4.1.2.17 DSI additional packet operations

### 4.1.2.17.1 DSI AES counter packet support

Encrypted digital data can be transferred over DSI. If data encryption uses 128-bit AES operating in counter (CTR) mode, as specified in HDCP 2.1 specification, then ensure that a counter is sent. The required counter must be sent as a generic long write packet in high-speed mode. The counter value must contain `{streamCtr[31:0], inputCtr[63:0], and message_id[7:0]}`. The DSI controller must only send out the counter packet, if the frame is encrypted. When pixel data is encrypted, it is transferred at 24 bits per PCLK cycle from the MDP to the DSI controller.

Configure the following fields in `DSI_0_AES_CTRL` register to enable AES counter packet generation:
* For a video mode panel: `AES_EN` = 1, and `AES_SEL` = 0.
* For a command mode panel: `AES_EN` = 1, and `AES_SEL` = 1.
<!-- page 807 -->
### DSI read back packets

The datatype field for each type of packets read back from the panel can be configured through the following registers:
* `DSI_0_RDBK_DATATYPE0`
* `DSI_0_RDBK_DATATYPE1`

The default values of these registers follow the MIPI Alliance Specification v1.01 for Display Serial Interface. These settings can be changed, if a panel does not follow the specification and requires different values.

The `RDBK_DATA_CLR` field in `DSI_0_RDBK_DATA_CTRL` register clears the read-data stored in `DSI_0_RDBK_DATA3` through `DSI_0_RDBK_DATA0` registers. The number of read data returned from the DSI panel can be read from the `RDBK_DATA_COUNT` field of `DSI_0_RDBK_DATA_CTRL` register.

### DSI end of transmission (EOT) packet

The EOT packet is used to indicate the end of an HS transmission. It enhances the overall system reliability. It is recommended to enable insertion of EOT packet for panels that support this feature. To enable EOT packet generation, set the `TX_EOT_APPEND` bit in `DSI_0_EOT_PACKET_CTRL` register to 1. The EOT packet content can be configured in `DSI_0_EOT_PACKET` register.

### DSI packet byte flip

At the protocol layer, the output byte endian order is controlled in three different ways to support panels that are not compliant with MIPI Alliance Specification for Display Serial Interface.

The `PACKET_BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP` configuration field in `DSI_0_CTRL` register provides the following options:
* **0**: Bit order is as specified in MIPI Alliance Specification for Display Serial Interface.
* **1**: Flip the bit order of each byte in the payload.
* **2**: Flip the bit order of each byte in the entire packet.

### 4.1.2.17.2 DSI error detection

DSI controller provides error detection capabilities for the following cases (with registers containing the kind of error that has occurred):
* Operation never completes (`DSI_0_STATUS` register)
* Contention of video mode and command mode packets (`DSI_0_STATUS` register)
* Video mode packet drop (`DSI_0_STATUS` register)
* Internal FIFO overflow or underflow (`DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS` register)
* DSI panel (or peripheral) returns an error packet (`DSI_0_ACK_ERR_STATUS` register)
* DSI lanes stuck at a certain state (`DSI_0_LANE_STATUS` register)
<!-- page 808 -->
* Error detected by PHY layer (`DSI_0_PHY_ERR` register)
* Operation times out (`DSI_0_TIMEOUT_STATUS` register)
* DSI PHY PLL unlocks (`DSI_0_CLK_STATUS` register)

When an interrupt is generated for DSI controller, check the `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register to see what kind of event has generated the interrupt. For more details on error interrupts, see Section DSI error interrupts.

If the `DSI_ERROR_STAT` bit in `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register is set to 1, check the `DSI_0_ERR_INT_MASK0` register to see what event is allowed to generate an error interrupt.

The DSI PHY error register (`DSI_0_DLN0_PHY_ERR`) reports errors returned from the PHY. If the mask bit for a specific error is set to 1, the turn request is de-asserted, if the corresponding error occurs. The DSI controller waits for the link to return to a forward stop state.

> [!NOTE]
> Turn request abort or interrupt is generated, if the mask fields in `DSI_0_DLN0_PHY_ERR` register are set to 1. Interrupt is generated, if the mask fields in `DSI_0_INT_CTRL` register are set to 1. Error status is generated, if the mask fields in `DSI_0_ERR_INT_MASK0` register are set to 0.

When a `DLN*_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW` or `DLN*_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW` field in `DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS` register is set (* = 0 to 3), verify the following:
* Ratio between PCLK and BYTE_CLK (see DSI clock configuration).
* Frame size configuration between the MDP and the DSI controller.
* If a read command is sent in the middle of video mode operation, check the HSYNC period and see whether it is greater than 8us. If it is not, then the frame width is probably too short for the read command and panel read response to complete within one line time.

### 4.1.2.17.3 DSI timeout timers

The following must be considered for the timeouts and watchdog that the software must maintain on the DSI controller:
* If a frame is triggered to be sent in video or command mode, the fastest it can complete is about the total $number\_of\_pixels \times pclk$. For example, if the clocks are configured for 60 Hz (that is, 60 frames per second), a frame is sent out in about 16.6ms.
* If a burst of DMA command packets is triggered, the minimum time required to complete the transfer is as follows:
  * High-speed data transmission = $size\_of\_the\_burst \times byte\_clk / number\_of\_data\_lanes$.
  * Low-power data transmission = $size\_of\_the\_burst \times esc\_clk$.

> [!NOTE]
> Some overhead is added for packet header and footer, and transmission start and stop time. Some operations depend on memory access latencies. Memory latency is not taken into account in the equations above.
<!-- page 809 -->
The DSI controller includes a timeout timer, which ensure the following types of operations run for a long time:
* High-speed data transmission
* BTA
* Reverse data transmission

The timer step size is adjusted by a power of two ESC_CLK cycles for each timeout timer.

To configure the timeout timer step, set the power value in `TIMER_RESOLUTION` field of `DSI_0_HS_TIMER_CTRL` register. For example, set to 0 for a step size of 1 ESC_CLK cycles, 1 for a step size of 2 ESC_CLK cycles, 2 for a step size of 4 ESC_CLK cycles.

When the high-speed timer times out, the host stops the high-speed data transmission smoothly per MIPI Alliance Specification v1.01 for Display Serial Interface. This feature can be enabled by setting to 1 the `HS_TX_TO_STOP_EN` field of `DSI_0_HS_TIMER_CTRL` register.

The timeout duration for high-speed data transmission can be configured in the `HS_TX_TO` field of `DSI_0_HS_TIMER_CTRL` register.

The timeout duration for BTA and reverse data transmission can be configured in the `BTA_TO` and `LP_RX_TO` fields of `DSI_0_LP_TIMER_CTRL` register, respectively.

The timeout status of all three timers can be read from the corresponding fields in `DSI_0_TIMEOUT_STATUS` register. The status fields are sticky.

## 4.1.2.18 DSI MISR configuration

### 4.1.2.18.1 DSI 32-bit protocol layer MISR

The following configuration generates 32-bit multiple-input signature register (MISR) values for the protocol layer output. There are separate registers for video mode (VIDEO) and command mode (CMD) operation.

1. Set the `WIDTH_SEL` field in `DSI_0_MISR_CMD_CTRL` register to 1.
2. Set the `WIDTH_SEL` field in `DSI_0_MISR_VIDEO_CTRL` register to 1.
3. Set the `EN` field in `DSI_0_MISR_CMD_CTRL` register to 1.
4. Set the `EN` field in `DSI_0_MISR_VIDEO_CTRL` register to 1.
5. Read the MISR values from the following registers:
   a. `DSI_0_MISR_CMD_MDP0_32BIT`
   b. `DSI_0_MISR_CMD_MDP1_32BIT`
   c. `DSI_0_MISR_CMD_DMA_32BIT`
   d. `DSI_0_MISR_VIDEO_32BIT`
<!-- page 810 -->
### 4.1.2.18.2 DSI 16-bit lane MISR

The following configuration generates 16-bit MISR values for each datalane during high-speed data transmission. Each lane module at the PHY side accumulates MISR values. The PHY MISR values are compared with the DSI controller lane MISR values to ensure correct high-speed data transmission between the DSI controller and PHY.

1. To enable lane MISR accumulation, set the `EN` field in `DSI_0_LANE_MISR_CTRL` register to 1.
2. Read the MISR values from the `DSI_0_LANE0_MISR` through `DSI_0_LANE3_MISR` registers.
3. To reset the MISR values, set `EN` field in `DSI_0_LANE_MISR_CTRL` register to 0.

### 4.1.2.18.3 DSI PHY triggers

The DSI controller supports two reset triggers to the PHY: a panel reset trigger, and escape trigger.

A panel reset can be triggered by writing 1 to the `DSI_0_RESET_SW_TRIGGER` register.

A generic escape mode command can be triggered by the following sequence:
1. Configure the escape sequence in the `DSIPHY_TIMING_CTRL_11` register.
2. Trigger the escape command by writing 1 to the `DSI_0_GENERIC_ESC_TX_TRIGGER` register.
