##### 4.1.2.19.3 MDSS_DSI_0 register definitions

###### 0x4 DSI_0_CTRL
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

DSI Control Register provides general control to the protocol, lane management, and PHY layers.

**DSI_0_CTRL**

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 30 | NEW_INTERLEAVE_MODE_EN | Unused (Enable new interleave mode with H/W arbitration between long commands and BLLP periods.) |
| 29:28 | PACKET_BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP | Swap the bit ordering of each byte of a packet:<br>0: no swap (bit 0 is lsb, bit 7 is msb)<br>1: swap each byte of payload (bit 0 is msb, bit 7 is lsb)<br>2: swap each byte of packet (bit 0 is msb, bit 7 is lsb) |
| 26 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 24 | CRC_CHK_EN | Enable CRC verification of the received packets |
| 20 | ECC_CHK_EN | Enable ECC verification of the received packets |
| 8 | CLKLN_EN | Enable clock lane of the PHY |
| 7 | DLN3_EN | Enable data lane 3 of the PHY |
| 6 | DLN2_EN | Enable data lane 2 of the PHY |
| 5 | DLN1_EN | Enable data lane 1 of the PHY |
<!-- page 817 -->
**DSI_0_CTRL (continued)**

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4 | DLN0_EN | Enable data lane 0 of the PHY |
| 2 | CMD_MODE_EN | Enable the Command Mode Engine. |
| 1 | VIDEO_MODE_EN | Enable the Video Mode Engine. |
| 0 | DSI_EN | Enable the DSI controller. |

###### 0x8 DSI_0_STATUS
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000

DSI Status Register provides status of the DSI controller

**DSI_0_STATUS**

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | INTERLEAVE_OP_CONTENTION_CLR | W | Writing a 1 to this field clears this bit |
| 31 | INTERLEAVE_OP_CONTENTION | R | The controller generates command mode packets and video mode packets at the same time (that is: the command mode packets are longer than one BLLP period) |
| 6 | PHY_RESET_BUSY | R | DSI interface is busy sending the panel reset through the link |
| 5 | GENERIC_TRIGGER_BUSY | R | DSI interface is busy sending the generic trigger through the link |
| 4 | BTA_BUSY | R | DSI interface is busy waiting for read response, acknowledge, or tearing effect signal from the peripheral |
| 3 | VIDEO_MODE_ENGINE_BUSY | R | Video mode engine is busy sending data from display engine |
| 2 | CMD_MODE_MDP_BUSY | R | Command mode engine is busy sending data from display engine |
| 1 | CMD_MODE_DMA_BUSY | R | Command mode engine is busy sending data from memory or reading data from the display panel |
| 0 | CMD_MODE_ENGINE_BUSY | R | Command mode engine busy |

###### 0xC DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS
- **Type:** RW
- **Reset State:** 0x11111000

Status of FIFOs in the DSI controller
<!-- page 818 -->
**DSI_0_FIFO_STATUS (continued)**

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | DLN3_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW_CLR | W | Writing a 1 to this field clears this bit |
| 31 | DLN3_HS_FIFO_UNDERFLOW | R | The FIFO for HS data on Lane 3 underflows |
| 30 | DLN3_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW | R | The FIFO of Lane 3 overflows |
| 30 | DLN3_HS_FIFO_OVERFLOW_CLR | W | Writing a 1 to this field clears this bit |

Active horizontal display region register.

| Bits | Name | Description |

### 0x84 DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL

**Type:** RW
**Reset State:** 0x00000000

DSI trigger control register

When DSI is enabled and CRTC1 or 2 is used for other non-DSI panels, the display engine path trigger must be set to manual internal, otherwise the CRTC will be stalled.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | TE_SEL | Select TE path<br>0: Tearing effect (external trigger) returns from data link<br>1: Tearing effect (external trigger) returns from a dedicated pin |
| 28 | COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER | This bit field indicates whether DMA or MDP path will win the arbitration if both request the link at the same time<br>0: DMA has higher priority than display processor<br>1: Display processor has higher priority than DMA |
<!-- page 837 -->

### DSI_0_TRIG_CTRL (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 24 | COMMAND_MODE_MDP_REQ_ORDER | If PHY TE is required for one of the MDP streams while the other stream is ready to transmit, this field determines which will win the arbitration<br>0: Command Mode MDP PHY TE request has higher priority than Command Mode MDP data transmission request<br>1: Command Mode MDP Data transmission request has higher priority than Command Mode MDP PHY TE request |
| 12 | BLOCK_DMA_WITHIN_FRAME | If Command Mode DMA operation is triggered in the middle of a frame of the stream selected by COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL, delay the operation until end of frame, otherwise service the dma operation right away |
| 9:8 | COMMAND_MODE_DMA_STREAM_SEL | If COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL = SOF/EOF or both COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL and COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL = TE or software+TE, the Command Mode DMA path is triggered at frame boundary of the MDP stream selected by this field.<br>0: stream 0<br>1: stream 1<br>2: stream 2<br>3: reserved |
| 6:4 | COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL | TRIGGER_SEL field is used to select which trigger is used for Command Mode display processor path.<br>0: none<br>1: reserved0<br>2: TE<br>3: reserved1<br>4: Software trigger<br>5: reserved2<br>6: Software trigger and TE<br>7: reserved3 |
| 2:0 | COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL | DMA_TRIGGER_SEL field is used to select which trigger is used for Command Mode DMA path.<br>0: none<br>1: Start/end of frame (determined by COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER)<br>2: TE<br>3: reserved0<br>4: Software trigger<br>5: Software trigger and start/end of frame (COMMAND_MODE_DMA_MDP_ORDER)<br>6: Software trigger and TE<br>7: reserved1 |

### 0x10C DSI_0_ERR_INT_MASK0

**Type:** RW

> Interrupt will be generated if the mask field(s) in `DSI_INT_CTRL` is set to 1; error status will be generated if the mask field(s) in `DSI_ERR_INT_MASK0` is set to 0.

| 28 | DPHY_DSIPLL_UNLOCK_MASK | Mask dsipll unlock (to avoid sending out unnecessary interrupts, set this bit to 1 before dsipll locks)<br>0: allow generation of error status<br>1: no error status generated |

## DSI_0_IOBIST_CTRL

* **Offset:** 0x114
* **Type:** RW
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

DSI IOBIST control register

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | DSI_IOBIST_CTRL | This register has 2 modes of operation: command and timing mode. All configuration fields should be written first, then enable (bit 0) should be set to 1 next and start (bit 5) is set to 1 last.<br><br>**COMMAND MODE**<br>- **bit 0:** DSI IOBIST ENABLE. Active high;<br>- **bit 5:** IOBIST start. Active high;<br>- **bit 6:** Select power mode for data transfer. 0 = high speed (HS), 1 = low power (LP)<br>- **bit 7:** Data pattern mode.<br>  - 0 = Use data pattern word<br>  - 1 = PRBS pattern.<br>- **bit 10:8:** multiple of finite random run (N): if bit 12 is finite, the finite run is 256 x (N+1) runs for HS PRBS and user data, or 16 x (N+1) for LP PRBS<br>- **bit 12:** Infinite run<br>  - 0 for infinite<br>  - 1 for 256 x (N+1) runs of HS PRBS, 16 x (N+1) runs of LP PRBS, 256 x (N+1) runs of HS user data, or 8 runs of LP user data.<br>- **bit 14:13:** DSIBIST_DSIPHY_LANE_SWAP, select which lane is used as lane0 for LPDT:<br>  - 0 = DLN0<br>  - 1 = DLN1<br>  - 2 = DLN2<br>  - 3 = DLN3<br>- **bit 15:** Select instruction type<br>  - 0 = command mode<br>  - 1 = DSI timing control mode.<br>- **bit 23:16:** data pattern byte (used when bit 7 is set to 0) other bits = reserved<br><br>**TIMING MODE**<br>- **bit 0:** DSI IOBIST ENABLE. Active high;<br>- **bit 5:** IOBIST start. Active high;<br>- **bit 15:** Select instruction type<br>  - 0 = command mode<br>  - 1 = DSI timing control mode.<br>  *(If you write one DSI timing data with the select instruction type == 1, you have to change the select instruction type from 1 to 0 for timing data latch control.)*<br>- **bit 23:16:** DSI timing data;<br>- **bit 28:24:** DSI timing register selection:<br>  - 0x10 = DSI_T_CLK_PRE (data width[5:0])<br>  - 0x11 = DSI_T_CLK_POST (data width[5:0]) |
<!-- page 855 -->

| 13:12 | `CMD_MDP_STREAM1_PATTERN_SEL` | Test pattern for command mode pixel (MDP) stream1 data<br>0: PRBS pattern generated from polynomial and init value<br>1: incremental starting from init value<br>2: fixed to init value |
| 9:8 | `CMD_MDP_STREAM0_PATTERN_SEL` | Test pattern for command mode pixel (MDP) stream0 data<br>0: PRBS pattern generated from polynomial and init value<br>1: incremental starting from init value<br>2: fixed to init value |
| 5:4 | `VIDEO_PATTERN_SEL` | Test pattern for video mode operation<br>0: PRBS pattern generated from polynomial and init value<br>1: incremental starting from init value<br>2: fixed to init value |
| 2 | `TPG_DMA_FIFO_MODE` | TPG DMA fifo write mode (used when `CMD_DMA_PATTERN_SEL` = 3)<br>0: fifo write through `TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL`, `TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL2` and `TPG_DMA_FIFO_WRITE_TRIGGER`<br>1: fifo write through `TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_DMA_INIT_VAL` only |
| 1 | `CMD_DMA_TPG_EN` | DSI test pattern enable for CMD DMA only. When the EN bit is set to 1, there is no need to explicitly set this bit. |
| 0 | `EN` | DSI test pattern enable. This is the global enable of the pattern generator. Once this bit is set to 1, it is ready to generate data for video mode, command mode pixel, or dma data. Video mode data is started by `DSI*_VIDEO_ENABLE`; Command mode pixel data can be started by `DSI*_TEST_PATTERN_GEN_CMD_STREAM[012]_TRIGGER` or triggered by the trigger source set in `COMMAND_MODE_MDP_TRIGGER_SEL`; Command mode dma data is generated when a memory read request is received (the application layer will generate memory read request when it is triggered by the trigger source set in `COMMAND_MODE_DMA_TRIGGER_SEL`). |

Idle insertion between command MDP packets

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

### 0x1B8 DSI_0_COMMAND_MODE_MDP_CTRL2

**Type:** RW  
**Reset State:** 0x00000006

Command mode MDP control2

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | `BURST_MODE` | Enable frame transfer in one burst<br>0: a frame can be transferred in multiple High-Speed data bursts<br>1: enable frame transfer in one High-Speed data burst if there is no gaps between lines from MDP |
| 14:12 | `INPUT_RGB_SWAP` | Swaps the R, G, and B channels of the input command mode pixels from MDP. This field should be used when different R,G, and B orderings are required. |
| 10:8 | `RGB_SWAP2` | Swaps the R, G, and B channels of the dst pixels. This field should be used when different R,G, and B orderings are required.<br>For example, if RGB_SWAP = 1 , RGB565 becomes RBG556. |
| 7 | `BYTE_MSB_LSB_FLIP2` | Swap the bit ordering of each byte of the dst pixel (this is done after the RGB swap and R/G/B_SEL).<br>0: bit 0 is lsb, bit 7 is msb<br>1: bit 0 is msb, bit 7 is lsb |
| 6 | `B_SEL2` | Bit Swaps the B Channel of the dst pixel. This field is used to reverse the ordering of the bits that are outputted for the color red (sic).<br>For example, for RGB888 color format, if the red component is 10000000 then if this field is enabled, 00000001 is output. |
| 5 | `G_SEL2` | Bit Swaps the G Channel of the dst pixel. This field is used to reverse the ordering of the bits that are outputted for the color red (sic).<br>For example, for RGB888 color format, if the red component is 10000000 then if this field is enabled, 00000001 is output. |

| 3:0 | `DST_FORMAT2` | Pixel format for stream 2<br>0 = RGB111<br>1 = reserved<br>2 = reserved<br>3 = RGB332 (data_src_width must be in multiple of 2 pixels)<br>4 = RGB444 (data_src_width must be in multiple of 2 pixels)<br>5 = reserved<br>6 = RGB565<br>7 = RGB666<br>8 = RGB888<br>Others = reserved |

## 4.2 Camera Subsystem (CAMSS)

> [!NOTE]
> This section describes only the top-level functionality of the camera subsystem (CAMSS). For more details (such as interrupts, clocks, resets, pins, hardware macros, and registers) of each camera functional sub-module, see the respective chapters.

### 4.2.1 CAMSS overview

The CAMSS is an encapsulated set of hardware modules that provides the infrastructure and functions to implement high quality camera, camcorder, and image processing applications.

The CAMSS takes input data from either an image sensor or external memory. The input data is then processed into output images (JPG, RAW, YUV, and so on.) to be further used by the rest of the SoC modules.

The I2C and GPIO pins control and configure the image sensor. Statistics are generated and passed to the 3A (auto white balance, auto focus, auto exposure) algorithms which are run on the main Arm CPU (APSS). The software interacts with the CAMSS through an AHB slave interface which provides a memory-mapped register interface. The global clock controller (GCC) handles the camera subsystem clocks. Interrupts are gathered from the CAMSS sub-modules into the IRQ router, which re-routes them to the APSS interrupt controller (APSS_QGIC2).

Figure 4-102 shows a high-level overview of the CAMSS megacell in the SoC.

#### Figure 4-102: CAMSS overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the Camera Subsystem (CAMSS) architecture and its connections to the rest of the SoC.
Inside CAMSS, an internal AHB Interface connects:
* IRQ Router (provides interrupts to the APSS)
* CAMSS TOP CSR
* MICRO
* JPEG processing engine (utilizes VBIF_JPEG for memory access)
* CPP (Camera Image Processor / Post Processor, utilizes VBIF_VFE for memory access)
* VFE_0 (Video Front End 0, utilizes VBIF_VFE for memory access)
* CSID (Camera Serial Interface Decoder) which contains ISPIF, CSID0, and CSID1.

On the right side of CAMSS:
* Sensor resets and standby signals
* Sensor master clocks
* CCI (Camera Control Interface) provides I2C / GPIO Sensor control
* CSI_PHY0 blocks interface between external MIPI Sensors and the CSID block:
  * MIPI Sensor 4 lanes interfaces through a CSI_PHY0 block to CSID0.
  * MIPI Sensor 2 lanes interfaces through another CSI_PHY0 block to CSID1.

On the left:
* GCC (Global Clock Controller) provides clocks and resets to CAMSS.
* APSS receives interrupts from the IRQ Router.

Below CAMSS:
* VBIF_JPEG and VBIF_VFE connect the JPEG, CPP, and VFE_0 blocks to the MMSS NoC (AXI) bus.
* MMSS NoC (AXI) connects to System NoC.
* System NoC connects to OCMEM (On-Chip Memory) and SMMU (System MMU), which connects to External Memory.
* System NoC also interfaces with CAMSS via an AHB slave bus.
<!-- page 903 -->

Table 4-101 lists the CAMSS main features.

#### Table 4-101 CAMSS features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| CAMSS | <ul><li>JPEG offline encoding via the JPEG engine</li><li>Image fine tuning such as de-noising, digital zoom, scaling, sharpening to enhance image after de-noising via the camera post processing (CPP) engine</li><li>Sensor control via the camera control interface (CCI)</li><li>Sensor resets, standby and master clocks.</li></ul> |

| Module | Feature | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CSID/VFE | High speed raw capture | Captures pixel data from CSID at full interface speed up to 4 Gbps; formats include DPCM6, DPCM8, MIPI Raw8/10/12 |
| CSID/VFE | MIPI CSI-2 DPCM 6-bit | Supports CSI-2 6-bit DPCM modes |
| CSID/VFE | MIPI CSI-2 Virtual channel / data type support | Supports 4 virtual channels, each with up to 4 data types |
| VFE | Read formats | Supports reading DPCM6, DPCM8, MIPI RAW8/10/12, Plain16 |
| VFE | Co-sited RGB | Support for 4 channel fully co-sited output from sensors |
| VFE | Frame drop | Dynamically programmable frame drop |
| VFE | High frame rate support | Grouped interrupts and output formats to reduce ISR rates for driver |
| VFE | Dedicated video path | Dedicated video path with field-of-view crop, down-scaler, and spatial filter |
| CPP | Up scaling/Downscaling | Arbitrary Scaling for digital zoom |
| CPP | Rotation/flip | Rotation/flip support for YUV images |
| CPP | Adaptive Spatial Filter | Adaptive Spatial Filter processing |
| CCI | I2C/GPIO controller | Dedicated queue-based I2C / GPIO controller for synchronizing commands to image sensor timing |
| JPEG encode | File size control stats | Statistics to predict file size for a 2nd pass JPEG encoding |
| JPEG encode | Up/down scaling/Rotation | Scaling for digital zoom, thumbnail generation |
| JPEG encode | Pitch | Support to read/write image data from buffers with pitch |

#### 4.2.1.2 CAMSS use cases

The camera design supports five primary operating modes:
* CAMSS viewfinder mode
* CAMSS snapshot mode
* CAMSS camcorder mode
* CAMSS live snapshot mode
<!-- page 905 -->

* CAMSS high frame rate camcorder mode

The following data flow overviews describe the most common configurations.
<!-- page 906 -->

#### 4.2.1.2.1 CAMSS viewfinder mode

The viewfinder mode provides images for the preview display. This is the most basic of the camera modes. A typical flow diagram is shown in Figure 4-103.

#### Figure 4-103: CAMSS viewfinder data flow
*Description:* A data flow diagram showing the CAMSS viewfinder pipeline.
Data starts at the **Sensor** and enters the **CAMIF -> VFE -> FIFO** block. From the **FIFO**, data is stored in **YCbCr Buffers x3**.
From these buffers, data passes through a **Rotator** block and is stored in another **Buffer**.
This buffer feeds into the **Display Controller -> RGB I/F** block, which also receives overlay data from an **OSD Generation** block via an **Overlay Surface** buffer.
Finally, the display controller outputs the combined data to the **LCD**.

#### 4.2.1.2.2 CAMSS snapshot mode

Snapshot mode captures the snapshot picture and encodes it for storage. The sensor, VFE, and JPEG engines play a part in this data flow as shown in Figure 4-104. The digital zoom image can be up sampled as it is encoded. This procedure is done off-line during a second pass encoding to decouple the operation from the real-time data rate requirements imposed by the image sensor. Note that there is only one JPEG engine for off-line encoding only. The flow diagram also illustrates how the thumbnail image is produced as an uncompressed image to memory by the VFE and can be used for immediate display.

#### Figure 4-104: CAMSS snapshot data flow
*Description:* A data flow diagram showing the CAMSS snapshot pipeline, which is split into real-time and off-line processing paths.
**Real-time Path:**
* Data flows from the **Sensor** to **CAMIF -> Image Processing -> FIFO**.
* From **FIFO**, an uncompressed **YCbCr Thumbnail** is generated.
* The thumbnail path splits:
  * **Display flow**: Passes through **Rotator** -> **Buffer** -> **Display Controller -> RGB I/F** -> **LCD** (with optional **OSD Generation** overlay via **Overlay Surface**).
  * **Encoding flow**: Flows to a **JPEG Encoder**, which outputs directly to a **JPEG File** buffer.

**Off-Line Path** (labeled with a bracket):
* Starts at **IMEM** (Internal Memory).
* Flows to **UpScale -> JPEG Encoder** for second-pass zoom and encoding.
* The output of the upscale/encoder is saved as a **JPEG File**.
* The **JPEG File** buffer is then read by the **SDCC -> SDIO** controller to be written to the **SD Card**.
<!-- page 907 -->

#### 4.2.1.2.3 CAMSS camcorder mode

In camcorder mode, the CAM produces two VFE outputs: display and video encoder as shown in Figure 4-105. These outputs can differ in aspect ratio and resolution.

#### Figure 4-105: CAMSS camcorder data flow
*Description:* A data flow diagram showing the CAMSS camcorder pipeline.
Data from the **Sensor** goes to **CAMIF -> VFE -> FIFO** and then splits into two paths:
1. **Display Path (Top):**
   * Stored in **YCbCr Buffers x3 or more**.
   * Processed by **Rotator**.
   * Stored in a **Buffer**.
   * Read by the **Display Controller -> RGB I/F** to be displayed on the **LCD** (with overlay support from **OSD Generation -> Overlay Surface**).
2. **Video Path (Bottom):**
   * Stored in another set of **YCbCr Buffers x3 or more**.
   * Processed by **VPE / Post Processing** (Video Processing Engine).
   * Stored in a **Buffer**.
   * Processed by **Video Encoder**.
   * Encoded data is put into **Video Buffers and Bitstream**.
   * Read by **SDCC -> SDIO** to be saved on the **SD Card**.

#### 4.2.1.2.4 CAMSS live snapshot mode

The live snapshot mode, a camcorder sub-mode, enables a still image capture during video encoding as shown in Figure 4-106. This mode uses the preview data path to supply the snapshot image while providing an uninterrupted video frame stream for the video encoder. It is a hybrid of the snapshot and viewfinder / camcorder modes.

#### Figure 4-106: CAMSS live snapshot data flow
*Description:* A data flow diagram showing the CAMSS live snapshot data flow, split into a real-time path and an off-line path.
**Real-time Path (Top):**
* Flows from **Sensor** -> **CAMIF -> VFE -> FIFO** -> **YCbCr Buffers x3 or more** -> **VPE / Post Processing** -> **Buffer** -> **Video Encoder** -> **Video Buffers and Bitstream** -> **SDCC -> SDIO** -> **SD Card**.
* This path represents the active video recording.

**Off-Line Path (Bottom, bracketed):**
* Starts at **IMEM** (Internal Memory), which holds the frame captured for the snapshot.
* The path splits into two parallel encoding paths:
  1. **DownScaler -> JPEG Encoder** (typically for thumbnail generation).
  2. **UpScale -> JPEG Encoder** (typically for the main snapshot image).
* Both encoders output their results to the **JPEG File** buffer.
* The **JPEG File** is then written by **SDCC -> SDIO** to the **SD Card**.

### 4.2.1.3 CAMSS high frame rate camcorder mode

The high frame rate camcorder mode groups the data formats and interrupts so that the driver handles interrupts once every N frames. This grouping lowers the interrupt rate to avoid overwhelming the processor.
<!-- page 908 -->

#### 4.2.1.4 CAMSS external connectivity

Figure 4-107 shows the CAMSS external interface signals.

#### Figure 4-107: CAMSS external connectivity
*Description:* A block diagram showing the routing of CAMSS external connectivity signals.
On the left, the **GCC** (Global Clock Controller) generates four clock signals: **CAM_MCLK0**, **CAM_MCLK1**, **GP_CLK0**, and **GP_CLK1**. These signals pass through the **CAMSS** block.
The **CAMSS** block also generates three control signals: **CAM0_STANDBY_N**, **CAM0_RST_N**, and **CAM1_RST_N**.
All seven of these signals exit **CAMSS** and enter the **TLMM** (Top-Level Mode Multiplexing) block, which is controlled by **SoC I/O Muxing Logic**.
The **TLMM** multiplexes these signals onto the physical I/O pins of the SoC on the right boundary.

Table 4-104 lists the CAMSS external signals and their respective attributes.

#### Table 4-104 CAMSS external connectivity signal attributes

| Module | Signal | Type¹ | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CAMSS | CAM0_STANDBY_N | O | Camera standby signal sensor 0 |
| | CAM0_RST_N | O | Camera reset signal sensor 0 |
| | CAM1_RST_N | O | Camera reset signal sensor 1 |
| | CAM_MCLK0 | O | Camera master clock sensor 0 |
| | CAM_MCLK1 | O | Camera master clock sensor 1 |
| | GP_CLK0 | O | Camera general purpose clock 0 |
| | GP_CLK1 | O | Camera general purpose clock 1 |

¹ I = Input, O = Output, B = Bidirectional, Z = High impedance, L = Loopback

> [!NOTE]
> Some signals can be multiplexed on a particular SoC GPIO pin via the TLMM registers. For the full list and configuration of CAMSS signals mapping to GPIO pins, see the table TLMM signal multiplexing and attributes in the TLMM chapter.
<!-- page 909 -->

#### 4.2.1.5 CAMSS internal connectivity

Figure 4-108 shows the CAMSS internal interface signals.

#### Figure 4-108: CAMSS internal connectivity
*Description:* A block diagram showing the internal connectivity (resets, clocks, interrupts, and bus interfaces) of CAMSS.
**Resets and Clocks from GCC to CAMSS:**
* GCC sends 6 resets: **GCC_CAMSS_AHB_ARES**, **GCC_CAMSS_TOP_AHB_ARES**, **GCC_CAMSS_GP0_ARES**, **GCC_CAMSS_GP1_ARES**, **GCC_CAMSS_MCLKO_ARES**, and **GCC_CAMSS_MCLK1_ARES**.
* GCC sends 6 clocks: **GCC_CAMSS_AHB_CLK**, **GCC_CAMSS_TOP_AHB_CLK**, **GCC_CAMSS_GP0_CLK**, **GCC_CAMSS_GP1_CLK**, **GCC_CAMSS_MCLK0_CLK**, and **GCC_CAMSS_MCLK1_CLK**.

**Interrupts to APSS:**
* **CSI_PHY0** blocks on the right send **MIPI_CSI0_CSIPHY_IRQ** and **MIPI_CSI1_CSIPHY_IRQ** directly to APSS.
* The internal **IRQ router** receives interrupts from camera sub-modules and outputs 8 interrupts to APSS: **CAMSS_IRQ[0:3]**, **CAMSS_IRQ[6:8]**, and **CAMSS_IRQ10**.
* The internal **VBIFs** block outputs **CAMSS_VBIF_IRPT_0** and **CAMSS_VBIF_IRPT_1** to APSS.

**Buses:**
* **System NoC** connects to CAMSS via an **AHB slave bus** and to the internal **VBIFs** block via an **AXI bus**.

## 4.2.1.6 CAMSS functional description

### 4.2.1.6.1 CAMSS power and clock management

> **NOTE:** This subsection gives top level power and clock details. See each CAMSS module sub-chapter for particular module’s internal power and clock management.

Figure 4-109 shows the CAMSS power management.

#### Figure 4-109: CAMSS power management
*Description:* This block diagram illustrates the power collapsible boundary of the Camera Subsystem (CAMSS). A thick red line outlines the power collapsible hardware domain, with a power switch icon at the top right. Inside this boundary, the following modules are connected to a common horizontal AHB Interface bus:
- IRQ Router
- CAMSS TOP CSR
- MICRO
- JPEG: Connected to the VBIF_JPEG block at the bottom, which interfaces outside the CAMSS boundary.
- CPP: Connected to the VBIF_VFE block at the bottom.
- VFE_0: Also connected to the VBIF_VFE block. The VBIF_VFE block interfaces outside the CAMSS boundary.
- CSID: Contains the ISPIF block, which is driven by CSID0 and CSID1.
- CCI (Camera Control Interface): Connected to the CSID block.

Outside the power collapsible boundary:
- Two CSI_PHY0 blocks on the right feed inputs into the CSID0 and CSID1 blocks inside the CAMSS boundary.

When none of the sub-modules are being used, the highlighted macro can be power collapsed. The standard sequence for initiating a power collapse is used. For more information, see Global Clock Controller (GCC) chapter for details. If any of the sub-modules within the CAMSS is being used, the entire CAMSS must be enabled.

The sub-module clocks can be disabled for power savings if sub-modules are not being used. Each sub-module has a clock block controller that can turn off clocks from the CGC_EN and FORCE_CLK_ON registers. In addition, because of its multi-input and crossbarring, unlike other camera blocks, CSID and CSI_PHY use many clocks. So there are CSI MUX_SEL register which control the RDI and PIX pipe clock sources for maximum flexibility and depending on the use case needs.

The GCC_CAMSS_AHB_CLK and GCC_CAMSS_TOP_AHB_CLK bus clocks must be active to access any software register within the camera subsystem.
<!-- page 913 -->

### CAMSS clock and memory bring up sequencing

The VBIF performs clock domain crossing between each camera sub-module and the QSB bus to DDR. In order to ensure VBIF logic is properly reset before use, the asynchronous reset from each clock domain must be asserted before any clock is enabled to the VBIF. Once the VBIF is properly reset at bring up, independent async and software synchronous resets may be applied for a given camera submodule without dependency on or affecting functionality of other camera sub-modules.

At CAMSS top level Power on Only, software asserts the asynchronous resets to CPP and VFE_0 clock domains, as well as the associated AHB and AXI clocks to VBIF as described in the section below.

Ensure that no clocks to the VBIF are running during periods in which async reset is being asserted to the VBIF. It is recommended to add the following reset sequence as shown in the following, after CAMSS GDSC power up sequencing and before enabling any clocks within the CAMSS.

Upon CAMSS Power up, the following async resets are applied to VBIF:
- GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AXI_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK
- GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_CPP_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_ARES
- GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_ARES

The CAMSS bring up sequence is as follows:
1. Write `0x1` in the `SW_COLLAPSE` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_GDSCR` register.
2. Write `0x1` in the `SW_COLLAPSE` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_GDSCR` register.
3. Write `0x1` in the `BLK_ARES` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_BCR` register. This asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_ARES` to VFE_0 and `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_ARES` and `GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_ARES` to the VBIF and VFE0. This also asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_ARES` to CPP and `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_ARES` again to the VBIF and CPP.
4. Write `0x0` in the `BLK_ARES` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_BCR` register. This de-asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_ARES` to VFE_0 and `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_ARES` and `GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_ARES` to the VBIF and VFE0. This also de-asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_ARES` to CPP and `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_ARES` to the CPP.
5. Write `0x1` in the `BLK_ARES` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_BCR` register. This asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_ARES` to JPEG and `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AXI_ARES` and `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_ARES` to the VBIF and JPEG.
6. Write `0x0` in the `BLK_ARES` bit field of the `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_BCR` register. This de-asserts the async reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_ARES` to JPEG and `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AXI_ARES` and `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_ARES` to the VBIF and JPEG.
<!-- page 914 -->

> **NOTE:** The above steps give example configuration for VFE_0/CPP and JPEG that have their own VBIF. Same approach is performed for other CAMSS modules as well. Perform step 5 and 6 for the CSIDs, CSI_PHYs, CCI, and MICRO.

7. Write `0x1` in the `CLK_ENABLE` bit field in the `GCC_CAMSS_*_CBCR` (where `*` is any sub-module camera clock needed)

> **NOTE:** Module clocks are NOT enabled until requested by the CAMSS sub-module driver(s).

#### CAMSS AHB clocks

All software register programming for the CAMSS is performed through an AHB interface. Each of the sub-modules within the CAMSS has their own AHB slave port and to perform any register accesses, the AHB clock must be active for that sub-module. If the AHB clock is disabled and software tries to access individual module, the AHB bus can hang.

There are individual AHB clocks driven to each of the sub-modules from the GCC, however it is required that all AHB clocks are set to the same frequency. If a sub-module is not being used, the AHB clock can be enabled/disabled independently from the GCC. The exception is the `GCC_CAMSS_TOP_AHB_CLK` clock domain which must remain active to access any register in the CAMSS top level.

### 4.2.1.6.2 CAMSS resets

The CAMSS supports three levels of reset capability:
- CAMSS power on reset
- CAMSS clock domain reset
- CAMSS functional module reset

#### CAMSS power on reset

Power-on reset (RESIN_N) is straightforward. During power on, this reset brings the sub-modules to a known state without requiring external clocks. The CAMSS supports asynchronous reset so that when the SoC powers on, all flops are set to a known state even if no clocks are present.

#### CAMSS clock domain reset

At the SoC level, the global clock block (GCC) provides the capability to independently enable/disable each clock going to the camera subsystem. Each clock has a corresponding reset signal that is also software controlled and asynchronously resets the sub-module logic. The resets are functionally grouped at a higher level into integration modules (IM) that enable software to reset a group of clock domains with a single command. see CAMSS sub-chapters for each sub-module clock domain resets.
<!-- page 915 -->

#### CAMSS functional module reset

Each sub-module (CSIDs, CCI, VFE_0, JPEG, MICRO) within the CAMSS contains a reset controller block that provides software with the capability to finely control the resets that are applied to the hardware. The reset controller within each sub-module provides the following capabilities:
- **Functional block resets**: Individual module blocks can be reset independently. The partitioning and granularity of this control is module dependent. For example, in the case of VFE_0, the bus interface block can be reset after a bus overflow condition to recover without needing to reset the software registers. This is advantageous because if the software registers had to be reset, this would result in the need to reconfigure the whole sub-module.
- **Software register reset**: All AHB software registers can be reset to their default state through a software command without disturbing hardware state.
- **Reset IRQ**: When a reset command is issued, an IRQ is returned when the reset operation is complete. If a clock is not running and a reset is issued, no IRQ is returned.

### 4.2.1.6.3 CAMSS interrupts

#### CAMSS IRQ router

At the highest SOC level, the APSS_QGIC2 controller services all individual module hardware IRQs and produces a single IRQ to the main CPU. This IRQ is general serviced by an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) which is implemented on the OS running on the device. In general, the ISR dispatches the triggered IRQ to different Interrupt Service Threads (IST). Depending on the execution environment and the HLOS, there may be restrictions for how the IST is structured. For example, on WinMobile, there must be a 1:1 mapping between a hardware IRQ and IST. This constraint impacts the software driver structure and also restricts the ability to support the usage of multiple hardwares as a single entity.

As the CAMSS consists of a multiple hardware modules working together, software may want to service multiple hardware modules with a single IRQ/IST, that is, combining VFE+JPEG IRQ for example.

To address this, the IRQ router is used to handle consolidation and mapping of the camera hardware modules to external IRQ lines driving to the QGIC chip level interrupt controller. Each of the camera modules feeds their IRQ outputs to the IRQ router which can be used to consolidate multiple IRQ sources into a single IRQ line. This capability enables software to be able to group multiple hardware modules to appear as a single entity to the HLOS. The configuration of the IRQ router is expected to be static for a given application and not changed dynamically.

There are 17 IRQ router slices that can map the input IRQs to the output IRQs. However, only seven slices are mapped to APSS_QGIC2 lines (see, Section 4.2.1.5) and six slices for the micro controller. Figure 4-110 shows how they are structured.
<!-- page 916 -->

#### Figure 4-110: CAMSS IRQ router
*Description:* This block diagram shows how interrupts from different camera modules are routed through the IRQ router to the APSS_QGIC and the MICRO controller.
- Left side (Interrupt Sources):
  - `VFE_0` generates `VFE_IRQ` to the IRQ router.
  - `CPP` generates `CPP_IRQ` to the IRQ router.
  - `CSIDs` generates three interrupts: `CSID_0_IRQ`, `CSID_1_IRQ`, and `ISPIF_IRQ`.
  - `CCI` generates `CCI_IRQ`.
  - `JPEG` generates `JPEG_IRQ`.
  - `MICRO` generates `MICRO_IRQ`.
- Center: The `IRQ router` receives all these input interrupts.
- Right side (Outputs to APSS_QGIC):
  - The IRQ router outputs 8 combined interrupts to the `APSS_QGIC`: `CAMSS_IRQ0`, `CAMSS_IRQ1`, `CAMSS_IRQ2`, `CAMSS_IRQ3`, `CAMSS_IRQ6`, `CAMSS_IRQ7`, `CAMSS_IRQ8`, and `CAMSS_IRQ10`.
- Bottom (Outputs to MICRO):
  - A 6-bit bus `MICRO_COMPOSITE_IRQ[0-5]` runs from the IRQ router back to the `MICRO` block.

The implementation of each IRQ router slice is shown in Figure 4-111.

#### Figure 4-111: CAMSS IRQ router slice implementation
*Description:* This diagram details the internal implementation of the CAMSS IRQ router and a single IRQ router slice.
- Top Diagram (CAMSS IRQ router overview):
  - Inputs: 13 level-based IRQ inputs (`irq0_in` to `irq12_in`) enter a block containing `demet` (demetallization) and `edge_detect` stages.
  - The resulting 13-bit edge-based IRQ bus (`irq_in[12:0]`) is routed into multiple parallel `ROUTER SLICE` blocks.
  - Outputs: The router slices output individual signals like `irq0_out`, `irq1_out`, `irq2_out`, etc.
  - Control Registers/Clocks: The router is controlled by `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_xx` registers, `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_RESET_CTRL` register, and the `GCC_CAMSS_TOP_AHB_CLK` clock.
- Bottom Diagram (IRQ router slice detailed logic):
  - For a single input index `i`:
    - The input interrupt `irq_in(i)` is gated with a mask bit `mask(i)` from the composite mask register using an AND gate, which then sets a `RESET REG` latch.
    - The `RESET REG` latch can be reset via an OR gate by the global `reset` signal, the inverted `mask(i)` signal, or a feedback signal.
    - The outputs of all `RESET REG` latches in the slice are combined using a comparator block and an OR-reduction (`OR_RED`) block.
    - The combined result is passed through an AND gate to the `d` input of a clocked `MASK REG` D-flip-flop, which outputs `irq_out`.
    - The output of the AND gate (before the MASK REG) feeds back to the OR gate reset input of the `RESET REG` latches.

Each IRQ router slice allows SW to map one or more incoming IRQs to a single output IRQ. The registers that are used to control the IRQ router logic are listed below:
- `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_0` through `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_12`
- `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MICRO_MASK_0` through `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MICRO_MASK_5`
- `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_RESET_CTRL`
<!-- page 917 -->

The `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_xx` is a register (1 register per IRQ router slice) that is used to select which IRQs to map to the given output IRQ. The register is one-hot encoded and setting an input IRQ bit to `0x1` enables capturing of that IRQ to contribute to the final output IRQ. The `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_RESET_CTRL` register is used to reset the state of the IRQ combining logic to an idle initial state. To apply a reset, software should write a `0x1` to the `CAMSS_IRQ_COMPOSITE_RESET_CTRL` register bit, followed by a `0x0` to complete the sequence. Whenever the MASK value is changed on an IRQ router slice, software must issue a reset to the corresponding slice to initialize it.

The default power on reset behavior of the IRQ router is such that the sub-module IRQs are mapped to the camera subsystem IRQs as follows in Table 4-109.

### Table 4-109 CAMSS IRQ router power on reset mapping

| Camera subsystem IRQ | Default power on mapping |
| :--- | :--- |
| CAMSS_IRQ0 | MICRO_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ1 | CCI_RQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ2 | CSID_0_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ3 | CSI_1_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ6 | ISPIF_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ7 | CPP_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ8 | VFE_IRQ |
| CAMSS_IRQ10 | JPEG_IRQ |

#### CAMSS status interrupts

The CAMSS does not have any status interrupts at the top hardware level.

#### CAMSS error interrupts

The CAMSS does not have any error interrupts at the top hardware level.

### 4.2.1.6.4 CAMSS timeouts

To detect and recover from system level problems, use a software based system timeout watchdog in conjunction with the CAMSS hardware. The image sensor generates image data which is processed in a streaming architecture in real time. That way, if there is a problem with the sensor sending the data, no further outputs (and interrupts) are generated by the hardware. Reasons the image sensor may send incorrect data include:
- I2C command did not complete correctly, or command is corrupted due to noise
- ESD shock
- Incorrect software configuration
<!-- page 918 -->

## 4.2.2 MIPI Camera Serial Interface 2 Decoder (CSID) and Physical Layer (CSI PHY)

This section describes the mobile industry processor interface (MIPI) camera serial interface-2 (CSI-2) decoder (CSID) and its companion interface physical layer (PHY).

### 4.2.2.1 CSID overview

CSID is the major camera interface used in image processing. It is responsible for decoding MIPI CSI-2 encoded data coming from the external camera sensor through the CSI PHY into unprocessed pixels for consumption down the pipe of the camera subsystem.

Figure 4-112 shows a high-level overview of the two CSID interfaces and the CSI PHY integrated within the camera subsystem and in the SoC.

#### Figure 4-112: CSID overview
*Description:* Block diagram of the Camera Subsystem within the SoC.
- **Camera Subsystem boundary** contains CCI, CSID (CSID0, CSID1), CSI PHY (CSI PHY0, CSI PHY1), ISPIF, and VFE0.
- **External Connections:**
  - **CCI** (Camera Control Interface) connects to an external **I2C/GPIO sensor** for control.
  - **CSI PHY0** connects to an external **MIPI sensor (4 lanes)**.
  - **CSI PHY1** connects to an external **MIPI sensor (2 lanes)**.
- **Internal Connections:**
  - **CSI PHY0** connects to **CSID0**.
  - **CSI PHY1** connects to **CSID1**.
  - **CSID0** and **CSID1** connect to **ISPIF**.
  - **ISPIF** connects to **VFE0**.
  - **VFE0** connects to **System NoC**.
- **Control and Interrupts:**
  - **GCC** (Global Clock Controller) provides **Clocks** and **Resets** to the Camera Subsystem.
  - **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem) receives **Interrupts** from the Camera Subsystem.

<!-- page 950 -->

#### 4.2.2.1.1 CSID 2D snapshot

This is the most common use where a user takes a simple picture.

Figure 4-113 shows the camera pipeline through several major blocks.

#### Figure 4-113: CSID high level data flow for a 2D snapshot
*Description:* Flow diagram showing the path of image data from the sensor to external memory.
- **Camera sensor** (outputs CSI-2 encoded image serially)
- -> **CSI PHYx** (converts serial data to byte data)
- -> **CSIDx** (decodes byte data into unprocessed pixels)
- -> **Pixel pipe** (inside **ISPIF / CSID**; routes the data)
- -> **VFE** (performs pixel processing)
- -> **External memory** (writes processed pixels to memory)

When a snapshot is taken, the camera sensor sends the CSI-2 encoded image to the CSI PHY serially. The CSI PHY converts this data into byte data, which the CSID decodes into unprocessed pixels. The data is then passed to the ISPIF, which routes it through one of its pipes to the VFE where the pixel processing and writing to external memory happens.


<!-- page 951 -->
#### 4.2.2.1.2 CSID 2D snapshot with embedded data

This scenario is similar to the 2D snapshot except that the camera sensor also sends an interleaved stream of non-pixel embedded data. The embedded data is more prevalent because it transfers information such as auto-focus values that can be used to improve quality and the user experience.

#### Figure 4-114: CSID 2D snapshot with embedded data
*Description:* A block diagram showing the data flow from the Camera Sensor to External Memory.
- **Camera Sensor** sends interleaved pixel and embedded data streams (represented by thick arrows) to **CSI PHYx**.
- **CSI PHYx** passes the streams to **CSID**.
- **CSID** splits the stream into:
  - **RDI pipe**: carries non-pixel or still-encoded pixel data (embedded data).
  - **Pixel pipe**: carries decoded pixel data.
- Both pipes pass through the **ISPIF CSID** block.
- From **ISPIF CSID**, they enter **VFE 0**.
- **VFE 0** routes:
  - Embedded data from RDI pipe to **External memory (Address M)** directly, without processing.
  - Pixel data from Pixel pipe to **External memory (Address N)** after processing.

In Figure 4-114, the thick arrows represent the interleaved pixel and embedded data streams. Interleaving is performed as described in the CSI-2 specification.

The CSID processes both streams and sends them to its pixel-only and data-only output interfaces. These outputs are routed to their respective ISPIF pipes (RDI pipes for non-pixel or still-encoded pixel data; pixel pipes for decoded pixel data) and sent downstream to VFE. Once in VFE, pixel data (the image) is processed and saved to external memory address N. Similarly, RDI data (the embedded data) is written to external memory address M without any processing.
<!-- page 952 -->
#### 4.2.2.1.3 CSID acronyms and terms

Table 4-150 lists the common acronyms and terms used throughout this section.

##### Table 4-150 CSID acronyms and terms

| Acronym or term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| SOT | Start of data transition |
| EOT | End of data transition |
| ISPIF | Image signal processors interface |
| DPCM | Differential pulse-code modulation compression |
| VFE | Video front end interface |
| CCI | Dedicated queue-based I2C and GPIO camera control interface for synchronizing commands to image sensor timing |
| MIPI CSI-2 virtual channel (VC) | Support of four virtual channels, each with up to four data types |
| RDI data | Raw dump interface embedded data passed to the image pipe along the pixel image data |
| ULPM | Ultra-low power mode, generally known as standby |

#### 4.2.2.3 CSID internal connectivity

Figure 4-116 shows the CSID internal interface signals.

#### Figure 4-116: CSID internal connectivity
*Description:* Diagram showing the clock, interrupt (IRQ), and control connectivity for the Camera Subsystem (CAMSS) blocks including CSI PHYs, CSID, ISPIF, and VFE.

##### Clock Tree & Control Paths
1. **Global Clock Controller (GCC) Clocks:**
   - `CAMSS_CSIPHY0_TIMER_CLK_SRC` and `CAMSS_CSIPHY1_TIMER_CLK_SRC` feed timer clocks to `CSI_PHY0` (`GCC_CAMSS_CSI0PHYTIMER_CLK`) and `CSI_PHY1` (`GCC_CAMSS_CSI1PHYTIMER_CLK`).
   - `CAMSS_CSI0_CLK_SRC` and `CAMSS_CSI1_CLK_SRC` generate `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI0PHY_CLK` and `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI1PHY_CLK`.
     - Through muxes controlled by APSS via `CAMSS_CSI0/1PHY_MUX_SEL_0/1` and clock gates enabled via `CAMSS_CSI0/1PHY_CGC_EN_0/1`, these generate:
       - `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI0PHY_MUX0_CLK` and `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI0PHY_MUX1_CLK` for `CSI_PHY0`.
       - `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI1PHY_MUX0_CLK` and `GCC_CAMMSS_CSI1PHY_MUX1_CLK` for `CSI_PHY1`.
   - `CAMSS_VFE0_CLK_SRC` generates `GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_CLK` which becomes `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_VFE0_CLK` for `ISPIF`.
   - `CAMSS_AHB_CLK_SRC` generates `GCC_CAMSS_AHB_CLK` which supplies the AHB interface clocks for:
     - `CSID0` (`GCC_CAMSS_CSI0_AHB_CLK`)
     - `CSID1` (`GCC_CAMSS_CSI1_AHB_CLK`)
     - `ISPIF` (`GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`)

2. **Pixel and RDI Clock Muxing:**
   - Clocks `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0PIX_CLK` and `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1PIX_CLK` are multiplexed based on control signals from APSS (`CAMSS_CSI_PIX/RDI_0/1_MUX_SEL` / `_CGC_EN`) to generate:
     - `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0PIX_MUX_CLK` for `CSID0`.
     - `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1PIX_MUX_CLK` for `CSID1`.
   - Clocks `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0RDI_CLK` and `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1RDI_CLK` are similarly multiplexed to generate:
     - `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0RDI_MUX_CLK` for `CSID0`.
     - `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1RDI_MUX_CLK` for `CSID1`.

##### Interrupt Paths (to APSS)
- `CSI_PHY0` asserts `CSIPHY_0_IRQ` (to camera subsystem IRQ router).
- `CSI_PHY1` asserts `CSIPHY_1_IRQ`.
- `CSID0` asserts `CSID_0_IRQ` which maps to `CAMSS_IRQ2`.
- `CSID1` asserts `CSID_1_IRQ` which maps to `CAMSS_IRQ3`.
- `ISPIF` asserts `ISPIF_IRQ` which maps to `CAMSS_IRQ6`.

##### Downstream Data Flow
- CSID0 and CSID1 feed into `ISPIF`.
- `ISPIF` feeds into `VFE`.
- `VFE` interfaces with `System NoC` (Network-on-Chip) to store data in memory.

### 4.2.2.4 CSID functional description

The CSID comprises of two CSID interfaces (CSID0 and CSID1), each of which can source data from any of the PHYs. In turn, the PHYs are hooked up to the camera sensors.

The CSID also contains the image signal processor interface (ISPIF), which routes the output of each CSID core to its appropriate destination VFE pixel pipeline and VFE bus master for writing directly to external memory.

Figure 4-117 shows the CSID data stream.

#### Figure 4-117: CSID data stream diagram
*Description:* A flow diagram representing how data streams from the physical layer (PHYs) to the Video Front End (VFE0) through the CSID and ISPIF.
- **Inputs (PHYs):** `CSI_PHY0` (PHY 0) and `CSI_PHY1` (PHY 1) receive data from camera sensors.
- **CSID Crossbar & Processing:**
  - Both `CSID0` and `CSID1` can select inputs from either `PHY 0` or `PHY 1`.
  - `CSID0` outputs:
    - `C0 PIX` (Pixel stream)
    - `C0 RDI` (RDI stream)
  - `CSID1` outputs:
    - `C1 PIX` (Pixel stream)
    - `C1 RDI` (RDI stream)
- **ISPIF Routing (Pipes):**
  - **Pixel Pipes:** `C0 PIX` and `C1 PIX` are routed to **Pixel pipe 0** and **Pixel pipe 1**. They support features like 2D bypass and alt. merge.
  - **RDI Pipes:** `C0 RDI` and `C1 RDI` are routed to **RDI pipe 0** and **RDI pipe 1**. They include 2x byte counters.
- **Outputs (to VFE0):**
  - Pixel pipes feed the Pixel input(s) of `VFE0`.
  - RDI pipe 0 feeds the `RDI 0` port of `VFE0`.
  - RDI pipe 1 feeds the `RDI 1` port of `VFE0`.

#### 4.2.2.4.1 CSID power and clock management

Because of its multi-input and crossbarring, unlike other camera blocks, CSID uses many clocks. Primarily, the clocks are configured with respect to clocking and streaming from D-PHY (2-phase) sensor.

In general, clocks can only:
- Be shut down when the CSID core (or ISPIF pipe) is not in use
- Dynamically changed if no glitches are introduced and the equations are satisfied.

Clocks can be controlled using the GCC software registers. See the Global Clock Controller (GCC) chapter for details on enabling or gating the CSID and CAMSS top level clocks.

In addition, the CSID clocks can be gated and controlled within the CAM itself. See the CAMSS top level chapter for details.

> [!NOTE]
> Software must not change the clocks while CSID is active. Configuration changes must also be made only when not streaming.

CSID does not have power modes (except for in-use and low power idle), yet it is highly configurable through its software registers.

When CSID is not in use, to achieve low power idle, software should disable clocks from the GCC clock controller to minimize power dissipation.
<!-- page 959 -->
Clocks that can be disabled are:
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSIxPHY_CLK`
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK`
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSIxPIX_CLK`
- `GCC_CAMSS_CSIxRDI_CLK`

##### CSID clock muxing

The CSID ISPIF core pixel and RDI pipe clocks are muxed to provide a synchronous path from the CSID core being sourced. The inputs to the clock mux are the CSID core clocks, and each pipe is able to select a CSID core clock independently of the other pipes enabling for a large number of connectivity permutations. Figure 4-116 shows the global clock muxing for CSI within the CAMSS. Figure 4-118 shows the CSID ISPIF pixel and RDI pipe clock muxing.

#### Figure 4-118: CSID ISPIF pixel and RDI pipe clock muxing
*Description:* A block diagram showing the clock selection (muxing) for the pixel and RDI pipelines in the ISPIF.
- **CSID Core Clock:** `CAMSS_CSIx_CLK_SRC` is divided/gated to generate `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK` for `CSIDx`.
- **Pixel Pipe Clock Mux:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0PIX_CLK` and `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1PIX_CLK` are inputs to a mux that outputs `GCC_CAMSS_CSIxPIX_MUX_CLK` to drive `Pixel pipe [x]` (where x is the pipe index).
- **RDI Pipe Clock Mux:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0RDI_CLK` and `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1RDI_CLK` are inputs to a mux that outputs `GCC_CAMSS_CSIxRDI_MUX_CLK` to drive `RDI pipe [x]`.

##### CSID D-PHY (2-phase) clock structure

Figure 4-119 shows the clock structure when streaming from a D-PHY sensor.

#### Figure 4-119: CSID streaming from a D-PHY (2-phase) sensor
*Description:* A high-level block diagram showing the clock domains and data path from a D-PHY sensor to VFE0.
- **Data Path:**
  - **Sensor** sends data to **CSI PHYx** (associated with `PIXEL_CLK`).
  - **CSI PHYx** forwards data to **CSIDx** (associated with `DDR_CLK`).
  - **CSIDx** routes the streams through either the **Pixel pipe** or **RDI pipe** (within ISPIF) to **VFE0**.
- **Clock Domains:**
  - **Sensor side:** `PIXEL_CLK`
  - **PHY to CSID interface:** `DDR_CLK`
  - **CSID core:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK`
  - **VFE core:** `GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_CLK`
<!-- page 960 -->
The clock relationships are as follows:

$$F_{PIXEL\_CLK} = H_{Active} \times W_{Active} \times (1 + blanking\_pct) \times FPS = H_{Active} \times W_{Active} \times (1 + blanking\_pct) \times BPP \times FPS$$

$$F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_CSIx\_CLK} \ge \frac{F_{DDR\_CLK}}{4}$$

$$F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_VFE0\_CLK,PIXEL} \ge \frac{8 \times num\_active\_lanes \times F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_CSIx\_CLK}}{BPP}$$

$$F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_VFE0\_RDI} \ge \frac{8 \times num\_active\_lanes \times F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_CSIx\_CLK}}{64}$$

> [!NOTE]
> $F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_VFE0\_CLK,PIXEL}$ is the required VFE frequency if a pixel pipe is used, whereas $F_{GCC\_CAMSS\_VFE0\_CLK,RDI}$ is the required VFE frequency if an RDI pipe is used. If both pixel and RDI pipes are used, the required VFE frequency is the maximum of the two.

#### 4.2.2.4.2 CSID resets

This section describes the software CSID resets only. There are also global hardware resets asserted by the GCC that can also reset the CSID. For more information about resets asserted to CSID, see subsection GCC reset controller in the SoC Clock Management (GCC) chapter.

From a hardware reset, CSID is in an unconfigured state, yet it can receive data from a sensor. To move CSID to the correct configured state, software must set the required clocks in the GCC, and set the corresponding CSID software registers for normal operation.

The software reset is initiated manually by writing to `CSID_RST_CMD` command register.

Furthermore, two types of software resets are available:
- **Non-clearing clock domain resets**, which should be used for debug only. These resets are initiated for CSID via the `CSID_RST_CMD [CSID_CLK_DOMAIN]` and `CSID_RST_CMD [AHB_CLK_DOMAIN]` bitfields. The CSID ISPIF clock domain resets are initiated via `ISPIF_RST_CMD_0 [CLK_DOMAIN_RST]` and `ISPIF_RST_CMD_1 [CLK_DOMAIN_RST]` bitfields.
- **Self-clearing strobed block resets** (for all major CSID sub-blocks), which can be used when entering the camera application to move CSID to a known state. These resets are initiated via the rest of the `CSID_RST_CMD`, `ISPIF_RST_CMD_0`, and `ISPIF_RST_CMD_1` bitfields. To use strobed resets, the following steps apply:
  a. Stop all streaming.
  b. Set the appropriate reset bits in the first reset register.
  c. Wait for the `RESET_DONE` IRQ.
  d. Repeat steps b and c for every reset register containing resets that must be asserted.
  e. Resume streaming.

Generally, a software reconfiguration is not required unless the software register strobed reset is asserted.


<!-- page 961 -->

### 4.2.2.4.3 CSID interrupts

#### CSID error interrupts

Table 4-156 lists the errors using interrupts that the CSID core can detect. The interrupts are configured from CSID_IRQ_MASK register and serviced from the CSID_IRQ_CLEAR_CMD and CSID_IRQ_STATUS registers.

##### Table 4-156 CSID warning and error interrupts

| Interrupt | Triggering condition |
| :--- | :--- |
| WARNING_ECC | CSID receives a short packet or a long packet header with one bit of corruption that is corrected. Even though the error was corrected, it indicates a poor signal quality somewhere along the path from the sensor to the CSID. <br>No software intervention is required. Check for abnormal voltages and/or other types of interference that may be adversely affecting the data stream (for example, termination resistors, board connectivity, and so on). |
| ERROR_PHY_DL[m]_FIFO_OVERFLOW, m=[0-3] | Input FIFO on the PHY data lane [n] interface overflows, which is usually caused by one of the following:<br>- GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK is running too slow relative to the camera sensor DDR clock<br>- There is too much skew between the data lanes coming from the PHY<br>This is a fatal error and requires the user to reset the CSID before continuing. |
| ERROR_CRC | CSID core receives a long packet and calculates a CRC that does not match the transmitted (expected) CRC. A CRC mismatch indicates the payload is corrupted. The pixels of the received line were corrupted, which may result in artifacts in the final image. Software may choose to drop the current frame (using the VFE) and attempt to recapture an uncorrupted one. |
| ERROR_ECC | Following events occur:<br>- A corrupted short packet that cannot be recovered is received<br>- A corrupted long packet header that cannot be recovered is received<br>The erroneous packet is dropped. If it was a short packet (SOF/EOF), frame timing is corrupted and likely results in an ERROR_UNBOUNDED_FRAME IRQ, which indicates incorrect connectivity between the sensor and the PHY, incorrect lane configuration (that is, the number of lanes on the sensor does not match the configured number of lanes in the corresponding CSID), or there is a significant interference with the data transmission. Each of these issues requires user intervention. |
| ERROR_MULTIMAPPED_VC_DT | CSID core receives a long packet with a VC/DT combination that is mapped to more than one CID. The header of the erroneous long packet is captured in the CSID_CAPTURED_MMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR register.<br>Software must verify the configuration of CSID_CID_LUT_VC_[n] software registers. There is a duplicate resulting in a VC/data type combination being mapped to different CIDs. The CSID_CAPTURED_MMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR register contains information on the multimapped long packet. |
| ERROR_UNMAPPED_VC_DT | CSID receives a long packet with a VC/DT combination that is not mapped to a CID or is mapped to a CID that is disabled. The header of the first error packet is captured in the CSID_CAPTURED_UNMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR register.<br>The received VC/data type combination was not programmed in CSID_CID_LUT_VC_[n] software registers. The CSID_CAPTURED_UNMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR register contains information on the unmapped long packet. |
<!-- page 962 -->

##### Table 4-156 CSID warning and error interrupts (Continued)

| Interrupt | Triggering condition |
| :--- | :--- |
| ERROR_STREAM_UNDERFLOW | CSID receives less bytes of payload in a long packet than specified in the long packet's header (word count). If this occurs, the sensor is most likely incorrectly programming the packet header compared to the payload size. Check its settings. Either the sensor is terminating early or its transmitter timing violates the MIPI D-PHY specification (in particular, TEOT) of the PHY being reset during streaming. This requires user intervention. |
| ERROR_UNBOUNDED_FRAME | Following events occur:<br>- FS (frame start) for VC n, <0 or more packets that are not FE for VC n>, FS for VC n<br>- FE (frame end) for VC n, <0 or more packets that are not FE for VC n>, FE for VC n.<br>If this error is not accompanied by any other errors, the sensor is likely at fault (it is not sending SOF, EOF pairs) and its configuration should be verified. If this error is accompanied by ERROR_ECC, the ERROR_UNBOUNDED_FRAME is the result of ECC errors. Debug the ERROR_ECC issue first, fixing that usually fixes this error too. |
| ERROR_6PP_FIFO_OVERFLOW | 6p (pixel) packer FIFOs overflow. By design, these FIFOs should never overflow. This bit exists in case there is a bug in the design. |
| ERROR_TG_FIFO_OVERFLOW | Test generator output FIFOs overflow. By design, these FIFOs should never overflow. This bit exists in case there is a bug in the design. |

Table 4-157 lists errors using interrupts that the ISPIF core can detect. The interrupts can be configured from the ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_MASK_0, ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_MASK_1, and ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_MASK_2 registers and serviced from the ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_0, ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_1, and ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_2 registers.

##### Table 4-157 ISPIF error interrupts

| Interrupt | Triggering condition |
| :--- | :--- |
| PIX_INTF_m_OVERFLOW, m=[0-1] | Pixel interface pipe FIFO overflows. The event occurs when the VFE clock (read clock) is too slow compared to the input data rate (write clock, GCC_CAMSS_CSIxPIX_CLK, x=[0-1] a function of the sensor data rate).<br>The rate of data consumption by the VFE does not match or exceeds the rate of data generation by the sensor.<br>Either increase the VFE frequency or decrease the sensor transmission rate to adhere to the CDC FIFO equation. |
| RAW_INTF_m_OVERFLOW, m=[0-1] | RDI pipe FIFO overflows. The event occurs when the VFE clock (read clock) is too slow compared to the input data rate (write clock, GCC_CAMSS_CSIxRDI_CLK, x=[0-1], a function of the sensor data rate).<br>The rate of data consumption by VFE does not match or exceeds the rate of data generation by the sensor. In this case, the rate of data generation is that of the sensor and the rate of data consumption is equal to 64 bits/VFE clock cycle.<br>Either increase the VFE frequency or decrease the sensor transmission rate so that it is less than 64 bits/VFE clock cycle. |
<!-- page 963 -->

#### CSID status interrupts

The CSID core includes several status interrupts, which can be configured from the CSID_IRQ_MASK register and cleared by setting the appropriate bit in the CSID_IRQ_CLEAR_CMD register.

##### Table 4-158 CSID status interrupts

| Interrupt | Triggering condition |
| :--- | :--- |
| INFO_PHY_DL[m]_SOT_CAPTURED, m=[0-3] | Received the beginning of a transmission on data lane [m] |
| INFO_PHY_DL[m]_EOT_CAPTURED, m=[0-3] | Received the end of a transmission on data lane [m] |
| INFO_LONG_PKT_CAPTURED | Captured a long packet corresponding to the settings configured in CSID_CORE_CTRL_1 |
| INFO_SHORT_PKT_CAPTURED | Captured a short packet corresponding to the settings configured in CSID_CORE_CTRL_1 |
| INFO_TG_DONE | Completed sending the configured number of frames |
| INFO_RST_DONE | Reset controller has completed sending the strobed resets written to CSID_RST_CMD |

Also, the ISPIF core provides status interrupts. All interrupts can be cleared by setting the appropriate bit in the ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_0, ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_1, and ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_2 software register.

##### Table 4-159 ISPIF status interrupts

| Interrupt | Triggering condition |
| :--- | :--- |
| PIX_INTF_[m]_VC_[n]_[p], m=[0-1], n=[0-3], p=[SOF, EOF, EOL] | Pixel interface pipe [m] has received an SOF, EOF, or EOL strobe on virtual channel [n] |
| RAW_INTF_[m]_VC_[n]_[p], m=[0-1], n=[0-3], p=[SOF, EOF, EOL] | Raw interface pipe [m] has received an SOF, EOF, or EOL strobe on virtual channel [n] |
| RST_DONE_IRQ | ISPIF core reset controller has completed sending out the strobed resets written to ISPIF_RST_CMD_0 and ISPIF_RST_CMD_1. |

### 4.2.2.4.4 CSID internal architecture

#### CSID interfaces

Table 4-160 lists the major interfaces of CSID.

##### Table 4-160 CSID interfaces

| CSID interface | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| CAMSS clock controller | Generates all CSID clocks and external resets. CSID also includes several software resets that can be accessed through its AHB interface. |
| APSS application processor | Programs CSID and handles all IRQs (even though the camera subsystem has a dedicated microprocessor, it is not used to program CSID or handle its IRQs). |
| AHB | Programming CSRs and IRQ handling |
| CSI PHY | CSI-2 Physical layer interface that receives sensor data |
| VFE | Interface that receives the decoded pixel and RDI data |
| CCI | Interface that receives sensor frame and line timing strobes from the CSID and sent to CCI. |
| Camera subsystem test bus and IRQ consolidation | Contains the CSID test buses and IRQs that are consolidated in the camera subsystem. The consolidated test bus and IRQs are sent to CAMSS_IRQ_ROUTER where a similar consolidation is performed. This continues until the test bus reaches TLMM, and the IRQs reach their intended destinations in the APSS_QGIC2. |

### 4.2.2.4.5 CSID defining the concurrency scenario

CSID is a configurable module that can service multiple sensors simultaneously. Consequently, the concurrency scenario must be determined to know the CSID components that are required.

##### Table 4-161 CSID scenarios

| Scenario | Requirements |
| :--- | :--- |
| 2D preview | A single CSID core and a single ISPIF pixel pipe. |
| snapshot | - The sensor output is decoded by a CSID with output being routed to an ISPIF pixel pipe and then to the corresponding VFE.<br>- The maximum speed is limited by the processing speed of the VFE. |
| Embedded unprocessed data | A single CSID core and a single ISPIF RDI pipe.<br>- For sensors that output embedded data and sensors that output data that VFE does not process.<br>- CSID core output is routed to the ISPIF RDI pipe and then to the corresponding VFE. |
| Combined | - CSID, with its multiple CSID cores and ISPIF pipes, can handle multiple scenarios simultaneously; in fact, it's common for a sensor to output multiple scenarios.<br>- Sensors output data sequentially. For example, a sensor may output a 2D preview stream interleaved with an embedded data stream and each stream identifiable by a unique data ID (virtual channel and data type) according to the MIPI CSI-2 specification. |
<!-- page 965 -->

### 4.2.2.4.6 CSID data flows

The primary operation of CSID is to transform CSI-2 encoded data into pixels for consumption by the VFE or direct writing to memory.

Table 4-162 shows the supported data flows.

##### Table 4-162 CSID supported data flows

| Data flow | What is supported |
| :--- | :--- |
| Input virtual channels | All virtual channels on its sensor input |
| Input data types | All 6-bit, 8-bit, 10-bit, and 12-bit pixel types and DPCM 10-6-10, 10-8-10, 12-6-12, and 12-8-12 compression types |
| Output CIDs | Channel IDs (distinguish virtual channels and data types from the rest of the processing pipeline).<br>Up to four CIDs per virtual channel for a total of 16 CIDs and denoted as CIDs 0 through 15.<br>- Each stream that is processed by CSID is assigned a unique CID that follows the data stream as it is processed and output.<br>- All RDI outputs output a CID that VFE can use to differentiate between separate streams. However, unlike the pixel interfaces, VFE does not support CIDs on its RDI inputs. Therefore, CSID does not provide a CID output on its output pixel interfaces.<br>- Mapping virtual channels and data types to CIDs is done using four look-up tables (See Table 4-163). |

Table 4-163 show details of the CSID CSID_CID_LUT_VC_0 register virtual channel bits.

##### Table 4-163 CSID virtual channel data stream bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 29:24 | CID_3_DT | Any stream received with virtual channel 0 and data type present in this field |
| 21:16 | CID_2_DT | Any stream received with virtual channel 0 and data type present in this field |
| 13:8 | CID_1_DT | Any stream received with virtual channel 0 and data type present in this field |
| 5:0 | CID_0_DT | Any stream received with virtual channel 0 and data type present in this field |

> [!NOTE]
> A virtual channel and data type combination cannot be assigned to more than one CID. If this multi-mapping occurs and a stream with the erroneous virtual channel and data type combination is received, the receiving CSID core asserts its ERROR_MULTIMAPPED_VC_DT IRQ and drops the stream. This is a fatal programming error and should be corrected.

Similarly, all received data streams must be mapped to only one CID. If a received data stream contains a virtual channel and data type that is not mapped to a CID, the receiving CSID core asserts its ERROR_UNMAPPED_VC_DT IRQ and drops the stream. This is also a fatal programming error and should be corrected.

### 4.2.2.4.7 CSID operation timeline

#### CSID 2D preview and snapshot timeline

Figure 4-120 shows the operational timeline of 2D preview, which is the most commonly used camera action.

#### Figure 4-120: CSID 2D preview timeline

*Description:* Sequence diagram of the CSID 2D preview timeline involving four actors: User, Processor, CSID, and Sensor.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    actor Processor
    actor CSID
    actor Sensor

    Note over User: Starts camera
    Processor->>Processor: Programs other cores
    Processor->>CSID: Programs CSID for 2D preview
    CSID->>Sensor: Programs sensor for 2D preview
    CSID->>Sensor: Sends start streaming command
    Sensor->>CSID: Streaming data
    CSID->>Processor: SOF IRQ
    Note over Processor: Start of frame processing
    CSID->>Processor: EOF IRQ
    Note over Processor: End of frame processing
    Note over Sensor: Vertical blanking
    
    Note over Sensor: (Streaming repeats)
    CSID->>Processor: SOF IRQ
    Note over Processor: Start of frame processing
    CSID->>Processor: EOF IRQ
    Note over Processor: End of frame processing

    Note over User: Stops camera
    Processor->>Processor: Halts VFE
    Processor->>CSID: Resets CSID
    CSID->>Sensor: Sends stop streaming command
    Note over Sensor: Places sensor in low power standby
```

### 4.2.2.4.8 CSID PHY initialization

#### CSID PHY power sequence

As 28nm is a thin-oxide deep submicron process, it is critical to power up lower supply voltages before higher ones to avoid circuit reliability failures which can cause part destruction. Similarly, the power-down sequence requires higher voltages to be disabled first, followed by the lower ones.

To power down all PHY lanes the following bit need to be set accordingly:

##### Table 4-164 CSID PHY power sequence

| Register | Value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MIPI_CSIPHY_GLBL_PWR_CFG | 0x00 | Power down all lanes |

MIPI CSI PHY can be programmed into either 4 lane or 2-1 lane mode (combo mode). The following sections describe these configurations.
<!-- page 969 -->

Assumptions include:
- CSI_PHY0
- Number of data lanes: 4 (lane 0, 2, 3, 4)
- Number of clock lanes: 1 (lane 1)

| MIPI_CSIPHY_GLBL_PWR_CFG | 0x3F | Power up all lanes. One bit for each lane and one global power up |

| MIPI_CSIPHY_LNn_CFG2 | 0x10 | Enable LP receiver for lane 1 (clock lane), n = [1] |
| MIPI_CSIPHY_LNn_CFG2 | 0x10 | Enable LP receiver for lane 2, n = [2] |
| MIPI_CSIPHY_LNn_TEST_IMP | 0x17 | Enable HS termination, n = [0] |
| MIPI_CSIPHY_LNn_TEST_IMP | 0x17 | Enable HS termination, n = [1] |
| MIPI_CSIPHY_LNn_TEST_IMP | 0x17 | Enable HS termination, n = [2] |

#### 4.2.2.4.9 CSID initialization

Initialization follows this sequence:
1. Optionally, reset the CSI_PHY(s), CSID, and VFE to move the blocks into a known state. See Section 4.2.2.4.2.
2. Program the sensor and ensure that it is not streaming, which can be in the form of ULPM (generally known as standby) or LP-11.
3. Program the CSI_PHY(s). See Section 4.2.2.4.8.
4. Program CSID; generally, register configuration is static except for all command registers (`*_CMD`).
5. Program the VFE0
6. Start the sensor

### CSID single 3-lane 2D stream example

Assumptions include:
* 3-lane sensor connected to CSI_PHY0

* Sensor data lane 0 connected to PHY lane 1 (for board connectivity error)
* Sensor data lane 1 connected to PHY lane 2
* Sensor data lane 2 connected to PHY lane 3
* Sensor data lane 3 connected to PHY lane 0
* Stream 0: virtual channel 1
* RAW10 (data type 0x2B)
* Processed by CSID0
* Mapped to CID 5 (arbitrarily chosen from CIDs 4 to 7; virtual channel 1 streams must be mapped to CIDs 4 through 7)
* Routed to VFE0 pixel pipe

### CSID two independent 2D streams

Table 4-170 lists the two types of independent streams.

### Table 4-170 CSID independent streams

| Stream | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| Multiple streams from same sensor | The streams can be denoted independent by assigning them to different virtual channels. Because the streams are being sent by the same sensor, the streams are sent sequentially (meaning they cannot be sent at the same time). As a result, all the streams can be handled by the same CSID core, which can only accept a single stream at a time. |
| Streams from different sensors | Always independent and can be sent at the same time. Because a CSID core can accept only a single stream at a time, streams from multiple sensors should be sent to different CSID cores. |

Assumptions include:
* Streams are coming from different sensors and thus, must be routed to different CSID cores.
* 4-lane sensor connected to CSI_PHY0
* Sensor data lane 0 connected to PHY lane 1 (due to board connectivity error)
* Sensor data lane 1 connected to PHY lane 0
* Sensor data lane 2 connected to PHY lane 3
* Sensor data lane 3 connected to PHY lane 2
* Stream 0: virtual channel 0
* DPCM 10-6-10 (data type 0x30)
* Processed by CSID0
* Mapped to CID 3 (arbitrarily chosen from CIDs 0 - 3)
* Routed to VFE0 pixel pipe
* 2-lane sensor connected to CSI_PHY1
* Sensor data lane 0 connected to PHY lane 3 (due to board connectivity error)
* Sensor data lane 1 connected to PHY lane 2
* Stream 1: virtual channel 3
* YUV422 8-bit (data type 0x1E)
* Processed by CSID1
* Mapped to CID 14
<!-- page 976 -->

* Routed to VFE0 RDI pipe 2

### CSID dynamic update of software registers

CSID does not have double-buffered software registers. Therefore, few cases exist for a core's (CSID0, CSID1, ISPIF) software registers to be updated while processing.

Generally, CSID software registers are configured at application launch and remain static while the camera is streaming.

Table 4-172 lists only the software registers that can be modified during processing.

### Table 4-172 CSID software registers that can be set during processing

| Register | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CSID** | |
| CSID_RST_CMD | Reset portions of the CSID core |
| CSID_IRQ_CLEAR_CMD | Clear IRQs that have fired |
| **ISPIF** | |
| ISPIF_RST_CMD_0 | Reset portions of the ISPIF core |
| ISPIF_RST_CMD_1 | Reset portions of the ISPIF core |
| ISPIF_IRQ_GLOBAL_CLEAR_CMD | Clear all the set bits in VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_0, VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_1, and VFE_m_IRQ_CLEAR_2<br>• Can be set simultaneously |
| ISPIF_VFE_m_INTF_CMD_0 | Start or stop data transfer to the various ISPIF processing pipes.<br>Disabling data transfer immediately requires a subsequent reset to continue (disabling data transfer does not). m = [0] |
| ISPIF_VFE_m_INTF_CMD_1 | Start or stop data transfer to the various ISPIF processing pipes.<br>Disabling data transfer immediately requires a subsequent reset to continue (disabling data transfer does not). m = [0] |

### CSID input output buffers and formats

Each CSID includes a set of input FIFOs in its PHY interface block, which are used to:
* Pack the PHY data stream for consumption by the rest of the CSID core pipeline
* Remove any skew between the PHY data lines that occurs because of chip or PHY timing, or both.

Besides the transparent FIFOs, the ISPIF core uses two memories that act as de-skew. Writing to and reading from these memories is automatic, no user intervention is required.
<!-- page 978 -->

### 4.2.2.5.3 CSID register definitions

#### 0x0 CSID_HW_VERSION
* **Type**: R
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`, x = 1 or 2
* **Reset State**: `0x30030000`

This register contains the CSID hardware version, which can be used to identify the exact version of hardware present.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR | |
| 27:16 | MINOR | |
| 15:0 | STEP | |

#### 0x4 CSID_CORE_CTRL_0
* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`, x = 1 or 2
* **Reset State**: `0x00032103`

#### 0x10 CSID_CID_LUT_VC_0
* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`, x = 0 or 1
* **Reset State**: `0x00000000`

This register contains the DT (data type) to MDT (mapped data type) mappings for CIDs 0x0 - 0x3, which are associated to VC 0. The format of the CIDs in this software register is as follows:

`CID[3:0] = {2'b00, MDT}`
<!-- page 988 -->

**NOTE:** No two MDTs may be mapped to the same DT. Furthermore, FS/FE (frame start/end) packets for VC 0 will apply to CIDs 0x0 - 0x3 since frame timing packets do not have an associated DT (that is, FS/FE packets apply to all DTs/MDTs within the same VC).

#### 0x10 CSID_CID_LUT_VC_0 (continued)

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 29:24 | CID_3_DT | DT mapped to CID 3. CID 3 is associated with VC 0. |
| 21:16 | CID_2_DT | DT mapped to CID 2. CID 2 is associated with VC 0. |
| 13:8 | CID_1_DT | DT mapped to CID 1. CID 1 is associated with VC 0. |
| 5:0 | CID_0_DT | DT mapped to CID 0. CID 0 is associated with VC 0. |

### 0x64 CSID_IRQ_MASK

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`, x = 0 or 1
- **Reset State**: 0x00000800

This register contains the CSID core IRQ mask. The IRQ mask is used to configure the events that the system processor(s) will handle (unmasked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x1) and ignore (masked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x0).
<!-- page 992 -->

> [!NOTE]
> A masked IRQ will still assert in this software register if the corresponding event occurs. The mask only prevents the CSID core from notifying the system processor(s).
