### 0x68 CSID_IRQ_STATUS

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_AHB_CLK`, x = 0 or 1
- **Reset State**: 0x00000000

This register contains the CSID core IRQ status.

> [!NOTE]
> Masking an IRQ will only prevent the CSID from notifying the processor of the corresponding event. The corresponding IRQ bit in this register will still be set to 0x1.

### CSID_IRQ_STATUS

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | ERROR_TG_FIFO_OVERFLOW | This IRQ fires when one of the test generator output FIFOs overflows. By design, these FIFOs should never overflow. This bit is present in case there is a bug in the design. |
| 30 | ERROR_6PP_FIFO_OVERFLOW | This IRQ fires when one of the 6p packer pixel FIFOs overflows. By design, these FIFOs should never overflow. This bit is present in case there is a bug in the design. |
| 29 | ERROR_UNBOUNDED_FRAME | This IRQ fires when one of the following events occur:<br><ul><li>FS (frame start) for VC n, &lt;0 or more packets that are not FE for VC n&gt;, FS for VC n.</li><li>FE (frame end) for VC n, &lt;0 or more packets that are not FE for VC n&gt;, FE for VC n.</li></ul> |
<!-- page 994 -->

### CSID_IRQ_STATUS (cont.)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 28 | ERROR_STREAM_UNDERFLOW | This IRQ fires when the CSID core receives less bytes of payload in a long packet than specified in the long packet's header (word count).<br>This is a fatal error which requires the user to reset the CSID core before continuing. |
| 27 | ERROR_UNMAPPED_VC_DT | This IRQ fires when the CSID core receives a long packet with a VC/DT combination that is not mapped to a CID. The header of the first error packet will be captured in `CSID_CAPTURED_UNMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR`. |
| 26 | ERROR_MULTIMAPPED_VC_DT | This IRQ fires when the CSID core receives a long packet with a VC/DT combination that is mapped to more than one CID. The header of the erroneous long packet will be captured in `CSID_CAPTURED_MMAPPED_LONG_PKT_HDR`. |
| 25 | ERROR_ECC | This IRQ fires when one of the following events occur:<br><ul><li>A corrupted short packet which cannot be recovered is received.</li><li>A corrupted long packet header which cannot be recovered is received.</li></ul> |
| 24 | ERROR_CRC | This IRQ fires when the CSID core receives a long packet and calculates a CRC that does not match the transmitted (expected) CRC. A CRC mismatch indicates the payload is corrupted. |
| 23 | ERROR_PHY_DL3_FIFO_OVERFLOW | This IRQ fires when the input FIFO on the PHY DL3 (data lane 3) interface overflows. This is usually caused by one of the following:<br><ul><li>`GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK` is running too slow relative to the camera sensor DDR clock.</li><li>There is too much skew between data lanes coming from the PHY.</li></ul>This is a fatal error which requires the user to reset the CSID core before continuing. |
| 22 | ERROR_PHY_DL2_FIFO_OVERFLOW | This IRQ fires when the input FIFO on the PHY DL2 (data lane 2) interface overflows. This is usually caused by one of the following:<br><ul><li>`GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK` is running too slow relative to the camera sensor DDR clock.</li><li>There is too much skew between data lanes coming from the PHY.</li></ul>This is a fatal error which requires the user to reset the CSID core before continuing. |
| 21 | ERROR_PHY_DL1_FIFO_OVERFLOW | This IRQ fires when the input FIFO on the PHY DL1 (data lane 1) interface overflows. This is usually caused by one of the following:<br><ul><li>`GCC_CAMSS_CSIx_CLK` is running too slow relative to the camera sensor DDR clock.</li><li>There is too much skew between data lanes coming from the PHY.</li></ul>This is a fatal error which requires the user to reset the CSID core before continuing. |
<!-- page 995 -->

## 4.2.2.5.4 ISPIF register definitions

### 0x8 ISPIF_RST_CMD_0

- **Type**: W
- **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`
- **Reset State**: 0x00000001

**RST_CMD**

This register is used to reset the ISPIF core to a known state. This is a command register and the software needs to set the bits on the clock domains it wishes to reset. A composite interrupt is generated when all the clock domains that were reset is complete. A second global reset command should not be issued until the reset acknowledge is received from the first command.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | VFE_0_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to the `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_VFE0_CLK` domain registers. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br>0x0: FUNCTIONAL<br>0x1: RESET |
| 30 | PIX_INTF_1_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to the `GCC_CAMSS_CSI1PIX_CLK` domain registers. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br>0x0: FUNCTIONAL<br>0x1: RESET |
| 29 | PIX_INTF_0_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to the `GCC_CAMSS_CSI0PIX_CLK` domain registers. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br>0x0: FUNCTIONAL<br>0x1: RESET |
| 28 | RDI_INTF_2_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to the `GCC_CAMSS_CSI2RDI_CLK` domain logic in ISPIF raw interface. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br>0x0: FUNCTIONAL<br>0x1: RESET |

### 0x208+0x200\*m ISPIF_VFE_m_IRQ_MASK_0, m=\[0..0\]
**Type:** RW
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK
**Reset State:** 0x08000000

This software register contains the ISPIF core IRQ mask. The IRQ mask is used to configure the events that the system processor(s) will handle (unmasked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x1) and ignore (masked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x0).

> [!NOTE]

### ISPIF_VFE_m_PIX_INTF_n_CROP

**Address:** `0x278 + 0x200 * m + 0x4 * n` where `m = [0..0]`, `n = [0..1]`
**Type:** RW
**Clock:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`
**Reset State:** `0xFFFF0000`

This register controls horizontal cropping.
<!-- page 1023 -->
#### ISPIF_VFE_m_PIX_INTF_n_CROP (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | END_PIXEL | Specifies the last pixel that will not be cropped. All pixels after this value will be cropped. For example, if this field is set to 0x234 and crop is enabled, pixels 0x235 and beyond will be cropped.<br>NOTE: The value 0x0 refers to pixel 0 (i.e., the first pixel). |
| 15:0 | START_PIXEL | Specifies the first pixel that will not be cropped. All pixels before this value will be cropped. For example, if this field is set to 0x234 and crop is enabled, pixels 0x0 to 0x233 will be cropped.<br>NOTE: The value 0x0 refers to pixel 0 (i.e., the first pixel). |

### ISPIF_VFE_m_3D_THRESHOLD

**Address:** `0x288 + 0x200 * m` where `m = [0..0]`
**Type:** RW
**Clock:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`
**Reset State:** `0x00000000`

This register is used for setting the threshold value for the HW FIFO that deskews the incoming sensor data during 3D merge mode. It is recommended to program this register to `CEILING((left_line_width_in_pixels / (2 * 6)))`.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10:0 | TX_THRESHOLD | This register sets the threshold value for the HW FIFO that deskews the incoming sensor data during 3D merge mode. The unit is in terms of 6 pixels. It is recommended to program this register to `CEILING((left_line_width_in_pixels / (2 * 6)))` |

### ISPIF_VFE_m_PIX_INTF_n_STATUS

| 2 | VC2_PIX_HALT | This bit indicates the current status of the ISPIF pixel 0 interface for Virtual Channel 2 (VC2)<br>0x0: The VC2 Pix interface is busy<br>0x1: The VC2 Pix Interface is idle |
| 1 | VC1_PIX_HALT | This bit indicates the current status of the ISPIF pixel 0 interface for Virtual Channel 1 (VC1)<br>0x0: The VC1 Pix interface is busy<br>0x1: The VC1 Pix Interface is idle |
| 0 | VC0_PIX_HALT | This bit indicates the current status of the ISPIF pixel 0 interface for Virtual Channel 0 (VC0)<br>0x0: The VC0 Pix interface is busy<br>0x1: The VC0 Pix Interface is idle |

### ISPIF_VFE_m_3D_DESKEW_SIZE

**Address:** `0x2E4 + 0x200 * m` where `m = [0..0]`
**Type:** R
**Clock:** `GCC_CAMSS_CSI_ISPIF_AHB_CLK`
**Reset State:** `0x00000000`

This register indicates the skew between the arrival of RIGHT and LEFT start-of-frames during 3D merge mode. The unit of the `DESKEW_SIZE` is in terms of number of VFE clock cycles. One can convert the `DESKEW_SIZE` value to the time unit by multiplying the `DESKEW_SIZE` by the VFE clock period.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:0 | DESKEW_SIZE | This register indicates skew between the arrival of RIGHT and LEFT start-of-frames during 3D merge mode. |

(With max Tclk-miss spec being 60 ns and the timer clock set to 8 ns, default value is set to ~40 ns)<br><br>Clock MISS timing parameter setup calculation is as follows:<br>To setup Tclk_miss, the following conditions need to be met:<br>- **Condition 1:** `Tclk_miss * Ttimerclk_period > Tddrclk_period` (when `Ttimerclk_period < Tddrclk_period`)<br>- **Condition 2:** `Tclk_idle > 3 * Ttimerclk_period`<br>- `Tclk_miss = Tclk_idle / Ttimerclk_period - 1`<br><br>*Note:* If configured as data lane, this register description is not applicable. If configured as clock lane, use the following descriptions:<br>- `Tclk_miss` : the clock miss timing parameter software register value. Count by Timer clock.<br>- `Tclk_idle` : the period of ddr clock miss time for PHY to detect.<br><br>**Example of usage mode:**<br>`Tddrclk_period = 2ns` (500MHz), `Ttimerclk_period = 8ns` (125Mhz)<br>`Tclk_idle` must be > 24ns.<br>`Tclk_miss` has to be greater than 3.<br>For detecting 60 ns clk miss period (`Tclk_idle = 60ns`), set `Tclk_miss = 6`. |

## 4.2.3 Camera Post Processing (CPP)
This section describes the camera post processing (CPP) engine.

### 4.2.3.1 CPP overview
The CPP provides post image capture processing capabilities. It provides image denoising capability, digital zoom scaling support, image sharpening to enhance image after denoising, and image scaling capability. It supports 0/90/180/270 degree rotation of the image, along with horizontal and vertical flip. The source of images to be processed is read from memory.

Figure 4-123 shows a high-level overview of the CPP module within the camera subsystem in the SoC.

#### Figure 4-123: CPP overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the Camera Post Processing (CPP) module and its integration within the system.
- Inside the **Camera Subsystem**, the **CPP** module connects to **VBIF** with "Data in" (VBIF to CPP) and "Data out" (CPP to VBIF).
- **GCC** provides "Clocks" and "Reset" inputs to the **CPP** module.
- The **CPP** module sends an "Interrupt" signal to **APSS**.
- **VBIF** communicates bidirectionally with the **System NoC**.
- The **Camera Subsystem** communicates bidirectionally with the **System NoC** via the "AHB slave bus".
- The **System NoC** is also connected bidirectionally to **OCMEM** and **SMMU**.
- **SMMU** is connected bidirectionally to **External Memory**.
<!-- page 1074 -->

Table 4-177 lists the CPP supported features.

##### Table 4-177 CPP features
| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| CPP | <ul><li>Image 0/90/180/270 degree rotation</li><li>Up and down scaling</li><li>Digital zoom</li><li>Image sharpening and denoising</li><li>Image cropping</li><li>Horizontal and vertical flip</li></ul> |

Table 4-178 lists some of the CPP key use cases.

##### Table 4-178 CPP key use cases
| Use case | Example scenario |
| :--- | :--- |
| Camera viewfinder, snapshot, and video | Real-time image-processing operations for camera and video and offline processing for post capture frames |
| Multiple software control for quick image processing | See Figure 4-125 |

### 4.2.3.2 CPP internal connectivity
Figure 4-124 shows the CPP internal interface signals.

#### Figure 4-124: CPP internal connectivity
*Description:* Detailed signal block diagram of the CPP module within the Camera Subsystem, highlighting clocks, reset, interrupt, and data paths.
- **GCC Connections:**
  - Provides reset signal `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_ARES` to **CPP**.
  - Provides clock source `CAMSS_CPP_CLK_SRC` which maps to **CPP** input clock `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_CLK`.
  - Provides AHB clock source `CAMSS_AHB_CLK_SRC` which maps to **CPP** input clock `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK` and also to the Camera Subsystem block input clock `GCC_CAMSS_AHB_CLK`.
- **APSS Connections:**
  - Receives interrupt signal `CAMSS_IRQ7` from **CPP** output `CPP_IRQ`.
- **Data Path:**
  - `Data in` goes from **VBIF** to **CPP**.
  - `Data out` goes from **CPP** to **VBIF**.
- **System NoC Connections:**
  - Bidirectional interface between **VBIF** and **System NoC**.
  - Bidirectional "AHB slave bus" between Camera Subsystem and **System NoC**.

Table 4-180 through Table 4-183 list the CPP internal connectivity attributes, such as information on each controller power domain belonging, clocks, resets, and interrupts.

### 4.2.3.3 CPP functional description
The CPP is used for camera applications in support of such camera features as viewfinder, snapshot, and video. CPP is needed for both real time operations for camera and video and the offline processing for post capture frames.

The camera micro controller (MICRO) is a small stand-alone hardware block within the camera subsystem that encapsulates all the functionality to enable real time embedded control for camera hardware.

Multiple software pieces and hardware blocks are involved in the operations when the CPP is needed. In the following scenario, a real time operation is used to describe the entire operation.

Figure 4-125 shows a high-level theory of operation of the CPP and surrounding camera entities.

#### Figure 4-125: CPP theory of operation
*Description:* Block diagram showing the interaction of software drivers and hardware modules (VFE, Micro Controller, CPP) using control, data, and interrupt paths.
- Legend:
  - **Interrupt**: Red line
  - **Frame Data**: Blue line
  - **Control**: Black line
- **ARM Host Software:**
  - **Upper layer Camera Software** interacts with **VFE Driver**.
  - **VFE Driver** controls **VFE** and receives "All VFE IRQs" from it.
  - **VFE Driver** communicates with **MC Driver**.
  - **MC Driver** controls the hardware **Micro Controller** and receives "Frame Done IRQ" from it.
- **Data Flow:**
  - **VFE** output is directed to **Ping** and **Pong** buffers.
  - **CPP** reads data from **Ping** / **Pong** buffers.
  - **CPP** writes processed data to **Output Buffer**.
- **Hardware Control:**
  - **Micro Controller** controls **CPP** and receives "All CPP IRQs" from it.
<!-- page 1078 -->

Figure 4-126 shows a high-level overview of the CPP functional blocks.

#### Figure 4-126: CPP functional block diagram (labeled as CSID functional block diagram in original PDF)
*Description:* Block diagram showing the CPP internal processing pipeline and its clock domains.
- **Clock Domains:**
  - **GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK domain:** Contains **AHB2AHB** block connecting to the external **AHB** bus.
  - **GCC_CAMSS_CPP_CLK domain:**
    - Register interface: **AHB2CRIF** connects to **AHB2AHB**. It interfaces with **Reset Controller**, **SW Registers**, and **IRQ Generator**.
    - Data path pipeline: **Fetch Engine** -> **Denoise** -> **Crop** -> **Upscale** -> **Sharpen (ASF)** -> **Crop** -> **Rotate** -> **Write Engine**.
- **External Interfaces:**
  - **AHB** bus at the top.
  - **VBIF** at the bottom, which interfaces with **System NoC**.
  - **Fetch Engine** reads from **VBIF**.
  - **Write Engine** writes to **VBIF**.

### 4.2.3.3.1 CPP power and clock management
The CPP is a separate hard macro within the camera subsystem, similar to the VFE and JPEG. The CPP is a power collapsible hard macro.

After a power-on sequence, ensure that the following is performed before using the CPP:
1. The CPP is reset to a known state, see Section 4.2.3.3.2.
2. Appropriate clocks to the CPP and VBIF instance in CPP hard macro are enabled:
   - For the CPP to be used, the `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_CLK` must be on.
   - The peripheral `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK` must be on.
   - The appropriate `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_CLK` must be on.

Upon enabling the controller from power collapsed state, the CPP must be reset from the global clock controller (GCC).

> [!WARNING]
> Resetting the CPP from the GCC must only be done upon power-up. If CPP hardware is actively processing and a reset from the GCC is applied, it can result in detrimental operation.
<!-- page 1079 -->

If the software is unsure of the state of CPP, it must perform a reset via the `CPP_RST_CMD_0` register. The software reset requires `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_CLK` and peripheral `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK` clocks to be running.

The required clocks for CPP are listed in Table 4-184.

##### Table 4-184 CPP required clocks
| Data Source | Data Sink | GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK / GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_CPP_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_CLK |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DDR | DDR | ON | ON | ON |

The registers in the GCC control the assertion of reset and enablement of clocks.

The register access to the VBIF requires the AHB clocks to be on because the CPP interfaces with the VBIF for AXI bus interfacing.

### 4.2.3.3.2 CPP resets
This section describes only the software CPP reset. There are also global hardware resets asserted by the GCC that can also reset the CPP.

Software must configure the CPP to an appropriate mode after a power-on-reset or a software reset via the `CPP_RST_CMD_0` register. Without proper configuration, issuing a start command to the hardware is meaningless and may result in unintended behavior.

The CPP (by default) is in a low-power state because key module processing blocks are disabled by default.

### 4.2.3.3.3 CPP interrupts
Interrupts are enabled from the `CPP_IRQ_MASK_0` register, polled from the `CPP_IRQ_STATUS_0` register, and cleared from the `CPP_IRQ_CLEAR_CMD_0` register.

The hardware IP returns interrupts upon hardware completed tasks, buffer management, and error conditions. Hardware completed task events include completion of stripe processing, with results written to memory. Buffer management interrupts include indication of consumed buffers. Table 4-185 lists the interrupts provided by the CPP.
<!-- page 1080 -->

##### Table 4-185 CPP interrupts
| No. | IRQ Name | IRQ Type | IRQ Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | `INFO_RST_DONE` | Status/Task Completion | Indicates that reset request is completed |
| 1 | `INFO_AXI_HALT_ACK_DONE` | Status/Task Completion | Indicates that AXI bus halt request is completed |
| 2 | `INFO_SESSION_DONE` | Status/Task Completion | Indicates that processing for session is completed. |
| 3 | `INFO_WE_WR_BUF_PLN_0_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a write plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 4 | `INFO_WE_WR_BUF_PLN_1_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a write plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 5 | `INFO_WE_WR_BUF_PLN_2_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a write plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 6 | `INFO_WE_WR_BUF_PLN_3_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a write plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 7 | `INFO_FE_0_RD_BUF_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a read plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 8 | `INFO_FE_1_RD_BUF_DONE` | Status/Buffer Management | Indicates that a read plane buffer specified by software is consumed. |
| 9 | `ERROR_CBCR_SIZE_MISMATCH` | Error | Indicates that CB plane and CR plane are of unequal size resulting in error during interleaving before writing to external memory. |

### 4.2.3.4.3 CPP register definitions

#### 0x0 CPP_HW_VERSION

* **Type**: R
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State**: 0x40010000

This software register contains the CPP hardware version, which can be used to identify the exact version of present hardware.

##### CPP_HW_VERSION Bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR_VERSION | Used to track the CPP generations. Generations are differentiated by feature-set. |
| 27:16 | MINOR_VERSION | Used to track lateral changes within a generation. The major feature-set remains the same but the implementation may be different (for example, an AHB interface in one design and an AXI interface in another, but both versions have similar feature-sets). |
| 15:0 | REVISION | Used to track individual RTL releases. |

#### 0x4 CPP_HW_CAPABILITY

* **Type**: R
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State**: 0x0000023F

This register can be read to determine capability of the CPP controller.

##### CPP_HW_CAPABILITY Bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10:8 | NUM_PROCESSING_PIPES | This field indicates number of processing pipelines. |
| 5 | ROTATOR | This field indicates that the CPP supports frame rotation. |
| 4 | ASF_CROP | This field indicates that the CPP supports frame cropping following adaptive spatial filtering (ASF). |
| 3 | ASF | This field indicates that the CPP supports ASF. |
<!-- page 1082 -->

##### CPP_HW_CAPABILITY Bits (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2 | SCALE | This field indicates that the CPP supports upscaling (continuous scaling - 1x-32x). |
| 1 | DENOISE_CROP | This field indicates that the CPP supports frame cropping following denoise. |
| 0 | DENOISE | This field indicates that the CPP supports denoising. |

#### 0x8 CPP_RST_CMD_0

* **Type**: W
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000

This software register allows the user to reset the entire CPP controller or individual blocks. When a reset is complete, the `INFO_RST_DONE` IRQ fires. A second reset command should not be issued until the reset acknowledgment is received from the first command.

##### CPP_RST_CMD_0 Bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | RST_BYPASS | 0x0: The reset controller for the individual functional module is active, and the `*_DOMAIN_RST` fields are not meaningful. A reset done interrupt is generated.<br>0x1: The reset controller is bypassed and the software must manually assert/de-assert reset to each clock domain using the `*_DOMAIN_RST` fields. The individual functional module reset is inactive. No reset done interrupt is generated. |
| 24 | CPP_DOMAIN_RST | This bit is used to manually assert/de-assert reset to the CPP clock domain registers. |
| 13 | PERF_MON_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 12 | MISR_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 11 | PACKER_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 10 | UNPACKER_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
<!-- page 1083 -->

##### CPP_RST_CMD_0 Bits (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 9 | PIPE_1_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 8 | PIPE_0_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 6 | WE_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 5 | FE_1_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 4 | FE_0_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 2 | SW_REG_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 1 | AXI_BRIDGE_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. When the reset is complete, an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |
| 0 | CORE_RST_STB | 0x0: Has no effect<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued. This resets all misc. logic in the CPP controller. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the CPP interrupt controller. |

#### 0xC CPP_IRQ_MASK_0

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: `GCC_CAMSS_CPP_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset state**: 0x00000001

This software register contains the CPP controller IRQ mask. The IRQ mask is used to configure the events that the system processors handle (unmasked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x1) and ignore (masked IRQ; setting the IRQ mask bit to 0x0).
<!-- page 1084 -->

> [!NOTE]
> If the corresponding event occurs, a masked IRQ still asserts in this software register. The mask only prevents the CPP controller from notifying the system processor(s).

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 9 | ERROR_CBCR_SIZE_MISMATCH | This IRQ fires when there is a size mismatch on the CB and CR stream. |

| 7 | INFO_FE_0_RD_BUF_DONE | This IRQ fires when read engine completes reading a buffer. |

| 3 | INFO_WE_WR_BUF_PLN_0_DONE | This IRQ fires when write engine completes writing a buffer. |
| 2 | INFO_SESSION_DONE | This IRQ fires when session is completed. |
| 1 | INFO_AXI_HALT_ACK_DONE | This IRQ fires when the AXI Bridge halt request completes. Halt request is initiated by writing to `AXI_HALT_REQ`. |
| 0 | INFO_RST_DONE | This IRQ fires when the CPP controller completes a software reset initiated by writing to `CPP_RST_CMD_0`. |

## 4.2.4 Camera Control Interface (CCI)

This section describes the camera control interface (CCI).

### 4.2.4.1 CCI overview

CCI controls camera sensors and peripherals with precise timing requirements over the I2C (interintegrated circuit) bus interface. CCI is within the camera subsystem that serves two I2C masters managing queues to be loaded with executable commands.

CCI also has GPIO (general-purpose I/O) queues loaded with commands to control the assertion or de-assertion of GPIOs for camera peripheral devices such as focus lens, optical zoom, mechanical shutter, and strobe flash.

Figure 4-127 shows a high-level overview of the CCI module within the camera subsystem and in the SoC.

#### Figure: Figure 4-127 CCI overview
*Description:* Block diagram showing the Camera Control Interface (CCI) within the Camera Subsystem and its integration into the SoC:
* The **CCI** is a block located inside the **Camera Subsystem**.
* It interfaces bidirectionally with the **System NoC**.
* It receives **Clock** and **Reset** lines from the **GCC** (Global Clock Controller).
* It sends **Interrupt** signals to the **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem).
* Within the Camera Subsystem, the **CSID0** and **CSID1** blocks feed **Sensor Timing Strobes** into the CCI.
* The CCI outputs **I2C / GPIO Sensor control** lines externally through a boundary pad of the SoC.
<!-- page 1088 -->

Table 4-188 lists the CCI supported features.

### Table 4-188 CCI features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| CCI | <ul><li>Philips Semiconductors I2C Specification, version 5.0, October 2012 compliance</li><li>MIPI Alliance Standard for Camera Serial Interface 2 v1.01.00 (CSI-2) compliant</li><li>Two I2C masters and camera GPIO control</li><li>Dedicated queue-based I2C and GPIO controllers for synchronizing commands to image sensor timing</li><li>Ability to generate precision timing signals to drive external stepper motors, VCM, piezo, and flash triggers synced with the line timing</li></ul> |

Table 4-189 lists some of the CCI key use cases.

| Use case | Example scenario |
| :--- | :--- |
| Off chip camera sensor control | Real time external sensor control during snapshot, preview, or camcorder modes. See CCI off-chip camera sensor control. |
| GPIOs precision timers | Control of external sensors with precise timing. See CCI GPIO control. |

| VC | Virtual channel |

### 4.2.4.3 CCI key uses

#### 4.2.4.3.1 CCI off-chip camera sensor control

**Prerequisite:** Before configuring a camera sensor, it must be powered up and in a known state. The sensor power-up or -down sequence is manufacturer-specific to the sensor and is not covered here.

When the sensor is powered up and in a known state, the main processor can:
* Configure the camera serial interface decoder (CSID) core and other camera cores such as the video front end (VFE), JPEG, and denoiser.
<!-- page 1089 -->

* Load the CCI I2C queue with required commands and enable CCI to send the I2C commands to the camera sensor over the I2C bus
* Wait for an interrupt indicating the sequence completion

Figure 4-128 shows the active CCI and other blocks (green) in 2D mode assuming a 4-lane sensor.

#### Figure: Figure 4-128 CCI data and control flow in 2D mode
*Description:* Block diagram showing the active components and the data and control flow paths during 2D mode camera operations using a 4-lane sensor:
* **Active Components** (indicated in green):
  * **Sensor 0** (external camera sensor)
  * **CSI_PHY0 4-lane** (external physical interface)
  * **CSID0** (internal camera subsystem decoder)
  * **TLMM** (SoC IO Multiplexer)
  * **AHB Decode** (internal bus decoder)
  * **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem)
* **Inactive Components** (indicated in white/gray):
  * **Sensor 1**, **CSI_PHY1 2-lane**, **CSID1**
* **Control and Data Flow paths**:
  * **Data**: Data flows from active **Sensor 0** through **CSI_PHY0 4-lane** data lanes into the **CSID0** block inside the Camera Subsystem.
  * **I2C Control**: The active **CCI (I2C)** block connects to **TLMM**, which drives **I2C BUS #0** to control **Sensor 0**. (**I2C BUS #1** to **Sensor 1** is inactive).
  * **Timing Strobes**: **CSID0** (and CSID1) send **Sensor Timing Strobes** back to the **CCI (I2C)** block.
  * **Processor Bus**: **APSS** controls the subsystem configuration through the **AHB Decode** block which routes to **CSID0** and **CCI (I2C)**.
  * **Interrupts**: The **CCI (I2C)** block asserts a **CCI_IRQ** back to the **APSS**.
<!-- page 1090 -->

### 4.2.4.4 CCI GPIO control

Figure 4-129 shows the GPIO and real-time control of the camera peripheral devices. For example, camera peripherals such as Xenon flash are triggered by GPIOs at the set time while capturing the image.

#### Figure: Figure 4-129 CCI GPIO data and control flow
*Description:* Block diagram showing the active components and control paths when Sensor 1 is active and GPIO is used to control external Camera Peripherals:
* **Active Components** (indicated in green):
  * **Sensor 1** (external camera sensor)
  * **CSI_PHY1 2-lane** (external physical interface)
  * **CSID1** (internal camera subsystem decoder)
  * **Camera Peripherals** (external components like focus lens, flash, etc.)
  * **TLMM** (SoC IO Multiplexer)
  * **AHB Decode** (internal bus decoder)
  * **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem)
* **Inactive Components** (indicated in white/gray):
  * **Sensor 0**, **CSI_PHY0 4-lane**, **CSID0**
* **Control and Data Flow paths**:
  * **Data**: Data flows from active **Sensor 1** through **CSI_PHY1 2-lane** data lanes into the **CSID1** block.
  * **I2C Control**: The **CCI (I2C)** block connects to **TLMM**, which drives **I2C BUS #1** to control **Sensor 1**.
  * **GPIO Peripheral Control**: **TLMM** has bidirectional connection to external **Camera Peripherals** to control them (e.g., triggering flash).
  * **Timing Strobes**: **CSID1** sends **Sensor Timing Strobes** back to the **CCI (I2C)** block.
  * **Processor Bus**: **APSS** controls the subsystem configuration through the **AHB Decode** block which routes to **CSID1** and **CCI (I2C)**.
  * **Interrupts**: The **CCI (I2C)** block asserts a **CCI_IRQ** back to the **APSS**.

#### 4.2.4.4.2 CCI protocol, timing diagrams, and data formats

Figure 4-131 shows the CCI I2C THIGH and TLOW timing dependencies for 400 KHz mode.

#### Figure: Figure 4-131 CCI I2C TLOW and THIGH combined for 400 KHz mode
*Description:* Timing diagram illustrating the relationship between the SCL physical signal and the internal `SCL_OUT` control signal for 400 kHz Fast-mode I2C. The reference clock is $F(\text{GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK}) = 19.2\text{ MHz}$, where one cycle time $T(\text{GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK})$ is approximately $52.08\text{ ns}$. The total period for 400 kHz is $2500\text{ ns}$, equivalent to 48 clock cycles.
- $t_f$ (fall time) must be between $20 + 0.1C_b$ and $300\text{ ns}$.
- $t_{\text{LOW}}$ (SCL low period) must be $> 1300\text{ ns}$.
- $t_r$ (rise time) must be $< 300\text{ ns}$, measured between 30% and 70% thresholds.
- $t_{\text{HIGH}}$ (SCL high period) must be $> 600\text{ ns}$.
- `TLOW` duration is set by `CCI_I2C_Mx_SCL_CTL[HW_TLOW]` and must be at least $25 \times T(\text{GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK})$.
- `THIGH` duration is set by `CCI_I2C_Mx_SCL_CTL[HW_THIGH]` and must be at least $18 \times T(\text{GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK})$.

Table 4-192 shows possible combinations of TLOW and THIGH to meet the I2C AC specification.

#### Table 4-192 CCI TLOW and THIGH combinations

| CCI_I2C_Mx_SCL_CTL [HW_TLOW] field value | CCI_I2C_Mx_SCL_CTL [HW_THIGH] field value |
| :---: | :---: |
| 25 | 23 |
| 26 | 22 |
| 27 | 21 |

#### Figure: Figure 4-133 CCI I2C SDA timings
*Description:* (Note: The diagram in the source document appears to depict a general-purpose I/O (GPIO) control sequence, likely for a camera actuator/VCM, rather than standard I2C SDA timings).
The diagram shows five waveforms: `EN` (Enable), `DIR` (Direction), `IN1`, `IN2`, and `Busy (in)`.
Below the waveforms is a flowchart sequence mapping to the signal transitions:
1. `GPIO CTL Init all '0'`
2. `WAIT 1 ms`
3. `GPIO CTL EN to '1'` (triggers `EN` signal high, which also causes `Busy (in)` to go high).
4. `WAIT 'x' us`
5. `GPIO CTL DIR to '1'` (triggers `DIR` signal high, labeled "Drive to infinite direction").
6. `WAIT 'y' us`
7. `REPEAT CMDs 'N' TIMES` (bracketed section controlling `IN1` and `IN2` pulses):

   - `WAIT 'v' us`
   - `GPIO CTL IN2 to '0'` (triggers `IN2` low)
   - `WAIT 'w' us`
8. After `tdir` duration, `DIR` goes low (labeled "Drive to macro direction").
9. A delay `t` occurs, after which `Busy (in)` has a brief low pulse before returning high, then eventually goes low when `EN` goes low.
10. Timing parameters defined include: `ten` (enable duration), `tperiod`, `tpw` (pulse width), `tdir` (direction high duration), and delays `x`, `y`, `z`, `u`, `v`, `w`, `s`, `t`.

#### Figure: Figure 4-135 CCI internal connectivity

#### 4.2.4.6 CCI functional description

Figure 4-136 shows a high-level overview of CCI functional blocks, which include:
* I2C master 0 and master 1
* I2C command queue 0 (64 words) and 1 (16 words for both master 0 and master 1)
* GPIO command queues (queue 0 is 32 words, queue 1 and 2 are 16 words each)
* Sync timers
* Interrupt controller
* Reset controller

#### Figure: Figure 4-136 CCI functional block diagram
*Description:* Detailed functional block diagram of the CCI, illustrating the division between two clock domains: `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` (green blocks) and `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK` (blue blocks).
- **`GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` domain (Green)**:
  - **Timers Block**: Contains *Fixed Delay Timers* and *Sync Timers*. The Sync Timers receive strobe signals: `CSID0_SOF_STB`, `CSID0_SOL_STB`, `CSID1_SOF_STB`, and `CSID1_SOL_STB`.
  - **I2C Masters**: Handles the physical I2C interface, connecting to external `SDAs` and `SCLs` lines.
- **`GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK` domain (Blue)**:
  - **I2C Command Queues**: Interacts with both the Timers Block and the I2C Masters.
  - **GPIO Command Queues**: Interacts with the Timers Block, I2C Command Queues, and Registers. It connects to external `GPIOs` (likely the CCI_TIMER and CCI_ASYNC lines).
  - **Registers**: The central configuration block, connected via the internal `AHB Bus` to the external `System NoC`. It has control paths (thin arrows) to all other functional blocks.
  - **IRQ Control**: Manages interrupts, outputting the `CCI_IRQ` signal.
  - **Reset Control**: Receives the external `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_ARES` reset signal.
<!-- page 1099 -->

#### 4.2.4.6.1 CCI power and clock management

CCI is a small core operating at a low frequency (19.2 MHz). When the core is not in use software disables the CCI clocks from GCC to save the dynamic power.

The CCI core does not support dynamic voltage scaling or dynamic clock frequency changes.

> [!NOTE]
> Before using CCI, software must ensure that the clocks to the CCI core are enabled and the core is reset to a known state. These operations are controlled by the registers in the GCC.

Table 4-198 list the CCI clocks and their recommended settings.

#### Table 4-198 CCI recommended clock settings

| Clock | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` | (Recommended 19.2 MHz CXO) Fixed frequency clock for the CCI I2C master and the timers to generate timing requirements. Does not change dynamically when the CCI core is in a busy state. The I2C timing control registers have limited bit-widths. These registers control the timing of the SCL/SDA I2C lines to generate the 100 KHz, 400 KHz modes of operation. <br>Recommendation: Limit the fixed frequency of the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` to under 50 MHz. Any clock faster than 50 MHz affects the sub 100 KHz mode I2C operation. |
| `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK` | Same as the fast peripheral bus clock (AHB clock) provided by the system. |

#### 4.2.4.6.2 CCI resets

CCI can be reset in two ways, by using the:
* Core asynchronous resets triggered by the GCC
* `CCI_RESET_CMD` register in the CCI core, used to reset individual CCI hardware blocks to a known state.

Software must set the bits in this register to enable the resets of the individual blocks. A composite interrupt is generated when the reset is complete.

> [!NOTE]
> Do not execute a second global reset command by setting the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register until the reset acknowledgement is received from the first command.

To reset CCI blocks:
1. Enable the `RST_DONE_IRQ` bit in the `CCI_IRQ_MASK_0` register.
2. Based on the preferred reset function, set bits in the `CCI_RESET_CMD`.
3. Wait for the `CCI_IRQ`.
4. Verify that the `RST_DONE_IRQ` bit is set in the `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_0` register.
<!-- page 1100 -->

5. Set the `RST_DONE_IRQ` bit in the `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_0` register.
6. Clear the reset done interrupt by setting the `CCI_IRQ_GLOBAL_CLEAR_CMD` register to 1.

> [!NOTE]
> `CCI_RESET_CMD` register bits [18:1] apply only when bit [0] `STROBED_RST_EN` is set to 1.

For `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers, the clear occurs only after setting the `CCI_IRQ_GLOBAL_CLEAR_CMD` register to 1. Only status bits that are set to 1 in the corresponding `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_0` and `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_1` registers are cleared.

#### 4.2.4.6.3 CCI Interrupts

CCI uses interrupts to indicate the operating state of the I2C masters, I2C queues, and the GPIO queues.
Interrupt status is contained in `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_0` and `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers.

##### Mask register

CCI includes corresponding IRQ mask registers to enable or disable interrupt triggering according to bits set in the `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_0` and `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers. By default all interrupt bits are disabled in the `CCI_IRQ_MASK_0` and `CCI_IRQ_MASK_1` registers.

##### Clear and global clear registers

CCI also has corresponding IRQ clear registers to clear the interrupt status in the `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_0` and `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers (clear registers: `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_0` and `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_1`).

While software selects the interrupt bits to be cleared in the `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_0` and `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers, when one interrupt is processed (and software clears it) and another is pending during the ISR (interrupt service routine), CCI generates an interrupt immediately.

##### Status interrupts

Table 4-199 describes the CCI status interrupts.

#### Table 4-199 CCI status interrupts

| IRQ name | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `RST_DONE_IRQ` | Reset done. Triggered when hardware finishes resetting the CCI blocks by enabling the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register (set bit 0 to 1). |
| `I2C_M0_RD_DONE` | I2C master 0 status interrupt. Triggered when I2C master 0 finishes reading the specified number of bytes from the I2C slaves. Software reads the I2C read data buffer after this interrupt is triggered. |
| `I2C_M0_Q0_REPORT` | I2C master 0 queue 0 status interrupt. Triggered when REPORT command is executed from queue 0 assigned to I2C master 0. Software reads the report details from the `CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_REPORT_STATUS` register after this interrupt is triggered. |

| **I2C_M1_RD_DONE** | I2C master 1 status interrupt. Triggered when I2C master 1 finishes reading the specified number of bytes from the I2C slaves. Software reads the I2C read data buffer after this interrupt is triggered. |

### Error interrupts

When an error interrupt is triggered, the error status is latched to a register. Software reads the error status register to determine the command and time of the failure. Table 1-13 describes the CCI error interrupts. through describe the CCI error interrupts.

### Table 4-200 CCI error conditions detected

| Error | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Invalid slave address** | When I2C master sends a slave address and receives a NACK, it issues a STOP. The NACK indicates that the slave with that slave ID is not present. |
| **Byte NACKed** | When a byte (other than the slave address) transmitted by the master is not ACKed by the slave, it issues a STOP |
| **Unknown command loaded in the queue** | – |
| **Underflow/overflow of the queue** | – |
| **Underflow/overflow of the I2C read buffer** | – |
<!-- page 1102 -->
### Table 4-201 CCI I2C master 0 error interrupts

| IRQ name | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **I2C_M0_RD_UNDERFLOW** | Triggered when the read buffer in the I2C master 0 underflows. Underflows occur when software tries to read more data than is present in the I2C read buffer. <br>For example, if software issues a I2C read command for 10 bytes (three words) from the I2C slave while reading the I2C read buffer, software tries to read four words, this underflow interrupt triggers.<br>To reset the read buffer after this interrupt is triggered, set `I2C_M0_RD_FIFO_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |
| **I2C_M0_RD_OVERFLOW** | Triggered when read buffer in the I2C master 0 overflows. Overflows occur when the software does not empty the I2C read buffer; then issues a new I2C read command with the bytes to be read from a I2C slave is more than the available space of the read buffer (can only up to four 32-bit words).<br>For example, if software issues two I2C read commands that exceed 16 bytes and does not empty the read buffer after the first read an overflow occurs.<br>To reset the read buffer after this interrupt is triggered, set the `I2C_M0_RD_FIFO_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |
| **I2C_M0_NACK_ERR** | Asserts when the I2C master 0 receives a NACK during I2C write. To reset the I2C master 0, set the `I2C_M0_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |

| :--- | :--- |

| :--- | :--- |
| **GPIO_Q<n>_UNDERFLOW** | Triggered when the command queue <n> of `GPIO_QUEUE_<n>` underflows. Underflows occur when software does not load the queue with the number of words specified in the `CCI_GPIO_Q<n>_EXEC_WORD_CNT` register.<br>To reset the queue, set the `GPIO_Q<n>_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |
| **GPIO_Q<n>_OVERFLOW** | Triggered when the queue <n> overflows. Overflows occur when software loads more words then the space available in the queue.<br>To reset the queue, set the `GPIO_Q<n>_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |
| **GPIO_Q<n>_UNKNWN_CMD** | Triggered when an invalid command is loaded into the command queue <n>. This queue does not require a reset after the interrupt is triggered. Hardware ignores this command and proceeds to the next command in the queue.<br>To reset the queue, set the `GPIO_Q<n>_RST_STB` bit in the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register to 1. |

#### 4.2.4.6.4 CCI initialization

To initialize CCI, perform the following steps:

**Power up and enable clocks**
1. Power up the chip. CCI does not require a separate power-up sequence.
2. Reset the CCI core by asserting the asynchronous resets generated by the GCC.
3. Enable the CCI clocks `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` and `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK`.
4. (Optional depending on the mode) Enable interrupts, see `CCI_IRQ_STATUS_1` registers, the clear occurs only after setting the `CCI_IRQ_GLOBAL_CLEAR_CMD` register to 1. Only status bits that are set to 1 in the corresponding `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_0` and `CCI_IRQ_CLEAR_1` registers are cleared.
<!-- page 1106 -->
5. (Optional depending on the mode) Enable the CSID core so CCI can synchronize the command execution to the sensor timing.

**Configure timers**
1. (Optional depending on the mode) Configure the sync timers in the CCI. Configure the CID for sync timers only if the queue commands must be synchronized to the sensor timing.
2. Configure the I2C master in the CCI to operate at the intended speed (100 KHz, 400 KHz, 1 MHz). Configure an I2C master only when CCI must access I2C slaves (GPIO queues do not require the I2C master).

**Setting up queues**
1. Determine the queue to be loaded with new commands. Software must verify that the queue has enough space to hold the new commands.
2. Load the appropriate I2C and GPIO queues with commands.
3. Set the number of commands to be executed for each queue.

**Execute command**
1. Enable the command execution by setting the `CCI_QUEUE_START` register.
2. Wait for interrupts or poll the queue level register to determine the command execution progress.
3. Clear the interrupts.

#### CCI enable sync timers and the CID

Software must enable the sync timers before loading the sync commands in the I2C or GPIO queues.

The CCI hardware has two sync timers that correspond to two CSI camera sensors in the system.

Each CSI sensor can generate up to four virtual channels (VCs), see Figure 4-137.

For each VC, the sensor can send long packets of a data type (DT). The camera serial interface decoder (CSID) core supports the decoding of up to four DTs within each VC.

A VC/DT combination is called a CID (CSID mapped ID). 16 CIDs are decoded by a CSID core from a single sensor.

The CCI supports synchronization of a timer to only one CID per sensor. The software always synchronizes the timers to the base VC.
<!-- page 1107 -->
#### Figure 4-137: CCI to CSID virtual channels

*Description:* The diagram illustrates the relationship between Sync Timers, CSI sensors, Virtual Channels (VC), Data Types (DT), and CIDs. It shows four parallel paths. In each path, a "Sync timer" block is connected to a "CSI sensor" block. Each "CSI sensor" outputs up to four Virtual Channels (represented by red horizontal arrows). A note indicates that "Each VC can send long packets of a DT (data type)". The combination of a Virtual Channel (VC) and a Data Type (DT) is labeled as "CID" (CSID mapped ID), shown as a span covering a VC arrow and an extending DT arrow (blue arrow).

#### CCI configure I2C master 0 registers

The I2C master can be configured to an I2C bus speed (100 KHz, 400 KHz, 1 MHz).

### Table 4-209 CCI registers to configure I2C master 0

| Register | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CCI_I2C_M0_SCL_CTL** | I2C master clock (SCL) period; set these two fields:<br>**HW_THIGH**: Specifies the high period of the SCL clock in `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` cycles using this equation:<br>$HW\_THIGH = CEIL(\text{minimum SCL high time } \mu\text{sec} \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ freq MHz})$<br>For example, to generate a 100 KHz mode SCL clock, a minimum high time of 4 $\mu$sec and `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` of 19.2 MHz: $HW\_THIGH = CEIL(4 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2\text{ MHz}) \approx 77 = 0x4D \text{ cycles}$<br>**HW_TLOW**: Specifies the low period of the SCL clock in `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` cycles using this equation:<br>$HW\_TLOW = CEIL(\text{minimum SCL low time } \mu\text{sec} \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ frequency MHz})$<br>For example, to generate a 100 KHz mode SCL clock, a minimum high time of 4.7 $\mu$sec and the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` of 19.2 MHz:<br>$HW\_TLOW = CEIL(4.7 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2\text{ MHz}) \approx 91 = 0x5B \text{ cycles}$<br>Always reprogram this register if there is a change in the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` period. CCI I2C TLOW and THIGH combined for 400 KHz mode shows the possible values of TLOW and THIGH to meet the 400 KHz SCL I2C AC specification. |
| **CCI_I2C_M0_SDA_CTL_0** | I2C master data (SDA) timing to SCL; set these two fields:<br>**HW_TSU_STO**: Specifies the setup time for the stop condition on the bus using this equation:<br>$HW\_TSU\_STO = CEIL(\text{minimum setup time } \mu\text{sec} \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ frequency MHz})$<br>For example, to generate 100 KHz mode, a minimum setup time of 4 $\mu$sec and `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` of 19.2 MHz:<br>$HW\_TSU\_STO = CEIL(4 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2 \text{ MHz}) \approx 77 = 0x4D \text{ cycles}$<br>**HW_TSU_STA**: Specifies the setup time for a repeated start condition using this equation:<br>$HW\_TSU\_STA = CEIL(\text{repeated start setup time } \mu\text{sec} \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ frequency MHz})$<br>For example, to generate 100 KHz mode, a minimum bus free time between a stop and a start condition of 4.7 $\mu$sec and `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` of 19.2 MHz: the HW_TBUF:<br>$HW\_TSU\_STA = CEIL(4.7 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2 \text{ MHz}) \approx 91 = 0x5B \text{ cycles}$, see CCI I2C SDA timings. |
<!-- page 1109 -->
### Table 4-209 CCI registers to configure I2C master 0 (Continued)

| Register | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CCI_I2C_M0_SDA_CTL_1** | I2C master data (SDA) timing to SCL; set two fields:<br>**HW_THD_DAT**: Specifies the hold time for the data on SDA; using this equation:<br>$HW\_THD\_DAT = CEIL(\text{maximum hold time } (\mu\text{sec}) \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ freq MHz}) \quad (1)$<br>For example, in 100 KHz mode, the I2C specification sets a maximum hold time of 3.45 $\mu$sec; if the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` is 19.2 MHz:<br>$HW\_THD\_DAT = CEIL(3.45 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2 \text{ MHz}) \approx 67 = 0x43 \quad (2)$<br>**HW_THD_STA**: Specifies the hold time for a start condition using this equation:<br>$HW\_THD\_STA = CEIL(\text{minimum hold time start condition } (\mu\text{sec}) \times GCC\_CAMSS\_CCI\_CLK \text{ frequency MHz})$<br>For example, in 100 KHz mode the I2C specification sets the hold time for a start condition to be 4 $\mu$sec. With a `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` of 19.2 MHz:<br>$HW\_THD\_STA = CEIL(4 \mu\text{sec} \times 19.2 \text{ MHz}) \approx 91 = 0x5B \text{ cycles}$<br>Do not modify this register when the I2C master is bus; always reset the value of this register if there is a change in the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` clock period. |

| **CCI_I2C_M0_MISC_CTL** | Digital filter in the I2C master to enable removal of glitches on the input SDA and SCL lines.<br>**HW_DBG_I2C_WR_LOOPBACK_EN**: (Debug only) One-bit field to enable the loopback of data transmitted by the I2C master. When enabled, the loopback data can be read by the software from the read data buffer through the `CCI_I2C_M0_READ_DATA` register. An interrupt is generated when the specified bytes in the I2C write command are loopbacked to the read data buffer.<br>**HW_SCL_STRETCH_EN**: Set this one-bit field to 1 to enable the support for I2C SCL clock stretch. Default is 0 meaning disable the SCL clock stretch.<br>**HW_TRDHLD**: Specifies the hold time in terms of CCI clocks (3 bits) for the SDA signal to bridge the undefined region of the falling edge of SCL.<br>**HW_TSP**: Corresponds to filtering of the number of glitches less than the specified number of CCI clocks on the input I2C lines (SCL and SDA).<br>- 00: No filtering (default)<br>- 01: One CCI clock (recommended)<br>- 10: Two CCI clocks<br>- 11: Three CCI clocks |

#### 4.2.4.6.5 CCI data flow

The CCI queues can be loaded at any time if there is enough space in the command queues. The `CCI_QUEUE_START` register controls the sequential execution of the commands.

If multiple queues are enabled at the same time, the commands from both the queues are executed in a round-robin.

> [!CAUTION]
> When an explicit LOCK command has already executed from a queue. If another queue is ready to execute a LOCK command, the other queue is blocked until an UNLOCK command is executed from the same queue that placed a lock.

If an I2C queue (say, queue A) is executing the `WAIT`, `WAIT_SYNC`, or `WAIT_GPIO` command and another queue (say, queue B) contains commands to be executed, queue B is granted access if an explicit lock is not set by queue A (executing the `WAIT` command).

The queues generate an interrupt only when queue executes a report command with the `IRQ_EN` bit set to 1.
<!-- page 1114 -->

Figure 4-139 shows the flow of command execution in the CCI.

#### Figure 4-139 CCI I2C command execution flow

*Description:* A flowchart illustrating the CCI I2C command execution loop.
1. **Start**
2. Check if **Exec Cmd Cnt > 0**:
   - If **No (N)**, loop back to the check.
   - If **Yes (Y)**, **Pop Cmd from Queue**.
3. Evaluate the command type:
   - **Lock CMD?**
     - Yes: Check if **Arbiter Lock Available?**
       - If No, wait/loop.
       - If Yes: **Set Arbiter Lock** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Unlock CMD?**
     - Yes: **Remove Arbiter Lock** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Set Params CMD?**
     - Yes: **Set Slave ID** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Report CMD?**
     - Yes: **Send IRQ to Host** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Wait CMD?**
     - Yes: **Wait for X Delay** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Sync CMD?**
     - Yes: **Wait for Sync Event** -> Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
     - No:
   - **Reg Access CMD?**
     - Yes: Check if **Arbiter Free or Available**:
       - If No, wait/loop.
       - If Yes: **Send I2C CMD** -> Check if **CMD Successful?**
         - If Yes: Proceed to **Decrement Exec Cmd Cnt** and loop back to step 2.
         - If No: Check if **Retry Limit Reached?**
           - If No: Loop back to "Arbiter Free or Available" check.
           - If Yes: **Report I2C Execution ERROR** (Terminal).
     - No: **Report Unknown CMD** (Terminal).
<!-- page 1115 -->

#### 4.2.4.6.6 CCI operating modes

The CCI supports these modes of operation:
- I2C access in 2D mode by enabling one queue of the I2C master
- I2C access in 2D mode by enabling both the queues of the I2C master
- I2C access along with GPIO control

#### 4.2.4.6.7 CCI execution of commands

The CCI has a global `CCI_QUEUE_START` register to execute commands that are loaded into the queues.

Each bit in the register corresponds to the queue number to execute. Before setting this register, the software must verify that the corresponding queue is loaded with the number of commands and the `QUEUE*_EXEC_CMD_CNT` is set appropriately.

Enabling multiple bits of this register at the same time starts multiple queues simultaneously.

Setting either of these registers to 0 has no effect in triggering a queue or executing commands from a queue already in progress.

#### Table 4-214 CCI QUEUE START register

| Bitfield | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| GPIO_Q2_START | Starts GPIO queue 2 command execution, which continues until the set number of commands executes |
| GPIO_Q1_START | Starts GPIO queue 1 command execution, which continues until the set number of commands executes |
| GPIO_Q0_START | Starts GPIO queue 0 command execution, which continues until the set number of commands executes |
| I2C_M1_Q1_START | Enables I2C queue 1 of master 1 to execute the commands, which continue until the set number of commands executes |
| I2C_M1_Q0_START | Enables I2C queue 0 of master 1 to execute the commands, which continue until the set number of commands executes |
| I2C_M0_Q1_START | Enables I2C queue 1 of master 0 to execute the commands, which continue until the set number of commands executes |
| I2C_M0_Q0_START | Enables I2C queue 0 of master 0 to execute the commands, which continue until the set number of commands executes |

  - Bits [3:0]: `REPORT`

#### Table 4-215 CCI I2C queue command set

| Field | Bit | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SET_PARAM** | 3:0 | (Value: 0x1) Software loads this command before executing any other I2C write or read or WAIT_SYNC command.<br>Software is not required to issue another SET_PARAM command until access to a different I2C slave or synchronization to a different sensor is needed |
| SID | 10:4 | Specify the I2C slave ID |
| RETRY | 17:16 | Specify the number of times the hardware retries the I2C command when it fails |
| ID_MAP | 19:18 | Specify the sensor number to be synchronized to the I2C command. The WAIT_SYNC command uses this ID to synchronize to the selected sensor timing. |
| Unused | 31:20 | – |
| **WAIT** | 3:0 | (Value: 0x2) Wait for a specified number of `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` cycles before executing the next command in the queue.<br>This is a 28 bit counter and counts up to 256 mega cycles; for example, if the `GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK` clock is set to 19.2 MHz, executing this command allows a maximum wait of ~13.98 sec before the next command in the queue can be executed. |
| WAIT_COUNT | 31:4 | Specify the wait count value in CCI clocks cycles |
| **WAIT_GPIO_EVENT** | 3:0 | (Value 0x4) Synchronizes the execution of the queue commands; always use with the TRIGGER GPIO EVENT |
| GPIO_QUEUE | 5:4 | Specify the GPIO queue number to synchronize to the commands; values are 0, 1, and 2 corresponding to the three GPIO queues |
| Unused | 31:6 | – |
| **TRIG_I2C_EVENT** | 3:0 | (Value is 0x5) Triggers a strobe event to the GPIO queues; always use with the WAIT_I2C_EVENT command |
| Unused | 31:4 | – |
| **LOCK** | 3:0 | (Value is 0x6) Enables execution the atomic queue commands without interruption from the other queue commands; locks the arbiter from approving a grant to the other queue.<br>Always pair this command with the unlock command; otherwise the commands from the other queues are not executed. |
| Unused | 31:4 | – |
| **UNLOCK** | 3:0 | (Value is 0x7) Removes the lock placed on the arbiter by the queue. Always pair with the lock command; otherwise the commands from other queues are not executed. |
| Unused | 31:4 | – |
| **REPORT** | 3:0 | (Value is 0x8) Indicates the progress of queue commands by placing it appropriately in the loaded queue commands |

#### Table 4-215 CCI I2C queue command set (continued)

### CCI I2C master operation sequence

Figure 4-141 shows the I2C master operation sequence timeline.

#### Figure 4-141 CCI I2C master operation sequence (I2C write)

*Description:* A timeline diagram illustrating the sequence of events during a CCI I2C Master Write operation. The timeline flows from top to bottom, showing interactions between Software (SW), CCI Queue, CCI Master (CCIM), and I2C Slave.
1. **SW** writes a command block to the **CCI Queue** via **AHB I/F**: `SID | Other parameters | Byte2 | Byte1 | Byte0 | CNT=6 | Byte5 | Byte4 | Byte3 | Other commands`.
2. **SW** triggers execution by writing `I2C_M#_Q#_START` to the **CCI Queue**.
3. **CCI Queue** sends the byte count and Slave ID (`CNT=6 | SID`) to **CCIM** over **CCIM-CCI I/F**, followed by the signal `CCIM_CMD_RDY`.
4. **CCIM** initiates transmission over the **I2C I/F**, sending the `SID` (with 'W' write bit) to the **I2C Slave**.
5. The **I2C Slave** responds with an ACK (`K`) to **CCIM**.
6. **CCIM** sends `CCIM_POS_ACK` back to the **CCI Queue**.
7. **CCI Queue** sends `Byte0` to **CCIM**, which in turn sends `Byte0` to the **I2C Slave**.
8. The **I2C Slave** ACKs (`K`) the byte, and **CCIM** sends `CCIM_POS_ACK` to the **CCI Queue**.
9. This sequence repeats for `Byte1` (with ACK from Slave and CCIM).
10. After a timeline break (representing bytes 2 to 4), the final byte `Byte5` is sent by **CCI Queue** to **CCIM**, and then to the **I2C Slave**.
11. The **I2C Slave** ACKs (`K`) the final byte, and **CCIM** sends the final `CCIM_POS_ACK`.
12. **CCIM** sends `CCIM_DONE` to the **CCI Queue**.
13. **CCI Queue** asserts an interrupt `IRQ (Report)` to the **SW**.

### CCI read data from I2C slave by I2C master 0 or master 1

In the I2C read command, software specifies the number of bytes to be read from an I2C slave. When the read command executes, the hardware waits for the set number of bytes to be received from the I2C slave. Then, it generates an interrupt that alerts software that the data is available in the read buffer.

Software reads the data from the `CCI_I2C_M0_READ_DATA` (for master 0) register or the `CCI_I2C_M1_READ_DATA` register four bytes at a time. Software must ensure that the data is read from the buffer to avoid an overflow.

> [!TIP]
> **Recommendation:** Software inserts the I2C read command within the lock and unlock commands to guarantee the atomic execution of I2C read command sequence.

Figure 4-142 shows the command sequence during I2C reads.


<!-- page 1121 -->

#### Figure 4-142: CCI I2C read command sequence
*Description:* A vertical block diagram showing a sequence of steps for a CCI I2C read command. The sequence consists of six steps, from top to bottom:
1. **Set Param** (Blue block)
2. **LOCK** (Red block)
3. **I2C WR** (Light beige/green block)
4. **I2C RD** (Light beige/green block)
5. **REPORT** (Light green block)
6. **UNLOCK** (Dark green block)

CCI I2C access in 2D mode with one queue for I2C master

To enable queue 0 of I2C master 0:
1. In the CCI_SET_CID_SYNC_TIMER_x register (where x= 0, 1, 2 or 3) set the CID that corresponds to the sensor to be synchronized with sync timers.
2. In the CCI_IRQ_MASK register, enable interrupt.
3. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_LOAD_DATA register, load the queue by repeatedly setting the 32-bit words.
4. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_EXEC_WORD_CNT register, set the word count to be executed.
5. In the CCI_QUEUE_START register, set the value to execute the command.
6. More commands can be loaded to the same or a different queue depending on the mode.
7. Wait for the CCI IRQ interrupt.
8. In the CCI_IRQ_STATUS register, read the value to verify that the correct interrupt triggered.
9. In the CCI_IRQ_CLEAR register, set to clear the interrupt.
<!-- page 1122 -->

Figure 4-143 shows the I2C master queue for 2D.

#### Figure 4-143: I2C access in 2D mode using single I2C master
*Description:* Block diagram of the CCI queue and command interface for a single I2C master in 2D mode.
- **Central Block:** Contains "Command and Queue" and a "CMD" register/block.
- **Top Block:** "I2C Master" receives commands from the "CMD" block.
- **Bottom Block:** "AHB interface" connects to the central block with two signals:
  - `QUEUE_RESET` (input to queue)
  - `PROGRAM_QUEUE` (input to queue)
- **Control Inputs (Left):**
  - `QUEUE_START` (triggers execution)
  - `EXEC_CMD_CNT` (number of commands to execute)
- **Status Outputs (Right):**
  - `CURR_CMD`
  - `REPORT_CMD_STAT`
  - `QUEUE_STATUS`
  - `CURR_WORD_CNT`
  - `IRQ_STATUS`

CCI I2C access in 2D mode with two queues for I2C master

To enable queue 0 and queue 1 of I2C master 0:
1. In the CCI_SET_CID_SYNC_TIMER_x register (where x is 0, 1, 2 or 3), set the CID that corresponds to the sensor to be synchronized with sync timers.
2. In the CCI_IRQ_MASK register, enable interrupt.
3. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_LOAD_DATA register, load queue 0 by repeatedly setting the 32-bit words.
4. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_EXEC_WORD_CNT register, set the word count to be executed.
5. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q1_LOAD_DATA register, load queue 1 by repeatedly setting the 32-bit words.
6. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q1_EXEC_WORD_CNT register, set the word count to be executed.
7. In the CCI_QUEUE_START register, set the value to bit 0 and bit 1 to execute the command.
8. More commands can be loaded to the same or a different queue depending on the mode.
9. Wait for the CCI IRQ interrupt.
10. In the CCI_IRQ_STATUS register, read the value to verify that the correct interrupt triggered.
11. In the CCI_IRQ_CLEAR register, set to clear the interrupt.
<!-- page 1123 -->

CCI I2C access at different time with two queues for I2C master

To enable two queues for I2C master 0:
1. In the CCI_SET_CID_SYNC_TIMER_x register (where x is 0, 1, 2 or 3), set the CID that corresponds to the sensor to be synchronized with sync timers.
2. In the CCI_IRQ_MASK register, enable interrupt.
3. Load the queue by repeatedly setting the number of 32-bit words in the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_LOAD_DATA register.
4. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_EXEC_WORD_CNT register, set the word count to be executed.
5. In the CCI_QUEUE_START register, set the value to bit 0 to execute the command.
6. Load the queue by repeatedly setting the number of 32-bit words in the CCI_I2C_M0_Q1_LOAD_DATA register.
7. In the CCI_I2C_M0_Q1_EXEC_WORD_CNT register, set the word count to be executed.
8. In the CCI_QUEUE_START register, set the value to bit 1 to execute the command.
9. Wait for the CCI IRQ interrupt.
10. In the CCI_IRQ_STATUS register, read the value to verify that the correct interrupt triggered.
11. In the CCI_IRQ_CLEAR register, set to clear the interrupt.

### 4.2.4.6.10 CCI halting command execution

CCI halting command execution occurs under the following scenarios:
1. Asynchronous termination of Camera application at the system level
2. CCI errors (underflow, overflow, unknown command, I2C NACK)

To terminate the execution of CCI commands a software reset needs to be issued. The software reset can happen in the middle of a I2C transaction leaving the I2C bus in an unknown state. To address this concern the proposed solution a simple “HALT REQUEST/ACK” mechanism is implemented in the CCI.

With the HALT REQ/ACK mechanism the CCI termination sequence will be as follows:
1. Async camera termination request or CCI Error happens
2. Software then issues a HALT request to the CCI hardware via a `CCI_HALT_REQUEST` register.
3. The CCI internally waits for the completion of the current command in flight.
4. On completion of the current command the CCI stops the execution of commands.
5. The CCI then generates a HALT ACK interrupt
6. Software issues a reset via the `CCI_RESET_CMD` register
7. The CCI generates a `RESET_DONE` interrupt indicating the idling of the CCI.

With this sequence, it is guaranteed that the software reset of the CCI will never happen in the middle of a command execution.

With the HALT mechanism there is no abruptly halting of the I2C Master. Instead, there is waiting for the I2C Master to gracefully complete the current I2C transaction and then stop the queues from presenting a new command to the Command processor. If, for some reason, the I2C bus goes into an unknown state when a HALT request is issued, then I2C command may not complete. In such a scenario, software issues a reset if the HALT ACK is not received before the expiry of the software-based Watchdog timer. The software is expected to enable the watchdog timer during step 3.

There are two HALT bits in the `CCI_HALT_REQUEST` register corresponding to two I2C masters. This provides the ability to independently halt the two I2C Masters if necessary.
<!-- page 1128 -->

### 4.2.4.6.11 CCI Timeouts

Software maintains timeouts on CCI to identify issues such as:
*   Lock up on the I2C bus.
*   Software can estimate the time to execute a set of commands from the queue by the CCI clock and the I2C bus speed.
*   If software does not receive a report interrupt (corresponding to the `REPORT` command) in the expected time, reset the CCI hardware and retry the commands.
*   Lock up waiting for an external GPIO trigger event.

#### 4.2.4.7.3 CCI register definitions

##### 0x0 CCI_HW_VERSION

*   **Type:** R
*   **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK


<!-- page 1131 -->

### CCI_HW_VERSION
**Reset state:** `0x10000008`

This register has the CCI hardware version information.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR_VERSION | Indicates different interface version. Major version changes are not backward compatible. |
| 27:16 | MINOR_VERSION | Indicates expanded functionality. Minor version adds functionality while being backward compatible for existing features. |
| 15:0 | STEP | Indicates a change in the CCI HW, which is not intended to impact software compatibility. It is used to track individual RTL releases. |

---

### 0x4 CCI_RESET_CMD
**Type:** W  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000001`

This register is used to reset the hardware to a known state. This is a command register and the software needs to set the bits to reset the intended logic. A composite interrupt is generated when all the clock domains that were reset is complete. A second global reset command should not be issued until the reset acknowledge is received from the first command.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | AHB_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to all the AHB domain logic in the CCI core excluding the AHB bridge. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br/>`0x0`: FUNCTIONAL<br/>`0x1`: RESET |
| 30 | CCI_CLK_DOMAIN_RST | This reset is to manually assert/deassert reset to all the logic in the CCI clock domain. This bit is NOT self-clearing.<br/>`0x0`: FUNCTIONAL<br/>`0x1`: RESET |
| 27 | SYNC_TIMER_3_RST_STB | Only applies when `STROBED_RST_EN` is (1)<br/>`0x0`: Has no effect. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the CCI interrupt controller.<br/>`0x1`: Triggers a self-clearing reset. |
| 26 | SYNC_TIMER_2_RST_STB | Only applies when `STROBED_RST_EN` is (1)<br/>`0x0`: Has no effect. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the CCI interrupt controller.<br/>`0x1`: Triggers a self-clearing reset. |

### 0x8 CCI_QUEUE_START
**Type:** W  
*(Description continues on next page)*
<!-- page 1134 -->

### 0x8 CCI_QUEUE_START (Continued)
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register is used to kick start the execution of commands that are loaded in a Queue. Each bit in the register corresponds to the Queue# to be kicked off. Before writing to this register the software should ensure that the corresponding 'QUEUE*_EXEC_CMD_CNT' register is programmed to a valid value and the Queue is loaded with the intended number of commands. Enabling multiple bits of this register at the same time kick starts the execution of commands from multiple queues at the same time.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6 | GPIO_Q2_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 5 | GPIO_Q1_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 4 | GPIO_Q0_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 3 | I2C_M1_Q1_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 2 | I2C_M1_Q0_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 1 | I2C_M0_Q1_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |
| 0 | I2C_M0_Q0_START | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Start Queue command execution. The command execution continues until the intended number of commands have been executed |

---

## 4.2.4.7.9 0x34 CCI_HALT_REQ
**Type:** W  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register is used to halt the execution of I2C Queue commands. All the bits of this register are self-clearing.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | I2C_M1_Q0Q1_HALT_REQ | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Halts the execution of commands from the queues assigned to I2C Master 1. After a successful halt the halt-ack interrupt will be generated |
| 0 | I2C_M0_Q0Q1_HALT_REQ | `0x0`: Has no effect.<br/>`0x1`: Halts the execution of commands from the queues assigned to I2C Master 0. After a successful halt the halt-ack interrupt is generated |

## 4.2.4.7.10 0x100 CCI_I2C_M0_SCL_CTL
**Type:** RW  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register is used to control the I2C Master Clock (SCL) low and high period.

> [!NOTE]
> Do not change this register when the I2C Master is in a busy state. Always reprogram this register whenever there is a change in the GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 27:16 | HW_THIGH | Specify the high period of the SCL clock in terms of GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK cycles. The hw_tHIGH is given by the following equation:<br/>`hw_tHIGH >= (Minimum SCL HIGH Time as per spec(usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 19.2 MHz, Min spec High time is 4 usec and hardware margin of 0:<br/>`tHIGH = CEIL(4 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 77 = 0x4D cycles` |
| 11:0 | HW_TLOW | Specify the Low period of the SCL clock in terms of GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK cycles. The hw_tLOW is given by the following equation:<br/>`hw_tLOW >= (Minimum SCL LOW Time as per spec(usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 19.2 MHz, Min spec Low time is 4.7usec and hardware margin of 0 then:<br/>`hw_tLOW = CEIL(4.7 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 91 = 0x5B cycles` |

---

## 4.2.4.7.11 0x104 CCI_I2C_M0_SDA_CTL_0
**Type:** RW  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register is used to control the I2C Master Data (SDA) timing for SCL.

> [!NOTE]
> Do not change this register when the I2C Master is in a busy state. Always reprogram this register whenever there is a change in the GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK.

*(Fields continue on next page)*
<!-- page 1138 -->

### 0x104 CCI_I2C_M0_SDA_CTL_0 (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 23:16 | HW_TSU_STO | Specify Set-up time for STOP condition.<br/>`tSU_STO >= (Min setup-time (usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 24.576 MHz and spec setup time is 4 usec and hardware margin of 0 then:<br/>`tSU_STO = CEIL(4 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 77 = 0x4D cycles` |
| 7:0 | HW_TSU_STA | Specify Set-up time for Repeated START condition.<br/>`tSU_STA >= (Min setup-time (usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 24.576 MHz and spec setup time is 4 usec and hardware margin of 0 then:<br/>`tSU_STO = CEIL(4.7 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 91 = 0x5B cycles` *(Note: Example in original text uses 4.7 usec and refers to tSU_STO)* |

## 4.2.4.7.12 0x108 CCI_I2C_M0_SDA_CTL_1
**Type:** RW  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register is used to control the I2C Master Data (SDA) timing for SCL.

> [!NOTE]
> Do not change this register when the I2C Master is in a busy state. Always reprogram this register whenever there is a change in the GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 23:16 | HW_THD_DAT | Specify Hold time for the Data.<br/>`hw_tHD_DAT <= (Max Hold time (usec) + hardware Margin) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 24.576 MHz and spec data hold time is 3.45 usec and hardware margin of 0 then:<br/>`tHD_DAT = CEIL(3.45 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 67 = 0x43 cycles` |
| 7:0 | HW_THD_STA | Specify Hold time for START Condition.<br/>`hw_tHD_STA <= ((Min Hold time (usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)`<br/>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 24.576 MHz and spec hold time is 4 usec then:<br/>`tHD_STA = CEIL(4 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 91 = 0x5B cycles` *(Note: Calculation in original text matches 4.7 usec at 19.2 MHz)* |

#### CCI_I2C_M1_SCL_CTLCCI_v0.3

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 27:16 | HW_THIGH | Specify the high period of the SCL clock in terms of GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK cycles. The hw_tHIGH is given by the following equation:<br>hw_tHIGH >= (Minimum SCL HIGH Time as per spec(usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)<br>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 19.2 MHz, Min spec High time is 4 usec and HW margin of 0:<br>tHIGH = CEIL(4 usec * 19.2MHz) ~= 77 = 0x4D cycles |
| 7:0 | HW_TLOW | Specify the Low period of the SCL clock in terms of GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK cycles.<br>The hw_tLOW is given by the following equation:<br>hw_tLOW >= (Minimum SCL LOW Time as per spec(usec) + hardware Margin(usec)) * GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK (MHz)<br>For example: For 100 KHz mode if GCC_CAMSS_CCI_CLK is 19.2 MHz, Min spec Low time is 4.7 usec and hardware margin of 0 then:<br>hw_tLOW = CEIL(4.7 usec * 19.2 MHz) ~= 91 = 0x5B cycles |

### 4.2.4.7.26 0x300 CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_EXEC_WORD_CNT

Type: RW

Clock: GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK

Reset state: 0x00000000

This register is used to specify the number of words (32 bit) to be executed from the I2C Command Queue. The software has the flexibility to load this register at any time. But, it takes into effect only when the corresponding bit in the QUEUE_START register is set. This register is not zero based that is, value of 0 means that no commands are there to be executed. The maximum value that can be programmed in this register is 64 that is, 0x40.

> [!NOTE]
> The software should program this register only after all the intended commands have been loaded into the queue.
<!-- page 1146 -->
#### CCI_I2C_M0_Q0_EXEC_WORD_CNTCCI_v0.3

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6:0 | EXEC_WORD_CNT | Specify the number of words to be executed |

### 4.2.4.7.56 0x900 CCI_GPIO_Q2_EXEC_WORD_CNT

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: GCC_CAMSS_CCI_AHB_CLK
- **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register is used to specify the number of words to be executed from the GPIO Command Queue. The software has the flexibility to load this register at any time. But, it will take into effect only when the corresponding bit in the QUEUE_START register is set. This register is not a zero based, that is, the value of 0 means no commands are there to be executed. The maximum value that can be programmed in this register is 16 which is, 0x10.

> [!NOTE]
> The software should program this register only after all the intended commands are loaded into the queue.
<!-- page 1157 -->
#### CCI_GPIO_Q2_EXEC_WORD_CNT

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4:0 | EXEC_WORD_CNT | Specify the number of words to be executed |
