The command can be bad due to following reasons:<br>- The command type field value of the command is unsupported<br>- The command is a normal I2C Write or a repeated start I2C Write command but, the specified byte_count field value is greater than 10 bytes.<br>- The commands is a normal I2C Read or a repeated start I2C Read command but, the specified byte_count field value is zero bytes (unsupported value).<br>- The command is a wait_gpio_queue command but, the specified queue number field value is 3 (CCI has only 3 GPIO queues. Hence the legal values for this field are 0, 1 and 2) |

| 1 | GPIO_Q0_UNDERFLOW | This bit asserts when GPIO Queue0 underflows |
| 0 | GPIO_Q0_REPORT | This bit asserts when the Report command is executed from the GPIO queue0 |

## 4.2.5 JPEG Encoder (JPEG)

This section describes the JPEG encoder engine.

### 4.2.5.1 JPEG overview

The JPEG encoder engine performs JPEG encoding of image data. The image data to be encoded are read from memory.

Figure 4-145 shows a high-level overview of the JPEG engine within the camera subsystem and in the SoC.

#### Figure 4-145: JPEG overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the connections of the JPEG module within the Camera Subsystem and the wider SoC. 
- The **Camera Subsystem** contains:
  - The **JPEG** core, which receives "Clocks" and "Reset" inputs from the external **GCC** (Global Clock Controller).
  - The JPEG core outputs an "Interrupt" signal to the external **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem).
  - The JPEG core connects to a local **VBIF** block via "Data in" and "Data out" lines.
  - The VBIF block communicates bi-directionally with the **System NoC** (Network-on-Chip) and also connects to an **AHB slave bus** communicating with the System NoC.
- The **System NoC** connects the Camera Subsystem to other system resources:
  - **OCMEM** (On-Chip Memory) via a bi-directional link.
  - **SMMU** (System MMU) via a bi-directional link, which in turn connects bi-directionally to **External Memory**.

### 4.2.5.3 JPEG functional description

Figure 4-147 shows a high-level overview of JPEG functional blocks.

#### Figure: Figure 4-147 JPEG functional block diagram
*Description:* The diagram shows the functional blocks of the JPEG module, their clock domains, and interfaces.
- **Buses:**
  - **AHB Bus** at the top for register access.
  - **System NoC** at the bottom, which connects to **OCMEM** and **DDR**.
- **Clock Domains:**
  - **GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK Domain:** Contains the **AHB2AHB** bridge which interfaces with the AHB bus.
  - **GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK Domain:** Contains the core JPEG processing blocks:
    - **Reset Controller**, **SW Registers** (connected to AHB2AHB), and **IRQ Generator**.
    - **Fetch Engine**: Reads input data from the **VBIF** (Virtualizing Bus Interface).
    - **JPEG Encoder**: The main processing core, connected to internal **RAMs**. It receives data from the Fetch Engine.
    - **Write Engine**: Receives encoded data from the JPEG Encoder and writes it to the **VBIF** via three channels.
- **Interfaces:**
  - **VBIF (Virtualizing Bus Interface)**: Interfaces the Fetch and Write engines with the **System NoC**.
  - **System NoC**: Connects to **OCMEM** (On-Chip Memory) and **DDR** (External Memory).

### 4.2.5.3.1 JPEG power and clock management

The JPEG can be power collapsed when not in use. However, if any JPEG engine blocks are used, it cannot be collapsed.

The power collapse sequences use the standard procedure for all power collapsible modules. By setting registers in the GCC, the JPEG hard macro can be brought out of a Power Collapsed state.

Reset the JPEG from the GCC, after enabling the engine from the Power Collapsed state. Perform this reset only to power up if any of the JPEG blocks are actively processing. Applying a reset from the GCC can cause detrimental chip operation.

If software is unsure of the state of the JPEG, a software reset is performed by setting the JPEG_0_RESET_CMD register. The software reset requires the GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK and peripheral GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK to be running.

Table 4-223 lists the required clocks for JPEG for the valid offline encode functional mode.

The JPEG has a virtualizing bus interface (VBIF) to the Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) bus, register access to the VBIF requires the GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK and GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AXI_CLK clocks to be on.
<!-- page 1173 -->

### Table 4-226 JPEG required clocks

| JPEG mode | Data source | Data sync | GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AXI_CLK |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Offline encode | DDR | DDR | On | On | On |

### 4.2.5.3.2 JPEG resets

In addition to the available software reset in GCC, software can reset the JPEG engine through:
- **JPEG_0_RESET_CMD** register. Software controls whether specific clock domains or individual blocks can be reset.
- Registers are accessed through the Advanced High-performance Bus (AHB) port; however, software cannot reset the VBIF through JPEG engine registers.

Apply a software reset only when the engine and AXI buses are idle. Also, before initiating a software reset, the engine (`GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK`) and register (`GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK`) clocks must be enabled.

To program the reset sequence, write to the reset bitfields in the `JPEG_0_RESET_CMD`.

The reset sequence is complete when software reads the `RESET_ACK_IRQ` in the `JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS` register.

> [!NOTE]
> Software must set the start command `HW_START` field in the `JPEG_0_CMD` register so the hardware executes correctly following a power-on reset. The default mode is inline JPEG awaiting a software start command to be issued in the `JPEG_0_CMD` register. Therefore, without a correct software setup, issuing a start command to the hardware is not needed and may result in unintended behavior. In addition, hardware must be reset after issuing the `HW_STOP` command.

### 4.2.5.3.3 JPEG interrupts

The JPEG engine issues interrupts for the following:
- When hardware completes tasks. This includes completion of JPEG encoding of a frame and results written to memory
- Following buffer management to indicate consumed buffers and hardware requests for more buffers to complete tasks
- After detecting processing
- For error conditions
<!-- page 1174 -->

### Table 4-227 JPEG interrupts description

| IRQ name | IRQ type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| SESSION_DONE | Status of task completion | Processing for session has completed |
| SWC_RD_DONE | Status of task completion | Software initiated block fetch has completed |
| RD_BUF_PLN0_DONE <br> RD_BUF_PLN1_DONE <br> RD_BUF_PLN2_DONE | Status of buffer management | A read plane buffer specified by software is consumed |
| RD_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN <br> RD_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN <br> RD_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN | Status of buffer management | A read plane buffer is issued to hardware to complete session |
| WR_BUF_PLN0_DONE <br> WR_BUF_PLN1_DONE <br> WR_BUF_PLN2_DONE | Status of buffer management | A write plane buffer specified by software is consumed |
| WR_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN <br> WR_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN <br> WR_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN | Status of buffer management | A write plane buffer is issued to hardware to complete session. |
| STOP_ACK | Status of task completion | Hardware stop command has completed |
| RESET_ACK | Status of task completion | Reset command has completed |
| VIOLATION | Error | A fatal and unexpected hardware condition |

### 4.2.5.3.4 JPEG data flows

Data flow in JPEG occurs in a session term – A session occurs from the time the software issues a processing start command to the hardware until the hardware returns either a session done IRQ indicating a complete task, or an error IRQ indicating an incomplete task.

In offline encode mode, the hardware reads one, two, or three streams of YCbCr image data. JPEG offline encoding data flow shows the hardware data path.

The encode engine can encode H1V1, H1V2, H2V1, H2V2, and monochrome image formats. JPEG expects that every encode session is a new image.

Software specifies image width and height to be encoded in MCUs. For each session, the region to be encoded and fetched must be rectangular. Assuming the hardware is appropriately configured, it can report this encoding status through read only registers: bytes and bits output to memory during session and statistics for MCUs encoded.

Internal state information of the encode pipeline is also exposed in registers to enable encoding from a prior session. Software can read these values and use these values in another session as initialization values to resume encoding from a prior session.
<!-- page 1175 -->

#### Figure: Figure 4-148 JPEG offline encoding data flow
*Description:* The diagram illustrates the data flow during offline JPEG encoding.
- **Fetch Engine (Rotate):** Reads the input data (single stream) and can perform rotation. It outputs three parallel streams (likely Y, Cb, Cr).
- **JPEG Processing:** A large block containing:
  - **Scaler:** Performs scaling on the three streams.
  - **Block Format:** Formats the scaled data into blocks.
  - **Encode Engine:** Encodes the formatted blocks.
- **Write Engine:** Receives the encoded data (three streams) from the Encode Engine and writes them out (three streams).

### Table 4-228 JPEG supported operations

| Mode | Rotate | Upscale | Downscale | Crop |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Offline encode | Yes | Yes, arbitrary from 1x to 8x | Yes, arbitrary from 1x to 16x | Yes, via buffer specification |

JPEG general software and hardware flow shows the general software and hardware interaction for each mode. A FIFO-based addressing scheme (see Section ) is assumed.
<!-- page 1176 -->

#### Figure: Figure 4-149 JPEG general software and hardware flow
*Description:* Flowchart illustrating the interaction between software (SW) and hardware (HW) during JPEG processing (decode/encode). The flow starts with SW setup and command, then splits into parallel read and write loops managed by HW with SW intervention for buffer queueing.
- **Initialization:**
  - SW sets up HW for decode/encode by programming appropriate registers.
  - SW issues start command to HW.
  - The flow splits into parallel **Read** (left) and **Write** (right) loops.
- **Read Loop (HW managed, SW assisted):**
  - HW reads data from the read buffer.
  - Upon "Read Buffer Done Event":
    - HW latches the address for reporting.
    - Checks if "Necessary Read Data Read":
      - If **Yes**: Transition to **Session Read Done** (termination of read session).
      - If **No**: Checks if "Read Buffer in Read Queue":
        - If **Yes**: HW continues reading (loops back to start of read).
        - If **No**: HW stops reading from memory and waits for SW.
          - SW checks: "SW adds read buffer to Read Queue?":
            - If **Yes**: HW resumes reading (loops back to start of read).
            - If **No**: SW remains in a wait loop.
- **Write Loop (HW managed, SW assisted):**
  - HW writes output to the write buffer.
  - Upon "Write Buffer Done Event":
    - HW latches the address for reporting.
    - Checks if "Necessary Write Data Written":
      - If **Yes**: Transition to **Session Done** (termination of write session/overall session).
      - If **No**: Checks if "Write Buffer in Write Queue":
        - If **Yes**: HW continues writing (loops back to start of write).
        - If **No**: HW stops writing to memory and waits for SW.
          - SW checks: "SW adds write buffer to Write Queue?":
            - If **Yes**: HW resumes writing (loops back to start of write).
            - If **No**: SW remains in a wait loop.

### 4.2.5.3.5 JPEG offline encode control sequences

When the hardware is configured for offline JPEG encoding, the source and sync of the data to be encoded is external memory and the output is a bit stream and statistics.

There are three offline encoding scenarios:
- JPEG single pass encode, single read buffer
- JPEG single pass encode, multiread buffer
- JPEG multipass encode, multiread buffer (context switching)
<!-- page 1177 -->

### JPEG single pass encode, single read buffer

In this scenario, all image data and prescaling are available in a single buffer.

1. Software sets up hardware for encode by programming configuration registers including the number of MCUs to encode to be the image size after scaling.
   - Load a single address pointer for each image plane to the read address queue. The number of planes is determined by the memory format of the input image.
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR`
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN1_RD_PNTR`
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN2_RD_PNTR`
   - Configure and load up to eight address pointers to hardware write address queue for each output stream used; hardware can output up to three streams. These streams are the encoded bit stream and statistics (if enabled).
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_PNTR`
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN1_WR_PNTR`
     - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN2_WR_PNTR`
2. Software issues a start command to hardware by writing in the `HW_START` bitfield in the `JPEG_0_CMD` register. Hardware reads the data until configured number of MCUs are encoded.
3. Hardware returns an IRQ upon completion of all data written to memory in the `SESSION_DONE_IRQ` bitfield of the `JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS` register.

> [!NOTE]
> For certain scaling cases, the last several lines in a buffer may not be consumed.

Figure 4-150 shows the single pass encode, single read buffer flow diagram.
<!-- page 1178 -->

#### Figure: Figure 4-150 JPEG single pass encode, single read buffer flow diagram
*Description:* This flowchart is identical in structure to Figure 4-149, but highlights the active path for a single read buffer scenario using green arrows.
- **Highlighted Path (Green):**
  1. Software setup and start command execution.
  2. Hardware starts reading from the single read buffer.
  3. A "Read Buffer Done Event" occurs.
  4. Hardware latches the address.
  5. The check "Necessary Read Data Read?" evaluates to **Yes** (since all data fits in the single buffer).
  6. The read session terminates at **Session Read Done**.
- The write path (right side) and other loop branches (buffer queues) are shown but not highlighted, indicating they are not the primary focus of this specific scenario's read phase.

### JPEG single pass encode, multiread buffer

In this scenario, all image data is available in a number of buffers (X); however, the number of MCUs post scaling per each of the X buffers is not necessarily known by software.

1. Software sets up hardware for encode by programming appropriate configuration registers including the number of MCUs to encode to be the image size after scaling.
2. Load up to two address pointers for each plane to the hardware read address queue.
   - Let $N = \{1, 2\}$
   - For ($i=0$; $i < N$; $i$++)
     - Configure bitfield `PNTR[i]` of the `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR` register
     - Configure bitfield `PNTR[i]` of the `JPEG_0_PLN1_RD_PNTR` register
     - Configure bitfield `PNTR[i]` of the `JPEG_0_PLN2_RD_PNTR` register
<!-- page 1179 -->

3. Load up to eight address pointers to hardware write address queue for each output stream used. Hardware can output up to three streams. These streams are the encoded bit stream and statistics (if enabled).
   - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_PNTR`
   - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN1_WR_PNTR`
   - Configure `JPEG_0_PLN2_WR_PNTR`
4. Software issues start command to hardware by writing in the `HW_START` bitfield in the `JPEG_0_CMD` register. Hardware attempts to read data until the configured number of MCUs are encoded. If hardware detects that the current block row to be fetched has a block height exceeding the current specified buffer (without another available buffer), hardware issues `RD_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN` in the `JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS` register.
5. Software must provide another buffer pointer so hardware can resume encoding. The buffer pointer should contain the image data following the previous buffer’s image data.
6. Hardware returns an IRQ upon completion of all data written to memory in the `SESSION_DONE_IRQ` bitfield of the `JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS` register.

Figure 4-151 shows the single pass encode, multiread buffer flow diagram.
<!-- page 1180 -->

#### Figure: Figure 4-151 JPEG single pass encode, multiread buffer flow diagram
*Description:* This flowchart is identical in structure to Figure 4-149, but uses color-coded paths to illustrate different scenarios in a multiread buffer setup.
- **Green Path:** The initial flow where hardware reads a buffer, completes it ("Read Buffer Done Event"), latches the address, and determines that more data is needed ("Necessary Read Data Read?" is No). It then checks the read queue.
- **Blue Path:** Loops back from "Read Buffer in Read Queue? (Yes)" to "HW reads data...", indicating the next buffer was already queued and processing continues without stopping.
- **Red Path:** Follows from "Read Buffer in Read Queue? (No)", leading to "HW stops reading from memory". It then waits for "SW adds read buffer to Read Queue? (Yes)" to loop back to "HW reads data...", illustrating the flow when hardware has to pause and wait for software to provide new buffers.
- **Purple Path:** The final iteration flow where "Necessary Read Data Read?" evaluates to **Yes**, leading to **Session Read Done**.

### JPEG multipass encode, multiread buffer (context switching)

In this scenario, the image data is available in X buffers; software or firmware may not know the number of MCUs postscaling per each of the X buffers (or are not necessarily available).

Hardware is to be transitioned in and out of encode and possibly transitioning between other image encode sessions.

The sequence of events for this model is the same as single pass, multiread buffer sequence except context switching when software sets buffers with >= MCUs to encode to hardware.

This permits the hardware to successfully complete the session and prevents halting further sessions. This implies that before setting up a session, software, or firmware must estimate with scaling ratios and buffer heights. Otherwise, hardware cannot encode the number of MCUs programmed. It waits indefinitely for a buffer that does not exist.


<!-- page 1181 -->

For JPEG encoding, the JPEG_0_PLN0_BUFFER_SIZE_WIDTH, JPEG_0_PLN1_BUFFER_SIZE_WIDTH, JPEG_0_PLN0_BUFFER_SIZE_HEIGHT, and JPEG_0_PLN1_BUFFER_SIZE_HEIGHT parameters in are configured based on the required buffer size. As the buffer size increases, the granularity of the buffer is larger.

For the encoder write engine, it has taken the advantage of writing bit stream to memory in a linear fashion to maximize burst transactions and therefore maximizing performance. As a result, concept of buffer width, height, and plane stride no longer apply.

From the programming point of view, since the encoded bit stream is written linearly, software only needs to program the buffer size and the start pointer. The other registers still exist (JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_STRIDE, JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_VSTEP and JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_HSTEP), but they are not used in encode write engine.

The register that software writes to for buffer size is still the same JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_BUFFER_SIZE, but instead of programming it with width and height, software programs it directly with buffer size.

> [!NOTE]
> This is only for the encode write engine; block processing for Fetch Engine does not change.

#### JPEG downscale configuration

#### Figure 4-152: JPEG downscale configuration
*Description:* This diagram illustrates the relationship between the read (input) buffer and write (output) buffer during JPEG downscaling.
- **Read Buffer (Left):** Represents the input image buffer with dimensions `READ BUFFER_WIDTH` and `READ BUFFER HEIGHT`.
  - The active image area is divided into a grid of 3x3 orange blocks.
  - The dimensions of each block are defined by `HSTEP * H_SCALE_RATIO` (width) and `VSTEP * V_SCALE_RATIO` (height).
  - The right and bottom edges of the read buffer contain `PADDING` (shown in blue-gray) to align with block boundaries.
- **Write Buffer (Right):** Represents the downscaled output image buffer with dimensions `WR BUFFER WIDTH` and `WR BUFFER HEIGHT`.
  - The active image area is also represented as a grid of 3x3 orange blocks, but scaled down.
  - The dimensions of each output block are defined by `HSTEP` (width) and `VSTEP` (height).
  - The configuration indicates `BLOCKS_PER_ROW = 3` and `BLOCKS_PER_COL = 3`.
  - There is a small `CROPPED` section on the right edge of the write buffer.

In the downscale mode, the configuration is as follows:
* Enable both fetch engine (see Section JPEG fetch engine configuration) and write engine (see Section JPEG write engine configuration), enable the scale engine (see Section JPEG scaling configuration), and enable the bridge.
* The fetch and write engines must be configured more than once unless this is a single plane image (one for luma processing and one for chroma processing).
* The BLOCK_WIDTH field in the JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN0_OUTPUT_CFG/ JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN1_OUTPUT_CFG / JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN2_OUTPUT_CFG register is programmed according to the horizontal scale ratio values listed in Table 4-239.

##### Table 4-239 JPEG scale ratio

| Scale ratio | BLOCK_WIDTH | HSTEP |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1x <= ratio < 2x | 4 | 255 |
| 2x <= ratio < 4x | 3 | 127 |
| 4x <= ratio < 8x | 2 | 63 |
| 8x <= ratio < 16x | 1 | 31 |
| 16x <= ratio <= 128x | 0 | 15 |
<!-- page 1187 -->

* The BLOCK_WIDTH field determines the HSTEP in the write configuration registers (JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN0_HSTEP, JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN1_HSTEP, and JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN2_HSTEP). The horizontal and vertical step corresponds to the block width and height. With block width N, HSTEP is programmed as N-1. The VSTEP registers values (JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN0_VSTEP, JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN1_VSTEP, and JPEG_0_SCALE_PLN2_VSTEP) is always 0.
* The last_HSTEP is the last block width; it is calculated by out_img_width%wr_HSTEP. The same as HSTEP / VSTEP, the last_HSTEP N is programmed as N-1 and last_VSTEP is 0.
* The output image dimension is simply the scaled input image (scale range ratio is 1-128).
* Given the output image dimension and the block dimension, the block per row and block per column can be calculated. With a value of N blocks, BLOCKS_PER_ROW and BLOCKS_PER_COL fields (in JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_BLOCK_CFG, JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_BLOCK_CFG, and JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_BLOCK_CFG registers) are programmed as N-1.
* Choose MN_DOWNSCALE as the vscale and hscale algorithm in the scale configuration JPEG_0_SCALE_CFG register. Enable horizontal and vertical scale. Disable upsample and downsample.

#### JPEG Huffman table specification

For JPEG encoding, the engine supports the selection of a programmable custom Huffman table in addition to using the standard Huffman table. The hardware DMI registers (JPEG_0_DMI_CFG, JPEG_0_DMI_ADDR, and JPEG_0_DMI_DATA) are used to load the quantization tables.

Software must write 164 * 2 + 12 * 2 = 352 entries.

### JPEG quantization table specification

The engine requires a quantization table to be loaded into hardware prior to encoding. DMI registers (`JPEG_0_DMI_CFG`, `JPEG_0_DMI_ADDR`, and `JPEG_0_DMI_DATA`) are used to load the quantization tables.

The quantization LUT requires 128 entries, with an address range of 0 to 127. Address ranges of:
* 0 to 63 contain the Luma quantization values
* 64 to 127 contains the Chroma quantization values

The first entry for each of the lower or higher portion of the LUT is the quantization value that applies to pixel 1 within a 64-pixel block.

Each address entry N within each half of the LUT is the quantization value that applies to pixel number (N+1).

> [!NOTE]
> For JPEG encoding, the quantization table is not programmed in zigzag coefficient order.

### JPEG quantization table load sequence

Software configures the DMI registers before loading the quantization table.
* Address value 0 is set in `JPEG_0_DMI_ADDR` so the first RAM address accessed is location 0.
  * To load the Luma quantization value for pixel 1, set `JPEG_0_DMI_CFG` to select the quantization LUT.
  * Set the auto increment field in the `JPEG_0_DMI_CFG` to be enabled.
  * Set the quantization value for pixel 1 in the `JPEG_0_DMI_DATA` register.
  * Set the quantization value for pixel 2 in the `JPEG_0_DMI_DATA` register.
* Continue until 128 entries are loaded. Although `JPEG_0_DMI_DATA` consists of 32 bits, the quantization values are 16 bits in value. The hardware expects the 16 bit quantization values to be set to the 16 least significant bits of the 32 bit register.

After the LUT loading completes, software sets the `DMI_MEM_SEL` field in `JPEG_0_DMI_CFG` register to select no memory selected before processing can begin. Otherwise, unintended JPEG processing results.

The following pseudo code shows how the quantization table should be loaded using DMI registers:

```c
task load_quantization_lut() {
    integer index;

    jpeg_dmi_addr.field_dmi_addr.set_fd_data(0);
    jpeg_dmi_addr.write_t();

    jpeg_dmi_cfg.field_auto_inc_en.set_fd_data(1);
    jpeg_dmi_cfg.field_dmi_ram_sel.set_fd_data(QUANTIZATION_LUT_RAM);
    jpeg_dmi_cfg.write_t();

    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    //Load Y Quantization values to lower portion of Quantization LUT
    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    for each (gd.luma_inv_quantize, index) {
        jpeg_dmi_data_lo.field_dmi_data_lo.set_fd_data(gd.luma_inv_quantize[index]);
        jpeg_dmi_data_lo.write_t();
    }
    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    // Load C Quantization values to upper portion of Quantization LUT
    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    for each (gd.chroma_inv_quantize, index) {
        jpeg_dmi_data_lo.field_dmi_data_lo.set_fd_data(gd.chroma_inv_quantize[index]);
        jpeg_dmi_data_lo.write_t();
    }
    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    // Disable DMI capabilities
    //-----------------------------------------------------------------
    jpeg_dmi_cfg.field_auto_inc_en.set_fd_data(0);
    // Note: The original documentation page ends here, likely missing jpeg_dmi_cfg.write_t(); and closing brace.
}
```

### JPEG buffer addressing resolution

The JPEG engine allows software to specify byte granularity stride and buffer pointer addressing for image planes.

For JPEG bit stream reads, hardware provides bit level resolution.

### JPEG input and output buffer modes

The JPEG engine can read data from OCIMEM or external memory, such as DDR. The source of the read data is configured in the `JPEG_0_FE_CFG` register.

The engine has a set of registers for buffer configuration, for example, for plane 0 `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR`, `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_OFFSET`, `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR_CNSMD`, `JPEG_0_RD_PNTR_CN`, `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_BUFFER_SIZE` and `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_STRIDE`.

JPEG supports addressing in FIFO mode. It supports both fetch and write paths for Luma. Hardware expects software to provide a sequence of buffer address pointers that are set in registers (up to two pointers per read plane and up to eight pointers per write plane).

Address pointers are stored in individual queues, one queue for each plane. The JPEG engine pulls a new address pointer from the queue as buffers are consumed during hardware operation.

As buffers are returned by hardware, software replaces consumed buffers in the queue. Software can track the buffers used for writing and reading through a status register `JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR_CNSMD` with the address of last buffer completed.

The following hardware restrictions apply:
* Data size to fetch or write for each buffer is fixed and cannot change unless hardware processing is stopped.
* There is no mechanism to replace address pointers already residing in a queue. To empty a queue, software must apply queue reset or even an entire JPEG engine reset command. See CCI is a small core operating at a low frequency (19.2 MHz). When the core is not in use software disables the CCI clocks from GCC to save the dynamic power..

### JPEG minimum access length support

Minimum access length (MAL) requirements are imposed to maximize DDR efficiency, which ultimately results in better system performance and possible reduced time to complete hardware tasks.

The JPEG engine accumulates sequential memory transactions and splits transactions that cross the specified byte boundaries for efficient access to the memory.

Software can configure the engine to perform MAL alignment on specified byte boundaries through the `MAL_BOUNDARY` field in the `JPEG_0_FE_CFG` and `JPEG_0_WE_CFG` registers, which must be configured for read and write memory transactions.

The hardware supports MAL break boundaries at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 bytes. For example, software configures the MAL byte boundary break to 128 bytes for both the fetch and write paths.

### JPEG maximum access length support

The JPEG allows software to control the maximum transaction size to memory. The size can be configured independently for write and read transactions using the `JPEG_0_FE_CFG` and `JPEG_0_WE_CFG` registers.

The VBIF hardware limits the programmable size to 8, or 128 bytes, for read and writes memory accesses.

For example, software configures the burst length for reads and writes with a maximum burst length of 8 and a multiple of the MAL byte breakup.

### JPEG register on-the-fly reconfiguration

When issuing a start command, software cannot modify configuration registers until hardware returns the `SESSION_DONE` IRQ in the `JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS` register.

Table 4-247 lists the only registers that can be modified while the hardware is actively processing.

### 4.2.5.3.7 JPEG memory packing

Table 4-248 lists the memory packing formats in the JPEG engine.

#### Table 4-248 JPEG packing formats

| Format | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| NV12 | Two streams and a semi-planar format consisting of a Y stream and an interleaved Cb and Cr stream. Each stream consists of an 8 bit data unit (Figure 4-153). |
| NV21 | Two stream and a semi-planar format consisting of a Y stream and an interleaved Cb and Cr stream (same as NV12 except Cb and Cr are swapped); each stream consists of an 8 bit data unit (Figure 4-153) |
| YV12 | Three stream format consisting of a Y stream, a Cb stream, and a Cr stream; each stream consists of an 8 bit data unit (Figure 4-154) |
| IYUV | Three stream format consisting of a Y stream, a Cb stream, and a Cr stream (same as YV12 except Cb and Cr are swapped; each stream has an 8 bit data unit (Figure 4-155) |
| Monochrome | A single stream format consisting of the Y plane only (Figure 4-156) |

### 4.2.5.3.8 JPEG performance

At JPEG engine level the engine supports static QoS settings.

At system level, the QoS latency settings must be recalibrated when the `GCC_CAMSS_JPEG0_CLK` clock changes frequencies since hardware latency counters run on the JPEG main processing functional clock domain.
<!-- page 1207 -->

### 4.2.5.3.9 JPEG command registers

Command registers are write-only registers that allow software to initiate hardware tasks. There are two command registers, `JPEG_0_RESET_CMD` and `JPEG_0_CMD`. The reset commands are grouped into one register such that a single write command may initiate multiple reset commands in parallel. Non-reset commands are found in the `JPEG_0_CMD` register and are listed in Table 4-249.

#### Table 4-249 JPEG Nonreset commands

| Command¹ | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `CLEAR_WR_PLNx_QUEUE` | Clear buffer queue contents |
| `CLEAR_RD_PLNx_QUEUE` | Clear buffer queue contents |
| `HW_STOP` | Stop hardware processing |
| `HW_START` | Start hardware processing |

¹ The commands are color-coded to show grouped usage.

While the commands are grouped into a single register, there is no meaning when all bits are set or commands are issued simultaneously to the hardware. On a given register write, software must set the bits or issue commands within one of the color groups only. In the blue command group (which consists of both a start and stop command), if the stop command is issued the hardware always executes the stop command regardless of whether the start command is set.

#### JPEG clear RD/WR queue

When these fields are set, they remove any address pointers still present in the address queue by resetting the FIFO used to store the address pointer for the read/write planes. The clearing of the queue is immediate and no IRQ is returned by the hardware.

#### JPEG HW_STOP

The `HW_STOP` is used to move the hardware from an active to an idle state before task completion. This stop mechanism ensures that all bus activity for the JPEG is stopped. After the stopping process is done, `INFO_AXI_HALT_ACK_DONE` (TBD) IRQ is returned by the hardware. If `HW_STOP` is used, software should perform a software reset to the JPEG engine. Doing so puts the engine back in a known good state.

#### JPEG HW_START

The `HW_START` is always issued at the start of any session to initiate processing. Configure the engine properly before informing the hardware to start the process. After the process is done, the hardware returns `SESSION_DONE` IRQ.

#### 4.2.5.3.12 JPEG register definitions

##### 0x0 JPEG_0_HW_VERSION
* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x30020000

This register is read to allow software to identify the hardware version of the JPEG engine.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR | This value identifies the major version of the JPEG engine. |
| 27:16 | MINOR | This value represents the minor version of the JPEG engine. |
| 15:0 | STEP | This value represents the step version of the JPEG engine. |

##### 0x4 JPEG_0_HW_CAPABILITY
* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000211

This register is read to determine the capabilities of the JPEG engine.
<!-- page 1213 -->

##### 0x4 JPEG_0_HW_CAPABILITY (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10:8 | DOWNSCALE | This field indicates the downscale factor (if any) the engine supports.<br>0x0: No Downscale Support<br>0x1: Discrete 8x<br>0x2: Continuous 8x |
| 6:4 | UPSCALE | This field indicates the upscale factor (if any) the engine supports.<br>0x0: No Upscale Support<br>0x1: Continuous 16x |
| 1 | DECODE | This field indicates that the engine supports JPEG decoding. |
| 0 | ENCODE | This field indicates that the engine supports JPEG encoding. |

##### 0x8 JPEG_0_RESET_CMD
* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register is used to reset the hardware to a known state. A composite interrupt is generated when all the resets are completed. A second reset command should not be issued until the reset acknowledge is received from the first command.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is a command register - writes to this register produced strobe commands to the hardware.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | RESET_BYPASS | 0x0: The reset controller for the individual functional module is active, and the `*_DOMAIN_RESET` fields are not meaningful. A reset done interrupt is generated.<br>0x1: The reset controller is bypassed and software must manually assert / de-assert reset to each clock domain using the `*_DOMAIN_RESET` fields. The individual functional module reset is inactive. No reset done interrupt is generated. |
| 29 | JPEG_DOMAIN_RESET | This bit is used to manually assert/de-assert reset to the JPEG clock domain registers. |
<!-- page 1214 -->

##### 0x8 JPEG_0_RESET_CMD (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 17 | CORE_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the engine. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 16 | MISR_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the hardware MISRs. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 13 | REGISTER_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the register block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 7 | SCALE_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the scale block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 6 | BLOCK_FORMATTER_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the block formatter block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 5 | DECODER_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the decoder block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. This bit resets the quantization/inverse quantization module hardware. |
| 4 | ENCODER_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the encoder block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. This bit resets the DCT/IDCT module hardware. |
| 2 | INLINE_INTERFACE_RESET | RESERVED |
| 1 | WE_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the write engine block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |
| 0 | FE_RESET | 0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Causes a reset to be issued to the fetch engine block. When the reset is complete an interrupt is generated back to the JPEG interrupt controller. |

##### 0xC JPEG_0_CORE_CFG
* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 1215 -->

##### 0xC JPEG_0_CORE_CFG (continued)

This register controls the data path configuration for the JPEG engine. See the JPEG HDD for details on the data path.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 26:24 | MODE | These bits indicate the operation the hardware is to perform.<br>0x0: IN_LINE_JPEG_ENCODE<br>0x1: OFFLINE_JPEG_ENCODE<br>0x2: JPEG_DECODE |
| 20 | INLINE_AUTO_RESYNC_EN | RESERVED<br>0x0: NO_RESYNC_ON_SOF<br>0x1: RESYNC_ON_SOF |
| 19 | TESTBUS_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the JPEG engine test bus.<br>0x0: TESTBUS_DISABLED<br>0x1: TESTBUS_ENABLED |
| 17 | BLOCK_FORMATTER_OUTPUT | This bit selects the output sequencing for the Block Formatter.<br>0x0: Write Gathering Sequence<br>0x1: JPEG Sequence |
| 16 | SCALE_INPUT_SEL | This bit selects the input source for the scale block.<br>0x0: Fetch engine is input source.<br>0x1: JPEG Decoder is input source. |
| 7 | SCALE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the SCALE block.<br>0x0: SCALE_DISABLED<br>0x1: SCALE_ENABLED |
| 6 | BLOCK_FORMATTER_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the BLOCK FORMATTER block.<br>0x0: BF_DISABLED<br>0x1: BF_ENABLED |
| 5 | JPEG_DECODE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the JPEG Decoder block.<br>0x0: JPEG_DECODE_DISABLED<br>0x1: JPEG_DECODE_ENABLED |
| 4 | JPEG_ENCODE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the JPEG Encoder block.<br>0x0: JPEG_ENCODE_DISABLED<br>0x1: JPEG_ENCODE_ENABLED |
| 3 | BRIDGE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the BRIDGE block.<br>0x0: BRIDGE_INTERFACE_DISABLED<br>0x1: BRIDGE_INTERFACE_ENABLED |
| 2 | INLINE_INTERFACE_ENABLE | RESERVED<br>0x0: VFE_INTERFACE_DISABLED<br>0x1: VFE_INTERFACE_ENABLED |
<!-- page 1216 -->

##### 0xC JPEG_0_CORE_CFG (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | WE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the WRITE ENGINE block.<br>0x0: WRITE_ENGINE_DISABLED<br>0x1: WRITE_ENGINE_ENABLED |
| 0 | FE_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the FETCH_ENGINE block.<br>0x0: FETCH_ENGINE_DISABLED<br>0x1: FETCH_ENGINE_ENABLED |

##### 0x10 JPEG_0_CMD
* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register is used to issue commands to the HW.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is a command register - writes to this register produced strobe commands to the HW.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 11 | APPLY_SWC_RD_PARAMS | 0x1: Kick off read of register specified block. |
| 10 | CLEAR_WR_PLN2_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear WR PLN2 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN2 write queue is discarded. This command should be used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 9 | CLEAR_WR_PLN1_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear WR PLN1 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN1 write queue is discarded. This command is used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 8 | CLEAR_WR_PLN0_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear WR PLN0 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN0 write queue is discarded. This command should be used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 6 | CLEAR_RD_PLN2_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear RD PLN2 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN2 read queue is discarded. This command should be used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 5 | CLEAR_RD_PLN1_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear RD PLN1 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN1 read queue is discarded. This command should be used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 4 | CLEAR_RD_PLN0_QUEUE | 0x1: Clear RD PLN0 buffer queue. Any address present in the PLN0 read queue will be discarded. This command should be used only when the hardware is not actively processing. |
| 3 | INLINE_STOP | RESERVED |
<!-- page 1217 -->

##### 0x10 JPEG_0_CMD (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2 | INLINE_START | RESERVED |
| 1 | HW_STOP | 0x1: Halt the bus bridge and engine processing. A CORE_STOP_ACK IRQ is returned after the bridge and engine has stopped in a safe state. |
| 0 | HW_START | 0x1: Start the hardware engine processing session. |

##### 0x14 JPEG_0_CORE_STATE_STATUS
* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register is read to determine the state of the JPEG engine.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 9 | TOP_LVL_CGC_STATE | This field reports the current state of the top-level CGC EN.<br>0x0: Top-level CGC is DISABLED.<br>0x1: The top-level CGC is ENABLED. |
| 8 | BUS_STATE | This field reports the current state of the bus/bridge.<br>0x0: Bus/bridge is IDLE.<br>0x1: Bus/bridge is ACTIVE. |
| 4 | REALTIME_STATE | This bit indicates the current state of the VFE interface.<br>0x0: the VFE interface is idle.<br>0x1: the VFE interface is monitoring VFE signals. |
| 2 | SCALE_STATE | This bit indicates the status of the scale path.<br>0x0: the scale path is idle.<br>0x1: the scale path is active. |
| 1 | DECODE_STATE | This bit indicates the status of the decoding path.<br>0x0: the decode path is idle.<br>0x1: the decode path is active. |
| 0 | ENCODE_STATE | This bit indicates the status of the encoding pipeline.<br>0x0: the decode path is idle.<br>0x1: the encode path is active. |

##### 0x18 JPEG_0_IRQ_MASK
* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
<!-- page 1218 -->

##### 0x18 JPEG_0_IRQ_MASK (continued)
* **Reset state:** 0x10000000

This register allows software to control which set of events trigger an Arm IRQ.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | MASK | This mask is used to enable/disable an interrupt source for the JPEG engine interrupt to the CAMSS_IRQ_ROUTER (and the APSS QGIC respectively).<br>0x0: The interrupt source is disabled.<br>0x1: The interrupt source is enabled.<br><br>Event mappings:<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(0)` <= `SESSION_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(4)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN0_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(5)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN1_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(6)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN2_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(7)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(8)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(9)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(10)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN0_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(11)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(12)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_DONE` [sic: `WR_BUF_PLN2_DONE`]<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(13)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(14)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(15)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(19)` <= `DCD_UNESCAPED_FF`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(20)` <= `DCD_HUFFMAN_ERROR`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(21)` <= `DCD_COEFFICIENT_ERROR`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(22)` <= `DCD_MISSING_BITSTUFF`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(23)` <= `DCD_SCAN_UNDERFLOW`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(24)` <= `DCD_INVALID_RSM`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(25)` <= `DCD_INVALID_RSM_SEQ`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(26)` <= `DCD_MISSING_RSM`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(27)` <= `STOP_ACK`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(28)` <= `RESET_ACK`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(29)` <= `VIOLATION` |

##### 0x1C JPEG_0_IRQ_CLEAR
* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register is a command register to clear hardware interrupts.
<!-- page 1219 -->

##### 0x1C JPEG_0_IRQ_CLEAR (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CLEAR | This register is used to clear an interrupt source.<br>0x0: Has no effect.<br>0x1: Clears the interrupt status in IRQ_STATUS.<br><br>Event mappings:<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(0)` <= `SESSION_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(4)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN0_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(5)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN1_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(6)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN2_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(7)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(8)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(9)` <= `RD_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(10)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN0_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(11)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_DONE`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(12)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_DONE` [sic: `WR_BUF_PLN2_DONE`]<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(13)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN0_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(14)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN1_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(15)` <= `WR_BUF_PLN2_REQ_ATTN`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(19)` <= `DCD_UNESCAPED_FF`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(20)` <= `DCD_HUFFMAN_ERROR`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(21)` <= `DCD_COEFFICIENT_ERROR`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(22)` <= `DCD_MISSING_BITSTUFF`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(23)` <= `DCD_SCAN_UNDERFLOW`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(24)` <= `DCD_INVALID_RSM`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(25)` <= `DCD_INVALID_RSM_SEQ`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(26)` <= `DCD_MISSING_RSM`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(27)` <= `STOP_ACK`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(28)` <= `RESET_ACK`<br>- `JPEG_IRQ_SRC(29)` <= `VIOLATION` |

##### 0x20 JPEG_0_IRQ_STATUS (continued)

### JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_PNTR

* **Offset:** 0x38
* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

Hardware fetches data from OCIMEM or external memory. Writing the RD_PNTR registers enters the written address into the hardware buffer queue. Each image plane can store up to two read buffer address pointers. Once a read pointer is written to the queue, it can only be removed from the queue by issuing a CLEAR_PLN*_QUEUE command via the CMD register.

> [!NOTE]
> When a buffer is switched over, an interrupt is generated. This mechanism allows the definition of the last used buffer to be updated so that it is not overwritten the next time that it is used.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | PNTR | Read buffer address pointer. |

---

* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 28:0 | OFFSET | Bit offset from corresponding buffer address pointer for hardware to start fetching data for processing. |
| 31:29 | — | Reserved |

### JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_BUFFER_SIZE

* **Offset:** 0x60
* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

When hardware is used for JPEG encoding, the `*_RD_HEIGHT` and `*_RD_WIDTH` fields are interpreted directly as height and width of the image plane by hardware. The maximum plane size supported for JPEG encoding is $2^{16} = 65536$ bytes (pixels) for image width and $2^{16} = 65536$ bytes (pixels) for image height.

When hardware is used for JPEG decoding, the hardware concatenates `*_RD_HEIGHT` and `*_RD_WIDTH` to determine the buffer size holding the bit stream. That is, bits 31:0 are treated as the total buffer size in bytes. For JPEG decoding, the maximum bit stream buffer size is then $2^{32}$ bytes.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | HEIGHT | Read plane buffer height. |
| 15:0 | WIDTH | Read plane buffer width. |

---

### 0x74 JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_HINIT

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

The PLN\*_RD_HINIT value is a Q9.21 value, requiring 30 bits. The PHASE_INIT value should be computed as follows:

* **Plane 0 - Luma Plane**:
  * Upscaling:
    * PHASE_INIT = (1/2)\*(1/s) - 1/2 (1 <= s <= 8)
  * Downscaling:
    * PHASE_INIT = 0 Always
* **Plane 1,2 - Chroma Plane**:
  * Interstitial:
    * Upscaling:
      * PHASE_INIT = (1/2)\*(1/s) - 1/2 (1 <= s <= 8)
    * Downscaling:
      * PHASE_INIT = 0 Always
  * Cosited:
    * Upscaling:
      * PHASE_INIT = (1/4)\*(1/s) - 1/4 (1 <= s <= 8)
    * Downscaling:
      * PHASE_INIT = (1/4)\*s + 1/4 (1 <= s <= 16)

#### Register Bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20:0 | FRACTIONAL | Pixel fractional co-ordinate. |

### 0xC0 JPEG_0_WE_CFG

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register is used to configure the write engine.

#### Register Bits

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | H_FLIP | This bit sets the horizontal orientation of the image when data is fetched. |
| 30:29 | ROTATION | This field sets the orientation of the image when data is fetched. The orientation is counter clockwise for the original image.<br>0x0: ROT_0_DEGREE (Image is rotated 0 degrees.)<br>0x1: ROT_90_DEGREE (Image is rotated counter clockwise 90 degrees.)<br>0x2: ROT_180_DEGREE (Image is rotated counter clockwise 180 degrees.)<br>0x3: ROT_270_DEGREE (Image is rotated counter clockwise 270 degrees.) |
| 28 | POP_BUFF_ON_EOS | |
| 27 | MAL_EN | This bit enables Minimum Access Length Alignment. |
| 26:24 | MAL_BOUNDARY | This field sets the Minimum Access Length Alignment on data writes to memory.<br>0x0: MAL_32_BYTES<br>0x1: MAL_64_BYTES<br>0x2: MAL_128_BYTES<br>0x3: MAL_256_BYTES<br>0x4: MAL_512_BYTES<br>0x5: MAL_1024_BYTES<br>0x6: MAL_2048_BYTES<br>0x7: MAL_4096_BYTES |
<!-- page 1238 -->

#### JPEG_0_WE_CFG Register Bits (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 18 | PLN2_EN | This bit enables writes to plane 2. |
| 17 | PLN1_EN | This bit enables writes to plane 1. |
| 16 | PLN0_EN | This bit enables writes to plane 0. |
| 12 | CBCR_ORDER | This bit indicates to the hardware how CbCr pixels are packed in memory.<br>0x0: Cb pixel is in the least significant bit of the word<br>0x1: Cr pixel is in the least significant bit of the word |
| 9:8 | MEMORY_FORMAT | This field dictates the output memory format.<br>0x0: PLANAR (Three plane input data: PLN0 = Y, PLN1 = Cb, PLN2 = Cr)<br>0x1: PSEUDO_PLANAR (Two plane input data: PLN0 = Y, PLN1 = Interleaved CbCr)<br>0x2: MONOCHROME (Single plane input data: PLN0 = Y) |
| 7:4 | BURST_LENGTH_MAX | This field limits the length of the read transaction onto the bus.<br>0x0: Burst length 1<br>0x1: Burst length 2<br>0x2: Burst length 3<br>0x3: Burst length 4<br>0x4: Burst length 5<br>0x5: Burst length 6<br>0x6: Burst length 7<br>0x7: Burst length 8<br>0x8: Burst length 9<br>0x9: Burst length 10<br>0xA: Burst length 11<br>0xB: Burst length 12<br>0xC: Burst length 13<br>0xD: Burst length 14<br>0xE: Burst length 15<br>0xF: Burst length 16 |

### 0xCC JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_PNTR

* **Type**: W
* **Clock**: GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

Hardware writes data to external memory. Writing the WR_PNTR registers enters the written address into the hardware buffer queue. Each image plane can store up to eight write buffer address pointers. Once a write pointer is written to the queue, it can only be removed from the queue by issuing a CLEAR_PLN\*_QUEUE command via the CMD register.


<!-- page 1241 -->

> [!NOTE]
> When a buffer is consumed, an interrupt is generated.

### JPEG_0_PLN0_WR_PNTR (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | PNTR | Buffer address pointer. |

This register configures the JPEG encode path. The Huffman encodes lookup table is controlled by this register. This register also controls the restart marker interval. Allowable restart marker intervals are from 0 to 65535.

| 11 | FSC_ENABLE | This bit enables/disables the File Size Control module in the JPEG encode pipeline.<br>0x0: FSC_DISABLED<br>0x1: FSC_ENABLED |

### 0x14C JPEG_0_ENCODE_FSC_REGION_SIZE

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

This section describes the registers that are used for file size control. These registers need to be programmed only when File Size Control functionality is enabled. With File Size Control, the image is divided into 16 horizontal or 16 vertical regions. Software must specify the bit budget for each of these regions, as well as the number of MCU rows per region. This register establishes the region size in number of MCU rows.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 8 | HV_REGION | This field determines whether the vertical sequencing.<br>When set (1), regions are vertical for the original input image orientation.<br>When clear (0), regions are horizontal for the original input image orientation. |
| 4:0 | REGION_SIZE | This value is programmed to the number of MCU rows. If there are N MCU rows per region, this register should be programmed as N-1. This implies that there is a minimum setting on 1 MCU row per region. |

### 0x180 JPEG_0_ENCODE_OUTPUT_SIZE_STATUS

* **Type:** R
<!-- page 1259 -->

### JPEG_0_ENCODE_OUTPUT_SIZE_STATUS (Continued)

* **Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK
* **Reset state:** 0x00000000

Reading this register after receiving the session_done_irq returns the total number of bytes used to encode the input image. The read value includes the addition of the EOI and restart markers. This register is updated at the end of each session. The maximum image that are encoded in a single session is 8196 x 8196. For a H1V1 image with 2:1 expansion and no marker insertion, this could result in an output bit stream of 403,046,496 bytes. The hardware supports size reporting of up to 536,870,912. If the bit stream exceeds the max value supported by this register, the hardware saturates the value.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 28:0 | OUTPUT_SIZE_BYTES | Total number of bytes used to encode the input frame. |

### 0x2EC JPEG_0_PLN0_RD_HINIT_INT

**Type:** RW  
**Clock:** GCC_CAMSS_JPEG_AHB_CLK  
**Reset state:** 0x00000000  

The PHASE_INIT value should be computed as follows:
* **Plane 0 - Luma Plane:**
  * Upscaling: `PHASE_INIT = (1/2)*(1/s) - 1/2` (1 <= s <= 8)
  * Downscaling: `PHASE_INIT = 0` Always
* **Plane 1,2 - Chroma Plane:**
  * **Interstitial:**
    * Upscaling: `PHASE_INIT = (1/2)*(1/s) - 1/2` (1 <= s <= 8)
    * Downscaling: `PHASE_INIT = 0` Always
  * **Cosited:**
    * Upscaling: `PHASE_INIT = (1/4)*(1/s) - 1/4` (1 <= s <= 8)
    * Downscaling: `PHASE_INIT = (1/4)*s + 1/4` (1 <= s <= 16)
<!-- page 1267 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16:0 | INTEGER | Pixel integer co-ordinate. |

## 4.2.6 Camera Video Front End (VFE)

This section describes the video front end (VFE) within the camera subsystem (CAMSS).

### 4.2.6.1 VFE overview

The VFE performs various image processing actions such as, lens rolloff correction, bad pixel correction, demosaicing, noise suppression, color enhancements, and downscaling. Figure 4-158 shows a high-level overview of the VFE engine within the CAMSS and in the SoC.

#### Figure: Figure 4-158 VFE overview

*Description:*  
This block diagram illustrates the integration of the Video Front End (`VFE_0`) within the Camera Subsystem and its connections to other SoC components.
- **Camera Subsystem:**
  - Contains `VFE_0` (a shaded block), a `CSID` block (Camera Serial Interface Decoder), and a `VBIF` block (Video Bus Interface).
  - The `CSID` block contains two decoder sub-blocks, `CSID0` and `CSID1`, both feeding into an `ISPIF` (Image Sensor Interface) block.
  - The `ISPIF` outputs directly to `VFE_0`.
  - `VFE_0` communicates with `VBIF` via "Data in" and "Data out" paths.
- **External Inputs & Control:**
  - `GCC` (Global Clock Controller) provides "Clocks" and "Reset" signals to `VFE_0`.
  - `VFE_0` sends "Interrupt" signals to `APSS` (Application Processor Subsystem).
  - Two external `CSI_PHY0` blocks receive inputs from MIPI Sensors:
    - The top `CSI_PHY0` connects to a "MIPI Sensor 4 lanes".
    - The bottom `CSI_PHY0` connects to a "MIPI Sensor 2 lanes".
    - Both `CSI_PHY0` blocks connect to the `CSID` block inside the Camera Subsystem.
- **Memory & Interconnect:**
  - `VBIF` connects to the `System NoC` (Network on Chip) via the "AHB slave bus" and data pathways.
  - The `System NoC` routes data to/from:
    - `OCMEM` (On-Chip Memory).
    - `SMMU` (System MMU), which interfaces with `External Memory`.

Table 4-253 lists the VFE supported features.


<!-- page 1271 -->

### Table 4-253 VFE features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| VFE_0 | - Supports reading DPCM6, DPCM8, MIPI Raw8/10/12, Plain16<br>- Bayer exposure, histogram, and auto focus statistics<br>- Auto exposure and auto white balance<br>- Bad pixel correction<br>- Green imbalance correction<br>- Demosaic<br>- Global and local tone mapping<br>- Chromatic aberration correction<br>- Programmable frame drop |

#### 4.2.6.2 VFE internal connectivity

Figure 4-159 shows the VFE internal interface signals.
<!-- page 1272 -->

#### Figure 4-159 VFE internal connectivity

*Description:* Block diagram showing the external and internal connections for the Video Front End (VFE_0) within the Camera Subsystem.
- **GCC (Global Clock Controller):** Sends signals `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_ARES`, `CAMSS_VFE0_CLK_SRC` (becomes `GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_CLK`), `CAMSS_AXI_CLK_SRC` (becomes `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_CLK`), and `CAMSS_AHB_CLK_SRC` (becomes `GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_CLK` and routes to `GCC_CAMSS_AHB_CLK` for VBIF) to the VFE_0.
- **APSS (Application Processor Subsystem):** Receives interrupt signal `CAMSS_IRQ0` from VFE_0's `VFE_IRQ`.
- **Camera Subsystem:**
  - **CSID ISPIF:** Sends `Pixel pipe` and `RDI pipes` data signals to VFE_0.
  - **VFE_0:** The central processing unit. Receives reset/clocks from GCC, inputs from CSID ISPIF, sends interrupt to APSS, outputs `Data out` to VBIF, and receives `Data In` from VBIF.
  - **VBIF:** Connected to VFE_0 (`Data out` and `Data In`) and communicates with the `System NoC` via bidirectional connections including the `AHB slave bus`.
- **System NoC:** Shared interconnect at the bottom connecting to VBIF.

#### 4.2.6.3 VFE functional description

Figure 4-160 shows a high-level overview of VFE functional blocks.

#### Figure 4-160 VFE functional block diagram

*Description:* Block diagram illustrating the VFE_0 subsystem and its internal components, segmented into two main clock domains:
- **GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_CLK Domain:** Contains the `AHB2AHB` block which interfaces with the external `AHB` bus.
- **GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_CLK Domain:** Contains:
  - `SW Registers` (interfaces with `AHB2AHB`).
  - `Reset Controller` and `IRQ Generator` connected to the register block.
  - `VFE_0` main processing block (green).
  - `Fetch Engine` (blue) which receives input from the `VBIF` and feeds into a multiplexer (MUX).
  - A MUX that selects between the input from `CSID ISPIF` and the `Fetch Engine` to feed into `VFE_0`.
  - `VFE_0` outputs data to the `VBIF`.
- **VBIF:** Interconnects the `VFE_0` and `Fetch Engine` block with the `System NoC` at the bottom.
- **System NoC:** Connects bidirectionally to `OCMEM` (On-Chip Memory) and `DDR` memory.

#### 4.2.6.3.1 VFE power and clock management

The required VFE clocks can be enabled by setting registers in the GCC (see Global Clock Controller chapter).

Table 4-258 lists the required clocks for VFE for the valid bypass functional mode.

Because the VFE instantiates a VBIF for interfacing to the AXI bus, register access to the VBIF requires the GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_CLK and GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_CLK clocks to be on.

### Table 4-258 VFE required clocks

| VFE mode | Data source | Data sync | GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AHB_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_VFE0_CLK | GCC_CAMSS_VFE_AXI_CLK |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Bypass | DDR | DDR | On | On | On |
<!-- page 1275 -->

#### 4.2.6.3.2 VFE resets

The VFE has available software reset in GCC (see Global Clock Controller chapter).

#### 4.2.6.3.3 VFE interrupts

The VFE interrupts can be configured from the `VFE_0_IRQ_MASK_0`, `VFE_0_IRQ_MASK_1`, `VFE_0_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_0` and `VFE_0_IRQ_COMPOSITE_MASK_1` registers.

Software can check the interrupt statuses by polling the `VFE_0_IRQ_STATUS_0` and `VFE_0_IRQ_STATUS_1` register and clear interrupts by writing in the `VFE_0_IRQ_CLEAR_0` and `VFE_0_IRQ_CLEAR_1` register. In addition, there is also a global clear method by setting the `GLOBAL_CLEAR` bitfield in the `VFE_0_IRQ_CMD` register.

##### 4.2.7 Camera Micro Controller (Micro)

This section gives a high level overview of the camera micro controller (MICRO) within the camera subsystem.

##### 4.2.7.1 MICRO overview

The camera MICRO a simplified microprocessor that offloads main processor to perform simple ALU instructions, access of camera sub-modules register space, and enable real time embedded control for camera hardware. It’s main goal is to deliver control and coordination to the hardware modules in the camera subsystem with guaranteed low latency IRQ response. After a power-up, the main APSS first uploads a firmware (micro program) to MICRO’s internal code-data memory that implements several key functionalities listed in Table 4-262.

Figure 4-161 shows a high-level overview of the MICRO within the camera subsystem and in the SoC.

#### Figure 4-161: MICRO overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the Camera Subsystem and its connections to external blocks: GCC (Global Clock Controller), APSS (Application Processor Subsystem), and the System NoC (Network on Chip).
Inside the Camera Subsystem:
- **MICRO**: The Camera Micro Controller, which receives Clock and Reset signals from GCC, and Control signals from APSS. It has a bidirectional interrupt interface with the CAMSS IRQ router. It also sends Control signals to the CPP (Camera Pre-Processor).
- **CAMSS IRQ Router**: Receives interrupts from MICRO and CPP, and routes interrupts to the APSS. It also routes interrupts back to MICRO.
- **CPP (Camera Pre-Processor)**: Receives control from APSS and MICRO. It sends interrupts to the CAMSS IRQ router. It has a data interface (Data in/out) with a VBIF block, and a "Ping/Pong" interface with VFE_0.
- **VFE_0 (Video Front End)**: Has a data interface (Data in/out) with a VBIF block, and connects to CPP via the Ping/Pong interface.
- **VBIF (Video Bus Interface)**: Two VBIF blocks are shown, one for CPP and one for VFE_0. Both connect bidirectionally to the System NoC.
- **AHB slave bus**: Connects System NoC to the Camera Subsystem.
System-level blocks connected to System NoC:
- **OCMEM**: On-Chip Memory.
- **SMMU**: System MMU, which interfaces with External Memory.

Table 4-262 lists the MICRO supported features.


<!-- page 1291 -->

### Table 4-262 MICRO features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| MICRO | - Command based interface to the APSS<br>- Command parser and data process algorithm<br>- AHB write/read interface to the CPP<br>- Interrupt service routines for interrupt requests from the CPP<br>- Interrupt requests to the APSS |

The list below describes a typical camera real time operation for a camera frame data.
1. A frame is generated by the VFE, and the VFE interrupts the APSS indicating the completion of a frame.
2. The APSS process the frame information as well as other configuration required for the CPP such as de-noise, ASF, rotation, upscale, etc., then sends a frame processing command and data to MICRO via the MICRO firmware command interface.
3. The MICRO firmware configures the CPP for the frame and its first stripe. MICRO commands the CPP to process for the first stripe.
4. The CPP interrupts MICRO when the first stripe process completes.
5. The MICRO firmware configures the CPP for the second stripe, and commands the CPP to start the process.
6. The CPP interrupts MICRO when the second stripe process completes.
7. The MICRO firmware and the CPP iterates step 5 and 6 until all the stripes for the frame are processed.
8. The MICRO firmware interrupts the APSS to notify the completion of the process.

### 4.2.8 Virtualizing Bus Interface (VBIF)
This section describes the virtualizing bus interface (VBIF).

#### 4.2.8.1 VBIF overview
Each multimedia module (Camera Subsystem, MDSS) requires common functions, such as aggregation of the data streams from their various internal engines, address virtualization, transaction formatting, protocol conversion, trace, and debug data formatting. All these functions are grouped in a single module called virtualizing bus interface (VBIF).

Figure 4-162 shows a high-level overview of the VBIF.
<!-- page 1292 -->

#### Figure 4-162 VBIF overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing how the Virtualizing Bus Interface (VBIF) blocks integrate the multimedia modules (Camera Subsystem, MDSS) with the System NoC, Memory, and other control units.
- **GCC (Global Clock Controller)** provides Clocks and Resets to the JPEG, CPP, and VFE engines in the Camera Subsystem, and to the MDSS.
- **APSS (Application Processor Subsystem)** receives interrupt signals from the JPEG, CPP, VFE, and MDSS modules.
- **Camera Subsystem** contains:
  - **JPEG** engine, which interfaces with the system via **VBIF_JPEG** (supporting Data in and Data out).
  - **CPP** (Camera Pre-Processor) and **VFE** (Video Front End) engines, which share the **VBIF_VFE** interface (supporting Data in and Data out for both).
- **MDSS** (Mobile Display Subsystem) interfaces with the system via **VBIF_MDSS** (supporting Data in and Data out).
- **System NoC** (Network on Chip) connects the VBIF interfaces (**VBIF_JPEG**, **VBIF_VFE**, **VBIF_MDSS**) to:
  - **OCMEM** (On-Chip Memory)
  - **SMMU** (System Memory Management Unit), which in turn connects to **External Memory**.

The VBIF is a highly configurable and provides these functions to each of the multimedia modules.

Table 4-263 lists the VBIF supported features.
<!-- page 1293 -->

### Table 4-263 VBIF supported features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| VBIF | - ARMv7 compliant virtual to physical address translation<br>- Provide signaling to the dynamic clock divide circuitry (DCD) to indicate when the VBIF requires a full speed AXI clock<br>- Support for multiple request routing schemes including: Fixed assignment, virtual address range, virtual address bit, physical address range, and physical address bit<br>- Support for debugging through test bus outputs and an advanced trace bus (ATB) connection<br><br>**VBIF client interface features:**<br>- Support for the Qualcomm generic protocol and more support for a subset of the QSB2.1 and AXI1.0 protocols.<br>- Software-controlled transaction limits to limit the number of outstanding transactions separately for reads and writes.<br>- Support for a heterogeneous mix of client configurations with different data bus, MID, and TID widths.<br>- Support for addressing resolution equal to the client data bus width:<br>  - 64-bit addressing for 64-bit data buses<br>  - 128-bit addressing for 128-bit data buses<br>  - 256-bit addressing for 256-bit data buses<br>- Support for CSIZE and ASIZE signaling (for some client port configurations the addressing resolution is required to have byte granularity).<br>- Ability to reinitialize individual client ports, either under hardware or software control, without affecting the other VBIF clients.<br>- Separate clocking for each client interface.<br>- Ability to re-order transaction responses to the clients if they require them in the same order in which they were originally issued.<br>- Write data timeout feature to avoid hanging the master port if the client does not provide data. A programmable timeout value is used, and an interrupt is generated if this event occurs to allow software to diagnose.<br>- Signal any error responses that have occurred from downstream components back to the initiating client.<br>- Break up transactions that cross the 1 Kb boundary into 2 transactions for QSB compliance.<br>- Ability to limit the maximum number of beats in a transaction under software control.<br><br>**Master port interfaces and arbiter blocks features:**<br>- Support the QSB2.1 protocol.<br>- Present transactions to the downstream components as out-of-order (OOO) capable, regardless of whether the transaction is returned in-order to the upstream clients.<br>- Support of independent clocks for the DDR and OCIMEM paths.<br>- Support of multiple arbitration schemes such as fixed priority, longest time waiting, round robin, and a modified round robin for QoS.<br>- Software-controlled transaction limits to limit the number of outstanding transactions separately for reads and writes.<br>- Ability to request the VBIF to halt traffic under software control as a prelude to power collapsing the subsystem that integrates the VBIF.<br>- Optional software control (override) for many of the QSB sideband signals. |
<!-- page 1294 -->

#### 4.2.8.1.1 VBIF acronyms and terms

Table 4-264 lists the common acronyms and terms used throughout this section.

##### Table 4-264 VBIF acronyms and terms

| Acronym or term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| VBIF | Virtualizing bus interface |
| DCD | Dynamic clock divide |
| ATB | Advanced trace bus |
| QoS | Quality of service |
| OOO | Out of order |
| MMSS | Multimedia subsystem |
| xPU | Address protection unit |

#### 4.2.8.1.2 VBIF key use cases

The VBIF provides a way for the multimedia processors to communicate with the system memory.
Figure 4-163 illustrates the flow of address requests along the OCIMEM path. This is a simplification of the DDR path as it does not involve the MMU. Requests are processed as follows:

The integrated MMSS processor sends a request to a particular VBIF client interface. This request is captured in the command FIFO in the XIN block and this request is sent out to the appropriate OCIMEM arbiter block. Any request, which crosses the 1kB boundary, is broken up into two requests during this stage.

The arbiter block arbitrates between the various XIN blocks and then the request is sent out to the appropriate QSB-AXI slave port. This request can potentially be broken into a number of smaller requests at this stage based on software programming.
<!-- page 1295 -->

#### Figure 4-163 Address request data flow on the OCIMEM path
*Description:* A detailed block diagram illustrating the data flow for address requests, highlighting the OCIMEM path (which bypasses the MMU) with numbered blue (1) and red (2) arrows. The diagram is divided into XIN block, MMU block, and ARB (Arbitration) block, showing how they interface between the Client I/F and the AXI bus.
- **Path 1 (Blue):** Shows the request starting from the **Client I/F (Request)**, entering the **XIN block**, passing through the **Request Pipeline & Queue**, and bypassing the MMU to enter the **Request Queue Physical Address**.
- **Path 2 (Red):** Shows the request continuing from the **Request Queue Physical Address**, passing into the **ARB block** through an **ARBITRATION** node (which also receives inputs from other XINs and MMUs), and finally exiting to the **AXI (Request)**.
- **MMU Path (Bypassed in this view):** Shows how requests can alternatively flow from the **Request Pipeline & Queue** to an **ARBITRATION** node in the **MMU block**, then to the **MMU** itself, which outputs a Physical Address (PA) Request back to the **Request Queue Physical Address** in the XIN block. The MMU also handles Hardware Table Walk (HTW) Requests and Returns.
- **Read Data Path:** Shows read data flowing from **AXI (Read)** to **RDATA RAM** in the ARB block, through a read **ARBITRATION** node, then to **Bus sizing** and **Read Data & RESP Buffer** in the XIN block, and finally to the **Client I/F (Read)**.
