#### Reference generator

(The following discussion assumes a 1.8 V supply voltage. If Micbias is enabled to a voltage other than 1.8 V, the thresholds scale accordingly.)

The reference generator is a resistor string DAC, which allows the reference voltage to be programmed from 0-787.5 mV in 12.5 mV steps. It consists of a coarse resistor string, which has 8 kΩ unit resistors and a fine resistor string, which also has 8 kΩ unit resistors, for a total of 56 kΩ in the fine resistor string. At any given time the fine resistor string is switched in parallel with one of the resistors in the coarse string. This parallel combination is 8 kΩ \|\| 56 kΩ = 7 kΩ. The additional 1 kΩ at the top of the string ensures uniform 12.5 mV steps.

In addition, reference voltages from 1.3 V - 1.6 V are provided for headset accessory detection and 1.8 V for electrical removal detection.

The various functions that the button detection system can provide are as follows.

*   If the microphone voltage is below 800 mV, it could be one of the five buttons being pressed and is determined by the programmed button thresholds to determine which of the buttons is being pressed. For example, consider the case of the typical button voltages being 0 mV, 100 mV and 200 mV for buttons 0, 1, and 2 respectively. In this case, software would program the button detection thresholds to 50 mV, 150 mV, and 250 mV for these buttons. If hardware detects that the mic voltage is between 50 mV and 150 mV, it indicates that button 1 was pressed.
*   If software is trying to determine the type of accessory, it measures the microphone voltage. If it measures a voltage below button 0 threshold, it types the accessory as a headphone. For headphones, the mic pole and ground pole are a single conductor. If it measures a voltage above the button 0 threshold, but below the headset threshold (typically 1.5 V), it determines that the inserted accessory is a headset. The microphone impedance typically results in the mic voltage being between 30 mV-1.48 V.
*   If hardware indicates that the mic voltage is above the headset threshold of 1.5 V, this indicates that the accessory has been removed and an electrical removal interrupt may be issued.
<!-- page 1480 -->

#### Figure 4-234 Reference generator voltage taps
*Description:* Schematic diagram of the reference generator DAC. It consists of a Coarse Resistor String on the left and a Fine Resistor String on the right.
*   **Coarse String**: Connected between VDD (1.8V) and Ground. It has an 80 kΩ resistor at the top, a 1 kΩ resistor, and seven 8 kΩ resistors. Taps are available at 0, 100 mV, 200 mV, 300 mV, 400 mV, 487.5 mV, 587.5 mV, 687.5 mV, and 787.5 mV.
*   **Fine String**: Consists of seven 8 kΩ resistors in series (total 56 kΩ). It is shown switched in parallel across the 400 mV to 487.5 mV segment of the coarse string (creating an $8\text{ k}\Omega \parallel 56\text{ k}\Omega = 7\text{ k}\Omega$ equivalent resistance).
*   **Taps on Fine String**: When connected, they provide intermediate voltage steps of 12.5 mV: 400 mV, 412.5 mV, 425.0 mV, 437.5 mV, 450.0 mV, 462.5 mV, 475.0 mV, and 487.5 mV.

#### Autozero mode

The autozero mode is used to minimize the input offset of the comparator. However, there are issues with using the autozeroing on the TX2 input. The clock frequency used for auto zeroing is 32 kHz, which can alias down to the audio band. In addition, the reference voltage cycles through the button thresholds at a 4 kHz rate, which causes 4 kHz tone and harmonics on the TX2 path. Hence, autozeroing must be disabled when recording is enabled on the TX2 path. The internal hardware uses the Micbias enable register bit (0x144: bit 7) to determine the status of TX2 as a recording path. Software is not required to do any additional settings to disable autozero mode.

However, debug modes are available to manually enable or disable the autozero mode. These can be found in MBHC_AZ_CTL (0x144: bits 4:3).

#### Current sources

The current sources are used for button and accessory detection when MicBias are turned off. A trimmed current, programmable from 50 μA-200 μA is sourced into the MicBias terminal. The current source is disabled when MicBias are turned on.


<!-- page 1481 -->

### Impedance detection

The impedance detection solution uses the headphone PA and the resulting software overhead is considerable, since it involves both MBHC and HPH PA drivers. Hence, a new impedance detection system that operates independently within the MBHC is also implemented.

The system requirements for ULT Codec impedance detection require the hardware to identify which of the following ranges the headphone load impedance is in Table 4-62.

#### Table 4-62 Impedance detection specification

| Impedance Range | Impedance detection result |
| :--- | :--- |
| 4 Ω-100 Ω | Low |
| 100 Ω-23000 Ω | High |

The actual hardware implementation uniquely identifies the impedance value instead of dividing it into two levels.

To implement this, the hardware goes through the following routine.

* The electrical detection current source drives 5 μA into the HPH output for insertion detection. If the load impedance is above 200 Ω, this creates a voltage of above 1 mV. The reference generator can be stepped from 1 mV to 63 mV to provide an impedance value of 100 Ω-23 kΩ in 0.2 kΩ steps.

To achieve these numbers with the accuracy table shown above, the following formula is needed to calculate the value:

$$\text{Impedance} = \frac{\text{RESULT\_CODE} \times 400 - 200}{0.96} - 230$$

* If the voltage on the HPH due to the 5 μA current source is below 200 Ω, one of two methods is used to create a voltage on the HPH output to compare it with a reference.
  * Legacy solution forces a DC voltage on the HPH output, senses the PA output stage current and source a scaled down version into a resistor.
  * New solution slowly ramps the current to the HPH output to 1 mA and then uses this as the input voltage to the comparator.

To achieve these numbers with the accuracy table shown above, the following formula is needed to calculate the value:

$$\text{Impedance} = \frac{\text{RESULT\_CODE} \times 2 - 1}{1.165} - 1.3$$
<!-- page 1482 -->

#### 4.5.8.3.7 Digital microphone operation

The SoC supports two digital microphones. These signals are brought out through the TLMM. Access is only through AHB bus. Only digital codec core is needed for digital microphone operation. No Analog codec functionality is required for digital microphone operation beyond potentially microphone bias.

#### Figure 4-235 Digital microphone interfaces
*Description:* This block diagram shows the digital microphone interface connections. At the top, the external interface consists of `DMIC_DATA` and `DMIC_CLK` connected to the `TLMM` block. Below `TLMM`, two 1-bit lines connect `TLMM` with a blue block labeled `DMIC 1,2`. The line from `TLMM` to `DMIC 1,2` and the line from `DMIC 1,2` to `TLMM` each pass through a yellow circular node. The `DMIC 1,2` block has two output signals on the left labeled `DMIC 1` (with a small yellow '1' above it) and `DMIC 2`.

The system clock (MCLK) determines how the digital microphone functions. When the MCLK is 12.288 MHz, there are five operational modes for the digital microphone interface (768 kHz, 2.048 MHz, 3.072 MHz, 4.096 MHz, and 6.144 MHz). When the MCLK is 9.6 MHz, four operational modes are supported for the digital microphone interface (600 kHz, 2.4 MHz, 3.2 MHz, and 4.8 MHz). The selection of the clock frequency is done via the LPASS_CDC_CLK_DMIC_B1_CTL. DMIC0_CLK_SEL bit. There are five options (DIV2, DIV3, DIV4, DIV6, and DIV16). Each DIV option means that the MCLK rate is divided by that amount to generate the digital mic clock rate. For instance, when running from 9.6 MHz, selecting DIV4 produces a digital mic clock rate of 2.4 MHz.

> [!NOTE]
> For 9.6 MHz MCLK, DIV6 is not valid.

> [!NOTE]
> DMIC0_CLK_SEL refers to bits in register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_DMIC_B1_CTL. DMIC0_CLK_SEL supports DMIC1 and DMIC2.

Also, in register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_DMIC_B1_CTL are the physical enables for the digital microphone clock (which are sent to the physical digital microphones). There is only one digital microphone interface.
<!-- page 1483 -->

Once an interface clock rate has been decided upon, the decimator input must also be set up properly to accept this input. First, the decimator must be set to “DMIC” mode. Second, the appropriate DMIC must be chosen for the decimator input – in some cases the decimator accepts more than one DMIC, so the input must also be selected properly. Lastly, the digital mic clock selection must match what the digital microphone interface is running at. To do this, in each decimator block, there is a control called LPASS_CDC_TXn_DMIC_CTL (where n is the decimator number) which sets the input for the DMIC clock. This control simply needs to match the value, which the digital microphone interface is operating at. So if the digital microphone interface is set to DIV4, the LPASS_CDC_TXn_DMIC_CTL needs to also be set to DIV4.

> [!NOTE]
> When only one DMIC (primary) is connected to a particular digital microphone data line, the “other” (secondary) channel (could be right or left depending on what the configuration of the one physical microphone is) becomes a phantom channel when the signal is decimated. This is because there is not a second microphone to change the state of the data the primary microphone had driven on the line. Therefore the primary and secondary data are the same. This is an inherent behavior of the digital microphone multiplexing the data line. It is suggested that if only one physical digital microphone is used on a data line that the secondary input is not enabled in the decimator.

Selecting a DMIC clock frequency depends on the use case appropriate and whether the digital mics installed on the device supports the clock in question. Assuming, a platform does have mics, which support all rates; the following table, provides the recommended setting per use case type. In mixed use case modes, use the highest clock needed.

#### Table 4-63 Suggested DMIC clock rates per use case

| Use Case Type | 9.6 MHz MCLK | 12.288 MHz MCLK |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Standard voice call | 2.4 MHz | 2.048 MHz or 3.072 MHz |
| Voice memo | 2.4 MHz | 2.048 MHz or 3.072 MHz |
| Audio record or Camcorder | 3.2 MHz | 3.072 MHz |
| Ultrasound | 4.8 MHz | 4.096 MHz or 6.144 MHz |

> [!NOTE]
> Ultrasound is not supported for this SoC.
<!-- page 1484 -->

The digital mapping from external clocking phase to internal signal is shown in Figure 4-236.

#### Figure 4-236 Digital microphone clock phase to signal mapping
*Description:* The figure consists of three parts: a circuit diagram, a mapping table, and a timing diagram.
1. **Circuit Diagram:** Shows connections between the APQ8016 SoC, two digital microphones (`Dmic L` and `Dmic R`), and the `PM8916 Micbias`. Both microphones have their `Vs` pins connected to `PM8916 Micbias`, each with a 0.1 uF capacitor to GND. `Dmic L` has its `Sel` pin floating (which maps to GND internally as per the table), while `Dmic R` has its `Sel` pin tied to `Vs`. The APQ8016 outputs a clock signal (`Clk0 / Clk1`) that is routed to the `clk` input of both microphones. The data outputs from both microphones (`Data2` from `Dmic L` and `Data1` from `Dmic R`) are tied together and routed to a single input on the APQ8016.
2. **Mapping Table:**
   | Select (Sel) | Mode | Internal Signal |
   | :--- | :--- | :--- |
   | Vs | Right (Data1) | DMIC 1 |
   | GND | Left (Data2) | DMIC 2 |
3. **Timing Diagram:** Shows the relationship between the clock `Clk0 / Clk1` and the data lines.
   - `Clk0 / Clk1` is a square wave.
   - `Data1` is active (valid "data") when the clock is high. It starts driving after a delay (t2) from the rising edge, and ceases driving (high-impedance) after a delay (t1) from the falling edge.
   - `Data2` is active (valid "data") when the clock is low. It starts driving after a delay (t2) from the falling edge, and ceases driving after a delay (t1) from the rising edge.

As can be seen, when the select line on the microphone is pulled high, the data will be a “right” channel; likewise, when the select line on the microphone is pulled low, the data will be a “left” channel. The microphone interface then dictates which channel group the data belongs to. For the DMIC0 interface, the signals will be DMIC 1 and DMIC 2 internally.

#### Figure 4-237 Decimators
*Description:* This diagram details the signal paths for Decimator 1 and Decimator 2. Each path is identical. 
For a given path (e.g., Decimator 1 / DEC 1):
A multiplexer selects from five input sources: `ADC 1`, `ADC 2`, `ADC 3`, `DMIC 1`, and `DMIC 2`. The ADC inputs are marked with a yellow '2', while the DMIC inputs are marked with a yellow '1'. The multiplexer's output is routed to a `Decimator` block. The output of the `Decimator` block goes through an `HPF` (High Pass Filter) block, then through a multiplier block labeled `(X)`, and finally outputs as `DEC 1` (or `DEC 2`). The signal lines connecting the `Decimator` output to the `HPF`, the `HPF` to the multiplier, and the multiplier to the output are all marked with a yellow '21'.

#### 4.5.8.3.9 Rx PCM and interpolation configuration

For the Rx paths, there are several different configurations. The differences are fairly minor but are of some note. Each section below will highlight the features for the three main types of output paths (HPH/EAR, and Speaker/EAR).

Loopback and test mode inputs are ignored in the path descriptions below.
<!-- page 1487 -->

##### EAR/HPHL path

The HPH/EAR interpolation paths are shown on Figure 4-238.

#### Figure 4-238 Block diagram of HPHL/EAR interpolation paths
*Description:* This detailed block diagram illustrates the processing pipeline from digital audio inputs to the analog headphone and earpiece outputs.
1. **Digital Processing Section (Left):**
   - **Input Mixer (Rx Mux 1):** Selects from inputs including `IIR 1`, `IIR 2`, `Rx1`, `Rx2`, and `Rx3`. The output passes through a summation node where loopback signals can be mixed, and then to a second summation node where sidetone signals (selected from `IIR 1` or `IIR 2`) are added.
   - **Filtering & Gain:** The combined signal passes through a High Pass Filter (`HPF`) block, a multiplier `(X)` for volume control, and an Interpolator (`INT`) block.
   - **Quantization & Shaping:** The interpolated signal is truncated (`Trunc`), processed by an `Rx shaper` (with associated `MDFT` and `LUT` blocks), and finally converted to a 1-bit stream by a `Serializer`.
2. **PDM Routing & Deserialization (Center):**
   - The 1-bit serialized stream is output as `rxfe_pdm_rx0_01` and also routed to a multiplexer that selects between this stream and `pdm_tx1_01`.
   - The selected stream is processed by a `De-serializer` block, which splits the signal path. One branch goes directly to a multiplexer, and the other goes through `Dithering` and `LUT` blocks first.
3. **DAC & Analog Output Section (Right):**
   - The deserialized 4-bit signal is processed by a `FIR` filter and a `DEM` (Dynamic Element Matching) block.
   - **RDAC #1 Path:** The output of the `DEM` block is routed to Resistor DAC 1 (`RDAC #1`). The differential analog output from `RDAC #1` is amplified and can be routed to either:
     - Earpiece Output (`Ear Out`, Class G): Amplified to output `CDC_EAR_P` and `CDC_EAR_M`.
     - Headphone Left Output (`HPH left`, Class AB): Amplified to output `CDC_HPH_L`.
   - **RDAC #2 Path:** The output of the `DEM` block is also inverted/buffered and routed via a multiplexer to Resistor DAC 2 (`RDAC #2`). The differential analog output from `RDAC #2` is amplified and routed to:
     - Headphone Right Output (`HPH right`, Class AB): Amplified to output `CDC_HPH_R`.

### 4.5.8.3.11 Digital gain controller system

There are two modes of operation for the digital gain controller; the first is “Automatic” mode and the second is “Manual” mode.

In addition, a half-dB step has been added to allow for finer gain adjustments. This half-dB adjustment is accomplished through a single bit that is independent of the main 8-bit volume control and is always a +0.5 dB step. This means that to achieve -0.5 dB of gain, the main volume control must be set to -1 dB, and the half-dB bit is set to yield -0.5 dB.

The outline below shows the behavioral characteristics of the digital gain controller.

1. In Automatic mode
    a. Timeout = 0 ms (default register value)
        i. Once a programmed update occurs, the gain update is immediate
    b. Timeout ≠ 0 ms; must be programmed to value greater than 0 ms to get the timeout feature
        i. Once a programmed update occurs, the gain is updated after a ZCD occurs or the timeout occurs
2. In Manual mode
    a. Timeout = 0 ms (default register value)
        i. Once a programmed update occurs, the gain update occurs immediately after the update bit is set (even if the programmed value matches the existing value)
    b. Timeout ≠ 0 ms; must be programmed to something greater than 0 ms to get the timeout feature
        i. Once a programmed update occurs, the gain update is gated by the update bit and after a ZCD occurs or the timeout occurs (even if the programmed value matches the existing value)
3. There is one timeout register for each gain controller blocks of the codec
    a. Rx has three gain controllers
    b. Tx has two gain controllers
    c. IIR has 2 x 4 gain controllers
    d. This means that for gains running at different sample rates, to maintain a real world constant timeout, the software will have to batch process gains using the single timeout, example:
        i. Set 32 kHz timeout
        ii. Do all needed updates for 32 kHz
        iii. Set 48 kHz timeout
        iv. Do all needed updates for 48 kHz and so on
<!-- page 1493 -->

4. There is one update bit for the entire codec
    a. Each gain register has the option to disable or enable the update bit (that is, switch between Automatic mode and Manual mode)
    b. When the update bit is set, all registers, which are in Manual, are updated
        i. Though if the gain value is unchanged from its previous state, no glitch occurs as a result of setting the update bit
    c. This bit is `0x3D0` (`CDC_TOP_GAIN_UPDATE`) bit 0, `UPDATE`
5. In Automatic mode
    a. Each gain will be updated after the corresponding gain register is written to (even if the programmed value matches the existing value)
        i. No glitch occurs for registers with no gain value update
6. For the 0.5 dB step usage in Automatic mode
    a. Timeout = 0 ms (default register value)
        i. If the whole number portion of the gain value XXXdB is updated, the value updates immediately
        ii. If the fractional portion of the gain value. XdB is update, the value with update immediately
        iii. This means that the gain updates twice when transitioning from 10 dB to 11.5 dB
            (a) If this is deemed a problem, manual update mode can be used to mitigate this
    b. Timeout ≠ 0 ms; must be programmed to something greater than 0 ms to get the timeout feature
        i. The user has manage this dual register update properly to ensure the timeouts are not violated
7. The digital gain implementation requires that the specific decimator or interpolation path be enabled for the digital gain to be physically implemented in the signal path. If the gain is set prior to enabling the decimator/interpolator path, the register shows the programmed gain value correctly, but it will not be implemented in the signal chain. Setting a digital gain value and then enabling the decimator/interpolator path will not cause the gain to be implemented. The only way for the programmed gain value to be implemented correctly is to first enable the decimator/interpolator path and then set the digital gain of the path.

#### Gain timeout configuration

1. The timer function in the gain controller is sample rate dependent. A few examples are shown below using 48 kHz and 8 kHz as examples.
2. At 48 kHz sampling rate (Fs), the maximum timeout is 1.37s; $((256 \times \text{TIMER\_VAL} + 255)/\text{Fs})$
3. 11111111 $\rightarrow (256 \times 255+255)/48k = 1.365\text{ s}$; $(256 \times 255+255)/8k = 8.19\text{ s}$
4. 10000000 $\rightarrow (256 \times 128+255)/48k = 0.69\text{ s}$; $(256 \times 128+255)/8k = 4.13\text{ s}$
5. 01000000 $\rightarrow (256 \times 64+255)/48k = 0.347\text{ s}$; $(256 \times 64+255)/8k = 2.08\text{ s}$
<!-- page 1494 -->

6. 00000000 $\rightarrow$ Immediate gain update without timer expiration and zero crossing detection. Software control mode.

### 4.5.8.3.12 Low frequency HPF (DC blocker)

The corner frequency of the HPF is not dependent on the sample rate. When the sample rate changes, the internal circuitry is adjusted properly to keep the corner frequency constant for the sample rate change. This maintains the programmed corner frequency constant regardless of sample rate.

The corner frequency is variable to three values. The values are 4 Hz, 75 Hz, and 150 Hz. As well, the HPF can be bypassed.

### 4.5.8.3.13 Charge pump configuration

The charge pump only is needed for headphone operation. As the headphone is class AB mode only, the charge pump is only required for negative voltage generation so that the output is still 0 V (ground) referenced.

### 4.5.8.3.14 Tx to Rx pass through options

This section highlights several ways in which signals may be passed from the Tx to Rx chains.

#### Mission mode pass through

The only approved Tx to Rx pass through configuration for nontest modes is described here. Such a pass through might be needed for users that use FM Radio chips with analog outputs or for real time monitoring of a stereo recording with two onboard mics via the HPH output.

An input may be routed to an output via the following chain: Input $\rightarrow$ ADC $\rightarrow$ Decimator $\rightarrow$ IIR filter $\rightarrow$ Interpolation mixer $\rightarrow$ Interpolator $\rightarrow$ DAC $\rightarrow$ PA

### 4.5.8.3.15 Microphone bias

Since there is only one microphone bias in the system, there is no selection option for the microphone bias voltage reference.
<!-- page 1495 -->

#### Figure 4-241 Microphone bias block

*Description:* A block diagram of the microphone bias module. A buffer amplifier (yellow triangle) has an input range of 1.6 V to 2.85 V. It is supplied from the top by a voltage source of 1.95 - 3.075 V (labeled `CDC_VDD_MIC_BIAS = USB supply`). The output of the buffer splits into two paths:
*   The top path goes through a switch, has a node labeled "Mbias #1" branching off, passes through a terminal (represented by an empty yellow circle), and outputs as `Mbias #1 (CDC_MIC_BIAS1)`.
*   The bottom path goes through a switch, has a node labeled "Mbias #2" branching off, passes through a terminal labeled "33" (represented by a yellow circle containing "33"), and outputs as `Mbias #2 (CDC_MIC_BIAS2)`.

The microphone bias module (MB Ref + microphone bias buffer) requires 0.225 V volts of overhead to guarantee performance from its supply. With PMIC L13 regulator set to 3.075 V, the maximum voltage microphone bias can deliver is 2.85 V.

The voltages available are:
*   1.6 V to 2.85 V bias output, in ~50 mV steps, L13 = 3.075 V

> [!NOTE]
> This SoC has only one microphone bias module available. There are, however, two physical pins on the device that can be selected appropriately for the use case appropriate. The two pins on the device are independently selectable. Closing the switch allows the microphone bias to be enabled on that pin.

There are also pull up and pull down options on the two-microphone bias pins to allow connectivity to VDD or GND.

There are certain limitations that need to be met. For example, if digital microphones are being used, the microphone bias must be programmed to 1.8 V to match digital voltage I/O levels. This means that any analog microphones must also operate at this bias level (whether internally or externally biased) if used concurrently with digital microphone usage.

For optimal performance, star connecting microphones with common mic biases as close as possible to the chip increases isolation between two mic signals. This means that having as little common microphone bias trace between microphones improves isolation as the parasitic resistance of the trace makes the AC ground of the microphone bias less optimal.

Along with the optimization recommendation above, placing the microphone bias resistor as close to the chip as possible lowers the capacitance on the microphone bias trace. This is important for capacitor-less microphone bias mode.

#### Internal biasing option (for ECM type microphones only)

Along with capacitor free TxFE feature comes the option to bias an external microphone from the audio lines that are directly connected to the microphone.
<!-- page 1496 -->

Differential mode inputs are not available. There are two configuration options available. These are shown in Figure 4-242 below. One is the choice of connecting the negative terminal of the input amplifier to microphone bias via a pull-up, or to ground inside the chip. The second is if the ground connection to negative terminal of the input amplifier is chosen, a second bit allows the choice of connecting this terminal to chip ground, or the `HPH_REF` pin. The `HPH_REF` pin can be seen as a ground sense node near the ground.

The pull-up option to microphone bias exists in microphone bias design. It is been found that this helps the systems when connecting to electret type microphones. This switch is shown closed in sub figures from the Figure 4-242. Based on measurements, this switch helps improve supply noise injection, ground noise injection, and improves PSRR. With some basic math, it can be shown that since the electret microphone is roughly 8kΩ AC impedance, all of these benefits are seen.

#### Figure 4-242 Internal bias resistor options

*Description:* Two schematic diagrams side-by-side showing configuration options for the internal bias resistors of an input amplifier within the PM8x16 chip, connected to an external microphone.
*   **Common elements in both diagrams:**
    *   An external microphone connected to the positive input of a variable gain amplifier (yellow triangle) inside the PM8x16.
    *   A "Mbias" node at the top.
    *   A 2.2k resistor connected between the Mbias node and the microphone input line.
    *   Feedback paths with open switches.
*   **Left Diagram (Mbias Pull-up Configuration):** A switch in the path connecting the negative input of the amplifier to the Mbias node is closed. A switch in the path connecting the negative input to ground is open. This connects the negative terminal to the microphone bias.
*   **Right Diagram (Ground Configuration):** The switch connecting the negative input to the Mbias node is open. The switch connecting the negative input to ground is closed (conceptually, to represent the alternative configuration). This connects the negative terminal to ground.

For the register description:
*   `MICB_1_INT_RBIAS`
*   `TXn_INT_RBIAS_EN`
    *   `DISABLE` VALUE `0x0`
    *   `ENABLE` VALUE `0x1`
*   `TXn_INT_PULLUP_EN`
    *   `TXnN_CONNECT_TO_GND` VALUE `0x0`
    *   `TXnN_CONNECT_TO_MBIAS_OUTPUT` VALUE `0x1`
*   `TXnN_GND_SEL` BIT
    *   `TX_GND` VALUE `0x0`
    *   `HPH_REF` VALUE `0x1`

When `TXn_INT_RBIAS_EN` is not set, none of the internal bias resistor switches disabled. When `TXn_INT_PULLUP_EN` bit is set to `TXnN_CONNECT_TO_MICBIAS_OUTPUT`, the negative input of the input amplifier [is connected] to microphone bias.
<!-- page 1497 -->

The dotted line in Figure 4-242 shows this logic. When `TXn_INT_PULLUP_EN` is set to `TXnN_CONNECT_TO_GND`, the negative input of the input amplifier is connected to ground, the ground connection point is decided by `TXnN_GND_SEL`.

> [!NOTE]
> The IN3 input controls for the `TXn_INT_PULLUP_EN` bit described above is in the `MICB_1_EN` register due to space constraints.

Any MEMs microphones should use the microphone bias directly and not use the internal bias option at all.

#### Internal microphone bias source options

As there is only one microphone bias in the system, but there are two physical pins on the device, the two-sub micbias nodes bias different inputs.

### 4.5.8.3.16 Headphone and ear PA overcurrent protection (OCP) circuits

There is also a separate OCP circuit for the speaker amp to be covered in Section 4.5.8.3.17 section.

The OCP circuit is just that, a circuit, which determines whether too much current, is leaving the amplifier pins and protects the system in the event of an over current event. This could be the result of a short circuit to ground/VDD or it could be the result of too low of a load impedance. In either case, if the signal level is sufficiently large enough such that the current leaving the codec amplifier pins exceeds the programmed current limits, the OCP circuit will be enacted. Once the over current event is encountered, the PA’s output stage shuts down immediately to stop the large current flow that would exist otherwise. There are some details beyond this simple description that are important and will be described below.

It should be noted that the OCP is not a short circuit detection feature. The PAs will not shut down simply because the outputs are shorted to ground, there must be some signal level accompanying the short circuit event before the OCP will be triggered, thus it really is an over current protection circuit.

The intent of the OCP is two-fold. First, while it is believed that the amplifiers will not be damaged by the over current event, shutting down the PA protects the codec from physical damage. Second, it reduces the excess loading from an over current event on the power management supply, which furnishes current to the headphone and ear PAs. This reduces the chance that the supply has a drastic drop out event caused by large current demands of the headphone and/or ear PAs. The drop out of the supply could have much wider consequences in the system than just impacting the codec alone.

There are several options for configuring the OCP circuit. Some of the parameters are global to both headphone PAs and ear PA. Those controls are at SPMI1 `0x91` and SPMI1 `0x92`. The configurations in these registers affect both the headphone and ear OCP elements (but not Speaker). `0x19F` controls how many times the PA will be re-enabled after and OCP event prior to stopping for good. Bits [3:0] set the finite number of attempts that the PA will try to re-enable itself after an over current event is found. `0x1A0` sets the duty cycle for “run” and “wait” times. The “wait” time is the time between when an over current event is found and when the next enable
<!-- page 1498 -->

attempt will occur. The “run” time determines how long the PA needs to be enabled before the system OCP determines that everything is ok. These timers also control internal states of the OCP. It is recommended to leave these as default.

The headphones have a specific top-level register, which controls certain aspects of the OCP for headphones. Register `0x1AA` has the current threshold for both left and right PAs. This is the current limit that must be met by either PA before the event is found by the circuitry. It also has state machine enables for the OCP state machine. These need to be enabled for proper OCP functionality. Likewise, the ear PA has bits in register `0x1BC`, bit [2:1], which need to, be enabled for the OCP to function for this PA. For both headphone and ear PAs, the `FSM_LOCK_EN` (`OCP_FSM_LOCK_EN` for ear PA) determines whether the PA will constantly try and re-enable itself or whether it will only try the number of times programmed in the global settings.

Each PA has its own OCP detection enable bits. For headphone left, this is `0x1AF` (`RX_HPH_L_TEST`) bit 0. For headphone right, this is `0x1B5` (`RX_HPH_R_TEST`) bit 0. For ear PA, this is `0x1BC` (`RX_EAR_EN`) bit 2. These can be left at their default value.

Once an overcurrent fault condition is found, the PA with the fault condition goes into a local shutdown mode. This is where the PA will try to re-enable itself a certain number of times before finally giving up or will find that the fault condition no longer exists and will continue without issue. If the number of re-attempts times out, the PA shuts down for good and assert an interrupt to the interrupt controller. This, in turn issues a hardware interrupt if the OCP interrupt bits are unmasked. If it is appropriate to renew the PA to try again after a lock event, the `OCP_FSM_EN` bit must be toggled to get the PA functional again. Disabling and re-enabling the PA will not reset the OCP state machine.

As mentioned above, the OCP depends signal current leaving the amplifier. If the load is reduced significantly, this can cause the OCP to trigger. For example, the ear PA nominally supports a load of 32 $\Omega$, but we also support loads down to 8 $\Omega$. However, for the same voltage output, the current increases by 4 fold with the same load change. This can cause unwanted OCP events.

A similar effect can happen on the HPH, though fortunately 16 $\Omega$ is generally the lowest that will nominally be plugged in. A scenario, which could cause issue with the headphone amplifiers, is with a “Y” splitter and two 16 $\Omega$ headsets plugged in. Effectively the loading is 8 $\Omega$ per channel, and this could cause OCP events depending on the setting of the current threshold.

> [!NOTE]
> It’s been noted that the HPH PA `OCP_DET_EN` enable bits cause extra leakage while the PA is not enabled. It is recommended to keep these disabled while the PAs are disabled and only enabling them prior to HPH PA enablement.

### 4.5.8.3.17 Speaker driver overcurrent protection

The speaker driver incorporates Over Current Protection (OCP) in the PA output stage. This circuit monitors the current through each of the four transistors in the output stage independently. It triggers immediately when the current through any of the transistors in the output stage exceed the programmed threshold. When the OCP triggers, it forces the output stage to be in high impedance mode and generates the speaker OCP interrupt.

The speaker driver OCP triggers on the first high current event it detects. Unlike the OCP for the headphone driver, there is no filter since the speaker is hard-wired in the phone and there is no jack to generate spurious OCP events. There is an internal state machine that guarantees that the
<!-- page 1499 -->

interrupt signal is held high for a minimum of two PWM clock cycles when it is generated and held low for a minimum of two PWM clock cycles before the power stage is re-enabled. This prevents glitches on the interrupt signal.

It should be noted that the OCP is not a short circuit detection feature. The PAs will not shut down simply because the outputs are shorted to ground, there must be some signal level accompanying the short circuit event before the OCP will be triggered, thus it really is an over current protection circuit.

The OCP operates independently of the speaker protection circuit. The speaker protection is a precise, low-bandwidth circuit that monitors the impedance of the speaker coil. The OCP is a course circuit that operates quickly. Since the impedance of the power stage is low, it can provide a large amount of current and potentially damage the chip if the OCP circuit does not intervene.

There are two modes of operation for the OCP logic, free-running and one-shot. In free-running mode, the Class D output stage is re-enabled after each OCP event. In this mode, the OCP acts as a current limiter where the Class D output stage is switched on and off to prevent the current from exceeding the limit. This generates audible artifacts.

In one-shot mode, the OCP circuit does not re-enable the Class D output stage after an OCP event. In this mode, the software has to read the interrupt and explicitly re-enable the PA. If the software does not re-enable the PA, the output stage is in the high-impedance mode indefinitely. This behavior is controlled by bit 6 of register `0x1E2`. Setting this bit to 0 puts the OCP circuit in free-running mode and setting it to 1 puts the OCP circuit in one-shot mode.

All of the controls for the speaker driver OCP circuit are in register `0x1E2`. Bit 7 is the enable bit and is on by default. Bit 6 controls whether the OCP circuit is in free-running or one-shot mode (default is free-running). Bits 5-4 control the glitch filter inside the OCP circuit (default is 64 ns). This glitch filter suppresses any transient signals that could generate a spurious OCP event. Bits 3-0 set the current threshold (default is 3.00 A). The limit can be set from 0 A to 5.625 A in steps of 375 mA.

> [!NOTE]
> The default value of `OCP_HOLD` was not set in the correct default configuration, which meant that the PA would continue to try and reconnect to the output, which was causing some potentially high current conditions and possibly burning the chip. The PMIC SBL was supposed to set this by default, but if it is not set while setting up the speaker amplifier, it should be set prior to enabling the device.

### 4.5.8.3.18 Headphone, ear, and speaker click and pop mitigation

The following sections go through each PA type and details the specific needs of each PA type.

#### Headphone PA

As there are no analog gains for HPH amplifiers, gain is statically set in analog to -4.5dB, there is no ability to mitigate the click and pop with any analog gain settings. The circuitry has a click and pop suppression circuit, which tries to minimize click and pop. The enable bit for the HPH amplifiers is all that is needed to minimize the click and pop from the hardware perspective. Of course, following the proper system sequencing is also required.
<!-- page 1500 -->

#### Ear PA

The Ear PA is effectively a new design, but is intending to meet the 1.26 mVpp (A-weighted) level for turn on and turn off. Actual performance pushed the spec to 2 mVpp (A-weighted)

#### Speaker PA

Software should be able to enable and disable the block without violating the 10 mVpp (A-weighted) spec. The enable/disable control is bit 7 (`CLASSD_PA_EN`) of register SPMI1: `0xB2` (`SPKR_DRV_EN`). Write a 1 to enable the driver and a 0 to disable it.

As the speaker PA has only one fixed gain value, the performance of the click and pop is guaranteed by design through only using the enable bit described above.

### Reset functionality

In the Digital codec core, there is a block reset register `AUDIO_CORE_BCR` in GCC, which resets ULT audio and digital codec core.

For Analog codec, since it is housed on the PMIC device, will use the standard reset mechanism provided by PMIC for each peripheral. This is detailed below.

First, there are two peripherals in Analog codec. One is digital and the other is analog. There are effectively four types of resets that come to the digital peripheral and three types that come to the analog peripheral. The extra reset for the digital peripheral is special to the digital; otherwise the three remaining resets are the same for each peripheral.

The three common resets for both peripherals are:

#### Hardware generated resets

#### FOLLOW_GLOBAL_SOFT_RB – another reset bit

#### LOCAL_SOFT_RESET – register bit

The hardware generated resets are out of software control usually. Once each peripheral has been set up to respond to particular reset signals from PMIC, it resets if any of these signals fires. The reaction to PMIC hardware reset signals can be alter by software by writing the register below (offset `0xDA`). There are certain hardware reset signals that cannot be avoided, if this signal set, the peripherals will reset without notice. The following are the configurable values. They will be set appropriately by hardware as defaults.

*   `PERPH_RESET_CTL3` ADDRESS `0x00DA` RW
*   `PERPH_RESET_CTL3` RESET_VALUE `0x0F`
*   `FOLLOW_OTST2_RB` BIT[3]
*   `FOLLOW_WARM_RB` BIT[2]
*   `FOLLOW_SHUTDOWN1_RB` BIT[1]
*   `FOLLOW_SHUTDOWN2_RB` BIT[0]

The `FOLLOW_GLOBAL_SOFT_RB` signal is a bit that can be set in each peripheral that will allow response to a global reset bit in PMIC register space (not in the Analog codec peripherals).




<!-- page 1501 -->

Reaction to this bit is defined in both Analog codec peripherals at offset 0xD9. If set, and if the PMIC bit is also set, the entire peripheral is reset. This will likely have limited use in functional mode.

**PERPH_RESET_CTL2** ADDRESS 0x00D9 RW

**PERPH_RESET_CTL2** RESET_VALUE 0x01

* **FOLLOW_GLOBAL_SOFT_RB** BIT[0]

The LOCAL_SOFT_RESET bit is another peripheral reset bit. Setting this bit resets the entire peripheral back to default. This reset bit is located in both Analog codec peripherals at offset 0xDB.

**PERPH_RESET_CTL4** ADDRESS 0x00DB RW

**PERPH_RESET_CTL4** RESET_VALUE 0x00

* **LOCAL_SOFT_RESET** BIT[0]

The last reset only applies to the Analog codec digital peripheral. It only affects the memory components of Analog codec digital; things like FIR memory. Setting this reset bit does not reset CSR values. This is only at digital peripheral offset 0x46. This reset value

**CDC_RST_CTL** ADDRESS 0x0046 RW

**CDC_RST_CTL** RESET_VALUE 0x00

* **DIG_SW_RST_N** BIT[7]
  * RESET VALUE 0x0
  * REMOVE_RESET VALUE 0x1

##### 4.5.8.3.19 Clock configuration

The SoC supports two possible clock frequencies: 9.6 MHz and 12.288 MHz.

The clock enters into the digital codec core (from the top clock controller block) and then is distributed to the rest of the codec, including via delivering the PDM clock to the Analog codec portion.

There are several top-level clocks to achieve this:

**Digital codec "Top"**
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_MCLK_CTL.MCLK_EN` – MCLK (master clock) enable
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL.PDM_CLK_SEL` – Enable PDM clock feedback
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL.PDM_EN` BIT – Enables the clock to the PDM interface

**Analog codec "Top"**
* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.D_MCLK_EN` – MCLK (from the PDM interface) enable for Analog codec
<!-- page 1502 -->

* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.A_MCLK_EN` – MCLK (again, derived from the PDM interface) for analog
* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.A_MCLK2_EN` – MCLK/2 for analog usage

There are individual clock controls for each of these devices:
* DMICs - `LPASS_CDC_CLK_DMIC_B1_CTL.DMIC0_CLK_EN`
* Interpolators - `LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL.RXn_CLK_EN`
* Decimators - `LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL.TXn_CLK_EN`
* IIRs - `LPASS_CDC_CLK_SD_CTL.IIRn_CLK_EN`

Not only the “top” level clocks need to be enabled for general clock enables, but the sub-branches of each circuit also have clock enables that are distinguished between digital and analog controls.

The digital controls are:
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.RXDn_CLK_EN` – Enable for each of the Rx (DAC) paths
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.TXD_CLK_EN` – Enable for both of the Tx (ADC) paths

The analog controls for analog Rx components are:
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.SPKR_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.BOOST_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.NCP_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.EAR_HPHL_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.EAR_HPHR_CLK_EN`

The analog control for analog Tx components is:
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.TXA_CLK25_EN` – ADC clock enable

Details of sequencing are provided in Section 4.5.8.4
<!-- page 1503 -->

#### Figure 4-243: Codec clock system
*Description:* The diagram illustrates the clock architecture between the APQ8016 SoC and the PM8916 PMIC. 
Within the APQ8016:
- The **Top Level Clock Block** feeds the **Digital CODEC Core**.
- The Digital CODEC Core clock input is gated by an AND gate controlled by `MCLK_EN`.
- Once inside the Digital CODEC Core, the clock goes to a **Clock generation and distribution** block which feeds:
  - Decimator 1 and Decimator 2
  - Interpolator 1, Interpolator 2, and Interpolator 3
  - DMIC Interface
  - IIR
- An **I2S Interface** receives `I2S_SCL Clocks` directly from outside the core.
- The output from the Digital CODEC Core to the PM8916 is gated by an AND gate controlled by `PDM_CLK_EN`.

Within the PM8916:
- A **PMIC 19.2MHz** clock source distributes clocks via:
  - A `÷500` divider to **MBHC Analog HW**.
  - A `÷6` divider to **Boost** (via a multiplexer).
  - A `÷6` divider to **NCP** (via a multiplexer).
- The **Analog CODEC** block receives the gated master clock from the APQ8016 Digital CODEC Core.
- This incoming clock is gated by an AND gate controlled by `D_MCLK_EN`.
- The output of the `D_MCLK_EN` gate is routed to:
  - **PDM Interface**, **4->9 bit FIR**, and **DEM**.
  - A `÷2` divider, which then feeds:
    - **RDAC/PA (EAR, HPHL, HPHR, SPKR)** via individual enables.
    - **TX digital Paths (TX1 & TX2)** via an enable.
    - **RX digital Paths (RX1, RX2, RX3)** via individual enables.
    - **Analog Timers** via an AND gate controlled by `A_MCLK2_EN`.
  - An AND gate controlled by `A_MCLK_EN` which routes directly and also through a `25% / 75% DC; ÷2` duty cycle / divider block to enable **TXFE/ADC (IN1, IN2)**.

##### Boost, MBHC, and NCP clock

The boost, NCP, and MBHC modules have the ability to select the PMIC clock system directly (and internally to the chip). The MBHC module, in fact, can only select the PMIC derived clock. Boost and NCP can select the PMIC clock or the PDM clock for their source. Speaker can also choose between PDM clock and a PMIC clock source, but that clock source is NCP clock.

##### Internal RC oscillator

No internal RC oscillator is available on Analog codec. The MBHC system receives a clock directly from the PMIC device for usage.

##### Interrupts

The Digital codec core does not have any interrupt capabilities.

##### 4.5.8.3.20 Codec control interfaces

###### Control register map

Since part of the codec is in the SoC and part is in the PMIC die, there are two control interfaces, which are needed to control the entire codec system. The SoC portion of the codec is on the AHB bus that is internal to the SoC. There is a single block of address space reserved for codec control on the AHB bus.

For Analog codec, the interface is SPMI. For Analog codec, there are two cores, which are peripheral devices in the PMIC. One core contains the registers for digital hardware controls. The other core contains the analog controls. In some cases, like interrupts, each core has interrupt status/controls within them.

#### Figure 4-244: Analog codec control register map
*Description:* The diagram shows the division of PMIC SPMI address space for the Analog codec controls into two separate cores:
- **Core 0 – digital hardware control (0x00 – 0xFF)**: located at Peripheral Address `0x1F000`.
- **Core 1 – analog hardware control (0x00 – 0xFF)**: located at Peripheral Address `0x1F100`.

The register accesses are 32 bits wide, where only the lower 8 bits are used in the device to maintain backward compatibility. As can be seen in Digital codec control register map, the only core used is “Core 0” (though this is not an official name it is used here for simplicity). Each valid subsequent register is addressed by an addition of 0x4. The addressable space between these steps of 4 (0x0, 0x4, 0x8…,and so on) contains no useful control register information.

#### Figure 4-245: Digital codec control register map
*Description:* The diagram illustrates a single 32-bit register access for the Digital codec on the AHB bus at offset address `0x771C000`. The 32-bit register access is mapped as follows:
- **Bits <7:0>**: Core 0 – digital hardware control (`0x00` – `0x1FC`, in steps of `0x4`), AHB offsetAddress = `0x771C000`.
- **Bits <15:8>**: Core 1 – unused (`0x01` – `0x1FD`, in steps of `0x4`), AHB offsetAddress = `0x771C000`.
- **Bits <23:16>**: Core 2 – unused (`0x02` – `0x1FE`, in steps of `0x4`), AHB offsetAddress = `0x771C000`.
- **Bits <31:24>**: Core 3 – unused (`0x03` – `0x1FF`, in steps of `0x4`), AHB offsetAddress = `0x771C000`.

##### 4.5.8.3.21 I2S

The only option for transporting data to and from the device is through I2S connected to ULT audio. There are effectively two interfaces on the device; one for the Rx data and one for the Tx data. There are two data lines on each interface. The Rx interface can support three discrete channels of information. The Tx can support four channels of discrete information, though since the SoC only has two decimators, the other channels are reserved for echo canceller feedback. Each interface has its own I2S bit clock and word select for that interface. This allows the Rx and Tx interfaces to operate at different sample rates from each other. But individual channels on each interface must be the same sample rate as dictated by the single clock and word select for each interface.

In order for I2S data to flow between the physical interface and the internal PCM buses, the `CONN_CLK_EN` bit in `LPASS_CDC_CLK_OTHR_CTL` (AHB) must be enabled.

#### Figure 4-246: Rx I2S port
*Description:* The diagram shows the Rx I2S routing configuration within the digital codec. Two I2S Rx blocks receive clocks and data:
- `I2S RX 0`: Receives data from `cdc_i2s_rx_sd0`, word select from `cdc_i2s_rx_ws`, and clock from `cdc_i2s_rx_clk`. Outputs Left channel to `RX1 Port` (`Rx1`, 24-bit/23-bit) and Right channel to `RX2 Port` (`Rx2`, 24-bit/23-bit).
- `I2S RX 1`: Receives data from `cdc_i2s_rx_sd1`, and shares the `cdc_i2s_rx_ws` and `cdc_i2s_rx_clk` lines. Outputs Left channel to `RX3 Port` (`Rx3`, 24-bit/23-bit).

#### Figure 4-247: Tx I2S port
*Description:* The diagram shows the Tx I2S routing configuration. Two I2S Tx blocks receive internal signals and output to the external pins:
- `I2S TX 0`: Receives Left channel from `DEC 1` (21-bit) via `TX1 Port`, and Right channel from `DEC 2` (21-bit) via `TX2 Port`. Gated by shared `cdc_i2s_tx_ws` and `cdc_i2s_tx_clk` clocks. Outputs data to `cdc_i2s_tx_sd0`.
- `I2S TX 1`: Receives Left channel from `Rx Mix 1` (21-bit) via `TX3 Port`, and Right channel via `TX4 Port` from a multiplexer selecting between `Rx Mix 2` (21-bit) and `Rx Mix 3` (21-bit). Shares the `cdc_i2s_tx_ws` and `cdc_i2s_tx_clk` clocks. Outputs data to `cdc_i2s_tx_sd1`.

##### 4.5.8.3.22 Concurrent Ear PA + HPH

There are two limitations, which impact concurrent Ear PA and HPH PA usage.

###### Interpolation restriction

First, the interpolator for the Ear PA and HPHL is shared. This can be seen in Interpolation path #1 with Ear PA and HPHL PA below. RDAC #1 and RDAC #2 can both source their signal from the same interpolation path (interpolation path #1).

#### Figure 4-248: Interpolation path #1 with Ear PA and HPHL PA
*Description:* The block diagram details the Rx signal processing chain (Interpolation Path 1) from the Digital CODEC inside the APQ8016 SoC to the Analog CODEC and PA drivers inside the PM8916 PMIC.
1. **APQ8016 (SoC Digital side)**:
   - Inputs `IIR 1` (23-bit), `IIR 2` (23-bit), `Rx1`, `Rx2`, `Rx3` enter a multiplexer/mixer (`Rx Mix 1`).
   - The selected signal (23-bit) goes to a summing block `+` with a `Gain` adjustment (21-bit output, `RX1 PATH`).
   - A second summing block `+` adds the selected sidetone (`IIR 1`/`IIR 2`, 23-bit).
   - The combined signal goes through a **High-Pass Filter (HPF)** (23-bit) -> multiplier `x` (23-bit) -> **Interpolator (INT)** (23-bit) -> **Volume control** (`V_vol`, 23-bit) -> **Rx shaper** (4-bit output, utilizing `SDM1` 2-bit control and `Dither` 4-bit).
   - The 4-bit output is serialized by the **Serializer** and sent as a 1-bit PDM stream (`cdc_pdm_rx0_d1`) to the PMIC via the physical pad `rx1_pdm_d`.

2. **PM8916 (PMIC Analog side)**:
   - The 1-bit PDM stream is received on pad `rx1_pdm_d`.
   - A multiplexer selects between this line and the external test input `pmic_ext_tst_d0`.
   - The signal goes to a **De-serializer** (green block), producing a 4-bit parallel output.
   - The 4-bit output is either sent directly or through a **Demap/LUT** block (which splits it into two 2-bit streams `rx_lh_ch1` and `rx_lh_ch2`) to a multiplexer.
   - The multiplexed 4-bit stream goes through a **FIR** filter (8-bit output) and a **DEM (Dynamic Element Matching)** block.
   - The output of the DEM block splits to feed:
     - **RDAC #1** (producing differential outputs + and -) which drives the class G **Ear Out (CDC_EAR_P / CDC_EAR_M)** or the class AB **HPH left (CDC_HPH_L)** amplifier.
     - **RDAC #2** (after passing through a phase inverter, producing differential outputs + and -) which drives the class AB **HPH right (CDC_HPH_R)** amplifier.
   
This layout shows that both RDACs and the Ear/HPH drivers share this single Interpolation Path #1.

Second, the Ear PA and the HPH PA share common hardware. Given this, EAR and HPH L and R cannot operate at the same time. This enforces that the proper sequencing is done when switching between the two PAs.

##### 4.5.8.3.23 Power supply options

The default power option for Analog codec is as follows:
* **Circuits supplied by 1.85 V (but will transition to 2.15 V when RF is active)**
  * HPH PAs VDD
  * Negative charge pump
* **Circuits supplied by 1.8 V system I/O voltage**
  * All analog circuits except charge pump
  * All digital hardware
  * All I/O pads
* **Circuits supplied by Vbatt**
  * 5 V boost
  * Speaker Driver (unless connected to an external 5 V boost)
  * Ear Speaker (unless speaker driver supply connected to 5-V boost – there is a boost bypass mode that can be used to effectively connect to battery)

#### 4.5.8.4 End-to-end Enable Sequencing

This section is intended to document the sequencing required to bring up and down blocks of the codec system.

##### 4.5.8.4.1 Clock system control

The clock system should be enabled in this order, and as applicable. Meaning, if an ADC path is being used, use the correct portions of the ADC clock system. Likewise for the DAC and DMICs.

**Digital codec "Top"**
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_MCLK_CTL.MCLK_EN`
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL.SEL_PDM_CLK_FB`
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL.PDM_EN`

**Analog codec "TOP"**
* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.D_MCLK_EN`
* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.A_MCLK2_EN`
* `CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL.A_MCLK_EN`

**I2S on Digital codec**
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_OTHR_CTL.CONN_CLK_EN` (also required for Tx connectivity to decimators)

**ADC Path**
* **Digital codec**:
  * `LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL.TX1_CLK_EN` – Decimator 1 enable
  * `LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL.TX2_CLK_EN` – Decimator 2 enable
* **Analog codec**:
  * `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.TXA_CLK25_EN` – ADC clock enable
  * `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.TXD_CLK_EN` – Digital Tx path enable (for either ADC path)

**DAC Path**
* **Digital codec**:
  * `LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL.RX3_CLK_EN` (SPKR)
  * `LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL.RX2_CLK_EN` (HPHR)
  * `LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL.RX1_CLK_EN` (EAR and HPHL and optionally HPHR)
<!-- page 1509 -->

* **Analog codec**:
  * `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.RXD3_CLK_EN` (SPKR)
  * `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.RXD2_CLK_EN` (HPHR)
  * `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.RXD1_CLK_EN` (EAR and HPHL and optionally HPHR)

**Clocks for specific PAs, denoted**
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.SPKR_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.BOOST_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL.NCP_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.EAR_HPHL_CLK_EN`
* `CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL.EAR_HPHR_CLK_EN`

**DMIC (Digital codec Only)**
* `LPASS_CDC_CLK_DMIC_B1_CTL.DMIC0_CLK_EN`

Some of this clock information needs integration into the sequences below.

##### Top-level codec blocks

###### Codec local bandgap enable

While the actual PM8916 bandgap resides in PMIC hardware, there is a local enable for the bandgap distribution in the Analog codec portion of the device.

**MASTER_BIAS_CTL** ADDRESS 0x0046 RW

**MASTER_BIAS_CTL** RESET_VALUE 0x00

* **MASTER_BIAS_EN** BIT[5]
  * DISABLE VALUE 0x0
  * ENABLE VALUE 0x1
* **V2I_BUFFER_EN** BIT[4]
  * DISABLE VALUE 0x0
  * ENABLE VALUE 0x1

##### 4.5.8.4.2 Rx path

There are sequences shown below for usage of state machines.
<!-- page 1510 -->

##### 4.5.8.4.3 General prerequisites

###### Rx master bias

For all DAC/PA devices in the Rx path, the Rx master bias must be enabled. This is done by:
1. Write a 1 to bit 7 of register SPMI1: 0x93 (`RX_COM_BIAS`)
   a. This asserts `RX_BIAS_EN`

When no DAC/PA devices in the Rx paths are needed:
1. Write a 0 to bit 7 of register SPMI1: 0x93 (`RX_COM_BIAS`) – Default
   a. This de-asserts `RX_BIAS_EN`

###### Negative charge pump for HPH

**Prerequisites**
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* PDM clk is enabled or PMIC clock source
  * The NCP clock can be sourced from either PDM clock or PMIC clock system, choose which is applicable.
* `A_MCLK2` is enabled
* Ensure that `NCP_EN.NCP_BYPASS` is set to b’0 (`NO_BYPASS_NCP` VALUE) for headphone mode (this is also covered in the HPH enable sequence)

###### Case 1: Standard bringup for HPH or EAR path

**Sequence:**
1. Enable the CP clock in Analog codec
   a. Write a 1 to bit 6 in register SPMI0: 0x4A (`CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL`)
2. Enable the NCP analog hardware
   a. Write a 1 to bit 0 in register SPMI1: 0x80 (`NCP_EN`)
3. Wait 100 μs before enabling HPH PA

###### Case 5: Standard shutdown

**Sequence:**
1. Disable the NCP analog hardware
   a. Write a 0 to bit 0 in register SPMI1: 0x80 (`NCP_EN`)
2. Disable the CP clock in Analog codec
   a. Write a 0 to bit 6 in register SPMI0: 0x4A (`CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL`)


<!-- page 1511 -->
#### 4.5.8.4.4 Earpiece

##### Prerequisites
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* Rx digital gain = mute

##### Case 1: Start up with state machine

###### Sequence
1. Enable Ear/HPH PA clock
   a. Set bits 0 and 1 to 1 of register SPMI0; 0x49 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL)
2. Write a 1 to bit 7 of SPMI1: 0x9E (PA_SEL)
   a. This selects the EAR PA operation mode
3. Write bit 4 to 1 of SPMI1: 0x80 (NCP_EN)
   a. This selects the correct ground (BYPASS_NCP_GND) for the EAR PA
4. Write a 1 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9B (RX_HPH_L_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Enables the HPHL DAC, needed for EARPA operation
5. Write a 1 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9D (RX_HPH_R_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Enables the HPHR DAC, needed for EARPA operation
6. Write bit 6 to 1 of SPMI1: 0x9E (RX_EAR_CTL)
   a. This enables the PA
7. Wait for interrupt
8. Disable Rx digital mute

##### Case 2: Disable Ear PA
1. Mute Rx digital gain
2. Disable Ear PA (in reverse order of sequences shown above)
   a. Write bit 6 to 0 of SPMI1: 0x9E (RX_EAR_CTL)
3. Wait for interrupt
4. Write a 0 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9B (RX_HPH_L_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Disables the HPHL DAC, needed for EARPA operation
5. Write a 0 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9D (RX_HPH_R_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Disables the HPHR DAC, needed for EARPA operation
6. Disable Ear PA clock
   a. Clear bits 0 and 1 of register SPMI0: 0x49 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL)
7. Disable remaining blocks
<!-- page 1512 -->
#### 4.5.8.4.5 Headphone

##### Prerequisites
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* The clock system is active
* The Rx master bias is enabled
* Charge Pump is active (or follow sequence in Case 1, which shows included NCP enable point)
* Rx digital gains = mute

##### Case 1: Start up with state machine

###### Sequence
1. Write a 0 to bit 7 of SPMI1: 0x9E (PA_SEL)
   a. This selects the HPH PA operation mode
2. Enable HPH PA clock
   a. Set bit 0 of register SPMI0: 0x049 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL) for HPHL
   b. Set bit 1 of register SPMI0: 0x049 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL) for HPHR
3. Set bit 1 of register SPMI1: 0x93 (RX_COM_BIAS_DAC)
   a. Enable the DAC reference
4. Set bit 2 of registers SPMI1: 0x9B and SPMI1:0x9D (RX_HPH_L_PA_DAC_CTL and RX_HPH_R_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Puts the DACs for HPHL and HPHR into reset
5. Enable signal source DAC
   a. Write a 1 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9B (RX_HPH_L_PA_DAC_CTL) for HPHL
   b. Write a 1 to bit 3 of SPMI1: 0x9D (RX_HPH_R_PA_DAC_CTL) for HPHR
6. Set bit 2 of registers SPMI1: 0x9B and SPMI1:0x9D (RX_HPH_L_PA_DAC_CTL and RX_HPH_R_PA_DAC_CTL)
   a. Removes the resets for HPHL and HPHR DACs
7. Write bit 4 to 0 of SPMI1: 0x80 (NCP_EN)
   a. This selects the correct ground (NO_BYPASS_NCP) for the HPH PA
8. Enable NCP per NCP sequence
9. Enable HPH PA
   a. Left HPH: write register SPMI1: 0x97 (RX_HPH_CNP_EN) bit 5
   b. Right HPH: write register SPMI1: 0x97 (RX_HPH_CNP_EN) bit 4
10. Wait for interrupt
11. Disable Rx digital mute
<!-- page 1513 -->
##### Case 2: Shutdown
1. Mute Rx digital gain
2. Disable HPH PA (in reverse order of sequences shown above) except for:
   a. Set and clear of DACs not needed
   b. Bypass for NCP (step 7) does not need altering
   c. PA_SEL does not need to be reconfigured
3. Wait for interrupt
4. Disable HPH PA clock
   a. Clear bit 0 of register SPMI0: 0x049 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL) for HPHL
   b. Clear bit 1 of register SPMI0: 0x049 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL) for HPHR
5. Disable remaining blocks

#### 4.5.8.4.6 Boost
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* Class D amplifier is disabled on start-up and shutdown
* No other excess loading is enabled on the boost output
* The clock system is active

> [!NOTE]
> Be ensured that bit 7 is set to 1 before enabling any boost functionality.

##### BOOST_CURRENT_LIMIT (ADDRESS 0x00C0, RW)
* RESET_VALUE: 0x02
* MAX_CURR_LIM_DISABLE: BIT[7]
  * DISABLE VALUE: 0x0
  * ENABLE VALUE: 0x1

##### Case 1: Enable

###### Sequence
1. Enable the boost clock
   a. Write a 1 to bit 5 of SPMI0: 0x4A (CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL)
      i. Enable clock from PMIC (if used)
2. Enable boost
   a. Set bit 7 of register SPMI1: 0xC3 (BOOST_EN_CTL)
3. Wait 500us before enabling any loading on boost
4. Write a 3 to bits 2:0 of SPMI1: 0xC0 (BOOST_CURRENT_LIMIT)
<!-- page 1514 -->
5. Program the appropriate output voltage
   a. Write proper value into SPMI1: 0xC1 (BOOST_OUTPUT_VOLTAGE)

##### Case 2: Disable

###### Sequence
1. Disable boost
   a. Clear bit 7 of register SPMI1: 0xC3 (BOOST_EN_CTL)
2. Disable the boost clock
   a. Write a 0 to bit 5 of SPMI0: 0x4A (CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL)
      i. Disable clock from PMIC (if used)

##### Case 3: "Enable" boost in bypass mode

###### Sequence
1. Set the PFET to be forced on
   a. Write a 1 to bits 6 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
2. Set the boost bypass registers
   a. Write a 1 to bits 7 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
3. Set the NFET to be controlled by register
   a. Write a 1 to bits 2 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
4. Enable boost
   a. Set bit 7 of register SPMI1: 0xC3 (BOOST_EN_CTL)

##### Case 4: "Disable" boost in bypass mode

###### Sequence
1. Set the boost bypass registers
   a. Write a 0 to bits 7 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
2. Set the NFET to be controlled by internal hardware
   a. Write a 0 to bits 2 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
3. Disable the boost bypass registers
   a. Write a 0 to bits 7 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
4. Set the PFET to be forced off
   a. Write a 0 to bits 6 and 1 of SPMI1: 0xC2 (BOOST_BYPASS_MODE)
<!-- page 1515 -->
#### 4.5.8.4.7 Speaker

##### Prerequisites
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* The Rx master bias is enabled
* The Clock Block is active
* Interpolation path is enabled
* VDD_SPKDRV or boost is up
* Rx digital gain = mute

##### Case 1: Start up Speaker PA

###### Sequence
1. Enable Speaker PA clock
   a. Set bit 4 of register SPMI0: 0x49 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL)
2. Turn on Vbatt LDO
   a. Set bit 0 of SPMI1: 0x9E (RX_EAR_EN) to 1
3. Wait 20us
4. Set bit 7 of SPMI1: 0xB5 (SPKR_PWRSTG_CTL) to 1
5. Set bit 2 of SPMI1: 0xB5 (SPKR_PWRSTG_CTL) to 1
6. Set bit 1 of SPMI1: 0xB5 (SPKR_PWRSTG_CTL) to 1
7. Set bit 2 of SPMI1: 0xB2 (SPKR_DRV_CTL) to 1
8. Enable the PA
   a. Set bit 7 (CLASSD_PA_EN) of register SPMI1: 0xB2 (SPKR_DRV_EN) to 1
9. Delay 400us
10. Disable Rx digital mute and start digital stream

##### Case 2: Shut down Speaker PA

###### Sequence
1. Mute Rx digital gain
2. Disable the PA
   a. Set bit 7 (CLASSD_PA_EN) of register SPMI1: 0xB2 (SPKR_DRV_EN) to 0
3. Disable Line PA clock
   a. Clear bit 4 of register SPMI0: 0x49 (CDC_ANA_CLK_CTL)
4. Shut off VDD_SPKDRV supply if applicable (that is, when using a 5V boost)
5. Disable remaining blocks
<!-- page 1516 -->
#### 4.5.8.4.8 Digital Rx

##### Case 1: Enable Rx Interpolators
1. Enable MCLK to digital block
   a. Write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_MCLK_CTL
      i. Do not disable this bit hereafter
2. Enable PDM clock
   a. Write 0x01 (set bit 0) of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL
3. Enable Analog codec Clocks
   a. Write 0x0E to register SPMI0: 0x048 (CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL)
4. Mute the Digital Rx gain
5. For interpolation paths, configure all appropriate elements of the interpolator then enable the block by turning on the clock to the interpolator
   a. RX1: write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL
   b. RX2: write 0x02 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL
   c. RX3: write 0x04 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_B1_CTL
6. Enable appropriate Rx path on Helicon die
   a. RX1: write 0x01 to register SPMI0: CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL
   b. RX2: write 0x02 to register SPMI0: CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL
   c. RX3: write 0x04 to register SPMI0: CDC_DIG_CLK_CTL
7. Once the analog section is correctly configured, unmute the digital Rx

##### Case 2: Disable Rx Interpolators
1. Mute the Digital Rx gain
   a. Turn off active PAs in the signal path
   b. Turn off the clock to the interpolators
   c. Toggle reset to the interpolator block, this allows proper restart of the interpolator block if re-enabled
      i. RX1: write 0x01 -> 0x00 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_RESET_CTL
      ii. RX2: write 0x02 -> 0x00 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_RESET_CTL
      iii. RX3: write 0x04 -> 0x00 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_RX_RESET_CTL
2. Disable PDM clock (if applicable)
   a. Clear bit 0 of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL
3. Disable Analog codec Clocks
   a. Write 0x00 to register SPMI0: 0x4A (CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL)
<!-- page 1517 -->
#### 4.5.8.4.9 Tx path

##### Analog input

##### Prerequisites
* The codec BG distribution is enabled
* The Clock Block is active
* Tx digital gain = mute

##### Case 1: Start up

###### Sequence
1. Configure the mode and gain of the path
   a. Gain
2. Set "initialization" bit for TxFE
   a. TXFE1: Write a 1 to bit 5 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
   b. TXFE2: Write a 1 to bit 4 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
   c. TXFE3: Write a 1 to bit 4 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
      i. Since TXFE3 is essentially a mirror to TXFE2, this is the only control where "TXFE3" requires a "TXFE2" register config
3. Enable the channel
   a. TXFE1: Write 0x80 (set bit 7) of register SPMI1: 0x60 (TX_1_EN)
   b. TXFE2: Write 0x80 (set bit 7) of register SPMI1: 0x61 (TX_2_EN)
   c. TXFE3: Write 0x80 (set bit 7) of register SPMI1: 0x68 (TX_3_EN)
4. Wait 1 ms
5. Clear "initialization" bit for TxFE
   a. TXFE1: Write a 0 to bit 5 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
   b. TXFE2: Write a 0 to bit 4 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
   c. TXFE3: Write a 0 to bit 4 of register SPMI1: 0x63 (TX_1_2_TEST_CTL_2)
      i. Since TXFE3 is essentially a mirror to TXFE2, this is the only control where "TXFE3" requires a "TXFE2" register config
6. Wait 1 ms
7. Enable high pass filter in digital hardware
8. Disable Tx digital mute
<!-- page 1518 -->
##### Case 2: Shutdown
1. Mute Tx digital gain
2. Disable all Tx blocks

##### Digital Microphone input

##### Prerequisites
* The Central BG is active in audio mode
* The Clock Block is active
* Tx digital gain = mute

##### Case 1: Start up
1. Enable MCLK to digital block
   a. Write 0x01 to AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_MCLK_CTL
      i. Do not disable this bit hereafter
2. Select the DMIC signal input for the appropriate decimation stage
   a. DEC1: Write bits <3:0> of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CONN_TX_B1_CTL
   b. DEC2: Write bits <7:4> of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CONN_TX_B1_CTL
3. Set up the decimator path for DMIC input
   a. Write 0x01 to bit <0> of LPASS_CDC_TXn_MUX_CTL
4. Set the clock frequency for the digital microphone. The clock frequency equals the MCLK divided by the DIV# selection (where # is 2, 3, 4, 6 or 16). For instance, when MCLK is 9.6 MHz, selecting DIV4 sets the digital mic clock to 2.4 MHz.
   a. DMIC1 and DMIC2:
      i. Choose an appropriate DIV by writing to bits <3:1> of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_TXn_DMIC_CTL. Be ensured that the decimators also selects the appropriate (that is, matching) Clock Mode as the digital microphone source
5. Enable the digital mic clock
   a. DMIC1 and DMIC2:
      i. Set bit 0 (DMIC0_CLK_EN) of register LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL to 1

##### Case 2: Shutdown
1. Mute Tx digital gain
2. Disable all Tx blocks
<!-- page 1519 -->
#### Digital Tx

##### Case 1: Enable Tx decimators
1. Enable MCLK to digital block
   a. Write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_MCLK_CTL
      i. Do not disable this bit hereafter
2. Enable PDM clock
   a. Write 0x01 (set bit 0) of register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_PDM_CTL
3. Enable Analog codec Clocks
   a. Write 0x0F to register SPMI0: 0x048 (CDC_TOP_CLK_CTL)
4. Mute the Digital Tx gain
5. For decimation paths, configure all appropriate elements of the decimator then enable the block by turning on the clock to the decimator
   a. TX1: write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL
   b. TX2: write 0x02 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL
6. Enable Tx paths on Helicon
   a. TX1: write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL
   b. TX1: write 0x01 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_CLK_EN_B1_CTL [sic]
7. Once the analog section is correctly configured, unmute the digital Tx

##### Case 2: Disable Tx decimators
1. Mute the Digital Tx gain
   a. Turn off the clock to the decimators
   b. Toggle reset to the decimator block, this allows proper restart of the decimator block if re-enabled
   c. TX1: write 0x01 -> 0x00 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_RESET_B1_CTL
   d. TX2: write 0x02 -> 0x00 to register AHB: LPASS_CDC_CLK_TX_RESET_B1_CTL

#### 4.5.8.4.10 Microphone bias output

##### Microphone Bias

##### Prerequisites
* Master Bias enabled
<!-- page 1520 -->
##### Case 1: Microphone bias power-up for audio processing
1. Select the microphone bias capacitor mode for particular hardware
   a. Microphone bias buffer 1: set bit 6 for installed no bypass capacitor; clear for bypass capacitor in register 0x12B (MICB_1_EN)
2. Program the microphone bias output voltage
   a. Configure bits <7:3> in register SPMI1: 0x41 (MICB_CFILT_1_VAL - MICB_1_VAL)
3. Enable microphone bias (common microphone bias module is the logical or of these two signals)
   a. Microphone bias 1: set bit 7 in register SPMI1: 0x40 (MICB_1_EN)
   b. Microphone bias 2: set bit 7 in register SPMI1: 0x44 (MICB_2_EN)

##### Case 2: Microphone bias power-down
1. Disable appropriate microphone bias buffers
   a. Microphone bias 1: clear bit 7 in register SPMI1: 0x40 (MICB_1_EN)
   b. Microphone bias 2: clear bit 7 in register SPMI1: 0x44 (MICB_2_EN)

### 4.5.9.3 ULT Audio register definitions

#### 4.5.9.3.1 0x00000000 ULTAUDIO_HW_VERSION

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** LCC_CORE_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x10000000
* **Description:** This register indicates the hardware version.

##### ULTAUDIO_HW_VERSION Fields
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR | Not backward compatible |
| 27:16 | MINOR | Expanded functionality. Backward compatible for existing features. |
| 15:0 | STEP | Changes in hardware that does not impact software compatibility |

#### 4.5.9.3.2 0x00000158 LPASS_AHBIX_EN

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** LCC_CORE_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000012
* **Description:** This register controls the masking of bus interrupts.
<!-- page 1527 -->

##### LPASS_AHBIX_EN Fields
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7 | Q6TCM_WRITE_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable Q6TCM_WRITE_ERROR interrupt. |
| 6 | Q6TCM_READ_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable Q6TCM_READ_ERROR interrupt. |
| 5 | AHBX_DECODE_BOUNDARY_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable AHBX_DECODE_BOUNDARY_ERROR interrupt. |
| 4 | AHBX_DECODE_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable AHBX_DECODE_ERROR interrupt. |
| 3 | AHBX_MISALIGNED_INT_EN | Enable AHBX_MISALIGNED interrupt. |
| 2 | AHBI_DECODE_BOUNDARY_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable AHBI_DECODE_BOUNDARY_ERROR interrupt. |
| 1 | AHBI_DECODE_ERROR_INT_EN | Enable AHBI_DECODE_ERROR interrupt. |
| 0 | AHBI_MISALIGNED_INT_EN | Enable AHBI_MISALIGNED interrupt. |

#### 4.5.9.3.3 0x00000188 LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_STATUS

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** LCC_CORE_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Description:** This register provides the status of invalid lpass csr address.

##### LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_STATUS Fields
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | LPASS_CSR_RIF_ADDR_INVALID | Invalid address is the one, which there is no register address corresponding to it. |

#### 4.5.9.3.4 0x0000018C LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_ACK

* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** LCC_CORE_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Description:** This write-only register is used to clear the status bits set in LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_STATUS.
<!-- page 1528 -->

##### LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_ACK Fields
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | LPASS_CSR_RIF_ADDR_INVALID | Acknowledge of lpass csr address invalid address |

#### 4.5.9.3.5 0x00000190 LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_EN

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** LCC_CORE_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Description:** This register controls the masking of CSR address invalid interrupt.

##### LPASS_LPASS_CSR_ADDR_VALID_EN Fields
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | LPASS_CSR_RIF_ADDR_INVALID_INT_EN | Enable or disable of the interrupt |

* **Type:** RW

### 4.5.9.5 AVSync register definitions

#### 4.5.9.5.1 LPASS_AUD_SYNC_CTL (0x00007000)

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: lcc_avs_xclk
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000

Control register
<!-- page 1559 -->
LPASS_AUD_SYNC_CTL (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | VFR_INT_SEL | Selects either the external device interrupt or the internal DSP interrupt.<br>0x0: INTERNAL<br>0x1: EXTERNAL |
| 13 | FM_PH_ADJ_NEG_WE | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit decrements sample counter by 1 |
| 12 | FM_PH_ADJ_POS_WE | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit increments sample counter by 1 |
| 11 | FM_XO_DIV_EN | Enables XO divider<br>0x1: ENABLE |
| 10 | FM_PH_TRK_EN | FM Phase Tracker Enable<br>0x1: ENABLE |
| 9 | FM_XO_DIV_RESET | FM XO divider Reset<br>0x1: RESET |
| 8 | FM_PH_TRK_RESET | Resets FM Phase Tracker.<br>0x1: RESET |
| 7 | BT_PH_ADJ_NEG_WE2 | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit decrements sample counter by 1 for DPLL 2 |
| 6 | BT_PH_ADJ_POS_WE2 | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit increments sample counter by 1 for DPLL 2. |
| 5 | BT_PH_ADJ_NEG_WE1 | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit decrements sample counter by 1 for DPLL 1 |
| 4 | BT_PH_ADJ_POS_WE1 | In software tracking method, writing 1 to this bit increments sample counter by 1 for DPLL 1 |
| 3 | BT_XO_DIV_EN | Enables XO divider<br>0x1: ENABLE |
| 2 | BT_PH_TRK_EN | Enables Bluetooth SCO Tx Phase Tracker.<br>0x1: ENABLE |
<!-- page 1560 -->
LPASS_AUD_SYNC_CTL (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | BT_XO_DIV_RESET | Resets Bluetooth SCO Tx divider<br>0x1: RESET |
| 0 | BT_PH_TRK_RESET | Bluetooth SCO Tx Phase Tracker Reset<br>0x1: RESET |

| 2 | BT_COUNT_OVF_XO2 | Bluetooth SCO Tx overflow status for sample counter 2 |
| 1 | BT_COUNT_OVF_REF1 | Bluetooth SCO Tx overflow status for reference counter 1 |
| 0 | BT_COUNT_OVF_XO1 | Bluetooth SCO Tx overflow status for sample counter 1 |

This is necessary only when multiple masters are connected to the same data line. When clear, the PCM block drives the data signal always and must be the only master. |
<!-- page 1570 -->
##### LPASS_LPAIF_PCM_CTLa (continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 17:15 | RATE | Software: RW, hardware: R<br>These bits define the number of bits clocks per PCM frame for long and short frame sync formats. This allows to support PCM rates other than 2.048 MHz (PCM Mode) and 128 kHz (AUX PCM mode). These bits MUST ALWAYS be set regardless of whether the SYNC_SRC is set for EXTERNAL or INTERNAL. The number of slots available per frame is the number of bits per frame divided by the number of bits per slot (TPCM_WIDTH and RPCM WIDTH). The number of bits per frame is common between the transmit and receive data but the slot width and slot selection are independent. Assuming a appropriate frame rate of 8 kHz:<br>0x0: ENUM_8 (8 (64 kHz))<br>0x1: ENUM_16 (16 (128 kHz, AUX PCM mode))<br>0x2: ENUM_32 (32 (256 kHz))<br>0x3: ENUM_64 (64 (512 kHz))<br>0x4: ENUM_128 (128 (1024 kHz))<br>0x5: ENUM_256 (256 (2048 kHz, PCM mode, default value)) |
| 14 | LOOPBACK | Software: RW, hardware: R<br>When set, the PCM DOUT is looped back to PCM DIN internally. |
| 13 | SYNC_SRC | Software: RW, hardware: R<br>When set, the PCM block generates a sync signal to drive off chip and for internal use. When cleared, the PCM block uses an external sync. The type of sync generated or expected is selected by AUX_MODE.<br>0x0: EXTERNAL (EXTERNAL)<br>0x1: INTERNAL (INTERNAL) |
| 12 | AUX_MODE | Software: RW, hardware: R<br>Selects between PCM (short sync) and Aux PCM (long sync) modes. In short sync mode, the sync pulse is one clock period wide and comes before the MSB of the first slot. In long sync mode, the sync pulse has a 50-% duty cycle and its rising edge is coincident with the MSB of the first slot:<br>0x0: PCM (PCM)<br>0x1: AUX (AUX) |


<!-- page 1571 -->

| Bits | Field | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 11 | RPCM_WIDTH | **Software: RW, hardware: R**<br>Selects between 8 bit and 16 bit samples in the incoming stream:<br>0x0: ENUM_8_BIT (8_bit)<br>0x1: ENUM_16_BIT (16_bit) |
| 10 | TPCM_WIDTH | **Software: RW, hardware: R**<br>Selects between 8 bit and 16 bit samples in the outgoing stream:<br>0x0: ENUM_8_BIT (8_bit)<br>0x1: ENUM_16_BIT (16_bit) |
| 9:5 | RPCM_SLOT | **Software: RW, hardware: R**<br>Specifies the incoming slot #0 to use in the PCM stream.<br>The number of slots available per frame is the number of bits per frame divided by the number of bits per slot (TPCM_WIDTH and RPCM WIDTH). The number of bits per frame is common between the transmit and receive data but the slot width and slot selection are independent.<br>00000 = (slot0, first slot)<br>00001 = (slot1, second slot)<br>...<br>11111 = (slot31, 32nd slot) |
| 4:0 | TPCM_SLOT | **Software: RW, hardware: R**<br>Specifies the outgoing slot #0 to use in the PCM stream.<br>The number of slots available per frame is the number of bits per frame divided by the number of bits per slot (TPCM_WIDTH and RPCM WIDTH). The number of bits per frame is common between the transmit and receive data but the slot width and slot selection are independent.<br>00000 = (slot0, first slot)<br>00001 = (slot1, second slot)<br>...<br>11111 = (slot31, 32nd slot) |

Interrupt status. A bit set in this status register indicates that the interrupt event occurred AND it is enabled in LPASS_LPAIF_IRQ_ENa for this interrupt output. Typical interrupt handling operation would read this register, note the interrupt sources, and write the value read back to the LPASS_LPAIF_IRQ_CLRa register to clear the interrupts.

Interrupt status. The definitions of the fields are as follows:

* **ERR_CHX** = When set, a bus error (AHB) occurred on channel X and is enabled.
* **OVR_CHX** = When set, an overrun occurred on channel X and is enabled. (Applicable to write DMA channels 0-3)
* **UNDR_CHX** = When set, an underrun occurred on channel X and is enabled. (Applicable to read DMA channels 0-4)
* **PER_CHX** = When set, channel X reached the period count and is enabled.

Raw status of the interrupt sources. A bit set in this status register indicates that the interrupt event occurred whether it was enabled or not. This register can be used for polling operations or debug. The raw status is cleared when a '1' is written to the corresponding bit in the LPASS_LPAIF_IRQ_CLEARa register.
