## 6.1.4 QUP functional description
Figure 6-25 shows a high-level functional overview of QUP.

#### Figure 6-25: QUP functional block diagram
*Description:* A functional block diagram showing the integration of the QUP (Qualcomm Universal Peripheral) and UART modules within the BLSP (BAM Low-Speed Peripheral) subsystem:
- **Peripheral and system configuration NoC** connects via the **Configuration AHB bus** to the QUP[1-6] and UART[1-2] modules.
- **Secure BAM-lite** is connected to QUP and UART modules using the **BASI** (BAM Aware Slave Interface) and **eDML** interfaces.
- The **QGIC** (Qualcomm Generic Interrupt Controller) handles interrupts from the subsystems.
- The **TLMM** (Top-Level Mode Multiplexer) handles physical pin multiplexing (GPIOs).

Figure 6-26 shows the internal architecture blocks along with the data flow and relevant components.
- The transmitted data is written to the output FIFO using the AMBA high-performance bus (AHB) interface, and the received data is read from the input FIFO.
- The protocol-specific features are controlled by the QUP control status registers (CSR), control data flows, and protocol-specific CSRs.
- The BAM aware slave interface (BASI) is a set of non-software accessible signals (not applicable in FIFO and block modes) that manage the data flows using the DMA capabilities of BAM.
- QTimer is a System on Chip (SoC) global time reference bus that uses timestamps. The I2C interface uses the global timestamp to tag a transaction on the I2C bus.
<!-- page 1693 -->

#### Figure 6-26: QUP internal architecture diagram
*Description:* A detailed internal architecture block diagram of the QUP subsystem showing data paths, clock distributions, registers, and external interfaces:
- **QUP Subsystem**:
  - Contains **QUP CSR**, **QUP output FIFO**, **QUP input FIFO**, **SPI CSR**, **SPI**, **I2C CSR**, and **I2C** modules.
  - Generates the interrupt signal **QUP_IRQ**.
  - Receives the core clock **CC_QUP_CORE_CLK** and the reset signal **QUP_RESET**.
- **Data Paths**:
  - The **AHB slave bus** writes data into the **QUP output FIFO** via "Data path in" and reads data from the **QUP input FIFO** via "Data path out".
  - **BAM (Bus Access Manager)** connects to the FIFOs through **BASI (BAM Aware Slave Interface)** via **eDML**:
    - **BASI (consumer)** transfers data from the QUP output FIFO.
    - **BASI (producer)** transfers data into the QUP input FIFO.
- **Protocol Controllers & Clocks**:
  - **SPI** is driven by the SPI functional clock **CC_QUP_SPI_CLK** and configured by **SPI CSR**.
  - **I2C** is driven by the I2C functional clock **CC_QUP_I2C_CLK**, takes input from the **QTimer bus** (for timestamping), and is configured by **I2C CSR**.
- **External Interfaces**:
  - Both SPI and I2C modules interface with the external world through **External I/O via SOC muxing**.

### 6.1.4.1 QUP power and clock management
The QUP has a simple power management that is based on clock gating. The power collapse is not supported and there are no memories, and hence the retention is not applicable.

The QUP internal clock gating is disabled by default and must be enabled by configuring the following fields in the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`):
- `APP_CLK_ON_EN`
- `CORE_CLK_ON_EN`
- `FIFO_CLK_GATE_EN`

As the QUP is not large, a considerable portion of its power is dissipated on the pads.

The QUP toggles a clock only when driving the data. The only exception is when the `CLK_ALWAYS_ON` bit of the `QUP_SPI_IO_CONTROL` register (address `0x00000304`) is set to `0x1`, which forces the `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` to always on. Set this bit to `0x0` when in functional mode.
<!-- page 1694 -->

All clocks are assumed to be off during an asynchronous reset. To save power, configure the QUP to transition to a reset state between transfers.

#### 6.1.4.1.1 QUP clocks functional description

##### CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
The `CC_QUP_CORE_CLK` is a high-speed clock accessing QUP registers and FIFOs. The clock can always be scaled, and when not accessing QUP it can be gated by setting the `CORE_CLK_ON_EN` or `FIFO_CLK_GATE_EN` bits of the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`) to `0x1`.

The clock is internally gated when QUP is in reset state and there is no active AHB transfer to it. It is not associated to the `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` or `CC_QUP_I2C_CLK` clocks.

##### CC_QUP_SPI_CLK
The `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` drives the `BLSPx_SPI_CLK` pad. The clock must be configured to the desired SPI operating frequency. By default, the `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` is always running and must not be gated or scaled while the QUP is active.

The clock is internally gated when:
- The `MINI_CORE` bit of the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`) does not enable the SPI feature.
- QUP is not in `RUN_STATE`.
- QUP is not in `PAUSE_STATE`.
- QUP is in `RUN_STATE` and both input and output paths are idle.

Clock gating can be disabled by setting the `APP_CLK_ON_EN` bit of the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`) to `0x0`. This bit should be set to `0x1` in functional mode.
<!-- page 1695 -->

The clock can be actively disabled by:
- (Preferred) Disabling the clock source when particular QUP SPI/I2C interface is not used
- Using a QUP configuration that inherently gates the clock (for example, moving the QUP to `PAUSE_STATE`)

##### CC_QUP_I2C_CLK
The `CC_QUP_I2C_CLK` does not drive the `BLSPx_I2C_SCL_A` pad directly (the pad is driven the same way as any data line).

The clock source is configured to a fixed frequency of 19.2 MHz from the oscillator (TCXO). The clock is nongated and nonscalable outside the QUP while the QUP is active, that is, when an I2C transfer is active or when the I2C is preparing on a transfer.

The clock is internally gated when:
- The `MINI_CORE` bit of the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`) does not enable the I2C feature
- QUP is not in `RUN_STATE`
- QUP is not in `PAUSE_STATE`
- QUP is in `RUN_STATE` and both input and output paths are idle

Clock gating can be disabled (clock is always on) by setting the `APP_CLK_ON_EN` bit of the `QUP_CONFIG` register (address `0x00000000`) to `0x0`. This bit should be set to `0x1` in functional mode.

The clock can be actively disabled by:
- (Preferred) Disabling the clock source when particular QUP SPI/I2C interface is not used
- Using a QUP configuration that inherently gates the clock

#### 6.1.4.1.2 QUP I2C clock dividers
The I2C specification has set limits on the high and low period of the I2C clock pulse. Table 6-17 lists the I2C specification clock limits.

### Table 6-17 QUP I2C clock limits
| Symbol | Parameter | Standard mode Min | Standard mode Max | Fast mode Min | Fast mode Max | Fast mode plus Min | Fast mode plus Max | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| fSCL | SCL clock frequency | 0 | 100 | 0 | 400 | 0 | 1000 | kHz |
| tLOW | Low period of the SCL clock | 4.7 | – | 1.3 | – | 0.5 | – | μs |
| tHIGH | High period of the SCL clock | 4.0 | – | 0.6 | – | 0.26 | – | μs |

To meet these limits, the `HIGH_TIME_DIVIDER_VALUE` and `FS_DIVIDER_VALUE` bits of the `QUP_I2C_MASTER_CLK_CTL` register (address `0x00000400`) can be programmed for setting the I2C clock dividers.
<!-- page 1696 -->

Table 6-18 lists the I2C default divider values.

### Table 6-18 QUP I2C default divider values
| Output clock frequency | FS divider | High-time divider |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| 100 kHz | 124 | 62 |
| 400 kHz | 28 | 14 |
| 1 MHz | 8 | 5 |

The FS divider value is responsible for the low period (tLOW). Reducing the HS value by 1 shortens tLOW by 52 ns (assuming the source clock is TCXO 19.2 MHz).

The SCL period is calculated as:
$$T = \text{TCXO} \times ((\text{FS\_DIV} + \text{HT\_DIV}) + 6 + \text{NR}) + T_{\text{rise}}$$

where:
- $\text{TCXO}$ is 52 ns.
- $\text{NR}$ is the noise rejection level.
- $T_{\text{rise}}$ is the SCL rise time.

Since $T_{\text{rise}} > 0$, the actual output clock frequency ($1/T$) will be slightly less than the target value (e.g. 400 kHz).

### 6.1.4.2 QUP reset options
The QUP supports two reset options: hardware and software. Hardware and software resets transition the QUP into the power-on reset (POR) state. All the previous software settings are erased.

The hardware reset `QUP_RESET` is an asynchronous reset per clock domain and is asserted from the RPM, and is used for power-on reset. The software reset is triggered by setting the `QUP_SW_RESET` register (address `0x0000000C`).

> [!NOTE]
> A software reset is usually not recommended for use with a normal operation sequence.

When the `QUP_SW_RESET` register (address `0x0000000C`) is set during a BAM transfer, the BAM continues sending data to the QUP. However, this data is not consumed by the output FIFO.

> [!NOTE]
> To avoid unexpected results, use the `QUP_SW_RESET` register (address `0x0000000C`) with a BAM pipe reset of dedicated pipes.

### 6.1.4.3 QUP operational states
The QUP operates according to the value in the `STATE` bit field of the `QUP_STATE` register (address `0x00000004`).

On the transition from `RESET_STATE` to `RUN_STATE`, the `QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT` (where `*` = `INPUT`/`OUTPUT`/`READ`/`WRITE`) counters associated with each register are initialized with the `QUP_MX_*_COUNT` (where `*` = `INPUT`/`OUTPUT`/`READ`/`WRITE`) values.
<!-- page 1697 -->

If a register is not initialized during `RESET_STATE`, it is set from the last `RESET_STATE` or `RUN_STATE` setting. The registers to reconfigure per run state are:
- `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` (address `0x00000100`)
- `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` (address `0x00000150`)
- `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` (address `0x00000200`)
- `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` (address `0x00000208`)
- `QUP_CONFIG` (address `0x00000000`) (`NO_INPUT` and `NO_OUTPUT` bits)

#### 6.1.4.3.1 RESET_STATE
Indicated by `QUP_STATE` [STATE] = `0x0` (address `0x00000004`). `RESET_STATE` is the default state after the QUP reset occurs (software or hardware). The SPI/I2C interfaces, FIFOs, and counters are held in reset. This is the only state used for software configuration of FIFO and the SPI/I2C interfaces.

Writing data to FIFO in `RESET_STATE` is not allowed. Any remaining data in the input and output FIFO is discarded when reset is configured. For example, the I2C mode releases SCL and SDA lines and creates an invalid condition on the I2C bus.

Hardware prevents moving from `RESET_STATE` to `RUN_STATE` if the register value is incorrect:
- I2C mode: in the `QUP_IO_MODES` register (address `0x00000008`), only $N = 7$ (tag version 2) or $N = 15$ (tag version 1) is valid. If $N$ is set to an invalid value, the QUP stays in `RESET_STATE`.
- SPI mode: the QUP does not transition to `RUN_STATE` if $N$ is configured less than 3.

The state should not be confused with a hardware or software reset. The `RESET_STATE` setting preserves previous software register programming, sets the internal counters to zero, and sets the internal state machine to idle. The `RESET_STATE` setting is an operational reset.

#### 6.1.4.3.2 RUN_STATE
Indicated by `QUP_STATE` [STATE] = `0x1` (address `0x00000004`). `RUN_STATE` is when SPI/I2C is brought out of reset and protocol-related activity is initiated based on the register settings during reset.

#### 6.1.4.3.3 PAUSE_STATE
Indicated by `QUP_STATE` [STATE] = `0x3` (address `0x00000004`). `PAUSE_STATE` is when SPI/I2C stops the bus activity based on:
- **I2C write operation**: SCL line is held low after ACK or NACK from the slave.
- **I2C read operation**: SCL line is held low after receiving the whole byte and before transmitting the ACK or NACK to the slave.
- **SPI operation**: Stops after transmitting or receiving $N$ bits on the bus ($N$ is configuration-dependent).

The SPI/I2C stops fetching new data from the output FIFO, sending new data to the input FIFO, and initiating new transfers.
<!-- page 1698 -->

### 6.1.4.4 QUP interrupts
The QUP is a single interrupt-based controller. The `QUP_IRQ` interrupt remains asserted as long as an error, an input service request, or an output service request is outstanding (unless it is masked).

The following status registers determine the nature of the interrupt:
- `QUP_OPERATIONAL` (address `0x00000018`) for input and output servicing
- `QUP_ERROR_FLAGS` (address `0x0000001C`) for FIFO-related errors
- `SPI_ERROR_FLAGS` or `I2C_MASTER_STATUS` for protocol-specific errors, depending on the enabled mode.

When the `QUP_IRQ` interrupt is asserted by a FIFO-related input and output service request, the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit and `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit of the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) is set.

A read of the other `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register status bits determines the nature of the interrupt. To deassert the interrupt, set the relevant service flag to `0x1` to clear it.

Table 6-19 and Table 6-20 provide details on the input and output service triggered interrupts for the different operating modes. For configuring the different operational modes, see Section 6.1.4.8.4.
<!-- page 1699 -->

### Table 6-19 QUP output service triggered interrupts
| Mode | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **FIFO** | The `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit of the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) is asserted as infinite or finite.<br><br>**Infinite**:<br>- The `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register (address `0x00000150`) is `0x0` and hardware sets the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` when the `OUTPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register changes from `0x1` to `0x0`, indicating that the software can write more data to the output FIFO.<br>- Software sets the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` to clear it to `0x0`, which means that the software knows to return to fill the output FIFO with data.<br><br>**Finite**:<br>- The `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register (address `0x00000150`) is nonzero and hardware sets the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` when `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit is asserted.<br>- Software sets the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` to clear it to `0x0`, which means that software acknowledges the setting and does not need to write any more data to the output FIFO.<br>- After a reset, the output FIFO is empty. Software can directly write to the FIFO without waiting for a service interrupt. |
| **Block** | The `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) is set to `0x1` when the `OUT_BLOCK_WRITE_REQ` bit or the `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register is set to `0x1`.<br>- When the `OUT_BLOCK_WRITE_REQ` bit is set, the output FIFO has space for a `BLOCK_SIZE` worth of data.<br>- Software should set the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` to clear it, which means that software knows to return to fill the output FIFO with a block of data. Only one block of data should be written to the output FIFO for each `OUT_BLOCK_WRITE_REQ` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register.<br>  - Clearing the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit when `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit is not set generates an `out_service_ack` signal to the QUP output FIFO to acknowledge that the flag was serviced. Clearing the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` also clears the `OUT_BLOCK_WRITE_REQ` flag.<br>- When `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit is set, then `MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` bit in `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` (address `0x00000100`) specifies the number of words sent from the output FIFO to the SPI/I2C. If `EN_EXT_OUT_FLAG` bit in `QUP_CONFIG` (address `0x00000000`) is not set, SPI/I2C might still process the last byte. If `EN_EXT_OUT_FLAG` bit is set, the `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` in `QUP_OPERATIONAL` interrupt is received when the SPI/I2C is idle.<br>- Software sets the `OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` to `0x1` to clear it, which means that software acknowledges the setting and no further data is to be written to the output FIFO. The `MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit is cleared in `RESET_STATE`. |
| **BAM** | `QUP_IRQ` is only used for error handing. BAM producer and consumer interrupts are used for functional data flow. |

> [!NOTE]
> The `OUTPUT_FIFO_FULL` and `OUTPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` status bits in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) are set and cleared regardless of the setting of the `OUTPUT_MODE` bit in the `QUP_IO_MODES` register (address `0x00000008`). However, the `OUTPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` bit can generate an interrupt in `FIFO_MODE`.
<!-- page 1700 -->

### Table 6-20 QUP input service triggered interrupts
| Mode | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **FIFO** | The `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit of the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) is asserted as infinite or finite. For both, the software should set the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` to clear it, which means that software knows to return to read from the input FIFO.<br><br>**Infinite**:<br>- The `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register (address `0x00000208`) is `0x0` and hardware sets the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` when the `INPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register changes from `0x1` to `0x0` [sic].<br>- When the software starts reading the input FIFO, there can be more than one word. To use a zero `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT`, set the `PACK_EN` bit in the `QUP_IO_MODES` register (address `0x00000008`) to `0x0` to disable packing for the input FIFO. This ensures that there is one instance of $N$ bits for each FIFO entry. If `PACK_EN` is set to `0x1`, software must verify that the number of $N$-bit instances exactly fits one FIFO 32-bit word entry. Otherwise, the input FIFO stalls waiting for the next $N$-bit instance to be shifted from the interface.<br><br>**Finite**:<br>- The `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register (address `0x00000208`) is nonzero and hardware sets the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` when `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit is asserted.<br>- If another transaction is required after the current has completed, first the SPI/I2C must be placed into `RESET_STATE` (`QUP_STATE` register, address `0x00000004`), the appropriate QUP FIFO-related registers set, then returned to `RUN_STATE`. Hardware clears the `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit after moving to `RESET_STATE`.<br>- Reading from the input FIFO before the interrupt is asserted is not supported. |
| **Block** | The `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) is set to `0x1` when the `IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ` bit or the `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register is set to `0x1`.<br>- When the `IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ` bit is set, there is a `BLOCK_SIZE` worth of data in the input FIFO to be read. Only one block of data should be read from the input FIFO for each `IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ`.<br>- When the `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` is set, the programmed number of data has been received by the input FIFO. The `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` is cleared in the `RESET_STATE`.<br>- Software should set the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit to `0x1` to clear it, which means that software knows to return to read from the input FIFO.<br>  - Clearing the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` bit generates an `in_service_ack` signal to the input FIFO as an acknowledgment only when the `IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ` is set to `0x1`. Clearing the `INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG` also clears `IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ`. The `MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` is cleared in the `RESET_STATE`. |
| **BAM** | `QUP_IRQ` is only used for error handing. BAM producer and consumer interrupts are used for functional data flow. |

> [!NOTE]
> The `INPUT_FIFO_FULL` and `INPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` bits in the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register (address `0x00000018`) are set and cleared, regardless of the setting of the `INPUT_MODE` bit in the `QUP_IO_MODES` register (address `0x00000008`). However, the `INPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY` bit can generate an interrupt in `FIFO` mode.




<!-- page 1701 -->

#### 6.1.4.5 QUP DMA request
The QUP supports DMA using BAM. When DMA with BAM is enabled and the QUP_DMA signal is asserted, the BAM consumer pipe-transmitted data is written to the output FIFO and the BAM producer pipe-received data is read from the input FIFO.

Each QUP is independent of the other QUP instances regardless of the selected modes (SPI/I2C, BAM/block/FIFO, and so on). When different modes are used for the same QUP, the modes can only be changed when the QUP is in a reset state. For detailed programming information of QUP with BAM DMA transactions, see Section 6.1.4.8.8.

#### 6.1.4.6 QUP architecture
Table 6-21 lists the QUP internal architecture components.

##### Table 6-21 QUP architecture components
| Element | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| Bus interfaces | <ul><li>AHB slave with BASI signals when integrated with BAM</li><li>SoC global QTimer bus</li></ul> |
| Internal FIFOs | Independent output and input FIFOs with size determined by values in the following bits of 0x0000 0008 `QUP_IO_MODES` register:<br><ul><li>`OUTPUT_BLOCK_SIZE`</li><li>`OUTPUT_FIFO_SIZE`</li><li>`INPUT_BLOCK_SIZE`</li><li>`INPUT_FIFO_SIZE`</li></ul> |
| Clock crossing boundaries | The clock domain crossing between `CC_QUP_CORE_CLK` and SPI/I2C clock occurs at the FIFO interfaces to the respective SPI/I2C. There are no domain crossings or signals between SPI/I2C.<br><ul><li>The `CC_QUP_CORE_CLK` controls data flow and component timing, including the AHB and BASI.</li><li>The `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` controls the SPI interface and associated functional block.</li><li>The `CC_QUP_I2C_CLK` controls the I2C interface and associated functional block.</li></ul> |
| Interrupt signal | Single `QUP_IRQ` signal |
| Register organization | Manages the following:<br><ul><li>**QUP**: Overall QUP operation and interrupts</li><li>**Output FIFO**: Output data flow and contains the output FIFO AHB interface</li><li>**Input FIFO**: Input data flow and contains the input FIFO AHB interface</li><li>**SPI**: SPI protocol-specific features</li><li>**I2C**: I2C protocol-specific features</li></ul> |

#### 6.1.4.7 QUP operations overview
The following list gives a high-level overview of the QUP operations to be configured:
1. Select a QUP instance to be used. All six QUP instances within the SoC are identical.
2. Set the QUP mode to SPI or I2C in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register.
<!-- page 1702 -->

3. At the SoC level, establish the following:
   a. External I/O muxing that is appropriate for the selected QUP instance and its related SPI/I2C
   b. Value of the `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK` or `CC_QUP_I2C_CLK`, depending on the functional block used
4. Use the `SPI_*` or `I2C_*` registers to initialize the functional block (see Section 6.1.4.8.3 and Section 6.1.4.8.2).
5. Use the 0x0000 0008 `QUP_IO_MODES` register to determine the data transfer mode to use, as shown in Table 6-22.

##### Table 6-22 QUP data transfer mode transaction sizes
| Data transfer mode | Transaction size |
| :--- | :--- |
| Programmed IO using FIFO mode | Less than the FIFO size |
| Programmed IO using block mode | Less, equal to, or greater than the FIFO size |
| DMA using BAM | Appropriate for any transaction size |

6. Set up for a transaction in the `RESET_STATE` (see Section 6.1.4.3.1), except for the bus lock-unlock feature that complies with the Microsoft SPB specification (see Section 6.1.4.8.7).
7. Perform the transaction data transfer in the `RUN_STATE` (see Section 6.1.4.3.2) based on the selected data transfer mode.
8. Repeat the last two steps for more transactions.

#### 6.1.4.8 QUP configuration

##### 6.1.4.8.1 QUP initialization sequence
The QUP initialization sequence sets up the QUP environment, FIFOs, and SPI/I2C for actions during the reset state. Configure the QUP environment parameters as shown in Table 6-23, which are not specific to any of the SPI/I2C functional block within.

##### Table 6-23 QUP environment parameters
| Register | Field | Category |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG` | `CORE_CLOCK_ON_EN`, `APP_CLK_ON_EN`, and `FIFO_CLK_GATE_EN` | Dynamic clock gating for `CC_QUP_CORE_CLK`, `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK`, and FIFO clock |
| `0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG` | `EN_EXT_OUT_FLAG` | Input and output service flag behavior |
| `0x0000 0020 QUP_ERROR_FLAGS_EN` | `QUP_ERROR_FLAGS_EN` | FIFO-related error reporting fields |
| `0x0000 0028 QUP_OPERATIONAL_MASK` | `INPUT_SERVICE_MASK` and `OUTPUT_SERVICE_MASK` | Input and output service flag interrupt masking for the `QUP_IRQ` signal. |

##### 6.1.4.8.2 QUP I2C initialization
1. Set the `MINI_CORE` bit in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x2 to select the I2C master controller.
<!-- page 1703 -->

2. Set the `EN_VERSION_TWO_TAG` bit in the 0x0000 0408 `QUP_I2C_MASTER_CONFIG` register to 0x0 for Section 6.1.4.8.11 or to 0x1 for Section 6.1.4.8.12 (nonlegacy tag usage is recommended).
3. Configure the `N` bit in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to the transfer size, depending on the tag version. The value for the setting starts at 0x0; for example, 0x0 means 1-bit and 0xF means a 16-bit transfer, as shown in Table 6-24.

##### Table 6-24 QUP tag version
| Tag version | N field setting | Transfer size |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| QUP I2C master tag programming version (legacy mode only) | 0xF | 16 bits |
| QUP I2C master tag programming version (non-legacy) | 0x7 | 8 bits |

4. Configure the `SDA_NOISE_REJECTION` bit and `SCL_NOISE_REJECTION` bit in the 0x0000 0400 `QUP_I2C_MASTER_CLK_CTL` register to reject the external noise, if required. The default value of 0x0 does not reject the external noise.
5. Configure the `FS_DIVIDER_VALUE` bit in the 0x0000 0400 `QUP_I2C_MASTER_CLK_CTL` register with the required clock divider value based on the frequency of the `CC_QUP_I2C_CLK` to determine the I2C operational clock frequency.
6. Configure the `HIGH_TIME_DIVIDER_VALUE` bit in the 0x0000 0400 `QUP_I2C_MASTER_CLK_CTL` register if the SCL required duty cycle is not 50%.

##### 6.1.4.8.3 QUP SPI initialization
1. Set the `MINI_CORE` bit in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x1 to select SPI.
2. Configure the `N` bit in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to a transfer size of at least four bits (set to three for a transfer size of four bits).
3. Set the `SLAVE_OPERATION` bit in the 0x0000 0300 `QUP_SPI_CONFIG` register to 0x0 for SPI master configuration (slave configuration is not supported).
4. Configure the wait time (number of cycles of `CC_QUP_SPI_CLK`) through the `DEASSERT_WAIT` bit in the 0x0000 0310 `QUP_SPI_DEASSERT_WAIT` register.
5. Set the other fields in the 0x0000 0300 `QUP_SPI_CONFIG` register and the 0x0000 0304 `QUP_SPI_IO_CONTROL` register, as needed.

> [!NOTE]
> Set either the `MX_CS_MODE` bit or the `CLK_ALWAYS_ON` bit of the 0x0000 0304 `QUP_SPI_IO_CONTROL` register to 0x1; but, do not set both to 0x1.

6. For clock-related error reporting, configure the corresponding bits in the 0x0000 030C `QUP_SPI_ERROR_FLAGS_EN` register.
<!-- page 1704 -->

##### 6.1.4.8.4 QUP I/O programming
The operation mode and the input and output transaction sizes are configured when in the reset state. The input and output paths support three modes of operation: FIFO, block, and BAM.

FIFO and block modes use direct software-programmed I/O and direct communication between the QUP and software. FIFO mode is for low-bandwidth applications, such as configuration and control interfaces, while the other two modes are for moving large chunks of data.

The QUP supports independent input and output in different modes. If BAM is used, both input and output must be configured for `BAM_MODE`.

The modes differ from one another in the following ways:
* When the service interrupt is generated
* When in a run state, communication between the processor (software driver) and the QUP is controlled through interrupts and service flags. If `BAM_MODE` is used, software communicates primarily with BAM, and the QUP communicates with BAM using BASI.
* How the service interrupt should be interpreted
* Which function (software or BAM) performs the data transfer

Set the `OUTPUT_MODE` bit and the `INPUT_MODE` bit in the 0x0000 0008 `QUP_IO_MODES` register to select the output transaction mode and the input transaction modes, respectively based on Table 6-25.
<!-- page 1705 -->

##### Table 6-25 QUP `OUTPUT_MODE` and `INPUT_MODE` field settings
| Field value | Setting | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0x0 | `FIFO_MODE` | Used for transactions less than or equal to the FIFO size.<br><br>**OUTPUT_MODE**<br><ul><li>Infinite operation if the 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register is set to 0x0. The software is interrupted when the QUP output FIFO changes state from nonempty to empty.</li><li>Finite operation if the 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register is not set to 0x0. The software is interrupted once per `RUN_STATE`, when the programmed number of words written to the output FIFO are sent.</li></ul>**INPUT_MODE**<br><ul><li>Infinite operation if the 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register is set to 0x0. The software is interrupted when the QUP input FIFO changes state from empty to nonempty.</li><li>Finite operation if the 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register is not set to 0x0. The software is interrupted once per `RUN_STATE`, when the programmed number of words is shifted in the FIFO from outside.</li></ul>The software should not set the 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` and 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` registers to more than the FIFO depth (`BLOCK_SIZE_INPUT` * `FIFO_SIZE_INPUT`). |
| 0x1 | `BLOCK_MODE` | Used for transactions less than, equal to, or greater than the FIFO size.<br><br>**OUTPUT_MODE**<br><ul><li>When interrupted, the software writes a block size of data to the QUP output FIFO until the programmed number of words have been sent, after which a final interrupt (`MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit in the 0x0000 0018 `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register) is issued. The 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register must be set to a nonzero value.</li></ul>**INPUT_MODE**<br><ul><li>When interrupted, the software reads the QUP input FIFO when it obtains a block-size worth of input data until the programmed number of words has been input. A final interrupt (`MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG` bit in the 0x0000 0018 `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register) is issued after the input FIFO receives the programmed number of words. The `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register must be set to a nonzero value.</li></ul> |
<!-- page 1706 -->

| Field value | Setting | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0x2 | Reserved | Not used |
| 0x3 | `BAM_MODE` | Used for transactions of any size using BAM.<br><br>**OUTPUT_MODE**<br><ul><li>The transaction size is a function of the `EOT` bit in the current consumer descriptor and the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register not being used. ##### 6.1.4.8.5 QUP data path initialization
1. To determine the input and output size, configure the following bits in the 0x0000 0008 `QUP_IO_MODES` register:
   * `OUTPUT_BLOCK_SIZE`
   * `OUTPUT_FIFO_SIZE`
   * `INPUT_BLOCK_SIZE`
   * `INPUT_FIFO_SIZE`
   
   Although it is set as a hardware constant, the size varies between different QUP SPI/I2C features. The `BLOCK_SIZE` determines the interval between `SERVICE_FLAG` interrupts in the block mode (how often an interrupt is received).
2. If needed, set either the `NO_INPUT` or `NO_OUTPUT` bits of the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x1 to disable QUP input or output FIFO.
   Both `NO_INPUT` and `NO_OUTPUT` cannot be set to 0x1. If the I2C master is enabled, `NO_OUTPUT` cannot be set to 0x1.
3. See Table 6-26 to configure the fields in the 0x0000 0008 `QUP_IO_MODES` register.

##### Table 6-26 QUP IO_MODES configuration
| Fields | Configuration details |
| :--- | :--- |
| `INPUT_MODE`, `OUTPUT_MODE` | Used as a mode for input and output FIFOs: `FIFO_MODE`, `BLOCK_MODE`, `BAM_MODE` (for BAM, input and output must both be `BAM_MODE`) |
| `PACK_EN`* | Enable or disable the transfer packing of size N into 32-bit words in the QUP input FIFO. For I2C, always use packed for most efficient use of input FIFO. |
<!-- page 1707 -->

| Fields | Configuration details |
| :--- | :--- |
| `UNPACK_EN`* | Enable or disable the unpacking of 32-bit words into N-sized transfers in the QUP output FIFO. For I2C, use unpacked for most efficient use of output FIFO. |
| `OUTPUT_BIT_SHIFT_EN`* | Set as required. For I2C, always set to 0x0. |

4. See Table 6-27 to configure the `QUP_MX_*_COUNT` registers (where * = INPUT/OUTPUT/READ/WRITE).

##### Table 6-27 QUP count configuration
| Mode | Configuration details |
| :--- | :--- |
| FIFO | Configure the 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register for the input FIFO and 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register for the output FIFO. Alternatively, one or both can remain at 0x0 (interrupts are a function of FIFO or empty, see Section 6.1.4.4). Values in either register should not exceed the FIFO depth (`BLOCK_SIZE` × `FIFO_SIZE`). |
| Block | Configure the 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` for the input FIFO and the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register for the output FIFO. If configured as 0x0, the associated input or output data flow is assumed infinite, which is not recommended because there is no graceful way to end a data flow. |
| BAM | 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register is not used, and must be programmed to 0x0. |

5. SPI only: In BAM mode, the BAM consumer transaction size determines the output transaction size (there is no need to configure the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register). The size of the producer transaction is:
   * If both the `NO_OUTPUT` and `NO_INPUT` bits of 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register are set to 0x0, the output (consumer pipe) and input (producer pipe) transactions happen simultaneously.
   * If 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` is set to 0x0, the producer transaction size is the same as the consumer transaction size.
   * If 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` is not set to 0x0, the producer transaction size is the same as `MX_INPUT_COUNT` bit of 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register.
   * If the `NO_INPUT` bit of 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register is set, there is no producer transaction, and the value of 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` is not used.
   * (BAM mode) Do not set the `NO_INPUT` bit of 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x1. If the output is not needed, software must send a zero length transfer (ZLT) with notify when done (NWD) before the real data descriptor.
6. I2C only: The output and input transfer sizes are determined by the TAG sequence. Set the 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` to 0x0.
7. BAM mode: The 0x0000 0104 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_CNT_CURRENT` and 0x0000 0204 `QUP_MX_INPUT_CNT_CURRENT` registers are used to indicate the number of bytes transferred on the bus. `0x0000 0200 QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` increases each time a new
<!-- page 1708 -->

data is received from the SPI/I2C. 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` increases each time a new data is sent to SPI/I2C.

##### 6.1.4.8.6 QUP using the RESET_STATE
After the QUP is initialized through register configuration during reset (`RESET_STATE`), including the SPI/I2C and data path, serial protocol transactions can start by entering a run state.

Transactions from one state to another follow these rules:
1. `RESET_STATE` is the default state after software or hardware reset of the QUP.
2. To transition from a reset state, the following conditions must be met. Otherwise, the hardware prevents the move to the run state.
   * Configure the N field in the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register according to Table 6-28.
   
##### Table 6-28 N field configuration
| Feature | N field setting | Transfer size |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| SPI | 0x3 or greater | 4 bits or greater |
| QUP I2C master tag programming version (legacy mode only) | 0xF | 16 bits |
| QUP I2C master tag programming version (non-legacy) | 0x7 | 8 bits |

   * Configure either the `NO_INPUT` bit or `NO_OUTPUT` of the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x0 (one must be set to 0x0).
   * SPI: Configure either the `MX_CS_MODE` bit or the `CLK_ALWAYS_ON` bit of the 0x0000 0304 `QUP_SPI_IO_CONTROL` register to 0x0 (both fields cannot be set to 0x1).
   * BAM mode: Do not configure the `NO_OUTPUT` bit of the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x1 and 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register to 0x0.
   * Block mode: Configure the 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` and the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` registers to a nonzero value.

> [!WARNING]
> Do not transition directly from a reset state to a pause state as the outcome is undefined.

3. Before configuring the STATE bit of 0x0000 0004 `QUP_STATE` register, verify that the `STATE_VALID` bit of 0x0000 0004 `QUP_STATE` register is 0x1. If it is set to 0x0, do not set the STATE bit. Any value read from it is invalid.
4. To ensure that the value written to the STATE bit of 0x0000 0004 `QUP_STATE` register is valid, software must read the `STATE_VALID` bit of 0x0000 0004 `QUP_STATE` register after the STATE field is set. Hardware sets the `STATE_VALID` bit to 0x1 to validate the STATE field.
<!-- page 1709 -->

##### 6.1.4.8.7 QUP reconfiguration during run
To comply with the Microsoft SPB specification, I2C supports the reconfiguration during run feature (also known as lock-unlock).

The application takes control of (locks) the I2C bus and, without issuing a stop event, writes and reads bytes. Drivers are aware of only one current sub-transfer. It is prohibited to enter `RESET_STATE` between sub-transfers because it resets the I2C and releases the SCL and SDA lines.

To use this feature:
1. All subtransfers (between lock and unlock) should be executed in the same. [sic]
2. Initialize the first transfer during `RESET_STATE` (during the initial state in which the I2C and SPI are reset and FIFOs are reset).
3. Initialize any subsequent transfers during `RUN_STATE` after receiving all data interrupts.
4. To schedule a new sub-transfer, reconfigure the next register, as shown in Table 6-29.

##### Table 6-29 QUP reconfiguration during run
| Mode | Configuration details |
| :--- | :--- |
| FIFO | <ul><li>Set the `MX_CONFIG_DURING_RUN` bit of the 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT` register to 0x1</li><li>Set the `MX_CONFIG_DURING_RUN` bit of the 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` register to 0x1</li></ul> |
| Block | <ul><li>Set the `MX_CONFIG_DURING_RUN` bit of the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT` register to 0x1</li><li>Set the `MX_CONFIG_DURING_RUN` bit of the 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register to 0x1</li></ul> |
| BAM | No reconfiguration is needed in BAM mode. The current implementation has a hardware issue with compilation indication. |

5. For a write sub-transfer, configure only the `NO_INPUT` bit of the 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register to 0x1.
   Setting the 0x0000 0100 `QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT`, 0x0000 0150 `QUP_MX_WRITE_COUNT`, 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT`, or 0x0000 0208 `QUP_MX_READ_COUNT` registers resets the output or input FIFOs.
6. Write the tagged data to the output FIFO.

##### 6.1.4.8.8 QUP BAM mode transactions
Each transfer should end with the `NWD` bit of the `QUP_OPERATIONAL` register configured. As a result, a new transfer does not start until the QUP indicates to the BAM that all the data has been processed.

The conditions for transfer completion are:
* All output data has completely shifted out of the external interface.
<!-- page 1710 -->

* All input data has completely shifted into the input FIFO and the FIFO has been completely emptied.
* The SPI/I2C is in idle mode (see Section [sic]).

After the software completes all transfers in the run state, it moves the QUP to the reset state to save power.

> [!NOTE]
> Before scheduling a new BAM data descriptor, QUP must be moved to the run state.

Table 6-30 shows the BAM mode transaction behavior when the different INPUT/OUTPUT fields are set. The 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register is used in legacy mode only. See Section 6.1.4.8.11.

##### Table 6-30 QUP BAM mode transactions
| Field | Configuration details |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register<br>Bit configuration:<br><ul><li>`NO_INPUT`: 0x0</li><li>`NO_OUTPUT`: 0x0</li></ul> | After the `RUN_STATE` is established, a new transaction starts with the first consumer AHB data write. The transaction continues until EOT indication is received from the BAM and 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` is exhausted. |
| 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register<br>Bit configuration:<br><ul><li>`NO_INPUT`: 0x1</li><li>`NO_OUTPUT`: 0x0</li></ul> | Same as previous except `MX_INPUT_COUNT` bit of the 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` register is not used and the input FIFO status is not considered. |
| 0x0000 0000 `QUP_CONFIG` register<br>Bit configuration:<br><ul><li>`NO_INPUT`: 0x0</li><li>`NO_OUTPUT`: 0x1</li></ul> | After set to `RUN_STATE`, new transaction starts and ends when 0x0000 0200 `QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT` is exhausted. |

###### QUP EOT signal
BAM indicates the end of a transfer with the EOT signal, which it sends to the QUP over the BASI interface. Software can request notification of transfer completion by setting the NWD signal.

* **SPI mode**: The EOT signal deasserts the `BLSPx_SPI_CS_N` line.
* **I2C mode**: The EOT tag defines the transfer boundaries by sending an EOT signal to BAM. A BAM transfer can contain multiple EOT tags.

###### QUP SPI and I2C idle condition
* **I2C**: Idle after the stop condition has been sent on the bus.
* **SPI**: Idle after all last N bits were transmitted and `BLSPx_SPI_CS_N` has been deasserted.


<!-- page 1711 -->

##### QUP output back-to-back transactions

After configuring the RUN_STATE, a write transaction begins with the first consumer write from BAM. After BAM signals EOT for the transaction, a new transaction can start without additional QUP or I2C setup.

When I2C tags are used, the QUP remains in the run state. It does not have to return to the reset state except to clear FIFOs for error recovery.

##### QUP input back-to-back transactions

Any tag following the EOT tag always starts a new input transaction. There is no fixed relationship between output and input transactions. One output transaction can generate multiple input transactions.

(SPI mode) If NO_OUTPUT bit of the 0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG register is asserted, the QUP must transition to a reset state, then back to the run state to maintain data integrity.

#### 6.1.4.8.9 QUP FIFO status flags behavior

The 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL register has four FIFO status flags:
* two for input (INPUT_FIFO_FULL and INPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY)
* two for output (OUTPUT_FIFO_FULL and OUTPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY)

The behavior of the `*_NOT_EMPTY` (where `*` = INPUT/OUTPUT) flags is the same for input and output. However, the `*_FULL` (where `*` = INPUT/OUTPUT) flags behave differently for input and output: FIFOs keep their `*_FULL` flags asserted when their reset is held asserted.

The input FIFO cannot be reset when the QUP_MX_INPUT_CNT is reached because the data cannot have been read by the system. The input FIFO is held in reset during:
* Hardware reset (QUP_RESET) assertion
* Software reset (0x0000 000C QUP_SW_RESET) assertion (usually one clock cycle)
* Reset state
* When no input (NO_INPUT bit of the 0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG register is set to 0x1)
* When performing reconfiguration during run (one clock cycle), see Section 6.1.4.8.7.

After these resets are deasserted or after exiting the reset state, the INPUT_FIFO_FULL bit of the QUP_OPERATIONAL register reads its functional value based on the FIFO contents.

The output FIFO is held in reset when the QUP_MX_OUTPUT_CNT is reached and the MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG bit of the 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL register is asserted. No other action is required for the output FIFO because it has finished its work.

The output FIFO is held in the reset state and:
* During a hardware reset (QUP_RESET) assertion
* During a software reset (0x0000 000C QUP_SW_RESET register) assertion (a few clock cycles)
<!-- page 1712 -->

* While MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG bit of the 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL register is kept asserted

The OUTPUT_FIFO_FULL bit of the 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL register remains asserted after a hardware or software reset (because it is in RESET_STATE) and after MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG bit of the 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL register is asserted.

#### 6.1.4.8.11 QUP I2C master tag programming version (legacy mode only)

I2C supports version 1 tags as the legacy behavior. Do not use this tag with any new software. Version 1 tags are not supported in BAM mode.

The data written to the output FIFO comprises of 16 bits divided into an 8-bit tag for the upper bits and an 8-bit data for the lower bits.

##### Table 6-32 QUP I2C output FIFO tagging

| Name | Value | Data value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| NOOP | 0x00 | 0xCC | Wait CC*9 number of CC_QUP_I2C_CLK (I2C operating mode frequency) cycles; CC value of 0 means 256 |
| START | 0x01 | 0xAA | LSB indicates write (0) or read (1); 7-bit address occupies the seven MSBs |
| MO_DATA | 0x02 | 0xDD | Master output data |
| MO_STOP | 0x03 | 0xDD | Master output data with STOP |
| MI_REC | 0x04 | 0xCC | Receive CC number bytes and NACK the last byte and STOP; CC value of 0 means a 256 byte read |

| Sequence | Tag | Data |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | START | 7-bit address, 1-bit read/write set for write |
| 2 | MO_DATA | Data |
| 3 | MO_STOP | Data |

| Sequence | Tag | Data |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| Bits 31:16 | Bit 15:0 |
| :--- | :--- |
| Tagged data 2 (second instruction in original) | Tagged data 1 (first instruction in original) |

Data received in the input FIFO is also tagged. Each byte is tagged with an 8-bit tag that indicates if the byte is not the last byte, is the last byte, or if a bus error happened during receipt of the byte.

##### Table 6-36 QUP I2C input FIFO tagging

| Tag name | Tag value | Data value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MI_DATA | 0x05 | 0xDD | Master input data |
| MI_STOP | 0x06 | 0xDD | Last byte of master input data |
| MI_NACK | 0x07 | 0xFF | Invalid master input data |

##### QUP I2C NOOP

For accurate timing results, use the I2C no operation (NOOP) tag only when the output FIFO is loaded with data in the pause state. NOOP wait duration counting begins on the falling edge of SCL from the previous byte's ACK cycle and continues counting for a multiple of nine SCL cycles.

Assuming that I2C tagged data is only loaded in the pause state and not in the run state, I2C NOOPs can be inserted:
* Into the middle of an I2C write transaction
  For example, a NOOP can be inserted into an I2C write between two bytes that are transmitted to an I2C slave.
* Between two separate I2C transactions
  For example, a NOOP can be inserted after one read transaction completes and before the next read transaction starts.

The following is not supported:
* A NOOP instruction must not be the first instruction of the transfer (must follow another tag).
* Back-to-back NOOPs is not supported. If a back-to-back NOOP is required, insert a repeated start between the two NOOPs.
<!-- page 1715 -->

* A NOOP cannot be inserted between a START tag for a read transaction and the following MI_REC tag.

#### 6.1.4.8.12 QUP I2C master tag programming version (non-legacy)

The I2C tagging strategy supports the QUP and BAM concept of a transaction by organizing write and read operations into transactions.

A single I2C write operation defines one QUP BAM output consumer transaction. Multiple write operations can be grouped into one QUP BAM output consumer transaction.

A single I2C read operation defines one QUP BAM input producer transaction. Multiple read operations can be grouped into one QUP BAM input producer transaction.

A transaction begins with a start tag in the LSB of the first 32-bit word of the data stream written into the output FIFO, followed by the address byte (or bytes if using a 10-bit address), and then a data tag and byte count.
* If the data operation is a write, the data bytes follow in the output FIFO.
* If the data operation is a read, the data bytes are read from the slave and moved to the input FIFO.

Transactions are byte-oriented but always begin with the LSB in the first word of the transaction. A transaction can end on any byte boundary. See Table 6-37 for details.

##### Table 6-37 QUP I2C nonlegacy tags, start, and data

| Tag | Value | 1st byte after tag | 2nd byte after tag | Additional bytes | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **START** | 0x81 | Slave address | N/A | N/A | LSB of address indicates write (0) or read (1) |
| **START_STOP** | 0x8A | Slave address | N/A | N/A | Same as START, but terminates the transfer immediately after slave address |
| **DATA_WRITE** | 0x82 | Byte count [0:7] | Data | Data | Byte count specifies the amount of data; 0 means 256. <br>Tag and data combination can be followed by additional DATA_WRITE tag and data combinations or a final DATA_WRT_STOP tag and data combination. <br>Any START tag that follows is a repeated start. <br>Data read tags are illegal in this context. |
| **DATA_WR_STOP** | 0x83 | Byte count [0:7] | Data | Data | Same as for DATA_WRITE, but terminates data with a STOP. <br>No data tags can follow until START. |
<!-- page 1716 -->

| Tag | Value | 1st byte after tag | 2nd byte after tag | Additional bytes | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DATA_READ** | 0x85 | Byte count [0:7] | N/A | N/A | Reads count data, but does not NACK the last byte; must be followed by another DATA_READ, DATA_READ and NACK, or DATA_READ and STOP. Leaves slave stalled waiting for read. <br>For all read tags: <br>• Copy the tag and associated count from output FIFO to input FIFO.<br>• Read the count bytes from the I2C slave and move bytes to the input FIFO.<br>• After completing the read, return to processing any remaining tags from the output FIFO. |

### 6.1.4.8.13 QUP I2C timestamp usage

Timestamp is an I2C tag that writes the QTIMER_GLOBAL_COUNTER[31:8] value after copying the tag from output to input FIFO. It helps determine when specific tags or data were written to the input FIFO.

In this implementation, only bits [31:8] of the full 56-bit bus are copied into memory. This achieves a 13.44 μs (256/19.2 MHz) granularity with a time span of 3.76 s (2^32/19.2 MHz), which
<!-- page 1724 -->

is sufficient for all existing applications. Because the time span is more than the usual transfer, software can use a simple minimum distance calculation to handle the timestamp rollover.

### 6.1.4.8.14 QUP I2C high-speed mode

The I2C high-speed (HS) supports transfers up to 3.4 MHz.
To start a HS transfer:
* Set the I2C clock to 50 MHz (this configuration is outside QUP)

A HS data transfer starts with a START tag with reserved HS-mode master code, followed by a START tag with a slave ID. A HS transfer finishes after issuing a STOP tag.

### 6.1.4.8.15 QUP BAM mode with command descriptors

SPI mode: The QUP and SPI must be reconfigured between transfers. To allow queuing transfers, the BAM command descriptors are inserted between the data descriptors, which configures the QUP before the next data transfer.

Use the command descriptor with the NWD signal to allow stalling the next operation until the current command is complete. For example, to stall the data processing until STATE_VALID bit of the 0x0000 0004 QUP_STATE register is asserted after transitioning to the run state, use a separate command descriptor with NWD to write to the QUP_STATE register to transition to a run state.

> [!WARNING]
> BAM mode: Do not set the NO_OUTPUT bit of the 0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG register to 0x1. If the output is not needed, software must send a ZLT with NWD before the real data descriptor.

#### QUP BAM command descriptor mask

The command descriptor includes a mask field. This option allows the software to modify specific bits in the register in the same way as a read-modify-write operation.

### 6.1.4.8.16 QUP hardware cancel support

Because of the SPB requirement, the application can request to cancel any transfer that it previously scheduled for the QUP driver. The QUP driver must then cancel the transfer as soon as possible.

The request to cancel a transfer occurs when the transfer was:
* Not scheduled in the hardware. If canceling the transfer is required, software must handle it without the hardware support.
* Scheduled and finished in hardware and hardware has notified the driver. The driver notifies the application that the transfer was already completed, and a cancellation does not occur.
* Already scheduled in the hardware but not finished. To cancel the transfer, a hardware sequence must be used.
  When this occurs, the possible scenarios are that the transfer:
  * BAM only: Is scheduled in BAM, but it has not reached QUP (nonstarted transfer)
<!-- page 1725 -->

* All modes: Partially reached QUP (on-going transfer)
* All modes: Has completed in QUP, but the software has not received the notification

### 6.1.4.8.17 QUP BAM mode cancel

All software transfers are tagged with a LOCAL_ID (recommendation is to increment the previous value (LOCAL_ID + 1)).

#### Figure 6-27: QUP software transfer sequence
*Description:* This diagram illustrates a timeline of sequential I2C/SPI transfers, where each transfer has an associated incrementing identifier.
* Transfer 1: `LOCAL_ID=1`
* Transfer 2: `LOCAL_ID=2`
* ...
* Transfer n: `LOCAL_ID=n`

#### Figure 6-28: QUP hardware support determination flowchart
*Description:* A flowchart showing the decision process when an application requests to cancel a transfer.
* **Start:** Application request to cancel transfer X is received by a driver.
* **Queue Status:** There is a queue containing `Queue transfer 1 *` through `Queue transfer N *`.
* **Decision:** Is Transfer X already scheduled to HW and driver did not receive a completion yet?
  * **Yes:** HW support is required to cancel.
  * **No:** Cancel should be taken care of in SW without HW support.
<!-- page 1726 -->

#### Figure 6-29: QUP cancel sequence with hardware flowchart
*Description:* A flowchart detailing the hardware-assisted cancellation sequence.
* **Start:** "HW support is required" (from Figure 6-28).
* **Step 1:** Write transfer ID `X` to `QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL[TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID]`, and write `1` to `QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL[TRANSFER_CANCEL]`.
* **Step 2 (Parallel Operations):**
  * Wait for transfer done.
  * Wait for `TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt.
* **Decision:** Did `TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt occur?
  * **No (Completion interrupt is received instead):**
    1. RESET the cancel state machine.
  * **Yes:**
    1. Read `QUP_*_FIFO_WORD_CNT`, `QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT`, and other registers (driver determines how much data was written/read).
    2. Move to `RUN_STATE` (to trigger flush of BAM data).
    3. Wait for `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt (HW transitions to pause state).
    4. Move to `RUN_STATE` (to resume normal operation).

After receiving the `TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt and transitioning to a run state, QUP flushes all data it receives from the BAM.

### 6.1.4.8.18 QUP back-to-back cancel

Figure 6-30 shows a possible scenario when two consecutive scheduled transfers are requested to be cancelled, where transfer x and x + 1 are required to be cancelled.
<!-- page 1727 -->

#### Figure 6-30: QUP back-to-back consecutive transfers cancelled
*Description:* Timeline demonstrating how to perform back-to-back cancel operations for two consecutive transfers (transfer `x` and `x+1`).
* **Transfers:** A sequence of transfers labeled with `LOCAL_ID = x-1`, `LOCAL_ID = x`, `LOCAL_ID = x+1`, and `LOCAL_ID = x+2`.
* **Events:**
  1. A cancel command for transfer `x` is sent.
  2. Once the cancel completion interrupt for transfer `x` is received, the new cancel command for transfer `x+1` must be scheduled immediately, before transitioning the QUP to `RUN_STATE`.

The procedure is as follows:
1. Cancel transfer `x`, as shown in Figure 6-30.
2. After receiving `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt and before moving QUP to `RUN_STATE`, schedule `x+1` transfer for cancellation by writing to `0x0000 0014 QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL` register.

### 6.1.4.8.19 QUP I2C cancel

The I2C `LOCAL_ID` is set with a special I2C tag. For I2C, it requires to check if the `QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT` (where `*` = `INPUT`/`OUTPUT`/`READ`/`WRITE`) counters are `0x0` or not. If both the counters are equal to `0x0`, the transfer scheduled for cancel is already finished in the hardware. The cancel state machine must be reset by writing to the `RESET_CANCEL_FSM` bit of the `0x0000 0414 QUP_I2C_MASTER_COMMAND` register before moving to `RUN_STATE`; otherwise, a wrong transfer (next to the required) is cancelled. The transfer cancel boundary is tagged by `FLUSH_STOP` tag. Upon encountering this tag, the cancel procedure is stopped, and `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt is issued.
<!-- page 1728 -->

#### Figure 6-31: QUP I2C specific cancel flowchart
*Description:* A flowchart detailing the I2C-specific transfer cancellation sequence.
* **Decision:** Did `TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt occur?
  * **Yes:**
    1. Read `QUP_*_FIFO_WORD_CNT`, `QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT`, and other registers (driver determines how much data was written/read).
    2. **Decision:** Are the counters zero? (If the counters (`MX_COUNT_CURRENT`) are zeros, a new transfer has started, but the interrupt is still pending for the old transfer, and no cancel should be done).
       * **Yes:**
         1. RESET the cancel state machine.
         2. Move to `RUN_STATE`.
       * **No:**
         1. Move to `RUN_STATE`.
         2. Wait for `qup_irq` with source `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` (HW will transition to pause state).
         3. Move to `RUN_STATE`.

### QUP I2C cancel with NACK handling

Cancel and NACK are independent events and might occur on the same byte. This occurrence requires a different handling mechanism.
<!-- page 1729 -->

#### Figure 6-32: QUP I2C cancel with NACK flowchart
*Description:* Flowchart illustrating how to handle a transfer cancel when a NACK (Negative Acknowledge) occurs.
* **Start:** Application request to cancel transfer X is received by the driver.
* **Step 1:** Write `X` to `QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL[TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID]` and `1` to `QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL[TRANSFER_CANCEL]`.
* **Step 2:** Wait for `QUP_IRQ` (hardware transitions to pause state).
* **Decision:** Was a `PACKED_NACKED` interrupt received?
  * **Yes:**
    * **Decision:** Is the active `LOCAL_ID == X` (i.e. did the NACK happen on the transfer currently being canceled)?
      * **Yes:**
        1. Abort the cancel operation for transfer `X` by asserting `RESET_CANCEL_FSM`.
        2. Handle the NACK (I2C flush).
      * **No:**
        1. Handle the NACK (I2C flush).
  * **No:**
    1. Handle the received interrupt.
    2. **Decision:** Was it a `CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt?
      * **Yes:**
        1. Handle transfer `X` cancel procedure as described (e.g. in Figure 6-31).

### 6.1.4.8.20 QUP SPI cancel

The SPI `LOCAL_ID` is set using a command descriptor interface.

#### Figure 6-33: QUP SPI command descriptor
*Description:* A representation of consecutive SPI command descriptors with NWD (Notify When Done) enabled.
* 1st descriptor with NWD.
* 2nd descriptor with NWD.

The data flushing is stopped when a new `LOCAL_ID` is set to QUP by the command descriptor. QUP transitions to a run state.
<!-- page 1730 -->

> [!CAUTION]
> If cancel was scheduled before a transfer was started in QUP, the first N bit word is received by QUP. If the transfer is single N bit long, an interrupt does not occur. This case is with unexpected behavior and no output is produced.

### 6.1.4.8.21 QUP multitransfer cancel

In SPI mode, sometimes multiple BAM transfers are used to send or receive a single SPI transfer. The `LOCAL_ID` remains the same for more than one BAM transfer.

Each BAM transfer at a single SPI transfer is called an SPI subtransfer. Because `QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT` (where `*` = `INPUT`/`OUTPUT`/`READ`/`WRITE`) number of registers are reset at each subtransfer, a mechanism is required (`EXTENDED_ID`) to determine which subtransfer is executing.

`EXTENDED_ID` and `LOCAL_ID` are in the `0x0000 0314 QUP_SPI_MASTER_LOCAL_ID` register. The purpose is to write the field with ascending number (see Figure 6-34). When the `TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH` interrupt triggers, the software reads the register to know the subtransfer the QUP is processing. The value in `MX_*_CNT_CURRENT` shows the data that was transmitted or received from the slave.

#### Figure 6-34: QUP multitransfer cancel timing diagram
*Description:* Timing diagram showing a single logical SPI transfer mapped to multiple BAM subtransfers.
* **I2C/SPI transfer 1:** Comprises multiple BAM subtransfers:
  * BAM transfer 1: `LOCAL_ID = 1`, `Extended_ID = 1`
  * BAM transfer 2: `LOCAL_ID = 1`, `Extended_ID = 2`
  * BAM transfer n: `LOCAL_ID = 1`, `Extended_ID = n`
* **I2C/SPI transfer 2:** Begins with a new `LOCAL_ID = 2`.
* **BLSP_SPI_CS_N:** The active-low SPI chip select remains low across all BAM subtransfers belonging to the first SPI transfer, ensuring uninterrupted communication.

The `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt behavior in SPI mode issues `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt only when a new `LOCAL_ID` is written and QUP is moved to the `RUN_STATE`.

Multiple transfers can be queued to BAM, while the latest queued transfer finished with command descriptor, which moves QUP to `RESET_STATE`. No new `LOCAL_ID` is written after this latest transfer. If this latest transfer is cancelled, `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt is not received when the cancel is done (due to hardware implementation TBD). If new transfer (with a new `LOCAL_ID`) is scheduled after the cancelled transfer, `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` is received at the beginning of this new transfer. This behavior is undesirable. To avoid this, after receiving the completion interrupt from BAM, reset the cancel state machine by writing to the `RESET_CANCEL_FSM` bit of the `0x0000 0318 QUP_SPI_MASTER_COMMAND` register.

If the transfer being cancelled is not the latest queued, it would be good to receive the `TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE` interrupt in order, if necessary, to cancel the following transfer.

### 6.1.4.8.22 QUP non-BAM mode cancel

In this type, the assumption is that the cancel is executed only for an ongoing transfer.


<!-- page 1731 -->
## QUP I2C non-BAM mode cancel

Canceling a transfer requires a valid stop condition on the bus. To force the stop condition, use the BAM mode cancel mechanism.

1. At the beginning of each non-BAM transfer, write the LOCAL_ID tag to set the value of the LOCAL_ID bit in the 0x0000 0410 QUP_I2C_MASTER_LOCAL_ID register. The value of the tag can be any number.
2. Send the cancel command and wait for the TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID_MATCH interrupt. Continue to process the transfer using the input or output service flag until the interrupt is received.
3. Read the QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT (where * = INPUT/OUTPUT/READ/WRITE) register to determine how much data was transmitted to the slave.
4. Transition to the run state.
5. Continue to write or read data belonging to the current processed tag. Hardware sends a top event on the bus after the data of the current tag is processed.
6. Check that the CANCEL_FSM_STATE bit of the 0x0000 0404 QUP_I2C_MASTER_STATUS register is equal to the FLUSH_STATE, which is entered after the data of the processing tag is queued and the stop event on the I2C bus is issued.
   Alternatively, instead of pulling the CANCEL_FSM_STATE bit, write the FLUSH_STOP tag to the output FIFO immediately after the processed tag. This triggers the TRANSFER_CANCEL_DONE interrupt after the stop event is sent.
7. Transition the QUP to a reset state. The remaining data in the FIFOs is removed, and new transfers can be scheduled.

## QUP SPI non-BAM mode cancel

In non-BAM mode, the SPI cancel must be performed in the SPI N boundary.

To cancel a transfer:
1. Move QUP to a PAUSE_STATE and wait until the current N-bit word is finished.
   The command to transition to the pause state can execute during the SPI N-bit word transfer. It must be performed on an N-bit word boundary. After the transition to the pause state, a delay is required to complete the transfer of the N-bit word.

#### Equation: Maximum wait time for SPI N-bit word transfer
*Description:* Formula to calculate the maximum wait time ($t_{max}$) based on word length ($N$) and SPI clock frequency ($CC\_QUP\_SPI\_CLK$).
$$t_{max} = \frac{N}{CC\_QUP\_SPI\_CLK}$$

   Assuming the CC_QUP_SPI_CLK is 1 MHz and N is 32, the worst case requires a wait of 32 μsec.
<!-- page 1732 -->
2. Read the QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT (where * = INPUT/OUTPUT/READ/WRITE) counter to determine the data that was transmitted. Read the remaining data from the input FIFO through the 0x0000 0218+ QUP_INPUT_FIFOc, c=[0..15] register.
3. Transition to a reset state, which removes the remaining data in the FIFOs and deasserts the BLSPx_SPI_CS_N signal.
4. Schedule a new transfer by transitioning the QUP to the run state and write the new data to the output FIFO.

### 6.1.4.9 QUP error detection and handling

#### 6.1.4.9.1 QUP FIFO errors

This error is reported in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register. Each bit can be masked by setting the corresponding bit in the 0x0000 0020 QUP_ERROR_FLAGS_EN register. The QUP error can be cleared by setting the related bit in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register to 0x1.

Misusing FIFOs cause errors such as the output FIFO overflow (OUTPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR bit in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register) and input FIFO overflow (INPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR bit in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register). These two should not occur if the QUP interrupts guidelines are followed—interrupts should never occur in BAM mode. Although they can be handled by resending or ignoring the last word (in FIFO mode) or block (in block mode) they can be masking a more serious software issue, so should be treated as fatal errors.

Other (theoretical) errors are output FIFO underflow (OUTPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR bit in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register) or input FIFO underflow (INPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR bit in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register).

Overflow cannot occur because masters can stop the clock and throttle the data. Scenarios that cause these errors are unknown and must be assumed to be fatal and unrecoverable.

#### 6.1.4.9.2 QUP SPI errors
This error is related to the SPI slave, which is not supported in this SoC.

#### 6.1.4.9.3 QUP I2C errors

This error is reported in the 0x0000 0404 QUP_I2C_MASTER_STATUS register. It is related to the data integrity and bus errors. Clear these errors by setting the related bit in the 0x0000 0404 QUP_I2C_MASTER_STATUS register to 0x1.

> [!NOTE]
> Any I2C error causes a transition of the QUP to PAUSE_STATE. For more details, see Section and Section .

QUP I2C errors: data integrity related
* **INVALID_READ_SEQ**: The error is reported when MI_REC tag does not follow the START tag for an I2C READ. These errors should not occur in a bug free software stack. Although
<!-- page 1733 -->
                        recoverable, these errors are treated as fatal errors as there could be a more severe software issue. The error can happen when START tag with read address is not followed by an MI_REC tag. This is only applicable when using legacy tags.
* **INVALID_TAG**: The error means that the I2C controller is trying to process data from the output FIFO that is improperly tagged.

QUP I2C errors: bus related
* **BUS_ERROR**: The error occurs when there is an unexpected start or stop condition on the I2C bus. In a multi master I2C system, this error indicates an improper behavior of the other master. In a single master I2C system, this error indicates excessive bus noise. Data can be retransmitted, but board design should be revised. Also, modify the SDA_NOISE_REJECTION and SCL_NOISE_REJECTION bits in the 0x0000 0400 QUP_I2C_MASTER_CLK_CTL register.
* **PACKET_NACKED**: The error occurs upon NACK receipt from the I2C device. See Section .
* **ARB_LOST**: The error occurs when arbitration is lost. This is possible to happen either when the data is retransmitted in a multimaster environment or (more common) excessive bus noise in a single master mode. For recovery, retransmit the data again and revise the hardware.
* **INVALID_READ_ADDR**: The error occurs upon receipt of NACK from the I2C device for the address byte. This error indicates that the I2C device does not exist or is not functional. For recovery, retransmit the data and revise the hardware.

#### QUP I2C handling device NACK
A slave device should acknowledge every byte transmitted from the I2C master (by sending a NACK or ACK). If not, hardware sends an interrupt to the software.

The QUP stops sending data, issues a stop condition on the I2C bus, and transitions to the pause state, which stops the data transfer but preserves the register values for debug.

To determine the part of data sent on the I2C link, read these registers for transfer status:
* QUP_MX_*_CNT_CURRENT (where * = INPUT/OUTPUT/READ/WRITE)
* QUP_I2C_MASTER_STATUS
* QUP_I2C_MASTER_LOCAL_ID

In BAM mode, a NACK can occur in the middle of a batch of scheduled transfers. To handle the NACK and reschedule the remaining batch transfers, execute the I2C_FLUSH command by setting the I2C_FLUSH bit in the 0x0000 0004 QUP_STATE register to 0x1. I2C_ FLUSH flushes both the input and output FIFOs, and terminates the current transmission (if exists) after the STOP bit. This causes the I2C to consume and ignore all data and tags, except the following:
* **INPUT_EOT** tag, which causes the I2C to move the INPUT_EOT_FLUSH tag to the output FIFO-helping software receive the scheduled interrupts and decode the input data stream.
* **FLUSH_STOP** tag, which ends the flush operation. This flow assumes that the software moved the FLUSH_STOP tag (probably at the end of each I2C transfer) in advance.

In a non-BAM mode, transition to a reset state to clear the remaining data in the FIFOs, and then configure new transfers.

### 6.1.5.3 QUP register definitions

#### 6.1.5.3.1 0x0000 0000 QUP_CONFIG

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

Unless otherwise stated, register bits written return the value when read.

The contents of this register should only be changed when in the RESET_STATE (see the 0x0000 0004 QUP_STATE register). The value written to the QUP output FIFO is shifted left towards the MSB before passing it to the mini-core as follows:
* N equals 8 or less: shift 24
* N equals 16 to 9: shift 16
* N equals 24 to 17: shift 8
* N equals 32 to 25: no shift

#### 6.1.5.3.3 0x0000 0008 QUP_IO_MODES

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x000000A5

Unless otherwise stated, register bits written return the value when read.

Notes:
1. Packing occurs as follows:
   * N equals 8 or less: pack four values into each QUP input FIFO word.
   * N equals 16 to 9: pack two values into each QUP input FIFO word.
   * N equals 32 to 17: no packing. Each mini-core value is moved to a QUP input FIFO word.
2. Unpacking occurs as follows:
   * N equals 8 or less: unpack four values from each QUP output FIFO word.
   * N equals 16 to 9: unpack two values from each QUP output FIFO word.
   * N equals 32 to 17: no packing. Each QUP output FIFO value is moved to the mini-core.
3. Both the `INPUT_MODE` and `OUTPUT_MODE` should be in `BAM_Mode` or in `non BAM_Mode`.

| 4:2 | OUTPUT_FIFO_SIZE | R | 0x0 = 2X BLOCK_SIZE<br>0x1 = 4X BLOCK_SIZE<br>0x2 = 8X BLOCK_SIZE<br>0x3 = 16X BLOCK_SIZE |
| 1:0 | OUTPUT_BLOCK_SIZE | R | Indicates the block size associated with Block_Mode for output<br>0x0 = 04 bytes (FIFO mode only)<br>0x1 = 16 bytes<br>0x2 = 32 bytes<br>0x3 = Reserved |

### 6.1.5.3.4 QUP_SW_RESET (0x0000 000C)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
- **Reset state**: 0x00000000

A write to this register resets the entire QUP core and all mini-cores. The internal registers are brought back to their reset values. Reading of this register returns zero. The AHB clock domain reset stays asserted until either the CC_QUP_SPI_CLK or CC_QUP_I2C_CLK domains are reset.
It is prohibited to write to any QUP register during this period and failing to do so causes an ERROR response on the AHB bus. In order to avoid this, software should poll the STATE_VALID bit of the 0x0000 0004 QUP_STATE register until it is asserted.

#### QUP_SW_RESET Bits
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | QUP_SW_RESET | A write to this register resets the entire QUP core and all the mini-cores. |
<!-- page 1742 -->

### 6.1.5.3.5 QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL (0x0000 0014)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
- **Reset state**: 0x00000000

#### QUP_TRANSFER_CANCEL Bits
| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:8 | TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID | RW | This field include the ID of the transfer that is scheduled for cancellation. This field is valid when asserting TRANSFER_CANCEL bit.<br>0xFF (W) = Cancels the current transfer regardless of its LOCAL_ID. Canceling an I2C transfer requires using non-legacy tags. |
| 7 | TRANSFER_CANCEL | W | 0x0 (W) = Disabled<br>0x1 (W) = Causes the hardware to go to pause_state when the LOCAL_ID = TRANSFER_CANCEL_ID. This allows flushing the rest of the transfer to implement cancel API. Canceling an I2C transfer requires using non-legacy tags. |

### 6.1.5.3.6 QUP_OPERATIONAL (0x0000 0018)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
- **Reset state**: 0x000000C0

See Section 6.1.4.4 regarding the correct interpretation of the various service interrupts generated by QUP and their relation to these register bits.

#### QUP_OPERATIONAL Bits
| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15 | NWD | R | Notify when done (NWD) status bit, which when set indicates a NWD acknowledgment is outstanding.<br>0x0 (R) = Cleared by QUP hardware when the NWD request is acknowledged by assertion of done_toggle. This bit is always unconditionally cleared in RESET_STATE.<br>0x1 (R) = Set by QUP hardware when NWD is signaled from BAM. |
| 14 | DONE_TOGGLE | R | Status bit that provides the current state of the side-band done_toggle signal sent to BAM. At each NWD acknowledgment, this bit toggles. |
| 13 | IN_BLOCK_READ_REQ | R | 0x0 (R) = No pending flag<br>0x1 (R) = QUP input FIFO has BLOCK_SIZE_INPUT amount of data ready for reading. Valid only in Block_Mode |
<!-- page 1743 -->

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12 | OUT_BLOCK_WRITE_REQ | R | 0x0 (R) = No pending flag<br>0x1 (R) = QUP output FIFO needs BLOCK_SIZE_OUTPUT amount of data to be written. Valid only in Block_Mode. |
| 11 | MAX_INPUT_DONE_FLAG | R | 0x0 (R) = No pending flag<br>0x1 (R) = QUP input FIFO has reached the programmed 0x0000 0200 QUP_MX_INPUT_COUNT value. Valid in FIFO_Mode (only if MX_READ_COUNT is nonzero), Block_Mode and Bam_Mode (for debug only). |
| 10 | MAX_OUTPUT_DONE_FLAG | R | 0x0 (R) = No pending flag<br>0x1 (R) = QUP output FIFO has reached the programmed 0x0000 0100 QUP_MX_OUTPUT_COUNT value. Valid in Block_Mode and Bam_Mode (for debug only). |
| 9 | INPUT_SERVICE_FLAG | RW | 0x0 (RW) = 0x0 (R) = No pending flag. Writing a 'zero' to this bit does nothing.<br>0x1 (R) = QUP input FIFO has an outstanding input service request. At the point in time this bit is set, the hardware also asserts qup_irq.<br>0x1 (W) = Clears it and acknowledges software has or will read the data. Valid in all modes, recommended to be masked in BAM mode. |
| 8 | OUTPUT_SERVICE_FLAG | RW | 0x0 (RW) = Writing a 'zero' to this bit does nothing.<br>0x1 (R) = QUP output FIFO has an outstanding output service request. At the point in time this bit is set, the hardware also asserts qup_irq.<br>0x1 (W) = Clears it and acknowledges software has or will read the data. Valid in all modes, recommended to be masked in BAM mode. |
| 7 | INPUT_FIFO_FULL | R | 0x0 (R) = The input FIFO is not full<br>0x1 (R) = The input FIFO is full and can accept no more data from the QUP mini-core. |
| 6 | OUTPUT_FIFO_FULL | R | 0x0 (R) = The output FIFO is not full<br>0x1 (R) = The output FIFO is full and can accept no more CRIF writes. |
| 5 | INPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY | R | 0x0 (R) = The input FIFO is empty<br>0x1 (R) = The input FIFO has at least one value in it to be read |
| 4 | OUTPUT_FIFO_NOT_EMPTY | R | 0x0 (R) = The output FIFO is empty<br>0x1 (R) = The output FIFO has at least one value in it to be shifted out |

### 6.1.5.3.7 QUP_ERROR_FLAGS (0x0000 001C)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
<!-- page 1744 -->

- **Reset state**: 0x00000000

All bits in this register are set by hardware and remain set until cleared by software. Writing a one to a bit clears it while writing a zero leaves the bit unchanged.

#### QUP_ERROR_FLAGS Bits
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 5 | OUTPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR | 0x0 = No error<br>0x1 = The output FIFO was full when a CRIF write was attempted to the FIFO. The write is discarded. |
| 4 | INPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR | 0x0 = No error<br>0x1 = The input FIFO was empty when a CRIF read was attempted to the FIFO. The read value returns is indeterminate. |
| 3 | OUTPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR | 0x0 = No error<br>0x1 = The output FIFO was empty when an output shift operation required a value. |
| 2 | INPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR | 0x0 = No error.<br>0x1 = The input FIFO was full when an input shift operation provided a new value. When this happens, the new value is discarded. |

### 6.1.5.3.8 QUP_ERROR_FLAGS_EN (0x0000 0020)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
- **Reset state**: 0x0000003C

Each bit in this register controls the setting of a corresponding error flag. If set, each bit enables generation of qup_irq and the setting of the corresponding error flag in the 0x0000 001C QUP_ERROR_FLAGS register for the specified error case. At reset, all error enable bits are set to '1'.

#### QUP_ERROR_FLAGS_EN Bits
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 5 | OUTPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR_EN | 0x0 = Error flag disabled<br>0x1 = Enables output over run error generation |
| 4 | INPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR_EN | 0x0 = Error flag disabled<br>0x1 = Enables input under run error generation |
| 3 | OUTPUT_UNDER_RUN_ERR_EN | 0x0 = Error flag disabled<br>0x1 = Enables output under run error generation |
| 2 | INPUT_OVER_RUN_ERR_EN | 0x0 = Error flag disabled<br>0x1 = Enables input over run error generation |

### 6.1.5.3.9 QUP_OPERATIONAL_MASK (0x0000 0028)

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_QUP_CORE_CLK
<!-- page 1745 -->

- **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register masks several 0x0000 0018 QUP_OPERATIONAL flags from creating an interrupt.

#### QUP_OPERATIONAL_MASK Bits
