### 6.4.5 HS USB programming guide

The digital USB controller is an augmented version of a Chip Idea USB controller. This is true for the register map as well. For a programming guide on registers, see the corresponding programmer manuals listed in Section 6.4.5.2.

This section provides details on the additional registers added to this controller and theory of operation surrounding those registers.

This section covers the following operational modes and features that are added on top of the USB controller:
- ULPI_VIEWPORT usage
- ULPI low-power mode
- Smart peripheral subsystem (SPS)
- Link power management (LPM)
- PHY control register
- General controller configuration options in addition to provided
- Software control for SESS_VLD


#### 6.4.5.1 USB_HS hardware configuration

The `USB_OTG_HS_GENERIC1` and `USB_OTG_HS_GENERIC2` registers represent the hardware configuration of the `USB_HS` instance. This hardware configuration is set during hardware design process.

This register includes the following information about the controller instance:
- **USB_HS_TX_DEPTH** – The number of words in Tx buffer. 2048 words for HS instances, 64 for FS instances. The word is 36 bits – 32 bits for data and 4 bits for tag that holds hardware internal information, which is used by the controller for correct data flow management.
- **USB_HS_RX_DEPTH** – The number of words in Rx buffer. 256 words for HS instances, 16 for FS instances. The word is 36 bits – 32 bits for data and 4 bits for tag that holds hardware internal information, which is used by the controller for correct data flow management.
- **USB_HS_DEV_EP** – The number of endpoints supported by the controller. 16 endpoints for HS instances, 4 endpoints for FS instances. Actual number of endpoints is `USB_HS_DEV_EP` x 2 – there is the same number of IN and OUT endpoints.
- **UTMI_PHY_SW_IF_EN** - Specifies if a software control register interface to UTMI PHY block is enabled. For controller instance connected to PHY, this parameter is 1. It is 0 in all other cases (FS 3-wire, FS 2-wire).
- **USE_SPS** – Specifies if BAM is connected to USB controller. 1 means BAM is connected. 0 means BAM is not connected.
- **USE_SPS_AHB2AHB** – Specifies if AHB2AHB bridge is connected between BAM and SPS Fabric AHB.
- **MAX_PIPES** – The number of supported SPS pipes; 16 BAM pipes are used.
<!-- page 1925 -->

#### 6.4.5.2 Chip Idea controller software procedures and sequences

All original software procedures and sequences of USB controller are defined in *CI13320A - USB 2.0 High Speed Controller Reference Manual* and *CI13320A - High Speed Controller Programmer's Manual*.

The operational model in the host mode is based on EHCI standard. For more information on the EHCI deviations in host mode of the Chip Idea controller and the operational model in device mode, see *CI13320A - USB 2.0 High Speed Controller Reference Manual*.

For more information on the host data structures and device data structures used by the Chip Idea controller, see *CI13320A - High Speed Controller Programmer's Manual*.


#### 6.4.5.3 Additions to the Chip Idea Controller

##### 6.4.5.3.1 Hardware limitations and software recommendations

1. Always make data transfers 4 byte aligned both in host and device - QCTDD01906466. Nonaligned transfers might reduce performance significantly.
2. When working with BAM, set this BAM register bit to 1:
   `BAM_CTL [BAM_EN_ACCUM] = 1`
   BAM optimized processing of INCR unspecified arriving from USB controller (Rx direction performance impact).
3. In host mode USB scratch registers `USB_OTG_HS_SCRATCH_RAMn` must be accessed only when the USB is in Idle – that is during initialization, during or after suspend, and so on. Otherwise, access to scratch may collide with Tx transfer – shared resource – Tx buffer. QCTDD01947542
4. When working with BAM mode in device, ensure that the following field in the eTD descriptor is always 0:
   `Total_bytes_enable = 0`
   This means that the USB BAM mode transfer size is controlled by BAM and not by the USB software.
5. Ensure that the maximum packet length (MPL) is $\ge$ 512 or $\le$ 256. Do not use MPL in this range – 257 < MPL < 511.
6. Always use unspecified length bursts (default value): `USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST [AHB_BURST] = 0`
7. Only when working with streaming mode disabled:
   `USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE [SDIS] = 1`
   Configure this register (fix to streaming mode disabled mode)
   `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2 [TX_BUF_PREFETCH_FIX_EN] = 1`
   Otherwise do not modify this register.
<!-- page 1926 -->

##### 6.4.5.3.2 General configuration

Several registers are used to configure the USB controller during initialization mode. These configuration registers must be written before the software driver sets Run/Stop bit in `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD [RS]` register to 1.

###### USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST

The `USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST` register must be always configured to `0x0` to ensure correct operation of the USB controller.

###### USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE

The USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE software driver must set the `XTOR_BYPASS` bit to `0` to enable the AHB transactor within the USB module. The AHB transactor is used for AHB master transactions when BAM is disabled or not connected at all.

The software driver must set `HPROT_MODE` to `0b10` to allow posted AHB write transactions for OUT data movement and nonposted AHB write transactions for device queue head (dQH) and device transfer descriptor (dTD) updates.

The `ASYNC_BRIDGES_BYPASS` bit allows bypassing the AHB2AHB bridge on the AHB master interface.
- The default reset value of `ASYNC_BRIDGES_BYPASS` bit is 0: AHB2AHB bridge is enabled.
- Software driver can write 1 to `ASYNC_BRIDGES_BYPASS` bit if the peripheral NoC clock frequency is above 55 MHz. The target PNoC frequency is 100 MHz.
- In case peripheral NoC clock frequency is below 55 MHz, software driver must write 0 to `ASYNC_BRIDGES_BYPASS` bit. This is the case in SVS mode – PNoC clock goes below 50 MHz.

> [!NOTE]
> USB controller reset is required if there is switch in `ASYNC_BRIDGES_BYPASS` bit during active operation.

###### USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG

Bits 15:0 of the `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG` register must be configured to `0x0C90` to ensure correct operation of the USB controller.

- `TESTMUX_SEL_3_0` = 0000
- `PE_DP_TXFIFO_IDLE_FORCE` = 1
- `ULPI_SERIAL_EN` = 0
- `STREAM_RX_BYPASS_ENABLE` = 0
- `PE_RX_BUF_PENDING_EN` = 1
- `HOST_SIM_TIMERS_EN_*` = 0
- `DSC_PE_RST_EN` = 1
<!-- page 1927 -->

- `ISO_FIX_EN` = 1
- `DMA_HPROT_CTRL` = 0
- `USB_BAM_DISABLE` = 0
- `TESTMUX_SEL_4` = 0
- `SYS_CLK_SW_EN` = 0

###### USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2

The `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` register must be configured to `0x1F60` to ensure correct operation of the USB controller.

- `SCRATCH_RAM_EN` = 1
- `SESS_VLD_CTRL_EN` = 0
- `CI_T_WTSUSRSTHS_EN` = 1
- `CI_T_UCH_EN` = 1
- `DP_RESET` = 0
- `ZLP_PRIME` = 0
- `NO_SOF_RX_FIFO_FULL` = 0
- `WRONG_OPMODE_SUSP` = 0
- `RESUME_END_INTR` = 0

> [!NOTE]
> During HS host operation, ensure to configure the `ULPI_TX_PKT_EN_CLR_FIX = 0` bit.


##### 6.4.5.3.3 Software control for SESS_VALID

Typically, the PHY generates the `SESS_VALID` signal based on the VBUS state and reports it to the link via RX CMD.

The `USB_HS` controller provides a method to ignore the `SESS_VALID` information from the PHY and controls the `SESS_VALID` directly by the software.

To do this, the software driver must perform the following steps:
1. Write 1 to the `SESS_VLD_CTRL_EN` bit of the `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` register.
2. Write 1 to the `SESS_VLD_CTRL` bit of the `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register to enable operation of USB2 controller.
3. In Device mode, when VBUS is detected by PMIC and not routed to the PHY to enable the DP pull-up, the software sets `VBUSVLDEXT` and `VBUSVLDEXTSEL` in `ULPI_REG MISC_A`.
<!-- page 1928 -->

4. Write 0 to the `SESS_VLD_CTRL` bit of the `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register to disable operation of USB2 controller.

> [!NOTE]
> The method described previously can be used if PHY does not provide VBUS indication and VBUS is detected by some other external circuit.


##### 6.4.5.3.4 Software control for chirp timing in device mode

USB_HS controller provides a software configurable value for the chirp timing in device mode. There are two parameters that affect device chirp K timing that are controlled by the software.
- `ci_t_uch_en`: When this bit is 0, the device port control state machine drives chirp K for 1 ms. When this bit is 1, the device port control state machine drives chirp K for 2 ms. Default value is 1 - legacy behavior.
- `ci_t_wtsusrsths_en`: When this bit is 0, the device port control state machine waits 2.5 μs from USB reset detection until starting driving chirp K. When this bit is 1, the device port control state machine waits 1.5 ms from USB reset detection until starting driving chirp K. Default value is 1 - legacy behavior.

These configuration bits are used to reduce wait time from the time USB reset is detected by the device until chirp K is transmitted by the device.

###### USB_OTG_HS_SCRATCH_RAMn

The Scratch RAM is a set of 16 registers ranging from `0x40` to `0x7C`, required for passing USB software information between different images. To enable software accesses to these registers, `SCRATCH_RAM_EN` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` must be set to 1.

###### USB_OTG_HS_TXFILLTUNING

The host transmits prebuffer packet tuning fields of register control performance tuning associated with how the host controller posts data to the TX latency FIFO before moving the data onto the USB bus.

The software driver must set `TXFIFOTHRES` bits in this register to at least `0x2`.


##### 6.4.5.3.5 Power on Reset

USB_HS controller is part of `CORE_PD`. Its power initialization is same as the power initialization of the `CORE_PD` and is described in the Power Management section.

After MPM asserts VDD, TCXO On and there is hardware Power on Reset $\rightarrow$ Boot is Up
- Software vote for `VDD_MIN` off
- Vote for `TCXO`
- USB 3.3 V on
- USB 1.8 V on

Initialize following clocks:
- `USB_HS_SYSTEM_CLK`
<!-- page 1929 -->

- `USB_HS_AHB_CLK`

Reset the PHY by GCC register `GCC_USB_HS_PHY_BCR[0]`. Analog configurations are set after the power on reset (parameter override) only for USB2 PHY. See Section 6.4.5.3.8 for more information.

Continue with the GPIO configuration as described in Section 6.4.5.3.6 and initialization sequence as described in Section 6.4.5.3.7.


##### 6.4.5.3.6 GPIO configuration

`GPIO_110` must be associated with USB ID interface signal.


##### 6.4.5.3.7 Initialization sequence

These configuration registers must be written before the software driver sets Run/Stop bit in `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD [RS]` to 1.

> [!NOTE]
> After software reset via `USBCMD`, software must start initialization sequence again.

1. Software writes 0 to `USB2_PHY_IDHV_CLAMP_EN` and must not assert IDHV signal (ID detection is done by PMIC).
2. Software sets following register to achieve 60 MHz with minimal jitter (this can be done as part of the parameter override sequence since the PHY must be reset (POR) after changing those values):
   a. FSEL: 000
   b. PLLBTUNE: 1
3. Set `CM` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE`:
   a. 0x3 for HOST mode
   b. 0x2 for DEVICE mode
4. For DEVICE mode only: Set `SLOM` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE` register to 1.
5. Set `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register:
   a. Set `PTS` bits to:
      i. ULPI: 0x2
   b. Set `PSPD` bits to:
      i. ULPI: 0x2 (HS)
   c. Set `PP` bit to 1.
6. For DEVICE mode only:
   a. Configure `ENDPOINTLISTADDR` register. It is on the `USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR` register address (shared address).
7. Set Run/Stop bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` to 1.
<!-- page 1930 -->

##### 6.4.5.3.8 Writing parameter override

1. Software writes `0b10` to `PTS` bits of the `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register.
2. Software writes the required value to `PARAMETER_OVERRIDE_A/B/C/D` registers through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
3. Software asserts bit 0 in `GCC_USB_HS_PHY_BCR` for at least 10 μs to reset the PHY.

> [!NOTE]
> The PHY POR is controlled by GCC register `GCC_USB_HS_PHY_BCR[0]` and not by `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [0]`.


##### 6.4.5.3.9 ULPI_VIEWPORT usage

The `ULPI_VIEWPORT` register allows access to the PHY registers through the ULPI interface from the link.
To access the ULPI, `PTS` bits of the `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register must be set to `0b10`. Also, the ULPI interface must be out of reset.

###### ULPI sync state

The `ULPISS` (read only) is an indication of the state of PHY. The software must read this bit to ensure it can access the PHY register through the `ULPI_VIEWPORT`. When the PHY is in Low Power mode or Serial mode, this bit reads as 0.

###### Register reads

To read a PHY register, in `USB_OTG_HS_ULPI_VIEWPORT` register:
1. Set `ULPIADDR` to the required register address.
2. Set `ULPIRUN` to start a read operation.
3. Poll `ULPIRUN` until cleared.
4. Read result is stored in `ULPIDATRD` bits.

###### Register writes

To write a PHY register, in `USB_OTG_HS_ULPI_VIEWPORT`:
1. Set `ULPIADDR` to the required register address.
2. Set `ULPIDATWR` to the required data to be written.
3. Set `ULPIRW` to 1.
4. Set `ULPIRUN` to start a read operation.
5. Poll `ULPIRUN` until cleared.


<!-- page 1931 -->

#### ULPI FORCE

It might be required sometimes to abort the PHY when it controls the ULPI interface (ULPI_DIR is high). To do so, software must set the ULPIFORCE bit when performing read/write operation. This allows the link to abort the PHY, complete its access, and give control back to the PHY.

##### 6.4.5.3.10 USB bus operations

Bus operations include SUSPEND, Resume, RESET, and Remote Wakeup. For detailed Sequences, see *CI13320A - USB 2.0 High Speed Controller Reference Manual* and *CI13320A - High Speed Controller Programmer's Manual*.

##### 6.4.5.3.11 ULPI low power mode

Low Power mode is a feature defined by the ULPI specification. This feature is designed to signal a PHY that it can go to its low power state and turn-off PLL. The idea is that the link controller clears the SuspendM bit in the function control register. After that, the PHY stops the ULPI clock to the link and turns off its internal PLL. When the PHY is in Low Power mode, the Linestate is reflected on ULPI data 0 and data 1 lines and the PHY interrupt is reflected on ULPI data 3. ULPI data 0, 1, and 3 can then be used to generate an asynchronous interrupt from the link to the Process and trigger the exit from the Low Power mode to a synchronous operational mode of ULPI between the link and the PHY.

After entering the ULPI Low Power mode, the PHY can be put into Retention mode in which it must consume less power.

###### Entering low power mode in suspend state

1. Software driver receives Suspend interrupt (SLI bit in `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` register) and decides to enter Low Power mode.
2. Software sets the `OTGDISABLE` bit of the `POWER_AND_CLOCK_MANAGEMENT` register to 0x1 through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
3. Software clears `ACAENB`, `DCDENB`, `VDATSRCENB0`, `VDATDETENB0`, and `CHRGSEL` in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
4. Software driver writes 1 to `PHCD` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register. Software must poll up to 100 μs until `PHCD` bit is set. If `PHCD` fails, this could be due to RESUME or RESET being received between step 1 and 2. In this case, entering low power mode for SUSPEND must be canceled by skipping rest of the steps.
5. Software driver writes 1 to `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
6. Software driver checks `SUSP` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register. If this bit is 0, then software performs the following:
    a. Clears `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
    b. Clears `PHCD` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register.
    c. Skips steps 7-12.
<!-- page 1932 -->

7. Software driver writes 1 to `USB2_PHY_CLAMP_MPM_DPSE_DMSE_EN_N` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` register.
8. For retention from Suspend, software driver writes 1 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]`.
9. Software driver stops `USB_SYSTEM_CLK`.
10. Software driver votes for stopping the bus clock and for TCXO shutdown.
11. Software driver votes against `VDD_MIN`.
12. If retention from suspend is supported, software can vote for VDD minimization if PHY was put into retention. If not, software driver votes against `VDD_MIN`.

###### Host mode PHY low power mode

**Preconditions:**
* Software ensures that `OTGDISABLE` bit of `POWER_AND_CLOCK_MANAGEMENT` register is set to 0x1 through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
* `ACAENB`, `DCDENB`, `VDATSRCENB0`, `VDATDETENB0`, and `CHRGSEL` in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register are cleared. If ID is routed to the PHY, software sets the `IDPULLUP` to `OTG_CTRL_REG[0]` through the ULPI VIEW PORT.

When PHY is used and the software driver sets `SUSP` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register, the USB controller automatically goes into the Low Power mode. Hence, regardless if the software wants to enter Low Power mode or not, `PHCD` must not be set by the software driver.

Software needs to wait for the `PHCD` to get set for at least 5 ms before moving forward with the LPM sequence.

After the PHY is put into SUSPEND (and before software puts the PHY in retention), software asserts the `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[0]]` for at least 10 ns and de-asserts it. This enables the Autoresume (in Host mode only).

**For retention from Suspend:**
1. Software driver writes 1 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL[USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]`.
2. Software can vote for VDD min.

###### Exiting low power mode when USB is in suspend state and chip is not in TCXO shutdown and remote wakeup is issued

1. USB software driver detects an application request and decides to proceed with the Remote Wakeup.
2. Software driver enables `USB_SYSTEM_CLK`.
3. Software driver writes 0 to `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
4. Software driver writes to `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register:
    a. Clears `PHCD` bit. Software must poll up to 100 μs until `PHCD` bit is cleared.
    b. Sets `FPR` bit.
<!-- page 1933 -->

5. If the retention bit was asserted, software exit retention by writing 0 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]`.

###### Exiting low power mode when USB is in suspend state and host event is detected

1. One of the possible external wakeup events occurs:
    a. Host signals Resume.
    b. Host signal Reset.
    c. Cable is disconnected/VBUS drops.
2. USB controller detects a linestate change via ULPI data 0 and 1 or an interrupt from the PHY via ULPI data 3.
3. USB controller generates an asynchronous interrupt to the MPM via the Interrupt Controller. If there was TCXO shut down/VDD min, a change of DPHV/DMHV is detected by the MPM and interrupt is generated.
4. MPM starts the wake-up sequence of TCXO and the processor. (Only when the chip is in TCXO shutdown)
5. TCXO is turned on, stabilized and running. (Only when the chip is in TCXO shutdown)
6. Processor is awake and running. (Only when the chip is in TCXO shutdown)
7. The bus clock is resumed and starts toggling.
8. Software driver enables `USB_SYSTEM_CLK`.
9. Software driver writes 0 to `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
10. If the retention bit was asserted, software exit retention by writing 0 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]`.
11. Software driver proceeds to a standard Resume/Reset sequences as described in *CI13320A - USB 2.0 High Speed Controller Reference Manual* and *CI13320A - High Speed Controller Programmer's Manual*.

###### Exiting low power mode with retention when the cable is disconnected with or without VDD_MIN

1. HV interrupts are not routed to controller instead USB IRQ will be generated from `ulpi_rx_data`.
2. In case of VDD_MIN: Increase DVDD to a valid operating level, after DVDD has stabilized and returned to a valid operating level continue to next step.
3. Software driver writes 0 to `USB2_PHY_CLAMP_MPM_DPSE_DMSE_EN_N` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` register.
4. Disable the `USB2_PHY_IDHV_INTEN`, `USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_INTEN`, `USB2_PHY_DPSE_INTEN`, and `USB2_PHY_DMSE_INTEN` of the `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL`.

> [!NOTE]
> Software must not set `USB2_PHY_IDHV_INTEN`; ID detection is done by the PMIC.
<!-- page 1934 -->

5. Software driver writes 0 to `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
6. Disable Retention mode by writing 0 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]`.
7. Read `PHCD` bit in `PORTSC` to see if it was cleared.

###### Entering low power mode with retention when the cable is disconnected with VDD_MIN

1. Software driver checks that there is no active session (cable is disconnected, `PHY_SESS_VLD` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` register is 0, Run/Stop bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register is 0) and decides to enter Low Power mode.

> [!NOTE]
> The VBUS from the PMIC must also be disabled.

2. Software writes 0b10 to `PTS` bits of the `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register.
3. Set the `OTGDISABLE` bit of the `POWER_AND_CLOCK_MANAGEMENT` register to 0x1 through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
4. Clear `ACAENB`, `DCDENB`, `VDATSRCENB0`, `VDATDETENB0`, and `CHRGSEL` in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
5. Software sets the `IDPULLUP` by writing 1 to `USB_OTG_HS_OTGSC [IDPU]` and to `OTG_CTRL_REG[0]` through the ULPI VIEW PORT.
6. Software driver writes 1 to `PHCD` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register. Keep the reference clock active for a minimum of 2.5 μs after setting the `PHCD` bit to 1 and ensure that `PHCD` is changed to 1 by polling `PHCD` bit (`SUSPENDM` bit is changed to 0 inside the PHY) to ensure that all power-down signals are set.
7. Software driver writes 1 to `ULPI_STP_CTRL` and `ASYNC_INTR_CTRL` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.
8. Software driver writes 1 to the `USB2_PHY_CLAMP_MPM_DPSE_DMSE_EN_N` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` register.
9. Software driver writes 1 to `USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_INTEN` (`USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_INTEN` is set only in Device mode), `USB2_PHY_DPSE_INTEN`, and `USB2_PHY_DMSE_INTEN` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` register.

> [!NOTE]
> Software must not set `USB2_PHY_IDHV_INTEN`. In addition, ID detection is done by the PMIC.

10. Software driver writes 1 to `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL[USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]` register bit.
11. Software driver stops `USB_SYSTEM_CLK` and votes for stopping the bus clock, TCXO shutdown, and `VDD_MIN`.

###### Going to VDD_MIN with VDD180 power collapse

1. All domains are active and cable is unplugged.
<!-- page 1935 -->

2. Software follows the steps described in Section [blank].
3. After the USB software votes for `VDD_MIN`, it must know that the plan is to Power Collapse VDD180.
4. Software sets the `PHY_MPM_HV_CLAMP_EN`, `USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_CLAMP_EN`, `USB2_PHY_IDHV_CLAMP_EN` and `USB2_PHY_CLAMP_MPM_DPSE_DMSE_EN_N` bits in `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` to 0.
5. Interrupt to propagate through PMIC.
6. USB software indicates to MPM that VDD330 and VDD180 can be collapsed.
7. VDDCX lowered to SVS level or `VDD_MIN` and potentially – Power Collapse of VDD180 and VDD330.

###### Coming out of power collapse of VDD180 with VDDCX nominal/min/SVS

1. **Initial state:**
    a. VDD180 in Power Collapse.
    b. `Freezeio_n` is low (if VDDCX is MIN).
    c. `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [USB2_PHY_PLLITUNE[1]]` of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` is high.
2. Interrupt from PMIC (or other source) wakes up the system.
3. VDDCX to SVS or Nominal.
4. Software driver writes 0 to `USB2_PHY_IDHV_INTEN` and `USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_INTEN`, `USB2_PHY_DPSE_INTEN`, and `USB2_PHY_DMSE_INTEN` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` register.
5. Software enables VDD180.
6. Software set `PHY_MPM_HV_CLAMP_EN` and `USB2_PHY_OTGSESSVLDHV_CLAMP_EN` bits in `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL` to 1.

> [!NOTE]
> `USB2_PHY_IDHV_CLAMP_EN` must not be set.

7. Software sets `USB2_PHY_RETEN` `USB_OTG_HS_PHY_CTRL [1]` to 1.
8. Software reads `PHCD` bit to check if it was cleared.
9. Software asserts `GCC_USB_HS_PHY_BCR[0]` to POR reset the PHY for at least 10 μs.
10. USB software and hardware sets up the system to start the USB connection (Restart the USB controller).

###### Entering suspend in HOST mode (not compatible with EHCI standard)

1. Software sets `ASE` and `PSE` of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` to 0.
2. Software sets `R/S` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` to 0.
3. Software sets `SUSP` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register to 1.
<!-- page 1936 -->

##### 6.4.5.3.12 Charger detection

###### Data contact detection

1. Run/Stop bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register is 0.
2. Software clears the `OTG_CTRL_REG`.
3. Software sets `OPMODE` to 0b01 in `FUNCTION_CTRL_REG`.
4. Software checks that there is a valid VBUS voltage (`SESS_VLD`).
5. Software writes 0b10 to `PTS` bits of `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC`.
6. Software clears `DCDENB` and `ACAENB` bits of the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register.
7. Software clears `DCDINTSTS` in `INTR_STS_REG_ADDR`.
8. Software sets `DCDINTENB` of `ALT_INTERRUPT_ENABLE` register.
9. Software sets the `DCDENB` and `ACAENB` bits of `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL`.
10. Software starts a long-term timer (~500 ms) to wait for DCD detection timeout.
11. A Positive DCD is established if:
    a. Timeout happens before receiving DCD interrupt.
    b. On receiving BC interrupt, software checks `ALT_INTERRUPT_LATCH` and finds that `DCDINTSTS` is high.
    c. Software finds that `RIDFLOAT` is low for more than 10 ms (detection is done by PMIC).
12. Software clears `ACAENB`, `DCDENB` of `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL`.
13. Software clears `DCDINTENB` of `ALT_INTERRUPT_ENABLE`.
14. Software clears `DCDINTSTS` and `RIDFLOATINTSTS` of `ALT_INTERRUPT_LATCH`.
15. Software continues to charging port detection.

> [!NOTE]
> When there is a reset (`USB2_PHY_ARES`/POR or `ULPIPOR` in `HS_PHY_CTRL` register, software ensures that the `ALT_INTERRUPT_LATCH` was cleared.

> [!NOTE]
> It is possible to use polling of the interrupt status signal instead of using the Interrupt mechanism.

##### 6.4.5.3.13 Charging port detection (primary port detection)

This section outlines how a dedicated charging port (DCP), CDP, and docking station may be detected.

1. Software detects VBUS and completes DCD detection first.
2. If in Host mode, software sets `DMPULLDOWN`, `DPPULLDOWN` in `OTG_CTRL_REG`.
3. Software sets `CHRGSEL`, `VDMSRCAUTO` bits in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register to 0.
<!-- page 1937 -->

4. Software sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` bit in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register to 1 and starts a 40-ms timer.
5. The PMIC must detect the resistance on the ID line and if it is not floating go to ACA procedure.
6. On timeout, software checks `CHGDET` for detection output.
7. If `CHGDET` is 1, then port is a charging port (DCP, CDP or ACA_A Docking Station).
8. Software sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` to 0 to end detection procedure and continues to docking station detection/DCP/CDP detection.

> [!NOTE]
> It is possible to use polling of the interrupt status signal instead of using the Interrupt mechanism.

###### Docking station detection (ACA-Dock)

After port detection (see Section 6.4.5.3.13 for more information), if `CHGDET` is 1, software can check `RID` value (detected by the PMIC). If the port is a docking station, `RID` value is `RID_A`, else continue to DCP/CDP detection.

> [!NOTE]
> A low-speed device connected to the accessory port of an ACA may also be detected as a charging port with `RID_A`. To rule out this possibility, software must check the line-state bits in `USB_OTG_HS_PORTSC` register. For a low-speed device that is asserting the D- pull-up, this indicates a high on D-, while for a docking station D- will be less than VLGC (see *Battery Charging Specification Rev. 1.1* http://www.usb.org/developers/docs/devclass_docs/) and therefore, line-state indicates a logic low on D-.

###### DCP detection

1. After primary detection, if `CHGDET` in `CHARGING_DETECTION_OUTPUT` register was 1 and the ID line has `RID_FLOAT`, it must be determined whether it is DCP or CDP.
2. To differentiate between DCP and CDP, software can either enable the D+ pull-up and monitor line-state or use DCP detection as follows.
3. Software sets the `CHRGSEL` to 1 and sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` bits in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register to 1 and starts 40-ms timer.
4. On timeout, software checks `CHGDET` in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_OUTPUT` register for detection output.
5. If `CHGDET` is 1, then port is a DCP (otherwise CDP).
6. Software sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` to 0 in a `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` to end detection procedure.

###### Accessory Charger Adapter detection

1. When VBUS is on or ID pad is grounded (through a resistor), the `ID_GND` detection circuitry in the PHY must be disabled first by disabling the ID pull-up bit 5 in `USB_OTG_HS_OTGSC` register.
2. Then ACA detection must be turned on in the PMIC.
<!-- page 1938 -->

3. Software must monitor the `RID` value and move to the right ACA state based on the new `RID` value.
4. If ID is not `RIDA`, software can decide ACA is connected.
5. If `ID = RIDA`, it must be checked whether it is ACA-A or ACA-Dock.
6. Software sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` bit in the `CHARGING_DETECTION_CONTROL` register to 1 and starts 40-ms timer.
7. On timeout, software checks `CHGDET` for detection output, when `CHGDET` is high it is ACA-Dock.
8. Software sets `VDATSRCENB` and `VDATDETENB` to 0.

Outside of monitoring interrupts, software must also determine whether ACA_A, ACA_B or ACA_C states are valid by looking at `RID` once device mode charging port detection is negative, that is, to differentiate between standard downstream port (SDP), which has `RID_FLOAT` from ACA_A/B/C, which have `RID_A/B/C`.

> [!NOTE]
> It is possible to use polling of the interrupt status signal instead of using the interrupt mechanism.

#### Figure 6-76: Battery charging operation

*Description:* Flowchart detailing the battery charging detection logic.
1. **Initial Check**: The algorithm checks VBUS. It loops until `VBUS > Votg_sess_vld`.
2. **DCD (Data Contact Detection)**: Once VBUS is detected, it starts a timer and enables DCD. It waits for DCD check conditions:
   - If `TDCD_TIMEOUT` occurs, or `D+ < VLGC` for `TDCD_DBNC`, or `ID != RID_FLOAT` for `TDCD_DBNC`, it enters the main detection flow.
   - Alternatively, if `ID != RID_FLOAT` for `TDCD_DBNC` is met, it can branch directly to the ACA detection branch.
3. **Primary Detection**: If the DCD conditions are met, it sets `D+ = VDP_SRC` and branches based on the line state:
   - **Path A (DCP/CDP)**: If `D- > VDAT_REF` & `D- < VLGC` & `ID = RID_FLOAT` are true, it branches to DCP/CDP detection.
     - If the device is ready to be enumerated, it connects as a DCP/CDP.
     - Otherwise, it performs **Secondary Detection** by setting `D- = VDM_SRC`.
       - If `D+ > VDAT_REF` is true, it is identified as a **DCP** (Idcp).
       - If `D+ < VDAT_REF` is true, it is identified as a **CDP** (Icdp).
   - **Path B (SDP)**: If `(D- < VDAT_REF + D- > VLGC)` & `ID = RID_FLOAT` is true, it is identified as a Standard Downstream Port (**SDP**, Isusp).
   - **Path C (ACA)**: If `ID != RID_FLOAT` is true, it proceeds to ACA branch.
4. **ACA Detection Branch**: Checks the resistance on the ID pin:
   - If `ID = RID_A` and `(D- > VDAT_REF & D- < VLGC)`, it is identified as **ACA-Dock** (Icdp).
   - If `ID = RID_A` and `(D- < VDAT_REF + D- > VLGC)`, it is identified as **ACA-A** (Idcp).
   - If `ID = RID_B`, it is identified as **ACA-B** (Idcp).
   - If `ID = RID_C`, it is identified as **ACA-C** (Idcp).
<!-- page 1939 -->

##### 6.4.5.3.14 Enabling/disabling DP when VBUS is not routed to PHY

When VBUS is detected by the PMIC, software sets `VBUSVLDEXTSEL` and `VBUSVLDEXT` in `MISC_A` register. This enables the DP pull-up during the Device mode.

When VBUS is disconnected, software can clear those bits.

##### 6.4.5.3.15 SPS mode operation

SPS presents a concept of transferring the data directly between two independent hardware modules without software copy operations. The data transfers are managed using a pipe mechanism. The hardware module that provides the data is a Producer on the pipe. The hardware module that retrieves the data from the pipe is a Consumer on the pipe. For more SPS architecture and design details, see *SPS and BAM documentation*.

The USB_HS link controller supports integration into SPS and it can operate as a Producer/Consumer of the pipe. The USB controller cannot interface the pipe directly because it is not compliant with SPS descriptors and pipe memory concept, therefore the USB controller has BAM. BAM provides an interface to the pipe memory from one side and a data control interface to the hardware controller on the other side.

USB_HS controller supports SPS mode of operation in device mode and it does not support SPS mode in host mode.

From a hardware-software interaction perspective, two additions to the original hardware-software interface of the USB controller are defined.

###### Mapping endpoints to pipes

The USB_HS controller has 16 IN and 16 OUT endpoints. Endpoints IN 0 and OUT 0 are always Control Endpoints. The USB_HS controller supports SPS mode of operation only for Bulk Endpoints (IN and OUT). SPS mode is not supported for Control, Interrupt, and Isochronous Endpoints.

The maximum number of supported pipes is defined during the design time of the target chip. For USB2 controller it is 16.

Any Bulk IN/OUT Endpoint can be associated with any pipe number. Only one specific endpoint can be connected to one pipe and vice versa.

USB2 controller has 15 registers that define the mapping between endpoints and pipes – `USB_OTG_HS_ENDPT_PIPE_IDn`, n=[1..15].

The software must map the endpoints to the pipes and write `USB_OTG_HS_ENDPT_PIPE_IDn`, n=[1..15] registers before writing `RS` bit of `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` register.

###### Enhanced transfer descriptor

A device driver of USB_HS controller uses `dQH` and `dTD` to set up data transfers for IN and OUT endpoint of the controller.
<!-- page 1940 -->

There is one `dQH` per each IN and OUT endpoint. `dQH` points to a linked list of `dTD`(s). `dTD` contains transfer length and pointers to the data buffers that software setups before queuing the `dTD`.

`dQH` and `dTD` data structures are defined in *CI13320A - USB 2.0 High Speed Controller Reference Manual* and *CI13320A - High Speed Controller Programmer's Manual*.

When operating in pipe mode, the USB2 controller moves the data to/from the pipe memory. A new special descriptor is used by the USB2 controller for pipe mode transfers – Enhanced Transfer Descriptor (eTD). eTD is based on the definition of `dTD` with several changes. eTD follows the same connectivity rules – it is linked to `dQH` or `dTD`.

#### Figure 6-77: Enhanced transfer descriptor

*Description:* Bitfield diagram of the Enhanced Transfer Descriptor (eTD) layout. It consists of 5 words (each 32-bit).
* **Word 0 (Read-Only)**:
  * Bit 31: `mult`
  * Bit 30: `zlt`
  * Bits 27-29: Reserved (`0`)
  * Bits 16-26: `Maximum Packet Length`
  * Bit 15: `ios`
  * Bits 0-14: Reserved (`0`)
* **Word 1 (Read/Write - part of ETD)**:
  * Bits 5-31: `Current dTD pointer`
  * Bits 0-4: Reserved (`0`)
* **Word 2 (Read/Write - part of ETD)**:
  * Bits 5-31: `Next dTD pointer`
  * Bits 2-4: Reserved (`0`)
  * Bit 1: `Type` (indicated in red)
  * Bit 0: `T` (Terminate)
* **Word 3 (Read/Write - part of ETD)**:
  * Bits 10-31: Reserved (`0`) (indicated in red)
  * Bit 9: `ioc` (Interrupt On Complete) (indicated in red)
  * Bit 8: `zlt` (Zero Length Termination Select) (indicated in red)
  * Bits 0-7: `status` (indicated in red)
* **Word 4 (Read/Write - part of ETD)**:
  * Bit 31: `tse` (indicated in red)
  * Bit 30: Reserved (`0`) (indicated in red)
  * Bits 0-29: `Total bytes` (indicated in red)

*Legend:*
* White blocks: Device Controller Read-Only
* Grey blocks: Device Controller Read/Write (Words 1-4 are bracketed as "ETD")

###### Description of the eTD fields:

* **Next dTD pointer**: This field contains the physical memory address of the next dTD/eTD to be processed. The field corresponds to memory address signals [31:5], respectively.
* **Type**: This bit is used to indicate the type of the next transfer descriptor - dTD/eTD.
  * 0 - The next transfer descriptor is a legacy transfer - dTD.
  * 1 - The next transfer descriptor is a pipe transfer - eTD.
* **Terminate (T)**: 1=pointer is invalid. 0=pointer is valid (points to a valid Transfer Element Descriptor). This bit indicates to the Device Controller that there are no more valid entries in the queue.
* **Interrupt On Complete (IOC)**: This bit is used to indicate if USBINT is to be set in response to device controller being finished with this dTD.
* **Zero Length Termination Select (ZLT)**: This bit is used to indicate when a zero-length packet is used to terminate transfers where the total transfer length is a multiple of the Maximum Packet Length. This bit overrides the bit in the Queue Head.
  * 0 – Enable zero length packets to terminate transfers equal to a multiple of the Maximum Packet Length (default).
  * 1 – Disable the zero length packets on transfers that are equal in length to a multiple Maximum Packet Length.


<!-- page 1941 -->

* **Status**: This field is used by the Device Controller to communicate individual command execution states back to the Device Controller software. This field contains the status of the last transaction performed on this qTD. The bit encodings are:
  * **Bit Status field description**
    * 7 – Active
    * 6 – Halted
    * 5 – Data Buffer Error
    * 3 – Transaction Error
    * 4, 2, 0 – Reserved
* **Total Bytes Enable (TBE)**: this field is used to enable the Total Byes field.
  * 1 – Total number of bytes that are moved with this transfer descriptor is defined by both the total bytes field and the sideband information signal’s coming from the BAM. BAM generates sideband information based on the BAM descriptors. The smaller between them defines the length of the transfer.
  * 0 – Total number of bytes that are moved with this transfer descriptor is defined by the sideband information signal’s coming from the BAM. BAM generates sideband information based on the BAM descriptors.
  * **Total Bytes**: This field specifies the total number of bytes to be moved with this transfer descriptor. This field is decremented by the number of bytes moved during the transaction and only on the successful completion of the transaction. If TBE = 0 then the controller ignores this field.

### Enhanced transfer descriptor – hardware limitation/software recommendation
* When BAM is not used, ensure `bam_en` = 0
* Always use TBE = 0
  For more details, see Section 6.4.5.3.1.
* When BAM is used, configure this bit to enhance performance:
  `BAM_CTL [BAM_EN_ACCUM] = 1`
  For more details, see Section 6.4.5.3.1.

### Operational model of enhanced transfer descriptors
There are two supported modes of operation for eTDs.
* First mode is used in case of an “infinite” data stream between the USB2 controller and pipe. A possible use case of this mode is an A2 block connected to USB_HS controller for IP packets traffic.
* Second mode is used if there are predefined data transfers between the USB2 controller and the pipe. A possible use case of this mode is an SDCC controller connected to USB2 controller for mass storage traffic.
<!-- page 1942 -->

#### "Infinite" pipe mode
In this mode dQH points to an eTD.

The “Next dTD Pointer” of the eTD points to the start address of itself creating a “loop” in such case.

The “Type” field is 1, which means the Transfer Descriptor is eTD and the USB_HS controller is expected to move the data to/from the pipe memory.

TBE bit is 0 that means the data transfer length is determined according to the BAM sideband information based on BAM descriptors.

For A2 use case, the ZLT bit is 0, which means USB transfers, can be terminated by a zero-length data transaction.

#### Total Bytes pipe mode
One possible use case for this mode is a Mass storage use case when USB2 controller communicates with SDCC. In this mode dQH can point to an eTD or dTD. The same endpoint is used to transfer the data both in direct mode using dTD and in pipe mode using eTD. eTD can point to dTD and dTD can point to eTD.

The Next dTD Pointer of the eTD points to the start address of next dTD and the Next dTD Pointer of the dTD points to the start address of next eTD. This allows smooth transition between the direct mode and pipe mode transfers on the same endpoint.

The Type field is 1 if the next linked TD is an eTD, and 0 if the next linked TD is a dTD.

TBE bit is 1 for the eTD, which means that the length of the data transfer is defined in Total Bytes field of the eTD.

For the mass storage case, the ZLT bit is 1 that means USB transfers never finishes with a zero-length data transaction even if the data transfer is an integer multiple of a Max Packet Length of the associated endpoint.

### 6.4.5.3.16 HBM mode operation
The HBM (Host Bus Manager) enables reducing software interfere in Host mode by generating “infinite” USB (Bulk) transfers. The HBM uses BAM as memory manager and substitutes software operation by manipulating the controller/software interface.

The HBM is EHCI compliant. The HBM section of HPG specifies the additional software sequences required for HBM operation.

#### HBM initialization sequence
To initiate the HBM, software must configure the HBM registers with the required modes and mapping the BAM pipes into the USB Endpoints.
1. Set HBM_EN in `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_CFG` register: Enable the HBM.
2. Set the EP-Pipe mapping into `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_QH_MAP_PIPE` registers.
<!-- page 1943 -->

    * For each HBM pipe, the software must write the related QH address from the Async schedule.
3. Set `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_PRODUCER` with the pipes in PRODUCER mode (pipes connected to IN EPs).
4. Optional setting of `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PARK_MODE_DISABLE` and `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_ZLT_DISABLE` registers:
    * Park mode enables executing up to 3 USB packets from each QH in the Async schedule before continuing to the next QH. The number of the executed packets is determined according to the amount of data available from BAM.
    * ZLT means that every USB transfer must be ended with a short packet. In case the transfer length is a multiple of Max Packet Size, the HBM generates a ZLP - zero length packet. If the ZLT is disabled, the HBM does not generate a ZLP (OUT EPs) when the transfer size is multiple of Max Packet Size.
    * The default values are both Park mode and ZLT enabled. Software must not access these registers in regular mode of work. In case software wants to disable Park mode or ZLT, it must set the bits according to the Pipe numbers. For example: setting bit #2 of `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_ZLT_DISABLE` disable ZLTs for Pipe number 2.
5. Set `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_EN` register with the active HBM pipes. Activating a pipe must be after all the HBM EP/pipes are configured.
6. BAM registers configuration and descriptor programming are required along with the HBM initialization.
7. QH and qTD must be activated after the HBM initialization is done. For QH and qTD requirements for HBM mode usage, see Section .

#### HBM initialization sequence – requirements for QH and qTD
1. QH and qTD must be EHCI compliant.
2. QH Horizontal Link Pointer must point to next QH Address (according to EHCI specification) to keep controller in endless loop.
3. Set `qTD.Buffer_Pointer` with 0x0. The qTD Buffer Pointer Address is not relevant for HBM. Data address is defined by the BAM descriptors. HBM might override these fields.
4. Total Bytes To Transfer qTD field are not relevant for HBM. The actual transfer length depends on the BAM descriptor programming and not on the qTD Total Bytes To Transfer field.
5. The `QH.Terminate` field and the `qTD.Status` field must have a valid Active bit (0x80 in the example) after the HBM initialization is done.

#### Figure: Queue Head (QH) Layout
*Description:* A diagram showing the 32-bit word layout of an EHCI Queue Head (QH). The structure consists of 12 words (offsets 0x00 to 0x2C).
- The first three words (0x00-0x08) contain QH Horizontal Link Pointer, Endpoint Capabilities/Characteristics, and Split Transaction State.
- The remaining nine words (0x0C-0x2C) are highlighted in yellow, representing the Transfer Overlay area (which mirrors a qTD structure): Current qTD Pointer, Next qTD Pointer, Alternate Next qTD Pointer, qTD Token (containing Total Bytes, Status, etc.), and five Buffer Pointers.
- Specific fields include: Maximum Packet Length, Device Address, EndPt, Status, Total Bytes to Transfer, and Buffer Pointers (Page 0 to 4).

#### Figure: Queue Element Transfer Descriptor (qTD) Layout
*Description:* A diagram showing the 32-bit word layout of an EHCI Queue Element Transfer Descriptor (qTD). It consists of 8 words (offsets 0x00 to 0x1C).
- Offsets 0x00 and 0x04 contain the Next qTD Pointer and Alternate Next qTD Pointer.
- Offset 0x08 contains the qTD Token, with fields: dt (Data Toggle), Total Bytes to Transfer, ioc (Interrupt on Complete), C_Page (Current Page), Cerr (Error Counter), PID Code, and Status.
- Offsets 0x0C to 0x1C contain five Buffer Pointers (Page 0 to 4). Buffer Pointer 0 also contains the Current Offset.
- Highlighted in yellow are: dt, Total Bytes to Transfer, C_Page, Cerr, Status, and Current Offset.

### HBM reset sequence
There are two kinds of software reset for the HBM – a general HBM reset and a pipe reset.

The general reset eliminates the entire HBM pipes configuration and counters and therefore a full initialization sequence is required after such an operation.

The recommended software sequence for the general reset:
1. Terminate all HBM related QHs and deactivate their qTDs.
2. Disable HBM: `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_CFG` register.
3. Generate a reset sequence for the BAM.
4. Reset the HBM (`USB_OTG_HS_HBM_SW_RST`).
5. Generate a full initialization sequence for the HBM.

The HBM pipe reset does not modify the HBM configurations and resetting only the internal counters of the chosen pipe. In this operation software must generate a BAM pipe reset and does not have to reconfigure the HBM:
1. Terminate the HBM pipe related QHs and deactivate their qTDs.
2. Disable HBM pipe: `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_EN` register.
3. Generate a pipe reset sequence for the BAM.
<!-- page 1946 -->

4. Reset HBM pipe sideband (`USB_OTG_HS_HBM_SB_SW_RST`).
5. Enable HBM pipe in `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_PIPE_EN` register.
6. Enable QH and qTD (software may reconfigure new QH and qTD, but in this case, the related `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_QH_MAP_PIPE` register must be reconfigured).

In both reset sequences, software may prepare a new QH and qTD structures and change the QH mapping (`USB_OTG_HS_HBM_QH_MAP_PIPE`).

### HBM pause/finish transfer
The HBM works with infinite USB transfers, therefore software must actively stop the HBM/USB operations. To stop USB EP working in HBM mode software stop the Asynchronous Schedule, pop the QH of the HBM EP from the Asynchronous List and enable the Asynchronous Scheduler.

The sequence:
1. Set 0 into `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` [ASE].
2. Polling on `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` [AS] until reading 0.
3. Remove the HBM EP QH from the Asynchronous List (link the previous QH to the next QH).
4. Set 1 into `USB_OTG_HS_USBCMD` [ASE].

### HBM test bus operations
The HBM contains debug capabilities through the controller test bus. Software can control the general USB test bus outputs by configuring the test bus mux from `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_CFG` register:
1. Set `HBM_TEST_BUS_SEL` accordingly.
2. Set `HBM_TEST_BUS_EN` field.
3. Software can sample the test bus values from `USB_OTG_HS_TEST_BUS` register.

### 6.4.5.3.17 APF operation
The APF (AXI pre-fetch) enhances the USB_HS performance, in normal operation the AHB read data through the AHB bus. When APF is enabled, the APF fetches larger chunks of data for the USB_HS controller, in this way the number of accesses to the PCNOC/SNOC is reduced significantly.

#### APF might exceed allocated buffer during BAM transfer
BAM transfers use cyclic data buffer, The APF does not have indication when this buffer is about to cycle so it brings data in opportunistic way.

It means that if there is large transfer, it brings 128 B even if the buffer is going to cycle after 1 B, when the buffer is cycled the extra data get flushed and the APF brings the data again from the beginning of the buffer.

BAM data buffer should be set to 128 B less than the allocation in the system memory in order not to exceed the allocated space for the buffer.
<!-- page 1947 -->

#### APF enable
To enable the APF/AXI bus operation, do the following sequence only during initialization or suspend:
1. Enable SMMU to work with the USB AXI bus.
2. Enable APF by setting 1 to `USB_OTG_HS_APF_CTRL` [APF_EN] register.

#### APF AXI hresp error handling
If there is hresp error over the AXI bus, software might receive interrupt from the CI controller.
1. Enable interrupt generation by writing to this register - `USB_OTG_HS_APF_CTRL` [APF_ERR_RESP_EN]
   The APF has set of registers that captures the AXI bus status during hresp = error. You can read those registers to analyze the hresp = error.
2. Ensure that hresp = error interrupt was triggered by reading 1 from this register - `USB_OTG_HS_APF_ERR_ADDR` [APF_ERR_INT].
   If not, hresp = error interrupt was not triggered.
3. Read those registers and analyze their values - `USB_OTG_HS_APF_ERR_ADDR`, `USB_OTG_HS_APF_ERR_CTRL`, `USB_OTG_HS_APF_ERR_DATA_LSB`, `USB_OTG_HS_APF_ERR_DATA_MSB`
4. To clear the interrupt register `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` [SEI]:
    a. Write to this register - `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` [SEI]
    b. Wait 1 μs or more.
    c. Read this register - `USB_OTG_HS_USBSTS` [SEI]
        i. If it is equal to 0, finish
       ii. If it still equal 1, return to step “a”

## 6.4.5.4 Hardware and software debug events

### 6.4.5.4.1 Hardware and software event buses
USB_HS block provides four outputs of 32 bits each:
1. `USB_OTG_HS_SW_EVENTS` - USB_HS software events.
2. `USB_OTG_HS_HW_EVENTS` - USB_HS hardware events.
3. `USB_OTG_HS_BAM_SW_EVENTS` - BAM software events.
4. `USB_OTG_HS_BAM_HW_EVENTS` - BAM hardware events.
<!-- page 1948 -->

### 6.4.5.4.2 USB_OTG_HS_SW_EVENTS description
USB_HS software events debug bus is enabled by bit 14 of `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` register (default value is 1 – enabled).

| USB_OTG_HS_SW_EVENTS bit number | Software event |
| :---: | --- |
| 0 | session start (VBUS rise) |
| 1 | session end (VBUS fall) |
| 2 | connect |
| 3 | disconnect |
| 4 | bus reset start |
| 5 | bus reset end |
| 6 | suspend start |
| 7 | suspend end |
| 8 | resume start |
| 9 | resume end |
| 10 | remote wake up |
| 11 | enter Low Power mode |
| 12 | exit Low Power mode |
| 13 | USB interrupt (USBSTS[0]) |
| 14 | USB error interrupt (USBSTS[1]) |
| 15 | port change interrupt (USBSTS[2]) |
| 16 | system error interrupt (USBSTS[4]) |
| 17 | frame rollover interrupt (USBSTS[3]) |
| 18 | async list advance interrupt (USBSTS[5]) |
| 19 | host async interrupt (USBSTS[18]) |
| 20 | host periodic interrupt (USBSTS[19]) |
| 21 | NAK interrupt (USBSTS[16]) |
| 22 | OTGSESSVLD interrupt |
| 23 | ID interrupt |
| 24 | DP/DM HV interrupt |
| 25 | PHY misc interrupt |
| 26 | IN EP priming is active |
| 27 | OUT EP priming is active |
| 28 | IN EP flush is active |
| 29 | OUT EP flush is active |
| 30 | At least one IN EP is primed and transfer is in progress |
| 31 | At least one OUT EP is primed and transfer is in progress |
<!-- page 1949 -->

### 6.4.5.4.3 USB_OTG_HS_HW_EVENTS description
USB hardware events debug bus is connected to the hardware debug bus of the USB_HS controller and HBM, if present. USB hardware events debug bus is enabled by bit 14 of `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` register (default value is 1 – enabled).

USB2 debug bus is a mux of 16 debug buses of the USB_HS controller and 16 debug buses of the HBM.

Bit 1 of `USB_OTG_HS_HBM_CFG` selects between the HBM debug bus and USB_HS controller debug bus. Value of 1 selects HBM, value of 0 selects USB2 controller.

Bits 0-3 and 14 of `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG` selects one of 16 debug buses of the USB_HS controller.

## 6.4.6 USB PHY registers

### 6.4.6.1 USB PHY registers overview
Software can access the registers that are described in this section via ULPI. To avoid confusion by overlap with vendor-specific registers defined for legacy USB PHYs, a starting address offset of 0x80 is chosen for these registers (from the 0x80 – 0xFF range allocated for vendor specific use in the extended register set per UTMI+ Low Pin Interface (ULPI) Specification Revision 1.1).

For some writable registers, a read/write register address is defined and two additional register addresses are defined for selectively setting or clearing specific bits in the register (similar to ULPI v1.1 specification convention).

> [!NOTE]
> While the interrupt latch register in the immediate register set (address 0x14) is cleared automatically on reading it, the alternate interrupt latch register in the extended register set (0x91-0x92) requires software to write a 1 to each bit to be cleared.

#### 6.4.7.3 USB_HS register definitions

##### 6.4.7.3.1 0x0000 0000 USB_OTG_HS_ID

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x0042FA05

The USB_OTG_HS_ID register is the identification register. It provides a simple way to determine if the USB-HS USB 2.0 controller is provided in the system. The ID register identifies the USB-HS USB 2.0 controller and its revision.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | RESERVED_BITS31_24 | These bits are reserved and must be set to zero. |
| 23:16 | REVISION | This field contains the revision number of the controller - 0x42. |
| 15:8 | NID | This field contains the complement version of ID[7:0] - 0xFA. |
| 7:0 | ID | This field is the configuration number. This number is set to 0x05 and indicates that the peripheral is the USB-HS USB 2.0 controller. |
<!-- page 1960 -->

##### 6.4.7.3.2 0x0000 0004 USB_OTG_HS_HWGENERAL

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000005C2

The 0x0000 0004 USB_OTG_HS_HWGENERAL register contains the general hardware parameters.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:11 | RESERVED_BITS31_11 | – |
| 10:9 | SM | VUSB_HS_PHY_SERIAL = 2 |
| 8:6 | PHYM | VUSB_HS_PHY_TYPE = 7 |
| 5:4 | PHYW | VUSB_HS_PHY16_8 = 0 |
| 3 | BWT | This bit is reserved for internal testing = 0 |
| 2:1 | CLCK | VUSB_HS_CLOCK_CONFIGURATION = 1 |
| 0 | RT | VUSB_HS_RESET_TYPE = 0 |

* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

### 6.4.7.3.5 0x0000 0010 USB_OTG_HS_HWTXBUF

**Type:** R

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x80070A08

The `USB_OTG_HS_HWTXBUF` register contains the Tx buffer hardware parameters.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | TXLCR | This bit is fixed to 1'b1 so that the local context registers are included in the design.<br>This means that the DMA context is implemented in flip-flops. |
| 30:24 | RESERVED_BITS30_24 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 23:16 | TXCHANADD | VUSB_HS_TX_CHAN_ADD - Defines the number of address lines needed per Endpoint per the TX latency buffer. Its reset value is taken from a GENERIC value passed to the controller. |
| 15:8 | TXADD | VUSB_HS_TX_ADD - Defines the number of address lines needed per the entire TX latency buffer. Its reset value is taken from a GENERIC value passed to the controller. |
| 7:0 | TXBURST | VUSB_HS_TX_BURST - Defines the data burst length of the AHB master interface in Quad-words (4-byte increments) of the TX data. Its reset value is taken from a GENERIC value passed to the controller.<br>Note: The actual burst lengths depend on the settings of USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE and USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST registers. |

| 15:8 | RX_ADD | VUSB_HS_RX_ADD - Defines the number of address lines needed per the entire RX latency buffer. Its reset value is taken from a GENERIC value passed to the controller. |
| 7:0 | RX_BURST | VUSB_HS_RX_BURST - Defines the data burst length of the AHB master interface in Quad-words (4-byte increments) of the RX data. Its reset value is taken from a GENERIC value passed to the controller.<br>Note: The actual burst lengths depend on the settings of USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE and USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST registers. |

### 6.4.7.3.8 0x0000 0080 USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER0LD

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER0LD` register is the general-purpose timer #0 load register. This register contains the timer duration or load value. See the `GPTIMER0CTRL` register for a description of the timer functions.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | RESERVED_BITS31_24 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 23:0 | GPTLD | General purpose timer load value. This field is the value to be loaded into the GPTCNT countdown timer on a reset action. This value in this register represents the time in microseconds minus 1 for the timer duration. Example: for a one millisecond timer, load 1000-1 = 999 or 0x0003E7.<br>Max value is 0xFFFFFF or 16.777215 seconds |
<!-- page 1963 -->
### 6.4.7.3.9 0x0000 0084 USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER0CTRL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER0CTRL` register is the general-purpose timer #0 control register. This register contains the control for the timer and a data field can be queried to determine the running count value. This timer has a granularity of 1 ms and can be programmed to a little over 16 seconds. There are two modes supported by this timer: the first is a one-shot and the second is a looped count, which is described in the following register table. When the timer counter value transitions to zero, an interrupt can be generated using the timer interrupts in the `USBTS` and `USBINTR` registers.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | GTPRUN | General purpose timer run<br>Read/write<br>Value 0 = Timer stop<br>Value 1 = Timer run<br>This bit enables the general-purpose timer to run. Setting or clearing this bit does not have an effect on the `GPTCNT`. |
| 30 | GPTRST | General purpose timer reset<br>Write-only<br>Value 0 = No action<br>Value 1 = Load counter value<br>Writing a one to this bit will reload the `GPTCNT` with the value in `GPTLD`. |
| 29:25 | RESERVED_BITS29_25 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 24 | GPTMODE | General purpose timer mode<br>Read/write<br>Value 0 = One shot<br>Value 1 = Repeat<br>This bit selects between a single timer countdown and a looped countdown.<br>In the one-shot mode, the timer counts down to zero, generates an interrupt, and stops until the counter is reset by the software.<br>In the repeat mode, the timer counts down to zero, generate an interrupt, and automatically reload the counter to begin again. |
| 23:0 | GPTCNT | General purpose timer counter<br>Read-only<br>This field is the value of the running timer. |

### 6.4.7.3.10 0x0000 0088 USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER1LD

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 1964 -->
The `USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER1LD` register is the general-purpose timer #1 load register (referred to as control register in the original text description). This register contains the timer duration or load value. See the `GPTIMER0LD` register for a description of the timer functions.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | RESERVED_BITS31_24 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 23:0 | GPTLD | General purpose timer load value. This field is the value to be loaded into the `GPTCNT` countdown timer on a reset action. This value in this register represents the time in microseconds minus 1 for the timer duration. Example: for a one millisecond timer, load 1000-1 = 999 or 0x0003E7.<br>Note: Max value is 0xFFFFFF or 16.777215 seconds. |

### 6.4.7.3.11 0x0000 008C USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER1CTRL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER1CTRL` register is the general-purpose timer #1 control register. See the description of the `USB_OTG_HS_GPTIMER0CTRL` register for details about this register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | GTPRUN | General purpose timer run<br>Read/write<br>Value 0 = Timer stop<br>Value 1 = Timer run<br>This bit enables the general-purpose timer to run. Setting or clearing this bit does not have an effect on the `GPTCNT`. |
| 30 | GPTRST | General purpose timer reset<br>Write-only<br>Value 0 = No action<br>Value 1 = Load counter value<br>Writing a one to this bit reloads the `GPTCNT` with the value in `GPTLD`. |
| 29:25 | RESERVED_BITS29_25 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 24 | GPTMODE | General purpose timer mode<br>Read/write<br>Value 0 = One shot<br>Value 1 = Repeat<br>This bit selects between a single timer countdown and a looped countdown. In the one-shot mode, the timer counts down to zero, generate an interrupt, and stop until the counter is reset by the software. In the repeat mode, the timer counts down to zero, generate an interrupt, and automatically reload the counter to begin again. |
| 23:0 | GPTCNT | General purpose timer counter<br>Read-only<br>This field is the value of the running timer. |
<!-- page 1965 -->
### 6.4.7.3.12 0x0000 0090 USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_AHB_BURST` register determines the AHB master mode of the USB HS controller.

> [!NOTE]
> If the `USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE` is configured to be 0x0 (the AHB Transactor is used), this register must be 0x0 as well, otherwise the AHB Master bus behavior is undefined. Use values other than 0x0 only if setting `USB_OTG_HS_AHB_MODE` to 0x1.
<!-- page 1966 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:3 | RESERVED_BITS31_3 | Must be set to zero. |
| 2:0 | AHB_BURST | AMBA AHB BURST. This is a read/write field that selects the following options for the `m_hburst` signal of the AMBA master interface:<br>- `3'b000`: INCR burst of unspecified length<br>- `3'b001`: INCR4, nonmultiple transfers of INCR4 are decomposed into singles<br>- `3'b010`: INCR8, nonmultiple transfers of INCR8 are decomposed into INCR4 or singles<br>- `3'b011`: INCR16, nonmultiple transfers of INCR16 are decomposed into INCR8, INCR4, or singles<br>- `3'b100`: This value is reserved and must not be used.<br>- `3'b101`: INCR4, nonmultiple transfers of INCR4 are decomposed into smaller unspecified length bursts<br>- `3'b110`: INCR8, nonmultiple transfers of INCR8 are decomposed into smaller unspecified length bursts<br>- `3'b111`: INCR16, nonmultiple transfers of INCR16 are decomposed into smaller unspecified length bursts<br><br>In all cases where the unspecified length burst is allowed, singles access may also occur, this is mostly true when the transaction is not 32-bit aligned.<br><br>Two consecutive single accesses must not happen. When a `INCRx` burst size is selected and the transfer is not multiple of the `INCRx` burst, the burst is decomposed in the different ways.<br><br>With `AHBBRST[2] = 1`, the smaller bursts are of unspecified length; with `AHBBRST[2] = 0`, the smaller bursts are smaller `INCRx` or singles. For example, assume that it is required at a given time, to transfer 22 words of information, for the following values of `AHBBRST` the master sequence is as follows:<br>- `3'b101`: INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR unspec. length<br>- `3'b110`: INCR8 + INCR8 + INCR4 + INCR unspec. length<br>- `3'b111`: INCR16 + INCR4 + INCR unspec. length<br>- `3'b001`: INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + INCR4 + SINGLE + SINGLE<br>- `3'b010`: INCR8 + INCR8 + INCR4 + SINGLE + SINGLE<br>- `3'b011`: INCR16 + INCR4 + SINGLE + SINGLE<br><br>This field after reset is set to a default value that can be configured in the file `vusb_hs_cfg.vhd`.<br><br>The `AHBBRST` field is only used when the AMBA-AHB system interface has been selected. It has no effect for controllers featuring BVCI interface. In the latter case, the read returns zeros.<br><br>When this field is different from zero, the value of the fields `TXBURST` / `RXBURST` in register `BURSTSIZE` 160h is ignored by the controller. Internally the `BURSTSIZE` is set to the value of the `INCRx` AMBA burst. Since this has a direct relation with the burst sizes, you must be careful with AHB burst selected. Although the `TXBURST` / `RXBURST` are bypassed, this register can still be written / read with no effect, while the `AHBBRST` field is nonzero. |
<!-- page 1967 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |

### 6.4.7.3.15 0x0000 009C USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000830

The `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG` register is used to configure various features that are added to the HS USB controller.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 15 | SYS_CLK_SW_EN | This bit is applicable only in SPS Device mode. When this bit is set then USB controller always voting for `USB_SYSTEM_CLK`. Default value is 0 - USB controller does not request `USB_SYSTEM_CLK` when in Low Power mode. |
| 14 | TESTMUX_SEL_4 | See `TESTMUX_SEL_3_0` the first 4 bits of this register. |
| 13 | USB_BAM_DISABLE | This bit disables the BAM logic inside the USB and makes it work in the Legacy mode. |
| 12 | DMA_HPROT_CTRL | When this bit is set, link controller always does nonposted dQH writes. |
| 11 | ISO_FIX_EN | This bit enables fix for Isochronous bug in CI controller |
| 10 | DSC_PE_RST_EN | This bit enables an automatic reset of Device PE state machine on disconnection event when operating as device. |
| 9 | HOST_SIM_TIMERS_EN_SUSP | When this bit is set (1), the timers used for the USB suspend process short for faster simulation and ATE time. When this bit is clear(0), the timers used for the USB suspend process are according to the USB specification. |
| 8 | HOST_SIM_TIMERS_EN_STD | When this bit is set (1), the timers used for the USB reset on the ULPI are short for faster simulation and ATE time. When this bit is clear(0), the timers used for the USB reset on the ULPI are according to the USB specification. |
<!-- page 1969 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7 | PE_RX_BUF_PENDING_EN | This is only valid in Device mode. Setting this bit causes to store a Transaction Status tag in the pending register instead of RX Buffer if the RX Buffer is full. The tag moves from pending register to RX Buffer as soon as it becomes not full. |
| 6 | STREAM_RX_BYPASS_ENABLE | This is only valid in Device mode. If SDIS bit is set (bit #4 of `USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE` (0x1A8)), that is streaming mode is disabled, setting this bit causes the RX traffic to override the SDIS bit, and to receive in streaming mode. TX will still be in nonstreaming mode. |
| 5 | ULPI_SERIAL_EN | This bit must be set to enable operation of ULPI Serial FS/LS mode. Default state is 1 - ULPI Serial mode is supported. |
| 4 | PE_DP_TXFIFO_IDLE_FORCE | This is only valid in Device mode. Setting this bit to 1 forces the `dp_tx_fifo_cmd_dev` to be equal to `PE_DP_TXFIFO_IDLE` when Device PE state machine in `REPORT_NAK` state and the RX Buffer is full. Reset value is 1. |
| 3:0 | TESTMUX_SEL_3_0 | With `TESTMUX_SEL_4` (bit 14) select one of the following test buses (values are binary 5-bit representation `{TESTMUX_SEL_4, TESTMUX_SEL_3_0}`):<br>- `00001`: Key state machines<br>- `00010`: dma_eng_0 dma_dev_sm_1<br>- `00011`: dma_eng_1 dma_context<br>- `00100`: dma_eng_2 dma_mem_arb<br>- `00101`: prot_eng_0<br>- `00110`: prot_eng_1<br>- `00111`: prot_eng_2<br>- `01000`: port_ctrl_0<br>- `01001`: port_ctrl_1<br>- `01010`: tx_buffer<br>- `01011`: rx_buffer<br>- `01100`: otg<br>- `10000`: dma_eng_3 dma_dev_sm_2<br>- `10001`: dma_eng_4 dma_traf, others zeros |
<!-- page 1970 -->

**Type:** RW

The `USB_OTG_HS_GEN_CONFIG_2` register is used to configure various features that have been added to the HS USB controller.

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |

| 25 | BVALID_SW_SEL | RW | BVALID_FROM_PHY = 0, BVALID_FROM_REG = 1, Default value 0 - BVALID_FROM_PHY |

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 10 | RX_FULL_NAK_EN | RW | When this bit is set the USB responds with NAKs for Host Tokens with slow AHB and when Streaming mode is enabled. Default value is 1. |
| 9 | ENDLESS_TD_EN | RW | When this bit is set, performance enhancements for 'infinite' Producer pipe (out endpoint with eTD that points to itself) are enabled. Default value is 1. |

| 5 | CI_T_UCH_EN | RW | When this bit is 0 then Device Port Control state machine drives Chirp K for 1 ms. When this bit is 1 then Device Port Control state machine drives Chirp K for 2 ms. Default value is 1 - legacy behavior. |

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

The convention is that the first N_PCC ports are assumed to be routed to companion controller 1, the next N_PCC ports to companion controller 2, and so on. In the previous example, the N_PCC could have been 4, where the first 4 are routed to companion controller 1 and the last two are routed to companion controller 2.<br>The number in this field must be consistent with N_PORTS and N_CC.<br>In this implementation, this field will always be clear (0). |
| 7:5 | RESERVED_BITS7_5 | Clear (0) these bits. |

### 6.4.7.3.25 0x0000 014C USB_OTG_HS_FRINDEX

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_USB_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_FRINDEX` register is the USB frame index register. This register is used by the host controller to index the periodic frame list. The register updates every 125 microseconds (once each microframe). Bits [N:3] are used to select a particular entry in the periodic frame list during periodic schedule execution. The number of bits used for the index depends on the size of the frame list as set by the system software in the frame list size field in the USBCMD register.
<!-- page 1989 -->

This register must be written as 32 bits. Byte writes produce undefined results. This register cannot be written unless the host controller is in the 'halted' state, as indicated by the HC halted bit. A write to this register while the run/stop bit is set (1) produces undefined results. Writes to this register also affect the SOF value.

In the device mode, this register is read-only and the device controller updates the `FRINDEX[13:3]` register from the frame number indicated by the SOF marker. Whenever a SOF is received by the USB bus, `FRINDEX[13:3]` is checked against the SOF marker. If `FRINDEX[13:3]` is different from the SOF marker, `FRINDEX[13:3]` is set to the SOF value and `FRINDEX[2:0]` is cleared (0) (that is, SOF for a 1 ms frame). If `FRINDEX[13:3]` is equal to the SOF value, `FRINDEX[2:0]` is incremented (that is, SOF for 125 μs micro-frame).

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:14 | RESERVED_BITS31_14 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 13:0 | FRINDEX | **Frame index**<br>The value in this register increments at the end of each time frame (for example, a microframe). Bits [N:3] are used for the frame list current index. This means that each location of the frame list is accessed eight times (frames or microframes) before moving to the next index.<br>The following data shows the values of N based on the value of the frame list size field in the USBCMD register when used in host mode:<br><br>\| USBCMD [Frame list size] \| Number of Elements \| N \|<br>\| :--- \| :--- \| :--- \|<br>\| 000b \| 1024 \| 12 \|<br>\| 001b \| 512 \| 11 \|<br>\| 010b \| 256 \| 10 \|<br>\| 011b \| 128 \| 9 \|<br>\| 100b \| 64 \| 8 \|<br>\| 101b \| 32 \| 7 \|<br>\| 110b \| 16 \| 6 \|<br>\| 111b \| 8 \| 5 \|<br><br>In the device mode, the value is the current frame number of the last frame transmitted. It is not used as an index. In either mode, bits 2:0 indicate the current micro frame. |

### 6.4.7.3.26 0x0000 0154 USB_OTG_HS_PERIODICLISTBASE

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_USB_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: 0x00000000
- **Constraint**: BANKED=host

The `USB_OTG_HS_PERIODICLISTBASE` register is the periodic list base address register. This 32-bit register contains the beginning address of the periodic frame list in the system memory. The HCD loads this register before starting the schedule execution by the host controller. The memory structure referenced by this physical memory pointer is assumed to be 4-Kbyte aligned. The
<!-- page 1990 -->

contents of this register are combined with the frame index register (FRINDEX) to enable the host controller to step through the periodic frame list in sequence.

> [!NOTE]
> This device is shared between the host controller and device controller operation. For host controller operation, this is the `USB_OTG_HS_PERIODICLISTBASE` register. For device controller operation, this is the `USB_OTG_HS_DEVICEADDR` register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:12 | PERBASE | **Base address (low)**<br>These bits correspond to memory address signals [31:12], respectively.<br>Only used by the host controller. |
| 11:0 | RESERVED_BITS11_0 | This field must be written as zeros. During runtime, the values of these bits are undefined. |

### 6.4.7.3.27 0x0000 0154 USB_OTG_HS_DEVICEADDR

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: CC_USB_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: 0x00000000
- **Constraint**: BANKED=device

The `USB_OTG_HS_DEVICEADDR` register is the USB device address register. The upper seven bits of this register represent the device address. After any controller reset or a USB reset, the device address is set to the default address (0). The default address matches all incoming addresses. The software shall reprogram the address after receiving a SET_ADDRESS descriptor.

The USBADRA is used to accelerate the SET_ADDRESS sequence by allowing the DCD to preset the USBADR register before the status phase of the SET_ADDRESS descriptor.

> [!NOTE]
> This device is shared between the host controller and device controller operations. For host controller operation, this is the `USB_OTG_HS_PERIODICLISTBASE` register. For device controller operation, this is the `USB_OTG_HS_DEVICEADDR` register.


<!-- page 1991 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:25 | USBADR | Device address<br>These bits correspond to the USB device address. |
| 24 | USBADRA | Device address advance<br>Default = 0<br>When this bit is clear (0), any writes to USBADR are instantaneous.<br>When this bit is set (1) at the same time or before USBADR is written, the write to the USBADR field is staged and held in a hidden register. After an IN occurs on endpoint 0 and is ACKed, USBADR will be loaded from the holding register.<br>The hardware will automatically clear (0) this bit on the following conditions:<br>1. IN is ACKed to endpoint 0 (USBADR is updated from staging register).<br>2. OUT/SETUP occur to endpoint 0 (USBADR is not updated).<br>3. Device reset occurs (USBADR is reset to 0).<br>Note: After the status phase of the SET_ADDRESS descriptor, the DCD has 2 ms to program the USBADR field. This mechanism will ensure this specification is met when the DCD cannot write of the device address within 2 ms from the SET_ADDRESS status phase. If the DCD writes the USBADR with USBADRA = 1 after the SET_ADDRESS data phase (before the prime of the status phase), the USBADR will be programmed instantly at the correct time and meet the 2-ms USB requirement. |
| 23:0 | RESERVED_BITS23_0 | These bits must be written as zeros. During runtime, the values of these bits are undefined. |

### 6.4.7.3.28 0x0000 0158 USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**BANKED=host**

The USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR register is the next asynchronous list address register.
This 32-bit register contains the address of the next asynchronous queue head to be executed by the host. Bits [4:0] of this register cannot be modified by the system software and will always return a zero when read.

> [!NOTE]
> The USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR register and the USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR register are shared between the host controller and device controller operations. For the host controller, this is the USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR register. For the device controller, this is the USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR register.
<!-- page 1992 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:5 | ASYBASE | Link pointer low (LPL).<br>These bits correspond to memory address signals [31:5], respectively. This field may only reference a queue head (QH). This field is only used by the host controller. |
| 4:0 | RESERVED_BITS4_0 | The values of these bits has no effect on circuit operation. |

### 6.4.7.3.29 0x0000 0158 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**BANKED=device**

The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR register is the endpoint list address register. In the device mode, this register contains the address of the top of the endpoint list in system memory. Bits [10:0] of this register cannot be modified by the system software and will always return a zero when read.

> [!NOTE]
> The USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR register and the USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR register are shared between the host controller and device controller operations. For the host controller, this is the USB_OTG_HS_ASYNCLISTADDR register. For the device controller, this is the USB_OTG_HS_ENDPOINTLISTADDR register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:11 | EPBASE | Endpoint list pointer (low)<br>These bits correspond to memory address signals [31:11], respectively. This field will reference a list of up to 32 queue heads (QH). That is, one queue head per endpoint & direction. |
| 10:0 | RESERVED_BITS10_0 | The values of these bits has no effect on circuit operation. |
