### 6.4.7.3.31 0x0000 0160 USB_OTG_HS_BURSTSIZE

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00001010

The USB_OTG_HS_BURSTSIZE register is the programmable burst size register. This register is used to control dynamically change the burst size used during data movement on the initiator (master) interface.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | RESERVED_BITS31_16 | The value of these bits has no effect on circuit operation. |
| 15:8 | TXPBURST | Programmable Tx burst length<br>This register represents the maximum length of the burst in 32-bit words while moving data from system memory to the USB bus. |
| 7:0 | RXPBURST | Programmable Rx burst length<br>This register represents the maximum length of the burst in 32-bit words while moving data from the USB bus to system memory. |

### 6.4.7.3.32 0x0000 0164 USB_OTG_HS_TXFILLTUNING

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The USB_OTG_HS_TXFILLTUNING register is the host transmit pre-buffer packet tuning register. The fields in this register control performance tuning associated with how the host controller posts data to the Tx latency FIFO before moving the data onto the USB bus. The specific areas of performance include the how much data to post into the FIFO and an estimate for how long that operation must take in the target system.

Definitions:
* **T0**: Standard packet overhead
* **T1**: Time to send data payload
* **Tff**: Time to fetch packet into TX FIFO up to specified level.
* **Ts**: Total packet flight time (send-only) packet
<!-- page 1994 -->

* **Ts** = T0 + T1
* **Tp** = Total packet time (fetch and send) packet = Tff + T0 + T1

Upon discovery of a transmit (OUT/SETUP) packet in the data structures, the host controller checks to ensure Tp remains before the end of the [micro] frame. If so it proceeds to pre-fill the TX FIFO. If at any time during the pre-fill operation the time remaining the [micro] frame is < Ts, then the packet attempt ceases and the packet is tried later. Although this is not an error condition and the host controller will eventually recover, a mark will be made the scheduler health counter to note the occurrence of a 'back-off' event. When a back-off event is detected, the partial packet fetched may require to be discarded from the latency buffer to make room for periodic traffic that will begin after the next SOF. Too many back-off events can waste bandwidth and power on the system bus, and thus must be minimized (not necessarily eliminated). Back-offs can be minimized with use of the TSCHHEALTH (Tff), as described in the register table.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:22 | RESERVED_BITS31_22 | The value of these bits has no effect on circuit operation. |
| 21:16 | TXFIFOTHRES | FIFO burst threshold<br>Default = 2<br>This register controls the number of data bursts that are posted to the TX latency FIFO in the host mode before the packet begins on to the bus. The minimum value is 2 and this value must be a low as possible to maximize USB performance. A higher value can be used in systems with unpredictable latency and/or insufficient bandwidth, where the FIFO may underrun because the data transferred from the latency FIFO to USB occurs before it can be replenished from system memory. This value is ignored if the stream disable bit in USBMODE register is set (1). |
| 15:13 | RESERVED_BITS15_13 | The value of these bits has no effect on circuit operation. |
<!-- page 1995 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:8 | TXSCHHEALTH | Scheduler health counter<br>Read/write to clear<br>Default = 0<br>This register increments when the host controller fails to fill the Tx latency FIFO to the level programmed by TXFIFOTHRES before running out of time to send the packet before the next start-of-frame. This health counter measures the number of times this occurs to provide feedback to selecting a proper TXSCHOH. Writing to this register will clear the counter and this counter will be at a maximum at 31. |
| 7:0 | TXSCHOH | Scheduler overhead<br>Default = 0<br>This register adds an additional fixed offset to the schedule time estimator described above as Tff. As an approximation, the value chosen for this register must limit the number of back-off events captured in the TXSCHHEALTH to less than 10 per second in a highly-utilized bus. Choosing a value that is too high for this register is not desired, as it can needlessly reduce USB utilization.<br>The time unit represented in this register is 1.267 ms when a device is connected in the high-speed mode for OTG and SPH. The time unit represented in this register is 6.333 ms when a device is connected in the low/full speed mode for OTG and SPH. The time unit represented in this register is always 1.267 times the MPH product. |

### 6.4.7.3.33 0x0000 0170 USB_OTG_HS_ULPI_VIEWPORT

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x08000000

The USB_OTG_HS_ULPI_VIEWPORT register provides indirect access to the ULPI PHY register set. Although the controller performs access to the ULPI PHY register set, there may be extraordinary circumstances where software may require direct access.

> [!CAUTION]
> Writes to the ULPI through the viewport can substantially harm standard USB operations. Currently, no usage model has been defined where the software must execute writes directly to the ULPI - see the exception regarding optional features below.

Executing read operations though the ULPI viewport must have no harmful side effects to standard USB operations.

> [!NOTE]
> The ULPI viewport is only synthesized in the design if the constant VUSB_HS_PHY_ULPI is set (1). If the ULPI interface is not enabled, this register will always read zeros.
<!-- page 1996 -->

Two operations can be performed with the ULPI viewport: wake-up and read/write operations. The wake-up operation is used to put the ULPI interface into normal operation mode and re-enable the clock, if necessary. A wake-up operation is required before accessing the registers when the ULPI interface is operating in the low power mode, serial mode, or car kit mode.

The ULPI state can be determined by reading the sync state bit (ULPISS). If this bit is set (1), then the ULPI interface is running in the normal operation mode and can accept read/write operations. If the ULPISS is clear (0), then read/write operations will not be able to execute. Undefined behavior will result if ULPISS = 0, and a read or write operation is performed.

To execute a wake-up operation, write all 32-bits of the ULPI Viewport where ULPIPORT is constructed appropriately, and the ULPIWU bit is set (1) and the ULPIRUN bit is clear (0). Poll the ULPI viewport until ULPIWU is zero for the operation to complete.

To execute a read or write operation, write all 32-bits of the ULPI viewport where ULPIDATWR, ULPIADDR, ULPIPORT, and ULPIRW are constructed appropriately, and the ULPIRUN bit is set (1). Poll the ULPI viewport until ULPIRUN is zero for the operation to complete. Once ULPIRUN is zero, the ULPIDATRD will be valid if the operation was a read.

The polling method above could also be replaced and an interrupt driven using the ULPI interrupt defined in the USBTS and USBINTR registers. When a wake-up or read/write operation completes, the ULPI interrupt will be set (1).

Several optional features may require to be enabled or disabled by the system software as part of system configuration. These bits are contained in the interface and OTG control registers of the ULPI PHY register set. These registers also contain bits that are controlled by the link dynamically and, therefore, must only be modified by the system software using the set/clear access method. Direct writes to these registers could have harmful side effects to the standard USB operations.

The following bits are optional bits:
* Bits 3 through 7 in the interface control register
* Bits 6 and 7 in the OTG control register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | ULPIWU | ULPI wake-up<br>Setting (1) this bit begins the wake-up operation. The bit will automatically transition to 0 after the wake-up is complete. Once this bit is set (1), the driver cannot clear it back to 0.<br>Note: The driver must never execute a wake-up and a read/write operation at the same time. |
| 30 | ULPIRUN | ULPI read/write run<br>Setting (1) this bit will begin the read/write operation. The bit will automatically transition to 0 after the read/write is complete. Once this bit is set (1), the driver cannot clear it back to 0.<br>Note: The driver must never execute a wakeup and a read/write operation at the same time. |
| 29 | ULPIRW | ULPI read/write control<br>This bit selects between running a read or write operation.<br>Value 0 = Read<br>Value 1 = Write |
<!-- page 1997 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 28 | ULPIFORCE | ULPI read/write force<br>This bit enables forcing register access during RX packet<br>Value 0 = register access is not forced during RX packet (default)<br>Value 1 = register access is forced during RX packet reception |
| 27 | ULPISS | ULPI sync state<br>Read Only<br>Value 1 = Normal sync state<br>Value 0 = In another state (for example, car kit, serial, low power)<br>This bit represents the state of the ULPI interface. Before reading this bit, the ULPIPORT field must be set accordingly if used with the multi-port host. Otherwise, this field must always remain 0. |
| 26:24 | ULPIPORT | ULPI port number<br>For the wakeup or read/write operation to be executed, this value selects the port number the ULPI PHY is attached to in the multi-port host. The valid range is 0 to 7. This field must always be written as a 0 for the non-multi-port products. |
| 23:16 | ULPIADDR | ULPI data address<br>When a read or write operation is commanded, the address of the operation is written to this field. |
| 15:8 | ULPIDATRD | ULPI data read<br>Read only<br>After a read operation completes, the result is placed in this field. |
| 7:0 | ULPIDATWR | ULPI data write<br>When a write operation is commanded, the data to be sent is written to this field. |

The host/device controller sets (1) this bit for all changes to the port device connect status, even if the system software has not cleared an existing connect status change. For example, if the insertion status changes twice before system software has cleared the changed condition, the hub hardware will be 'setting' an already-set bit (that is, the bit will remain set). The software clears this bit by writing a one to it. This field is zero if the port power (PP) bit in this register is zero in the host mode.<br>Device mode:<br>This bit is undefined in the device controller mode. |
| 0 | CCS | **Current connect status**<br>Read-only<br>Host mode:<br>- Value 1: Device is present on port<br>- Value 0: No device is present<br>Default = 0<br>This value reflects the current state of the port, and may not correspond directly to the event that caused the connect status change bit (bit 1) to be set (1). This field is clear if the port power (PP) bit in this register is clear (0) in host mode.<br>Device mode:<br>- Value 1: Attached<br>- Value 0: Not attached<br>Default = 0<br>If this bit is set (1), this indicates that the device successfully attached, and is operating in either high speed or full speed, as indicated by the high-speed port bit in this register. If this bit is clear (0), this indicates that the device did not attach successfully or was forcibly disconnected by the software clearing (0) the run bit in the USBCMD register. It does not state the device being disconnected or suspended. |

### 6.4.7.3.38 USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE (0x000001A8)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

The `USB_OTG_HS_USBMODE` register is the USB device mode register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:6 | RESERVED_BITS31_6 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 5 | VBPS | **VBUS power select**<br>- Value 0: Output is 0<br>- Value 1: Output is 1<br>This bit is connected to the `vbus_pwr_select` output and can be used for any generic control, but is named to be used by logic that selects between an on-chip VBUS power source (charge pump) and an off-chip source in systems when both are available. |


<!-- page 2011 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4 | SDIS | Stream disable mode<br>Value 0 = Inactive (default)<br>Value 1 = Active<br>**Device mode:**<br>Setting (1) this bit disables double priming on both the Rx and Tx for low bandwidth systems. This mode ensures that, when the Rx and Tx buffers are sufficient to contain an entire packet, the standard double buffering scheme is disabled to prevent overruns/underruns in bandwidth-limited systems.<br>*Note:* In the high-speed mode, a NYET handshake will respond to all packets received when the stream disable is active.<br>**Host mode:**<br>Setting (1) this bit ensures that overruns/underruns of the latency FIFO are eliminated for low bandwidth systems where the Rx and Tx buffers are sufficient to contain the entire packet. Enabling the stream disable also has the effect of ensuring that the Tx latency is filled to capacity before the packet is launched onto the USB.<br>*Note:* Time duration to pre-fill the FIFO becomes significant when the stream disable is active. See TXFILLTUNING and TXTTFILLTUNING [MPH only] to characterize the adjustments needed for the scheduler when using this feature.<br>*Note:* The use of this feature substantially limits of the overall USB performance. |
| 3 | SLOM | Setup lockout mode.<br>In the device mode, this bit controls the behavior of the setup lock mechanism. See Control Endpoint Operation Model.<br>Value 0 = Setup lockouts on (default)<br>Value 1 = Setup lockouts off (DCD requires use of a setup data buffer tripwire in USBCMD) |
<!-- page 2012 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2 | ES | Endian select<br>Read/write<br>This bit can change the byte ordering of the transfer buffers to match the host microprocessor bus architecture. The bit fields in the microprocessor interface and the DMA data structures (including the setup buffer within the device QH) are unaffected by the value of this bit, because they are based upon 32-bit words.<br>Value 0 = Little endian (default) - first byte referenced in the least significant byte of a 32-bit word.<br>Value 1 = Big endian - first byte referenced in most significant byte of a 32-bit word. |
| 1:0 | CM | Controller mode<br>Read/write once<br>The controller mode is defaulted to the proper mode for host-only and device-only implementations. For those designs that contain both host and device capability, the controller will default to an idle state and will require to be initialized to the desired operating mode after reset. For combination host/device controllers, this register can only be written once after reset. If it is necessary to switch modes, the software must reset the controller by writing to the RESET bit in the USBCMD register before reprogramming this register.<br>Value 00 = Idle [default for combination host/device]<br>Value 01 = Reserved<br>Value 10 = Device controller [default for device only controller]<br>Value 11 = Host controller [default for host only controller] |

### 6.4.7.3.39 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTSETUPSTAT (0x0000 01AC)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTSETUPSTAT register is the endpoint set-up status register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | RESERVED_BITS31_16 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 15:0 | ENDPTSETUPSTAT | Set-up endpoint status<br>For every set-up transaction that is received, a corresponding bit in this register is set (1). The software must clear or acknowledge the setup transfer by setting (1) a respective bit after it has read the setup data from the queue head. The response to a set-up packet as in the order of operations and total response time is crucial to limit bus time outs while the set-up lock-out mechanism is engaged.<br>This register is only used in the device mode. |
<!-- page 2013 -->
### 6.4.7.3.40 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTPRIME (0x0000 01B0)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTPRIME register is the endpoint initialization register. This register is only used in the device mode.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | PETB | Prime endpoint transmit buffer<br>For each endpoint, a corresponding bit is used to request that a buffer is prepared for a transmit operation to respond to a USB IN/INTERRUPT transaction. The software must set (1) the corresponding bit when posting a new transfer descriptor to an endpoint. The hardware will automatically use this bit to begin parsing for a new transfer descriptor from the queue head and prepare a transmit buffer. The hardware will clear (0) this bit when the associated endpoint(s) is (are) successfully primed.<br>*Note:* These bits will be momentarily set (1) by the hardware during hardware re-priming operations when a dTD is retired, and the dQH is updated.<br>PETB[15] - Endpoint #15<br>PETB[1] - Endpoint #1<br>PETB[0] - Endpoint #0. |
| 15:0 | PERB | Prime endpoint receive buffer<br>For each endpoint, a corresponding bit is used to request that a buffer is prepared for a receive operation for when a USB host initiates a USB OUT transaction. The software must set (1) the corresponding bit whenever posting a new transfer descriptor to an endpoint. The hardware will automatically use this bit to begin parsing for a new transfer descriptor from the queue head and prepare a receive buffer. The hardware will clear (0) this bit when the associated endpoint(s) is (are) successfully primed.<br>*Note:* These bits will be momentarily set (1) by the hardware during hardware re-priming operations when a dTD is retired, and the dQH is updated.<br>Bit 15 - Endpoint #15<br>Bit 1 - Endpoint #1<br>Bit 0 - Endpoint #0 |

### 6.4.7.3.41 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTFLUSH (0x0000 01B4)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 2014 -->
The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTFLUSH register is the endpoint de-initialize register. This register is only used in the device mode.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | FETB | Flush endpoint transmit buffer<br>Setting (1) a bit in this register will cause the associated endpoint to clear any primed buffers. If a packet is in progress for one of the associated endpoints, that transfer will continue until completion. The hardware will clear this register after the endpoint flush operation is successful.<br>FETB[15] - Endpoint #15<br>FETB[1] - Endpoint #1<br>FETB[0] - Endpoint #0 |
| 15:0 | FERB | Flush endpoint receive buffer<br>Setting a bit (1) will cause the associated endpoint to clear any primed buffers. If a packet is in progress for one of the associated endpoints, that transfer will continue until completion. The hardware will clear this register after the endpoint flush operation is successful.<br>Bit 15 - Endpoint #15<br>Bit 1 - Endpoint #1<br>Bit 0 - Endpoint #0 |

### 6.4.7.3.42 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTSTAT (0x0000 01B8)

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 2015 -->
The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTSTAT register is the endpoint status register. This register is only used in the device mode.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | ETBR | Endpoint transmit buffer ready<br>One bit for each endpoint indicates the status of the respective endpoint buffer. This bit is set (1) by the hardware as a response to receiving a command from a corresponding bit in the ENDPTPRIME register. There will always be a delay between setting (1) a bit in the ENDPTPRIME register and the endpoint indicating that it is ready. This delay time varies based upon the current USB traffic and the number of bits set (1) in the ENDPTPRIME register. The buffer ready status is cleared by a USB reset, by the USB DMA system, or through the ENDPTFLUSH register.<br>*Note:* These bits will be momentarily cleared by the hardware during hardware endpoint re-priming operations when a dTD is retired, and the dQH is updated.<br>ETBR[15] - Endpoint #15<br>ETBR[1] - Endpoint #1<br>ETBR[0] - Endpoint #0. |
| 15:0 | ERBR | Endpoint receive buffer ready<br>One bit for each endpoint indicates the status of the respective endpoint buffer. This bit is set (1) by the hardware as a response to receiving a command from a corresponding bit in the ENDPTPRIME register. There will always be a delay between setting (1) a bit in the ENDPTPRIME register and the endpoint indicating that it is ready. This delay time varies based upon the current USB traffic and the number of bits set (1) in the ENDPTPRIME register. The buffer ready status is cleared by a USB reset, by the USB DMA system, or through the ENDPTFLUSH register.<br>*Note:* These bits will be momentarily cleared by the hardware during hardware endpoint re-priming operations when a dTD is retired, and the dQH is updated.<br>ERBR[15] - Endpoint #15<br>ERBR[1] - Endpoint #1<br>ERBR[0] - Endpoint #0 |

### 6.4.7.3.43 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTCOMPLETE (0x0000 01BC)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 2016 -->
The register is the endpoint complete register. This register is only used in the device mode.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | ETCE | Endpoint transmit complete event<br>Each bit indicates that a transmit event (IN/INTERRUPT) occurred and the software must read the corresponding endpoint queue to determine the endpoint status. If the corresponding IOC bit is set (1) in the transfer descriptor, then this bit will be set (1) simultaneously with the USBINT. Writing a one will clear the corresponding bit in this register.<br>ETCE[15] - Endpoint #15<br>ETCE[1] - Endpoint #1<br>ETCE[0] - Endpoint #0 |
| 15:0 | ERCE | Endpoint receive complete event<br>Each bit indicates that a received event (OUT/SETUP) occurred and the software must read the corresponding endpoint queue to determine the transfer status. If the corresponding IOC bit is set (1) in the transfer descriptor, then this bit will be set (1) simultaneously with the USBINT. Writing a one will clear the corresponding bit in this register.<br>ERCE[15] - Endpoint #15<br>ERCE[1] - Endpoint #1<br>ERCE[0] - Endpoint #0 |

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CC_USB_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00800080

The USB_OTG_HS_ENDPTCTRL0 register is the endpoint control 0 register. Every device will implement endpoint0 as a control endpoint.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | RESERVED_BITS31_24 | Clear (0) these bits. |

It will continue returning STALL until the bit is cleared (0) by the software or it will automatically be cleared (0) upon receipt of a new SETUP request.<br>After receiving a SETUP request, this bit will continue to be cleared (0) by the hardware until the associated ENDPTSETUPSTAT bit is cleared (0).<br>*Note:* There is a slight delay (50 clocks maximum) between the ENDPTSETUPSTAT being cleared (0) and the hardware continuing to clear (0) this bit. ### 6.4.7.3.46 USB_OTG_HS_ENDPT_PIPE_IDn, n=[1..15]

**Address:** `0x0000 01FC+0x4*n`
**Type:** RW
**Clock:** `CC_USB_AHB_CLK`
**Reset State:** `0x001F001F`

The `USB_OTG_HS_ENDPT_PIPE_IDn` register is the endpoint pipe number register. There is an `USB_OTG_HS_ENDPT_PIPE_IDn` register for each endpoint in a device.

> [!NOTE]
> Reset value of `TX_PIPE_ID` and `RX_PIPE_ID` is `0x1F`, which means that Endpoint is not mapped to any pipe.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:21 | RESERVED_BITS31_21 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 20:16 | TX_PIPE_ID | This field indicate the pipe number that this Tx end point (n) will use in pipe mode. |
| 15:5 | RESERVED_BITS15_5 | Clear (0) these bits. |
| 4:0 | RX_PIPE_ID | This field indicate the pipe number that this Rx end point (n) will use in pipe mode. |

### 6.4.7.3.48 USB_OTG_HS_GENERIC1

**Address:** `0x0000 0244`
**Type:** R
**Clock:** `CC_USB_AHB_CLK`
**Reset State:** `0x00000000`

The `USB_OTG_HS_GENERIC1` register reset is `0xXXXXXXXX` for generics because the value of these registers changes per controller instance. Software can read these registers to identify the real hardware parameters of the controller instance.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | USB_HS_TX_DEPTH | TX_DEPTH is the number of words in the TX buffer. This number is calculated by the number of bytes allocated per Endpoint divided by 4, times the number of endpoints. In HS USB this value is typically 512 bytes per EP, and for FS ONLY USB it is typically 64 bytes per EP. |
| 15:0 | USB_HS_RX_DEPTH | RX_DEPTH is the number of words in the RX buffer. This number is typically 256, but can support powers of 2 up to 4096. |

### 6.4.7.3.49 USB_OTG_HS_GENERIC2

**Address:** `0x0000 0248`
**Type:** R
**Clock:** `CC_USB_AHB_CLK`

| 17 | RESERVED | Reserved |

| 15 | USE_SPS_AHB2AHB | USE_SPS_AHB2AHB generic specifies if AHB2AHB bridge is connected between BAM and SPS Fabric AHB. only applicable when USE_SPS = 1. 1 - the controller has AHB2AHB bridge between BAM and SPS Fabric AHB, 0 - the BAM connected directly to SPS Fabric AHB |

| Bits | Name | Description |

## 6.5 Secure Digital Card Controller (SDCC)

This section describes the SDCC. The SDCC is a simple, high-performance, serial interface. The SDCC provides bidirectional data transfer between the system memory and the storage device (eMMC, MMC, SD card, and SDIO device).

### 6.5.1 SDCC overview

Figure 6-78 shows a high-level overview of the two SDCC instances integrated in the SoC.

The SDCC1 supports 8-bit data bus and is used for connection to eMMC. The SDCC2 supports 4-bit data bus and is used for connection to SD card or SDIO device.

#### Figure 6-78: SDCC overview
*Description:* Block diagram showing the integration of the two SDCC instances (`SDCC[0-1]`) in the system:
* `SDCC[0-1]` is connected to the `APSS_QGIC` via Interrupts.
* `SDCC[0-1]` receives Clocks and Resets from `RPM`.
* `SDCC[0-1]` is connected to the Peripheral and system configuration NoC.
* `SDCC[0-1]` is connected to external pins/pads (labeled as `SDCC[0-1] pads` / `pDGs`).

Table 6-90 lists the SDCC supported features.
<!-- page 2033 -->

#### Table 6-90 SDCC features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| SDCC1 and SDCC2 | <ul><li>**Data bus:**<ul><li>Up to eight data lines for SDCC1</li><li>Up to four data lines for SDCC2</li></ul></li><li>**Support for the following standards:**<ul><li>SD version 3.01 and earlier</li><li>eMMC version 4.5 and earlier</li><li>SDIO version 3.00 and earlier</li></ul></li><li>Standard host controller interface (SDHCI)</li><li>**SD timing modes:**<ul><li>DS</li><li>HS</li><li>SDR12</li><li>SDR25</li><li>SDR50</li><li>SDR104</li><li>DDR50</li></ul></li><li>**eMMC timing modes:**<ul><li>DS</li><li>HS</li><li>DDR</li><li>HS200</li></ul></li><li>**Dual voltage:**<ul><li>3 V or 1.8 V I/O pads for SD cards</li><li>1.8 V or 1.2 V I/O pads for eMMC and SDIO devices</li></ul></li><li>Programmable delay line (SDCDC)</li><li>Flow control - clock is stopped to avoid FIFO overflow or underrun</li><li>FIFO mode - software writes the data directly into the FIFO on Write transactions and reads the data directly from the FIFO on Read transactions</li><li>ADMA mode - software prepares ADMA descriptors for SDCC and SDCC DMA engine executes Write or Read transfers according to ADMA descriptors</li><li>Two interrupt lines from SDCC core to CPU interrupt controller (some targets connect interrupt 0 line only)</li><li>eMMC high priority interrupt (HPI)</li><li>Detection of SDIO interrupts signaled by SDIO device</li></ul> |
<!-- page 2034 -->

#### Table 6-90 SDCC features (cont.)

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| SDCC1 and SDCC2 | <ul><li>**Wake-up capabilities:**<ul><li>DAT1 line can be used to wake up the SoC from shutdown state on SDIO protocol interrupt</li><li>DAT3 line can be used to wake up the SoC from shutdown state on SD card insertion</li></ul></li><li>eMMC boot sequence - normal and alternative</li><li>Supports dynamic bus clock scaling</li><li>No limitation for the ratio between AHB bus clock (HCLK) and SD interface clock (MCLK)</li><li>Autogeneration of CMD19 for SD and CMD21 for eMMC (SEND_TUNING_PATTERN) at read transaction start</li><li>Autogeneration of CMD12 (STOP_CMD) at the end of data transaction</li><li>Autodetection of the end of card programming state at the end of write transaction</li><li>**Dual voltage:**<ul><li>3 V or 1.8 V I/O pads for SD cards</li><li>1.8 V or 1.2 V I/O pads for eMMC and SDIO devices</li></ul></li></ul> |

Table 6-91 lists the SDCC not supported features.

#### Table 6-91 SDCC not supported features

| Module name | Not supported features |

### 6.5.4 SDCC functional description

The SDCC provides a simple, high-performance, serial interface to eMMC, MMC, SD cards, and SDIO devices.

Figure 6-81 shows a high-level overview of the SDCC functional blocks.

#### Figure 6-81: SDCC functional block diagram
*Description:* High-level functional block diagram of the SDCC (`SDCCn`, where n = 1 to 2):
* **SDCCn Internal Blocks:**
  * **DPSM** (Data Path State Machine)
  * **CPSM** (Command Path State Machine)
  * **SDCDC DLL** (Delay-locked loop / delay line)
  * **FIFO** (1 KB capacity)
  * **ADMA engine** (DMA controller)
  * **SDCC registers**
* **External and Power Connections:**
  * **PMIC** supplies power via `VDDPX_SDCn`
  * **MPM** connects to the hardware `RESET`
  * **TLMM / SoC I/O Muxing Logic** routes external signals: `SDCn_CLK`, `SDCn_CMD`, `SDCn_DATA_x`, `SD_CARD_DET_N`, `SD_WRITE_PROTECT`
* **Control and System Connections:**
  * **Clock control block** provides `HCLK` and `MCLK`
  * **Interrupts to APSS:** `IRQ0` and `IRQ1`
  * **Peripheral and system configuration NoC** connects to `SDCC registers` via `AHB slave` interface.
  * **System NoC** connects to `ADMA engine` via `AXI master` interface.
  * **APSS** and **System memory** interface via the System NoC.

### 6.5.4.1 SDCC functional block diagram

SDCC functional blocks:
* **Clock control block:** configures and provides HCLK and MCLK clocks to the SDCC.


<!-- page 2041 -->

* **PMIC**: configures and provides power to the SDCC.
* **Interrupt controller**: receives interrupts from the SDCC and generates an interrupt to the CPU (if the interrupt is enabled at the interrupt controller level).
* **TLMM**: provides connectivity from the SDCC to I/O pads that are assigned for SDCC usage.
* **Dual-voltage I/O pads**:
  * 3 V and 1.8 V I/O pads for SD cards.
  * 1.8 V and 1.2 V I/O pads for eMMC and SDIO devices.
* **MPM**: allows waking up the SoC from shutdown state. DAT1 and DAT3 I/O pads are connected to MPM.
  * DAT1 I/O pad can be used to wake up the chip on SDIO interrupt.
  * DAT3 I/O pad can be used to wake up the chip on SD card insertion.
* **Interfaces between the SDCC and Peripheral and System Configuration NoC**:
  * AHB slave port for software configuration and transferring data in FIFO mode.
  * AXI master port for transferring data in ADMA mode.
* **SDCDC DLL**: programmable delay line that provides a method to tune the best sampling point of the incoming data from the card or device in SDR104 and HS200 modes.
* **FIFO**: 1024-byte buffer for data transfer (transmit and receive).
* **CPSM**: command path state machine (handles commands).
* **DPSM**: data path state machine (handles data).
  * System memory (external DDR memory): used for data buffers when Tx or Rx transactions are performed.

The supported protocols have a common physical layer definition:
* The Host always supplies the clock to the Card.
* One line for command from the Host to the Card and for response from the Card to the Host.
* 8 (SDCC1) / 4 (SDCC2) lines for transferring the data between the Host and the Card.
* Every transaction starts with the Host sending a command to the Card on the bidirectional command line. The Card returns a response to the Host on the same bidirectional command line.
* The commands are used to initialize and configure the Card, and to start data transaction.
* Write data is transferred from the Host to the Card on the bidirectional data lines.
* Read data is transferred from the Card to the Host on the bidirectional data lines.

### 6.5.4.2 SDCC power and clock management

#### 6.5.4.2.1 Controller and system initialization sequence

1. Configure PMIC to turn on VREG to provide VDD power to the card.
<!-- page 2042 -->

2. Configure SDCC GPIOs in TLMM (see `TLMM_SDCn_HDRV_PULL_CTL`, where n = 1 to 2).
   a. Configure clock pad to no-pull.
   b. Configure CMD and DAT lines to pull up.

   > [!NOTE]
   > For the configuration of the SDCC pads, see the corresponding registers in Section 6.3.

3. Configure MCLK in clock control block to 100 kHz – 400 kHz.
4. For the configuration of the SDCC clocks, see the corresponding registers in Chapter GCC.
5. Set `SDCC_MCI_POWER[CONTROL]` bit to 0x1 (turn off).
6. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_CLK` register:
   a. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[ENABLE]` bit to 0x1.
   b. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit to 0x0.
   c. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[WIDEBUS]` bit field to 0x0: DAT[0] line is used for transferring data during initialization mode of the card.
   d. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit to 0x1.
   e. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[INVERT_OUT]` bit to 0x0: Output command and data are launched on falling edge.
   f. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SELECT_IN]` bit field to 0x2: Input command and data are sampled on rising edge of the internal feedback clock.
   g. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[HCLKON_SW_EN]` bit to 0x0.
   h. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SD_DEV_SEL]` bit field to 0x0.
   i. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[CLK_FB_DLY_SEL]` bit to 0x0.
   j. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[IO_PAD_PWR_SWITCH]` bit to 0x0.
   k. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[CLK_INV]` bit to 0x0.
   l. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SDC4_MCL_SEL]` bit field to 0x2.
   m. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[RX_FLOW_TIMING]` bit to 0x0.
7. Wait 1 ms to provide the free running SD clock to the card.
8. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit to 0x1 (turn on).
9. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK0` and `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK1` registers.
10. Write 0xFFFFFFFF to `SDCC_MCI_CLEAR` register.
11. Configure interrupt controller block to enable SDCC interrupts.

    > [!NOTE]
    > For the configuration of the SDCC interrupts, see the corresponding registers in the Chapter Interrupts.
<!-- page 2043 -->

#### 6.5.4.2.2 Clock control in legacy MCI mode

The SDCC stops the SD clock on the following conditions:
* `SDCC_MCI_POWER[CONTROL]` bit is 0x0.
* `SDCC_MCI_CLK[ENABLE]` bit is 0x0.
* The default reset state of `SDCC_MCI_POWER[CONTROL]` and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[ENABLE]` bits is 0x0. The SD clock stops after the SDCC reset is completed.
* The SDCC is in idle state (no active command or data transaction) and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit is 0x1.
* During an active Tx transaction, the FIFO becomes empty and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit is 0x1.
* During an active Rx transaction, the FIFO becomes full and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit is 0x1.
* Eight clock cycles after Tx transaction completes successfully (`PROG_DONE` event detected) and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit is 0x1.
* Eight clock cycles after Rx transaction completes successfully (`DATAEND` event detected) and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit is 0x1.
* Eight clock cycles after Tx or Rx transaction fails due to `DATA_TIMEOUT` or `DATA_CRC_FAIL` event and `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]` bit is 0x1.

> [!NOTE]
> For descriptions of the `PROG_DONE`, `DATAEND`, `DATA_TIMEOUT`, and `DATA_CRC_FAIL` events, see `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` register.

#### 6.5.4.2.3 Writes to legacy MCI registers (power, clock, command, and data control registers)

When the software writes to the `SDCC_MCI_POWER`, `SDCC_MCI_CLK`, `SDCC_MCI_CMD` and `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` registers, the register write operation is completed after 3 HCLK + 2 MCLK clock cycles. The software can access these registers only after the register write operation is completed. This synchronization delay cannot be ignored, especially when the MCLK is slow (for example: 400 kHz). Special status bit is defined to wait properly for register write completion – see `SDCC_MCI_STATUS2[MCLK_REG_WR_ACTIVE]` bit.

> [!NOTE]
> The software must always check the `SDCC_MCI_STATUS2[MCLK_REG_WR_ACTIVE]` bit after writing to one of these registers and before accessing them again.

#### 6.5.4.2.4 Power reduction modes

The following optional software bits reduce the power consumption of the core:
* `SDCC_MCI_CLK[PWRSAVE]`: Gates the clock to the card. The clock can be disabled during IDLE times to save power.
* `SDCC_MCI_CLK[HCLKON_SW_EN]`: Gates the AHB clock. The clock can be disabled during IDLE times to save power.
<!-- page 2044 -->

* `SDCC_MCI_CLK[INT_MCLK_ON]`: Gates the MCLK clock. The clock can be disabled during IDLE times to save power.
* `SDCC_MCI_DLL_CONFIG[PDN]`: Allows DLL to operate in low-power mode, see Section 6.5.4.12.3.

### 6.5.4.3 SDCC reset options

#### 6.5.4.3.1 Hard reset

The SDCC core has a reset input, which is controlled by a software register in the clock control block of the SoC (see `GCC_SDCCn_BCR`, where n = 1 to 2).

The SDCC hard reset asserts the SDCC core reset input. The hard reset is activated in two cases:
* SoC hardware power-on reset.
* The software writes 0x1 to `GCC_SDCCn_BCR[BLK_ARES]` bit.

In both cases, all software registers, state machines, and internal registers are reset to default values.

A hard reset can be used in error scenarios when the SDCC core detects one of the following error events in the `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` register:
* `CMD_CRC_FAIL`
* `DATA_CRC_FAIL`
* `CMD_TIMEOUT`
* `DATA_TIMEOUT`
* `TX_UNDERRUN`
* `RX_OVERRUN`
* `BOOT_ACK_ERR`
* `BOOT_TIMEOUT`
* `AUTO_CMD19_TIMEOUT`

#### 6.5.4.3.2 Soft reset

**Soft reset sequence using `SDCC_MCI_CMD` and `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` registers**

This sequence resets CPSM and DPSM. The sequence does not reset the configuration registers of the SDCC.
1. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register (resets CPSM).
2. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register (resets DPSM).
3. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_BOOT` register.
<!-- page 2045 -->

**Soft reset sequence using `SDCC_MCI_POWER` register**
1. Software writes 0x1 to `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST_REQ]` bit.
2. Software waits until `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST_REQ]` bit is 0x0.
3. Software writes 0x1 to the intended software reset bit:
   * `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST]`: Software reset bit for the core (CPSM and DPSM).
   * `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST_CONFIG]`: Software reset bit for the core without resetting the following configuration registers:
     * `SDCC_MCI_POWER`
     * `SDCC_MCI_CLK`
     * `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASKn` (n = 0 to 1)
     * `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASKINT2_n` (n = 0 to 1)
     * `SDCC_MCI_CCS_TIMER`
     * `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER`
     * `SDCC_MCI_PWRCTL_MASK_REG`
     * `SDCC_MCI_BOOT_ACK_TIMER`
     * `SDCC_MCI_DLL_CONFIG`
     * `SDCC_MCI_PWRCTL_CTL_REG[HC_WRITE_PROTECT]`
     * `SDCC_MCI_PWRCTL_CTL_REG[CARD_DETECT_PIN_LEVEL]`
4. Software polls on the same bit until it is 0x0.
5. Reset has been completed.

The software reset can be used in error scenarios when the SDCC core detected one of the error events in the `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` register as described in Section 6.5.4.3.1.

### 6.5.4.4 SDCC interrupts

The SDCC core has two interrupt enable registers:
* `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK0` – enables `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` events to trigger SDCC IRQ0 output of the core.
* `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK1` – enables `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` events to trigger SDCC IRQ1 output of the core.

The SDCC core has two separate IRQ outputs. This allows different events to be grouped to different IRQ outputs.

For example: normal status bits (`SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_RESPONSE_END]`, `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATAEND]`, `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[PROG_DONE]`) can be configured in `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK0` to trigger IRQ0. The error status bits (`SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_FAIL]`, `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_CRC_FAIL]`, `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_TIMEOUT]`) can be configured in `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK1` to trigger IRQ1.
<!-- page 2046 -->

All status events can be enabled in both `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK0` and `SDCC_MCI_INT_MASK1` registers.

> [!NOTE]
> When the software clears the interrupts in nonselective manner (writes 0xFFFFFFFF to `SDCC_MCI_CLEAR` register), there is possibility for missing reported events from the SDCC to the software. The `SDCC_MCI_CLEAR` register must be used to clear pending events in the `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` register only after they are detected and registered by the software.

#### 6.5.4.4.1 High priority interrupt (HPI)

The HPI feature is used for switching from low priority Tx to higher priority Rx in eMMC4.41 and above.

The following procedure is required:
1. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register.
2. Write 0x1 to `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST_REQ]` bit.
3. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_POWER[SW_RST_REQ]` bit is 0x0.
4. Send CMD12 with the appropriate fields:
   a. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[CMD_INDEX]` to 0xC (12).
   b. Set `SDCC_MCI_ARGUMENT[CMD_ARG]` to 0x0.
   c. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[MCIABORT]` to 0x1.
   d. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PROG_EN]` to 0x1.
5. Send CMD12 or CMD13 (according to the card HPI command support) with the appropriate fields:
   a. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[CMD_INDEX]` to 0xC (12) or 0xD (13).
   b. Set `SDCC_MCI_ARGUMENT[CMD_ARG]` to 0x1.
   c. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PROG_EN]` to 0x1.
6. Perform the sequence from section Section .
7. Perform Rx data transaction from the eMMC.

### 6.5.4.5 Hardware configuration

The `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS` register presents the hardware configuration of the SDCC core instance.
* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[SD_DATA_WIDTH]`: The number of the physical SD DAT lines of the SDCC core.
* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[RAM_SIZE]`: The size of the internal RAM of the SDCC core.
* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[USE_SPS]`: Specifies whether the SDCC controller includes the BAM and DML.
<!-- page 2047 -->

* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[MAX_PIPES]`: The number of supported SPS pipes (if the core operates with the BAM).
* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[USE_DLL_SDC4]`: Specifies whether the SDCC controller includes the programmable delay line (SDCDC).
* `SDCC_MCI_GENERICS[NUM_OF_DEV]`: Specifies the number of supported eSD/eSDIO devices connected through the shared bus to the SDCC core instance.

> [!NOTE]
> For more information about SDCCn (n = 1 to 2) instance hardware configuration, see Section 6.5.1.

### 6.5.4.6 Supported timing modes

#### 6.5.4.6.1 Default speed (DS), high speed (HS), SDR12, SDR25, and SDR50

Write 0x2 to `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SELECT_IN]` bit field. This setting programs the SDCC to sample received data using the rising edge of the feedback clock.

#### 6.5.4.6.2 DDR50

Write 0x3 to `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SELECT_IN]` bit field. This setting programs the SDCC to use DDR logic on transmit and receive paths. For DDR mode, the MCLK has to be programmed to be ×2 clock frequency on the SD interface. For example: to run DDR at 48 MHz, the provided MCLK must be 96 MHz.

> [!NOTE]
> For the configuration of the SDCC clocks, see the corresponding registers in Chapter GCC.

#### 6.5.4.6.3 SDR104

Write 0x4 to `SDCC_MCI_CLK[SELECT_IN]` bit field. This setting programs the SDCC to use the delay line (SDCDC) and asynchronous FIFO. When this setting is used, the tuning sequence must be executed (see Section 6.5.4.12.5).

### 6.5.4.7 Send of commands

Write the command argument into `SDCC_MCI_ARGUMENT` register.
1. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register:
   a. Set command index in `SDCC_MCI_CMD[CMD_INDEX]` bit field.
   b. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[RESPONSE]` bit to 0x1 for all commands except for commands that do not generate response (SD and eMMC commands: CMD0, CMD4, CMD15).
   c. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[LONGRSP]` bit to 0x1 for all commands that generate R2 response (SD and eMMC commands: CMD2, CMD9, CMD10). Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[LONGRSP]` bit to 0x0 for all other commands.
   d. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[INTERRUPT]` bit to 0x1 to disable command timeout.
<!-- page 2048 -->

> [!NOTE]
> If detection and reporting of command timeout is needed, set this bit to 0x0. In case some card needs more than 64 cycles to respond, set the bit to 0x1 to disable command timeout detection.

* e. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PENDING]` bit to 0x1 to send a request command automatically at the end of ongoing data transaction.
* f. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[ENABLE]` bit to 0x1.
* g. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PROG_ENA]` bit to 0x1 for commands that generate R1b response (SD commands: CMD7, CMD12, CMD20, CMD28, CMD29, CMD38; eMMC commands: CMD5, CMD6, CMD12, CMD28, CMD29, CMD38). Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PROG_ENA]` bit to 0x0 for all other commands.
* h. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[DAT_CMD]` bit to 0x1 for commands starting data transaction:
  * i. SD commands: CMD17, CMD18, CMD19, CMD24, CMD25, CMD27, CMD30, CMD40, CMD42, CMD56, ACMD13, ACMD22, ACMD51.
  * ii. SDIO commands: CMD53.
  * iii. eMMC commands: CMD8, CMD14, CMD17, CMD18, CMD19, CMD24, CMD25, CMD26, CMD27, CMD30, CMD31, CMD42, CMD56.

  Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[DAT_CMD]` bit to 0x0 for all other commands.
* i. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[MCIABORT]` bit to 0x1 when sending CMD12 to SD Combo card (SDIO + SD memory).
* j. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[CCS_ENABLE]` and `SDCC_MCI_CMD[CCS_DISABLE]` bits to 0x0.
* k. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[AUTO_CMD19]` bit to 0x1 only for SD CMD17 and CMD18 when running in SDR50 or SDR104 UHS-I mode to run CMD19 with tuning block before sending CMD17 or CMD18. This is required for the SDCDC autocalibration. Set `SDCC_MCI_CMD[AUTO_CMD19]` bit to 0x0 for all other commands and in all other cases.

2. Wait for interrupt or poll for 0x1 the following bits of `SDCC_MCI_STATUS` register:
   a. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_FAIL]` bit is set to 0x1, then the response was received from the card/device, but the CRC checks, check that of the received response failed.
      i. The `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_FAIL]` bit is expected to be 0x1 when a valid response is received for SD ACMD41, eMMC CMD1, SDIO CMD5.
      ii. The `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_FAIL]` bit can be set to 0x1 when response for SD CMD11, CMD19 is received. The software has to ignore `CMD_CRC_FAIL` error in that case.
   b. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_TIMEOUT]` bit is set to 0x1, then no response was received from card/device within 64 SD clock cycles.
   c. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_RESPONSE_END]` bit is set to 0x1, then the response was received from the card/device and the CRC check passed.
   d. The `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_SENT]` bit is set to 0x1 only after CMD0 is sent.
<!-- page 2049 -->

3. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_RESPONSE_END]` bit is set to 0x1 or `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_CRC_FAIL]` bit is set to 0x1 for SD ACMD41, eMMC CMD1, SDIO CMD5, read `SDCC_MCI_RESP_CMD` register to verify that the response index is equal to the command index.
4. If the response index is equal to the command index, then read the command response from `SDCC_MCI_RESPn` (n = 0 to 3) registers.
   a. For commands with R2 response (SD and eMMC CMD2, CMD9, CMD10) read `SDCC_MCI_RESP0`, `SDCC_MCI_RESP1`, `SDCC_MCI_RESP2`, and `SDCC_MCI_RESP3` registers.
   b. For all other commands read `SDCC_MCI_RESP0` register only.
5. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[CMD_ACTIVE]` bit is cleared to 0x0.
6. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register to reset CPSM.

### 6.5.4.8 Write data sequence

1. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit to 0x1.
2. Send ACMD23 to SD2.0 card to specify the number of the write blocks to be pre-erased before writing (used for multiple blocks write command).
3. Send CMD23 to SD3.0 card and eMMC to specify the number of the data blocks to be transferred.
4. Write 0x0 to `SDCC_MCI_DLL_CONFIG[CDR_EN]` bit in case automatic tracking is enabled.
5. Write the data transaction time limit into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
   a. The value is 250 ms multiplied by the actual frequency of MCLK.
6. Write the total length of the data transaction in bytes into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register. The value of `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register is an integer multiple of the value in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
7. If DATA_PEND feature is used (`SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit is 0x1), then write response error check mask to `SDCC_MCI_RESPONSE_MASK` register. Setting bits in `SDCC_MCI_RESPONSE_MASK` register causes the SDCC automatically to check corresponding bits of the command response. The SDCC does not start write data transaction if one of the corresponding bits in the command response is set.
8. If DATA_PEND feature is not used (`SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit is 0x0), then send write data command to the card/device to start a write data transaction. The possible commands are:
   a. SD commands: CMD24, CMD25, CMD27, CMD42, CMD56
   b. eMMC commands: CMD20, CMD24, CMD25, CMD26, CMD27, CMD42, CMD56
   c. SDIO commands: CMD53, CMD54 (QCT-specific command)
9. Check that a valid response was received.
10. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register:
    a. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[ENABLE]` bit to 0x1.
<!-- page 2050 -->

* b. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DIRECTION]` bit to 0x0.
* c. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to 0x1 for eMMC CMD20 and CMD19.
  Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to 0x0 for all other write data commands.
* d. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DM_ENABLE]` bit to 0x0 (FIFO mode).
* e. Write the block size used in data transaction into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
* f. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit to 0x0.
* g. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[INFINITE_TRANSFER]` bit to 0x0.
* h. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit to 0x1 for:
  * i. SD commands: CMD24, CMD25 if CMD23 (was sent prior to it)
  * ii. eMMC commands: CMD19, CMD24, CMD25 if CMD23 (was sent prior to it)
  * iii. SDIO commands: CMD53, CMD54 (QCT-specific command)
  In all other cases set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit to 0x0.
* i. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[RX_DATA_PEND]` bit to 0x0.

11. If DATA_PEND feature is used (`SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit is 0x1), then at first do step 7 with `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit set to 0x1 and after that do step 6 without checking the response (the SDCC does that automatically).
12. \[Optional\] After sending CMD25 and receiving a correct response for it, program `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register to send CMD12 with `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PENDING]` bit set to 0x1. In that case, the SDCC sends CMD12 automatically at the end of write data transaction. This step is not required if CMD23 was sent prior to CMD25.
13. Execute step 13a through 13d until all data is written into the FIFO or one of the error events is detected:
    a. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_CRC_FAIL]` bit is set to 0x1, then the card/device detects an CRC error during the data transfer.
    b. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_TIMEOUT]` bit is set to 0x1, then the card/device did not complete programming of the transmitted data within the time period specified in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    c. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[TX_UNDERRUN]` bit is set to 0x1, then the SDCC tried to send data to the card when no data was available for transmission. This bit is never expected to be set if `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit is set to 0x1.
    d. Write the data into the SDCC FIFO:
       i. Write 1 word to FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[TXFIFO_FULL]` bit is 0x0.
       ii. Write 8 words to FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[TXFIFO_EMPTY]` or `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[TXFIFO_HALF_FULL]` bit is 0x1.
       iii. To write more than 8 words of data, poll on `SDCC_MCI_FIFO_STATUS` register for the indications - `TX_FIFO_64`, `TX_FIFO_128`, `TX_FIFO_256` or `TX_FIFO_512` (to write 64, 128, 256 or 512 bytes).


<!-- page 2051 -->

14. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATAEND]` bit is set to `0x1`. This can be done using polling or interrupt.
15. Send `CMD12` to the card/device if the write data command was sent with `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit set to `0x0` and also if `CMD12` was not scheduled using PENDING command feature in step 11.
16. Wait until one of the following events is detected (can be done using polling or interrupt):
    a. The `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[PROG_DONE]` bit is set to `0x1`.
    b. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_TIMEOUT]` bit is set to `0x1`, then the card/device did not complete programming of the transmitted data within the time period specified in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
17. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[TXACTIVE]` bit is set to `0x0`.
18. Write `0x0` to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register to reset DPSM.

### 6.5.4.9 Read data sequence

1. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit to `0x1`.
2. Send `CMD23` to SD3.0 card and eMMC to specify the number of the data blocks to be transferred.
3. Write the data transaction time limit into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    a. The value is 100 ms multiplied by the actual frequency of MCLK.
4. Write the total length of the data transaction in bytes into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register. The value of `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register is an integer multiple of the value in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
5. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register:
    a. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[ENABLE]` bit to `0x1`.
    b. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DIRECTION]` bit to `0x1`.
    c. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to `0x1` for eMMC `CMD11` and `CMD14`.
       Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to `0x0` for all other read data commands.
    d. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DM_ENABLE]` bit to `0x0` (FIFO mode).
    e. Write the block size used in data transaction into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
    f. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x0`.
    g. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[INFINITE_TRANSFER]` bit to `0x0`.
    h. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit to `0x0`.
    i. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[RX_DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x1`.
6. Send read data command to the card/device to start a read data transaction. The possible commands are:
<!-- page 2052 -->

    a. SD commands: `CMD6`, `CMD17`, `CMD18`, `CMD19`, `CMD30`, `CMD40`, `CMD56`, `ACMD13`, `ACMD22`, `ACMD51`
    b. eMMC commands: `CMD8`, `CMD11`, `CMD14`, `CMD17`, `CMD18`, `CMD30`, `CMD31`, `CMD56`
    c. SDIO commands: `CMD53`, `CMD54` (QCT-specific command)
7. Check that a valid response was received.
8. [Optional] After sending `CMD18` and receiving a correct response for it, program `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register to send `CMD12` with `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PENDING]` bit set to `0x1`. In that case, the SDCC sends `CMD12` automatically at the end of read data transaction. This step is not required if `CMD23` was sent prior to `CMD18`.
9. Execute step 9a through 9d until all data is received and read from the FIFO or one of the error events is detected:
    a. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_CRC_FAIL]` bit is set to `0x1`, then a CRC error was detected on received data.
    b. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_TIMEOUT]` bit is set to `0x1`, then the card/device did not start sending a new block of data within the time period specified in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    c. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RX_OVERRUN]` bit is set to `0x1`, then the data was received and written into the FIFO when it was full. This bit is never expected to be set if `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit is set to `0x1`.
    d. Read the data from the SDCC FIFO:
        i. Read 1 word from FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_EMPTY]` bit is `0x0` or if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXDATA_AVLBL]` bit is `0x1`.
        ii. Read 8 words from FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_FULL]` or `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_HALF_FULL]` bit is `0x1`.
        iii. To read more than 8 words of data, the user should poll on `SDCC_MCI_FIFO_STATUS` register for the indications - `RX_FIFO_64`, `RX_FIFO_128`, `RX_FIFO_256` or `RX_FIFO_512` (to read 64, 128, 256 or 512 bytes).
10. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATAEND]` bit is set to `0x1`. This can be done using polling or interrupt.
11. Send `CMD12` to the card/device if there is multiblock read from SD or eMMC and also if `CMD12` was not scheduled using PENDING command feature in step 8.
12. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXACTIVE]` bit is set to `0x0`.
13. Write `0x0` to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register to reset DPSM.

#### 6.5.4.9.1 Read data sequence for eMMC4.5 device in HS200 timing mode

> [!NOTE]
> Use this sequence to calibrate the SDCDC automatically when operating with eMMC4.5 device in HS200 timing mode.

1. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit to `0x1`.
<!-- page 2053 -->

2. Write the data transaction time limit into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    a. The value is 100 ms multiplied by the actual frequency of MCLK.
3. Write 64 into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register.
4. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register:
    a. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[ENABLE]` bit to `0x1`.
    b. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DIRECTION]` bit to `0x1`.
    c. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to `0x0`.
    d. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DM_ENABLE]` bit to `0x0` (FIFO mode).
    e. Write 64 to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
    f. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x0`.
    g. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[INFINITE_TRANSFER]` bit to `0x0`.
    h. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit to `0x0`.
    i. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[RX_DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x1`.
    j. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[SW_SDC4_CMD19]` bit to `0x1`.
5. Send read data command `CMD21` to the device (to send the tuning data from the device to the SDCC).
6. Read the data from the SDCC FIFO:
    a. Read 8 words from FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_FULL]` or `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_HALF_FULL]` bit is `0x1`.
7. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATAEND]` bit is set to `0x1`. This can be done using polling or interrupt.
8. Write `0x0` to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register to reset DPSM.
9. Set `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit to `0x1`.
10. Send `CMD23` to SD3.0 card and eMMC to specify the number of the data blocks to be transferred.
11. Write the data transaction time limit into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    a. The value is 100 ms multiplied by the actual frequency of MCLK.
12. Write the total length of the data transaction in bytes into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register. The value of `SDCC_MCI_DATA_LENGTH` register is an integer multiple of the value in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
13. Set appropriate bit fields and write to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register:
    a. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[ENABLE]` bit to `0x1`.
    b. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DIRECTION]` bit to `0x1`.
    c. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to `0x1` for eMMC `CMD11` and `CMD14`.
    d. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[MODE]` bit to `0x0` for all other read data commands.
    e. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DM_ENABLE]` bit to `0x0` (FIFO mode).
<!-- page 2054 -->

    f. Write the block size used in data transaction into `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[BLOCKSIZE]` bit field.
    g. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x0`.
    h. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[INFINITE_TRANSFER]` bit to `0x0`.
    i. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[AUTO_PROG_DONE]` bit to `0x0`.
    j. Set `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL[RX_DATA_PEND]` bit to `0x1`.
14. Send read data command to the card/device to start a read data transaction. The possible commands are:
    a. SD commands: `CMD6`, `CMD17`, `CMD18`, `CMD19`, `CMD30`, `CMD40`, `CMD56`, `ACMD13`, `ACMD22`, `ACMD51`
    b. eMMC commands: `CMD8`, `CMD11`, `CMD14`, `CMD17`, `CMD18`, `CMD30`, `CMD31`, `CMD56`
    c. SDIO commands: `CMD53`, `CMD54` (QCT-specific command)
15. Check that a valid response was received.
16. [Optional] After sending `CMD18` and receiving a correct response for it, program `SDCC_MCI_CMD` register to send `CMD12` with `SDCC_MCI_CMD[PENDING]` bit set to `0x1`. In that case, the SDCC sends `CMD12` automatically at the end of read data transaction. This step is not required if `CMD23` was sent prior to `CMD18`.
17. Execute step 17a through 17d until all data is received and read from the FIFO or one of the error events is detected:
    a. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_CRC_FAIL]` bit is set to `0x1`, then a CRC error was detected on received data.
    b. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATA_TIMEOUT]` bit is set to `0x1`, then the card/device did not start sending a new block of data within the time period specified in `SDCC_MCI_DATA_TIMER` register.
    c. If `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RX_OVERRUN]` bit is set to `0x1`, then the data was received and written into the FIFO when it was full. This bit is never expected to be set if `SDCC_MCI_CLK[FLOW_ENA]` bit is set to `0x1`.
    d. Read the data from the SDCC FIFO:
        i. Read 1 word from FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_EMPTY]` bit is `0x0` or if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXDATA_AVLBL]` bit is `0x1`.
        ii. Read 8 words from FIFO address if `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_FULL]` or `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[RXFIFO_HALF_FULL]` bit is `0x1`.
18. Wait until `SDCC_MCI_STATUS[DATAEND]` bit is set to `0x1`. This can be done using polling or interrupt.
19. Send `CMD12` to the card/device if there is multiblock read from SD or eMMC and also if `CMD12` was not scheduled using PENDING command feature in step 16.
20. Write `0x0` to `SDCC_MCI_DATA_CTL` register to reset DPSM.
