### 7.1.4 EBI functional description

Figure 7-4 shows the EBI block diagram.

#### Figure: EBI block diagram
*Description:* The block diagram shows a detailed view of the External Bus Interface (EBI) within the Snapdragon 410E. The EBI consists of the BIMC (Bus Integrated Memory Controller), one CA DDRPHY, four DQ DDRPHYs (DQ0 to DQ3), and the AHB2PHY block. Inside the BIMC, five subcomponents are shown: BRIC, SCMO, DPE, SHKE, and DTE. The BIMC interfaces with various SoC blocks: SNOC (bidirectional), APSS (bidirectional), GPU (input), QDSP6 (input), SMMU (bidirectional), and PCNOC (bidirectional to both BIMC and AHB2PHY). Inside the EBI, the BIMC has bidirectional connections to the CA DDRPHY and each of the four DQ DDRPHYs. The DQ DDRPHYs and the CA DDRPHY are chained together with vertical control/clock lines, which also connect to the AHB2PHY at the bottom. Each of the CA DDRPHY and DQ0-DQ3 DDRPHYs has a bidirectional connection to the external SDRAM interface through chip pads.

### 7.1.4.1 BIMC functional description

BIMC comprises the following key subcomponents:
* AXI interconnect through Reusable Bus and Interconnect Components (BRIC)
* SDRAM Control and Memory Organizer (SCMO)
* DDR Protocol Engine (DPE)
* SDRAM Housekeeping Engine (SHKE)
* DDR Test Engine (DTE)

The BIMC architecture is partitioned into front-end AXI interface and back-end DDR portion. The front-end comprises BRIC and SCMO and is used as an interface to the rest of the chip. BRIC and SCMO are typically configured once after boot and are not updated by the system during normal operation. Main categories include slave address mapping, DDR memory density configuration, MPU configuration, arbitration settings, and performance monitoring.

The BIMC back-end comprises DPE and SHKE and handles the critical part of the initialization, self-refresh, frequency scaling, and so on.
<!-- page 2178 -->

##### 7.1.4.1.1 Initialization

The AXI interconnect portion of BIMC is part of the backbone of the SoC, which requires it to be functional for the SoC to boot the various processors. To meet this requirement, several configuration registers are reset with defaults to ensure minimal guaranteed functionality without any software programming. This minimal guaranteed functionality includes accurate routing of read and write transactions originating from all bus masters to system slaves, including system-wide registers, on-chip memories, and other on-chip components. External components, such as SDRAMs that require initialization before access are excluded and any transactions targeting them return errors. Upon successful boot of processors on the SoC or during the secondary boot process, it is recommended to program the various control and status registers for best performance and latency.

##### 7.1.4.1.2 Memory protection and external semaphore

The SCMO contains a memory protection unit (MPU) and software must configure the corresponding resource partitions appropriately for the entire DDR address region. In addition, global monitors inside SCMO provide shared memory access support and semaphore management. The BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_GLOBAL_MON_CFG register is the only one to program the following:
* Control the exclusive read responses when global monitors are not available via the EXRD_RESP bit.
* Enable/disable request generation whenever any exclusive monitor gets cleared via the CLR_EXMON_EN bit.
* Define the exclusive access address granularity to be either 128-bit or 64-bit via the EXCMD_ADDR_GRAN bit.

##### 7.1.4.1.3 SDRAM interface overview

The BIMC back-end, also called the SDRAM controller or generically referred to as a memory controller (MC), handles all aspects of dealing with the SDRAM interface. The MC functionality is split between three major components:
* **SCMO**:
  * Converts read and write transaction addresses into SDRAM addressing (rank, bank, row, and column).
  * Orders transactions to maximize hits to open rows thus minimizing row precharges and activates.
  * Buffers writes to coalesce and delay them thus allowing for critical transactions to take precedence.
* **DPE**:
  * Transacts with SDRAM for all commands and maintains signaling and signal timing requirements of SDRAM.
<!-- page 2179 -->

* **SHKE**:
  * Initializes SDRAM.
  * Maintains periodicity of periodic commands to SDRAM, for example, refresh, calibration, status register read, activity-based self-refresh, and power down modes.

##### 7.1.4.1.4 SDRAM address decoding

Every read and write transaction targeted to the external SDRAM must be decoded to determine in which SDRAM device and where a read or write must be performed. The key components that need identification are as follows:
* **Channel** – only one physical SDRAM interface called a channel is supported.
* **Rank** – Two ranks are supported. Each rank is accessed with a separate chip select. At any time, there can be an access to only one of the two ranks since all control and data pins are shared between the two ranks. Depending on total SoC memory needs either rank #0 or #1 or both are populated with SDRAM devices. Rank auto detect during initialization is used to determine the ranks populated with SDRAM devices.
  Depending on the density of SDRAM devices in each rank and the location of the address range in the memory map, rank selection uses up to 8 bits of address. Rank selection is programmed by writing to the following fields:
  * `RANK_EN` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register
  * `ADDR_BASE` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_BASE_CSn` register
  * `ADDR_MASK` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MASK_CSn` register
  
  `ADDR_MASK` determines which bits of the transaction address (`ADDR[33:25]`) to look for to match against `ADDR_BASE`. When a match is found, the transaction is determined as targeting the matched rank.
* **Bank** – Each LPDDR2 device has four or eight banks depending on the density. LPDDR3 has eight banks. Bank selection uses 2 or 3 address bits. The number of banks is programmed by writing to the `BANK_SIZE` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register and must match the number of banks in the SDRAM device populated.
* **Row** – Each LPDDR2 bank has from 4096 to 32768 rows depending on the density and data-width. Each LPDDR3 bank has from 16384 to 32768 rows. Row selection uses 12 through 16 address bits. The number of rows in each bank is programmed by writing to the `ROW_SIZE` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register and must match the number of rows in the SDRAM device populated.
* **Column** – Each LPDDR2 row has from 128 to 4096 columns depending on the density and data-width. Each LPDDR3 row has from 1024 to 4096 columns. Column selection uses 7 through 12 address bits. The number of columns in each row is programmed by writing to the `COL_SIZE` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register and must match the number of columns in the SDRAM device populated.
* **Addressing mode** – The `ADDR_MODE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register determines the order of slicing of incoming address to determine ranks, banks, rows, and columns. Rank, row, bank, and column (from MSB to LSB) is the only supported addressing mode.
<!-- page 2180 -->

It is required to program all register fields previously mentioned in this section before any accesses to the SDRAM. Changes to these fields when reads or writes are in progress result in unexpected behavior.

It is recommended to program the `RANK_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register last to prevent any intermediate settings from being applied. In addition, the starting address of each rank must be aligned to the size (density) of the DRAM devices populated in that rank. For example, a rank populated with 2 GB of total memory must start at 0, 2 GB, 4 GB, 6 GB, and so on. It must not start at 1 GB, 3 GB, 5 GB, and so on.

##### 7.1.4.1.5 Address remapping

An address remapping capability is available to remap read and write transaction addresses to be SDRAM address decode friendly. These remapped addresses do not affect any access control checks which are performed with the original transaction address from the bus master. Address remapping can provide more flexibility in changing addresses unlike enhancing the configuration register fields for each decoding rank.

Each address remapping configuration set includes register fields to specify an address range and up to two math operations to perform on addresses that fall in the range. The math operations available are de-interleave of 1 KB interleaving and change offset, in other words, move the address range into higher or lower regions in increments of 256 MB.

The address range of each remapping configuration set is configured using the `MASK_10` and `MASK_31_28` bits of the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_ADDR_MASK_LOWER` register and the `BASE_10` and `BASE_31_28` bits of the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_ADDR_BASE_LOWER` register. The `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_ADDR_MASK_LOWER` register specifies size of the address range by indicating which bits of the transaction address to match against the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_ADDR_BASE_LOWER`. The smallest address range configurable is 256 MB.

The de-interleave operation is optional and removes `addr[10]` and shifts `addr[31:11]` towards LSBs. It is enabled when the `OPCODE_ENABLE` bit in the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_OP0` register is set to `0x1`. Expressed as an equation, de-interleaving performs the following function:

$$RemappedAddr = \{1'b0, OriginalAddr[31:11], OriginalAddr[9:0]\}$$

The change offset operation is an optional change in offset of the address range in 256 MB increments and is performed on the address modified by the de-interleave operation. Depending on the `OPERAND` field value in the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_OP1` register, the entire matched address range can be moved up or down in the memory map using positive or negative offsets. Expressed as an equation, offset change performs the following function:

$$RemappedAddr = OriginalAddr + Offset \times 256\text{MB}$$

The change offset operation is enabled when the `OPCODE_ENABLE` bit in the `BIMC_BRIC_REMAPn_OP1` register is set to `0x1`.


<!-- page 2181 -->

##### 7.1.4.1.6 SDRAM initialization

The following sequence shows an LPDDR2-S4/LPDDR3 initialization assuming the timer clock is 32 kHz and the XO clock is 19.2 MHz:

1. Set to 0x1 the `RANK0_EN` or `RANK1_EN` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register depending on the ranks being initialized. If rank auto detect sequence is required to determine which ranks are populated, set both bits to 0x1.
2. Program the registers in the DPE and SHKE blocks. If memory device initialization is performed the following registers must be left at their power-on-reset values:
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR`
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL`
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL`
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL`
3. Program the registers in the BRIC and SCMO blocks.
4. Configure the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_0` through `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_16` registers.

> **NOTE:** The `RD_LATENCY` and `WR_LATENCY` fields in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_16` register must be programed based on the frequency of operation.

5. Set bit [0] at physical address 0x0044 C020 to 0x1.
6. Configure all required DDRPHY registers. See Section DDRPHY initialization for more details.
7. Turn on the memory clock by writing the following:
   * 0x1 to bit `WAIT_TIMER_DOMAIN` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
   * 0x5 to field `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
   * 0x1 to bit `CK_ON` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to start the memory clock.
   * 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 to field `RANK_SEL` in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.
8. Poll the `CK_ON` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
9. Drive CKE high and wait for at least 200 μs for LPDDR2 or 500 μs for LPDDR3 by performing the following:
   * Set to 0x1 the `WAIT_TIMER_DOMAIN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
   * Set to 0x11 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
<!-- page 2182 -->

* (Continuation of step 9)
  * Set to 0x1 the `CKE_ON` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the CKE signal.
  * Set to 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.
10. Poll the `CKE_ON` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
11. Issue RESET command to reset all SDRAM mode registers and wait 11 μs. This can be done by the following sequence:
    * Set to 0x0 the `WAIT_TIMER_DOMAIN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
    * Set to 0x2 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
12. If LPDDR2, perform the following:
    * Set to 0x3F the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register.
    * Set to 0x1 the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
    * Set to 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.
    * Poll the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
    * Go to step 14.
13. If LPDDR3, perform the following:
    * Set to 0x3F the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register.
    * Set to 0xFC the `MREG_WDATA` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register. This is required for symmetrical PE and NE values on the CA bus as it is not calibrated.
    * Set to 0x1 the `EXTND_MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
    * Set to 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.
    * Poll the `EXTND_MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
    * Set to 0x0 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
    * Perform CA calibration sequence if required.
14. Perform ZQ calibration. This can be done by the following sequence:
    * Set to 0x1 the `WAIT_TIMER_DOMAIN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
<!-- page 2183 -->

* (Continuation of step 14)
  * Set to 0x14 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
  * Set to 0x1 the `ZQCAL_LONG` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the ZQ calibration command.
  * Set either to 0x1 or 0x2 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the rank being initialized.
15. Poll the `ZQCAL_LONG` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
16. In case of two ranks, repeat steps 14 and 15.
17. Configure SDRAM MR1 by performing the following sequence:
    * Set to 0x1 the `WAIT_TIMER_DOMAIN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
    * Set to 0x5 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
    * Set to 0x01 the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register.
    * Set to 0xC3 the `MREG_WDATA` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register. This indicates BL of 8, sequential burst and memory burst type of wrapping nature. This needs to be changed appropriately when selecting a different BL.
    * Set to 0x1 the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the MR write command.
    * Set to 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.

> **NOTE:** Auto precharges are not supported and hence the value of nWR is not used. If certain high values need to be programmed in the nWR based on the clock frequency, the user is required to enable nWRE in SDRAM MR2 first before setting nWR in MR1.

18. Poll the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
19. Configure SDRAM MR2 by performing the following sequence:
    * Set to 0x02 the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register.
    * The `MREG_WDATA` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register needs to be programmed appropriately based on the read or write latency of the memory device and the current frequency of operation.
    * Set to 0x1 the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the MR write command.
    * Set to 0x1, 0x2, or 0x3 the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the ranks being initialized.
<!-- page 2184 -->

* (Continuation of step 19)
20. Poll the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
21. Set to 0x0 the `WAIT_TIMER_BEFORE_HW_CLEAR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_1` register.
22. If rank auto detect is required, perform the sequence as described in Section Rank auto detect.

##### 7.1.4.1.7 SDRAM MR read

To read from an LPDDR2 or LPDDR3 mode register the following sequence should be performed:

1. If not already done, perform initialization as described in Section SDRAM initialization.
2. Configure the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register to the mode register address that will be read from the SDRAM device.
3. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate which rank will be read from.
4. Set to 0x1 the `MODE_REGISTER_READ` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to start the MR read command. Note that only one manual command can be outstanding to the controller at any given time.
5. Poll the `MODE_REGISTER_READ` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
6. Read the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_RDATA_RANK0_L` or `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_RDATA_RANK1_L` register to obtain the SDRAM MR data.

> **NOTE:** Hardware ensures that any command that follows the MR reading meets the memory timing specifications.

##### 7.1.4.1.8 SDRAM MR write

To write to an LPDDR2 or LPDDR3 mode register the following sequence should be performed:

1. If not already done, perform initialization as described in Section SDRAM initialization.
2. Configure the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register to the SDRAM mode register address that will be written to.
3. Configure the `MREG_WDATA` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register with the write data for the SDRAM device.
4. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate which rank will be written to.
5. Set to 0x1 the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to start the MR write command. Note that only one manual command can be outstanding to the controller at any given time.
6. Poll the `MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.
<!-- page 2185 -->

* (Continuation of Section 7.1.4.1.8 SDRAM MR write)
> **NOTE:** Hardware ensures that any command that follows the MR writing meets the memory timing specifications.

##### 7.1.4.1.9 SDRAM EMR write

This operation only applies to LPDDR3 device types, which require CA calibration (calibration of the DDR command bus). See the LPDDR3 vendor specification on writable mode registers and their bit definitions.

The extended mode register (EMR) write sequence is as follows:

1. If not already done, perform initialization as described in Section SDRAM initialization.
2. Configure the `MREG_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register to the SDRAM mode register address that will be written to.
3. Configure the `MREG_WDATA` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_ADDR_WDATA_CNTL` register with the write data for the SDRAM device.
4. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate which rank will be written to.
5. Set to 0x1 the `EXTND_MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to start the MR write command. Note that only one manual command can be outstanding to the controller at any given time.
6. Poll the `EXTND_MODE_REGISTER_WRITE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register until 0x0.

> **NOTE:** Hardware ensures that any command that follows the MR writing meets the memory timing specifications.

Typically, an EMR write is used before the LPDDR3 device calibration. This command holds the CA bus stable for one more cycle before and after the chip select to guarantee sufficient setup and hold time, so the uncalibrated SDRAM can sample the command successfully.

##### 7.1.4.1.10 Rank auto detect

Software uses the rank auto detect sequence to determine if a memory device is present on a specific rank. The sequence is as follows:

1. If not already done, perform initialization as described in Section SDRAM initialization.
2. Ensure that the `DEVICE_CFG_RANK0` or `DEVICE_CFG_RANK1` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_CONFIG_0` register is set to a non reserved value.
3. Set to 0x0 the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE` or `RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
4. Ensure that periodic auto refresh and hardware activity-based self-refresh functions are disabled.
5. Execute MR read command to register MR32 or MR40 in the desired rank.
6. Read the `MREG_TIMEOUT` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_RDATA_STATUS` register.
<!-- page 2186 -->

* (Continuation of Section 7.1.4.1.10 Rank auto detect)
7. If `MREG_TIMEOUT` = 0x0 the rank is populated. In this case the following must be performed:
   * Set to 0x1 the `RANK0_EN` or `RANK1_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
   * Set to 0x1 the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE` or `RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
   * Set to 0x1 the `RANK_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register.
   * Go to step 9.
8. If `MREG_TIMEOUT` = 0x1 the rank is not populated. In this case the following must be performed:
   * Set to 0x0 the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE` or `RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
   * Set to 0x0 the `RANK_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register.
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the corresponding rank.
   * Set to 0x1 the `CKE_OFF` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to disable the CKE signal.
   * Poll the `CKE_OFF` bit until 0x0.
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the corresponding rank.
   * Set to 0x1 the `CK_OFF` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to disable the CK signal.
   * Poll the `CK_OFF` bit until 0x0.
9. If second rank needs to be detected, go to step 5.

##### 7.1.4.1.11 ZQ calibration

ZQ calibration is used for calibrating the output driver strength over process, voltage, and temperature variation over time. A ZQ-Cal command is sent during SDRAM initialization for the initial calibration. A periodic ZQ-Cal or a manual ZQ-Cal is used during normal operation after rank is initialized to compensate for any voltage and temperature changes.

ZQ calibration can be performed only when the SDRAM device is in idle state having all banks precharged. During ZQ calibration the DQ bus (including DQS) must be tri-stated. The memory controller enforces the same when executing a ZQ calibration request.

In a two-rank system, ZQ calibration cannot be performed on both ranks at the same time. In addition, because DQ bus (including DQS) is Hi-Z, data traffic cannot be sent to any of the two ranks during ZQ calibration time.

The timing parameters associated with ZQ calibration are set via the `TZQCL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_17` register and the `TZQCS` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_7` register.
<!-- page 2187 -->

###### Manual ZQ calibration

Software can trigger manual ZQ calibration using the following sequence:

**For Short ZQ-Cal command:**

1. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the corresponding rank.
2. Set to 0x1 the `ZQCAL_SHORT` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
3. Poll the `ZQCAL_SHORT` bit until 0x0.

**For Long ZQ-Cal command:**

1. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the corresponding rank.
2. Set to 0x1 the `ZQCAL_LONG` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
3. Poll the `ZQCAL_LONG` bit until 0x0.

###### Periodic ZQ calibration

Periodic ZQ calibration must be enabled only after all initialization and calibration sequences have been executed and the SDRAM device is ready for normal operation. To enable the periodic ZQ calibration perform the following:

1. The `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register must be set to 0x3 for a two-rank system or either to 0x1 or 0x2 depending on the corresponding rank that is enabled and initialized in case of single rank.
2. Specify the periodic interval between short ZQ calibrations via the `ZQCAL_INTERVAL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register. A non-zero value enables the periodic ZQ calibration feature.

After enabling the auto-ZQ calibration feature, the memory controller immediately issues a ZQ-Cal request to rank1. Then, after `ZQCAL_INTERVAL`/2, a ZQ-Cal request is issued to rank0 if enabled.

To disable the periodic ZQ calibration feature, software can change the `ZQCAL_INTERVAL` field from a non-zero value to 0x0. The `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register is synchronized to the timer clock domain. So, any write to this register is delayed until the last write to the same register is synchronized to the timer clock domain.
<!-- page 2188 -->

##### 7.1.4.1.12 SDRAM temperature status read

The memory controller can change the SDRAM refresh rate (SRR) based on the temperature range where the memory device is operating.

###### Manual SRR

Software can trigger a read of the temperature status register only after the rank initialization is complete. The mode register address is 0x4. Mode register read command can be issued from the SHKE using the sequence in Section 7.1.4.1.7.

The controller uses the memory configuration information in the `DEVICE_CFG_RANK1`/`DEVICE_CFG_RANK0` field of the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_CONFIG_0` register to determine if the x32 memory device is built as 1x32, 2x16, or 4x8. This determines the temperature information from each device and computes the highest refresh rate required by any device.

A manual SRR causes the refresh rate updates depending on the sampled values. To disable the refresh rate update set to 0x1 the `DISABLE_AUTO_REFRESH_TEMP_UPDATE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register.

The data for the SRR can be read from the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_RDATA_RANK0_L` or `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_MREG_RDATA_RANK1_L` register.

###### Periodic SRR

To enable auto adjustment of the periodic refresh rate, the following should be performed:

1. Set to 0x4 the `MRR_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register as MR4 provides the LPDDR2/LPDDR3 temperature status information.
2. Configure the `MRR_RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register to enable the periodic MRR feature to all ranks which are enabled.
3. Configure the `MRR_INTERVAL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register to any appropriate non-zero value.
4. The data from the periodic MRR can be read from the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR_RDATA_RANK0_L` or `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR_RDATA_RANK1_L` register.

After enabling the auto-MRR feature, the memory controller immediately issues an MRR request to rank1 if enabled. Then, after `MRR_INTERVAL`/2, an MRR request is issued to rank0 if enabled.

If the refresh rate changes, the new refresh rate is used for that rank upon the expiry of the current refresh interval. To disable the refresh rate changes, set to 0x1 the `DISABLE_AUTO_REFRESH_TEMP_UPDATE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register.

To disable the periodic MRR feature, software can change the `MRR_INTERVAL` field from a non-zero value to 0x0. The `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register is synchronized to the timer clock domain. So, any write to this register is delayed until the last write to the same register is synchronized to the timer clock domain.
<!-- page 2189 -->

###### Refresh rate update

When the DPE samples the temperature update flag (TUF) from the LPDDR2/LPDDR3 SDRAM in response to the SRR read, the temperature refresh update information (on a per-rank basis) is sent to the SHKE through the DPE-SHKE interface. The TUF bit indicates that there was a change from the last read of the SDRAM mode register. The DPE also sends update information based on the device configuration (1x32 or 2x16 or 4x8) on a per-rank basis.

If the SHKE is configured to accept refresh rate changes through the `DISABLE_AUTO_REFRESH_TEMP_UPDATE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register, the refresh rate is changed at the expiration of the current refresh interval.

##### 7.1.4.1.13 Interrupt signaling and status

The TUF bit from the SDRAM can be used to signal an interrupt event. If the temperature information has changed from the last read of the mode register, the SDRAM sets the TUF bit.

If the device is getting close to the low or high temperature threshold, software can use the interrupt event to take precautions. To set the low and high thresholds for interrupt generation, the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRUPT_ENABLE` register must be used.

Once a level interrupt is generated, software can read the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRUPT_STATUS` register to determine the exact cause of the interrupt. To clear an interrupt, set to 0x1 the corresponding bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRUPT_CLR` register.

It is unnecessary to set to 0x1 bit [0] at 0x0044 C020 for writes to the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRUPT*` registers. Software can then choose to change the threshold for the interrupt via the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRUPT_ENABLE` register.

The `RANK_0_TEMP_OOR` and `RANK_1_TEMP_OOR` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS_0` register indicate if the SDRAM operates outside the operating temperature range. The `RANK_0_DERATE` and `RANK_1_DERATE` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS` register indicate if the SDRAM operates in derate mode.

##### 7.1.4.1.14 Deep power down

Deep power down (DPD) is a low-power state of the SDRAM device where no data is retained. The only way to revert the memory to normal mode once DPD is entered is by using a complete reinitialization sequence.

###### Enter DPD

The following is the sequence to enter DPD:

1. If enabled, disable hardware (activity based) self-refresh for the rank to be placed in DPD. This is done via writing 0x0 to the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0`/`HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register. This triggers self-refresh exit if any of the ranks were in this state.
2. Poll the `RANK_0_SR`/`RANK_1_SR` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS_0` register until 0x0.
<!-- page 2190 -->

* (Continuation of Section 7.1.4.1.14 Deep power down - Enter DPD)
3. Issue manual DPD command to the appropriate ranks by configuring the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register. Note that if both ranks need to be placed in DPD, this must be done sequentially.
4. Set to 0x1 the `ENTER_DEEP_PD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
5. Poll the `ENTER_DEEP_PD` bit until 0x0.
6. Poll the `RANK_0_DPD`/`RANK_1_DPD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS_0` register until 0x1.
7. Disable the CKE signal for the rank which entered DPD:
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to the appropriate value.
   * Set to 0x1 the `CKE_OFF` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
8. Poll the `CKE_OFF` bit until 0x0.
9. Disable the CK signal for the rank which entered DPD:
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to the appropriate value.
   * Set to 0x1 the `CK_OFF` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
10. Poll the `CK_OFF` bit until 0x0.
11. Set to 0x0 the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
12. Set to 0x0 the `RANK0_EN`/`RANK1_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.

When SHKE receives the software-triggered DPD command, it causes SCMO and DFE to flush the data for the rank to be placed in DPD. Any new commands driven to that rank result in decoding errors from SCMO and DFE. When this situation occurs, the controller clears the `ENTER_DEEP_PD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.

The memory controller must not issue any commands to the rank in DPD state. Once the rank enable and rank initialization is complete, bits are cleared and the status of the rank is uninitialized. The DPD status may no longer indicate that the rank is in DPD.

###### Exit DPD

Once the SDRAM is in DPD mode, all its contents are lost. After exiting DPD, the entire SDRAM initialization sequence must be performed again to make the memory active again.

The following is the sequence to exit DPD:

1. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS_0` register to the appropriate value. Note that if both ranks need to be brought out of DPD, this must be done sequentially.
2. Set to 0x1 the `EXIT_DEEP_PD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.


<!-- page 2191 -->

3. Poll the `EXIT_DEEP_PD` bit until `0x0`.
4. Perform initialization for the corresponding rank. See Section SDRAM initialization.

   > [!NOTE]
   > Software must maintain the memory timing parameter tDPD. Therefore, if the `RANK_EN` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SCMO_ADDR_MAP_CSn` register has been set to `0x0` before entering DPD, it must be set to `0x1`.

### 7.1.4.1.15 Self-refresh

Self-refresh is a low-power mode of the memory device that can be used to retain the SDRAM data, even if the rest of the system is powered down. When the SDRAM has entered self-refresh mode, all external control signals except CKE are in don’t care. An external clock is not necessary in this mode.

To enable partial array self-refresh (PASR) mode directly, set up the mode registers in the SDRAM device. This has no impact on the controller.

All self-refresh controls in the DPE registers that must be set during memory controller initialization reside in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_9`, `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_10`, and `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_13` registers.

#### Hardware-based self-refresh

The controller enters self-refresh if it is idle for a programmable number of cycles. This assumes that software-triggered self-refresh does not interfere with the hardware initiated one. This is only supported after the memory device has been initialized.

To enable hardware-based self-refresh mode, perform the following sequence:

1. Set to `0x1` the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0`/`HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register to enable the hardware activity-based self-refresh.
2. Configure the `HW_SELF_RFSH_IDLE_TIMER` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register appropriately.

The controller monitors the number of idle cycles. When the timer expires, it places the memory rank in self-refresh. The controller exits from self-refresh to execute a periodic ZQ-Cal, manual software request or new transactions received by DPE command queue.

The condition for hardware self-refresh wakeup due to SHKE activity is based on any valid software manual command (valid post rank initialization) triggered to that rank, including:

* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[ENTER_DEEP_PD]`
* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE]`
* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_ASAP]`
* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[ZQCAL_SHORT]`
* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[ZQCAL_LONG]`
* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[MODE_REGISTER_READ]`
<!-- page 2192 -->

* `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0[MODE_REGISTER_WRITE]`
* Any periodic SRR or ZQ events occurring to that rank.

Hardware self-refresh wakeup can also be caused by DPE activity. In the absence of any DPE activity, the device reenters self-refresh as soon as the manual commands are complete. Therefore, in this case the idle timer is not restarted.

Another condition triggering a hardware self-refresh exit is the self-refresh enable bit switching to disable mode. In other words, when a rank is in self-refresh, it wakes up when the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0`/`HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register is deasserted.

To change the value of the `HW_SELF_RFSH_IDLE_TIMER` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register in the middle of operation, which is not a common practice, software must perform the following:

1. Disable self-refresh by setting to `0x0` the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0`/`HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register.
2. Update to the new value by setting the new timer value in the `HW_SELF_RFSH_IDLE_TIMER` field of the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register.
3. Re-enable the self-refresh for the corresponding rank via the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` or `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit depending on the rank-independent self-refresh mode or concurrent self-refresh mode of operation.

   > [!NOTE]
   > The previous three steps must be separate register write operations.

#### Software-based self-refresh

The memory controller allows software to enter and exit self-refresh, which is intended for debug and a few software system sequences.

##### Enter self-refresh

Software must execute this sequence to trigger the controller to issue a self-refresh request which is allowed only after the rank is initialized and for active ranks in the system.

In a two-rank system with both ranks active, the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register must be set to `0x3` reflecting the request goes to both ranks.

In a two-rank system when one of the ranks is not available (as in DPD), the `RANK_SEL` field must be set to indicate the active rank only. A software self-refresh request trigger is not allowed if one of the ranks is being placed into or brought out of DPD mode.

The memory controller does not process any commands after a software-triggered self-refresh executes. The memory controller resumes only after software triggers an exit.

The following sequence shows software self-refresh entry:

1. Disable hardware-based self refresh for the appropriate rank by setting to `0x0` the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0`/`HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register.
<!-- page 2193 -->

2. Disable the IO calibration engine in the DDRPHY as described in Section IO calibration disabling. This is required because memory controller will not respond to IO calibration requests from the DDRPHY when in software-triggered self-refresh.
3. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the appropriate rank or both ranks.
4. If immediate self-refresh entering is desired perform the following:
   * Set to `0x1` the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_ASAP` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
   * Poll the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_ASAP` bit until `0x0`.
   * Go to step 7.
5. If self-refresh entering when idle is desired perform the following:
   * Set to `0x1` the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
   * Poll the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE` bit until `0x0`.
6. Read the `SW_SELF_RFSH` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_STATUS` register to verify that software self-refresh has been entered.

##### Exit self-refresh

Software self-refresh requests are supported only for all active ranks in the system. In a two-rank system, with both ranks active, the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register must be set to `0x3` reflecting the request goes to both ranks.

In a two-rank system when one of the ranks is not available (as in DPD), the `RANK_SEL` field must be set to indicate the active rank only. Software self-refresh exit is not allowed if one of the ranks is being brought out of DPD and the self-refresh exit must occur before the DPD exit sequence starts.

Software must not set to `0x1` the `EXIT_SELF_REFRESH` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register unless it has already set to `0x1` the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE` or `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_ASAP` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register or a watchdog reset has occurred.

The following sequence shows software self-refresh exit:

1. Depending on the amount of time memory device is in self-refresh state, execute manual IO calibration.
2. Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register for the appropriate rank or both ranks.
3. Set to `0x1` the `EXIT_SELF_REFRESH` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to cause the controller to exit self-refresh immediately.
4. Poll the `EXIT_SELF_REFRESH` bit until `0x0`.
5. Check if the appropriate rank came out of self-refresh by reading the `RANK_0_SR` or `RANK_1_SR` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_STATUS_0` register.
6. Enable DDRPHY IO calibration as described in Section IO calibration.
<!-- page 2194 -->

7. Enable hardware self-refresh for the appropriate rank by setting to `0x1` the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` or `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register.

### 7.1.4.1.16 IO calibration setup

There is a request-acknowledge IO calibration interface between the DDRPHY and SHKE. The IO calibration request for the control and data signals is asserted by the DDRPHY for one XO clock cycle. The SHKE responds with an acknowledge which duration can be programmed in DPE clock cycles via the `IOCAL_UPDATE_PULSE_WIDTH` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.

The memory controller holds stable the corresponding address control and data outputs to the DDRPHY during the time the acknowledge is asserted. This enables the IO calibration engine in the DDRPHY to perform the PCNT/NCNT update to the pads.

For more information, see Section [section missing or unspecified in source text].

### 7.1.4.1.17 LPDDR3 CA training pattern

To perform LPDDR3 CA training pattern, execute the following sequence:

1. Drive CKE low for the rank being calibrated:
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the rank being calibrated.
   * Set to `0x1` the `CKE_OFF` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the memory clock enable low.
2. Load the address pattern that is to be driven to the CA bus for calibration by writing to the following registers:
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_CA_TRAIN_PRE_CS`
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_CA_TRAIN_CS`
   * `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_CA_TRAIN_POST_CS`
3. Set to `0x1` the `CA_TRAIN_PATTERN_CMD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.

   > [!NOTE]
   > Only one manual command can be outstanding to the controller at any time.

Hardware clears the `CA_TRAIN_PATTERN_CMD` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register once the pattern has been driven to the SDRAM bus. During CA calibration, the SDRAM samples the CA bus and drives the sampled value back to the DQ bus. Then, software can perform checks on the sampled data pattern by reading the PHY registers. Another CA training pattern can be triggered by repeating the sequence.

### 7.1.4.1.18 Training sequences

The training sequences shown in this section are one-time software-based sequences performed during boot.
<!-- page 2195 -->

#### Functions to be disabled before training

To disable periodic hardware events if already enabled, perform the following steps:

1. Disable periodic MRR by setting to `0x0` the `MRR_INTERVAL` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register. This is required for all DDRPHY training sequences.
2. Disable periodic ZQ by setting to `0x0` the `ZQCAL_INTERVAL` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register. This is required for all DDRPHY training sequences except for CA training.
3. Disable periodic auto refreshes by setting to `0x0` the `AUTO_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` and `AUTO_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register. This is required for all DDRPHY training sequences except for CA training.
4. Disable hardware-based self-refresh controls by setting to `0x0` the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` and `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register. This is required for all DDRPHY training sequences.

#### CA training for LPDDR3

The CA training sequence is required to calibrate the SDRAM characteristic of the command address (CA) bus to ensure that the setup and hold timings are satisfied. The sequence involves driving data patterns on the CA bus with the chip select to the SDRAM device.

The SDRAM device samples the CA bus on the positive and negative edge of the clock (qualified with chip select) and asynchronously sends the captured value on the DQ pins. CA delays can be adjusted to find the precise delay values to ensure that the setup and hold is met on the CA bus.

The CA training is required to be done sequentially for each rank. Additionally, for a two-rank system CA training cannot be performed while the other rank is actively receiving traffic. In other words, both the ranks are required to be initialized together.

The memory controller registers associated with CA training are involved in the following:

* Enable and disable CA training modes through mode register writes to the SDRAM.
* Drive the different data patterns on the CA bus.

The DDRPHY registers associated with CA training are involved in the following:

* Control the CA delays (individual CA bits, including fine and coarse delay control).
* Read the asynchronous DQ bus from the SDRAM.
* Override the DQ/DQS IE/OE signals from the memory controller to enable sampling of data required for training.

##### Enable CA training (first pass)

If CA training was performed after device and controller initialization, then set to `0x0` the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register. CA training for LPDDR3 devices can be enabled by setting the SDRAM mode register MR41 (Address = `0x29`, Opcode = `0xA4`). This mode calibrates the address pins CA0, CA1, CA2, CA3, CA5, CA6, CA7, and CA8.
<!-- page 2196 -->

An extra CA training mode can be enabled by setting the MR48. This mode is used to calibrate the remaining address pins CA4 and CA9. Software can initiate the mode register writes using the SHKE registers. See the SDRAM extended mode register write details in Section SDRAM EMR write.

The controller can be set up to drive patterns on the CA bus for CA training. Specifically, the registers in the controller must provide the ability to drive the CA bus (PE/NE) with a value one cycle before the chip select assertion, drive a value (PE/NE of CA bus) during the chip select assertion, and drive a value (PE/NE of CA bus) one cycle after the chip select assertion.

Software is required to set up the six different data values for each CA pattern (CA PE and CA NE) to be driven for the training. See the LPDDR3 CA training pattern details in Section [section missing or unspecified in source text].

##### Enable CA training (second pass)

After the software sequence produces an optimal setting, CA training mode can be enabled to the additional mode to calibrate the address pins CA4 and CA9 by setting LPDDR3 MR48 (Address = `0x30`, Opcode = `0xC0`). Before performing the mode register write, CKE must be turned on as follows:

* Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the rank being calibrated.
* Set to `0x1` the `CKE_ON` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the memory clock enable high.

Then perform the SDRAM extended mode register write (see Section [section missing or unspecified in source text]) to calibrate address pins CA4 and CA9. See the LPDDR3 CA training pattern details in Section LPDDR3 CA training pattern.

##### Disable CA training

After the software sequence produces an optimal setting, the CA training mode can be disabled by setting LPDDR3 MR42 (Address = `0x2A`, Opcode = `0xA8`). Before performing the mode register write, CKE must be turned on as follows:

* Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to indicate the rank being calibrated.
* Set to `0x1` the `CKE_ON` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register to drive the memory clock enable high.

If CA training was performed after device and controller initialization, reset to `0x1` the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.

#### Write leveling for LPDDR3

This sequence aligns the write DQS to the memory clock at the SDRAM. It is primarily used to compensate for the delay in the package to meet the strict tDQSS requirements of the LPDDR3 device. This SoC generates DQS pulses to the SDRAM device which samples the clock at the rising edge of DQS and sends the information to the SoC on the asynchronous DQ bus.
<!-- page 2197 -->

To enable write leveling for the specific rank, set to `0x1` the `OP7` bit in the LPDDR3 MR2. To disable write leveling after the software write leveling sequence is successful, set to `0x0` the `OP7` bit in the LPDDR3 MR2. If two ranks are present, then repeat the write leveling sequence for the second rank. For more information about MR write, see the SDRAM mode register write sequence in Section SDRAM MR write.

The memory controller registers associated with LPDDR3 write leveling are involved in the following:

* Enabling and disabling write leveling through mode register writes to SDRAM.

The DDRPHY registers associated with LPDDR3 write leveling are involved in the following:

* Control the DQS delays for each data byte (fine and coarse delay control).
* Trigger a DQS pulse to the SDRAM.
* Read the asynchronous DQ bus from the SDRAM.
* Override the DQ/DQS IE/OE signals from the memory controller to control driving and sampling of data required for training.

  > [!NOTE]
  > If both ranks of the controller are present, then write leveling must be performed on a rank individual basis.

#### DQS-DQ read calibration

This training sequence is used to position the read DQS and DQ for reliable capture of the read data by the controller. It involves a software-triggered master performing writes to initialize the SDRAM with a worst-case data pattern (because the writes have not been calibrated, the write data has not been successfully written to the SDRAM device).

Using the CPU master, software triggers many reads, compares, and adjusts the DQ delays through the DDRPHY registers. For this calibration, the IE and read capture windows in the controller must be set so that the controller can see all DQS edges from the SDRAM device. The register controls are in `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_14` and `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_15`.

The DDRPHY registers associated with DQS-DQ read calibration control the DQ delays – fine and coarse delay control and per-bit DQ.

#### DQS-DQ write calibration

This training sequence positions the write DQS and DQ to ensure that the write DQS edge is center-aligned to the write data. It involves a software-triggered master performing writes to initialize the SDRAM with a worst-case data pattern.

Using the CPU master, software triggers many reads and compares. Software has control over the write DQS delays (or DQ or both) which are adjusted for each write and read dataset. For this calibration, the IE and read capture windows in the controller must be set so that the controller can see all DQS edges from the SDRAM device. The register controls are in `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_14` and `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_DRAM_TIMING_15`. The DDRPHY registers associated with DQS-DQ write calibration control the DQ delays – fine and coarse delay control and per-bit DQ.
<!-- page 2198 -->

#### Functions to be enabled after training

The following steps enable periodic hardware events after the respective training sequences are completed:

1. After all DDRPHY training sequences except for CA training, enable periodic ZQ calibration:
   * Configure the `RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register based on the ranks present.
   * Configure the `ZQCAL_INTERVAL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_ZQCAL` register with optimal settings.
2. After all DDRPHY training sequences except for CA training, enable periodic auto refreshes by correctly setting the `AUTO_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` and `AUTO_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register based on the ranks present.
3. After all DDRPHY training sequences, enable periodic SRR:
   * Set to `0x4` the `MRR_ADDR` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register. The MR4 register in LPDDR2/3 provides temperature status information.
   * Configure the `MRR_RANK_SEL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register based on the ranks present.
   * Configure the `MRR_INTERVAL` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_PERIODIC_MRR` register with optimal settings.
4. Enable hardware-based self-refresh controls.
5. After all DDRPHY training sequences, set correctly the `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK0` and `HW_SELF_RFSH_ENABLE_RANK1` bits in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register based on the ranks present.

### 7.1.4.1.19 Low frequency behavior

The SHKE and DPE architecture separates the refresh requests from all other housekeeping commands. SHKE sends a separate pulse per rank to indicate when refresh is required. This allows DPE to know immediately when a new refresh is required on each rank independently. It improves the ability to keep up with refreshes at low frequencies. DPE uses this pulse to track the number of outstanding refreshes on a rank. For example, if DPE has received four refresh request pulses from SHKE but has only issued two, then two refreshes are outstanding. When a rank has outstanding refreshes, DPE immediately starts blocking page activities and traffic. This allows the controller in parallel prepare for and execute refreshes across two ranks.

However, the design also implements the LPDDR2/3 refresh bandwidth requirement (tREFBW) that limits no more than eight refreshes in any rolling window of 32*tRFCab. The refresh bandwidth can cause traffic blocks for long periods while it catches up on refreshes. At 9.6 MHz, 4X refresh rate, 3.9 μs tREFi, traffic can be blocked for almost 100 μs. Therefore, the recommendation is to never run the controller at 9.6 MHz.
<!-- page 2199 -->

The `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL_1` register can be used to define the refresh interval of rank 1 independently of rank 0. Ideally this register should be used to minimize the number of refreshes issued in a two-rank system where both ranks do not have the same refresh interval. Otherwise, tREFi is only specified in `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` that is common to both ranks. If so, the worst case must be used.

For example, if one rank = 3.9 μs and the other = 7.8 μs, 3.9 μs must be used.

A feature in SHKE avoids running at 4X refresh rate at 9.6 MHz if the normal refresh interval is 3.9 us. The `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL_2` register controls a delay timer that allows software to delay the automatic switch to the 4X refresh rate for up to 65535 timer clocks (up to 2 seconds). The intent of this timer is that software uses it to delay long enough for software to switch the clock frequency to a higher one before the controller actually starts issuing refreshes at the 4X rates (every 977 ns).

The DDRPHY requires a 2X memory clock input. The lowest frequency of operation is 9.6 MHz. Depending on the device configuration, the following special steps are recommended for the high temperature:

* Software must know which ranks have which nominal refresh interval, such as rank0 = 7.8 μs and rank1 = 3.9 μs.
* The `BIMC_S_DDR0_DPE_INTERRRUPT_ENABLE` register must be configured such that an interrupt is generated if the temperature reaches the 4X refresh rate level (`HIGH_TEMP_THRESHOLD` = `TREFI_0.25X_DERATE`).
* The `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL_2` register must be configured as follows:
  * `DLY_RFSH_CONDN` = `TREFI_0.25X` (only delay switch to 4X rate)
  * `RFSH_UPDATE_TIMER` = minimum number of timer clocks required to cover safely the time it takes to receive an interrupt from DPE due to temperature increase and to actually switch the frequency up from 9.6 MHz to a higher frequency (expected delay is in 5 ms range).
* If any 3.9 μs tREFi device is at or above the 4X refresh rate temperature, software should not switch frequencies to 9.6 MHz from a higher temperature.
* If it is already at 9.6 MHz, software switches to higher frequency if it receives an interrupt indicating the temperature of any 3.9 μs tREFi device has gone above the 4X refresh rate level (0.25X tREFi).

### 7.1.4.1.20 XO clock switch, shutdown, and resume

If the XO clock must be shut down to save power, memory contents, IO signal quality, and timing, margins must be maintained. Under normal circumstances, the XO clock is a continuously running clock with a constant rate. In a dual-channel system, typically the XO clock shutdown means that the clock to both channels is shut down. In that case, the following steps must be performed for both channels:

* Execute the enter self-refresh sequence as shown in Section Enter self-refresh to enter self-refresh. Software can safely disable XO clock and can restart XO clock as needed by the system.
<!-- page 2200 -->

* Software might need to reconfigure BIMC initialization.
* If the new XO clock frequency differs from the original one, software must reprogram the `HW_SELF_RFSH_IDLE_TIMER` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_SELF_REFRESH_CNTL` register and the `TREFI` field in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_AUTO_REFRESH_CNTL` register as they affect the timers running on the XO clock with the new XO clock period.
* Software might need to reconfigure the DDRPHY.
* Execute the exit self-refresh sequence as shown in Section Exit self-refresh.
* Depending on the duration of XO shutdown, a manual SRR, ZQ or IO calibration is recommended.
* Once all the preceding calibrations have completed, software may resume memory traffic.

### 7.1.4.1.21 Watchdog reset sequence flow

Memory contents should be maintained during a watchdog event without direct software interaction, so trace data stored in main memory before a system crash can be retrieved. If watchdog event occurs the memory is placed in self-refresh mode and a subsequent reset does not change this until directed by software. The controller automatically initiates an enter self-refresh command to all active ranks as soon as possible. The self-refresh status can be read from the `WDOG_SELF_RFSH` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_STATUS` register.

The memory controller is reset after the watchdog event, but it preserves its internal self-refresh state, the self-refresh state of the memory device, and the value of the `WDOG_SELF_RFSH` bit. Thus, CKE is preserved and maintains a value of “0” keeping the memory device in self-refresh state. As the memory controller register contents are lost during reset following a watchdog event, the DPE and SHKE registers must be reset to the optimal settings.

The following software workaround is required to handle a hardware issue when the TREFI is not loaded correctly:

1. Set to `0x0` the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register for the rank present.
2. Wait at least three XO clock cycles.
3. Set to `0x1` the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register for the rank present.
4. Repeat steps 1 through 3 for all channels.

After the reset deassertion and register reconfiguration, software can bring the memory device out of self-refresh by performing the exit self-refresh sequence as described in Section Exit self-refresh. At this point, software triggers the processor cache data to the SDRAM, so the same would be retained for debug. This is equivalent to the memory controller receiving a several writes to the SDRAM. Now software can read the SDRAM contents to determine what caused the failure that has triggered watchdog event.




<!-- page 2201 -->
### 7.1.4.2 DDRPHY functional description

The DDRPHY block is critical in accessing external SDRAM devices. All command address (CA) and data byte (DQ) SDRAM signals are routed through the DDRPHY. There are two DDRPHY types – CA PHY and DQ PHY. Each DQ PHY provides support for one byte of the SDRAM interface. Thus, there are four DQ PHY blocks for the 32-bit SDRAM interface. There is only one CA PHY block.

The DDRPHY includes the following sub-blocks:
* IO pads.
* Configuration registers.
* Calibrated delay circuits (CDC).
* Calibration controller for CDC and for IO pads.

There is also an AHB2PHY module that is used to access the DQ PHY configuration registers.

#### 7.1.4.2.1 AHB2PHY broadcast mode

Multiple DQ DDRPHY configuration registers can be set with a single write access using the AHB2PHY broadcast mode. For example, in broadcast mode a write access to the DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG register issues writes to the DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG registers of all DQ DDRPHYs accessed through a common AHB2PHY module.

The broadcast mode is only applicable to write accesses. Reads of the configuration registers must be issued for each DDR PHY separately.

> [!NOTE]
> For certain registers or sequences, setting the registers simultaneously for all DDRPHYs may not be practical.

#### 7.1.4.2.2 Calibrated delay circuit

Assertion of a software calibration trigger followed by its deassertion creates a trigger pulse that initiates the calibration engine. Subsequently, the hardware-based auto-calibration is enabled.

The auto-calibration interval must be set to recommended values. To avoid corner cases, the recommendation is that the auto-calibration interval value be greater than the time it takes to perform one calibration. Otherwise, the auto-calibration timer generates a trigger pulse during the calibration process. To safeguard against this, any trigger pulse generated while the calibration engine is in a non-idle state is ignored.

The CDC_REFCOUNT_CFG register helps determine the accuracy of calibration. As the value increases, more reference (fixed) frequency clock cycles are used for calibration, thereby increasing the accuracy of the calibration. However, this costs larger calibration times. Therefore, the recommended value of CDC_REFCOUNT_CFG balances the accuracy and speed of calibration. Conversely, smaller values of CDC_REFCOUNT_CFG may appear adequate for devices in the nominal region of the spread. However, these values may not work consistently for devices at the extremes of PVT (process, voltage, temperature) plot.
<!-- page 2202 -->
#### CDC initialization sequence

To function correctly, the calibration sequence requires fixed frequency clock in the range between 19.2 MHz and 27 MHz. Other fixed frequencies can also be suitable, but this range has been extensively verified and is recommended.

The calibration sequence is used at Power-on reset, as a part of the SDRAM initialization and in case of change in the voltage domain connected to CDC. Calibration of CDC is not required for a change in the SDRAM interface operating frequency.

The CDC initialization sequence is as follows:
1. Perform CDC register initialization sequence if not already done. See Section *CDC register initialization sequence*.
2. Assert software calibration trigger by writing `0x1` to the `SW_TRIG_FULL_CALIB` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
3. De-assert software calibration trigger by writing `0x0` to the `SW_TRIG_FULL_CALIB` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
4. If the DDR 1x clock frequency is in frequency zone 1, go to step 7.
5. Enable auto-calibration by setting to `0x1` the `HW_AUTOCAL_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
6. Enable auto-calibration timer by setting to `0x1` the `TIMER_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG0` register.
7. Poll the `CALIBRATION_DONE` bit in the `CDC_STATUS0` register until `0x1` to check if calibration is done.
8. Confirm that there was no error during calibration by reading `0x0` from the `CDC_ERROR_CODE` bit in the `CDC_STATUS0` register.
9. If `CDC_ERROR_CODE` = `0x1`, raise a flag to debug the root cause of CDC calibration error.

#### CDC register initialization sequence
1. Write recommended values to the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
2. Write recommended values to the `CDC_CTLR_CFG1` register.
3. Write recommended values to the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG0` register.
4. Write recommended values to the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG1` register.
5. Write recommended values to the `CDC_REFCOUNT_CFG` register.
6. Write recommended values to the `CDC_COARSE_CAL_CFG` register.
7. Write recommended values to the `CDC_DELAY_CFG` register.
8. Write recommended values to the `CDC_OFFSET_CFG` register.
9. Write recommended values to the `CDC_SLAVE_DDA_CFG` register.
<!-- page 2203 -->
#### CDC auto-calibration sequence disabling

To disable the CDC auto-calibration sequence perform the following steps:
1. If exiting rapid calibration, set to `0x0` the `FF_TIMER_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG1` register and go to step 3.
2. If not exiting rapid calibration set to `0x0` the `TIMER_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG0` register.
3. Disable auto-calibration by setting to `0x0` the `HW_AUTOCAL_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
4. Poll the `CTLR_SM_IDLE` bit in the `CDC_STATUS0` register until `0x1`.

#### CDC software calibration sequence

The software-triggered sequence can calibrate the CDC on-demand only after the CDC initialization sequence described in Section *CDC initialization sequence*. CDC auto-calibration is not in an enabled state when this sequence is executed as part of frequency switch from zone 1 to transition frequency. The software-triggered sequence is as follows:
1. If not already done, disable the CDC auto-calibration sequence as described in Section *CDC auto-calibration sequence disabling*.
2. Configure the `DELAY_VAL` field in the `CDC_DELAY_CFG` register.
3. Write recommended values to the `TMUX_CHAR` field in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
4. Write recommended values to the `CDC_OFFSET_CFG` register.
5. Write recommended values to the `CDC_SLAVE_DDA_CFG` register.
6. Assert software calibration trigger by writing `0x1` to the `SW_TRIG_FULL_CALIB` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
7. De-assert software calibration trigger by writing `0x0` to the `SW_TRIG_FULL_CALIB` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
8. Poll the `CALIBRATION_DONE` bit in the `CDC_STATUS0` register until `0x1` to check if calibration is done.
9. Confirm that there was no error during calibration by reading `0x0` from the `CDC_ERROR_CODE` bit in the `CDC_STATUS0` register. If `CDC_ERROR_CODE` = `0x1`, raise a flag to debug the root cause of CDC calibration error.
10. If transitioning to frequency zone 1, perform the following steps, otherwise exit the sequence:
    * Enable auto-calibration by setting to `0x1` the `HW_AUTOCAL_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register.
    * Enable auto-calibration timer by setting to `0x1` the `TIMER_ENA` bit in the `CDC_CAL_TIMER_CFG0` register.

Table 7-7 lists the possible sequences that require a CDC software triggered calibration sequence and the recommended setting for the `CDC_SLAVE_DDA_CFG` register and the `DELAY_VAL` field in the `CDC_DELAY_CFG` register.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
