## 7.1.5.21 DIM_D02_DDRPHY_DQ register definitions

### 7.1.5.21.1 DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG (0x00001800)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_DDR_DIM_CFG_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000031

The `DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG` register configures the following: DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG / DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_TOP_CFG
<!-- page 2403 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :---------- |
| 30 | DQ_LB_MODE_SEL | Selects external or internal loop back mode<br>1'b1: internal loop back mode<br>1'b0: external loop back mode (default) |
| 29 | DQ_LB_MODE_EN | Enables external or internal loop back mode<br>1'b1: loop back mode enabled<br>1'b0: loop back mode disabled (default) |
| 28 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 27 | MISR_DATA_CLK_SEL | selects b/w MISR data or SEED and Loopback clock or FF clock<br>1'b1: from dte<br>1'b0: seed from csr ff clk (default) |
| 26 | CDC_LDO_EN | Enablement of CDC LDO<br>1'b1: Enabled<br>1'b0: Disabled LDO and power provided from switches (default) |
| 25 | CDC_SWITCH_RC_EN | Enablement of CDC power RC (LPF) switch<br>1'b1: Enabled<br>1'b0: Disabled (default) |
| 24 | CDC_SWITCH_BYPASS_OFF | Enablement of CDC power bypass switch<br>1'b1: Disabled<br>1'b0: Enabled (default) |
| 16 | RCW_EN | Enablement of the Read Capture Window<br>1'b1: Enable the RCW<br>1'b0: Disabled (default) |
| 8 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 5 | WR_PIPE_EXTEND1 | Write pipe extend select (when hp_mode = 1'b1)<br>1'b1: with pipe extend (default)<br>1'b0: without pipe extend |
| 4 | WR_PIPE_EXTEND0 | Write pipe extend select (when hp_mode = 1'b0)<br>1'b1: with pipe extend (default)<br>1'b0: without pipe extend |
| 0 | WR_CLK_SEL | Write clock select<br>1'b1: With write CDC (default)<br>1'b0: Bypass write CDC, write clock from cdiv2 phi2 output |

### 7.1.5.21.11 DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_CDC_CTLR_CFG0 (0x00001830)

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_DDR_DIM_CFG_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x02000000

The `DIM_DQ_CDC_CTLR_CFG0` register configures the following: DIM_DQ_CDC_CTLR_CFG0 / DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_CDC_CTLR_CFG0
<!-- page 2409 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :---------- |
| 26 | ERROR_CODE_UPDATE_EN | 1'b1: Enable overwriting (default) the error code for subsequent calibrations.<br>1'b0: Disable overwriting the error code during subsequent calibrations |
| 25 | STAGGER_CAL_ENA | 1'b1: Stagger calibration of write and read CDCs once after the other to reduce peak voltage drop.<br>1'b0: Both write and read CDCs calibrated simultaneously<br>This bit is introduced on the x2 core, so not present on x0 and x1 versions of DIM/PHY. |
| 24 | TRACKING_CAL_ENA | 1'b1: Relationship between subunits and oscillator count is learnt and used for tracking calibration.<br>1'b0: Periodic calibration triggers cause full recalibration |
| 23:20 | OSC_COUNT_ERR_TOLERANCE | Magnitude of the difference between oscillator count and target count when the algorithm assumes convergence and stops further search. |
| 19 | TRACK_CALIB_MODE | 1'b0: Tracking calibration uses previous Target_count value.<br>1'b1 Accurate mode: Target_count is recomputed at the start of tracking calibration |
| 18 | FULL_DELAY | 1'b0: unitstep and subunit caps are from calibration or SW settings<br>1'b1: All unit step and subunit caps are selected for the delay arrays. |
| 17 | HW_AUTOCAL_ENA | 1'b1: Enables periodic auto calibration<br>1'b0: Periodic calibration is disabled |
| 16 | SW_TRIG_FULL_CALIB | A low to high transition on this register bit triggers the CDC calibration statemachine to initiate full calibration of the standby delay array. Also resets tracking mode for the delay arrays. |
| 13:12 | OSC_PRE_DIV | The factor by which the raw oscillator frequency is divided before being given to the counting logic.<br>2'b00 Divide by 1<br>2'b01 Divide by 2<br>2'b10 Divide by 4<br>2'b11 Divide by 8 |
| 10:0 | TMUX_CHAR | Cchar is a characterized constant equal to the ratio of output mux offset delay to average unit step delay. This register is programmed by multiplying the constant with 1024 and rounding to the nearest integer. E.g. if Cchar = 0.67, RO(0.67 * 1024) = 686, hence program TMUX_CHAR = 11'h2AE |

### 7.1.5.21.12 DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_CDC_CTLR_CFG1 (0x00001834)

| 23:20 | STANDBY_DELAY | This is the number of reference clock cycles from when a newly calibrated delay array is made active to when the current active delay array is put into standby mode.<br>4'b0: Disables the counter. Hardware waits for explicit acknowledgement of delay array switch from CDC.<br>Others: Explicit acknowledgement mode is disabled, and the counter is used |
| 18:16 | DEL_MODE_DELAY | Number of reference clock cycles between putting a newly calibrated delay array in delay mode to selecting it as the active delay array. The minimum allowed value is 1 |

| 10:8 | DECODER_DELAY | Number of reference clock cycles allowed for unitstep and subunit counts to be encoded into the unit and finecap select lines on the DDA. The minimum allowed value is 1. |

| 2:0 | MULTIPLIER_DELAY | Number of reference clock cycles allowed for arithmetic multiplication operations. The minimum allowed value is 1 |

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 11 | SW_OVRD_DA1_OSC_EN | In software override mode, 1'b1 written to this bit puts delay array 1 in oscillator-mode |

| 2 | SW_OVRD_LOAD_DA_SEL | In software override mode, this bit selects the delay array to which unit and subunit offset values from CDC_OFFSET_CFG register will be loaded. |

### 7.1.5.21.32 0x000018D0 DIM_D02_DIM_DQ_WR_CDC_STATUS0

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 26:24 | CDC_ERROR_CODE | Error code for internal errors:<br>3'b000: No error<br>3'b001: Programmed delay less than Tmux<br>3'b010: Programmed delay less than Tmin<br>3'b011: Unit-step overflow: Overflow during fine calibration. Desired delay cannot be realized even when all unit-steps are selected.<br>3'b100: Unit-step underflow<br>3'b101: Unit-step overflow: Overflow during coarse calibration. Estimated unit steps needed to realize the desired delay are greater than the total number of unit-steps in design.<br>Note: The CDC_ERROR_CODE is not a sticky register and is updated after each CDC calibration. |
| 23:16 | SW_REF_GATE_COUNT | Number of reference clock cycles in the software generated oscillation gate window doing SW override mode |
| 15:4 | OSC_COUNT | Current value of oscillator count |
| 3 | CURR_SEL_DA | This bit indicates the current active delay array connected to the output.<br>1'b0: DA0 is selected<br>1'b1: DA1 is selected |
| 2 | CTLR_SM_IDLE | 1'b1 Indicates that the calibration state machine is idle.<br>1'b0 indicates calibration statemachine is busy |
| 1 | OSC_DONE | This status register is set after oscillations count is finished by CDC. It gets reset when a new oscillator count is started. |
| 0 | CALIBRATION_DONE | 1'b1 indicates that calibration is done and CURR_SUBUNIT_STEPS, CURR_UNIT_STEPS status registers are valid. |

| Bits | Name | Description |

| 30 | DQ_LB_MODE_SEL | Selects external or internal loop back mode<br>1'b1: internal loop back mode<br>1'b0: external loop back mode (default) |
| 29 | DQ_LB_MODE_EN | Enables external or internal loop back mode<br>1'b1: loop back mode enabled<br>1'b0: loop back mode disabled (default) |
| 28 | RESERVED | Reserved |

| 25 | CDC_SWITCH_RC_EN | Enablement of CDC power RC (LPF) switch<br>1'b1: Enabled<br>1'b0: Disabled (default) |
| 24 | CDC_SWITCH_BYPASS_OFF | Enablement of CDC power bypass switch<br>1'b1: Disabled<br>1'b0: Enabled (default) |
| 16 | RCW_EN | Enablement of the Read Capture Window<br>1'b1: Enable the RCW<br>1'b0: Disabled (default) |
| 8 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 5 | WR_PIPE_EXTEND1 | Write pipe extend select (when hp_mode = 1'b1)<br>1'b1: with pipe extend (default)<br>1'b0: without pipe extend |
| 4 | WR_PIPE_EXTEND0 | Write pipe extend select (when hp_mode = 1'b0)<br>1'b1: with pipe extend (default)<br>1'b0: without pipe extend |
| 0 | WR_CLK_SEL | Write clock select<br>1'b1: With write CDC (default)<br>1'b0: Bypass write CDC, write clock from cdiv2 phi2 output |

| 18 | FULL_DELAY | 1'b0: unitstep and subunit caps are from calibration or SW settings. 1'b1: All unit step and subunit caps are selected for the delay arrays. |

| 13:12 | OSC_PRE_DIV | The factor by which the raw oscillator frequency is divided before being given to the counting logic.<br>2'b00 Divide by 1<br>2'b01 Divide by 2<br>2'b10 Divide by 4<br>2'b11 Divide by 8 |
| 10:0 | TMUX_CHAR | Char is a characterized constant equal to the ratio of output mux offset delay to average unit step delay. This register is programmed by multiplying the constant with 1024 and rounding to the nearest integer. E.g. if Char = 0.67, RO(0.67 * 1024) = 686, hence program TMUX_CHAR = 11'h2AE |

# 7.2 DMA Engine for Hardware Retention (DEHR)

This section describes the DMA Engine for Hardware Retention (DEHR).

## 7.2.1 DEHR overview

The DEHR is a DMA engine, which is used to save and restore BIMC configuration data during power collapse. Figure 7-5 shows the DEHR overview.

#### Figure 7-5: DEHR overview
*Description:* A block diagram of the DEHR system within the Snapdragon 410E SoC. The DEHR block, which contains an internal SRAM, is positioned in the center. It has a bidirectional Handshake interface with the GDHS block inside the GCC (Global Clock Controller), and also receives a Clock signal from the GCC. The DEHR also has a bidirectional Handshake interface with the xPU block inside the BIMC (Bus Integrated Memory Controller). Both the DEHR and the BIMC are connected bidirectionally to a shared "Peripheral and system configuration NoC" bus.
*Label:* DEHR_001

### 7.2.1.1 DEHR acronyms and terms

Table 7-12 lists the common acronyms and terms used throughout this section.

#### Table 7-12: DEHR acronyms and terms

| Acronym or term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| DEHR | DMA Engine for Hardware Retention |
| BIMC | Bus Integrated Memory Controller |
| GDHS | Globally Distributed Head Switch |
<!-- page 2448 -->

Figure 7-6 shows the DEHR internal connections.

#### Figure 7-6: DEHR internal connectivity
*Description:* A connectivity diagram showing how the DEHR is integrated into the Snapdragon 410E SoC. The GCC block sends a clock signal "GCC_DEHR_CLK" to the DEHR block, and has a bidirectional Handshake interface between its GDHS sub-block and the DEHR. The BIMC block has a bidirectional Handshake interface between its xPU sub-block and the DEHR. The DEHR block has a bidirectional connection to the "Peripheral and system configuration NoC" bus.
*Label:* DEHR_002

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DEHR | VDD_CX | Peripheral and system configuration NoC |

| Module | IM(1) clock | Source | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DEHR | GCC_DEHR_CLK | GCC | DEHR clock |

(1) IM = integration module in GCC

## 7.2.3 DEHR functional description

The DEHR functions as both master and slave on the PCNOC. This bus is used for software configuration of DEHR, DEHR xPU and DEHR VMIDMT. The PCNOC is also used to read or write data from or to the DEHR SRAM. It is also used by DEHR to do save and restore transactions.

DEHR has handshaking with GDHS controller to detect power collapse and perform save operation. The handshaking is also used to detect power up and perform restore operation. DEHR has handshaking signals with BIMC xPU too. DEHR saves and restores BIMC configuration data during power collapse.

### 7.2.3.1 DEHR operation

DEHR performs two operations: save and restore. It fetches the BIMC slave configuration data and saves it into the DEHR SRAM for save operation. It transfers the data back to BIMC for restore operation. The DEHR also provides ways to access its configuration space.

### 7.2.3.2 Save and restore operations

The configuration data address and length are programmed as linked list and loaded into DEHR SRAM first.

For save operation, DEHR gets the linked list descriptors from SRAM and decodes the descriptors. It then starts sending AHB read requests to BIMC to get its configuration data and save it into the DEHR SRAM.

For restore operation, DEHR gets the linked list descriptors from SRAM and decodes the descriptors. It then reads SRAM again to fetch the configuration data. When both address and data are ready, it starts sending AHB write requests to BIMC to transfer the configuration data back.

### 7.2.3.3 Linked list format

The configuration data that DEHR saves and restores is not a continuous data block. It has a lot of reserved (RSVD) holes in between the valid data blocks.

The linked list is used to descript each data block address and length. It also points to the next valid data block to avoid the RSVD holes.

There are two types of linked list descriptors: address type and link type. The address type holds the new base address and is shown in Table 7-15. The link type holds both length and offset for two data blocks and is shown in Table 7-16.

#### Table 7-15: Address type linked list descriptor

| Bits | 32 | 31:28 | 27:0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Field | AD | RSVD | Address |

In case of address type descriptor, the AD bit is 0x1. The Address field holds the new transfer base address. It reflects bits [31:4] of the actual address.
<!-- page 2450 -->
#### Table 7-16: Link type linked list descriptor

| Bits | 32 | 31:25 | 24:17 | 16:15 | 14:8 | 7:0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Field | AD | Len2 | Offset2 | RSVD | Len1 | Offset1 |

In case of link type descriptor, the AD bit is 0x0. The Offset1/Len1 fields are the first offset/length pair and the Offset2/Len2 fields are the second offset/length pair.

DEHR treats an empty link (all Len/Offset are 0x0) as the end of the linked list. In case there are odd number of links in the middle of linked list, Len2 should be set to 0x0 and Offset2 to 0x1.

There are many reserved holes in the BIMC configuration space. The DEHR won’t save and then restore them as the linked list descriptor is used to skip these reserved holes. Figure 7-7 shows an example for part of the BIMC configuration space.

#### Figure 7-7: Linked list descriptors example
*Description:* A diagram illustrating how a partially populated and fragmented BIMC configuration space is mapped to logical descriptors and finally encoded into 33-bit hardware linked list descriptors.
- **Left (BIMC configuration space):** Shows a vertical stack of memory addresses containing either valid register words (e.g. `0x1004` (1 word), `0x1010-0x1014` (2 words), `0x1020` (1 word), etc.) or reserved space (RSVD) holes (e.g., "51 words" between `0x1030` and `0x1100`).
- **Middle (Logical descriptors):** Translates the memory structure into logical parameters. Address type descriptors set the base address (e.g., `AD=1`, `Address=0x000 0100` for base `0x1000`). Link type descriptors specify pairs of offsets and lengths to skip reserved holes (e.g., `AD=0`, `Len2=2`, `Offset2=3`, `RSVD`, `Len1=1`, `Offset1=1`).
- **Right (Linked list descriptors):** Shows the final 33-bit binary representation of the descriptors, matching the logical tables (e.g., address descriptor `0x1` | `0x0000 0100`, link descriptor `0x0` | `0x2` | `0x3` | `0x0` | `0x1` | `0x1`).
*Label:* DEHR_003


<!-- page 2451 -->
#### 7.2.3.4 Save and restore sequence
The save and restore is kicked off when a power-collapse is triggered. It is atomic operation which cannot be interrupted. The accesses to the client and configuration ports of BIMC xPU are blocked from the beginning of the save process to the end of the restore process. However, the BIMC xPU ports are not blocked for DEHR.

Assuming the DEHR configuration has been done a priori, the save sequence is as follows:
1. Software must ensure that all accesses to BIMC have been completed and the memory in self-refresh.
2. Software triggers a power collapse by writing to the BIMC GDHS controller.
3. Power-collapse is initiated by sending notification to DEHR over the handshake interface.
4. DEHR requests from the BIMC xPU to block the accesses to the xPU client and configuration ports. Blocked means all transactions to these ports will return an error response.
5. BIMC xPU responds when ports are blocked.
6. DEHR saves BIMC and xPU configuration to its internal SRAM.
7. DEHR notifies GDHS that the save operation is complete and the power may be collapsed.
8. GDHS collapses the power.

The restore sequence is as follows:
1. Upon wakeup event the power collapse trigger asserted in step 2 of the save sequence is de-asserted, triggering power restore operation.
2. When the power restores, GDHS notifies DEHR.
3. DEHR restores BIMC xPU state.
4. DEHR requests from the BIMC xPU to unblock the accesses to the xPU client and configuration ports.
5. BIMC xPU is unblocked.
6. DEHR notifies GDHS that the restore operation is complete.
7. DEHR sets to 0x1 the `RESTORE_DONE` bit in the `DEHR_DMA_STATUS` register.
8. Software triggers BIMC GDHS power restore command.
9. DEHR restores the BIMC registers.
10. Software should set to 0x1 the `RANK0_INITCOMPLETE`/`RANK1_INITCOMPLETE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_CONFIG` register.
11. Software should set to 0x1 the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE` bit in the `BIMC_S_DDR0_SHKE_DRAM_MANUAL_0` register.
12. Software should poll the `ENTER_SELF_REFRESH_IDLE` bit until 0x0.
13. Normal operation resumes.
<!-- page 2452 -->
The following exceptions to the save and restore sequence apply:
- If the power collapse request is canceled during the save sequence before DEHR notifies GDHS that the save operation is complete, DEHR aborts the save operation and doesn’t notify GDHS for save completion.
- If power collapse is requested during the restore sequence, DEHR ignores the request until the restore sequence completes.

### 7.2.4 DEHR registers
The register bits and fields not shown in this section are considered reserved. Errors are not generated if write to these locations is performed. Reading the value of reserved bit or field returns unknown result.

## 7.3 On-chip internal memory (OCIMEM)
This section describes the on-chip internal memory (OCIMEM).

### 7.3.1 OCIMEM overview
There is one OCIMEM module in the device that supports 16 KB SRAM accessible through the SNOC. The SRAM is implemented as a single bank.

### 7.3.3 OCIMEM functional description

#### 7.3.3.1 OCIMEM architecture
OCIMEM contains two slave interface ports. The first one is a 64-bit AXI port connected to the SNOC and allows access to the internal memory resources (SRAM). The second one is a 32-bit AHB port connected to the PCNOC and allows programming of OCIMEM internal registers. There is also an MPU on the SNOC AXI port to protect the internal memory resources.

By default, the SRAM content is retained across resets.

#### 7.3.3.2 OCIMEM initialization
OCIMEM has minimum requirements for its initialization. Besides ensuring that the `GCC_IMEM_AXI_CLK` clock is turned-on in GCC, OCIMEM comes out of reset, ready to accept memory transactions without the need of programming any of its registers. By default, all memories are ON when coming out of reset.

There are optional programming steps to configure the MPU and interrupts but they are not required to access the memory. These optional steps are as follows:
1. Turn-on the `GCC_IMEM_CFG_AHB_CLK` clock through the GCC registers.
2. Program the OCIMEM MPU registers.
3. Program the OCIMEM interrupt registers.

#### 7.3.3.3 OCIMEM power management
The `OCIMEM_PSCGC_TIMERS` and `OCIMEM_PSCGC_M0_M7_CTL` registers are associated with the OCIMEM power management.

The OCIMEM SRAM bank can be put to sleep or waken-up by programming the `M0_PSCGC_CTL` field in the `OCIMEM_PSCGC_M0_M7_CTL` register.

After putting the memory to sleep, the software must verify that this has been done by checking if the `M0_PSCGC_CLKOFF` bit in the `OCIMEM_PSCGC_STAT` register is 0x1. After waking-up the memory from sleep, the software must also verify that this has been done by checking if the `M0_PSCGC_CLKOFF` bit is 0x0.

The `WAKEUP_COUNTER` field in the `OCIMEM_PSCGC_TIMERS` register specifies the number of OCIMEM clocks required to wake-up the memory from sleep. The `TO_SLEEP_COUNTER` field in the `OCIMEM_PSCGC_TIMERS` register specifies the number of OCIMEM clocks (`GCC_IMEM_AXI_CLK`) required to put the memory to sleep. The minimum timer value is 20 ns. It is recommended to leave the default value of these timers unchanged. It is not recommended to re-program these values as the OCIMEM clock may be scaled up or down based on the use case.
<!-- page 2460 -->
#### 7.3.3.4 OCIMEM reset
During OCIMEM reset state, all interrupts are disabled and the `OCIMEM_AXI_ERR_SYNDROME` register is cleared. The memory core logic is on (`M0_PSCGC_CTL` = 0x2), which is needed to retain the memory content across resets.

#### 7.3.3.5 OCIMEM interrupts
The OCIMEM has one non-MPU general purpose interrupt (`OCIMEM_NONSEC_IRQ`) and two MPU related interrupts (`OCIMEM_XPU2_NON_SECURE_INTR` and `OCIMEM_XPU2_SECURE_INTR`). The latter ones are activated when the OCIMEM MPU detects violation. These MPU related interrupts do not have associated registers that are described in the Section OCIMEM register definitions. The `OCIMEM_NONSEC_IRQ` interrupt is activated upon detection of address decode error or SRAM bank power-down access error, that is, sleep error.

The `AXI_ERR_INT_STAT` bit in the `OCIMEM_INTC_STAT` register is asserted for AXI errors on the SNOC port. See Section Errors detected on the SNOC port. Additional information regarding the errors can be obtained by reading the `OCIMEM_GEN_STAT` register. This register always logs the errors even when the interrupts are disabled. The `OCIMEM_NONSEC_IRQ` interrupt can be enabled or disabled by writing to the `AXI_ERR_INT_MSK` bit in the `OCIMEM_INTC_MASK` register. After the `OCIMEM_NONSEC_IRQ` is active, it can only be cleared by writing 0x1 to the `AXI_ERR_INT_CLR` bit in the `OCIMEM_INTC_CLR` register.

#### 7.3.3.6 OCIMEM error handling
This section describes the measures to be taken when each of the detected errors occur. In general, errors are detected but an error recovery sequence is not required.

##### 7.3.3.6.1 Errors detected on the PCNOC port
OCIMEM can detect an address out of range error on its PCNOC port. In this case, OCIMEM returns error response to PCNOC. The data returned on the 32-bit AHB read-data bus is 0x0 and should be considered invalid. There are no measures required to restore functionality on the OCIMEM configuration port. No interrupts are generated if this error occurs.

##### 7.3.3.6.2 Errors detected on the SNOC port
OCIMEM can detect errors on its SNOC port caused by an address out of range (address decode error) and by an access to memory that has been put to sleep (sleep error). In both cases, OCIMEM returns error response to SNOC. The data returned on the 64-bit AXI read-data bus is 0x0 and should be considered invalid. There are no measures required to restore functionality on the OCIMEM AXI port. Interrupts are generated if enabled. See section OCIMEM interrupts for more information.

The `OCIMEM_ERR_ADDRESS` and `OCIMEM_AXI_ERR_SYNDROME` registers log details associated with the request that caused errors on the OCIMEM SNOC port.

##### 7.3.4.11 0x0000 0060 OCIMEM_ERR_ADDRESS
* **Type:** R
* **Reset State:** 0x0000 0000

The OCIMEM_ERR_ADDRESS register contains the lower (from SNOC slave port) address of the request that caused the AXI bus error. This register is updated by hardware upon the detection of an AXI address decode or sleep error. Once set, the register is locked until the AXI_ERR_INT_CLR bit of the OCIMEM_INTC_CLR register is written to clear the error.

# 8 Device Resources

## 8.1 Resource Power Manager (RPM)
This section describes the resource power manager (RPM) that is available in the SoC.

### 8.1.1 RPM overview
The RPM is a dedicated engine for managing SoC shared resources to attain the lowest dynamic and static power profile of that SoC. The engine operates with low latency and low power.

Figure 8-1 shows a high-level overview of the RPM.

#### Figure 8-1: RPM overview
*Description:* Block diagram illustrating the RPM hardware architecture.
- **RPM hardware** block containing:
  - An **RPM** sub-block consisting of **Cortex-M3 with NVIC**, **Data RAM**, **Code RAM**, and **RPM CSR**, all interconnected via the **RPM AHB internal bus**.
  - Independent hardware blocks: **RBCPR**, **MPM SAW**, **PMIC_ARB SPMI**, and **Message RAM**.
- The **RPM hardware** block is connected via a bidirectional bus to the **Peripheral and System Configuration NoC**.
- The **Peripheral and System Configuration NoC** connects bidirectionally to four main external components: **GCC**, **PRNG**, **TLMM**, and **BIMC**.
<!-- page 2468 -->
#### 8.1.1.1 RPM functionality
The RPM consists of Cortex®-M3 processor with an integrated nested vectored interrupt controller (NVIC); 144 KB multibank code RAM; 64 KB multibank data RAM.
* **RPM processor:** The processor is based on the ARMv7-M architecture. The RPM processor has a native advanced high-performance bus (AHB) light interface and built-in embedded trace module/interrupt transfer mode (ETM/ITM). The processor frequency is 150 MHz. The Cortex-M3 supports a native suspend and wait for interrupt (SWFI) instruction, which allows the processor to turn off its own clock when the clock is not needed.
* **Interrupt controller:** The Cortex-M3 has a built-in NVIC. The RPM is configured to use 64 interrupts. The RPM interrupt controller provides priority queuing of interrupts and supports both edge-sensitive and level-sensitive interrupts. Sources external to the RPM include master power management (MPM), sleep power management (SPM), messaging, and nonmessaging masters. Sources internal to the RPM include general-purpose timers, and watchdog (WDOG) timer bark.
* **Code RAM:** The RPM code RAM serves as an instruction memory for the RPM processor.
* **Data RAM:** The RPM data RAM serves as data for RPM processor. Data RAM is used for stack pointer for interrupt vector table. The RPM has a 64 KB data RAM. The RPM data RAM operates at a clock frequency that is synchronous to the RPM AHB.
* **RPM CSR:** The RPM control/status register (CSR) provides interprocess communication (IPC) and general-purpose output (GPO) registers to generate IPC interrupts and general-purpose pulses, respectively. The RPM CSR also supports WDOG timer software interface registers and other miscellaneous use registers.
* **AHB:** The RPM AHB is synchronous to the RPM processor. The RPM AHB has Cortex-M3 as the default master for the bus. The RPM AHB allows byte, half-word, and word accesses for the code and data RAM. The RPM AHB allows only word accesses for CSR registers.

#### 8.1.1.2 Message RAM
The RPM message RAM provides memory for sending messages to and from the RPM controller.

#### 8.1.1.3 PMIC arbiter and system power management interface (SPMI)
The PMIC arbiter (PMIC_ARB) provides concurrent and autonomous PMIC access to the various software and hardware entities that need to communicate with the PMIC. The communication with an off-chip PMIC is via single SPMI bus.

Hardware power management blocks (such as SAW and RBCPR) also need to issue commands to the PMIC over the SPMI interface.
<!-- page 2469 -->
#### 8.1.1.4 MPM and SAW

##### 8.1.1.4.1 MPM functionality
MPM shuts down the clock source (CXO) and moves the SoC into power collapse (PC) mode or retention (MIN) mode. The MPM supports four sleep modes to save power. Table 8-1 describes the sleep modes.

###### Table 8-1 MPM sleep mode
| Sleep mode | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| CLK_OFF | Sleep state when MPM turns off the CXO oscillators |
| VDD_CX_MIN_VDD_MX_MIN | Both digital controller voltage (VDD_CX) and split-rail memory voltage (VDD_MX) are minimized while retaining all memory and logic (FF) states |
| VDD_CX_PC_VDD_MX_MIN | MPM can power collapse the VDD_CX voltage rail, and lower the VDD_MX to save power |
| VDD_CX_PC_VDD_MX_PC | Both VDD_CX and VDD_MX are shut down, which saves the most leakage |

For information about VDD_CX and VDD_MX, see Section 8.1.3.

##### 8.1.1.4.2 SAW functionality
SAW (subsystem power management (SPM) and adaptive voltage scaling (AVS)) provides the following functions:
1. **Interface to the PMIC arbiter (permits SAW to request voltage changes on a few regulators):** This interface is used by the AVS and SPM logic when they operate autonomously, and is also available for direct use by software. That is, once configured, software can write to a register in the SAW that causes a configuration value to be sent to the PMIC, changing the voltage provided by the PMIC supply regulator.
2. **AVS state machine:** This hardware accepts requests from the client controller to raise or lower the supply voltage, in response to process monitors in the client controller that indicate when the supply for the client can be lowered, and still operate at the current clock frequency. Thus, the CPU can be supplied with the minimum voltage required to support the clock frequency, which may be different among various chips, depending on the process variation. Optimizing (minimizing) the supply voltage for each individual chip allows most chips to be operated at a lower voltage than a worst-case chip might require, which makes the average user experience much better than the potential worst case. The interface from the client is simple, with just two signals to request a higher, or lower voltage. The AVS logic in the SAW calculates the appropriate supply voltage to request and sends requests via the PMIC arbiter interface. Other features include:
   * A configurable timer to avoid making multiple change requests before each incremental voltage change can settle and be evaluated by the hardware monitors in the client controller.
   * Limit registers that can be programmed to limit the range of voltages that can be used.
<!-- page 2470 -->
* Interrupts that can be generated if the AVS logic receives a request to adjust the voltage outside of the limited range.
3. **SPM state machine:** This hardware acts as a proxy for the client while the client is in a low power or sleep state, by sequencing the controls necessary for the client to enter and exit the sleep state. For example, a client CPU controller may be programmed to enter an idle state, which it accomplishes by sending a sleep request signal to the SPM. The SPM then gates the clock(s) used by the client, and optionally opens power switches, or even signals the PMIC to lower or remove the supply voltage. While the client is asleep, the SPM monitors a signal in the subsystem, which is conventionally a wake-up signal from an interrupt controller, and wakes up the client CPU when the signal is asserted.

> [!NOTE]
> The AVS and SPM state machines never run simultaneously. The AVS machine is only active while the client is operating normally, and the SPM is only active when the client controller is in a sleep mode.

##### 8.1.1.5 Rapid bridge core power reduction (RBCPR)
RBCPR is in VDD_CX top-level power domain, because its registers should not be affected by power collapse cases.

> [!NOTE]
> For more information about software and hardware power management architecture, see Snapdragon 410E (APQ8016E) System Power Overview.

#### 8.1.4 RPM API description

##### 8.1.4.1 RPM API overview

Figure 8-4 shows a high-level overview of the RPM functional blocks.

#### Figure 8-4 RPM functional block diagram
*Description:* A block diagram showing the functional architecture of the Resource Power Manager (RPM).
At the top, multiple external "Master" blocks ("Master 1" through "Master N") connect bidirectionally to the main "RPM" block.
Inside the RPM block, the components are layered:
- **RPM handler**: The top-level interface that communicates with the external Masters.
- **NPA (Node Power Architecture)** and **SLEEP**: The middle layer. The RPM handler connects bidirectionally to both the NPA block and the SLEEP block.
- **Drivers**: Below the NPA and SLEEP blocks. It contains drivers for `Clock`, `DDR`, `PMIC`, `Bus`, `MPM`, `WDOG`, and `SPMI`. Control paths (bidirectional arrows) run from the RPM handler, through the NPA block, to the `Clock`, `DDR`, `PMIC`, and `Bus` drivers. The SLEEP block connects bidirectionally to the `MPM` driver.
- **Kernel** (labeled "Kernal" in the diagram): The bottom layer of the RPM.
At the very bottom, external SPM (System Power Manager) blocks associated with different master cores (e.g., "Master 1 Core 0 SPM", "Master 1 Core 1 SPM", "Master 2 SPM", "Master N Core 0 SPM", "Master N Core N SPM") connect bidirectionally to the RPM's Kernel layer.
<!-- page 2479 -->

Modules in the RPM block diagram:
- **Kernel**: The kernel supports:
  - Interrupts
  - Intlock, priorities, and configuration
  - Busy waits
  - Timers
  - SWFI
- **RPM handler**: The RPM handler abstracts the RPM message protocol away from other software.
- **Drivers**: Drivers for each of the resources supported by the RPM register with the RPM handler to request notification when requests are received for the resource that the driver controls.
- **Node power architecture (NPA)**: A driver may use the NPA to represent resources controlled by the driver.
- **Clock driver**: The RPM clock driver directly handles the aggregating requests from each of the masters for any of the system-wide clock resources controlled by the RPM.
- **Bus arbitration driver**: The RPM bus arbiter driver takes bus arbiter settings as requests from different masters in the system and aggregates them to represent the frequency-independent system settings.
- **PMIC**: RPM power management IC driver directly aggregates requests from each of the masters for any of the system-wide PMIC resources controlled by the RPM.
- **Watchdog driver**: Watchdog driver is a fail-safe mechanism for incorrect or stuck conditions.
- **MPM driver**: Modem power manager driver is used to program the MPM hardware block during system-wide sleep to monitor the wakeup-capable interrupts.

Three main definitions are done in RPM messaging:
- **Masters**: Masters are the subsystems that make requests to the RPM.
- **Resources**: Resources are the physical components that the RPM is responsible for controlling. They are listed as follows:
  - Clocks
  - Bus arbitration
  - PMIC
  - Chip sleep wake-up interrupts
  - Processor wake-up deadlines
<!-- page 2480 -->

- **Configuration sets**: A configuration set is a collection of settings, one for each resource that fits a logical use case. Three sets are currently provided for each master:
  - **Active set**: This set contains the settings used when the subsystem is awake.
  - **Sleep set**: This set contains the settings used when the subsystem is sleeping (when an SPM handshake occurs).
  - **Next active set**: This set contains the settings used when the subsystem is awake and before the active set.

### 8.1.4.4 Function documentation

#### 8.1.4.4.1 static int msm_rpm_dev_probe(struct platform_device *pdev)

The APSS probes the RPM over SMD to communicate APSS to the RPM, and opens an RPM channel to communicate to the RPM.

**Parameters**
* `[in] pdev`: Platform device information

**Returns**
* If the probe is successfully done, it returns `TRUE`, otherwise it returns the `EPROBE_DEFER` error.

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` during the SoC RPM driver initialization.
<!-- page 2484 -->
#### 8.1.4.4.2 static int msm_rpm_send_data(struct msm_rpm_request *cdata, int msg_type, bool noirq)

Sends data over an SMD channel after checking for channel availability.

**Parameters**
* `[in] cdata`: Request to the RPM with a message header, KVP data, and the number of bytes to the SMD buffer.
* `[in] msg_type`: Message request type, such as clock, voltage, and so on
* `[in] noirq`: Do not enable interrupt

**Returns**
* If the API successfully writes to the SMD channel, it returns `TRUE`; otherwise it returns `EBUSY`.

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` before calling this function.

#### 8.1.4.4.3 static int msm_rpm_send_smd_buffer(char *buf, uint32_t size, bool noirq)

Writes data to the open SMD channel.

**Parameters**
* `[in] buf`: Data to be written to the SMD channel
* `[in] size`: Size of the buffer
* `[in] noirq`: Do not enable interrupt

**Returns**
* If the API successfully writes to the SMD channel, it returns `TRUE`; otherwise it returns `EBUSY`.

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` before calling this function.
<!-- page 2485 -->
#### 8.1.4.4.4 int msm_rpm_send_message(enum msm_rpm_set set, uint32_t rsc_type, uint32_t rsc_id, struct msm_rpm_kvp *kvp, int nelems)

Sends data or a message in KVP format.

**Parameters**
* `[in] set`: Set the active/sleep parameter for the resource
* `[in] rsc_type`: Unsigned 32-bit integer that identifies the type of the resource
* `[in] rsc_id`: Unsigned 32-bit integer that uniquely identifies a resource within a type
* `[in] kvp`: Array of KVP data
* `[in] nelems`: Number of KVP pairs associated with the message

**Returns**
* If an acknowledgment for the message is received from the RPM within the given time-frame, the API returns 0 on success, and an error on failure.

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` before calling this function.

#### 8.1.4.4.5 int msm_rpm_send_request(struct msm_rpm_request *handle)

Sends the RPM messages using SMD. The function assigns a message ID before sending the data out to the RPM. The RPM hardware uses the message ID to acknowledge the messages.

**Parameters**
* `[in] handle`: Pointer to the `msm_rpm_request` for the resource being modified

**Returns**
* Returns a nonzero message ID on success and zero on a failed transaction.
* The drivers use the message ID to wait for an acknowledgment from the RPM.

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` before calling this function.
<!-- page 2486 -->

Clears the RPM request handle created with `msm_rpm_create_request`.

**Parameters**

**Returns**
* None

**Dependencies**
* Call `msm_rpm_dev_probe` before calling this function.

**Returns**

## 8.2 PMIC Arbiter (PMIC_ARB)

This section describes the PMIC arbiter (PMIC_ARB) in the SoC.

### 8.2.1 PMIC_ARB overview

> [!CAUTION]
> The access to all system-wide PMIC resources through the PMIC_ARB is controlled by RPM. For more information about RPM, see chapter Resource Power Manager (RPM).

The PMIC_ARB serves to provide various hardware and software masters with concurrent and autonomous access to the PMICs.

The all of the off-chip PMICs are accessible via a single SPMI interface. The device contains multiple processors that may need to communicate with the PMIC. Furthermore, hardware power management blocks (SAW, RBCPR) also are issuing commands to the PMIC over the SPMI interface.

The PMIC_ARB prioritizes multiple clients that are attempting to access the PMIC. Software transactions all occur over the same bus, and are handled on first-come first-serve basis. Software requests are prioritized relative to hardware requests according to a fixed priority order that is programmable.

To facilitate concurrent and autonomous software access to the PMIC from multiple processors, a configurable number of data channels are provided. Each channel is located at a unique base address and consists of a set of registers used to initiate SPMI commands and read back results (data and status). It is intended that the PMIC_ARB be configured such that there is a unique virtual R/W channel and observable channel for each software master in the system. Each data channel for both R/W and observable can only have one outstanding transaction at a time.

The PMIC_ARB contains the SPMI controller and provides security for its configuration port.
<!-- page 2490 -->
Figure 8-5 shows a high level overview of the PMIC_ARB.

#### Figure: PMIC_ARB overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the PMIC_ARB (PMIC Arbiter) and its connections.
* The central block is **PMIC_ARB**.
* On the left, PMIC_ARB connects to the **Peripheral and System Configuration NoC** via an **AHB slave bus**. **Software Masters** connect to this NoC.
* At the bottom, PMIC_ARB connects to **Hardware Accesses** via **PVC Ports**.
* On the right, PMIC_ARB connects to external pins via an **SPMI interface**:
  * **PMIC_SPMI_DATA** (bidirectional signal)
  * **PMIC_SPMI_CLK** (output signal)
