### 8.3.3 GCC phase locked loops (PLLs)
A PLL is a mixed-signal element that creates an oscillating output, which is phased locked to a given reference source input. There are, in general, a number of PLLs instantiated within a CC block. The output of the resident PLLs is routed to the clock domain generators. The types of PLLs resident are related to the required quality or frequency range of the clock domains created.

#### 8.3.3.1 Clock source generation
The GCC has four PLLs as raw clock sources. The GCC also takes in the following external clock sources:
* XO (19.2 MHz)
* Sleep clock (32 kHz)

Careful configuration of the PLLs to generate appropriate frequencies minimizes the use of M/N counters in each clock regime. Figure 8-14 shows the GCC PLLs.

#### Figure: Figure 8-14 GCC PLLs
*Description:* A block diagram representing the GCC Phase Locked Loops (PLLs). A common input signal labeled `CXO` enters the main `GCC` block and branches to feed four internal PLL blocks in parallel:
- **GPLL0**: Contains a sub-block `SR` and an oscillator. It provides two output signals: `GPLL0_OUT_AUX` and `GPLL0_OUT_MAIN`.
- **GPLL1**: Contains a sub-block `SR` and an oscillator. It provides two output signals: `GPLL1_OUT_AUX` and `GPLL1_OUT_MAIN`.
- **BIMC_PLL**: Contains a sub-block `SR` and an oscillator. It provides one output signal: `BMIC_PLL_OUT_EARLY`.
- **GPLL2**: Contains a sub-block `SR` and an oscillator. It provides one output signal labeled `GPLL1_OUT_MAIN` (note: labeled as GPLL1 instead of GPLL2 in the diagram).
<!-- page 2572 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

#### 8.3.3.2 PLL clock sources
There are four PLLs in the GCC. They are all the same type – SRPLL.
* **GPLL0** – general PLL that provides clocks to the NoCs, QDSS, RPM, BIMC (Nominal), cryptos, multimedia modules, and all peripherals.
  * VCO = 800 MHz
* **GPLL1** – used for Audio cores and for GPU in Turbo mode.
  * VCO = 884.376 MHz
* **GPLL2** – provides clock sources for the VFE in Turbo mode.
  * VCO = 930 MHz
* **BIMC_PLL** – a dedicated PLL for BMIC/DDR.
  * VCO = 1066 MHz

Two more PLLs are available in the device controlled by the respective module – APSS and WCSS PLLs. They have a slightly different hardware characteristic from those in GCC. These two PLLs are SR2PLL, but the programming is the same. The control registers for APSS and WCSS PLLs are located in the corresponding module.

#### 8.3.3.3 PLL voting feature
A PLL voting feature is available for PLLs that are common resources and can be shared across all on-chip processors. All PLLs in the GCC are votable. The voting logic allows processor to cast its vote to enable a votable PLL. It is a vote for enable scheme, so no processor can disable the votable PLL for other processors to use. The PLL voting logic includes a PLL enable state machine that provides the automated steps to enable the PLL without software interference. When the corresponding PLL is enabled, the finite state machine (FSM) sends a PLL active flag that the software can poll to determine whether the PLL is active or not.

#### 8.3.3.4 PLL programming
Programming the PLLs is achieved through the CSRs in the GCC blocks housing the target PLL.

Table 8-109 lists the general set of register for PLL programming.

The PLL output value is calculated via:

$$V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot (L + M/N)$$

> [!NOTE]
> For programming a specific PLL, use the corresponding register. For example, to program GPLL0, use GCC_GPLL0_MODE, GCC_GPLL0_L_VAL, registers.
<!-- page 2573 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

##### Table 8-109 General set of register for PLL programming

| Generic register name | Register name | Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PLL_MODE** | GCC_GPLL0_MODE<br>GCC_GPLL1_MODE<br>GCC_GPLL2_MODE<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_MODE | Basic controls requiring a sequence |
| **PLL_USER_CTL** | GCC_GPLL0_USER_CTL<br>GCC_GPLL1_USER_CTL<br>GCC_GPLL2_USER_CTL<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_USER_CTL | Contains fields that are consistent across all PLLs, such as post-divide, pre-divide, output-enable bits. |
| **PLL_CONFIG_CTL** | GCC_GPLL0_CONFIG_CTL<br>GCC_GPLL1_CONFIG_CTL<br>GCC_GPLL2_CONFIG_CTL<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_CONFIG_CTL | Contains architecture-specific settings, such as charge-pump current |
| **PLL_L_VAL** | GCC_GPLL0_L_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL1_L_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL2_L_VAL<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_L_VAL | L value for frequency selection. |
| **PLL_M_VAL** | GCC_GPLL0_M_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL1_M_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL2_M_VAL<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_M_VAL | M value for frequency selection. |
| **PLL_N_VAL** | GCC_GPLL0_N_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL1_N_VAL<br>GCC_GPLL2_N_VAL<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_N_VAL | N value for frequency selection. |
| **PLL_STATUS** | GCC_GPLL0_STATUS<br>GCC_GPLL1_STATUS<br>GCC_GPLL2_STATUS<br>GCC_BIMC_PLL_STATUS | Status bits for PLL |

#### 8.3.3.4.1 PLL power-up sequence
Recommended power-up sequence for FSM/Non-FSM modes:

**FSM mode PLL power-up sequence (SBL):**
1. Configure `PLL_L`/`M`/`N`/`USER_CTL` registers.
2. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BIAS_COUNT]` = 24 (0x18), which creates 20 μs delay between bypass removal and reset removal.
3. Set `PLL_CONFIG_CTL` = 0x30031800.
<!-- page 2574 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

4. Assuming one of the processors already have voted for the PLL, enable the PLL FSM: `PLL_MODE [PLL_VOTE_FSM_ENA]` = 0x1.
5. Wait for `PLL_STATUS [PLL_ACTIVE_FLAG]` to be set.
6. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BIAS_COUNT]` = 0x1, if above SWA sequence is not to be used for further PLL power-ups taken care by FSM.

**Non-FSM mode PLL power-up sequence (SBL):**
1. Configure PLL `L`/`M`/`N`/`USER_CTL` registers.
2. Disable charge pump output by `PLL_CONFIG_CTL [FORCE_PFD_UP, FORCE_PFD_DOWN]` = 0x3 and `PLL_CONFIG_CTL [FORCE_ISEED]` = 0x1. Finally, `PLL_CONFIG_CTL` = 0x30031800.
3. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BYPASSNL]` = 0x1.
4. After 20 μs delay, set `PLL_MODE [PLL_RESET_N]` = 0x1.
5. Wait `PLL_STATUS [PLL_LOCK_DET]` to be set.
6. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_OUTCTRL]` = 0x1 to enable the PLL outputs.

**FSM mode PLL power-up sequence (from XO shutdown):**
1. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_VOTE_FSM_RESET]` = 0x1.
2. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BYPASSNL]` = 0x0.
3. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_RESET_N]` = 0x0.
4. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_OUTCTRL]` = 0x0.
5. Software waits (`HAL_clk_BusyWait(1)`).
6. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_VOTE_FSM_ENA]` = 0x1.
7. Software waits (`HAL_clk_BusyWait(1)`).
8. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BIAS_COUNT]` = 0x18, which creates 20 μs delay between bypass removal and reset removal.
9. Disable charge pump output by writing `PLL_CONFIG_CTL [FORCE_PFD_UP, FORCE_PFD_DOWN]` = 0x3 and `PLL_CONFIG_CTL [FORCE_ISEED]` = 0x1. So `PLL_CONFIG_CTL` = 0x30031800.
10. Assuming one of the processors already have voted for the PLL, remove the PLL FSM reset: `PLL_MODE [FORCE_ISEED]` = 0. *(Note: text says FORCE_ISEED, but might refer to PLL_VOTE_FSM_RESET)*
11. After 30 μs delay after enabling the PLL, set `PLL_CONFIG_CTL [FORCE_PFD_UP, FORCE_PFD_DOWN]` = 0x0. Finally, `PLL_CONFIG_CTL` = 0x00031800.
12. Wait for `PLL_STATUS [PLL_ACTIVE_FLAG]` to be set.
13. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BIAS_COUNT]` = 0x1, if above SWA sequence is not to be used for further PLL power-ups.
<!-- page 2575 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

#### 8.3.3.4.2 PLL shutdown
This procedure assumes starting from the "On State".

> [!NOTE]
> For FSM mode PLLs, all processors need to remove the vote.

1. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_OUTCTRL]` equal to zero.
2. Wait long enough for the outputs to switch off. The required wait time is two ticks of the output main clock. For example, if the output frequency is from a post divide of four, the delay requirement is eight VCO ticks or more. At the slowest VCO of 250 MHz, 8 ticks is only 32 ns, that is, less than one XO tick.
3. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_BYPASSNL]` and `PLL_MODE [PLL_RESET_N]` to zero.

#### 8.3.3.4.3 PLL bypass
This procedure assumes starting from the "intended default values" or the "Off State".
1. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_RESET_N]`, `PLL_MODE [PLL_BYPASSNL]`, and `PLL_MODE [PLL_OUTCTRL]` all low. Set all bits low in same write to this register.
2. Set `PLL_USER_CTL [PLLOUT_LV_EARLY]`, `PLL_USER_CTL [PLLOUT_BIST]`, `PLL_USER_CTL [PLLOUT_LV_AUX]`, and `PLL_USER_CTL [PLLOUT_LV_MAIN]` as intended.
3. Set `PLL_MODE [PLL_OUTCTRL]` equal to one.

This action provides a glitch free switch from clocks off to clocks running at `CLK_REF`. De-assert `PLL_OUTCTRL` to turn-off clocks in a glitch free fashion. `CLK_REF` appears on the early output also if enabled.

#### 8.3.3.4.4 PLL mode control
If the PLL supports glitch-free output gating, the sequence for controlling frequency changes at the PLL can be simplified. The output of the PLL can be halted, and this halts everything downstream without requiring branches and/or roots to be halted.

#### 8.3.3.4.5 PLL voting
For the votable PLL in the corresponding mode register, 1 bit is used for the `PLL_VOTE_FSM_RESET`, 1 bit for the `PLL_VOTE_FSM_ENA`, 6 bits for the `PLL_BIAS_COUNT` (counter value for the FSM to complete the bias stage), and 6 bits for the `PLL_LOCK_COUNT` (time for the PLL locking).

For SR and SR2 PLL, proper lock indication is provided. The PLL voting FSM takes advantage of the lock detect output and use it to figure out when the PLL is locked and enable the clock output. Therefore, the only counter bits that are programmed are the `PLL_BIAS_COUNT` bits. When the PLL lock detect output does not function as expected, programming the `PLL_LOCK_COUNT` bits can be used instead.
<!-- page 2576 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

Once these bits are programmed, there are `PLL_ENA` registers for each master on the chip. Each is protected by an ACR. Any one master can program the enable bit for a particular votable PLL and enable it. The enable bit, when set, triggers the FSM to bring up the PLL.

`PLL_LOCK_COUNT` = 0 means FSM is using `LOCK_BIT_DET` from the `PLL_STATUS` register.

#### 8.3.3.4.6 Sample sequence to enable the PLL in FSM mode from any processor
**Cast vote:** A particular processor can vote to enable the PLL by setting the corresponding PLL enable bit in its PLL enable register. For example, if APSS wants to vote GPLL0 to be on, software programs the GPLL0 bit of the `GCC_APCS_TZ_GPLL_ENA_VOTE` register in global clock controller.
1. Poll the `STATUS` register of the voted PLL to get an indication when the PLL voted on is locked and ready.
   For example, if we want to figure out whether GPLL0 is locked and ready or not, software polls the `PLL_LOCK_DET` bit or `PLL_ACTIVE_FLAG` in `GCC_GPLL0_STATUS` register. When the bit is asserted, GPLL0 is ready.
2. **Remove vote:** To turn off the vote, software must clear the corresponding PLL enable bit in its PLL enable register.

### 8.3.4 GCC root clock generator (RCG)
This section describes the root clock generator as a building block of a clock controller.

#### 8.3.4.1 RCG overview
Clock source selection for each regime is implemented within the clock block. For the GCC, clocks are generated by using root clock generators.

The following types of generators are used by the GCC:
* **RCG**: The RCG supports 8 functional clock source muxing and 5-bit, half-integer divide (HID) capability for dynamic clock source switching and frequency division.
* **MND_RCG**: The RCG supports 8 functional clock source muxing and fractional divide capability for dynamic clock source switching and frequency division. Both 8-bit MND and 16-bit MND are used. This generator consists of a 5-bit half-integer divider followed by the MND fractional post divider.

Additional optional blocks are:
* **CDIV**: This is a skew balanced integer clock divider, whose division ratio is dynamically switchable. Both 2-bit (DIV up to 4) and 4-bit (DIV up to 16) are used.

Figure 8-15 shows the generic clock generation diagram, which includes the most common sources used by most root clock generators in the GCC.
<!-- page 2577 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

#### Figure: Figure 8-15 GCC common clock generation
*Description:* A detailed block diagram of the **Root Clock Generator (RCG)**.
- **Central Block**: Labeled **ROOT CLOCK GENERATOR**.
- **Control Inputs (Left & Top-Left)**:
  - `SRC_SEL` (3-bit): Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_CFG_RCGR[SRC_SEL]`.
  - `SRC_DIV` (5-bit): Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_CFG_RCGR[SRC_DIV]`.
  - MND-specific inputs (grouped as "Only valid for MND generator"):
    - `M`: Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_M[M]` (blue).
    - `~(N-M)`: Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_N[NOT_N_MINUS_M]` (blue).
    - `~2D`: Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_D[NOT_2D]` (blue).
    - `MODE`: Fed by `<CLK_NAME A>_CFG_RCRG[MODE]` (blue).
  - `AO_PGM_CLK`: Always running clock fed by `AHB_CLK`.
  - `PGM_EN`: Fed by `WR_EN`.
  - `PGM_DATA`: Fed by `WR_DATA[UPDATE]`.
  - `HW_CLK_CONTROL`: Fed by the OR-gated `<CLK_NAMES>_CLK_HW_CONTROL_EN(s)` from downstream CBC(s) HW_CLK_CONTROL input.
  - `ASYNC_CLK_R_ENA`: Fed by the OR-gated `<CLK_NAMES>_CLK_SRC_ON(s)` from downstream CBC(s) and `<CLK_NAME A>_CMD_RCGR[ROOT_EN]`.
- **Clock Source Inputs (Bottom-Left)**:
  - `SRC0`: `CLK_XO_SRC` (19.2 MHz) from external `XO`.
  - `SRC1`: Primary PLL source (oscillator symbol).
  - `SRC2`: Secondary PLL source (oscillator symbol).
  - `SRC3`: Tertiary PLL source (oscillator symbol).
  - `SRC4`: Connected to Ground.
  - `SRC5`: Connected to Ground.
  - `SRC6`: `SLEEP_CLK` (32 kHz).
  - `SRC7`: Unconnected.
  - `ALT_SRC` and `ALT_SEL` inputs at the bottom are grounded.
- **Outputs (Right)**:
  - `ROOT_OFF`: Outputs `<CLK_NAME A>_CMD_RCRG[ROOT_OFF]`.
  - `UPDATE`: Outputs `<CLK_NAME A>_CMD_RCRG[UPDATE]`.
  - `CLK_OUT`:
    - Direct output path to `<CLK_NAME A>_CLK_SRC (MHz)`.
    - Secondary path routed through an integer clock divider block **CDIV** (which takes control input `<CLK_NAME B>_MISC[SRC_DIV]`) to produce:
      - `<CLK_NAME B>_CLK_SRC (MHz)` (for CDIV driving more than one CBC).
      - `<CLK_NAME C>_CLK_SRC (MHz)` (for generating an asynchronous clock source).

The primary clock element is the RCG, which selects raw clock sources and divides them down to generate the clock.

Raw clock sources include:
* Selection of PLL outputs
* XO
* Sleep clock.

GCC has two types of RCGs. One includes a half integer divider (HID), and is named RCG, and the other includes a HID followed by fractional divider – MND_RCG.

Despite the divider differences, both types of RCG support the following features:
* Stops the output clock during reset to support universal reset (UAR) methodology.
* Supports dynamic clock switching with the update software protocol. If the output clock is halted and the software has complete control of the halting, the clock source switching is done in a static fashion where the clock sources (both from and to) do not need to be on. If the output clock is halted and the hardware controls the halting or the output clock is not halted, the clock source switching is done in a dynamic fashion, where the clock sources (both from and to) have to be on before the switch can be complete.

The HID used by the RCG is 5-bit, which provides a division up to of 16. The HID handles 1.2 GHz in nominal voltage (0.81 V) and 600 MHz in SVS voltage (0.73 V). For MND_RCG, the
<!-- page 2578 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

HID is followed by an MND that contains a dual-edge M/N counter, which can be bypassed. The GCC uses two types of the MND_RCG, an 8-bit MND and 16-bit MND. The 8-bit MND handles 1.2 GHz in nominal voltage and 600 MHz in SVS voltage. The 16-bit MND handles 600 MHz in nominal voltage and 300 MHz in the SVS voltage.

In the GCC, because many clocks do not have strict and precise frequency requirement, half integer divide RCG is used mostly. For other clock regimes (such as peripheral clocks) where precise frequencies are required and cannot be obtained by half integer division from some raw clocks, MND_RCG are used.

The M/N:D counter is a phase-accumulator that increments in steps of M, rolling over when it crosses or equals the value of N. A single-edge M/N:D counter increments on the positive edges of the input clock. Because the edge of the output clock is aligned to the rollover point, the output clock can have a jitter varying from zero to the period of the input reference clock. This is because the minimum resolution for generating the edges of the output clock is the positive edges of the input clock. The dual-edge balanced M/N:D counter supports dual-edge mode with 1/2 cycle resolution and clock swallowing. The output frequency of this MND_RCG can be determined using the following formula, where P is the divide setting for HID and $f_{src}$ is the frequency of the chosen source:

$$f_{out} = \frac{f_{src}}{P} \cdot \frac{M}{N}$$

### 8.3.4.2 RCG registers

#### 8.3.4.2.1 Clock generator configuration register
The clock generator configuration register (`CFG_RCGR`) allows software configuration of the root clock generator. A clock generator generates a clock domain (tree), which is functionally independent of all other clock domains. The RCG is then instantiated a single time for each clock generator. The generator can select from eight inputs as a possible source to the internal divider.

##### Table 8-110 Clock generator configuration register (CFG_RCGR)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31:14 | Reserved |
| 13:12 | MODE |
| 11 | Reserved |
| 10:8 | SRC_SEL |
| 7:5 | Reserved |
| 4:0 | SRC_DIV |

The `SRC_SEL` bits select the input source for the RCG.

The `SRC_DIV` bits define the integer and half integer portion of the divider setting. The `HALF_INT` value is used along with the integer divide value. For example, when programming for divide by 2.5, the `SRC_DIV` is $(2 \cdot \text{DIV} - 1) = 4$. When `SRC_DIV` = 0 or 1, both mean (DIV - 1).
<!-- page 2579 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

The RCGs for hi-speed clocks contain only the 5-bit HID and hence require only the `SRC_DIV` value for complete divider programming. The RCGs allow for further divide ratios and contain MND dividers downstream of the 5-bit HID. To configure the MND values for those RCGs, see Section 8.3.4.3.2.

The `CFG_RCGR [MODE]` bits allow for software selection of the source division type within the generator. This 2-bit controls which mode the M/N:D divider is operating at. There are four valid modes:
* **Bypass mode** (`CFG_RCGR [MODE]` = 0x0)
  The M/N:D divider is bypassed (DIV - 1) in this mode. It is also recommended to have bypass mode as the default mode during power-on reset. In bypass mode, the M/NOT_2D/NOT_N_MINUS_M bit settings are don't care and are usually zeros.
* **Swallow mode** (`CFG_RCGR [MODE]` = 0x1)
  Swallow mode is used if and only if M/N > 2/3, in which case the M/N:D generates output clock by "swallowing" certain pulses of the input clock.
* **Dual-edge mode** (`CFG_RCGR [MODE]` = 0x2)
  This is recommended for all practical purposes. The output clock can rise/fall on both the rising edge and falling edge of the input clock, thus providing the finest resolution for cycle period and duty cycle.
* **Single-edge mode** (`CFG_RCGR [MODE]` = 0x3)
  In single edge mode, the output clock can only rise/fall on the rising edge of the input clock. Dual edge mode supersedes the single edge mode.

The default value of the `CFG_RCGR` is established upon `FUNC_ARES`.

#### 8.3.4.2.2 Clock generator command register
The clock generator command register (`CMD_RCGR`) allows software control of the RCG, see Table 8-111. The control register allows software to give a go trigger to the configuration data.

##### Table 8-111 Clock generator command register (CMD_RCGR)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31 | ROOT_OFF |
| 30:8 | Reserved |
| 7 | DIRTY_D |
| 6 | DIRTY_N |
| 5 | DIRTY_M |
| 4 | DIRTY_CFG_RCGR |
| 3:2 | Reserved |
| 1 | ROOT_EN |
| 0 | UPDATE |
<!-- page 2580 -->
APQ8016E Technical Reference Manual
Device Resources

The `CMD_RCGR [ROOT_EN]` bit (when set to 1) enables the output clock of the clock generator. This enable may be ORed with a hardware clock enable and then sent to the RCG. The output clock is controlled glitch-free via this mechanism.

The `CMD_RCGR [ROOT_OFF]` status allows software to determine if the generator is actively producing a clock. It is low (0) when the clock is active.

The `UPDATE` status bit is software and hardware modified. Software sets the bit when the configuration values are programmed and when they have taken effect, then hardware clears the bit to '0'. Software should not trigger another update when the update status (`CMD_RCGR[UPDATE]`) is high.

When a particular configuration register is programmed, the associated dirty bit is set in the CMD_RCGR register – `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_CFG_RCGR]`. Upon the `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit that is set, the dirty bits are cleared. `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]`, `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_N]`, and `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_M]` bits are valid bits only for MND_RCG. *(Note: The original manual text incorrectly mentions "DIRTY_D" three times: "CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D], CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D], and CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]")*

#### 8.3.4.2.3 MND registers
There are RCGs available with built-in MND at 8-bit, and 16-bit, which allows further dividing of the selected source. The values are LSB justified, so it always is X down to 0, where X is the divider width minus 1. The MND program values retain the hardware savings method, requiring the intended values to be formatted.

To simplify hardware implementation, M/N/D values are programmed in a special way. Specifically:
* **D value** is programmed as `NOT_2D` (that is, 1's complement of 2D)
* **M value** is programmed as is.
* **N value** is programmed as `NOT_N_MINUS_M` (that is, 1's complement of N-M).

Table 8-112 through Table 8-114 show these registers.

##### Table 8-112 M register

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31:X | Reserved |
| (X-1):0 | M |

##### Table 8-113 N register

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31:X | Reserved |
| (X-1):0 | NOT_N_MINUS_M |

The default value of the MND registers is established upon reset.


<!-- page 2581 -->

### 8.3.4.2.4 Miscellaneous clock generator register for CDIV

Table 8-114 shows the MISC register for CDIV. This type of register is implemented when the CDIV feeds more than one branch.

##### Table 8-114 MISC register for CDIV

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31:8 | Reserved |
| 7:0 | AUTO_SCALE_DIV |
| 3:1 | Reserved |
| 0 | AUTO_SCALE_DIS |

`MISC [AUTO_SCALE_DIV]` bit field is used to configure the div ratio when auto scaling is enabled.

`MISC [AUTO_SCALE_DIS]` bit controls whether RPM clock automatic clock scaling can be disabled.

### 8.3.4.3 Clock selection

All clock regimes stem from an RCG or BALANCE_ROOT (BR). From the output of RCG, the clock can be further divided down by passing it through a clock divider (CDIV). A single-phase clock out of the clock controller is generated by sending the clock source through a clock branch cell (CBC). There are two types of CBCs used in the device. A regular CBC for halting and unhalting of output clock (CBC) and a CBC that provides power switch controls to memories (PSCBC) while halting and unhalting the output clock. To be UAR-compliant, both types of CBCs halt their output clocks during reset time. For more information about CBC, see Section 8.3.5. For more information about resets, see Section 8.3.6.

All clock regimes coming from the same RCG or BR are either synchronous (skew balanced – same frequency) or isosynchronous (edge aligned – but divided ratio frequency).

#### 8.3.4.3.1 Enable and update of RCG

There is a `HW_CLK_CONTROL` port on the RCG. The `HW_CLK_CONTROL` port of the RCG is used to indicate to the RCG logic when the `ASYNC_CLK_EN` port of the RCG is under hardware control. The hardware control is wire-ORed from the hardware control of all the downstream CBCs. If any of the downstream CBCs are under hardware control, it enables the RCG under hardware control as well. In this case, whenever RCG receives an update, it always performs a dynamic switch.

If the RCG enable is under sole software control, the RCG enable state takes place based on whether the RCG can perform a static switch or dynamic switch. So the RCG enable must be staged apart from the update. Enabling the RCG in software should occur by enabling any downstream CBCs instead of direct RCG enabling via the `ROOT_EN` bit of the corresponding `CMD_RCGR` register. Software does not use this bit to enable the RCG and only in the special case when the CBC feedback to turn off the root feature is broken.

RCG enabling and updating the RCG is staged by construction since the bit to turn on any CBCs is in a separate register than the update bit of the RCG.
<!-- page 2582 -->

The RCG employs an "update" software protocol. The procedure to change the clock source and/or division ratio is the following:

> [!NOTE]
> In all programming sequences, replace the registers with the corresponding registers for the certain clock. For example, CBCR replaces with `<CLOCK_NAME>_CBCR`.

1. Software programs the new `CFG_RCGR [SRC_SEL]` and `CFG_RCGR [SRC_DIV]` values and sets the `CMD_RCGR[4] <CLOCK_NAME>_DIRTY_CFG_RCGR`, `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]`, and `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_M]` bits.
   
   > [!NOTE]
   > `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]` and `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_M]` bits are available only on MND_RCGs.

   a. The dirty bit `CMD_RCGR[4] <CLOCK_NAME>_DIRTY_CFG_RCGR` indicates that configuration registers are polluted and their values do not reflect what the RCG is using.
   b. Configuration can be done in multiple transactions.
2. Software writes to `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit to apply the settings.
   a. Asserting `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit should automatically clear `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_CFG_RCGR]`, `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]`, and `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_M]` bits.
   b. `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit being high means that a command is issued, but not yet completed.
3. Hardware clears `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit once new settings are applied.
   a. If all the `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]`, `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_CFG_RCGR]`, `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_D]`, and `CMD_RCGR [DIRTY_M]` bits are low, the configuration registers are current and reflect what the RCG is using.

> [!NOTE]
> This procedure is agnostic of clock on/off status.

The hardware programming interface for the `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit consists of three signals: `AO_PGM_CLK`, `PGM_EN`, `PGM_DATA`. When both `PGM_EN` and `PGM_DATA` are high, the `CMD_RCGR [0] UPDATE` bit is asserted. Software is not allowed to clear the `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]` bit.

The default value of the `CMD_RCGR` is established upon reset.

#### 8.3.4.3.2 Set up a source generator (RCG)

> [!NOTE]
> In all programming sequences, replace the registers with the corresponding registers for the certain clock. For example, CBCR replaces with `<CLOCK_NAME>_CBCR`.

The following sequence is followed to set up RCG:
1. Program the M, N, and D registers with divide and duty-cycle values for specific RCG (if MND present).
<!-- page 2583 -->

2. Program `CFG_RCGR` with divide (divider value is programmed as $(2N - 1)$) and source selection values.
3. Set update bit in `CMD_RCGR` register.
   a. Program the `CFG_RCGR [MODE]` if MND divider is to be used.
4. Poll on the update bit until it clears to indicate that the switch is complete.

`ROOT_EN` bit is set in software when the clock is in the hardware control or the clock is controlled in different processor and RCG is in different processor.

For more information about optional M/N:D setting sequence see Section 8.3.4.3.4 for the MND sequence.

#### 8.3.4.3.3 Set up a source generator (RCG) for GPU

Since a `CLK_ON` signal from GPU module turns on the GPU RCG as soon as GPU is out of power collapse, software should ensure that the PLL branch is enabled when software brings GPU out of power collapse and intends to do a frequency switch by changing source or division values.
1. PLL configured
2. GDSC disabled (power up)
3. PLL enabled
4. RCG configured
5. CBC enabled.

#### 8.3.4.3.4 Set up MND RCG

The software programming protocol for `MND_RCG` is the same as that of `RCG`. Nevertheless, `MND_RCG` has extra CSR bits for controlling M/N:D divider settings. This is detailed as follows:

In an M/N:D divider, M/N governs the division ratio, namely:

$$f_{out} = f_{src} \cdot \frac{M}{N}$$  (1-2)

D governs the duty cycle, namely:

$$DutyCycle = \frac{D}{N}$$  (1-3)

> [!NOTE]
> In all programming sequences, replace the registers with the corresponding registers for the certain clock. For example, CBCR replaces with `<CLOCK_NAME>_CBCR`.

Reconfigure MND:
1. The 5-bit predivider (half-integer) can be configured to any division ratio upon power-on-reset.
   a. After reset removal, it starts with divided clock directly.
<!-- page 2584 -->

2. The configuration registers holding MND values are running on output clock of the predivider.
3. Program `CFG_RCGR [MODE] = 0x2` (dual edge mode).
4. Program `M/NOT_2D/NOT_N_MINUS_M` to valid values.

Later reprogramming `M/NOT_2D/NOT_N_MINUS_M` can be done on-the-fly via `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]`.

Switching source and reconfiguring `CFG_RCGR[MODE]` is done by the following sequence:
1. Disable MND (`CBCR [CLK_ENABLE] = 0`).
2. Switch source.
3. Re-enable MND (`CBCR [CLK_ENABLE] = 1`).
4. Reconfiguring `CFG_RCGR [SRC_DIV]` can be on the fly.

#### 8.3.4.3.5 MMU clocking

The MMU clocks can be turned on:
* Either based on hardware activity within MMU:
  * Based on any TBU/TCU activity, `O_TXUN_CLKON` assertion.
  * Based on TCU/TBU configuration path access, `O_TXUN_CLKON` assertion.
* Whenever the master port AXI clocks are turned On (Only for TBUs)
* Through voting logic:
  * All the MMU clocks except `GCC_SMMU_XPU_CLK` are votable through dedicated votable registers for MMU clocks. There are four sets of registers each for voting by Hypervisor/TZ/HLOS and RPM (`<MASTER_NAME>_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE` and `<MASTER_NAME>_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE`). The vote for MMU clocks is a vote for On and not for OFF.
* The clocks are turned OFF only when there is no vote by software and there is no activity within MMU and all the master port clocks are OFF.

### 8.3.5 GCC integration modules (IM)

#### 8.3.5.1 Clock voting scheme

Several clock regimes are configured as votable clocks, because they are shared among different execution environments and all on-chip processors vote them. A particular processor casts its vote by configuring the corresponding voting registers that are protected by the GCC RPU. When the processor has nothing to do, it can enter into the IDLE (STANDBY) mode, where the processor clock and (optionally) the votable clocks are halted by executing a STANDBYWFI or processor idle instruction. See the corresponding registers `CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE` and `CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE`. Each bit in these registers of X:0 represent branch enable or sleep enable for a particular votable clock.
<!-- page 2585 -->

When the processor is finished gating internal clocks and flushing the write buffer, it asserts the `STANDBYWFI` signal or its `IDLE` signal. This signal is used to disable its clock enable vote for the votable clocks that are triggered with the corresponding `SLEEP_ENA` bit in its sleep enable vote register (`CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE`). The votable clocks are:
* `gcc_sys_noc_Apss_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_gmem_sys_noc_axi_clk`
* `gcc_blsp1_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_blsp1_sleep_clk`
* `gcc_prng_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_boot_rom_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_msg_ram_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_tlmm_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_tlmm_clk`
* `gcc_mpm_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_spmi_cnoc_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_crypto_clk`
* `gcc_crypto_axi_clk`
* `gcc_crypto_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_bimc_Apss_axi_clk`
* `gcc_apss_ahb_clk`
* `gcc_apss_axi_clk`
* `gcc_imem_axi_clk`

Figure 8-16 illustrates the detailed hardware implementation used in generating the branch enable for the votable clocks to give processor the ability to disable its clock enable vote and contribute to halting of the votable clocks and/or processor clocks upon a `STANDBYWFI` signal or processor idle assertion.
<!-- page 2586 -->

#### Figure 8-16: Clock voting enable logic

*Description:* The figure shows the hardware logic for combining clock votes from different processors/execution environments to control clock branches (CBC). It consists of two separate voting combiner networks.

**Left Combiner Network (controls general CBC):**
It ORs the votes from 6 sources:
1.  **RPM Vote:** Combined using an AND gate: `(NOT RPM_GCC_PROC_HCLK_EN) AND GCC_RPM_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0]`.
2.  **Application Processor Vote (Trust Zone):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_TZ_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_TZ_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
3.  **Application Processor Vote (Non-Trust Zone):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
4.  **MSS Q6 Vote:** Combined as: `GCC_MSS_Q6_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( MSS_GCC_Q6_CORE_IDLE AND GCC_MSS_Q6_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
5.  **Application Processor Vote (Hypervisor):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_HYP_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_HYP_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
6.  **WCSS Vote for Clocks:** Combined as: `GCC_WCSS_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( WCSS_GCC_ARM9_IDLE AND GCC_WCSS_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.

The outputs of these 6 blocks are inputs to a 6-input OR gate, the output of which drives the `CBC` enable.

**Right Combiner Network (likely for SMMU clocks):**
It ORs the votes from 4 sources:
1.  **RPM Vote:** Combined as: `GCC_RPM_SMMU_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( RPM_PROC_IDLE AND GCC_RPM_SMMU_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
2.  **Application Processor Vote (Non-Trust Zone):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_SMMU_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_SMMU_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
3.  **Application Processor Vote (Trust Zone):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_TZ_SMMU_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_TZ_SMMU_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.
4.  **Application Processor Vote (Hypervisor):** Combined as: `GCC_APCS_HYP_SMMU_CLOCK_BRANCH_ENA_VOTE[X:0] AND NOT ( (NOT APCS_SYSAHBCLKONREQ) AND GCC_APCS_HYP_SMMU_CLOCK_SLEEP_ENA_VOTE[X:0] )`.

The outputs of these 4 blocks are inputs to a 4-input OR gate, which outputs the combined SMMU vote.

---

#### 8.3.5.2 IM overview

An integration module (IM) consists of logic used to manage the reset, power, and clocks for a particular block. Reset logic, CBCs, and power controllers build an IM. GCC Integration module shows the template logic for these components. For information about the control registers used to configure these logics, see Section 8.3.5.3 and Section 8.3.6.2.1. The BCR register holds the block level software reset bit that resets the corresponding block (for more information see Section 8.3.6). The GDSCR register configures the global distributed switch controller (power controller). The CBCR register configures the corresponding CBC. These registers are used in all IMs to ensure a regular approach to control IMs.
<!-- page 2587 -->

#### Figure 8-17: GCC Integration module

*Description:* The block diagram shows the internal structure of a GCC Integration Module (IM), which manages power (via GDSCs) and clock gating (via CBCs) for functional blocks. This typical IM contains two GDSC blocks and two CBC blocks, sharing reset and clock inputs.

**GDSC (Global Distributed Switch Controller) Blocks:**
Each of the two GDSCs is controlled by registers:
*   Inputs:
    *   `SW_OVERRIDE` from `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[2]`
    *   `CONTROLS` from `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[10:3]`
    *   `SW_COLLAPSE` from `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[0]`
    *   `HW_CONTROL` from `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[1]`
    *   `ARES_IN` connected to common `HW_ARES`
    *   Clock input connected to common `CXO`
    *   `EN_FEW_ACK` and `EN_REST_ACK` are tied to '0'.
*   Outputs:
    *   `STATUS` mapped to `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[31]`
    *   `STATE` mapped to `<GDSABLE DOMAIN NAME>_GDSCR[30:27]`
    *   `EN_FEW` and `EN_REST` (module outputs)
    *   `RETAIN/SAVE/RESTORE_FF_SAVE` (module output)
    *   `CLAMP_IO` (module output)
    *   `CLK_DISABLE` (feeds the clock disable logic of CBC)
    *   `PD_ARES` (power domain reset, feeds CBC `PD_ARES`)

**CBC (Clock Branch Cell) Blocks:**
Each of the two CBCs controls one clock output.
*   Inputs:
    *   `CLK_IN` connected to common `CLK_SRC`
    *   `CLK_EN` directly controlled by software via `<CLK_NAME>_CBCR[0]`
    *   `CLK_DIS` controlled by an OR gate: `CLK_DISABLE` (from GDSC) OR `NOT <CLK_NAME>_CBCR[0]`
    *   `HW_ARES` connected to common `HW_ARES`
    *   `SW_ARES` controlled by software via `<BRANCH_NAME>_BCR[0]`
    *   `SS_ARES` connected to common `SS_ARES`
    *   `PD_ARES` connected to `PD_ARES` output of the corresponding GDSC
*   Outputs:
    *   `CLK_OUT` (the gated clock output of the module)
    *   `CLK_OFF` status mapped to `<CLK_NAME>_CBCR[31]`
    *   `CLK_ON` (clock active feedback signal, also output of the module)
    *   `ARES_OUT` (reset output of the module)

---

There are two types of CBCs. The simple type of CBC only controls the enabling and disabling of the clock branch. It also provides 'source-on' feedback, which basically ensures RCG is on when CBC is enabled to the root clock generation to enable the clock source. When a particular clock branch is used to clock memories, another type of CBC that also manages the power of the memories (RAMs and ROMs) is used. Power switch cells allow a memory core (RAMs and ROMs) and periphery power collapse and they are used to reduce leakage currents in deep submicron processes while increasing speed. This requires all clock regimes that interface with memories to have a power switch controller. For more information about CBC with power management, see Section 8.3.5.4.

For blocks with no power domains to control, the GDSCs and associated registers are not required.
<!-- page 2588 -->

#### 8.3.5.3 IM registers

##### 8.3.5.3.1 Clock branch controller register (CBCR)

The CBCR allows for software control of the CBC. This block contains combinational logic surrounding a branch clock gating cell (BCGC). Clock enables and higher priority disables are combined to feed the asynchronous enable of the BCGC, which asynchronously (and glitch-free) enables the output clock. The reset circuitry is also contained within the CBC.

Table 8-115 shows the register (CBCR) to control the CBC.

##### Table 8-115 Clock branch control register (CBCR)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31 | CLK_OFF |
| 30:28 | Reserved |
| 27:24 | NOC_FSM_CLKOFF_SLEEP |
| 23:20 | NOC_FSM_CLKON_WAKE |
| 19:16 | CLK_DIV |
| 15 | NOC_HANDSHAKE_FSM_EN |
| 14 | FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON |
| 13 | FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON |
| 12 | FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_OFF |
| 11:8 | WAKEUP |
| 7:4 | SLEEP |
| 3:2 | Reserved |
| 1 | HW_CTL |
| 0 | CLK_ENABLE |

The `CBCR [CLK_OFF]` bit connects to the enable on the CBC. If the disable `CBCR [CLK_ENABLE]` is not active, this may cause the clock to turn on.

`CBCR [HW_CTL]` is for hardware control. It is used to indicate when the CBC is clock enabled/disabled by downstream hardware.
* `HW_CLK = 0`, then software controls both `CMD_RCGR [ROOT_EN]` and `CMD_RCGR [UPDATE]`. Software should not write to `CMD_RCGR [ROOT_EN]` and update simultaneously.
* `HW_CLK = 1`, then software only does update at RCGR.

The force signals are used in the following way:
* `FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON` – Software forces `MEM_CORE_ON` to on when it is 1.
* `FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON` – Software forces `MEM_PERIPH_ON` to on when it is 1.
* `FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_OFF` – Software forces `MEM_PERIPH_ON` to off when it is 1.
<!-- page 2589 -->

The `CBCR [SLEEP]` and `CBCR [WAKEUP]` values are used to establish the count of clocks for the branch that holds off clock enable/disable relative to the memory power switch control. There are two programmable counters: the sleep counter and the wake-up counter. When the clock is disabled, the clock is gated immediately (up to a 2-cycle delay), but the memory control signals are not turned off until a delay of sleep clock cycles – `SLEEP` bitfield. When the clocks are enabled, the memory control signals are turned on immediately, but the clock remains gated until the wakeup clock cycles later – `WAKEUP` bitfield.

The clock divider value, `CLK_DIV`, applies only when there is a branch CDIV present.

> [!NOTE]
> If a CDIV is present, but feeds more than one branch, the control for that CDIV is in a MISCs register. See the Miscellaneous clock generator register for CDIV in Section 8.3.4.2.

The `NOC_FSM_CLKON_WAKE` is set when post PD analysis is run.

The `NOC_FSM_CLKOFF_SLEEP` is set when post PD analysis is run.

The default value of the CBCR is established upon `FUNC_ARES`.

##### 8.3.5.3.2 Globally distributed switch controller register (GDSCR)

The GDSCR allows for software control of the GDSC. The GDSC controls the switches that supply power to an on-chip power domain. The GDSC allows for hardware sequencing through the virtual power domain (PD) power-up/power-down steps. The trigger to put a power domain into or out of power collapse can be selected to be from hardware or software inputs. If no hardware PD control is available, the hardware input is tied-off and software maintains sole control.

Table 8-116 shows the register (GDSCR) to control the GDSC.

##### Table 8-116 Globally distributed switch controller register (GDSCR)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31 | PD_OFF |
| 30:27 | GDSC_STATE |
| 27:24 | Reserved |
| 23:20 | EN_REST_WAIT |
| 19:16 | EN_FEW_WAIT |
| 15:12 | CLK_DIS_WAIT |
| 11 | Reserved |
| 10 | RESTORE |
| 9 | SAVE |
| 8 | RETAIN |
| 7 | EN_REST |
| 6 | EN_FEW |
| 5 | CLAMP_IO |
<!-- page 2590 -->

##### Table 8-116 Globally distributed switch controller register (GDSCR) (continued)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 4 | CLK_DISABLE |
| 3 | PD_ARES |
| 2 | SW_OVERRIDE |
| 1 | HW_CONTROL |
| 0 | SW_COLLAPSE |

Although the process of entering and exiting the power collapse states are under hardware control via the GDSC, there is a software override mode. This mode allows software to control all steps of PD collapse. In this mode, the controls of the power domain are exposed to software. The state of the controls must adhere to the standard mode states, unless software is intentionally varying the controls for another purpose.

Table 8-117 lists three different power sequences.

##### Table 8-117 Power sequences

| SW_OVERRIDE | HW_CONTROL | Power sequencing |
| :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 0 | 0 | Hardware-controlled, software-triggered; software register: `SW_COLLAPSE` |
| 0 | 1 | Hardware-controlled, hardware-triggered |
| 1 | X | Software-overridden using below software registers: `RETAIN`, `SAVE`, `RESTORE`, `CLK_DISABLE`, `PD_ARES`, `CLAMP_IO`, `EN_FEW` and `EN_REST` |

The GDSC is not reset with the software block reset bit active.

The finite-state-machine (FSM) controls the steps for going in and out of PD collapse. The state transitions for the GDSC are timed relative to the CXO input clock. Most state transitions are timed via parameters in the HDL.

In addition to parameters, there are three states transitions that software can modify:
* `CLK_DIS_WAIT` – wait while all clocks in this PD are turned off
* `EN_FEW_WAIT` – wait while the first few PD transistors are turned on
* `EN_REST_WAIT` – wait while the remaining PD transistors are turned on

The parameters are set and reviewed, but the preceding state transitions allow for override if they are somehow incorrect. See the SWI for default values.

In the retention register mode, software should write 0 to `RETAIN` bit during chip power-up to reset all retention registers and then reconfigure to 1 before power-down if the data retention feature is required.

The GDSC is asynchronously reset (via `ARES_IN`) to the PD collapsed state. The power domains are not powered-up by default after reset. Software is required to bring all GDS-controlled power domains out of collapse after reset, except in cases where the default parameter is modified to PD noncollapse.


<!-- page 2591 -->

#### 8.3.5.4 Power switch clock control for memory core and periphery power collapse

Power switch cells reduce leakage currents in deep submicron processes while increasing speed. These CBC cells (PSCBC) allow memory (RAMs and ROMs) core and periphery power collapse. This requires all clock regimes that interface with memories have power switch control.

The power switch controller is responsible for:
* Turning off the memory periphery power switch (`CLK_SLP_RET_N`) and the memory core head switch (`CLK_SLP_NRET_N`) signals SLEEP cycles after the clocks are off.
* Turning the clocks back on WAKEUP cycles after the memory periphery footswitch and the memory core headswitch signals are on.

When the memory clock goes to sleep, asserting the `CLK_SLP_RET_N` (clock sleep retention) signal low power collapses the periphery circuitry of the memory. This has no effect on the content of the memory.

When the memory clock goes to sleep, asserting `CLK_SLP_NRET_N` (clock sleep nonretention) signal low power collapses the core circuitry of the memory. The content of the memory is lost.

##### 8.3.5.4.1 Memory sleep controller implementation

The default behavior of the memory sleep controller saves the leakage of the periphery circuitry of the memory, but it does not save the leakage of the core circuitry of the memory. If the memory contents need not be saved while the memory is in sleep mode, software can disable the `FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON` bit of the CBCR register. This enables the memory core head switch signal to be ACTIVE (`CLK_SLP_NRET_N` signal goes low) when the associated clock is halted. Therefore, the leakage of the memory core circuitry is saved.

By default, the memory periphery foot-switch signal is off (`CLK_SLP_RET_N` signal goes low) when the associated clock is halted (regime goes to the sleep mode).

The default behavior of the memory core headswitch signal is to remain on (`CLK_SLP_NRET_N` signal stays high) when the associated clock is halted (regime goes to the sleep mode).

Therefore, the default behavior of the memory sleep signals controller power collapses the memory periphery, but not the memory core. This saves the content of the memory whenever the memory clock is halted. Hence, the default behavior of the memory sleep controller saves the leakage of the periphery circuitry of the memory, but it does not save the leakage of the core circuitry of the memory.

If the memory content does not need to be saved while the memory is in sleep mode, the software can disable the `FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON` bit of the sleep controller. This enables the memory core headswitch signal to be ACTIVE (`CLK_SLP_NRET_N` signal goes low) when the associated clock is halted.

Therefore the leakage of the memory core circuitry is saved. When the clock regimes need to be off for a short period, the software can force the `FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON` bit so that the `CLK_SLP_RET_N` signal remains inactive (remains high) during the dynamic switch mechanism.
<!-- page 2592 -->

##### 8.3.5.4.2 Clock domains with memory sleep controllers

For clock domains with memory sleep controllers:
* All clock domains that interface with memories (RAMs and ROMs) are implemented with a memory controller to control the memory leakage in the sleep mode.
* Each clock regime in each memory group can set up its own WAKEUP and SLEEP count value in the CBCR register (in all cases, the wakeup value is identical to the sleep value).
* Each memory controller has bypass bits (`FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON` and `FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON` bits in the CBCR register), as well as programmable software values.
* Default values for all `CBCR[WAKEUP]` and `CBCR[SLEEP]` values is `0xF`. This ensures maximum time between the clock being shutdown and the sleep signals asserted low (clock going to sleep), it also ensures that a maximum time between the sleep signals asserted high (clock wake-up) and the clock is run again.
* A `0xF` default value can be decreased by the software for slower clock domains where timing requirements on the memory sleep pins is met with a smaller software value.
* Decreasing the software value decreases the overall latency to power collapse and wake-up the memories (go to power collapse faster and wake-up faster).

When the source to any clock regime is going to be switched, select one of the following options:
* Enough wait cycles are inserted to ensure that the clock source to the sleep counter does not glitch
* The `FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON` and `FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON` bits are asserted during the clock source switch.

For software implementation, the second option is easier.

#### 8.3.5.5 Programming IM

> [!NOTE]
> In all programming sequences, replace the registers with the corresponding registers for the certain clock. For example, CBCR replaces with `<CLOCK_NAME>_CBCR`.

##### 8.3.5.5.1 Assert force

> [!NOTE]
> Asserting force is valid only for power switch CBCs.

Write `CBCR[FORCE_MEM_CORE_ON]`, `CBCR[FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_ON]`, and `CBCR[12] FORCE_MEM_PERIPH_OFF` values of a particular PSCBC.

##### 8.3.5.5.2 Setting WAKEUP/SLEEP values

> [!NOTE]
> Asserting force is valid only for power switch CBCs.

Write `CBCR[WAKEUP]` and `CBCR[SLEEP]` bit fields.
<!-- page 2593 -->

##### 8.3.5.5.3 Turn on/off a clock branch

> [!NOTE]
> Hardware also has vote on the enable of output clock.

Software shall do the following for turning on or off a clock branch:
1. **Turn on**: set `CBCR[CLK_ENABLE]` bit.
   a. Clock turns on within a few clock cycles.
2. Wait for the `CBCR[CLK_OFF]` bit to go low. May also need to check the NoC interface FSM state bits (`CBCR[NOC_HANDSHAKE_FSM_STATUS]`).
3. **Turn off**: clear `CBCR[CLK_ENABLE]` bit.
   a. Clock turns off within a few clock cycles.
4. Wait for the `CBCR[CLK_OFF]` bit to go high. May also need to check the NoC interface FSM state bits (`CBCR[NOC_HANDSHAKE_FSM_STATUS]`).

> [!NOTE]
> Checking the FSM state bits is intended only for power switch CBCs.

> [!NOTE]
> Regarding votable clocks, masters can only request the bus clock to be ON. The bus clock is turned off only if all masters vote for the clock to be OFF.

##### 8.3.5.5.4 Set up a branch divider

Configure the `CBCR[CLK_DIV]` field for divide value.

This takes effect immediately.
1. The switch is glitch-free and thus does not require any downstream clock gate controls to be halted.

##### 8.3.5.5.5 Check status of a clock branch

The IM for a particular core houses the CBC cells. Each cell outputs a clock status indicating the clock state: enabled or disabled.

Read `CBCR[CLK_ENABLE]` bit. A ‘1’ indicates that the clock is disabled.

##### 8.3.5.5.6 Controlling power domains via GDSC

This section describes the control of power domains via GDSC.

> [!NOTE]
> In all programming sequences, replace the registers with the corresponding registers for the certain clock. For example, CBCR replaces with `<CLOCK_NAME>_CBCR`.

###### Hardware-controlled/software-triggered mode
The GDSC takes feedback from the hardware signals and controls the power-up/down (PU/PD) sequence, but software has control of when the PU/PD sequences occur.
<!-- page 2594 -->

Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE]`.

The procedures are as follows:

###### Collapsing power:
1. Write ‘1’ to `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE]`.
2. Poll status bit `GDSCR[PWR_ON]` for completion.

###### Bring-up power:
1. Write ‘0’ to `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE]`.
2. Poll status bit `GDSCR[PWR_ON]` for completion.

> [!NOTE]
> During the chip power-up in retention mode, software should write ‘0’ to `GDSCR[RETAIN]` bit to reset all retention registers and then reconfigure to 1 before power-down if data retention feature is required.

###### Hardware-controlled/hardware-triggered mode

The GDSC takes feedback from the hardware signals and controls the power-up/down sequence and also takes queues from hardware signals for when it executes the PU/PD sequences. In this mode, the software can only make itself aware of the current state of the Power Domain. This is accomplished by polling the `PWR_ON` bit (course knowledge), or polling the `GDSC_STATE` bits (fine grain knowledge).

Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 1`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE] = 0`.

The procedures are as follows:

###### Determining power state (course)
1. Poll status bit `GDSCR[PWR_ON]`.

###### Determining power state (fine)
1. Poll status bits `GDSCR[GDSC_STATE]`.

###### Switching from software trigger mode to hardware trigger mode

This section describes switching from software to hardware trigger for PU/PD sequence.

Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE] = 0` in `GDSCR` register.
1. Write ‘1’ to `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL]`.
2. Wait for at least 5 GDSC clock cycles after switch to hardware control is done before using it.

The reason is the hardware signal `HW_COLLAPSE_EN` is probably 1 when the control is switched to hardware for the first time and software is required to wait for the power-down sequence to start and reflect in the status signal before they start trying to turn it on again.
<!-- page 2595 -->

###### Switching from hardware trigger mode to software trigger mode

This section describes switching from hardware to software trigger for PU/PD sequence.

Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 1`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE] = 0`.
1. Write ‘0’ to `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL]`.
2. Wait for at least five GDSC clock cycles.
3. Poll `GDSCR[PWR_ON]` status bit for completion.

###### Switching from software trigger mode to hardware trigger mode when collapsed

This section describes switching from software to hardware trigger for PU/PD sequence.
Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE] = 1`.
1. Write ‘1’ to `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL]`.

###### Switching from hardware trigger mode to software trigger mode when collapsed

This section describes switching from hardware to software trigger for PU/PD sequence.

Assumption: `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL] = 1`, `GDSCR[SW_OVERRIDE] = 0`, `GDSCR[SW_COLLAPSE] = 1`.
1. Write ‘0’ to `GDSCR[HW_CONTROL]`.
2. Wait for at least five GDSC clock cycles.
3. Poll `GDSCR[GDSC_STATE]` status bits for completion.

##### Software override mode

The following is the standard mode state sequence to put the power domain in power collapse.

Assumption: `GDSCR[EN_FEW]` and `GDSCR[EN_REST]` are both ‘1’ (power to both sets of Head switches is on). This is the powered up state.

The procedure to power collapse domain is as follows:
1. Set to ‘1’ `GDSCR[CLK_DISABLE]` bit.
2. Poll the `CBCR[CLK_OFF]` status bits in one or more CBCRs of all CBCs in the power domain.
   * When all `CLK_OFF` bits are ‘1’, then clocks to controlled power domain are disabled.
3. Set to ‘1’ `GDSCR[RETAIN]`, `GDSCR[SAVE]`, and `GDSCR[PD_ARES]`.
4. Wait.
<!-- page 2596 -->

> [!CAUTION]
> The wait time is hardware-dependent. If time is critical, the time is derived for the nets controlled above for the specific GDSC PD in a worst-case manner OR if time is not critical, a 1 ms delay suffices.

5. Clear `GDSCR[SAVE]` and set to ‘1’ `GDSCR[CLAMP_IO]`.
6. Wait.

> [!CAUTION]
> The wait time here is hardware-dependent. If time is critical, the time must be derived for the nets controlled above for the specific GDSC PD in a worst-case manner OR if time is not critical, a 1 ms delay suffices.

7. Clear to ‘0’ both `GDSCR[EN_FEW]` and `GDSCR[EN_REST]` to turn off transistors.

The power domain is now in the power collapsed state.

###### To bring the power domain out of power collapse state:
1. Set to ‘1’ `GDSCR[EN_FEW]` to turn on the few switches.
2. Set to ‘1’ `GDSCR[EN_REST]` to turn on the rest of the switches.
3. Clear to ‘0’ `GDSCR[PD_ARES]` and `GDSCR[CLAMP_IO]` to remove reset and remove clamp.
4. `GDSCR[RESTORE]` is set to ‘1’ active and `GDSCR[RETAIN]` is cleared to ‘0’.
5. `GDSCR[RESTORE]` is cleared to ‘0’.
6. `GDSCR[CLK_DISABLE]` is cleared to ‘0’.
7. Poll the `CBCR[CLK_OFF]` status bits in the CBCRs and all CBCs in the power domain.
   * When all bits are ‘0’, then this is powered up state.

### 8.3.6 GCC reset controller

#### 8.3.6.1 GCC reset controller features

The logic in the reset controller (RST_CTL) block handles:
* Reset input conditioning for SoC supplied resets.
* Qualifying fuse sensing for functional resets.
* Creation of XO rail power-on-reset (POR).
* Facilitation of secure WDOG induced reset debugging.
* Resetting the alternate boot flow.
<!-- page 2597 -->

#### 8.3.6.2 GCC reset controller overview

The RST_CTL block is located in the GCC. Signal connections to all other associated blocks for reset control are shown in Figure 8-18.

#### Figure 8-18: Reset structure within the SoC

*Description:* A block diagram showing the reset generation and distribution within the SoC, centered on the `RST_CTL` block.
* Left side shows external inputs (`SRST_N`, `RESIN_N`, `CXO`, `SLEEP_CLK`) and peripheral blocks (`MPM`, `WDOG`, `QDSS`, `QFPROM`) interfacing with `RST_CTL`.
* `RST_CTL` internal contains `CX POR`.
* Right side shows outputs from `RST_CTL`:
  * `RESOUT_N` directly to external pad `RESOUT_N`.
  * `DEBUG_ARES`, `ACCESS_ARES`, `FUNC_ARES` going into an OR gate along with `BLK_ARES bit` and `PD_ARES bit` inputs.
  * The OR gate output is `ARES_IN` which enters the `Integration Module (IMn)` dashed boundary, connecting to `CBCs`.
  * `CBCs` output `ARES_OUT` to the `BLOCK`'s `Reset Tree`.
  * `Specific resets` line outputs to "To BMIC, IMEM, APSS".

The RST_CTL block communicates with various blocks and also takes some fundamental inputs from pads. Based on the software programmed state of the RST_CTL block and the inputs to the block, the RST_CTL block produces the appropriate resets. These output resets are sent to special linked blocks (shown left of RST_CTL in Figure 8-18), and to the IM blocks and specific other blocks within the SoC.

The resets from RST_CTL are used in the CC blocks to create the resets that go to the functional blocks.

Three main resets are distributed:
* `FUNC_ARES` – intended to reset registers related to functional logic
* `DEBUG_ARES` – intended to reset only logic for debug purposes
* `ACCESS_ARES` – intended to reset only logic for access control

The `BLK_ARES` bit in Figure 8-18 is located in the associated BCR register. This reset is not available for all CBC. For more information about `BLK_ARES`, see Table 8-120.

The `PD_ARES` bit in Figure 8-18 is located in the associated GDSC register. See Section 8.3.5.3 for more information about GDSCR registers.

The remaining resets that come from the RST_CTL block are intended to address special cases and to provide resets to the blocks closely tied to reset condition generation.
<!-- page 2598 -->

##### 8.3.6.2.1 Block control register

The block control register (BCR) is intended to allow efficient software control of features that affect the entire block. The scope of the control is a direct consequence of wiring, and so this must be reviewed and accepted by software.

Table 8-118 shows the register (BCR) to control the block.

###### Table 8-118 Block control register (BCR)

| Bits | Name |
| :--- | :--- |
| 31 | `DFD_STATUS` (optional) |
| 30:2 | Reserved |
| 1 | `DFD_EN` (optional) |
| 0 | `BLK_ARES` |

To reset a block, the `BLK_ARES` bit is set. When the `BLK_ARES` bit is set, the clocks from all the CBCs within the IM are disabled. They are enabled when this bit is cleared.

The clock frequency to individual CBCs determines how quickly the clocks are enabled/disabled. The asynchronous reset to the CBC is delayed by two cycles of `SLEEP_CLK` when `BLK_ARES` transitions to active.

If the block under control has a virtual power domain via GDSC, only the clocks are affected.

When the `BLK_ARES` bit is set, the clocks from all the CBCs are disabled. After 2 `SLEEP_CLK` cycles, the `ARES_OUT` signals from all the CBCs go active. The GDSC is not reset with the software block reset bit. This is essentially a byproduct of the wiring so that the power state of the PD is maintained post-reset.

The default value of the BCR is established upon `FUNC_ARES`.

##### 8.3.6.2.2 RESIN_N

The RST_CTL block in the device includes the external PMIC in the reset sequence. When there is a specific condition that is intended to cause a specific type of SoC reset, the RST_CTL block triggers the PMIC for RESIN_N and then waits for the RESIN_N before producing resets to SoC.

> [!NOTE]
> One exception is when the CXO power rail voltage is lowered sufficiently to cause the CX POR circuitry to trigger a power-on reset. The PMIC is notified, but the SoC is also simultaneously put into reset. The other exception is during debugger. The SRST can be held active by the debugger, independent of RESIN_N.

A reset uses the following sequence:
1. Reset causing condition occurs.
2. `PS_HOLD` pin connected to PMIC is brought low via RPM.
3. `RESIN_N` from PMIC goes active.
4. Resets to SoC go active.
<!-- page 2599 -->

#### 8.3.6.4 Reset controller structure

SoC resets are disassociated from clock control, except that all clocks are halted during active reset. This further drives the simplification of the CC block and allows all CC blocks to assume a homogeneous structure as long as the particular clock regimes support asynchronous reset methodology.

#### 8.3.6.5 SoC level reset

There are multiple ways in which the entire SoC is asynchronously reset:
* SoC power-on sequence
* CXO rail power-up (security block involved for QFPROM sensing)
<!-- page 2600 -->

* `RESIN_N` pin goes active
* Secure WDOG expires (debug mode setting may modify this)
* MPM temperature sensor reset (overtemperature)

The `FUNC_ARES` is the signal that carries the SoC level reset.

##### 8.3.6.5.1 SoC power-on sequence

When the device is powered-up, there is a capacitive circuit that holds the reset pin `RESIN_N` active. After the pin reset into the `RST_CTL` block goes inactive, the reset sequence will continue to completion.

##### 8.3.6.5.2 Reset button depressed

When the hardware reset on the device is depressed, the reset pin `RESIN_N` is active and the entire SoC is asynchronously reset. When released from this state, the SoC is left in a predetermined state, from which it goes through a boot sequence, and so on.

##### 8.3.6.5.3 Secure WDOG debug mode

If the software does not pet the secure WDOG (write a service pulse to it) in a specified amount of time, the circuit produces a bark (call for a service pulse). If more time elapses without a software pet, the WDOG expires and bites (issue a reset). For the device, there are multiple WDOG circuits, but only the secure WDOG generates a chip level reset via the `RST_CTL` block.

The `RST_CTL` block supports creation of reset sequencing to enhance the ability to debug though secure WDOG expiry. Along with reset sources and software control of configuration, the SoC will be presented with resets depicted in the reset table.

The secure WDOG, in the always on domain of MPM, causes the chip to reset in different modes.

The WDOG CPAS is the ultimate source for WDOG SoC reset timing flow.

###### Processor halting
When the external debugger is attached and the secure WDOG expires (bites), the software has the option to configure the hardware to set a CTI trigger that halts the processor. This is accomplished by the software setting the `GCC_PROC_HALT[PROC_HALT]` bit. A subsequent resin causes the trigger to go active.

###### WDOG reset status
The WDOG reset status bit – `GCC_RESET_STATUS[SECURE_WDOG_EXPIRE_STATUS]`, is used to allow the software to track and control the flow through the reset cycles when caused by the secure WDOG expiring in the debug mode.




<!-- page 2601 -->

### 8.3.6.6 Subsystem level reset

The subsystem reset can be created from the following two asynchronous reset sources:
* SoC in reset
* Software subsystem reset

#### 8.3.6.6.1 Full SoC reset

When the reset control block senses that the entire SoC requires a reset, then it asserts all of the `FUNC_ARES` reset signals. These signals are used by the clock controller blocks to create the corresponding mapped branch resets.

The `BLK_ARES` bit of BCR register is allocated to enable reset for the sequential elements associated with all of the clock branches for that block.

#### 8.3.6.6.2 PS_HOLD control

The `PS_HOLD` register is in the MPM. Hardware control of the `PS_HOLD` register is shared between logic in the MPM and logic in the RST_CTL block. The shared control is due to functions in each of the modules that cause the need for the PMIC to bring RESIN_N active, which is triggered by PS_HOLD going low.

#### 8.3.6.6.3 PS_HOLD_ARES signal

In the RST_CTL block the `PS_HOLD_ARES` is active in the following cases:
* Power-on reset (`SEC_CTL_POR_ARES`)
* Secure WDOG expires – `EXPIRED_STATUS` bit of the `APCS_WDOG_STATUS` register
* SRST assertion – `SW_SRST` bit of the `GCC_SW_SRST`

#### 8.3.6.6.4 PS_HOLD_ASET signal

The `PS_HOLD_ASET` is asserted on RESIN_N active in the first boot pass, but only when the `PROC_HALT` bit of the `GCC_PROC_HALT` register is enabled. If processor halt is enabled, then post resin, the processor cannot set PS_HOLD in time to avoid a subsequent RESIN_N.

#### 8.3.6.6.5 Additions to WDOG reset

WDOG reset flow is also enabled upon an abnormal reset from PMIC. Any reset from PMIC is considered as abnormal if it is not software initiated. For more information about the reset bits, see `GCC_RESET_STATUS` register.
<!-- page 2602 -->

#### 8.3.6.7 Subsystem and block reset generation

##### 8.3.6.7.1 Block reset generation

1. Ensure that `SLEEP_CLK` is enabled in region where BCR for reset is located.
2. Set particular reset bit in the BCR register.
3. Clear above reset bit.

The minimum clock turn on time after reset de-assertion is 4+ clock cycles. This time is used to guarantee the asynchronous reset de-assertion timing to all the downstream flops when the clock is still off. A further requirement is defined that this time should be at least 200 ns. With 4+ clock cycles, this makes the period of the clock to be at least 50 ns (20 MHz) if the branch is enabled before the de-assertion of the reset to satisfy this requirement.

If the CBC is enabled before reset de-assertion, the incoming clock to the CBC should be running at XO (19.2 MHz) speed.

If the CBC is not enabled before reset de-assertion, the CBC should not be enabled before 200 ns after de-assertion of the reset. This restriction applies to all reset conditions.

> [!CAUTION]
> `BLK_ARES` bit is specified to be used only in a debug or catastrophic recovery purposes only. It should not be used in functional cases. But if software should use it, then the requirement regarding reset and clock should be obeyed.

The clock rate restrictions for block resets are explicitly for the case when the clocks are enabled in CBCR registers. If the clocks are disabled by software and then the reset sequence is completed, the clocks can then be re-enabled at-speed, without throttling back to XO.

The GDSC-controlled power collapse sequence ensures that clock rates are properly set to the proper frequency before coming out of collapse. There is additional time for hardware reasons, and therefore proper timing even when clocks are running at full-speed is ensured completely via hardware controlled bring-up sequence with clocks at-speed.

##### 8.3.6.7.2 Restart a subsystem (SS)

1. Set particular reset bit in the reset register.
2. Clear above reset bit.

When a subsystem restart is initiated by software, the `FUNC_ARES` for the subsystem for which the `RESTART` bit of the `<SS_NAME>_RESTART` was set, becomes active. Two `SLEEP_CLK` before the `FUNC_ARES`, the `FUNC_CLK_DIS` goes active. This gives time to shut down clocks at the CBCs within the CC.

In addition, there is logic to automatically reset the CBCRs controlling the subsystem clocks sent by GCC when software sets the corresponding subsystem restart bit. The reset puts the CBCRs back to their default state, where the clock branch enable is 0. By doing that, hardware has stopped these clocks by the restart bit. When software clears the restart bit, these clock branches are off before the clearing of this bit.

> [!NOTE]
> Software system restart is available only for GPU and WCSS.
<!-- page 2603 -->

### 8.3.7 General purpose clocks setting

A general purpose (GP) clock output that lets the user configure an intended clock output by first selecting a clock source (GPLL0 or 19.2 MHz) and then programming an intended division ratio (M/N) and a duty cycle. For more information about the pads of the GP clocks, see Section 8.3.2.

`GCC_GP_CLK_n` settings are programmed via `GCC_GPn_CBCR`, `GCC_GPn_CMD_RCGR`, `GCC_GPn_CFG_RCGR`, `GCC_GPn_M`, `GCC_GPn_N`, and `GCC_GPn_D` registers, where n = 1 to 3. See Table 8-122 for more information.

See Section 8.3.5 to program `GCC_GPn_CBCR`.

For the rest of the registers, see Section 8.3.4.

### 8.3.8 Device-specific clock derivation

Table 8-122 lists the clocks and their associated registers for RCG and IM.

There are votable clocks, that use same registers. For more information about votable clocks and their masters, see Section 8.3.5.1.

For more information about programming the registers shown in Table 8-122, see Section 8.3.4 and Section 8.3.5.

`GCC_APSS_MISC` is used to enable or disable `GCC_APSS_AUX1_CLK` and `GCC_APSS_AUX2_CLK`.

Dynamic clock division is supported for the device NoCs. The enable of DCD, the allowance of division values and the hysteresis control are programmed via the following registers:
* For SNoC – `GCC_SNOC_DCD_CONFIG` and `GCC_SNOC_DCD_HYSTERESIS_CNT` registers.
* For PCNoC – `GCC_PCNOC_DCD_CONFIG` and `GCC_PCNOC_DCD_HYSTERESIS_CNT` registers.

During booting, if the `CLK_ENABLE` bit of the `GCC_USB_BOOT_CLOCK_CTL` is set, all clocks necessary to access USB 2 are turned on.

### 8.3.9 GCC AHB interface and CSR
Access to all CSRs within the GCC are via the AHB interface. The accesses do not support HREADY hold-off as all accesses immediately take effect.

The GCC registers are grouped, and their access is protected to particular processors or execution environment. All of these registers are protected behind an RPU. The RPU provides 32 resource groups, where each resource group protects 4KD words. This makes the RPU protect 1 MB of GCC address space.

## 8.3.10.3 GCC register definitions

### 8.3.10.3.1 0x00021000 GCC_GPLL0_MODE

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

GPLL0_MODE register configures and controls GPLL0.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 21 | PLL_VOTE_FSM_RESET | Resets PLL voting FSM<br>0: Deasserts Reset to PLL voting FSM<br>1: Resets PLL voting FSM |
| 20 | PLL_VOTE_FSM_ENA | Enable PLL voting FSM<br>0: Disabled<br>1: Enabled |
| 19:14 | PLL_BIAS_COUNT | Sets PLL bias count of PLL voting FSM. The count specifies X * 16 PLL reference clock cycles to wait for biasing the PLL during bringup. |
| 13:8 | PLL_LOCK_COUNT | Sets PLL lock time of PLL voting FSM. The count specifies the number of BIAS wait time interval to wait before determining PLL is locked. If lock count is Y, it waits Y * PLL_BIAS_COUNT * 16 PLL reference clock cycles before declaring PLL is locked. If this value is set to 0, the lock_det output of the PLL is used instead |
| 3 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 2 | PLL_RESET_N | This bitfield is used for reset of digital logic in PLL. This includes the MND counters and integer divider |
| 1 | PLL_BYPASSNL | Specify the PLL bypass mode<br>0: Bypass PLL<br>1: Use PLL |
| 0 | PLL_OUTCTRL | Specify the PLL output control<br>0: Disable PLL output and save power<br>1: Activate PLL outputs |

### 8.3.10.3.2 0x00021004 GCC_GPLL0_L_VAL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

Following equation is used to calculate the GPLL0 output frequency VCO = REF * [L+(M/N)]

Where R represents the predivider of 2 and P represents postdivider. The value of GPLL0 register is the given value of L for that equation.
<!-- page 2638 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:0 | PLL_L | This bitfield contains 8-bit L value. This specifies the PLL VCO feedback divide ratio. |

### 8.3.10.3.3 0x00021008 GCC_GPLL0_M_VAL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

Following equation is used to calculate the GPLL0 output frequency VCO = REF * [L+(M/N)]

Where R represents the predivider of 2 and P represents postdivider. The value of GPLL0 register is the given value of M for that equation.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 18:0 | PLL_M | This bitfield contains 19-bit M value. This specifies the PLL M-value for frac-N accumulator. |

### 8.3.10.3.4 0x0002100C GCC_GPLL0_N_VAL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000

Following equation is used to calculate the GPLL0 output frequency VCO = REF * [L+(M/N)]

Where R represents the predivider of 2 and P represents postdivider. The value of GPLL0 register is the given value of N for that equation.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 18:0 | PLL_N | This bitfield contains 19-bit N value. This specifies the PLL N-value for frac-N accumulator. |

### 8.3.10.3.5 0x00021010 GCC_GPLL0_USER_CTL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
<!-- page 2639 -->

This register contains register bits for specifying GPLL0 user configuration settings.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:25 | RESERVE_BITS31_25 | – |
| 24 | MN_EN | PLL fractional mode control.<br>0: Disable<br>1: Enable |
| 23:21 | RESERVE_BITS23_21 | – |
| 20 | VCO_SEL | VCO selection<br>1: Select low frequency VCO (100-500 MHz)<br>0: Select high-freq VCO (400-1400 MHz) |
| 19:13 | RESERVE_BITS19_13 | – |
| 12 | PRE_DIV_RATIO | Clk_ref predivide ratio.<br>0: 1<br>1: 2 |
| 11:10 | RESERVE_BITS11_10 | – |
| 9:8 | POST_DIV_RATIO | Output clock Post divide ration.<br>00: 1<br>01: 2<br>10: Reserved<br>11: 4 |
| 7 | OUTPUT_INV | Output invert state.<br>0: Output invert disable<br>1: Output invert enable |
| 6:5 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 4 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 3 | PLLOUT_LV_EARLY | Enable or disable of pllout_lv_early output.<br>0: Disable<br>1: Enable |
| 2 | PLLOUT_LV_BIST | Enable or disable of pllout_lv_bist output.<br>0: Disable<br>1: Enable |
| 1 | PLLOUT_LV_AUX | Enable or disable of pllout_lv_aux output.<br>0: Disable<br>1: Enable |
| 0 | PLLOUT_LV_MAIN | Enable or disable of pllout_lv_main output.<br>0: Disable<br>1: Enable |
<!-- page 2640 -->

### 8.3.10.3.6 0x00021014 GCC_GPLL0_CONFIG_CTL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00031000

This register contains register bits for specifying GPLL0 configuration control settings.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:30 | RESERVE_BITS31_30 | – |
| 29 | FORCE_PFD_UP | Force PFD Up (force_PFD\<1\>).<br>0 Normal operation (default).<br>1 Force PFD UP -> 1 |
| 28 | FORCE_PFD_DOWN | Force PFD down (force_PFD\<0\>).<br>0 Normal operation (default).<br>1 Force PFD DN -> 1 |
| 27:26 | NMOSC_FREQ_CTRL | Noise measurement oscillator frequency control.<br>00: Highest (2.8 GHz at TT / 1.05 V / 40°C) (default)<br>01: 1/2 highest<br>10: 1/3 highest<br>11: 1/4 highest |
| 25:24 | PFD_DZSEL | PFD reset pulse width adjustment (PFD_dzsel\<1:0\>).<br>00 1x delay (default)<br>01: 2x delay<br>10: 3x delay<br>11: 4x delay |
| 23 | NMOSC_EN | Noise measurement oscillator control (nmosc_en)<br>0: Disable (default)<br>1: Enable |
| 22 | RESERVE_BIT22 | – |
| 21:20 | ICP_DIV | Charge pump bias mirror multiplication factor(icp_div\<1:0\>).<br>00: 1 (default)<br>01: 3/2<br>10: 7/4<br>11: 9/4 |
| 19:18 | IREG_DIV | Regulator bias mirror multiplication factor (ireg_div\<1:0\>).<br>00: 1 (default)<br>01: 7/5<br>10: 9/5<br>11: 11/5 |


<!-- page 2641 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 17:16 | CUSEL | VCO decoupling cap unit size (cusel <1:0>).<br>00: 125 fF<br>01: 250 fF<br>10: 375 fF<br>11: 500 fF (default) |
| 15 | REF_MODE | Reference circuit mode (ref_mode).<br>0: Bandgap Mode: Seed currents source from bandgap circuit and N well reference circuit active. (default)<br>1: Supply-independent mode: Seed currents sourced from supply-independent circuit and N well reference pulled to VDDA. |
| 14 | RESERVE_BIT14 | – |
| 13:12 | CFG_LOCKDET | Lock detector phase error threshold (cfg_lockdet<1:0>).<br>00: 2pi/2<br>01: 2pi/15 (default)<br>10: 2pi/23<br>11: 2pi/31 |
| 11 | FORCE_ISEED | Seed current control (force_iseed).<br>0: Turn off seed currents when clock is detected. (default)<br>1: Keep seed currents on always. |
| 10:0 | RESERVE_BITS10_0 | – |

### 8.3.10.3.23 0x00023004 GCC_BIMC_PLL_L_VAL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

Following equation is used to calculate the BIMC_PLL output frequency VCO = REF * [L+(M/N)]

Where R represents the predivider of 2 and P represents postdivider

The value of BIMC_PLL register is the given value of L for that equation.

| Bits | Name | Description |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 7:0 | PLL_L | This bitfield contains 8-bit L value. This specifies the PLL VCO feedback divide ratio. |

| 11:8 | WAKEUP | RW | This bitfield specifies the number of clock cycles it takes for the clock to turn back on.<br>0x0: CLOCK0 (Zero cycle)<br>0x1: CLOCK1 (One cycle)<br>0x2: CLOCK2 (Two cycles)<br>0x3: CLOCK3 (Three cycles)<br>0x4: CLOCK4 (Four cycles)<br>0x5: CLOCK5 (Five cycles)<br>0x6: CLOCK6 (Six cycles)<br>0x7: CLOCK7 (Seven cycles)<br>0x8: CLOCK8 (Eight cycles)<br>0x9: CLOCK9 (Nine cycles)<br>0xA: CLOCK10 (Ten cycles)<br>0xB: CLOCK11 (Eleven cycles)<br>0xC: CLOCK12 (Twelve cycles)<br>0xD: CLOCK13 (Thirteen cycles)<br>0xE: CLOCK14 (Fourteen cycles)<br>0xF: CLOCK15 (Fifteen cycles) |
| 7:4 | SLEEP | RW | This bitfield specifies the number of clock cycles until complete sleep where headswitch of the corresponding memories will be opened.<br>0x0: CLOCK0 (Zero cycle)<br>0x1: CLOCK1 (One cycle)<br>0x2: CLOCK2 (Two cycles)<br>0x3: CLOCK3 (Three cycles)<br>0x4: CLOCK4 (Four cycles)<br>0x5: CLOCK5 (Five cycles)<br>0x6: CLOCK6 (Six cycles)<br>0x7: CLOCK7 (Seven cycles)<br>0x8: CLOCK8 (Eight cycles)<br>0x9: CLOCK9 (Nine cycles)<br>0xA: CLOCK10 (Ten cycles)<br>0xB: CLOCK11 (Eleven cycles)<br>0xC: CLOCK12 (Twelve cycles)<br>0xD: CLOCK13 (Thirteen cycles)<br>0xE: CLOCK14 (Fourteen cycles)<br>0xF: CLOCK15 (Fifteen cycles) |
