### 8.3.10.3.257 GCC_CLOCK_FRQ_MEASURE_CTL

**Address:** `0x00074004`

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** CLK

**Reset State:** `0x00000000`

The clock frequency measure control register holds the value to load in the XO DIV4 counter. It also contains the enable to turn on both up and down counters for measure frequency for the corresponding debug clock.

> [!NOTE]
> The XO DIV4 counter uses the GCC_XO_DIV4_CLK. One must enable the GCC_XO_DIV4_CLK by programming GCC_XO_DIV4_CBCR.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 | CNT_EN | This bitfield is used to enable both the Up and Down counter.<br>0x1: ENABLE (Enable.)<br>0x0: DISABLE (Disable.) |
| 19:0 | XO_DIV4_TERM_CNT | After it is loaded, this value is decremented and used to compare to figure out the frequency of the clock measured. Freq(measure clock) = Freq(XO_DIV4) * (MEASURE_CNT + 1.5) / (XO_DIV4_TERM_CNT + 3.5) |

### 8.3.10.3.258 GCC_CLOCK_FRQ_MEASURE_STATUS

**Address:** `0x00074008`

**Type:** R

**Clock:** CLK

**Reset State:** `0x00000000`

This register is read only register, which contains the status of the measurement counter and its value. It is used to figure out the frequency of the clock measured at the end.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 25 | XO_DIV4_CNT_DONE | This bitfield is automatically set (1) when the XO_DIV4 counter terminates. The microprocessor polls to determine when the value of the measurement counter is valid. |
| 24:0 | MEASURE_CNT | These read only register bits hold the value stored in the measurement counter, which is used to figure out the frequency of the clock measured. Freq (measure clock) = Freq(XO_DIV4) * (MEASURE_CNT + 1.5) / (XO_DIV4_TERM_CNT + 3.5) |
<!-- page 2838 -->

#### GCC_VFE0_CMD_RCGR Register Details

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |

| 0 | UPDATE | | This UPDATE bit is SW and HW modified. SW sets the bit when the configuration values are programmed, and when they have taken effect, then HW clears the bit to 0.<br>0: Not Active<br>1: Active |

## 8.4 Interconnects

This section describes the system interconnects.

The NoC is the chip interconnect that connects masters and slaves and allows them to communicate with each other. For operating in mission mode, the NoC has almost no software programming requirements. That is, no programming is required to get started.

There are two interconnects on system level:
* The system NoC (SNOC)
* The peripheral and system configuration NoC (PCNOC).

Figure 8-1 shows these NoCs along with the connected masters and slaves.

#### Figure: Interconnects overview
*Description:* A block diagram illustrating the chip-level interconnect architecture, highlighting the two primary Network on Chips (NoCs): the System NoC (SNOC) and the Peripheral and System Configuration NoC (PCNOC), along with their connected master and slave components.
- **SNOC (System NoC)**: Acts as the high-throughput backbone.
  - Connected to **BIMC** (Bus Interface Memory Controller), which interfaces with **SDRAM**, **SMMU**, and **GPU**.
  - Bidirectionally connected to **APSS** (Application Processor Subsystem), **CAMSS_VFE**, **CAMSS_JPEG**, **MDSS** (Multimedia Display Subsystem), **VENCDEC**, **MSS_NAV**, and **WCSS**.
  - Receives inputs from **MSS_DSP**, **QDSS_STM**, **QDSS_BAM**, and **QDSS_ETR**.
  - Outputs to **GMEM** (shared with GPU) and **IMEM**.
- **PCNOC (Peripheral and System Configuration NoC)**: Manages peripheral communication and configuration.
  - Bidirectionally connected to control and peripheral blocks: **QDSS_DAP** (two instances), **TCU**, **MSG_RAM**, **GCC**, **PRNG**, **PDM**, **TLMM**, **MPM**, **PMIC_ARB**, **BOOT ROM**, **SPDM**, **DEHR**, **TCSR**, **RPM**, **SDCC2**, **SDCC1**, **AUDIO**, **BLSP1**, and **USB**.
  - Drives configuration ports (CFG) for various subsystems: **EBI1_PHY_CFG**, **MSS_CFG**, **VENCDEC_CFG**, **RPM_XPU_CFG**, **DEHR_CFG**, **MMU_CFG**, **PRNG_XPU_CFG**, **GPU_CFG**, **SNOC_XPU_CFG**, **DISP_SS_CFG**, **CAMSS_CFG**, **PCNOC_XPU_CFG**, **RBCPR_CFG**, **QDSS_CFG**, **PCNOC_CFG**, **IMEM_CFG**, **SNOC_CFG**, and **BIMC_CFG**.
- **NoC Interconnection**: SNOC and PCNOC are bidirectionally connected to each other, allowing communication between the two domains.

**Table 8-125 Interconnects acronyms and terms**

| :--- | :--- |
| NoC | Network on Chip |
| Master | Module or subsystem on the NoC capable of initiating transactions |
| Slave | Module or subsystem on the NoC being accessed from masters. It is the master’s target that may or may not accept master’s transactions. |
| NIU | Network Interface Unit. The NIU is a NoC block that connects masters and slaves to the NoC. It converts their protocols to the NoC internal protocol. |

### 8.4.3 Interconnects functional description
The SNOC is the primary interconnect on the SoC and connects the modules that require the maximum bandwidth. The majority of module register configurations are set through the PCNOC which is connected to the SNOC.

The NoC consists of multiple QSB, AHB, and AXI ports originating from the various masters that request access to various slaves and to the external SDRAM.

### 8.4.3.2    AHB bus timeout (ABT) module

Most bus hangs occur to access to disabled AHB slaves. The slave receives the access, but its HReady signal is driven low indefinitely. The ABT module ensures that access to a slave never hangs the bus. It is implemented as slave on the AHB bus and monitors the HReady signal of each AHB slave to detect bus hangs. According to the AHB protocol, a slave can only drive its HReady low while it actively inserts wait-states into an in-progress transaction.

When a slave is idle, the slave must must drive its HReady high and drive OK on its HResp lines.

The ABT module uses a timer to track how long the HReady signal for any slave is asserted low. It decrements the timer while HReady is low. When the timer expires, a hang is detected. The ABT module responds on behalf of the hung slave and generates an interrupt. It also captures the syndrome information to identify the master and slave involved in the hung transaction.

The ABT module responds only on behalf of the hung slave but continues to monitor other slaves on the bus. If another slave also hangs before the interrupt is serviced, the ABT module responds on behalf of that slave too. These responses prevent bus hangs. Thus, bus traffic can continue.

The ABT module always accepts the AHB requests and always provides the response in the next clock cycle without inserting any wait states. Thus, the transactions targeted to it never cause bus hangs. This holds true even if the clock to the ABT module is disabled.

The PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT0 to PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT9 ABT modules are present in the SoC. These modules reside in the PCNOC.

#### 8.4.3.2.1 ABT module configuration

> **NOTE:** Throughout this section, n = 0 to 9.

The ABT module is disabled on power-on reset. To enable it, set to 0x1 the TIMEOUT_SLAVE_GLB_EN bit in the TCSR_TIMEOUT_SLAVE_GLB_EN register. Setting this bit to 0x1 enables all ABT modules in the SoC.

To configure how long the ABT module will track the low value of HReady signal before it detects bus hang and generates interrupt, write the desired value to the LOADVAL field in the PCNOC_n_ABT_TIMER_LOADVAL register. The formula to calculate LOADVAL is as follows:

LOADVAL=(ABT module time base frequency [kHz])×(Timer timeout period [ms])

For example, if the time base frequency is 32 kHz and the timeout period should be 2ms, the LOADVAL field should be set to 64 (32kHz × 2ms).

To enable the ABT module interrupt (PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUTn), set to 0x1 the INTRENABLE bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_INTR_ENABLE register. The interrupt should also be enabled at chip level through the corresponding bit in the TCSR_TIMEOUT_INTR_x_ENABLE register, where x = APSS, RPM.

To start the timer of the ABT module, which effectively enables the timeout feature, set to 0x1 the MODE bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_TIMER_MODE register.

<!-- page 3010 -->
The recommended sequence of ABT module configuration steps is as follows:

1. Enable the ABT module.
2. Configure the LOADVAL field.
3. Enable the ABT module interrupt locally at module level.
4. Enable the ABT module interrupt at chip level too.
5. Start the timer of the ABT module.
6. The ABT module and the chip level registers are not affected by a hardware reset, so they do not need to be programmed again.

#### 8.4.3.2.2 ABT module interrupts

> **NOTE:** Throughout this section, n = 0 to 9.

When a timeout event occurs, the ABT module generates an interrupt (PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUTn) that indicates a bus hang. The interrupt remains active until it has been explicitly cleared by setting to 0x1 the INTRCLEAR bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_INTR_CLEAR register. To determine if there are any active interrupts the chip level TCSR_TIMEOUT_INTR_STATUS register can be read. It contains interrupt status information for all ABT modules unlike the INTRSTATUS bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_INTR_STATUS register which holds the status only for the PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUTn module. In addition, the INTRSTATUS bit is asserted also if the interrupt is disabled.

The ABT module provides syndrome information associated with the interrupt. It can be read through the following registers:

* **PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_ID**: contains information about the transaction that caused the bus hang
* **PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_ADDR0**: contains the lower 32 address bits of the transaction that caused the bus hang
* **PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_ADDR1**: contains the upper 32 address bits of the transaction that caused the bus hang
* **PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_HREADY**: identifies the slave that caused the bus hung

In case of interrupt, if the SYNDVALID bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_VALID register is set to 0x1, then the syndrome information is valid. To clear the syndrome valid bit (SYNDVALID) and the syndrome information, set to 0x1 the SYNDCLEAR bit in the PCNOC_n_ABT_SYND_CLEAR register.

The following is the recommended sequence steps when servicing ABT module interrupts:

1. Determine if there are any active interrupts.
2. If any, read the syndrome information.
3. Based on syndrome information identify the hung slave and resolve the issue.
4. Clear the syndrome information.
5. Clear the interrupt.



<!-- page 3011 -->

> [!NOTE]
> The interrupt clear (INTRCLEAR) and syndrome clear (SYNDCLEAR) only take effect when the `TIMEOUT_SLAVE_GLB_EN` bit in the `TCSR_TIMEOUT_SLAVE_GLB_EN` register is set to `0x1`.

### 8.4.4 Interconnects registers

The register bits and fields not shown in this section are considered reserved. Errors are not generated if write to these locations is performed. Reading the value of reserved bit or field returns unknown result.

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT0_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00000000`

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INSTID | SW configurable field to provide unique number for each of the AHB Timeout Slaves in the chip. |

##### 8.4.4.2.2 0x00000008 PCNOC_0_ABT_NUM_SLAVES

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** `GCC_PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT0_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00000005`

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 5:0 | NUMSLAVES | Specifies the number of slaves on the AHB bus excluding the Timeout Slave. Valid values are from 1 to 32. |

##### 8.4.4.2.3 0x0000000C PCNOC_0_ABT_TIMER_LOADVAL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT0_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x000000FF`

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:0 | LOADVAL | Load the timer with this value, when the timer is in load mode, i.e, MODE field in ABT_TIMER_MODE is 0.<br/>*Note:* `LOADVAL` of 0 is not valid. |

##### 8.4.4.2.4 0x00000010 PCNOC_0_ABT_TIMER_MODE

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_PCNOC_BUS_TIMEOUT0_AHB_CLK`

* **Reset state:** `0x00000000`

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | MODE | Timer mode.<br/>0x0: The timer is in load mode and the `LOADVAL` field value in `ABT_TIMER_LOADVAL` is loaded into the timer.<br/>0x1: The timer is in run mode. |

## 8.5 Interrupts

### 8.5.1 Interrupt sources

This section describes the interrupt maps for the various processor subsystems in the device.

#### 8.5.1.1 APSS interrupt map

Table 8-134 shows the mapping for the APSS_QGIC2 PPI/SPI interrupt inputs. All unused PPI/SPI interrupts are not shown in this table. All APSS internal interrupts are highlighted in yellow.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| APSS_QGIC2_C0_PPI[4] | 20 | APSS | APC0_QGICQTMRVIRTIRPTREQ | Level | |
| APSS_QGIC2_C0_PPI[5] | 21 | APSS | APC0_DBGCOMMRXFULL | Level | |
| APSS_QGIC2_C0_PPI[6] | 22 | APSS | APC0_DBGCOMMTXEMPTY | Level | |

## 8.5.2 Qualcomm® Generic Interrupt Controller (QGIC2)

This section describes the QGIC2 integrated within the applications processor subsystem (APSS), in other chapters also referred to as APSS_QGIC2.

### 8.5.2.1 QGIC2 overview

The QGIC2 is a fully programmable interrupt controller designed to be paired with an ARM-compliant CPU controller. It performs the following functions:

- Receives interrupts from within the SoC or from private CPU peripherals
- Processes the interrupts with priority information set by software
- Directs the interrupts to the host CPU controller

In this device, the QGIC2 is integrated within the APSS and supports all four A53 controller by implementing individual interface (IRQ/FIQ) for each core.

Figure 8-21 shows a high-level overview of the QGIC2 module.

#### Figure 8-21: QGIC2 overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the structure of the QGIC2 (Qualcomm Generic Interrupt Controller). At the center is the QGIC2 distributor block.
- Input signals entering the QGIC2 distributor include:
  - SPIs (Shared Peripheral Interrupts)
  - CPU0 PPIs to CPU3 PPIs (Private Peripheral Interrupts)
- The QGIC2 distributor is connected to:
  - An AHB interface via the QGIC2 AHB block
  - Four CPU interfaces (CPU interface 0 through CPU interface 3)
- Each CPU interface outputs IRQ/FIQ signals to its respective host CPU core.

Table 8-140 lists the APSS QGIC2 supported features.
