### 8.5.2.4 QGIC2 functional description

#### 8.5.2.4.1 QGIC2 architecture

Figure 8-23 shows a high-level overview of the QGIC2 functional blocks:
* **The distributor** is a self-contained block that includes all interrupt configuration and routing registers, plus all routing and prioritization logic. The logic that determines the highest priority interrupt for each host CPU is repeated per CPU.
* **The CPU interface** contains logic that can be configured for specific CPU requirements: a priority threshold, secure vs. nonsecure interrupts, and tracking for interrupt priority levels. The CPU interface also provides the IRQ/FIQ signals to the host ARM core.
* **The hypervisor interface block** consists mostly of CSRs that work with hypervisor software to provide software-driven interrupts to guest virtualization-compliant OSs running on ARM cores.
* **The virtual CPU (VCPU) interface** is almost a carbon-copy of the CPU interface, except that it connects to the hypervisor interface instead of the distributor. As such, this block is the virtualized version of the CPU interface, and provides the virtual fast interrupt request (VFIQ) and virtual interrupt (VIRQ) signals to the virtualization-complaint host ARM CPU.

#### Figure 8-23: QGIC2 functional block diagram
*Description:* A functional block diagram showing the data flow and signals of the QGIC2:
- **Distributor**: Registers interrupt inputs:
  - Software Generated Interrupts (SGI_TRIGGER)
  - Private Peripheral Interrupts (PPIs)
  - Shared Peripheral Interrupts (SPIs)
  - Handles Enable signals, SPI_TARGET, priority, security decoding, and per-CPU pending interrupts and masking.
- **CPU Interface**: Receives HPPI information, priority, and security decoding from the Distributor. It provides interrupts (`irq_n`, `fiq_n`) and wake-up signals (`irq_wake_up`, `fiq_wake_up`, `wakeup`) to the CPU. It handles the `deactivate` signal.
- **Hypervisor Interface**: Interfaces with the Virtual CPU interface.
- **Virtual CPU Interface**: Generates virtual interrupts (`virq_n`, `vfiq_n`) for the CPU.
- **CRIF interface** and **int_ack/eoi interface** connect the various components to the system and CPU.

#### 8.5.2.4.2 QGIC2 interrupt basics and flow

##### Interrupt Types

The QGIC2 architecture defines the following interrupt types:
* **Software generated interrupts (SGIs)**: These are used for interprocessor communication, and are generated by a write to the APCS_GICD_SGIR register.
* **Private peripheral interrupts (PPIs)**: These are generated by private/internal peripherals within the APSS or the A53 processor itself.
<!-- page 3075 -->

* **Shared peripheral interrupts (SPIs)**: These are generated by system peripherals, outside the APSS.

##### Interrupt States

Interrupt states are relevant to all software interactions. Keep the following facts in mind when working with interrupt states:
* An interrupt that is asserted becomes pending.
* An interrupt becomes active when software acknowledges the interrupt by reading the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register.
* An interrupt that is reasserted when it is already active becomes active & pending.
* An interrupt becomes inactive when software, after it has completed processing the interrupt, writes to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register with the ID of an interrupt currently in the active state. If the interrupt was in active & pending, it transitions instead to pending.

> [!NOTE]
> The above do not include the effects of registers such as `APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn` or `APCS_GICD_ISACTIVERn`.

##### Interrupt Flow

The following steps breakdown the complete interrupt handling flow in the QGIC2. The actual software interaction process is explained in Section Software interaction scenarios.

An interrupt arrives at the QGIC2.
1. The interrupt arrival event is passed to a finite state machine (FSM) that, if the interrupt is not already pending, registers the change in state and the interrupt becomes pending. An interrupt that is already active, which means that software has acknowledged it, is not valid for assertion but can become pending again. In that case, the state is active & pending, which is not valid for assertion to a processor.

   > [!NOTE]
   > These transitions occur whether the interrupt is enabled or not. The enable determines only whether or not the interrupt can assert.

2. If the interrupt state is valid for assertion to a processor (enabled and pending), the interrupt priority is passed to a massive comparator tree that finds the highest priority interrupt for each CPU.
3. The interrupt information is passed to the CPU interface for which it was targeted. The CPU interface compares its internal settings and state with the interrupt priority.
4. If the CPU interface determines that the interrupt may proceed, the IRQ or FIQ line to the ARM host processor asserts low, flagging the interrupt to the processor.
5. Software must then read the interrupt acknowledge register (`APCS_GICC_IAR`) for the corresponding CPU interface, which returns an ID uniquely identifying the interrupt. Doing so changes the interrupt state in the QGIC2 from pending to active and the interrupt is no longer valid for assertion to the CPU. This causes the IRQ or FIQ line to reassert high, deactivating the assertion to the host CPU.
<!-- page 3076 -->

6. Software handles the interrupt and writes the interrupt ID – the same value returned by the `APCS_GICC_IAR` read – to the end of interrupt register (`APCS_GICC_EOIR`). This tells the QGIC2 that processing is complete, and the QGIC2 moves the interrupt from active to inactive. Alternatively, if the interrupt was asserted again while active, it is in the active & pending state and an `APCS_GICC_EOIR` write transitions the interrupt to the pending state, at which point it is again valid for assertion to the CPU.

#### 8.5.2.4.3 QGIC2 power and clock management

The QGIC2 automatically gates internal clocks, and there are no clock enable/disable registers that must be manipulated at reset. The automatic clock gating may be optionally disabled by a write to the `APCS_GICD_CGCR` register.

##### QGIC2 clocking

The QGIC2 has a single clock input that is synchronous to the incoming AHB connection.

The clock rate may be changed as needed. The clock rate does not matter for interrupt detection, only for the AHB bus interface and QGIC2 core logic.

Internal interrupt detection logic is clocked only when an interrupt arrives at the QGIC2. At that point, a clock is requested, enabled, and the interrupt’s physical state change is signaled to the FSM for that interrupt.

##### System level power management impacts

The QGIC2 has no state-retention flops, so any system-level power down or clock gating collapses or freezes the QGIC2. As such, software should save states for later restoration. See Section Saving and restoring state for details on how to save and restore the QGIC2 state.

#### 8.5.2.4.4 QGIC2 reset options

The QGIC2 has a single asynchronous reset input that resets the QGIC2 to the same known, default state: secure, all internal block disabled, all interrupts disabled.

#### 8.5.2.4.5 QGIC2 security

The QGIC2 supports two groups of interrupts in terms of secure/non-secure operations:
* **Group 0** refers to secure interrupts and settings
* **Group 1** refers to nonsecure interrupts and settings

Banking of certain features is operated by security and this allows an ARM Trustzone-compliant core (A53) to run both a secure OS and nonsecure user software, and also allows that division of permission to automatically extend to the interrupt controller. This way nonsecure software cannot modify the secure interrupts used by the host OS.
<!-- page 3077 -->

#### 8.5.2.4.6 QGIC2 connection to multicore host CPUs

The APSS QGIC2 supports all four A53 CPU controllers, has multiple CPU interfaces that provide interrupt routing to each controller. Certain internal registers are also banked to allow settings per CPU.

### 8.5.2.5 QGIC2 programming guide

This section describes common programming scenarios for the QGIC2 and how software is expected to interact with it.

> [!NOTE]
> The QGIC2 has no timing-sensitive configuration sequences, that is, requiring a write followed by a delay, followed by a write, and so on. However, the following sections are presented in order of their effect on the system. As such, this order should be maintained when possible.

#### 8.5.2.5.1 Enumeration of interrupts: Absolute vs. relative

The APSS QGIC2 supports 16 SGIs, 16 PPIs (including the hypervisor maintenance interrupt), and 256 SPIs. When addressing registers, these interrupt numbers all exist on a continuum, as shown in Figure 8-24.

#### Figure 8-24: QGIC2 interrupt enumeration
*Description:* Interrupt number mapping from absolute to relative:
- SGI: 0 to 15 (16 interrupts)
- PPI: 16 to 31 (16 interrupts)
- SPI: 32 to 287 (256 interrupts)

The absolute interrupt number is the number on the continuum and this is the number that the QGIC2 really uses when dealing with the interrupt. The relative number is its offset within its own type: SGI #0-15, PPI #0-15, and SPI #0-255.

For example, if the target interrupt to program is SPI #5, the QGIC2 actually considers this to be interrupt number 37 because it is indexed from 0 and includes the SGI and PPI interrupts. When using the addressing and indexing equations that follow in the rest of this section, then it would be the number 37 that should be used and not 5.

Use the following equations to determine the absolute interrupt number:
* **SGI**: Absolute = Relative
* **PPI**: Absolute = Relative + 16
* **SPI**: Absolute = Relative + 32

> [!NOTE]
> PPIs and SGIs are repeated per CPU controller, but their number ranges overlap and, rather than being given unique numbers, banked interrupts are accessed using banked
<!-- page 3078 -->

registers. For instance, PPI #5 on CPU0 and PPI #5 on CPU1 are two different interrupts with two different physical inputs, but they share the same interrupt number and are differentiated by the means by which they are accessed on the bus. PPI #5 on CPU0 is accessed through the registers banked for CPU0, while PPI #5 on CPU1 is accessed through the registers banked for CPU1.

#### 8.5.2.5.2 Enabling the QGIC2

The QGIC2 includes global enable bits for both the distributor and the CPU interface. These two blocks can be enabled and disabled separately.

##### Distributor enable

Because the distributor is the central control and routing hub for the QGIC2, it must be enabled via the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` register for the QGIC2 to function. If it is disabled entirely, there are no interrupts presented to the CPU interfaces, and subsequently no interrupts presented to the host CPU controllers.

The `APCS_GICD_CTLR` register contains the following two bits:
* **ENABLE** (bit position 0): This bit is the group 0 (secure) enable. It determines whether or not group 0 interrupts are considered for routing to a CPU interface. If this bit is set to `0x0`, no group 0 interrupt is considered for routing, and no pending interrupts in this group block the routing of a group 1 (nonsecure) interrupt.
* **ENABLE_NS** (bit position 1): This bit is the group 1 enable. It determines whether or not group 1 interrupts are considered for routing to a CPU interface. If this bit is set to `0x0`, no group 1 interrupt is considered for routing, and no pending interrupts in this group block the routing of a group 0 interrupt.

Use the scenarios in Table 8-145 to help determine which bits to program.

### Table 8-145 Distributor enable scenarios

| Bits Set | Scenarios |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Secure Only** | <ul><li>Most software verification</li><li>TrustZone-compliant CPU that does not use nonsecure interrupts or wishes to momentarily disable all processing of nonsecure interrupts</li></ul> |
| **Non-Secure Only** | <ul><li>TrustZone-compliant CPU that does not use secure interrupts or wishes to momentarily disable all processing of secure interrupts</li></ul> |
| **Secure + Non-Secure** | <ul><li>Standard configuration for ARM TrustZone-compliant cores for which interrupt security must be maintained</li><li>May also be set for software verification, as setting both bits high and then using only Group 0 or Group 1 interrupts is entirely permissible and has no ill effects</li></ul> |

##### CPU interface enable

The CPU interface can be enabled via the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register. As with the distributor, the CPU interface has associated group 0 and group 1 enable bits, as follows:
* **ENABLE** (bit position 0): This bit allows its associated CPU interface to present group 0 interrupts to the host CPU. Disabling this bit does not stop the processing of group 0 interrupts
<!-- page 3079 -->

for this CPU in the distributor, but it does stop all such interrupts from being presented to the host CPU on the IRQ/FIQ lines. If such an interrupt is currently the highest priority pending interrupt for this CPU Interface, disabling group 0 interrupts blocks any further interrupt assertions for this host CPU controller unless the highest pending interrupt security changes.
* **ENABLE_NS** (bit position 1): This bit allows this CPU interface to present group 1 interrupts to the host CPU. Disabling this bit does not stop the processing of group 1 interrupts for this CPU in the distributor, but it does stop all such interrupts from being presented to the host CPU on the IRQ/FIQ lines. If such an interrupt is currently the highest priority pending interrupt for this CPU interface, disabling group 0 interrupts blocks any further interrupt assertions for this host CPU controller unless the highest pending interrupt security changes. Setting this bit to `0x0` blocks the assertion of group 1 interrupts to the host CPU controller to which this interface is connected.

> [!NOTE]
> The `ENABLE` and `ENABLE_NS` bits in the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register need to be configured depending on the `ENABLE` and `ENABLE_NS` bits set in the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` register and depending on how the security/grouping of interrupts are configured.

Additionally, the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register also includes two important bits to provide control for secure destination and interrupt acknowledge:
* **S_DEST** (bit position 3): This is the secure destination bit. It controls to which output port, IRQ or FIQ, a group 0 interrupt is presented. For the setting of this bit to have any effect, the `ENABLE` bit in this register must first be set to `0x1`. If the `S_DEST` bit is set to `0x0`, group 0 interrupts are asserted to the host CPU controller on the IRQ line. If the `S_DEST` bit is set to `0x1`, they are presented to the host CPU controller on the FIQ line.
  This setting matters due to the behavior of handling interrupts in an ARM-compliant controller (A53). The IRQ and FIQ lines cause traps to different exception vectors. If there are separate exception handlers for each security level, this bit should be set to `0x1`. If software intends to use just one handler at the IRQ trap address and determine handling by interrupt ID only, this bit should be set to `0x0`, causing all interrupts to be routed through the IRQ line.
* **ACKCTL** (bit position 2): This is the acknowledgment control bit. It determines whether or not a secure access can acknowledge a non secure interrupt. When this bit is set to `0x0`, secure software that attempts to acknowledge a non secure interrupt receives a special code (`0x3FE`) that serves as notification that the highest pending interrupt is a non secure interrupt. Secure software may then surrender control to non secure software to allow the interrupt to be handled. When this bit is set to `0x1`, secure software may acknowledge a non secure interrupt and it receives no special notification that it has done so.

> [!NOTE]
> The `ACKCTL` bit is useful when the `S_DEST` bit is set to `0x0`. When `S_DEST` is set to `0x1`, non secure interrupts use the IRQ signal and secure interrupts use the FIQ signal, and each signal causes traps to different addresses in an ARM-compliant controller. They can then be handled with specialized code for secure vs. nonsecure. When `S_DEST` is set to `0x0`, both secure and nonsecure interrupts arrive on the same IRQ line and trap to the same exception address. Software then has no means of determining the security of the interrupt apart from reading the interrupt security register (`APCS_GICD_ISRn`).
<!-- page 3080 -->

> [!NOTE]
> The CPU interface is replicated per CPU controller, meaning that the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register is banked per CPU controller.

> [!NOTE]
> This register includes some other functional bits as well. For verification, do not write all 0xFs to this register, as doing so can have unintended side effects. Enable only the needed features.

##### Additional configuration: Priority mask

To allow interrupts to assert, there is an additional register in the CPU interface that must be configured: the priority mask register (`APCS_GICC_PMR`). This register serves as a threshold for interrupts coming from the distributor.

The `APCS_GICC_PMR` register causes the CPU to block the assertion of any interrupt with a numerical priority value greater than or equal to the setting in the register. This means that any logical priority value less than or equal to the setting in the register is blocked. The power-on-reset value of this register is all 0s, which means that all interrupts are initially blocked. As such, this register should be set above `0x0` to ensure that interrupts are not blocked. The exact value set is up to software and varies based on the priority values chosen for interrupts in the distributor.

#### 8.5.2.5.3 Setting up an interrupt

The following sections describe several registers that must be considered when setting up an interrupt. Some of optional, while others are required.

##### Enabling and disabling an interrupt

The following registers are used for enabling/disabling interrupts:
* Enabling interrupts: `APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn`
* Disabling interrupts: `APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn`

Rather than performing a read-modify-write operation on a single register to control interrupt enables, the QGIC2 maintains an internal enable tracker and then exposes control over that bit through command registers. Writing 1 to the correct bit in the correct `APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn` register number enables an interrupt, and writing 1 to the same bit number in the same `APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn` register number [sic: probably `APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn`] disables the interrupt. This way, enabling or disabling a single interrupt only requires one bus transaction and minimizes the chance of accidentally changing another interrupt.

The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to registers and bits. Let $n$ be the absolute interrupt number, $r$ be the register number, and $b$ be the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 32$$

$$b = n \text{ MOD } 32$$

To enable a specific interrupt, write 1 to bit position $b$ in `APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn` register number $r$. To disable a specific interrupt, write 1 to bit position $b$ in `APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn` register number $r$.


<!-- page 3081 -->

> [!NOTE]
> The registers corresponding to PPI and SGI interrupts are banked per CPU.

### Setting an interrupt targeting (SPI only)

If the interrupt being configured is a PPI or an SGI, routing does not need to be set, as PPIs and SGIs are banked per CPU controller and are always targeted and routed to the CPU controller, for which they are banked. If the interrupt being configured is an SPI, it must be targeted at one or more CPU controllers, or otherwise it is not routed to any CPU interface.

The register for this setting is the interrupt targets register (`APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn`). The fields are 8 bits wide, and this register is read-modify-write, so any changes must preserve existing data except for those bits being modified.

The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to register and bits, where $n$ is the absolute interrupt number, $r$ is the register number, and $b$ is the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 4$$

$$b = (n \text{ MOD } 4) \times 8$$

> [!NOTE]
> $b$ here is the base bit for modification. Bits $b+7$ through $b$ should be modified; [7:0] for interrupt 0, [15:8] for interrupt 1, [23:16] for interrupt 2, etc.

As an example, to target SPI #23 (absolute number 55) at CPU0 and CPU1, the write should be performed to the `APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn` register number 13. Bits [31:24] of this register should be set to 0000 0011, bitwise.

### Setting an interrupt priority

On reset, all interrupts come up to priority 0, the highest priority level. Priority comparisons among pending interrupts determine which interrupt is routed to the CPU interface first.

When multiple interrupts are pending and their priorities are all equal, the lowest absolute number interrupt is asserted first.

For example, if SPIs #24 and #36 are both pending and have the same priority, SPI #24 is routed to the CPU interface first. If SPI #24 and SGI #3 are both pending with the same priority, SGI #3 is routed to the CPU interface first.

To change the priority of an interrupt, use the interrupt priority register (`APCS_GICD_IPRIORITYRn`). The fields are 8 bits wide, and this register is read-modify-write, so any changes must preserve existing data except for those bits being modified.

The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to register and bits, where $n$ is the absolute interrupt number, $r$ is the register number, and $b$ is the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 4$$

$$b = (n \text{ MOD } 4) \times 8$$
<!-- page 3082 -->

> [!NOTE]
> $b$ here is the base bit for modification. Bits $b+7$ through $b$ should be modified; [7:0] for interrupt 0, [15:8] for interrupt 1, [23:16] for interrupt 2, and so on.

Because QGIC2 only supports 32 priority levels, the three least significant bits of each priority bit range are always masked off inside the QGIC2, so only bits [7:3] of each range retain priority information. The bit ranges for each interrupt are still given 8 bits of space, however, to provide backwards compatibility to QGIC1.

### Setting an interrupt detection (level vs. edge)

All interrupts that the QGIC2 receives on external ports are active high, but it can be configured to physically detect an interrupt using either level or edge detection, which is configured via the interrupt configuration register (`APCS_GICD_ICFGRn`):

*   **Level detection**: This is the default (on reset) mode. This option should be used when the peripheral providing the interrupt asserts its interrupt line to the QGIC2 and keeps it asserted until software writes to that peripheral to clear the interrupt. In this detection mode, the QGIC2 considers the interrupt to be pending as long as the peripheral keeps its interrupt line asserted. Deassertion clears the pending state.
*   **Edge detection**: This option is used for a peripheral that sends a pulse on its interrupt line. In this detection mode, the QGIC2 watches for the rising edge of a pulse and notes that edge as a signal that the interrupt should be set pending. After the pulse has passed, the interrupt remains pending in the QGIC2. Additional assertions are ignored as long as the interrupt is in some way already pending.

> [!NOTE]
> For information about the type of each interrupt that is mapped to QGIC inputs, see the Interrupt Mapping chapter. It is recommended that SPI inputs are configured accordingly, otherwise errors may occur.

Two bits are used per interrupt. The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to register and bits, where $n$ is the absolute interrupt number, $r$ is the register number, and $b$ is the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 16$$

$$b = (n \text{ MOD } 16) \times 2$$

Because each interrupt consumes two bits, bits $b+1$ through $b$ should be modified.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is read-modify-write, so existing data should be preserved except for the bits that are being modified.

For example, if SPI #45 (absolute number 77) needs to be set to edge detection, the write should be directed to the `APCS_GICD_ICFGRn` register number 4, and bits [27:26] should be set to 11, bitwise.

> [!NOTE]
> The interrupt detection setting does not apply to SGI interrupts, and attempting to change the `APCS_GICD_ICFGRn` register values for SGI interrupts has no effect. SGI interrupts are always assumed to be edge detections because they are triggered by AHB writes.
<!-- page 3083 -->

### Setting an interrupt security/grouping

Interrupts can be assigned to a security level/group by secure software. This is accomplished via the `APCS_GICD_ISRn` register.

This setting takes only 1 bit per interrupt. The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to register and bits, where $n$ is the absolute interrupt number, $r$ is the register number, and $b$ is the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 32$$

$$b = n \text{ MOD } 32$$

To make a certain interrupt nonsecure or part of group 1, write 1 to bit position $b$ in `APCS_GICD_ISRn` register number $r$.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is read-modify-write, so existing data should be preserved, except for the bits that are being modified.

Note the following when assigning security/grouping to interrupts:

*   Regardless of the enable set in the `APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn` register for any given interrupt, if the enable bit for that interrupt security level/group is not set to `0x1` in the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` register, that interrupt is effectively disabled. Thus, if only the group 0 (secure) enable bit is set to `0x1` in the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` register and an interrupt is made group 1 (nonsecure) via the `APCS_GICD_ISRn` register, that interrupt is now disabled. The `APCS_GICD_CTLR` and `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register settings should be checked so that the QGIC2 is configured to allow the security levels that are planned for use.
*   In security-aware system, a nonsecure master cannot change the settings of secure interrupts. A nonsecure master can only change the settings for nonsecure interrupts. Furthermore, only a secure master can assign security via a write to the `APCS_GICD_ISRn` register. A nonsecure master cannot change this setting. As such, caution should be taken, as this register affects interrupt setting accessibility for bus masters.

### Changing an interrupt pending status in software

When software tries to check or change the pending status of an interrupt without relying upon a physical assertion, the QGIC2 exposes this through a command/status register pair:

*   Interrupt set-pending register (`APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn`)
*   Interrupt clear-pending register (`APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn`)

These registers use just one bit per interrupt. The following equations identify the mapping of interrupt numbers to register and bits, where $n$ is the absolute interrupt number, $r$ is the register number, and $b$ is the bit number. DIV and MOD are integer division and modulo.

$$r = n \text{ DIV } 32$$

$$b = n \text{ MOD } 32$$
<!-- page 3084 -->

To set a certain interrupt pending, write 1 to bit position $b$ in `APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn` register number $r$. To clear interrupt pending status, write 1 to bit position $b$ in `APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn` register number $r$.

The current PENDING status of the interrupt may be obtained by reading bit position $b$ of register $r$ for either `APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn` or `APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn`. Both return the same information, with a value of 1 meaning pending.

Note the following precautions with these registers:

*   Interrupt security affects these registers. A secure read of these registers returns the pending status for all interrupts, and writing either register securely can affect any interrupt. However, a non-secure read of this register returns status information only for Group 1 interrupts. Similarly, a nonsecure write can only affect the pending status of Group 1 interrupts.
*   Interrupts change state even if they are not enabled, and an interrupt set pending in software can only be cleared from that state by either an interrupt acknowledge event or by a write to the `APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn` register.
*   These registers return the pending status for SGIs, but they may not be used to change the pending status of an SGI. For that, the `APCS_GICD_SPENDSGIRn` and `APCS_GICD_CPENDSGIRn` registers must be used.

#### 8.5.2.5.4 Software interaction scenarios

This section covers scenarios in which software may need to interact with the QGIC2 to handle an interrupt. This section assumes that an interrupt has been configured using the instructions in the preceding section.

This section also includes important operational notes about software interaction with the QGIC2. As such, it should be read along with the preceding sections.

Despite variations here, however, all examples are still variations of the basic flow discussed in Section Interrupt Flow.

##### Handling a secure edge SPI

This scenario assumes that the QGIC2 has been configured for full security support (registers `APCS_GICD_CTLR` and `APCS_GICC_CTLR` both set to enable both security levels). For this scenario, it is assumed that secure destination is set to `0x0` to cause group 0 (secure) interrupts to assert on the IRQ line, and that acknowledgement control is also set to `0x0`, so secure software cannot acknowledge a group 1 (nonsecure) interrupt.

The SPI used is SPI #23 (absolute number 55), enabled, set to group 0, a priority of `0x18`, and targeted to CPU0.

The scenario begins with the current running thread being a nonsecure guest program.

1.  Edge SPI interrupt #23 arrives at QGIC2. The QGIC2 detects the rising edge and changes interrupt state to pending in the distributor.
2.  SPI interrupt #23 is compared with other pending interrupts and, assuming there are no interrupts of higher priority, is then presented to the CPU interface based on its priority.
<!-- page 3085 -->

3.  The CPU interface passes the interrupt through to the host CPU controller on the IRQ line (not FIQ because secure destination is 0).
4.  The ARM controller receives the interrupt and traps to the IRQ handler address. The interrupt service routine (ISR) takes over.
5.  Control was still held by nonsecure software, so nonsecure software attempts to acknowledge that it has received the interrupt by reading the interrupt acknowledge register.
6.  However, because the interrupt was secure, nonsecure software is not allowed to acknowledge the interrupt, and a special value of `0x3FF` (called spurious, meaning the assertion of the IRQ line was valid but the interrupt that caused it has ceased to be pending or cannot be acknowledged) is returned. The IRQ line remains asserted.
7.  The ISR exits, because `0x3FF` is not a valid interrupt number and cannot be handled. The IRQ line remains asserted, however. The OS scheduler, in the meantime, begins execution of a secure thread.
8.  The IRQ causes another trap and another jump to the ISR, but this time the software is secure and the `APCS_GICC_IAR` read succeeds.

    The `APCS_GICC_IAR` read has three effects, two of which have previously been discussed.
9.  The interrupt is set to active in the distributor. As such, the interrupt is no longer under consideration for assertion to the processor. The IRQ line de-asserts.
10. A read to the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register returns an ID uniquely identifying this interrupt to software. The ID returned is always the absolute number of the interrupt.
11. The CPU interface notes the priority level of the interrupt that was acknowledged. That interrupt priority level is now considered active, and any interrupt that arrives at the CPU interface while that level is active is blocked if its priority is less than or equal to the active level. This is to prevent preemption – that is, re-assertion of the IRQ line while software is already handling an interrupt – by interrupts that are not of higher priority than the interrupt being handled.

    > [!NOTE]
    > This tracking is per CPU interface, so all priority levels could still assert on other CPU interfaces. The intent is only to prevent preemption by lower or equal priorities on the CPU controller that is currently processing an interrupt.

12. Software handles the interrupt.
13. When complete, software must notify the QGIC2 that it has finished handling the interrupt. As such, it writes the ID of the interrupt – its absolute interrupt number – back to the QGIC2 via the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register. The ID is the value that was returned on the original `APCS_GICC_IAR` read, so the read value may simply be written back. Writing the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register performs two functions.
14. The active state is cleared from the distributor. If the interrupt was in the active state, it becomes INACTIVE and is ready for use again. If the interrupt was active & pending due to receiving another signal while active, it becomes pending and is immediately valid for assertion to a CPU controller.
15. The highest priority level marked active in the CPU interface is cleared. This clear is called a priority drop. Because only higher priority interrupts can cause preemption, which causes
<!-- page 3086 -->

    another `APCS_GICC_IAR` read, the highest priority level marked active should be the last priority level acknowledged. As such, it is critical that software writes interrupt IDs to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register in the inverse order from which interrupts were received. So if interrupts 1, 2, and 3 are received and acknowledged, each preempting with higher priority than the last, the order of writes to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register should be 3, 2, and 1 as processing completes.

##### Handling a nonsecure level PPI

The process for handling this interrupt is slightly different, but the assumption for setup of the QGIC2 is the same as the last scenario.

The interrupt used is PPI #3 (absolute number 19), enabled, set to group 1, and a priority of `0x20`. Targeting is not needed, since PPIs are banked per CPU controller and always targeted at the controller for which they are banked.

1.  Level PPI #3 arrives at the QGIC2 and remains asserted, since the peripheral holds the line high until it is cleared. The QGIC2 notes the change in state and the interrupt becomes pending.
2.  PPI #3 is compared with other pending interrupts and, assuming there are no interrupts of higher priority, is then presented to the CPU interface based on its priority.
3.  The CPU interface passes the interrupt through to the host CPU controller on the IRQ line (never FIQ regardless of setting, since this interrupt is group 1).
4.  The ARM controller receives the interrupt and traps to the IRQ handler address. The interrupt service routine takes over.
5.  The interrupt service routine attempts to acknowledge the interrupt by reading the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register, but secure software currently has control. With acknowledgement control set to 0 in the QGIC2, secure software cannot acknowledge a group 1 interrupt, and so the QGIC2 returns a value of `0x3FE`, a special code that indicates to secure software that the highest priority interrupt is nonsecure.
6.  Secure software has been notified that the highest priority interrupt is nonsecure, so control is returned to the main execution thread until nonsecure software regains system control. At this point, nonsecure software can then read the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register to acknowledge the interrupt.
7.  The QGIC2 returns the ID (absolute number) of the interrupt, which is 19, sets it active in the distributor, and marks its priority level active in the CPU interface.

    > [!NOTE]
    > Non secure and secure priority levels are tracked separately in the CPU interface so that non secure software cannot affect the tracking of secure interrupts. Because the interrupt line is still asserted to the QGIC2, the interrupt actually becomes active & pending.

8.  Because this interrupt is a level type, software is now responsible for writing to the signaling peripheral to clear the interrupt from that peripheral. The interrupt line to the QGIC2 is then de-asserted, and the interrupt is active in the distributor.
9.  Software completes handling the interrupt.
<!-- page 3087 -->

10. Software then declares that it is finished to the QGIC2 by writing the interrupt ID of 19 to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register. The ID is the value that was returned on the original `APCS_GICC_IAR` read, so the read value may simply be written back. The QGIC2 marks the interrupt inactive in the distributor and the priority drop is performed, clearing the highest active priority level from the CPU interface.

##### Handling an SGI interrupt

This scenario assumes the same setup as the past two scenarios. This scenario additionally assumes a dual-core host CPU. The configuration of the CPU interface that sends the SGI interrupt does not matter for this scenario, only for the CPU interface that receives the interrupt.

The SGI used is SGI #6, absolute number 6, set to secure, priority `0x40`.

This case is not used to address matters of security handling, so it is assumed that both the interrupt and software are secure. The intent is to focus on handling SGI interrupts.

1.  CPU1 wishes to signal a software interrupt to CPU0, so it performs an AHB write to the software generated interrupt register (`APCS_GICD_SGIR`) to trigger the interrupt. A single write always triggers a single SGI interrupt number, though it can be triggered for the SGIs banked for more than one core. For example, a write from CPU1 to trigger SGI #6 could target that interrupt for itself (CPU1) or for CPU0 or for both. This is because SGI interrupts all share the same numbers (range 0-15), but are banked per core.
2.  The distributor receives the write and sets SGI #6 to pending, noting the CPU controller that made the request.
3.  SGI #6 is compared with other pending interrupts and is then presented to the CPU interface based on its priority.
4.  The CPU interface passes the interrupt through to the host CPU controller.

    > [!NOTE]
    > IRQ/FIQ is not discussed in this scenario, but the same rules apply as did in the past two examples.

5.  The A53 controller receives the interrupt and traps to the handler address. The interrupt service routine takes over.
6.  Software acknowledges the interrupt by reading the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register. As before, the interrupt is marked active in the distributor and the priority level of the interrupt is marked active in the CPU interface. The exception is, if it is pending from another core, in which case it becomes active & pending.

    SGIs differ from other interrupts in the following ways:
    *   SGI interrupts are tracked for each core from which they can be set, and acknowledging the interrupt only clears the request from one CPU controller. For example, if CPU0, CPU2, and CPU3 all send SGI #3 to CPU1, then CPU1 has SGI #3 pending from all three controllers. When software acknowledges the interrupt, the QGIC2 clears only one of those requests, and it does so in a fair round robin fashion. Thus, in this example, the request from CPU0 is cleared and returned (which is described in the following bullet) while the requests from CPU2 and CPU3 remain pending.
<!-- page 3088 -->

    *   As mentioned above, the controller where the request originated is returned on an `APCS_GICC_IAR` read along with the interrupt ID. An `APCS_GICC_IAR` read to CPU interface 0 for a request from CPU1 returns the interrupt ID in bits [9:0] of the result, but bits [12:10] are intentionally set to `0x1` to indicate that the request came from CPU1.
7.  Software now handles the interrupt.
8.  When handling has completed, software must signal the completion to the QGIC2 by writing the interrupt ID to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register. However, since this is an SGI, the write must be modified slightly. Bits [9:0] should still be the ID of the interrupt, but bits [12:10] of the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` write should contain the core number that was returned in bits [12:10] of the original `APCS_GICC_IAR` read. As always, the write to `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register should be the contents of the original read from the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register.

The QGIC2 performs the priority drop, clearing the highest active priority level from the CPU interface. It marks the interrupt inactive in the distributor only if it is not pending from any other core.

##### Scheduled interrupt handler: Use of split EOI

In cases of a scheduled operating system, interrupts may need to be scheduled for handling like any other thread. In the case that a thread is already running, an interrupt causes a trap to an exception handler, but the operating system simply acknowledges the interrupt by an `APCS_GICC_IAR` read, stores the ID, schedules the ID for later handling as another thread, and then writes the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register to signal the completion of processing at the QGIC2.

The problem with this method is that, especially for a level type, the interrupt may become pending again after the OS writes the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register. Yet, handling has only been scheduled and has not yet occurred, so the interrupt really should not re-occur until after it has been handled.

The QGIC2 introduces a method called split EOI created by ARM to handle this scenario without needing to disable the interrupt.

Split EOI separates the end of interrupt process into two steps/registers. The first step is the write to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register, and the second step is the write to the deactivate interrupt register (`APCS_GICC_DIR`).

For this scenario, all the settings for the QGIC2 are the same as the first SPI scenario in section *Handling a secure edge SPI*. The difference is that the EOI mode bits (EOIMODE and EOIMODENS) in the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register are both set high.

The SPI used is SPI #23 (absolute number 55), enabled, set to group 0, a priority of `0x18`, and targeted to CPU0.

1.  Fast forwarding, the interrupt has arrived, been routed, and signaled to the CPU, and software has acknowledged the interrupt with an `APCS_GICC_IAR` read. Nothing about these steps changes.
2.  Because this interrupt is scheduled for handling rather than handled immediately, the ID of the interrupt is added to a queue for later handling. At this point, software now writes its ID to the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register as it usually would.
<!-- page 3089 -->

3.  However, enabling split EOI mode changes the effect of the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` write. The priority drop is still performed, so the highest active priority level is cleared from the CPU interface. That is all. The interrupt is not set inactive in the distributor. It remains active or, even if it physically recurs, active & pending. It is not valid for assertion to the CPU interface again for as long as it is in some way active. Software thus does not need to disable the interrupt.
4.  Software handles the interrupt.
5.  Software now writes the interrupt ID – again, the absolute number of the interrupt, and the same value returned from the `APCS_GICC_IAR` register – to the `APCS_GICC_DIR` register. This register finally triggers the state change in the distributor and the interrupt is marked inactive (if it was active) or pending (if it was active & pending). Software has no need to re-enable the interrupt.

This process reduces the number of reads and writes necessary for scheduled handling from 4 to 3 and makes the inclusion of such scheduled handling a viable part of the QGIC2 operation.

Simply delaying the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` write until after the scheduled interrupt had been handled would not have been sufficient, and the reason is the active priority level tracking. Recall that an active priority level in the CPU interface blocks the assertion of all interrupts of lesser or equal priority. Thus, even if delaying the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` write would prevent re-assertion of the single interrupt, it would also prevent software from receiving and scheduling the handling of any interrupt of lesser or equal priority. Any software-only prioritization scheme would thus be overridden; and if software did not use hardware priority in the QGIC2 at all and left all priorities at 0, then only one interrupt would ever be scheduled at a time.

Separating the priority drop thus allows software to clear this active priority level from the CPU interface, which allows all interrupts to assert at the CPU interface again. Because the interrupt that asserted is not cleared, however, that interrupt is unable to re-assert until the final deactivation stage.

#### 8.5.2.5.5 Saving and restoring state

The QGIC2 can fully save and restore internal state. The QGIC2 CSRs allow software to read out internal state, which allows it to be saved before a power collapse and then restored once power is restored and the QGIC2 is reset.

Saving and restoring internal state is as simple as reading all applicable registers to gather state information and then, after power has been restored and the QGIC2 has been reset, writing that same data back to the registers from which it was read.

> [!NOTE]
> Only secure software can perform a full save and restore, because certain registers and state for any interrupts configured to be group 0 can only be accessed by secure software.

> [!NOTE]
> There is no means of freezing QGIC2 operation before state is saved, so software should ensure that the system is not providing any further interrupts to the QGIC2. Otherwise, a peripheral could provide an interrupt to the QGIC2 after the pending interrupt information has already been saved, resulting in the loss of that interrupt’s pending state.
<!-- page 3090 -->

The following registers should all be read and their contents saved:

*   **Distributor**
    *   `APCS_GICD_CTLR`
    *   `APCS_GICD_ISRn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_IPRIORITYRn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_ISACTIVERn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_SPENDSGIRn`, all registers, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICD_ICFGRn`, all registers, all banks
*   **CPU interface**
    *   `APCS_GICC_CTLR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICC_APR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICC_NSAPR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICC_BPR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICC_NSBPR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICC_PMR`, all banks
*   **Hypervisor block**
    *   `APCS_GICH_HCR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICH_APR`, all banks
    *   `APCS_GICH_LRn`, all registers, all banks
*   **Virtual CPU interface**
    *   None of the GICV registers need to be saved. All important bits for the GICV block are aliased into the hypervisor block in the `APCS_GICH_APR` and `APCS_GICH_VMCR` registers. This is so hypervisor software can quickly and efficiently save and restore state on this block should a virtualized guest OS be moved from one physical CPU to another.

> [!NOTE]
> If the QGIC2 virtualization features are not being used, the register contents in the hypervisor block do not need to be saved or restored.

After power has been restored and the QGIC2 has been reset, the data read from the registers listed above should be written back into the registers from which they were read. The data should not be masked before writing and data read from multiple registers and multiple banks should be written back into the register number and bank from which they were read. For instance, after reading `APCS_GICD_ICFGR1` from CPU1, the data the read returned should be written back into `APCS_GICD_ICFGR1` for CPU1 once the reset process is complete.


<!-- page 3091 -->

> [!WARNING]
> To keep the processor from being interrupted as it is restoring state, the `APCS_GICH_HCR` and `APCS_GICD_CTLR` registers can be restored last. Alternatively, interrupts can be masked in the host CPU controllers.

### 8.5.2.5.6 Use of QGIC2 virtualization features

The QGIC2 includes virtualization features that enable software to create virtual interrupts that can be provided to guest OSs or programs running in virtualization. The host OS and virtualization system run on the real, physical CPU and use the distributor and physical CPU interface. The virtualization software then configures a series of interrupts needed by the guest/virtual OS and loads those into the virtualization extensions on the QGIC2. Special virtual FIQ and virtual IRQ lines on the ARM CPU controller provide the interrupts to the virtual software and trap to special handling addresses that can be used by the guest OS to handle the interrupt.

The virtualization features are encapsulated in the hypervisor and virtual CPU blocks, each banked per CPU controller.

> [!NOTE]
> While interrupts can be set to group 0 or group 1, the virtualization blocks do not support access-based security. It is assumed that the virtualization software is always nonsecure, and so all features of the virtualization blocks must be accessible to nonsecure software. Any restrictions on access to these blocks have to be managed by page table settings in software. The virtualization blocks are aligned to 1K addresses to allow for this.

#### Virtual CPU configuration

The configuration of the virtual CPU block itself is not covered here because the setup of the block itself is identical to the setup for the physical CPU. The CSRs are identical except for the lack of banking by security, so Sections CPU interface enable and Additional configuration: Priority mask apply to this block as well. This is intentional, as the virtualization features are designed such that the software running as the guest in virtualization should not know that it is running in a virtualized environment.

#### Hypervisor block configuration and use

The hypervisor block is the core of the QGIC2 virtualization feature set. For virtualization, the virtual CPU interface replaces and imitates the physical CPU interface, and the hypervisor block replaces and imitates the distributor, though it is replicated per CPU and feeds interrupts only to its attached virtual CPU interface. However, the hypervisor block is not nearly as complex as the distributor, and is designed for explicit software control.

The intent is that the guest software running in the virtual world is still able to receive interrupts, but they must be routed by software from the physical world to the virtual world.

#### Configuring the hypervisor block

Before use, the hypervisor block must be configured via the hypervisor control register (`APCS_GICH_HCR`). At a minimum, the EN bit (bit 0) must be set high. The EOICOUNT field is not a setting, and the various interrupt enable bits within the `APCS_GICH_HCR` enable various maintenance interrupts.
<!-- page 3092 -->

Maintenance interrupts are level type interrupts asserted to the distributor on PPI #0, per core, by the hypervisor block. They serve as direct notification to software of a condition that requires intervention in the hypervisor block. The use of these interrupts is not required, but enabling each enables use of its bit in the maintenance interrupt status register (`APCS_GICH_MISR`), a useful interrupt syndrome register. The conditions these interrupts describe must still be serviced as they arrive, and detecting them without using maintenance interrupts requires keeping track of the full hypervisor state in software.

#### Routing hardware interrupts to the hypervisor block

A hardware interrupt is a PPI or SPI. The hypervisor software is responsible for acknowledging the interrupt at the CPU interface and then placing the interrupt into the hypervisor. The operation of the hypervisor software is not covered here, as it is expected that software fully drafts its own system. As such, only the details of writing an interrupt into the QGIC2 hypervisor block are covered.

Once a hardware interrupt is acknowledged at the CPU interface, software must then write the ID to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register and then place this interrupt into a list register (`APCS_GICH_LRn`) in the hypervisor block.

A software requirement is for the CPU interface to be operated in split EOI mode when using the hypervisor block. This ensures that the interrupt that has been routed to the hypervisor block does not recur at the physical CPU interface until it has been handled in the VCPU interface. Active & pending state for hardware interrupts is tracked in the distributor and not in the hypervisor block. Software should not attempt to mirror the state in the distributor by disabling split EOI and allow interrupts to reoccur at the CPU interface.

The fields within the `APCS_GICH_LRn` register breakdown as shown in Table 8-146 for hardware interrupts.

##### Table 8-146 List register description for hardware interrupts

| Field | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **HW** | Since this is a PPI or SPI, this bit should be set to `0x1`. |
| **GRP** | This is the security/group of the interrupt that is presented to the VCPU interface. As with the CPU interface, the security/group of an interrupt affects the behavior of the VCPU interface and which registers affect the interrupt. As noted previously, security of bus accesses is no longer checked, but interrupt security/grouping does still affect operation in the same way it did in the physical world. |
| **STATE** | For a new interrupt, this should always be set to pending (`0x1`). Any time an interrupt changes state in the hypervisor, this field is physically updated. This is exposed so that software can swap interrupts in and out as it has need without losing state information. |
<!-- page 3093 -->

##### Table 8-146 List register description for hardware interrupts (cont.)

| Field | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **PRI** | Just as interrupt priority is set in the distributor for each interrupt via the `APCS_GICD_IPRIORITYRn` register, so each interrupt in the hypervisor block must also be given a priority when it is placed into a list register. <br><br> *Note: The field is only five bits wide. This is because the QGIC2 only supports 32 levels of priority. It is analogous to the `APCS_GICD_IPRIORITYRn` register, wherein only bits [7:3] of each interrupt priority bit range are used. Since the hypervisor is a QGIC2-only block and no backward compatibility is required, the priority field may be sized according to the number of bits actually available.* <br><br> The hypervisor block compares all the interrupts in the `APCS_GICH_LRn` registers to one another to choose the highest priority pending interrupt just as is done in the distributor. |
| **PHY_ID** | The physical ID of the interrupt. This should be the value that was returned on bits [9:0] from the CPU interface when software acknowledged the interrupt. A feature provided by the hypervisor block for hardware interrupts – source was a PPI or SPI and hardware bit set to `0x1` in the `APCS_GICH_LRn` register – is to allow the EOIR or DIR write on the VCPU interface (that is, `APCS_GICV_EOIR` or `APCS_GICV_DIR`) to automatically propagate all the way to the distributor, which eliminates any requirement upon software to switch context and perform the DIR itself. The QGIC2 must know which interrupt should be deactivated, however, and providing the original interrupt ID in this field fulfills that requirement. |
| **VRTL_ID** | This is the ID of the interrupt that is returned when the guest software reads the interrupt acknowledge register on the VCPU interface (`APCS_GICV_IAR`). It does not have to be the same as the physical ID, and can in fact be anything software wishes it to be, as long as it is less than or equal to `0x3FC` (anything above is reserved), and as long as the ID is unique, multiple interrupts should not all share the same virtual ID. |

#### Routing software interrupts to the hypervisor block

A software interrupt is an SGI, and it comes with the additional requirement that the source CPU information be captured and maintained along with the interrupt itself. The hypervisor block also provides for this case, but use differs slightly.

The fields within the `APCS_GICH_LRn` register breakdown as shown in Table 8-147.

##### Table 8-147 List register description for software interrupts

| Field | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **HW** | Since this is an SGI, this bit should be set to `0x0`. |
| **GRP** | Unchanged from hardware interrupt usage. |
| **STATE** | Unchanged from hardware interrupt usage. |
| **PRI** | Unchanged from hardware interrupt usage. |
<!-- page 3094 -->

##### Table 8-147 List register description for software interrupts (cont.)

| Field | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **EI** | For software interrupts, the physical ID field is overloaded and is used for additional setting bits. The first is the EI bit, short for EOI interrupt. For software interrupts in the hypervisor, it is a requirement that the hypervisor software performs the final DIR of the interrupt to the CPU interface (not the VCPU Interface). The DIR is not automatically forwarded as in the case of a hardware interrupt. The EI bit determines whether or not, on final deactivation, an EOI interrupt is thrown in the hypervisor (also gated by the EI bit in the `APCS_GICH_HCR` register). Final deactivation transitions the interrupt state to INVALID (`0x0`), so the rule for EOI Interrupt assertion is `hardware==0` and `STATE==INVALID` and `EI==1`. <br><br> *Note: Since the physical ID information for this interrupt is not maintained in the hypervisor block, software is responsible for maintaining this information separately.* |
| **CPU_ID** | To preserve source CPU information for SGI interrupts, this 3-bit field is provided. It is returned in bits [12:10] of an `APCS_GICV_IAR` read to the VCPU interface, just as would an `APCS_GICC_IAR` read to the CPU Interface. |
| **VRTL_ID** | Unchanged from hardware interrupt usage. |

#### Routing more than 4 virtual interrupts

The Qualcomm implementation of the ARM GIC 2.0 specification provides 4 out of the 64 possible list registers. Therefore, it is quite easy to overflow the provided number of registers with interrupts routed to the hypervisor block. To prevent overflow, software is required to keep track of the interrupt overflow in a separate buffer. There are, however, rules for prioritizing interrupts for placement into list registers:

1. The highest priority pending interrupt should always be present in the list registers so that it may be presented to the VCPU interface. The VCPU interface then determines preemption.
2. If active or active & pending interrupts are maintained in the `APCS_GICH_LRn` registers, it should be the highest priority interrupts so that `APCS_GICV_EOIR`/`APCS_GICV_DIR` requests (that is, from the VCPU interface) affect those interrupts first. It is of prime importance for software to always maintain the highest-to-lowest priority ordering of `APCS_GICV_EOIR`/`APCS_GICV_DIR` replies.

When `APCS_GICV_EOIR`/`APCS_GICV_DIR` replies arrive (from the VCPU interface) for a virtual ID that the hypervisor software has not been able to place into a `APCS_GICH_LRn` register, the `EOICOUNT` field in the `APCS_GICH_HCR` register is provided. This field counts the number of interrupt deactivation requests (`APCS_GICV_EOIR` write when split EOI is disabled, `APCS_GICV_DIR` write when enabled) received from the VCPU interface for IDs that were not present in the `APCS_GICH_LRn` registers. Software may use this count to parse its internal buffer and manually perform the `APCS_GICC_DIR` write (that is, for CPU interface) for the highest priority buffered interrupts. Again, the `APCS_GICC_DIR` writes should proceed from highest priority to lowest, which should be the inverse order from their acknowledgment.

#### Context switching

When it becomes necessary to move data for a hypervisor block banked for one CPU to a hypervisor block banked for another CPU, move the data in the following registers:
- `APCS_GICH_HCR`
<!-- page 3095 -->

- `APCS_GICH_VMCR`
- `APCS_GICH_LRn`, all registers
- `APCS_GICH_APR`

These seven registers (this number includes the four-list registers) are all that are required for a full restoration of hypervisor and VCPU interface block state on the new target CPU controller.

#### Types of maintenance interrupts

Table 8-148 lists the maintenance interrupts that exist in the QGIC2 hypervisor block and what they mean to software. The names below use the bit field names from the maintenance interrupt status register (`APCS_GICH_MISR`), which functions as an interrupt syndrome register.

As long as the case that these interrupts describe holds true, they are asserted to PPI #0. Maintenance interrupts are always level type and remain asserted until the case is cleared or the interrupt itself is disabled. As such, software should typically enable these maintenance interrupts only when notification is required should the applicable case arise.

##### Table 8-148 List of hypervisor maintenance interrupts

| Acronym | Interrupt Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **VDNSI** | Virtual CPU disable nonsecure interrupt | If enabled, this interrupt asserts whenever the group 1 enable bit in the `APCS_GICV_CTLR` register is set low. Enabling this maintenance Interrupt in the `APCS_GICH_HCR` register allows software to receive an interrupt notifying it that the VCPU interface has disabled the receipt of group 1 interrupts. This can be useful if software has group 1 interrupts in its buffer. It can then re-enable the group 1 handling in the VCPU Interface or hold on to the group 1 interrupts until the VCPU Interface is fully re-enabled. |
| **VENSI** | Virtual CPU enable nonsecure interrupt | This interrupt is the opposite of the VDNSI. If enabled, this interrupt asserts whenever handling nonsecure interrupts is enabled in the VCPU interface. This interrupt can be used to provide notification that group 1 interrupt handling has been re-enabled on the VCPU interface. |
| **VDSI** | Virtual CPU disable secure interrupt | This is the group 0 version of the VDNSI interrupt. |
| **VESI** | Virtual CPU enable secure interrupt | This is the group 0 version of the VENSI bit. |
| **NPI** | No-pending interrupt | This interrupt asserts whenever there is no pending interrupt present in any of the list registers. This interrupt is used to notify software that all existing pending interrupts in the list registers have been acknowledged or cleared and it should swap out one of the interrupts in the list registers for any of the pending interrupts in its buffer; recall that software should always keep the highest priority pending interrupt in a list register instead of buffering it. This is so that the VCPU interface may properly determine preemption. |
<!-- page 3096 -->

##### Table 8-148 List of hypervisor maintenance interrupts (cont.)

| Acronym | Interrupt Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SKIDI** | Skid interrupt | Recall that the `EOICOUNT` field in the `APCS_GICH_HCR` register is used to count the deactivation requests (EOIR write when split EOI is disabled, DIR write when enabled) directed to IDs that do not exist in a list register. If enabled, this interrupt asserts whenever the `EOICOUNT` is nonzero to alert software that there are interrupts in its buffer for which it should manually perform a DIR write to the CPU interface. |
| **EI** | EOI interrupt | This interrupt asserts whenever a software (`HW==0`) interrupt in a list register has been fully handled (state returns to INVALID) and its EI bit is set high. This alerts software that a software type interrupt has completed processing and needs to be fully retired with a DIR write to the CPU interface. Software may determine exactly which list register holds the interrupt that is asserting the EOI Interrupt by reading the EOI interrupt status register (`APCS_GICH_HCR`). |

### 8.5.2.5.7 Debugging aids

This section answers some frequently asked questions about debugging the operation of the QGIC2 in software. A common scenario is an interrupt that asserts but QGIC2 does not provide an IRQ. In this case, things to try are as follows:

1. Ensure that the enable bits in the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` and `APCS_GICC_CTLR` registers are both set to `0x1`.
2. Ensure that the priority mask of the CPU interface is nonzero.
3. Ensure that any preceding interrupts were successfully completed with a write to the `APCS_GICC_EOIR` register. If split EOI is enabled and the same interrupt is failing to re-assert, ensure that a write to the `APCS_GICC_DIR` register was also performed.
4. Ensure that the detection type of the interrupt is correct. A level type provides a rising edge when it asserts, so a level type may be detected as edge, although this is risky. An edge type set to level detection, however, is lost.
5. Ensure that the security of the interrupt in the `APCS_GICD_ISRn` register is as expected and that the enable bits for that security level/group are set in the `APCS_GICD_CTLR` and `APCS_GICC_CTLR` registers.
6. Ensure that the priority of the interrupt is not set to `0xF8`, as this priority level never asserts. This is the maximum value of the priority mask in the CPU interface, so setting an interrupt priority to `0xF8` causes it to be masked even if the CPU interface mask is set as high as possible.
7. If it is an SPI, ensure that it is targeted via the `APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn` register.
8. Ensure that the correct registers were set by referring to Section *Enumeration of interrupts: Absolute vs. relative*, and then referring to the equations provided in Section *Setting up an interrupt*.
<!-- page 3097 -->

| `APCS_GICV_APR` | RW | `0x40D0` | `0x0B0040D0` |
| `APCS_GICV_IIDR` | R | `0x40FC` | `0x0B0040FC` |
| `APCS_GICV_DIR` | W | `0x5000` | `0x0B005000` |

### 8.5.2.6.3 QGIC2 distributor register definitions

#### 0x0 APCS_GICD_CTLR

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
- **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
- **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register controls if the distributor responds to external interrupt stimulus changes.

- **Nonsecure access:** Distributor provides access to the `ENABLE_NS` bit.
- **Secure access:** Distributor provides access to both the `ENABLE` and `ENABLE_NS` bits.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **ENABLE_NS** | This bit is an alias of the `enable_ns` bit. This bit is only usable by Secure software.<br> `0x0`: CLR<br> `0x1`: SET |
| 0 | **ENABLE** | This bit is the enable bit for both Secure and Nonsecure software. Secure software accesses `enable_s` at this location. Nonsecure software accesses `enable_ns`.<br> `0x0`: CLR<br> `0x1`: SET |
<!-- page 3100 -->

#### 0x4 APCS_GICD_TYPER

- **Type:** R
- **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
- **Reset State:** Undefined
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register provides information about the configuration of the QGIC2.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:11 | **LSPI** | Returns the number of lockable shared peripheral interrupts (LSPIs) that the QGIC2 contains.<br> *Note: QGIC2 does not support lockable SPIs, always reads back `0x0`.* |
| 10 | **TZ** | TrustZone support.<br> QGIC2 supports TrustZone, always reads back `0x1`. |
| 9:8 | **RESERVED_BITS9_TO_8** | |
| 7:5 | **CPU_NUM** | Returns the number of CPU interfaces that QGIC2 provides. QGIC2 provides either:<br> `0x0`: One CPU interface<br> `0x1`: Two CPU interfaces<br> `0x2`: Three CPU interfaces<br> `0x3`: Four CPU interfaces<br> `0x4`: Five CPU interfaces<br> `0x5`: Six CPU interfaces<br> `0x6`: Seven CPU interfaces<br> `0x7`: Eight CPU interfaces<br> *Note: QGIC2 supports four CPU interfaces, always reads back `0x3`.* |
| 4:0 | **IT_LINES** | Returns the number of INTIDs, to the nearest 32, that the distributor provides. Read as:<br> `0x0`: The distributor is configured for up to 32 INTIDs<br> `0x1`: The distributor is configured for up to 64 INTIDs<br> `0x2`: The distributor is configured for up to 96 INTIDs<br> `0x3`: The distributor is configured for up to 128 INTIDs<br> `0x7`: The distributor is configured for up to 256 INTIDs<br> `0x1E`: The distributor is configured for up to 992 INTIDs<br> `0x1F`: The distributor is configured for up to 1020 INTIDs<br> *Note: QGIC2 supports up to 256 INTIDs, always reads back `0x7`.* |




<!-- page 3101 -->

### 0x8 APCS_GICD_IIDR

* **Type**: R
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00001070
* **Security Treatment**: Common

This register provides the implementor of the distributor and the revision of the distributor.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:12 | REVISION | Returns the revision number of the distributor, 0x1 |
| 11:0 | IMPLEMENTOR | Returns Qualcomm JEP106 ID number, 0x70 |

### 0x20 APCS_GICD_ANSACR

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: Restricted

This is the auxiliary nonsecure access control register. It is used to control nonsecure access to the APCS_GICD_CGCR register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | GICD_CGCR | 0x0: SEC (Disallows nonsecure access)<br>0x1: NS (Allows nonsecure access) |

### 0x24 APCS_GICD_CGCR

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: Restricted

This is the clock gate control register. It is used to control localized clock gating override logic. Setting bits in this register disables the corresponding local clock gating logic. The local clock gating logic normally turns off a local (small subset) clock tree automatically if there is no need for the clock. If any error is found in the gating logic, these bits can be used to override it.
<!-- page 3102 -->

### APCS_GICD_CGCR (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:17 | RESERVED_31_TO_17 | |
| 16 | TOP | Controls the top-level clock gate (which gates entire QGIC2).<br>0x0: ENABLE<br>0x1: DISABLE |
| 15:4 | RESERVED_15_TO_4 | |
| 3 | DI_SGI_STATE | Controls the clock gate for Distributor interrupt state database registers for SGI interrupts.<br>0x0: ENABLE<br>0x1: DISABLE |
| 2 | DI_PPI_SPI_STATE | Controls the clock gate for distributor interrupt state database registers for PPI and SPI interrupts.<br>0x0: ENABLE<br>0x1: DISABLE |
| 1 | DI_DEMET | Controls the clock gate for distributor interrupt input demet registers.<br>0x0: ENABLE<br>0x1: DISABLE |
| 0 | DI_RD | Controls the clock gate for distributor CRIF read data.<br>0x0: ENABLE<br>0x1: DISABLE |

### 0x30 APCS_GICD_HW_VERSION

* **Type**: R
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x20000000
* **Security Treatment**: Restricted

Read-only register specifying unique hardware version for recognition by Qualcomm software.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | MAJOR | Indicates unique software interface lacking backward compatibility. Hard coded to [31:28] = 0x2, indicating QGIC2. |
| 27:16 | MINOR | Minor changes to design that add new features or updates but, which do not, break software compatibility. Hard coded to [27:16] = 0x0, indicating current minor revision 0. |
| 15:0 | STEP | A hardware change, which has no impact on software. Hard coded to [15:0] = 0x0, indicating stepping 0. |
<!-- page 3103 -->

### 0x80+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ISRn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: Restricted

Each bit in this register controls the security state of an interrupt, to be either secure or nonsecure. You can only access these registers with secure read or secure write accesses.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ISR0 register (at address offset 0x0080) is banked, that is there is one per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and controls that CPU's PPI and SGI interrupts. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT_NS | 0x0: SEC (Assigns INTID N to the secure state)<br>0x1: NS (Assigns INTID N to the non-secure state) |

### 0x100+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependant

Each bit in an APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn register controls the enabling of an interrupt.

Reading this register returns the currently enabled interrupts subject to NS-int dependant access rules.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ISENABLER0 register (at address offset 0x0100) is banked, that is, there is one per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and controls that CPU's PPI and SGI interrupts. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT | 0x0: N/A (No effect. Use the APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn register.)<br>0x1: SET (Enables INTID N.) |
<!-- page 3104 -->

### 0x180+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependant

Each bit in an APCS_GICD_ICENABLERn register controls the disabling of an interrupt.

Reading this register returns the currently enabled interrupts subject to NS-int dependant access rules.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ICENABLER0 register (at address offset 0x0180) is banked, that is there is one per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and controls that CPU's PPI and SGI interrupts. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT | 0x0: N/A (No effect. Use the APCS_GICD_ISENABLERn register.)<br>0x1: CLR (Disables INTID N.) |

### 0x200+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependent

Each bit in an APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn register provides the pending status of an interrupt. Writing a 1 to any of these bits transition the corresponding interrupt to the pending (or active & pending) state.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ISPENDR0 register (at address offset 0x0200) is repeated once per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and controls that CPU's PPI interrupts. SGI interrupt bits are read-only, however the distributor updates these using the APCS_GICD_SGIR register. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT | 0x0: NA (No effect. Use the APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn register.)<br>0x1: SET (Sets INTID N to the pending state.) |
<!-- page 3105 -->

### 0x280+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependant

Each bit in an APCS_GICD_ICPENDRn register provides the pending status of an interrupt. Writing a 1 to any of these bits transition the corresponding interrupt out of the pending (or active & pending) state.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ICPENDR0 register at (address offset 0x0280) is banked, that is there is one per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and controls that CPU's PPI interrupts. SGI interrupt bits are read-only, however the distributor updates these using the APCS_GICD_SGIR register. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT | 0x0: NA (No effect. Use the APCS_GICD_ISPENDRn register.)<br>0x1: CLR (Clears INTID N from the pending state.) |

### 0x300+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ISACTIVERn, n=[0..8]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependant

Each bit in an APCS_GICD_ISACTIVERn register provides the active status of an interrupt. Writing a 1 to any of these bits transition the corresponding interrupt to the active (or active & pending) state.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ISACTIVER0 register (at address offset 0x0300) is repeated once per CPU interface. It is only accessible from the designated CPU and provides information for that CPU's PPI and SGI interrupts. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | INT | 0x0: DO_NOTHING<br>0x1: SET |
<!-- page 3107 -->

### APCS_GICD_IPRIORITYRn (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:11 | INT1 | |
| 7:3 | INT0 | All bits cleared (0x0) is the highest priority. All bits set (0x1F) is the lowest priority. <br><br>For nonsecure write access, the MSB is always set (1). For nonsecure read access, the MSB is always clear (0). Nonsecure entities cannot use the highest priorities without secure software setting such a priority. The highest priorities are typically reserved for secure software. <br><br>On the other hand, secure software can, if needed, write and read the MSB. Secure entities have access to all priorities. Secure interrupts can use priority numbers 0x10-0x1F (the lower half of the priority spectrum) if needed. <br><br>Due to strict 'less than' comparisons used in the CPU interface, setting an interrupt's priority to 0x1F effectively disables that interrupt. <br><br>The number of priorities actually supported is 32. Software can determine this number by writing 0xFF and reading back the result. |

### 0x800+0x4*n APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn, n=[0..71]

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: NS-int dependant

Each field in an APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn register controls the destination CPUs of an interrupt.

> [!NOTE]
> The APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn registers at address offsets 0x0800 to 0x81C are not actually implemented. These are place holders for PPI and SGI interrupts. PPI interrupts, being private, only have one destination CPU. SGI interrupts are generated by APCS_GICD_SGIR register only and do not need APCS_GICD_ITARGETSRn register. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupt destinations.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is byte addressable.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | INT3 | |
| 23:16 | INT2 | |
| 15:8 | INT1 | |
| 7:0 | INT0 | Each bit represents one of eight CPUs. Bit 0 represents CPU0, bit 7 represents the CPU7. Setting this field to 0x0 disables the interrupt as no CPU sees it set. <br><br>For INTIDs < 32 (the SGI and PPI), reads return the bit corresponding to the CPU performing the read (that is, CPU0 reads back 0x01010101). Writes are ignored. <br><br>The number of CPUs actually supported is determined by NUM_CPU generic. Software can determine this number by writing 0xFF and reading back the result. |
<!-- page 3108 -->

Each field in the APCS_GICD_ICFGRn registers allows:

These are only accessible from the designated CPU and allow read access for that CPU's PPI and SGI interrupts. The remaining registers control the SPI interrupts. PPI #0 is the maintenance interrupt and must be configured as level type. This register is not byte addressable, interrupts should be disabled before configuring their type.
