### APCS_GICD_ICFGRn (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3:2 | INT1 | |
| 1:0 | INT0 | 0x0: LVL_N_TO_N<br>0x1: LVL_1_TO_N<br>0x2: EDGE_N_TO_N<br>0x3: EDGE_1_TO_N<br><br>These bits behave differently for each of the three-interrupt types as follows:<br>- For SGI, read back as 0x2 – SGI interrupts are edge-sensitive and use the N-N model.<br>- For PPI/SPI, read/writable as 0x1 or 0x3 – PPI/SPI interrupts can be edge or level sensitive and use the 1-N model. |

### 0xF00 APCS_GICD_SGIR

* **Type**: W
* **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State**: 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment**: Banked

This register provides the method by which software may cause interrupts to become pending for designated target CPUs. The QGIC2 maintains an internal database of all outstanding software interrupt requests pended to each CPU interface and rotates through them in round robin fashion. Signaling the same interrupt a second time before it is serviced result in only one interrupt from the source CPU to one or more target CPUs.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:26 | RESERVED_BITS31_TO_26 | |
| 25:24 | T_FILTER | Target filter<br>0x0: LIST (Use the T_LIST as is)<br>0x1: OTHERS (Send to all CPUs accept the CPU MID making the request, ignoring T_LIST)<br>0x2: MID (Send to only the CPU MID making the request, ignoring T_LIST)<br>0x3: N/A (Reserved) |
| 23:16 | T_LIST | Target list. Each bit set represents a CPU target for the INT_ID, subject to the T_FILTER field.<br>0x1: CPU0<br>0x2: CPU1<br>0x4: CPU2<br>0x8: CPU3<br>0x10: CPU4<br>0x20: CPU5<br>0x40: CPU6<br>0x80: CPU7 |
<!-- page 3110 -->

### APCS_GICD_SGIR (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15 | SATT | Security attribute. This bit is only programmable by secure software<br>0x0: SECURE (Secure interrupt is issued)<br>0x1: NONSECURE (Nonsecure interrupt is issued) |
| 14:4 | RESERVED_BITS14_TO_4 | |
| 3:0 | INT_ID | The INT ID number (0-15) of the SGI to be set as pending. |

## 8.5.2.6.4 QGIC2 hypervisor interface register definitions

### 0x1000 APCS_GICH_HCR

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register configures the QGIC2 hypervisor interface.

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 31:27 | EOICOUNT | Counts the number of EOIs, which have been received without a corresponding entry being found among the list registers. Incremented automatically by the CPU interface when such an EOI is received. EOIs, which do not clear a bit in the active priorities, register do not cause an increment. The maintenance interrupt is asserted whenever this field is nonzero and the SKIDIE bit is set (see below). |
| 7 | VDG1IE | If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever the ENABLE_ G1 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register is cleared.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 6 | VEG1IE | If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever the ENABLE_ G1 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register is set.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 5 | VDG0IE | If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever the ENABLE_ G0 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register is cleared.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 4 | VEG0IE | If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever the ENABLE_ G0 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register is set.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 3 | NPIE | No pending interrupt maintenance interrupt enable. If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever no list registers contain an interrupt in pending state.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 2 | SKIDIE | SKID maintenance interrupt enable. If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever the EOICOUNT bit in the APCS_GICH_HCR register is nonzero.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
<!-- page 3116 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | UIE | Underflow maintenance interrupt enable. If this bit is set, the maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever zero or one of the list entries are marked as valid.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 0 | EN | Enable or disable maintenance and by proxy virtual CPU interface interrupts.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |

### 0x1004 APCS_GICH_VTR

- **Type:** R
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x90000003
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register provides information about the configuration of the hypervisor interface (virtual QGIC2 type register).

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 31:29 | PRIBITS | Indicates the number of priority bits implemented, minus one. For this version of the specification the only acceptable value is 0x5, indicating 5 bits of priority (32 levels) |
| 28:26 | PREBITS | Indicates the number of preemption bits implemented, minus one. For this version of the specification the only acceptable value is 0x5, indicating 5 bits of preemption (32 levels) |
| 5:0 | LISTREGS | Indicates the number of implemented list registers, minus one. QGIC2 has 4 list registers. This is set to 0x3. |

### 0x1008 APCS_GICH_VMCR

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x004C0000
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register contains read/write aliases of all the virtual machine accessible state (aliases from the APCS_GICV_* registers). This alias allows the hypervisor to easily save and restore this state with a single read or write, and without needing to map in the virtual machine registers.

> [!NOTE]
> Various bits of this register include the terms group 0 (G0) or group 1 (G1) in their names. This is purely for compatibility with the physical QGIC2 interface and does not pertain to actual TrustZone security.
<!-- page 3117 -->

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 31:27 | VMPMR | Alias of the LEVEL bit field in the APCS_GICV_PMR register. |
| 23:21 | VMG0BP | Alias of the VAL bit field in the APCS_GICV_BPR register. |
| 20:18 | VMG1BP | Alias of the VAL bit field in the APCS_GICV_ABPR register. |
| 9 | VEM | Alias of the EOIMODE bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |
| 4 | VMGBPR | Alias of the GBPR bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |
| 3 | VMFIQEN | Alias of the FIQEN bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |
| 2 | VMACKCTL | Alias of the ACKCTL bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |
| 1 | VMENABLE_G1 | Alias of the ENABLE_G1 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |
| 0 | VMENABLE_G0 | Alias of the ENABLE_G0 bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register. |

### 0x1010 APCS_GICH_MISR

- **Type:** R
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register is the maintenance interrupt syndrome register in the hypervisor interface. This register indicates which maintenance interrupts are currently asserted. This takes into account the individual maintenance interrupt enable bits in the APCS_GICH_HCR register. However, the global enable in APCS_GICH_HCR(EN) is not factored in to these bits. Therefore, the maintenance interrupt is asserted if and only if at least one bit is set in this register and the EN bit in APCS_GICH_HCR is set.

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | VDNSI | |
| 6 | VENSI | |
| 5 | VDSI | |
| 4 | VESI | |
| 3 | NPI | |
| 2 | SKIDI | |
| 1 | UI | |
| 0 | EI | |

- **Security Treatment:** Common

| Bits | Name | Description |

| 3:0 | LR | 0x0: NOT_EOI<br>0x1: EOI |

This register provides information about the priorities currently active in the hypervisor interface.

| Bits | Name | Description |

| 31:0 | PRI | 0x0: INACTIVE<br>0x1: ACTIVE |
<!-- page 3119 -->

### 0x1100+0x4*n APCS_GICH_LRn, n=[0..3]

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000
- **Security Treatment:** Common

The APCS_GICH_LRn provides access to each of the list registers in the hypervisor interface.

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 31 | HW | Indicates that this is a hardware interrupt. When this bit is set, bits [19:10] contain the physical interrupt number, and when this interrupt is subject to an EOI request, a deactivate interrupt request will be sent to the interrupt distributor. |
| 30 | GRP | Indicates that this interrupt should be treated as group 1. This means that the interrupt presents as an IRQ if the ENABLEG1bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register is set.<br>If the GRP bit is clear, the interrupt is put into group 0 and present as either IRQ or FIQ depending on the setting of the FIQEN bit in the APCS_GICV_CTLR register but only if the ENABLEG0 bit in the same register is also set.<br>This bit is also used with the CBPR bit in APCS_GICV_CTLR to determine which binary point register is used in GICV for preemption calculations. |
| 29:28 | STATE | 0x0: IDL (Invalid)<br>0x1: PNA (Pending, not active)<br>0x2: A (Active)<br>0x3: PA (Active & pending)<br>Note: for hardware interrupts, the active & pending state is held in the physical distributor rather than the VCPU interface. The active & pending state (0x3) should only be used for software originated interrupts (virtual devices) or SGIs. |
| 27:23 | PRI | Indicates the priority of this interrupt. This is converted to a traditional 8-bit QGIC priority value by appending three zero bits. |
| 19:10 | PHY_ID | The physical ID of the interrupt.<br>When the hardware bit is set this field indicates the physical interrupt ID, which is forwarded to the distributor when this interrupt is subject to an EOI request.<br>If the physical ID is between 16 and 31 inclusive (PPI space), the deactivation applies to the PPI associated with the same physical CPU as the VCPU interface making the request.<br>If the physical ID is between 0 and 15 inclusive (SGI space), the deactivation will still apply to SGI associated with the same physical CPU as the VCPU interface making the request but it is expected that the hardware bit and physical ID will not be used for SGIs. |
| 9:0 | VIRTL_ID | Indicates the virtual ID. This ID is returned to the guest OS when this interrupt is acknowledged via the APCS_GICV_IAR register. |
<!-- page 3120 -->

### 0x1120 APCS_GICH_SW_LR

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000
- **Security Treatment:** Common

This register is not a real physical register or address in the design. It is placed here in the Software Manual to describe the alternate meanings for bits [19:10] in the APCS_GICH_LRn registers. Adding it here allows software to pick up defines for these alternate meanings and use them in APCS_GICH_LRn accesses.

The hardware uses these alternate definitions when bit 31 (hardware) is set to 0 – indicating a pure virtual interrupt written directly to this hypervisor interface or an interrupt generated due to an SGI that originated in the distributor. Bits [31:20] and [9:0] retain the normal APCS_GICH_LRn meanings.

| Bits | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 19 | EI | Indicates that this interrupt should trigger an EOI interrupt. When this bit is set, a maintenance interrupt will be asserted whenever this interrupt becomes invalid. |
| 12:10 | CPUID | If this interrupt is an SGI, indicate the requesting CPU ID. This appears in the relevant field of the VM interrupt acknowledge register.<br>If the interrupt is not an SGI, software must set this field to 0. |

## 8.5.2.6.5 QGIC2 CPU interface register definitions

### 0x2000 APCS_GICC_CTLR

- **Type:** RW
- **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State:** 0x00000000
- **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register configures the QGIC2 CPU interface.

Nonsecure access: Access is granted only to bits 0, 5, 6 and 9.

Secure access: Access is granted to all register bits. Nonsecure bits 0, 5, 6, and 9 are aliased into bits 1, 7, 8, and 10 for access by secure software. Modifying these aliased bits modify the nonsecure settings. Bits 0, 5, 6, 9 are physically banked into secure and nonsecure space.


<!-- page 3121 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 | EOIMODENS | For secure software, a read/writable alias of nonsecure EOIMODE. |
| 9 | EOIMODE | For secure software, controls the behavior of secure access to APCS_GICC_EOIR and APCS_GICC_DIR.<br>For nonsecure software, controls the behavior of nonsecure access to APCS_GICC_EOIR and APCS_GICC_DIR.<br>0x0: PD_AND_DI (both priority drop and deactivate Interrupt, APCS_GICC_DIR does not function)<br>0x1: PD (APCS_GICC_EOIR performs priority drop, APCS_GICC_DIR performs deactivate interrupt function) |
| 8 | IRQBYPDISABLENS | For secure software, a read/writable alias of non-secure version of IRQBYPDISABLE. |
| 7 | FIQBYPDISABLENS | For secure software, a read/writable alias of nonsecure version of FIQBYPDISABLE. |
| 6 | IRQBYPDISABLE | For nonsecure software, when CPU interface is disabled, prevents the legacy bypass IRQ signal from being forwarded to the CPU (if IRQ is under nonsecure control). For secure software, prevents bypass if FIQ is under secure control.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 5 | FIQBYPDISABLE | For nonsecure software, when CPU interface is disabled, prevents the legacy bypass FIQ signal from being forwarded to the CPU (if FIQ is under nonsecure control). For secure software, prevents bypass if FIQ is under secure control.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 4 | SBPR | Controls, which binary point register is used to, calculate preemption.<br>0x0: BANKED (Secure interrupts use the secure binary point register, nonsecure interrupts use the nonsecure binary point register)<br>0x1: RESTRICTED (All interrupts use the secure binary point register) |
| 3 | S_DEST | Controls destination of secure interrupts.<br>0x0: IRQ<br>0x1: FIQ |
| 2 | ACKCTL | Controls the side effect behavior of a secure read request to the APCS_GICC_IAR register in the case where the highest priority pending interrupt is nonsecure.<br>If ACKCTL is set to 0x0, a secure read request to the APCS_GICC_IAR returns an interrupt ID value of 1022, and the read request does not cause the interrupt to be acknowledged (that is, the pending status of the interrupt remains unchanged).<br>If ACKCTL is set to 0x1, a secure read request to the APCS_GICC_IAR returns the interrupt ID value of the nonsecure interrupt, and causes the interrupt to be acknowledged (that is, the interrupt becomes active, or active & pending).<br>0x0: DISABLE_ACK_OF_NS_PENDING<br>0x1: ENABLE_ACK_OF_NS_PENDING |
<!-- page 3122 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | ENABLE_NS | For secure software, a read/writable alias of nonsecure software's enable bit (bit 0 of this same register in nonsecure space).<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |
| 0 | ENABLE | For nonsecure software, this bit enables/disables nonsecure interrupts.<br>For secure software, this bit enables/disables secure interrupts.<br>0x0: CLR<br>0x1: SET |

### 0x2004 APCS_GICC_PMR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register configures the QGIC2 CPU interface priority mask. The priority mask can be used to limit the interrupts that can cause an interrupt request to the CPU based on priority levels.

**Nonsecure access:** Write access is granted only if bit 7 is 0x1, writes are ignored otherwise. Reads are always granted, however, bit 7 is always set in the data returned. Bit 0 is always zero.

**Secure access:** Access is granted to all register bits.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:3 | LEVEL | Set the priority mask level. The CPU interface asserts an interrupt request to CPU if the priority of the highest pending interrupt sent by the interrupt distributor is strictly higher than at least the mask set in priority mask register. |

### 0x2008 APCS_GICC_BPR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000002
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register configures the QGIC2 CPU interface binary point. The binary point is used to limit interrupts that can cause an interrupt request to the CPU based on the interrupt's priority and the interrupt priority that currently being serviced by the CPU (if there is one). If the CPU is not servicing an interrupt, the binary point register is not used.

**Nonsecure access:** Provides access to the nonsecure binary point register.

**Secure access:** Provides access to the secure binary point register. Secure software may access the nonsecure binary point register at offset 0x001C.
<!-- page 3123 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2:0 | VAL | The VAL setting is used to determine the priority bits used for preemption. |

### 0x200C APCS_GICC_IAR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000003FF
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register is used by the CPU to obtain the ID of the interrupt, which caused the assertion if IRQn or FIQn.
Performing this read has the side effect of causing the distributor to change the interrupt from the pending state to the active or active & pending state according to the description below.

Using three bits defined by AHB bus security state (1=non-secure), security of the HPPI (1=nonsecure) and the value of the ACKCTL bit in APCS_GICC_CTLR:
* **b00x:** respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (secure request to secure interrupt, ACKCTL is don't care)
* **b010:** respond with 1022 (secure request to nonsecure interrupt but ACKCTL=0 disabling secure handling of nonsecure interrupts)
* **b011:** respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (secure request to nonsecure interrupt with ACKCTL=1)
* **b10x:** respond with 1023 (nonsecure request to secure interrupt)
* **b11x:** respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (nonsecure request to nonsecure interrupt)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value returned in this field is dependent on the security state of the access to the register, the security state of any outstanding interrupts, the value of ACKCTL bit in the APCS_GICC_CTLR register as defined in the description above. |
<!-- page 3124 -->
### 0x2010 APCS_GICC_EOIR

* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

The end of interrupt register (APCS_GICC_EOIR) has two possible behaviors. By default it can be written to indicate when software has finished handling an interrupt.

If the EOIMODE bit is set to 0x1, writing this register has the priority drop (PD) effect. The PD effect is when the active priority bit for the highest priority active interrupt is cleared. The key difference, when EOIMODE is 0x1, is that the distributor is not notified that this happened – that is, the interrupt itself does not become inactive.

When EOIMODE is 0x0, writing to this register will, in addition to the PD effect described above, set the interrupt to inactive or pending (if prior to writing to this register, the interrupt was both active & pending it becomes pending) in the distributor.

In either case, the value written must be the interrupt ID, and the CPU source ID for SGIs, of the interrupt that is being completed.

The security status of the write to this register (NS-prot) must match the security status (NS-int) of the interrupt ID for the interrupt to be successfully cleared.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it must match the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt. The CPU source ID must match an active interrupt in order for the APCS_GICC_EOIR to take effect. The CPU_ID is written must match that delivered to software when APCS_GICC_IAR is read.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value must match the interrupt ID that software received when reading the APCS_GICC_IAR register. If the security settings match, a write causes the priority drop effect and if EOIMODE=0, the active state in the distributor for the corresponding interrupt will also be cleared. |

### 0x2014 APCS_GICC_RPR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000000F8
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

The running priority register (APCS_GICC_RPR) provides access to the highest priority of all the active interrupts on this CPU. The priority value returned is sensitive to the security status (NS-int) of the interrupt currently running and the NS-prot.
<!-- page 3125 -->
**Nonsecure access:** If the currently interrupt is secure (NS-int = 0), and a nonsecure read of the running priority register is attempted (NS-prot = 1), then the value 0 (maximum priority) is returned.

**Secure access:** Returns the true value in the register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:3 | VAL | Running priority value |

### 0x2018 APCS_GICC_HPPIR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000003FF
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

This register provides access to the highest priority pending interrupt to the CPU Interface.

> [!NOTE]
> Interrupts that are active & pending in the distributor are not considered candidates to become the highest priority pending interrupt.

Using three bits defined by AHB bus security state (1=nonsecure), security of the HPPI (1=nonsecure) and the value of the ACKCTL bit in APCS_GICC_CTLR:
* **b00x:** respond with the true interrupt number (secure request to secure interrupt, ACKCTL is don't care)
* **b010:** respond with 1022 (secure request to nonsecure interrupt but ACKCTL=0 disabling secure handling of nonsecure interrupts)
* **b011:** respond with the true interrupt number (secure request to nonsecure interrupt with ACKCTL=1)
* **b10x:** respond with 1023 (nonsecure request to secure interrupt)
* **b11x:** respond with the true interrupt number (nonsecure request to nonsecure interrupt)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value returned in this field is dependent on the security state of the access to the register, and the security state of any outstanding interrupts, as described above. |
<!-- page 3126 -->
### 0x201C APCS_GICC_ABPR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000003
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

This register provides a copy of the nonsecure binary point register for use by secure software. See the definition of the APCS_GICC_BPR register for details on the use of this register.

* **Nonsecure access:** No access.
* **Secure access:** Access granted, updates are reflected to nonsecure software at the APCS_GICC_BPR register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2:0 | VAL | Same as the APCS_GICC_BPR register – effects only nonsecure interrupts. |

### 0x2020 APCS_GICC_AIAR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000003FF
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

This register is used by the CPU to obtain the ID of the interrupt, which caused the assertion if IRQn or FIQn. This is a secure only register used to read nonsecure interrupts by secure software.

Performing this read has the side effect of causing the distributor to change the interrupt from the pending state to the active or active & pending state.

* **Nonsecure access:** No access. Read as zero.
* **Secure access:** See description below.

Based on the 2 bits defined by the AHB security of the request (1=nonsecure) and the security of the interrupt (1=nonsecure):
* **b00:** respond with 1023 (secure request that behaves as if it is a nonsecure request, to secure interrupt)
* **b01:** respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (secure request that behaves as if it is a nonsecure request, to nonsecure interrupt)
* **b1x:** RAZ/WI (nonsecure request cannot access this register)
<!-- page 3127 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. |

### 0x2024 APCS_GICC_AEOIR

* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

A secure write to this register has an identical effect to a nonsecure write to APCS_GICC_EOIR, with the exception of the EOIMODE bit; the value of the secure EOIMODE bit (bit 9) in APCS_GICC_CTLR is used to determine whether the interrupt is deactivated or just priority dropped rather than the nonsecure EOIMODENS bit (bit 10).

This register must be used by secure software to signal completion of nonsecure interrupts when the ACKCTL bit of the APCS_GICC_CTLR register is set to 0x0; APCS_GICC_EOIR cannot be used for this purpose since it would affect APCS_GICC_APR rather than APCS_GICC_NSAPRn.

* **Nonsecure access:** Ignored.
* **Secure access:** Signal completion of nonsecure interrupt.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it must match the ID of the CPU, which requested the Interrupt. The CPU source ID must match an active interrupt in order for the APCS_GICC_AEOIR to take effect. The CPU_ID is written must match that delivered to software when APCS_GICC_IAR is read.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value must match the interrupt ID that software received when reading the APCS_GICC_IAR register. A write cause the priority drop effect and if EOIMODE=0, the active state in the distributor for the corresponding interrupt will also be cleared. |

### 0x2028 APCS_GICC_AHPPIR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x000003FF
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

This is a secure-only register.
<!-- page 3128 -->
A read from this register has an identical effect to a nonsecure read from APCS_GICC_HPPIR. It can therefore be used to check for a pending nonsecure interrupt without the possibility of returning a secure interrupt ID value.

Interrupts that are active & pending in the distributor are not considered candidates to become the highest priority pending interrupt.

* **Nonsecure access:** No access. Read as zero.
* **Secure access:** See description below.

Using 3 bits defined by AHB bus security state (1=nonsecure), security of the HPPI (1=nonsecure) and the value of the ACKCTL bit in the APCS_GICC_CTLR register:
* **b00x:** respond with 1023 (HPPI is a secure interrupt)
* **b01x:** respond with the true interrupt number (HPPI is a nonsecure interrupt)
* **b1xx:** RAZ/WI (nonsecure request cannot access this register)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value returned in this field is dependent on the security state of the access to the register, and the security state of any outstanding interrupts, as described above. |

### 0x20D0 APCS_GICC_APR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Banked

Each bit in this register provides the active status of priorities in the CPU interface.

* **Nonsecure access:** Bits [15-0] represent priorities 31 to 16 of the nonsecure active priorities.
* **Secure access:** Bits [31-0] represent priorities 31 to 0 of the active secure priorities.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | PRI | Active status of priorities.<br>0x1: A (Active)<br>0x0: N/A (Not active) |
<!-- page 3129 -->
### 0x20E0 APCS_GICC_NSAPR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

Each bit in this register provides the active status of nonsecure priorities in the CPU interface.

* **Nonsecure access:** None – write ignore, read-as-zero.
* **Secure access:** Bits [31-0] represent priorities 31 to 0 of the active nonsecure priorities.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | PRI | Active status of nonsecure priorities.<br>0x1: A (Active)<br>0x0: N/A (Not active) |

### 0x20FC APCS_GICC_IIDR

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00020070
* **Security Treatment:** Common

This register provides information about the QGIC2 CPU interface version and device implementor information.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:20 | PART_NUM | Part Number: 0x0. |
| 19:16 | ARCH_VERSION | Architecture Version: 0x2. |
| 15:12 | REVISION | Revision number: 0x0. |
| 11:0 | IMPLEMENTOR | Bits [11:8] contain the implementor's JEP106 continuation code, 0x0.<br>Bit [7] is always 0<br>Bits [6:0] contain bits [6:0] of the implementor's JEP106 code. |

### 0x3000 APCS_GICC_DIR

* **Type:** W
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Banked
<!-- page 3130 -->
This register provides the mechanism by which software can deactivate a specific interrupt.

* Secure writes can deactivate secure and nonsecure interrupts.
* Nonsecure writes can only deactivate nonsecure interrupts.

> [!NOTE]
> Unlike APCS_GICC_EOIR and APCS_GICC_IAR, there is no restriction of the deactivation of nonsecure interrupts with secure accesses. The ACKCTL bit does not affect the behavior of APCS_GICC_DIR. This is because unlike APCS_GICC_IAR there is no chance of the access affecting an interrupt from an unexpected security state, and unlike APCS_GICC_EOIR there is no effect on APCS_GICC_APR or APCS_GICC_NSAPRn, so there is no need to indicate which register should be affected.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. INT_ID written should match value returned from APCS_GICC_IAR read. |

## 8.5.2.6.6 QGIC2 virtual CPU interface register definitions

### 0x4004 APCS_GICV_PMR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000000
* **Security Treatment:** Common

This register configures the QGIC2 virtual CPU interface priority mask. The priority mask can be used to limit the interrupts that can cause an interrupt request to the CPU based on priority levels.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:3 | LEVEL | Set the priority mask level. The CPU interface asserts an interrupt request to CPU if the priority of the highest pending interrupt sent by the interrupt distributor is strictly higher than at least the mask set in priority mask register. |

### 0x4008 APCS_GICV_BPR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
* **Reset State:** 0x00000002
* **Security Treatment:** Common


<!-- page 3131 -->
This register configures the QGIC2 virtual CPU interface binary point. The binary point is used to limit interrupts that can cause an interrupt request to the CPU based on the interrupt's priority and the interrupt priority that currently being serviced by the CPU (if there is one). If the CPU is not servicing an interrupt, the binary point register is not used.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2:0 | VAL | The VAL setting is used to determine the priority bits used for preemption. |

### 0x400C APCS_GICV_IAR

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x000003FF`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

This register is used by the CPU to obtain the ID of the interrupt, which caused the assertion if IRQn or FIQn.

Performing this read has the side effect of causing the GICH to change the interrupt from the pending state to the active or active & pending state according to the rules below.

Using the two bits defined by security of the HPPI (1=nonsecure) and the value of the ACKCTL bit in the `APCS_GICC_CTLR` register:
- `b0x`: respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (ignore APROTNS and consider as a secure request to secure interrupt, ACKCTL is don't care)
- `b10`: respond with 1022 (ignore APROTNS and consider as secure request to nonsecure interrupt but ACKCTL=0 disabling secure handling of nonsecure interrupts)
- `b11`: respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active (ignore APROTNS and consider as secure request to nonsecure interrupt with ACKCTL=1)

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU which requested the Interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier - a virtual interrupt number determined by the hypervisor software. |

### 0x4010 APCS_GICV_EOIR

- **Type**: W
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x00000000`
- **Security Treatment**: Common
<!-- page 3132 -->
The end of interrupt register (`APCS_GICV_EOIR`) has two possible behaviors. By default it can be written to indicate when software has finished handling an interrupt.

If the EOIMODE bit in the `APCS_GICV_CTLR` register is set to `0x1`, writing this register has the priority drop (PD) effect. The PD effect is when the active priority bit for the highest priority active interrupt is cleared. The key difference, when EOIMODE is `0x1`, is the interrupt itself does not become inactive.

When EOIMODE is `0x0`, writing to this register will, in addition to the PD effect described above, set the interrupt to inactive or pending (if prior to writing to this register, the interrupt was both active & pending it becomes just pending). However, if EOIMODE is `0x0`, then the CPU_ID and INT_ID must match an active interrupt for a state change to occur.

In either case, the value written must be the interrupt ID, and the CPU source ID for SGIs, of the interrupt that is being completed.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it must match the ID of the CPU, which requested the Interrupt. The CPU_ID is written must match that delivered to software when `APCS_GICV_IAR` is read.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. The value must match the interrupt ID that software received when reading the `APCS_GICV_IAR` register. |

### 0x4014 APCS_GICV_RPR

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x000000F8`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

The running priority register (`APCS_GICV_RPR`) provides access to the highest priority of all the active interrupts on this virtual CPU.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7:3 | VAL | Running priority value. |

### 0x4018 APCS_GICV_HPPIR

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x000003FF`
- **Security Treatment**: Common
<!-- page 3133 -->
This register provides access to the highest priority pending interrupt to the virtual CPU interface. If no interrupt is pending, responds with `0x3FF`.

> [!NOTE]
> Interrupts that are active & pending in the GICH (hypervisor) are not considered candidates to become the highest priority pending interrupt.

Using two bits defined by the value of the ACKCTL bit in the `APCS_GICV_CTLR` register and the NS bit of the HPPI (1=nonsecure):
- `b1x`: respond with the virtual interrupt number
- `b00`: respond with the virtual interrupt number
- `b01`: respond with 1022

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier. |

### 0x401C APCS_GICV_ABPR

- **Type**: RW
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x00000003`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

This register provides access to the nonsecure binary point register used by nonsecure interrupts when the GBPR bit of the `APCS_GICV_CTRL` register is `0x0`. See the definition of the `APCS_GICV_BPR` register for details on the use of this register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2:0 | VAL | Same as the `APCS_GICV_BPR` register - effects only nonsecure interrupts. |

### 0x4020 APCS_GICV_AIAR

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x000003FF`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

This register is used by the CPU to obtain the ID of the interrupt, which caused the assertion if IRQn or FIQn.

Performing this read has the side effect of causing the GICH to change the interrupt from the pending state to the active or active & pending state according to the rules below.
<!-- page 3134 -->
Using the security state of the pending interrupt:
- `0`: respond with 1023
- `1`: respond with the true interrupt number, transitioning to active

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it contains the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is read as 0 and should be ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt identifier - a virtual interrupt number determined by the hypervisor software. |

### 0x4024 APCS_GICV_AEOIR

- **Type**: W
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x00000000`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

This register presents the same programmers model as `APCS_GICC_AEOIR`.

The effect of writing to this register is identical to the effect of writing the same value to the `APCS_GICV_EOIR` register. This alias is provided for compatibility with the physical CPU interface, where the two registers have a different effect due to the provision of separate secure and nonsecure active priority registers.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12:10 | CPU_ID | CPU source ID value is only valid if the interrupt is a software interrupt, in which case it must match the ID of the CPU, which requested the interrupt. The CPU_ID is written must match that delivered to software when `APCS_GICV_IAR` is read.<br>For PPIs and SPIs the CPU source ID field is ignored. |
| 9:0 | INT_ID | Interrupt Identifier. The value must match the interrupt ID that software received when reading the `APCS_GICV_IAR` register. |

### 0x4028 APCS_GICV_AHPPIR

- **Type**: R
- **Clock**: GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK
- **Reset State**: `0x000003FF`
- **Security Treatment**: Common

This register presents the same programmers model as `APCS_GICC_AHPPIR`.
<!-- page 3135 -->
This register returns the interrupt ID of the highest priority pending interrupt if it has an NS value of 1. Reading this interrupt has no side effects and simply returns the highest priority pending interrupt among the list registers or a status code as explained below.

- `0`: respond with 1023

| Bits | Name | Description |

## 8.6 Qualcomm Timer (QTMR)

This section describes the QTMR controller available in the SoC.

### 8.6.1 QTMR overview

QTMR implements the ARM generic timer specification.

Each QTMR is synchronized with the device single SoC-global counter. QTMR is used to generate timer triggered events based on an equal-to or greater than comparison with a global counter. The use of a single global counter removes the need for interprocessor timer synchronization at initialization and after power collapse.

Figure 8-25 shows a high-level overview of the QTMR integrated within device application Cortex-A53 subsystem (APSS).

#### Figure 8-25: QTMR overview
*Description:* A block diagram illustrating the integration of the Qualcomm Timer (QTMR) within the Application Subsystem (APSS).
The diagram contains the following components:
- **APSS (Application Processor Subsystem)**: A block enclosing the QTMR and QGIC blocks.
  - **QTMR**: Comprises seven frames labeled Frame 0, Frame 1, up to Frame 6. It receives clocks and resets from the GCC, a 56-bit global counter input, and connects to an AHB Slave Port. It outputs interrupts to the QGIC block.
  - **QGIC**: Receives interrupts from the QTMR.
  - **AHB Slave Port**: Positioned on the boundary of APSS, interfacing the QTMR with the System NoC.
- **External to APSS**:
  - **56-bit global counter**: Feeds into the QTMR block.
  - **GCC (Global Clock Controller)**: Supplies "Clocks" and "Resets" signals to the QTMR block.
  - **System NoC**: Communicates with the APSS via the AHB Slave Port.

## 8.6.4 QTMR functional description

Figure 8-27 shows a high-level overview of QTMR functional blocks.

#### Figure 8-27: QTMR functional block diagram
*Description:* The diagram illustrates the Qualcomm Timer (QTMR) internal architecture and interfaces. A large QTMR block contains a "QTIMER CONTROL" block (consisting of FSM and AHB sub-blocks) and seven stacked "Frames x7 / QTIMER COMPARE" blocks (each containing a Physical Timer and a Virtual Timer).
* The APSS connects to the QTIMER CONTROL block via an external "AHB Slave Port" bidirectional bus.
* A "56-bit Global Counter" input enters the QTMR block from the bottom. It splits into a control path feeding the QTIMER CONTROL block, and a direct data path feeding the QTIMER COMPARE frames.
* Control and data signals are exchanged between the QTIMER CONTROL block and the QTIMER COMPARE frames.
* The QTIMER COMPARE frames generate external "Interrupts" to the right.

Integrated in the device is a single 56-bit global counter (placed in always-on domain) used for interprocessor timer synchronization. There is only one such hardware mechanism in the entire system that increments the timer counter every clock cycle. Each timer frame in the QTMR provides a separate memory-mapped view of this physical counter.

* **Counter sourcing:** Each increment of the counter represents 19.2 MHz or ~52.08 ns. During low-power modes, it switches to the sleep clock, implemented as the 19.2 MHz/586. Each clock switch results in an inaccuracy of up to +/- 52.08 ns (1 XO clock cycle).
* **Counter depth:** The depth of the counter is 56-bits, which give a resolution with the 19.2 MHz clock from 0 to 118.927924 years.

QTMR consists of the following main block:
* **QTIMER CONTROL:** The block includes logic to handle:
  * AHB interface
    The control block includes the following access control registers:
    * `QTMR_AC_CNTFRQ`
    * `QTMR_AC_CNTSR`
    * `QTMR_AC_CNTTID`
<!-- page 3143 -->

* (continued from previous page...)
  * `QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n`, n=\[0..6\]
  * `QTMR_AC_CNTVOFF_LO_n`, n=\[0..6\]
  * `QTMR_AC_CNTVOFF_HI_n`, n=\[0..6\]

### 8.6.4.1 QTMR architecture

Figure 8-28 shows a simplified functional overview of QTMR module.

#### Figure 8-28: QTMR internal architecture
*Description:* The diagram shows the internal structure of the QTMR within a larger "Subsystem". Inside the "QTMR" block:
* Multiple "Timer Frame" blocks (from "Timer Frame 0" to "Timer Frame 6") are present. Each "Timer Frame" contains a "Physical Timer" block and an optional "Virtual Timer (optional)" block.
* At the bottom of the QTMR block is a "Timer Access Control" block.
* Below the QTMR block, but still within the Subsystem, there is a red block labeled "xPU".

The QTMR controller consists of:
* Frames
* Timers
* Counters
* Second view (of a timer frame)

#### 8.6.4.1.1 Timer frames

A timer frame consists of a single physical timer entity and an optional virtual timer/counter entity. The QTimer instance consists of one or more timer frames. The number of timer frames is hardware-configurable. A timer frame consists of a single physical and an optional virtual timer entity. Each timer frame has a memory-mapped software view of the global physical counter.
<!-- page 3144 -->

APSS QTMR instance has 7 timer frames (F0-F6). Frame 0 supports second view, while all the other timer frames support only the first view. Each timer frame has an optional virtual timer.

#### 8.6.4.1.2 Physical timer

Each timer frame provides a physical timer. The physical timer generates events based on the global counter and a programmable physical compare value.

#### 8.6.4.1.3 Virtual timer

An optional virtual timer that generates events based on the virtual counter of the QTMR instance and a programmable virtual compare value.

#### 8.6.4.1.4 Virtual counter

Virtual counter is created by hardware by applying a programmable virtual counter offset to the 56-bit global physical counter. There is an optional virtual counter/timer for each frame of QTMR instance. This virtual counter/timer provides both a virtual counter offset value and a virtual timer compare value.

#### 8.6.4.1.5 Second view

Each timer frame has an optional software memory-mapped restricted view (mirror) of the "first view" timer frame registers, except for the `QTMR_V1_CNTPL0ACR`, `QTMR_V1_CNTVOFF_LO` and `QTMR_V1_CNTVOFF_HI` registers, which are blocked. These registers are restricted by registers in the first view. Having two views allows the MMU and xPU to apply different protection attributes to each view. This allows the software to use the first view and user to use the second view.

#### 8.6.4.1.6 Access control

The QTMR registers are protected by several protection stages. For more information about access control and security treatment, see Section 8.6.5.3.

### 8.6.4.2 QTMR power and clock management

QTMR is powered by the VDD_CX power domain and is power collapsed only when the entire domain is power collapsed. QTMR is not functional during XO shut down/deep sleep.

Low-power features of the QTMR include:
* Register level clock gating
* Output signal to support external dynamic clock gating

The QTMR module has the following two clocks:
* `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`
* `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK`

The QTMR module does not generate any internal clocks.
<!-- page 3145 -->

QTMR clocks can be gated. After the timer clocks are gated, the global counter broadcasts for a number of cycles before the QTMR enables its counter and captures this global count. This ensures that QTMR does not fall out of sync with the 56-bit global counter once the clock is back on. The broadcast time depends how long it takes to broadcast to the furthest point on the device.

#### 8.6.4.2.1 Clock synchronization

Most logic is synchronous with the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` clock except for the following registers that use the `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK`:
* `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_LO`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_HI`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_LO`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_HI`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CVAL_LO`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CVAL_HI`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CVAL_LO`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CVAL_HI`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTP_TVAL`
* `QTMR_V1_CNTV_TVAL`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_TVAL`
* `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_TVAL`

> [!NOTE]
> Software does not take care of gating the clocks.

When software writes to any of the above registers, `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` needs to be synchronized with the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`. The total number of cycles needed to achieve this synchronization is 3 `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` + 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`.

##### CVAL read/write

The corresponding `*_CVAL` registers are hereinafter referred to as `CVAL`.

Reads from the corresponding `CVAL` registers whether for physical or virtual frames are simple read operations. Writes to the corresponding `CVAL` registers for a physical frame are also simple write operations. However writes to the `CVAL` registers for a virtual frame is a little more involved and it is a multicycle operation (see Figure 8-29 for more details on the CNTV_CVAL_WR).
<!-- page 3146 -->

Figure 8-29 shows the virtual timer compare value `CNTV_CVAL` compared against the virtual count value, `CNTVCT` where `CNTVCT` = Global counter – Virtual offset. An interrupt signal is asserted when the global counter is greater than or equal to `CNTV_CVAL` + `VOFF`.

It takes 1 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` for a `CVAL` write without factoring in the number of cycles it takes for synchronization. The total wait time for writes to the `CVAL` is 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` + (3 `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` + 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`).

#### Figure 8-29: CNTV_CVAL write timing diagram
*Description:* A timing diagram representing a write operation to `CNTV_CVAL`. It shows the following signals:
* `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK`: The timer clock.
* `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`: The faster AHB system clock.
* `AHB_HSEL`: The AHB select line, pulsing high for one AHB clock cycle.
* `AHB_HADDR`: Shows addresses `A1` and `A2` sequentially.
* `AHB_HWDATA`: Valid write data `Data (A1)` corresponding to address `A1`.
* `AHB_FSM`: The AHB Finite State Machine which transitions from `IDLE` to `TCLK_CSR_WR` (which stays in this state for 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` and 3 `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` for synchronization) and then back to `IDLE`.
* `QTMR_HSEL`: A control signal which goes low during the active phase of the state machine.
* `CVAL`: Shows the register content updating to "New CVAL" at the end of the state machine write cycle.

##### TVAL read/write

The corresponding `*_TVAL` registers are hereinafter referred to as `TVAL`.

For the `TVAL` operations, physical and virtual operations are treated the same such that for physical frames the used virtual offset is 0. In this way, the same logic can be used for both physical and virtual frames.

`TVAL` read operations are performed with the following calculations that do the subtraction of `CNTVOFF` and then subtract that from the `CVAL`:
$$\text{TVAL} = (\text{CVAL} - (\text{CNTPCT} - \text{CNTVOFF}))$$

`TVAL` writes essentially write to the `CVAL` the following calculations that do the `signExtend` of `TVAL` before adding it to the result of `CNTPCT` - `CNTVOFF`:
$$\text{CVAL} = (\text{CNTPCT} - \text{CNTVOFF}) + \text{signExtend}(\text{TVAL})$$

Figure 8-30 shows the TVAL timing diagram. It takes 5 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` for a `TVAL` write without factoring in the number of cycles it takes for synchronization. The total wait time for writes to the `TVAL` = x `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` + (3 `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` + 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`).
<!-- page 3147 -->

#### Figure 8-30: TVAL write timing diagram
*Description:* A timing diagram illustrating the write operation for `TVAL`. The signals are:
* `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK`: The slower timer clock.
* `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`: The faster AHB system clock.
* `AHB_HSEL`: AHB select signal, high for 1 AHB clock cycle.
* `AHB_HADDR`: Shows address `A1` followed by `A2`.
* `AHB_HWDATA`: Shows `Data (A1)` corresponding to the write address.
* `AHB_FSM`: The state machine starts in `IDLE`, transitions through a short intermediate state, then 3 additional empty clock cycles, then enters the `TCLK_CSR_WR` state (which stays for 2 `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` and 3 `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` for synchronization), passes through a clock-crossing transition, and returns to `IDLE`.
* `QTMR_HSEL`: Active low control signal, remaining low during the state machine's active write period.
* `CVAL`: Updates to "New CVAL" at the end of the state machine sequence.

*(1) Stays in this state for 2 QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK and 3 QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK for synchronization*

### 8.6.4.3 QTMR interrupts

For each QTMR frame there could be up to two interrupts, `QTMR_PHY_IRQ` and `QTMR_VIRT_IRQ` (if a virtual timer is implemented).

APSS QTMR frame0 (F0) has two interrupts, `APSS_QTMR_PHY_IRQ_0` and `APSS_QTMR_VIRT_IRQ_0`. For every other QTMR frame (F1-F6), there is a single interrupt – `APSS_QTMR_PHY_IRQ_1` to `APSS_QTMR_PHY_IRQ_6`.

The interrupt occurs when the physical/TVAL count value is greater or equal to the compare value.

The interrupts are active high and level triggered. An interrupt remains active until that condition is no longer valid.

QTMR interrupts can be masked by setting the `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL`/ `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL`/ `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL`/ `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[IMSK]` bit.

Interrupt status can be polled before masking by checking the `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL`/ `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL`/ `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL`/ `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[ISTAT]` bit.

Reading the `*_CTL` register is a multicycle operation.

### 8.6.4.4 QTMR theory of operation

#### 8.6.4.4.1 Data Flow

The key data flow in the QTMR module is on the AHB interface. Operations include AHB writes to QTMR registers and AHB reads from the QTMR registers.

Some AHB operations in the QTMR module require insertion of wait states. For this purpose, there is an AHB FSM that controls the flow for these operations.

QTMR FSM is used to handle the following multicycle operations:
* Read of physical count
* Read of virtual count
<!-- page 3148 -->

* (continued from previous page...)
  * Read of physical TVAL
  * Read of virtual TVAL
  * Read/write of physical CTL
  * Read/write of virtual CTL
  * Write of physical CVAL
  * Write of virtual CVAL
  * Write of physical TVAL
  * Write of virtual TVAL

Figure 8-31 shows the FSM transitions.

#### Figure 8-31: QTMR FSM
*Description:* A state transition diagram for the QTMR Finite State Machine (FSM). It defines the following states and transitions:
* **IDLE**: The default state.
  * Loops back to **IDLE** if no multicycle operation is requested.
  * Transitions to **SYNC1_GLBL_CNT** on `(readCntPct | readCntVct | readCntpTval | writeCntpTval | readCntvTval | writeCntvTval)`.
  * Transitions to **CNTV_CVAL_WR** on `writeCntvCval`.
  * Transitions to **HRDATA_WR** on `readCntCtl`.
  * Transitions to **TCLK_CSR_WR** on `writeCntpCval | writeCntpCtl | writeCntvCtl`.
* **SYNC1_GLBL_CNT**: First stage of global counter synchronization.
  * Transitions unconditionally to **SYNC2_GLBL_CNT**.
* **SYNC2_GLBL_CNT**: Second stage of global counter synchronization.
  * Transitions to **HRDATA_WR** on `readCntPct`.
  * Transitions to **SUB_VOFF** on `readCntpTval | readCntvTval | readCntVct | writeCntpTval | writeCntvTval`.
* **CNTV_CVAL_WR**: Virtual compare value write state.
  * Transitions to **TCLK_CSR_WR**.
* **SUB_VOFF**: Virtual offset subtraction state.
  * Transitions to **HRDATA_WR** on `readCntVct`.
  * Transitions to **TVAL_CALC** (unconditionally).
* **TVAL_CALC**: Timer Value calculation state.
  * Transitions to **HRDATA_WR** on `readCntpTval | readCntvTval`.
  * Transitions to **TCLK_CSR_WR** on `writeCntpTval | writeCntvTval`.
* **HRDATA_WR**: Host Read Data/Write state.
  * Loops on `busy`.
  * Transitions to **IDLE** on `~busy`.
* **TCLK_CSR_WR**: Timer Clock Control Status Register Write state.
  * Loops on `busy`.
  * Transitions to **IDLE** on `~busy`.

Table 8-159 and Table 8-160 describe the functions of each of the QTMR FSM states.

### Table 8-159 QTMR FSM state descriptions

| QTMR FSM STATE | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| IDLE (0) | As long as none of the valid multicycle options present the FSM remains in this state. |
| SYNC1_GLBL_CNT (1) | This is the first stage of synchronizing the global counter. |
| SYNC2_GLBL_CNT (3) | This is the second stage of synchronizing the global counter. |
<!-- page 3149 -->

### Table 8-159 QTMR FSM state descriptions (continued)

| QTMR FSM STATE | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| HRDATA_WR (2) | This state is for the read data path. For all operations that need this stage EXCEPT for the read of the CTL register, the next cycle read data is available. For reads of the CTL register, because this register is clocked on the `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` it needs to synchronize with the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`, so it remains in this state as long as the busy flag for the clock synchronization is set. |
| SUB_VOFF (6) | This stage sets up the controls needed to subtract the virtual offset from the count since $\text{Virtual Count} = \text{Global Count} - \text{Virtual Offset}$. In the case of physical count, user subtract 0. |
| TVAL_CALC (7) | Controls for the TVAL calculation are carried out in this stage. For TVAL writes $\text{CVAL} = (\text{CNTP(CNTV)} + \text{signExtend(TVAL)})$, for TVAL reads, $\text{TVAL} = \text{CVAL} - \text{CNTP(CNTV)}$ |
| TVAL_CSR_WR (5) | This state is for any writes to a CSR register on the `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK`. The registers in the QTMR that are clocked on the `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` are: `CNTP_CTL`, `CNTV_CTL`, `CNTP_CVAL`, `CNTV_CVAL`, `CNTP_TVAL_WR`, `CNTV_TVAL_WR`. Because all these registers are clocked on the `QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK` it needs to synchronize with the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`, so it remains in this state as long as the busy flag for the clock synchronization is set. *(Note: Referenced as TCLK_CSR_WR in the transition diagram and table)* |
| CNTV_CVAL (4) | Controls for comparing the virtual compare value against the `CNTVCT` counter are set in this stage. *(Note: Referenced as CNTV_CVAL_WR in the transition diagram)* |

### Table 8-160 QTMR FSM state transitions

*Note: S1 = SYNC1_GLBL_CNT, S2 = SYNC2_GLBL_CNT*

| No. | Write/Read | Register | Cycle 1 | Cycle 2 | Cycle 3 | Cycle 4 | Cycle 5 | Cycle 6 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | RD | CNTP | S1 | S2 | HRDATA_WR | IDLE | – | – |
| 2. | RD | CNTV | S1 | S2 | SUB_VOFF | HRDATA_WR | – | – |
| 3. | WR | CNTV_CVAL | CNTV_CVAL_WR | TCLK_CSR_WR | IDLE | – | – | – |
| 4. | WR | CNTP_TVAL | S1 | S2 | SUB_VOFF | TVAL_CALC | TCLK_CSR_WR | IDLE |
| 5. | WR | CNTV_TVAL | S1 | S2 | SUB_VOFF | TVAL_CALC | TCLK_CSR_WR | IDLE |
| 6. | RD | CNTP_TVAL | S1 | S2 | SUB_VOFF | TVAL_CALC | HRDATA_WR | IDLE |

| 9. | RD | CNTP_CTL | HRDATA_WR | IDLE | – | – | – | – |

#### 8.6.4.4.2 Data Flow

The key data flow in the QTMR module is on the AHB interface. Operations include AHB writes to QTMR registers and AHB reads from the QTMR registers.

Some AHB operations in the QTMR module require insertion of wait states. For this purpose, there is an AHB FSM that controls the flow for these operations.

The QTMR FSM is used to handle the following multicycle operations:

* **Read of physical/virtual count using registers:**
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTPCT_LO`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTPCT_HI`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTVCT_LO`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTVCT_HI`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTPCT_LO`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTPCT_HI`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTVCT_LO`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTVCT_HI`

* **Write of physical/virtual CVAL using registers:**
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_LO`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_HI`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_LO`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_HI`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CVAL_LO`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CVAL_HI`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CVAL_LO`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CVAL_HI`

* **Read/write of physical/virtual TVAL using registers:**
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTP_TVAL`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTV_TVAL`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_TVAL`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_TVAL`

* **Read/write of physical/virtual CTL using registers:**
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL`
  * `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL`
  * `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL`


<!-- page 3151 -->
### 8.6.4.4.3 AHB interface

QTMR functions as a slave on an AHB-bus. The AHB slave port is used to read and write QTMR CSRs. It has the following features:
* 32-bit burst/non-burst transfers
* Only use AHB_HPRONTS[1] for privileged mode or user mode access.
* Insert appropriate number of wait states to synchronize to QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK. Most CSRs are clocked with QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK
* The AHB interface works for any frequency of QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK and QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK, that is QTMR_SYS_TMR_CLK can be slower than QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK and vice versa

After the AHB master has started the transfer with the assertion of any of the HSELs, QTMR de-asserts the QTMR_HREADY signal to extend the transfer. Figure 8-32 shows the AHB write transfer, and Figure 8-33 shows the AHB read transfer.

#### Figure: Figure 8-32 AHB write transfer
*Description:* A timing diagram showing an AHB write transfer to the QTMR over several cycles of the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` clock. The signals shown are:
* `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`: Clock signal.
* `AHB_HSEL`: Select signal, asserted high for one clock cycle.
* `AHB_WRITE`: Write control signal, asserted high during the address phase (coinciding with `AHB_HSEL` high), and then goes low.
* `AHB_HADDR`: Address bus, showing target address `A1` during the address phase.
* `AHB_HWDATA`: Write data bus, showing `Data (A1)` starting in the cycle after the address phase and held for 7 clock cycles.
* `QTMR_HREADY`: Transfer ready signal, pulled low by the slave in the cycle after `AHB_HSEL` assertion to insert wait states. It remains low for 7 cycles while the write is processed and then goes high to complete the transfer.

#### Figure: Figure 8-33 AHB read transfer
*Description:* A timing diagram showing an AHB read transfer from the QTMR over several cycles of the `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK` clock. The signals shown are:
* `QTMR_SYS_AHB_CLK`: Clock signal.
* `AHB_HSEL`: Select signal, asserted high for one clock cycle.
* `AHB_WRITE`: Write control signal, remains low (indicating read) during the address phase (coinciding with `AHB_HSEL` high), and then goes high.
* `AHB_HADDR`: Address bus, showing target address `A1` during the address phase.
* `AHB_HWDATA`: Data bus (labeled as `AHB_HWDATA` in diagram, representing read data output), showing read data `Data (A1)` only during the last cycle of the transfer before `QTMR_HREADY` goes high.
* `QTMR_HREADY`: Transfer ready signal, pulled low by the slave in the cycle after `AHB_HSEL` assertion to insert wait states. It remains low for 7 cycles and goes high once the read data is ready on the bus.
<!-- page 3152 -->
### 8.6.4.5 QTMR configuration

#### 8.6.4.5.1 Initial setup

The following setup sequence needs to be done once.
1. Configure the frequency count (`QTMR_AC_CNTFRQ`) to know the frequency of the counter. For example, for a 19.2 MHz global counter frequency, the value should be `0x124F800`, which corresponds to 19200000 Hz.
2. Configure the access control register `QTMR_AC_CNTSR` to provide the appropriate access to the individual elements of the timer as listed in Section 8.6.4.5.3.

> [!NOTE]
> This step is needed only for nonsecure accesses.

#### 8.6.4.5.2 QTMR modes

**Physical counter**
1. Programming using `*_CNTP_CVAL` register
   a. Read the physical count: `QTMR_V1_CNTPCT_LO`/`HI` and `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTPCT_LO`/`HI` registers.
   b. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTFRQ`/`F0_QTMR_V2_CNTFRQ` to know the frequency of the counter.
   c. Calculate the time interval (count) by which the interrupt is expected.
      * For example, if interrupt is expected to happen after 1 μs, then the time interval is $10^{-6} \times$ `QTMR_V1_CNTFRQ` (or `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTFRQ` for view 2 of frame 0) = 19.2 counts.
   d. Add the physical count and the count value calculated in step c and program the result in `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_LO`/`HI` register, or the `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CVAL_LO`/`HI` register for view 2 of frame 0.
   e. Enable the timer by setting `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL[EN]` bit to 1. For view 2 of frame 0, the corresponding register is `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL[EN]`.
   f. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL[ISTAT]` bit to verify interrupt for view 1 is asserted. To verify the interrupt for view 2 of frame 0, read `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL[ISTAT]` bit.
   g. See Section 8.6.4.5.4 for more information on exception handling to handle interrupts.
2. Programming using `*_CNTP_TVAL` register
   a. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTFRQ` (or `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTFRQ` for view 2 of frame 0) to know the frequency of the counter.
   b. Write the `QTMR_V1_CNTP_TVAL` or the `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_TVAL` register with the count value. This value is essentially the interval after which an interrupt (`QTMR_PHY_IRQ`) occurs.
      * For example: If `*_CNTP_TVAL` is programmed to be 10, then `*_CNTP_CVAL` gets programmed to `*_CNTPCT_LO`/`HI` + 10, which implies interrupt (`APSS_QTMR_PHY_IRQ`) will occur after 10 counts.
<!-- page 3153 -->
   c. Enable the timer by setting `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL[EN]` bit to 1. For view 2 of frame 0, the corresponding register is `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL[EN]`.
   d. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL[ISTAT]` bit to verify interrupt for view 1 is asserted. To verify the interrupt for view 2 of frame 0, read `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTP_CTL[ISTAT]` bit.
   e. See Section 8.6.4.5.4 for more information on exception handling to handle interrupts.

**Virtual counter**

Virtual counters are used to measure the passing of time on a particular virtual machine. Hence, in a real chip that runs on multiple OS there could be one physical timer and multiple virtual timers (add unique offsets to each virtual timer).

For programming virtual counters, the virtual offset register is configured by writing to `QTMR_V1_CNTVOFF_LO`/`HI` registers, with the unique offsets corresponding to each virtual timer.

1. Programming using `*_CNTV_CVAL` register
   a. Read the physical count: `QTMR_V1_CNTVCT_LO`/`HI` and `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTVCT_LO`/`HI` registers.
      * Virtual Count = Global Count – Virtual Offset
   b. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTFRQ`/`F0_QTMR_V2_CNTFRQ` to know the frequency of the counter.
   c. Calculate the time interval (count) by which the interrupt is expected. This is similar to step 1.c in physical counter section.
   d. Add the physical count and the count value calculated in step c and program the result in `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_LO`/`HI` register, or the `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CVAL_LO`/`HI` register for view 2 of frame 0.
   e. Enable the timer by setting `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL[EN]` bit to 1. For view 2 of frame 0, the corresponding register is `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[EN]`.
   f. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL[ISTAT]` bit to verify interrupt for view 1 is asserted. To verify the interrupt for view 2 of frame 0, read `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[ISTAT]` bit.
   g. See Section 8.6.4.5.4 for more information on exception handling to handle interrupts.
2. Programming using `*_CNTV_TVAL` register
   a. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTFRQ` (or `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTFRQ` for view 2 of frame 0) to know the frequency of the counter.
   b. Write the `QTMR_V1_CNTV_TVAL` or the `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_TVAL` register with the count value. This value is essentially the interval after which an interrupt (`APSS_QTMR_PHY_IRQ`) occurs.
      * For example: If `*_CNTV_TVAL` is programmed to be 10, then `*_CNTV_CVAL` gets programmed to `*_CNTVCT_LO`/`HI` + 10, which implies interrupt (`APSS_QTMR_VIRT_IRQ`) will occur after 10 counts.
   c. Enable the timer by setting `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL[EN]` bit to 1. For view 2 of frame 0, the corresponding register is `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[EN]`.
<!-- page 3154 -->
   d. Read `QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL[ISTAT]` bit to verify interrupt for view 1 is asserted. To verify the interrupt for view 2 of frame 0, read `F0_QTMR_V2_CNTV_CTL[ISTAT]` bit.
   e. See Section 8.6.4.5.4 for more information on exception handling to handle interrupts.

#### 8.6.4.5.3 Security handling

Security in the QTMR is divided into the following categories:
* NS-bit-based protection of each physical or virtual timer frame. This is programmable by setting the `QTMR_AC_CNTSR[NSN]` field.
* Protection of individual features of V1 view of a frame. This is programmable by setting the `QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n` register.
* Protection of individual features of V2 view of a frame. This is programmable by setting the `QTMR_V1_CNTPL0ACR` register.

#### 8.6.4.5.4 Exception handling

When an interrupt is asserted in QTMR module, it can be handled in two ways:
* Either mask the interrupt by setting the corresponding `IMSK` bit of the `*_CNTP_CTL` or `*_CNTV_CTL` register, or
* Reprogram the timer such that the condition that asserted the interrupt is no longer valid.

### 8.6.4.6 QTMR APSS specifics

There are seven timer frames (F0-F6) dedicated to Application Subsystem (APSS). Frame 0 supports second view, while all the other timer frames support only the first view. Each timer frame has an optional virtual timer.

### 8.6.5.3 QTMR_AC register definitions

Addresses are offsets from zero. When constants are exported, they are re-assigned to the appropriate base address.

Only word accesses are supported on these registers. Byte and half-word accesses are not supported.

There are three types of security treatment of QTMR registers:
* **Restricted** indicates that only secure requests may access this register. If nonsecure accesses are attempted, writes are ignored and read return zero.
* **NSN dependent** indicates that secure request can access this register regardless of the QTMR access control register setting. The nonsecure request can access this register, depending on the value set in the QTMR access control register. For nonsecure accesses to restricted QTMR register, writes are ignored and read return zero.
* **Both** indicate that secure and nonsecure requests may access this register.

#### 8.6.5.3.1 0x0000 0000 QTMR_AC_CNTFRQ

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

Counter frequency register. Counter frequency in ticks per second.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTFRQ | Counter frequency in ticks per second |
<!-- page 3158 -->
#### 8.6.5.3.2 0x0000 0004 QTMR_AC_CNTSR

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Restricted

The counter secure register (CNTSR) contains a bit for secure access to each timer frame, including both views of the timer frame and the access to the associated CNTACR and CNTVOFF registers in the access control region.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6:0 | NSN | Nonsecure access to frame N. N lies from 0 to NUM_FRAME-1 (number of configured frames)<br/>* `0x0`: `SECURE_ONLY` (Secure access only - nonsecure access is RAZ/WI)<br/>* `0x1`: `SECURE_OR_NONSECURE` (Secure or nonsecure access) |

#### 8.6.5.3.3 0x0000 0008 QTMR_AC_CNTTID

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Both

The counter timer ID (CNTTID) is 32-bit register that identifies the number of timer frames implemented, which frames have virtual offsets and timers, and which frames have second views.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:28 | F7_CFG | Frame 7 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 27:24 | F6_CFG | Frame 6 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 23:20 | F5_CFG | Frame 5 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 19:16 | F4_CFG | Frame 4 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 15:12 | F3_CFG | Frame 3 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 11:8 | F2_CFG | Frame 2 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 7:4 | F1_CFG | Frame 1 configuration (same definition as Frame 0) |
| 3:0 | F0_CFG | Frame 0 configuration:<br/>* `0x3`: `RSVD` (Reserved (Read as zero))<br/>* `0x2`: `FPLO` (Frame has second view)<br/>* `0x1`: `FVI` (Virtual frame implemented)<br/>* `0x0`: `FI` (Frame implemented) |
<!-- page 3159 -->
#### 8.6.5.3.4 0x0000 0040+0x4*n QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n, n=[0..6]

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Controlled by `QTMR_AC_CNTSR[NSN]` field

The Counter Access Control Register (CNTACR) provide access control to the individual elements of timer frame n, including the second view of that timer frame n.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 5 | RWPT | Read/Write access to `CNTP_*` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |
| 4 | RWVT | Read/Write access to `CNTV_*` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |
| 3 | RVOFF | Read access to `CNTVOFF` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |
| 2 | RFRQ | Read access to `CNTFRQ` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |
| 1 | RPVCT | Read access to `CNTVCT` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |
| 0 | RPCT | Read access to `CNTPCT` register<br/>* `0x0`: `ACCESS_DENIED` (Access denied)<br/>* `0x1`: `ACCESS_ALLOWED` (Access allowed) |

#### 8.6.5.3.5 0x0000 0080+0x8*n QTMR_AC_CNTVOFF_LO_n, n=[0..6]

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Controlled by `QTMR_AC_CNTSR[NSN]` field

The lower 32 bits of Virtual Offset register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTVOFF_LO | Lower bits [31:0] of virtual offset for Frame n |
<!-- page 3160 -->
#### 8.6.5.3.6 0x0000 0084+0x8*n QTMR_AC_CNTVOFF_HI_n, n=[0..6]

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `GCC_APSS_AHB_CLK`
* **Reset State:** `0x00000000`
* **Security Treatment:** Controlled by `QTMR_AC_CNTSR[NSN]` field

The upper 32 bits of Virtual Offset register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 23:0 | CNTVOFF_HI | Higher bits [31:0] of virtual offset for Frame n |

<!-- page 3163 -->
The Physical Timer Compare Value register is compare against the CNTPCT counter. The interrupt signal is asserted when the CNTPCT counter is greater than equal to CNTP_CVAL.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTP_CVAL_L0 | Lower bits [31:0] of compare value for interrupt for Frame |

#### 8.6.5.4.10 0x0000 0024 QTMR_V1_CNTP_CVAL_HI

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWPT] bit

The Physical Timer Compare Value register is compared against the CNTPCT counter. The interrupt signal is asserted when the CNTPCT counter is greater than equal to CNTP_CVAL.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 23:0 | CNTP_CVAL_HI | Higher bits [31:0] of compare value for interrupt for Frame |

#### 8.6.5.4.11 0x0000 0028 QTMR_V1_CNTP_TVAL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWPT] bit

An alternative 32-bit TVAL view to provide read or write CVAL register.

The TVAL reads:

TVAL = (CVAL - CNTP)

The TVAL writes CVAL with:

CVAL = (CNTP + signExtend(TVAL))

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTP_TVAL | Timer value in tick per second for Frame |
<!-- page 3164 -->
#### 8.6.5.4.12 0x0000 002C QTMR_V1_CNTP_CTL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWPT] bit

The Physical Timer Control Register, which can disable the timer and, can mask its interrupt. If the timer is disabled, interrupts are masked, but the timer value continues to count down.

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2 | ISTAT | R | Interrupt status before masking (Read Only)<br>0x0: INTERRUPT_NOT_PENDING<br>0x1: INTERRUPT_PENDING |
| 1 | IMSK | RW | Mask interrupt<br>0x0: UNMASK_INTERRUPT<br>0x1: MASK_INTERRUPT |
| 0 | EN | RW | Enable timer<br>0x0: DISABLED<br>0x1: ENABLED |

#### 8.6.5.4.13 0x0000 0030 QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_LO

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWVT] bit

The Virtual Timer Compare Value register is compared against the CNTVCT counter. The interrupt signal is asserted when the CNTVCT counter is greater than or equal to CNTV_CVAL. This register is functional if FVI (Virtual Frame implemented) for the Frame n is set in QTMR_AC_CNTTID register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTV_CVAL_L0 | Lower bits [31:0] of compare value for interrupt for Frame n |

#### 8.6.5.4.14 0x0000 0034 QTMR_V1_CNTV_CVAL_HI

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWVT] bit
<!-- page 3165 -->
The Virtual Timer Compare Value register is compared against the CNTVCT counter. The interrupt signal is asserted when the CNTVCT counter is greater than equal to CNTV_CVAL. This register is functional if FVI (Virtual Frame implemented) for the Frame n is set in QTMR_AC_CNTTID register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 23:0 | CNTV_CVAL_HI | Higher bits [31:0] of compare value for interrupt for Frame n |

#### 8.6.5.4.15 0x0000 0038 QTMR_V1_CNTV_TVAL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWVT] bit

An alternative 32-bit TVAL view to provide read or write CVAL register.

The TVAL reads:

TVAL = (CVAL - (CNTP - CNTVOFF)

The TVAL writes CVAL with:

CVAL = (CNTP - CNTVOFF) + signExtend(TVAL)

This register is functional if FVI (virtual Frame implemented) for the Frame n is set in QTMR_AC_CNTTID register.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | CNTV_TVAL | Timer value in ticks per second for Frame |

#### 8.6.5.4.16 0x0000 003C QTMR_V1_CNTV_CTL

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** GCC_APSS_TCU_CLK

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_AC_CNTACR_n [RWVT] bit

The virtual timer control register, which can disable the timer and, can mask its interrupt. If the timer is disabled, interrupts are masked, but the timer value continues to count down.
<!-- page 3166 -->
This register is functional if FVI (virtual Frame implemented) for the Frame n is set in QTMR_AC_CNTTID register.

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2 | ISTAT | R | Interrupt Status before masking (Read Only)<br>0x0: INTERRUPT_NOT_PENDING<br>0x1: INTERRUPT_PENDING |
| 1 | IMSK | RW | Mask interrupt<br>0x0: UNMASK_INTERRUPT<br>0x1: MASK_INTERRUPT |
| 0 | EN | RW | Enable timer<br>0x0: DISABLED<br>0x1: ENABLED |

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

**Security Treatment:** Controlled by QTMR_V1_CNTPL0ACR[PL0CTEN] bit

An alternative 32-bit TVAL view to provide read or write CVAL register.

The TVAL reads:

TVAL = (CVAL - (CNTP - CNTVOFF)

The TVAL writes CVAL with:

CVAL = (CNTP - CNTVOFF) + signExtend(TVAL)
