## 8.7 Bus Access Manager (BAM)
This section describes the bus access manager instances available in the SoC.

### 8.7.1 BAM overview
BAM is a component inserted between the peripheral module and the subsystem bus to act like DMA engine. It is designed to provide high throughput data flows for peripheral-to-peripheral devices and peripheral-to-software (both ways) running on the chip.

There are three variants of BAM instances integrated in the SoC:
* **BAM**: full performance version of BAM module.
* **BAM-lite**: an optimized version of BAM module–gathers slow peripherals and provides them with BAM capability.
* **BAM-NDP**: Non-data path version of BAM module–enables peripherals with fast fabric connectivity to access the data directly.

The BAM notifies the peripheral on data/space and addresses, and the peripheral notify the BAM on transferred data (and addresses).

BAM-NDP's software interface to the driver is similar to the BAM interface.

Figure 8-34 shows a high-level overview of BAM instances.
<!-- page 3172 -->

#### Figure 8-34: BAM overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the integration of various BAM (Bus Access Manager) instances within the SoC.
- **System NoC** connects to **USB HS BAM** (associated with USB 2.0 HS).
- **BAM-Lite** is positioned between peripherals (**BLSP**, **SDCC2**) and the system.
- **BAM-NDP** (Non-Data Path) instances are associated with **QDSS** and **Crypto5**.
- **SDCC1** is connected to the **Peripheral and system configuration NoC**.
- Other system components shown include: Audio / Codec Digital, LPA, RPM, MPM2, TCSR, Clock Ctl, SPDM, PMIC_ARB (connected via SPMI), PDM, Security controller, PRNG, TLMM, MSG RAM, Boot ROM, TIC, and Other CFG.

BAM module supports the following main features:
* BAM to BAM: direct data exchange between two peripherals
* System producer to BAM connections in which data blocks of an arbitrary size and at any address are gathered by hardware from memory.
* BAM to system consumer connection in which data is scattered by hardware into data blocks of an arbitrary size at any address boundary in memory.
* Multiple pipe connections with other BAMs (consumer/producer) or system memory for transferring and receiving data; only one pipe connection is active at a time.
* Pipe interleaving, an active pipe may be switched to efficient performance.
<!-- page 3173 -->

* Sideband signaling about available data to read or space available to write.
* Bursts or busy states on the peripheral side data AHB bus. (Not supported for BAM-lite)
* AHB error response values for recording. (Not supported for BAM-lite)
* Data retransmission in which producer may retransmit a block from the beginning and consumer may read a block from the beginning according to the retransmission mechanism. (Not supported for BAM-lite)
* Secured BAMs have an integrated APU to protect the BAM and the peripheral registers from malicious accesses.
* Power save mode in two implementations:
  * Inactivity counter that sends an interrupt to software about an inactive connection
  * Clock request mechanism that allows clock-gating of some inactive blocks
* Three operational pipe modes:
  * **SPS**: BAM works with either another BAM or with a system producer/consumer.
  * **Direct**: BAM passes through the data received from the peripheral module without altering it. (Not supported for BAM-lite)
  * **Legacy (BAM-disabled mode)**: Data from the peripheral completely bypasses BAM (via an external mux). (Not supported for BAM-lite)

### 8.7.3 BAM functional description
BAM connects to a peripheral component with a bridge component, which allows existing peripherals to add BAM when they are integrated into the system. Alternately, the bridge component integrates directly within the peripheral. The peripheral driver controls the bridge component.

The AMBA high performance bus (AHB) slave is the internal data interface between BAM and the peripheral. The AHB master is the gateway to the external AHB bus at the dedicated bus clock.

The system consists of several peripherals with BAMs connected on a bus structure. The hardware design is modular and therefore, the peripherals within the system vary between targets. For specific information about system peripherals with BAMs, see Section 8.7.3.6.

Figure 8-36 shows a high-level overview of BAM functional blocks.
<!-- page 3177 -->

#### Figure 8-36: BAM functional block diagram
*Description:* A block diagram showing the internal functional blocks of the BAM and its interfaces.
- **Interfaces**:
  - **Configuration AHB slave** connects via a **Configuration AHB bridge** to the internal configuration interface. It is protected by a **Secure block** (with **APU** and **AHB2CRIFC**).
  - **Data AHB master** connects to the **AHB arbiter** and is associated with **VMIDMT**.
  - **Internal data AHB slave** connects to the peripheral's internal data AHB.
  - **Interrupt AHB master** is also present.
  - **Sideband signals** interface with the **Sideband generation block**.
- **Internal Blocks**:
  - **BAM register block**
  - **Descriptor and event handler**
  - **Sideband generation block**
  - **Pipe state machines**
  - **AHB buffer**
  - **BOB** (BAM Operational Block) connected to the AHB arbiter.

* **Internal data AHB slave interface**: The data interface between BAM and the peripheral. When BAM is enabled, all data transfers go through this block, including both pipe mode and direct mode transfers. It includes standard AHB signals and is compliant with the AHB specification. It also handles sideband signals concatenated to the AHB bus to ensure synchronization between the BAM and the peripheral when needed.
* **Sideband signals**: Additional signals used by BAM that are valid during the AHB address phase, similar to other AHB control signals. The following sideband signals are used:
  * **PIPE_NUMBER [4:0]**: Pipe number being accessed.
  * **BLOCK_END**: Marks the end of a block from the peripheral (used in producer pipes); active on the address phase of the last AHB burst of a produced block or as a standalone message together with the `MESSAGING_ONLY` signal.
  * **TRANSACTION_END**: Marks the end of a transaction from the peripheral (used in producer pipes). Can be active on the address phase of the last AHB burst of a produced transaction or as a standalone message together with the `MESSAGING_ONLY` signal. When asserted, `BLOCK_END` must also be asserted.
  * **RETRANSMISSION**: Marks the data of the AHB transfer as retransmitted data. When this signal is asserted, both `DIRECT_MODE` and `MESSAGING_ONLY` are 0. This signal is active on the first address phase of the retransmitted AHB burst.
<!-- page 3178 -->

  * **MESSAGING_ONLY**: When the peripheral (as producer) wants to notify BAM that the last transmitted block was the end of a transaction without sending new data to the pipe, a single AHB transfer is sent with this bit set to 1 and `TRANSACTION_END` set to 1. The data phase of this transfer is disregarded.
  * **DIRECT_MODE**: This signal reflects the pipe operating mode:
    * When 1, the peripheral accesses the system memory space directly using the entire 32 bits of the `HADDR`. The address remains unchanged and the AHB transfer is directed to the external data AHB.
    * When 0, the peripheral accesses the pipe memory; the address is treated as a logical address, and the additional signaling is used to determine the pipe being accessed and its cause.

> [!NOTE]
> When the peripheral is not working with a pipe (`DIRECT_MODE` is set to 1), the bus is treated as a standard AHB interface. Otherwise, the BAM uses the signals and the sideband signaling to operate in pipe mode.

* **Configuration AHB interface**: Used to access the registers in BAM and peripherals.
* **BAM register block**: Contains the configuration registers of BAM and its pipes. It also:
  * Provides software access to the registers through the configuration AHB bus.
  * Software can also access the peripheral through this bus by not selecting the BAM selection bit in the address (using generic `BAM_CONF_AHBS_ADDR_WIDTH-1`).
  * BAM decodes software accesses; if BAM access is detected, BAM converts them to a simplified RAM access protocol in the BAM configuration bridge.
  * BAM registers are divided into two groups with one residing in RAM and the other in flip-flops (control, interrupt, and general BAM registers; though not duplicated in each pipe).
  * Because one bus limits a peripheral to one pipe at a time, BAM can handle only one pipe at a time (even though it operates many pipes).
  * Once a pipe switch is required, BAM switches context to the required pipe by storing the previous pipe's state and loading the new pipe's state.
  * Includes a RAM controller state machine that manages RAM access. Access can be software or internal BAM accesses for context storage and loading.
* **BAM operational block (BOB)**: Separates the data buses, both internal and external, from the pipe state machine. Pipe state machine does not fetch descriptors or generate control information on the AHB. Rather it requests an external agent. Additionally, the pipes handle control information to the AHB data, but not the data itself.
* **Pipe state machines**: Hardware logic that controls the pipes, which work at any time with a single pipe. The AHB slave, based on the request from the peripheral, determines the active pipe. Parameters for all pipes are stored in dedicated RAM; then, they are loaded and stored by the pipe context switch operation each time the peripheral changes the `PIPE_NUMBER` (indicating concatenation to the AHB address phase).
<!-- page 3179 -->

* **Pipe sideband generation**: The signal generation engine based on register values, pipe state, and information from the descriptor and event handler.
* **Descriptor and event handler**: Main functions are to:
  * Fetch and write descriptors.
  * Execute the read and write events to peer BAM components.
  * Consolidate all descriptor and events from all pipes into a single point of AHB requests to the external bus.
* **AHB buffer**: Used for data aggregation, alignment, and read prefetch for enhanced external AHB performance.
* **Interrupt AHB master**: Present for every pipe and responsible for outputting the sideband signals. It receives inputs from the AHB slave interface, the pipe state machine, and the descriptor and event handler to send information to the peripheral.
* **AHB arbiter**: A standard AHB arbiter for bus access between the descriptors, events, pipe data, and direct memory. It uses a fair round robin scheme to ensure in-order execution of pending AHB accesses (as long as the bus requests are in order).
* **Data AHB master**: The gateway to the external AHB bus at the dedicated bus clock.
* **Secure block**: The AHB slave (configuration) security. Unlike secured BAMs that have an integrated APU to protect from untrusted access, the non-secure BAM does not have one.
* **VMIDMT (Virtual machine ID mapping table)**: The AHB master (data) security.

> [!NOTE]
> For more information about APU and VMIDMT, see Section 8.7.3.5.

#### 8.7.3.1 BAM power and clock management

##### 8.7.3.1.1 BAM clock
`BAM_CLK` is BAM functional clock and drives the BAM state machines and operational modules. BAM can actively request this clock.

When BAM needs the `BAM_CLK`, it sets the `BAM_CLOCK_REQUEST` signal to 1.

BAM clears the signal to 0 when the bus clock is no longer required, starting from the ensuing clock cycle.
* On reset, the `BAM_CLOCK_REQUEST` is 1 until the internal registers have completed the reset procedures.
* Once asleep since staying idle, BAM may request clock periodically to support the inactivity clock domain pulse detected by BAM's clock domain.
* Once a `BAM_CLK` is received and the inactivity counter of each pipe is updated, the `BAM_CLOCK_REQUEST` returns to 0.

This request expects the `BAM_CLOCK` to be available within 2^(INACTIVITY_TIMER_WIDTH-1) cycles of the inactivity clock, allowing the maximum delay for setting the clock when using BAM and the inactivity clocks in the same frequency range.
<!-- page 3180 -->

> [!NOTE]
> `BAM_CLK` should be faster than `INACTIVITY_TIMERS_CLOCK`.

##### 8.7.3.1.2 Inactivity timer clock
`INACTIVITY_TIMERS_CLOCK` drives a slow time counter that does not need high accuracy.

This clock has two modes (hardware generic-based):
* **Timer per pipe**: All pipes track activity for an active pipe in case of lengthy inactivity, which may indicate a problem.
* **Global timer (single timer for all pipes)**: Like timer per pipe, but it monitors and notifies inactivity of all the active pipes within BAM.

#### 8.7.3.2 BAM reset options
There are two ways to reset the BAM: software reset and hardware reset. Both methods have the same effect.

After BAM reset, all registers are in their default values, and all state machines return to their idle-state.

##### 8.7.3.2.1 BAM hardware reset
BAM has an asynchronous reset (`ASYNC_RST`). This reset is accessible from the block control register of the corresponding module. For more information, see section GCC reset controller in chapter Clock Management (GCC).

##### 8.7.3.2.2 BAM software reset
BAM could be reset synchronously via register write. User should write 1 to the `BAM_CTRL [BAM_SW_RST]`, then write 0. Once the second write (0) operation is done, BAM would be out of reset.

> [!NOTE]
> BAM software reset is invalid if security is enabled and `BAM_TRUST_REG [BAM_RST_BLOCK]` is 0.

BAM has a universal software-controlled BAM reset; each pipe contains its own software-controlled reset.


<!-- page 3181 -->

### Table 8-171 BAM reset and enable

| To reset the | Do this |
| :--- | :--- |
| Whole register space (includes all pipes and all RAM-based registers in BAM) | Set the BAM_SW_RST bit in BAM_CTRL register. Software should wait several clock cycles before deasserting this bit (to 0). |
| Register space of the selected pipe (includes all RAM-based registers) | Set the P_SW_RST bit in each BAM_P_RSTn register.<br>The pipe software reset bit is self-deasserting (the register is write only so always returns 0 on read). Software must set bit to 0 to complete the pipe reset.<br>A delay is unnecessary here–in BAM to BAM mode, both ends of the pipe should reset simultaneously.<br>For example, to reset…<br>- Assert pipe reset at BAM 1 (write 1)<br>- Assert pipe reset at BAM 2 (write 1)<br>- Deassert pipe reset at BAM 1 (write 0)<br>- Deassert pipe reset at BAM 2 (write 0) |

The BAM_EN bit in the BAM_CTRL register controls whether any data from the peripheral module enters BAM in case that BAM has bypass (BAM_HAS_NO_BYPASS bit is low in the BAM_REVISION register).

> [!NOTE]
> Each pipe has a P_EN bit in its BAM_P_CTRLn register. If a peripheral attempt to access a disabled pipe, a fatal error occurs in BAM (see Table 8-172).

BAM is reset, either during initial bring-up or when in an error state, through the BAM_SW_RST. This reset disables BAM. After a reset, during the initial bring-up stage, BAM is enabled using the BAM_EN bit.

> [!NOTE]
> Once enabled, the only way to disable BAM is to reset it; setting a P_SW_RST bit is unnecessary.

During chip operation, software should use P_EN and P_SW_RST bits to change the pipe mode for the relevant pipes.

#### 8.7.3.2.3 Pipe software reset

> [!NOTE]
> Pipe software reset should be done only when the pipe is empty, that is, no data-transfer is ongoing.

Pipe software reset is done by writing 1 to the BAM_P_RSTn [P_SW_RST], then writing 0. The zero-write operation would finish only when the PIPE reset process is done. After pipe software reset, all configuration registers of the pipe must be reconfigured.

In case of PEER pipe, pipe software reset should be done to both the PEER pipes.
<!-- page 3182 -->

#### 8.7.3.2.4 Peripheral acknowledgment

BAM reflects the pipe software reset status to the peripheral, and waits for acknowledgment from the peripheral that it finished its pipe software reset from its side, then the BAM starts its own pipe software reset operation.

There are two kinds of peripherals from the pipe software reset perspective; peripherals that supports pipe software reset, does the pipe software reset internally, without software involvements and return acknowledgment software must ensure that incase peripheral doesn't support acknowledging pipe software reset, BAM_CNFG_REG [BAM_NO_EXT_P_RST] is set, otherwise pipe software reset would get stuck.

In case peripheral doesn't support pipe software reset hardware, software must reset the pipe in the peripheral, and hold the reset state until BAM pipe software reset is done, and only after that, the peripheral is allowed to exit the pipe software reset. Pipe must be reconfigured and enabled after peripheral is out of pipe reset state.

### 8.7.3.3 BAM interrupts

BAM has up to eight interrupts lane, one for each execution environment (EE) (see Section 8.7.3.6 for integration details). In case security is disabled, BAM works only with one EE, thus uses only bit 0 of the BAM_IRQ bus. The execution environment of the BAM, and of each of its pipes are configurable.

Apart from the BAM specific interrupt, BAM also outputs APU interrupts, which are the APU secured interrupt and APU non-secured interrupt.

> [!NOTE]
> When security is not used, or when the APU is not active (but is present - all accesses approved), interrupts are output on the interrupt line designated for EE0.
> When security is used, software must set up each pipe its interrupt output lane. By default, a pipe uses the EE0 interrupt output lane.

BAM specific interrupt are fully configured, each EE has a separate IRQ interrupt that indicates an interrupt was raised within the EE. An IRQ interrupt may indicate an interrupt in the BAM (incase the BAM belongs to the EE) or an interrupt that was raised from a pipe of the EE. There are two levels of interrupt masking, Figure 8-37 explains the interrupts masking scheme.

#### 8.7.3.3.1 Interrupts mechanism

The SPS interrupt sources are in a single interrupt controller block, which can provide an interrupt controller interface to each system CPU that requires SPS services.

The interrupt controller can route:
- Any of the interrupt sources to each controller
- Sources out of SPS to the CPUs' primary interrupt controllers.
<!-- page 3183 -->

After receiving an interrupt from BAM:
- The BAM_IRQ bit set in the BAM_IRQ_SRCS indicates that a BAM general interrupt occurred
  - BAM_IRQ_STTS register describes the cause of the outgoing interrupt
- Each set bit in P_IRQ indicates that an interrupt occurred for a specific pipe
  - BAM_P_IRQ_STTSn describes the cause for the ongoing interrupt

Figure 8-37 shows the BAM interrupt scheme.

#### Figure 8-37: BAM interrupt scheme

```mermaid
graph TD
    BAM_IRQ_STTS[BAM interrupt status RO]
    BAM_IRQ_EN[BAM interrupt enable RW]
    BAM_IRQ_STTS & BAM_IRQ_EN --> AND1[Bitwise AND]
    AND1 --> BAM_IRQ_SRCS[BAM interrupt sources RO]
    
    BAM_IRQ_SRCS --> AND3[Bitwise AND]
    BAM_IRQ_MSK[BAM interrupt mask RW]
    BAM_IRQ_MSK --> AND3
    AND3 --> BAM_GLOBAL_MSK[BAM global interrupt source masked]
    
    P_IRQ_STTS["Pipe interrupt status[n] RO"]
    P_IRQ_EN["Pipe interrupt enable[n] RW"]
    P_IRQ_STTS & P_IRQ_EN --> AND2[Bitwise AND]
    
    AND2 --> AHB_SEL[AHB pipe interrupt selector]
    
    INT_AHB_MASTER[Interrupt AHB master]
    
    BAM_GLOBAL_MSK --> AND4[Bitwise AND]
    AHB_SEL --> AND5[Bitwise AND]
    INT_AHB_MASTER --> AND4 & AND5
    
    AND4 & AND5 --> AND6[Bitwise AND]
    AND6 --> BAM_IRQ[BAM_IRQ line]
```

*Description:* A logic diagram showing the masking and routing of BAM interrupts.
- **BAM Interrupt path:** The BAM interrupt status register (BAM_IRQ_STTS, Read-Only) is bitwise ANDed with the BAM interrupt enable register (BAM_IRQ_EN, Read-Write) to produce the BAM interrupt sources (Read-Only). These sources are then bitwise ANDed with the BAM interrupt mask register (BAM_IRQ_MSK, Read-Write) to produce the BAM global interrupt source masked.
- **Pipe Interrupt path:** For each pipe `n`, the Pipe interrupt status register (`BAM_P_IRQ_STTSn`, Read-Only) is bitwise ANDed with the Pipe interrupt enable register (`BAM_P_IRQ_ENn`, Read-Write) to produce the pipe's interrupt.
- **Routing and Output:** The masked pipe interrupts are routed through the AHB pipe interrupt selector. The BAM global interrupt source masked, the selected pipe interrupts, and the Interrupt AHB master signal are combined through bitwise AND gates to produce the final `BAM_IRQ` line.

Table 8-172 and Table 8-173 show interrupt handling.
<!-- page 3184 -->

### Table 8-172 BAM interrupt handling

| Interrupt | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| BAM_ERROR_IRQ | Indicates a fatal error in BAM, which might occur after an unsuccessful pipe reset operation only. Software should reset the whole BAM. |
| BAM_HRESP_ERR_IRQ | Indicates that an error response received by BAM AHB master when accessing the bus; can be used to debug illegal memory address accesses. BAM_AHB_MASTER_ERR_* registers contain the error information as recorded in BAM. To clear this interrupt, reset BAM. |

### Table 8-173 Pipe interrupt handling

| Pipe interrupt | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| P_SW_RESET_ERROR_IRQ | Indicate an unsuccessful pipe reset operation, for this specific pipe. |
| P_HRESP_ERR_IRQ | Indicates that an error response received by BAM AHB master when accessing the bus, via the specific pipe access (data, descriptor or event); can be used to debug illegal memory address accesses. BAM_AHB_MASTER_ERR_* registers contain the error information as recorded in BAM. |
| P_PRCSD_DESC_IRQ | (Only for system modes) Issued when BAM processes a descriptor with an INT bit set.<br>Software may want to add more descriptors for BAM to work with and update the P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST field in BAM_P_EVNT_REGn. |
| P_TIMER_IRQ | Inactivity timer has expired; used to detect an inactive pipe. Pipe is active when accessed by a peripheral. If the BAM is performing pipe operations (descriptor reading) but peripheral does not access pipe, it remains inactive. |
| P_WAKE_IRQ | Triggered when a peer BAM or system producer or consumer writes to this BAM's event register. |
| P_OUT_OF_DESC_IRQ | Usually indicates an error; used for debug; software may add descriptors or configure a larger FIFO for pipe.<br>- In BAM with system producer/both consumers, the interrupt fires when a descriptor is needed in pipe but there are no more in the descriptor FIFO. Indicates to software that descriptors should be added to descriptor FIFO.<br>- In BAM as producer and another BAM as consumer: indicates erroneous configuration. Data has been written to data buffer and with no room in descriptor buffer to create a descriptor. Avoid by providing a bigger descriptor buffer. |
| P_ERR_IRQ | (Not used) Pipe error interrupt indicating an error occurred. |
| P_TRNSFR_END_IRQ | For producer BAM, triggered when the peripheral sends an EOT. For consumer, triggered when the peripheral acknowledges enough data has been consumed to close a transfer (selected with EOT bit in descriptor). |
<!-- page 3185 -->

#### 8.7.3.3.2 Interrupts configuration

To set BAM interrupts there are multiple registers which must be configured, starting with the BAM_IRQ_SRCS register, these registers define if one the BAM global interrupts is to be enabled or any of the pipe's interrupts. In case of using more than one EE, each EE would have its specific BAM_IRQ_SRCS_MSK_EEi [0-7] register.

Other than enabling the interrupts group (BAM-global or pipe), the desired interrupt group must also be masked via BAM_IRQ_SRCS_MSK_EEi [0-7]; for the interrupt group to cause and interrupt assertion on the IRQ interrupts lane, the group must be enabled in the BAM_IRQ_SRCS_EEi and set to 1 the matching bit in the BAM_IRQ_SRCS_MSK_EEi.

To indicate which interrupt of the interrupts-group may cause IRQ lane assertion, the matching bit in the BAM_P_IRQ_ENn must be set (for the pipe interrupts group), or BAM_IRQ_EN for the BAM global interrupt.

### 8.7.3.4 BAM operation

#### 8.7.3.4.1 Pipe overview

Data transactions occur between a producer, which has data to transfer, and a consumer to which it transfers the data. The producer and the consumer communicate through a pipe, which is an abstraction of a unidirectional data channel, containing some memory components and a set of configuration parameters.

Figure 8-38 presents the general overview of BAM operation. Section 8.7.3.4.3 and Section 8.7.3.4.4 provide more specific details depending on the used mode.

#### Figure 8-38: BAM data flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Producer
    participant DataMemory as Data Memory
    participant DescriptorFIFO as Descriptor FIFO
    participant Consumer

    Producer->>DataMemory: Writes Data
    Producer->>DescriptorFIFO: Writes Descriptor
    Producer->>Consumer: Creates write event
    Consumer->>DataMemory: Reads Data
    Consumer->>DescriptorFIFO: Reads Descriptor
    Consumer->>Producer: Sends read event
```

*Description:* A sequence diagram representing the basic data flow between a Producer and a Consumer in BAM.
1. The Producer writes data to the Data Memory.
2. The Producer writes the corresponding descriptor to the Descriptor FIFO.
3. The Producer triggers a write event to notify the Consumer.
4. The Consumer reads the descriptor from the Descriptor FIFO.
5. The Consumer reads the data from the Data Memory.
6. The Consumer sends a read event back to the Producer to acknowledge consumption of the data.

The producer and consumer may either both be hardware peripherals (BAM-to-BAM transaction mode) or one of them may be system process (system transaction mode).
<!-- page 3186 -->

A pipe describes one data flow, so a peripheral that communicates simultaneously on a number of channels requires several pipes. One example is a USB module, where each endpoint is mapped to a distinct pipe.

The BAM filters the communication between the peripheral modules and the pipe. The BAM notifies the peripheral of the current pipe state and manages data transfer between the peripheral and the pipe (for BAM and BAM-lite).

A pipe is set up with one or two continuous cyclic buffers:
1. **Data FIFO:** A relatively small block of memory organized as a circular buffer, used only in BAM-to-BAM mode. In this case, the producer writes the data to the data FIFO (and the matching descriptors to the descriptor FIFO), while the consumer reads the data from the data FIFO (after reading the matching descriptors from the descriptor FIFO). In system transactions, data transfer is through the system memory.
2. **Descriptor FIFO:** Another memory block through which peripheral reads or write descriptors of the data to be transferred and other further information (see Section 8.7.3.4.2). Descriptor FIFO is the main communication between the producer and the consumer. Producer (BAM or System) generates descriptor and puts them in the descriptor FIFO, after filling the data in the relevant memory places (defined by the descriptors), while the consumer reads those descriptors from the descriptor FIFO, to know where to read the produced data from.

Typically, the data and descriptor FIFOs are local to the peripheral subsystem to achieve maximum performance. However, they may be located anywhere in the system.

> [!NOTE]
> The maximum supported size of the data FIFO is 32K-1.

#### Pipe descriptors

Figure 8-39 presents the BAM pipe descriptor structure:

#### Figure 8-39: Descriptor structure

| DWORD | Bits | Field Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DWORD 0** | [31:0] | Data Start Address LSB | Lower 32 bits of the physical address of the data buffer. |
| **DWORD 1** | [15:0] | Descriptor Size | Number of bytes to transfer (maximum size is 32K-1). |
| | [19:16] | Data Start Address MSB | Upper 4 bits of the physical address of the data buffer (for 36-bit addressing). |
| | [31:20] | Flags | Control flags for the descriptor transfer:<br>- **INT** (bit 31): Generate interrupt on processing.<br>- **EOT** (bit 30): End of Transfer.<br>- **EOB** (bit 29): End of Block.<br>- **NWD** (bit 28): Notify Write Descriptor.<br>- **CMD** (bit 27): Command descriptor (commands to peripheral instead of data).<br>- **LOCK**: Lock bus group.<br>- **UNLOCK**: Unlock bus group.<br>- **IMM**: Immediate data flag. |

*Description:* The BAM pipe descriptor is a 64-bit structure consisting of two 32-bit words (DWORD 0 and DWORD 1). DWORD 0 contains the lower 32 bits of the buffer address. DWORD 1 contains the 16-bit descriptor size, the upper 4 bits of the buffer address (bits 16-19), and various control flags (bits 20-31) such as INT, EOT, EOB, NWD, CMD, LOCK, UNLOCK, and IMM.

> [!NOTE]
> The maximum descriptor size supported is 32K-1.
<!-- page 3187 -->

> [!NOTE]
> Zero size descriptor must come with EOT and supported only in BAM-lite system-consumer pipe.

- **Flags:** The following flags are supported:
  - **Interrupt (INT):** This flag is used in system consumer mode only. The software should set this bit in order to receive a notification (interrupt) from the BAM when the descriptor is completely consumed.
  - **End of transfer (EOT):** This flag is used to specify the end of transaction at the end of this descriptor.
  - **End of block (EOB):** This flag is used to specify the end of block at the end of this descriptor.
  - **Notify when done (NWD)** (only for BAM-lite and BAM-NDP): When set, NWD provides a handshake between peripheral and BAM indicating the transaction is truly done and data/command has delivered its destination.
    On receiving NWD, the peripheral asserts the signal `DONE_TOGGLE` back to the BAM only when all data associated with the transaction has been transferred to the external device or when command was completed. On the BAM end, it waits for done toggle from the peripheral before invoking any interrupt to software or processing the next descriptor.
    Software can use the NWD feature in order to make the BAM to separate between executions of consecutive descriptors. This can be useful for features like command descriptor.
    The NWD handshake is per pipe.
  - **Immediate (IMM)** (only for BAM-NDP): Allows the software to create descriptors of type immediate, which does not generate any data transmissions or registers configuration, it is simply supplied to the peripheral, the peripheral then parses its fields (which are irrelevant to the BAM). Only the flags of this descriptor are relevant to the BAM, address and size are irrelevant, and BAM simply passes them as is to the peripheral. This can be used for the software to operate peripheral-specific operations within regular data operations. Immediate descriptors are published on the sidebands as 1 byte size descriptor, once BAM_NDP fetches an immediate descriptor, it publishes all recently fetched descriptors including the immediate descriptor with immediate indication, to inform the peripheral that the last published descriptor was immediate descriptor.

> [!NOTE]
> Immediate descriptor must not have the CMD bit set.

  - **Lock/Unlock:** The lock and unlock bits are used to define a mechanism to lock certain pipes while other are in use, and is supported for command descriptors only. This provides the software to enter ordering between pipes execution. (Generally, the BAM pipes are total independent from each other and work in a parallel manner)
  - **Command (CMD)** (only for BAM-lite and BAM-NDP): Allows the software to create descriptors of type command. Descriptors of type command do not generate any data transmissions but configure registers in the peripheral (write and read registers operations).
    Using command descriptor enables the software to queue new configurations between data transfers in advance.
<!-- page 3188 -->

In command descriptor, the 36-bit address points to the start of the command block which holds the command elements and the 16-bit size defines the size of the command block.

> [!NOTE]
> Command descriptors are available only in the system mode.

#### Pipe event

Pipe event (read/write event) is a method of information passing and flow control between the producer and the consumer. It contains write/read pointers to locations in the data and descriptor FIFOs.

There are several conditions under which BAM generates a pipe event:
- **Writing to BAM_P_EVNT_REGn register:** If current BAM works as producer, it receives read events into this register from the consumer.
  - If the consumer is another BAM, it writes read events to this register.
  - If the consumer is a software process, it prepares the descriptors in the descriptor FIFO and updates the `P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST` value in this register.
- **BAM_P_EVNT_GEN_TRSHLDn register** (for BAM-to-BAM mode) configures the threshold value for read/write event generation by the BAM towards another BAM. When a BAM pushes/pops this number of bytes to/from the pipe, an event to the other BAM is generated. A counter summing up the bytes pushed/popped is reset when the event is issued, thus restarting the count for the threshold.
- **EOT:** Events are also issued after the End of Transfer (EOT) is received from the peripheral (producer case), regardless of whether the pushed bytes count has reached the threshold or not.
- **Virtual event:** Needed to prevent the case in which the producer succeeded in sending an event towards the consumer before it was halted. In that case, doing a regular event would confuse the BAM into thinking that it received a whole descriptor FIFO event.
  To construct the virtual event:
  - LSB bits of the 16-bit `SW_DESC_OFST` and MSB bit [31] is set to 1.
  - Formula: `0x1000_0000 | SW_DESC_OFST` (written to register `0x1000` BAM_P_SW_OFSTS).
  - Deassert the pipe halt at the pipe's consumer side (set 0 to `P_HALT` bit in `BAM_P_HALTn` register).

> [!NOTE]
> Read/write events are not applicable for system producers/consumers. Thus, interrupt requests are needed to inform software that the data was fully transferred.

#### Pipe operating modes

Three operational pipe modes are supported:
- **SPS (most common mode):** BAM works with another BAM serving as a producer or consumer, or with a system producer or consumer. Consequently, to operate a pipe combining producer-consumer transactions and legacy mode transactions, the peripheral must use the direct mode.
  In SPS mode, the data destination address from the peripheral module is altered by the BAM and sent to the relevant pipe.
  When the pipe works with another BAM (not with a system producer or consumer), there are...
<!-- page 3189 -->

- Each pipe may be in run or halt state, as configured by the pipe's `BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT]` bit.
  - **Run:** The normal operating state where the two BAMs connect through the pipe.
  - **Halt:** BAM does not communicate with its peer BAM over the pipe. This state is used primarily for pipe maintenance, such as pipe setup or disable to prevent loss of data or errors.
    Halt is used to temporarily stop data transfer through a BAM-to-BAM pipe. It causes a gradual pause, rather than an immediate one (see Section 8.7.3.4.5).
- **Direct (not supported for BAM-lite):** BAM passes the data received from the peripherals without altering it. When the pipe is enabled, the peripheral may choose to work either in direct mode or in SPS mode. When the pipe is disabled, direct mode is mandatory.
  In direct mode, the data flow from the peripheral is not affected by any pipe configurations.
  There are some configurations optimizing the BAM operation, see `BAM_CTRL` and `BAM_P_CTRLn` registers.
- **Legacy / BAM-disabled mode (not supported for BAM-lite):** Data from the peripheral bypasses the BAM (through an external mux). When `BAM_EN` bit is not set (BAM is not enabled), the BAM's connected peripherals work in legacy mode.
  Enabled by a hardware or software universal reset only.

Figure 8-40 shows different BAM modes and their interactions.

#### Figure 8-40: BAM software states

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Legacy Mode (BAM Disabled)" as Legacy
    state "Direct Mode" as Direct
    state "SPS Mode" as SPS
    
    [*] --> Legacy
    Legacy --> Direct : BAM_CTRL[BAM_EN] = 1
    Direct --> Legacy : BAM Reset
    Direct --> SPS : BAM_P_CTRLn[P_EN] = 1
    SPS --> Direct : BAM_P_CTRLn[P_EN] = 0
    
    state SPS {
        state "RUN" as Run
        state "HALT" as Halt
        [*] --> Run
        Run --> Halt : BAM_P_HALTn[P_HALT] = 1
        Halt --> Run : BAM_P_HALTn[P_HALT] = 0
    }
```

*Description:* State transition diagram showing the different operational modes of the BAM.
1. The BAM starts in **Legacy Mode** (disabled) after reset.
2. Enabling the BAM via `BAM_CTRL[BAM_EN] = 1` moves it to **Direct Mode**. A BAM reset returns it to Legacy Mode.
3. Enabling a specific pipe via `BAM_P_CTRLn[P_EN] = 1` moves the pipe operation into **SPS Mode**. Disabling the pipe (`P_EN = 0`) returns it to Direct Mode.
4. In SPS Mode, the pipe can be toggled between **RUN** and **HALT** states using the `BAM_P_HALTn[P_HALT]` register.
<!-- page 3190 -->

When BAM is enabled, the peripheral selects the SPS or direct mode, and it can alternate between them. The mode selected by the peripheral is not affected by the BAM configuration.

> [!NOTE]
> Software does not distinguish between direct and legacy modes.

Features of the SPS architecture:
- Software is not involved in data transfer between the two peripherals, only in configuring and starting relevant pipes.
- Interface errors are seamless: if the producer receives a packet with an error, it is not required to notify any other module.
- It writes over the space in the data FIFO containing the erroneous data. Similarly, the consumer can retransmit data not received by its link partner without buffering the entire transfer in the consumer module.
- Flow control between the producer and consumer is designed so that both sides know in advance if the other side does not have space for or data to transmit.

#### Pipe halt

##### Consumer only halt

In consumer mode, BAM stops sending bytes available information to the peripheral, causing the peripheral to stop consuming data from pipe. In case of PEER consumer, the pipe data-fifo would get filled by the PEER producer, still because the peripheral does not get any notification on the additional data (via byte_available side-band) no additional data would be transferred on the consumer pipe (that is, the consumer peripheral stops reading data from the FIFO).

If halting just the consumer side is enough for the desired effect, this is the preferred method. (On the consumer side; it has the same effect as halting both the producer and consumer sides and is simpler).
- **To invoke halt:** Assert pipe halt at the pipe's consumer side (Set `BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT]` to 1 register).
- **To remove halt:** Deassert pipe halt at pipe's consumer side (Clear `BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT]` to 0).

##### Full PEER pipes halt

To halt both PEER pipes, the PEER producer pipe is halted, thus the PEER producer pipe stops sending write events to the PEER consumer pipe, which causes the PEER consumer pipe to stop receiving information about data waiting in the pipe, thus data flow stops on both PEER pipes. This requires that software initiates the following (more complicated) flow.

1. **To initiate halt on both PEER pipes:**
   a. Invoke PEER producer pipe halt by setting the `BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT]` bit of the producer pipe.
   b. Invoke PEER consumer pipe halt by setting the `P_HALT` bit of the consumer pipe, and also setting the `P_PROD_HALTED` bits in `BAM_P_HALTn` register.
2. **To remove halt:**


<!-- page 3191 -->

a. Software reads the SW_DESC_OFST field of the BAM_P_SW_OFSTS register on the producer side-consequently, this automatically removes the producer halt.
b. Software sends a virtual write event to the consumer BAM (BAM_P_EVNT_REGn of the consumer) to notify it about the added descriptors.

##### Empty pipe

At the end of work or before pipe-SW-reset, user would want to make sure that the pipe is empty.
In system pipes, user should stop issuing events (write to BAM_P_EVNT_REGn), and wait until BAM_P_SW_OFSTS is equal to BAM_P_EVNT_REGn.

In case of PEER pipe, user should make sure the producer peripheral stops writing data, then in the producer-pipe, wait until BAM_P_EVNT_REGn is equal to BAM_P_SW_OFFSET and BAM_P_PRDCR_SDBNDn bit 16 (first bit of the BAM_P_CTRL field) is 0 (i.e. the descriptor is not full).

In case of PEER pipe, where the last descriptor generated by the producer-pipe is zero-sized descriptor with EOT, consumer-pipe will not send-an-event to the producer regarding that last descriptor (implementation constraint). Thus in that case, user should wait until BAM_P_SW_OFSTS = BAM_P_EVNT_REGn + 8 (on the producer-pipe), and make sure that last descriptor in the FIFO is zero-sized descriptor with EOT.

#### 8.7.3.4.2 Initial BAM configuration

To start working with the BAM, user should configure the BAM and it's pipes then enable it. For safer work, user should reset the BAM, before enabling it. The following should be configured prior to enabling the BAM:
1. If security is used: Trust register must be configured with the APU and VMIDMT.
2. Configure the BAM_CTRL register
3. Configure the BAM_CNFG_REG register
4. Configure the BAM_DESC_CNT_TRSHLD register (not valid for BAM-lite).
5. If inactivity timer is used, user should configure the BAM_TIMER_CTRL register (not valid for BAM-NDP)
6. Configure interrupt enabling registers (if system pipes are used, interrupts must be enabled).

##### BAM control register

BAM_CTRL register defines some basic configurations of the BAM, including the BAM_SW_RST bit.
1. BAM_EN: enable/disable the BAM operation. BAM registers and peripheral registers are accessible even when BAM is disabled.
2. BAM_EN_ACCUM: valid for direct mode in BAM only. Enables accumulation of peripheral's transactions into INCR8 burst transaction, for better bus utilization.
3. BAM_DESC_CACHE_SEL: BAM only, defines descriptor caching method, for system mode only.
4. BAM_CACHED_DESC_STORE: BAM only, controls storing of descriptor's cache in the RAM when doing context switching, for system mode only.
<!-- page 3192 -->

5. IBC_DISABLE: Disable inactivity-timer operation, for power saving, not valid for BAM-NDP.
6. LOCAL_CLOCK_GATING: Enable/disable local clock-gating for power saving.
7. CACHE_MISS_ERR_RESP_EN: (for BAM_NDP only) in case it is enabled, BAM_NDP will respond with AHB-ERROR-RESPONSE on the local_ahb interface when peripheral tries to read a descriptor that wasn't already read yet, i.e. not in the descriptor cache yet, to enable the peripheral to serve another pipe, and retry to fetch the descriptor afterwards.

   > [!NOTE]
   > This feature must be supported in the peripheral too, if not this may cause for the peripheral to hang.

8. BAM_MESS_ONLY_CANCEL_WB: BAM increments (by 8) the BAM_P_SW_OFFSET register once peripheral uses all the size of the descriptor, to release the already used descriptor. In case peripheral issues messaging-only EOT, before any more data transfer, BAM would temporally decrement the BAM_P_SW_OFFSET, write-back the EOT indication on the already released descriptor, then re-increment the BAM_P_SW_OFFSET register. Once BAM_MESS_ONLY_CANCEL_WB bit is set, BAM would simply ignore the messaging-only indication (in case the descriptor was fully used). This feature would allow the software to override the descriptor once it was released via BAM_P_SW_OFFSET, without worrying of any write-back that could occur on that descriptor.

##### BAM configuration register

BAM_CNFG register enables newly added features and bug fixes, recommended value is fffff7ff.

Make sure not to use value other than the recommended value for this register before consulting the BAM team.
1. BAM_NO_EXT_P_RST: Control whether BAM should wait for peripheral pipe software reset acknowledgment before finishing it's reset or not.
2. BAM_CD_ENABLE: Enables the command-descriptor support.

#### 8.7.3.4.3 Hardware transactions (BAM-to-BAM)

BAM-to-BAM is data transaction process, that occurs between a producer and consumer both of which are hardware peripherals with BAM.

##### BAM-to-BAM pipe configuration

To configure a producer or consumer in a pipe that works with another BAM using pipe memory (do the following for both the producer and the consumer BAMs):
1. Perform pipe software reset. If the pipe is allocated immediately after a BAM universal reset, this step can be skipped.
2. Mask or unmask the interrupts for this pipe in the corresponding bit in BAM_INTERRUPT_SOURCES_MASK register.
3. Enable the interrupts for the pipe by enabling the relevant bits in the BAM_P_IRQ_ENn register.
<!-- page 3193 -->

4. Set the address of the descriptor buffer for pipe in BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_LSB and BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_MSB registers.
5. Address should be aligned at 8 bytes and must be the same for the producer and the consumer BAMs - both use the same descriptor buffer.
6. Set the size (multiple of 8) of the pipe descriptor buffer field of BAM_P_FIFO_SIZESn register (value must be the same for the producer and the consumer BAMs, as both use the same descriptor buffer).
7. Write the data buffer address to the BAM_P_DATA_FIFO_ADDR_LSB and BAM_P_DATA_FIFO_ADDR_MSB registers. Must be the same for the producer and the consumer BAMs - both use the same data buffer.
8. Write the data buffer size to the PIPE_PHYSICAL_FIFO_SIZE field of the BAM_PIPE_PHYSICAL_FIFO_SIZE register. (Must be the same for the producer and the consumer BAMs - both use the same data buffer).
9. Set the BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR register to the peer BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR_LSB/MSB address (LSB register is aliased to the old BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR_ADDR).
   For example, pipe 7 of BAM A connects to pipe 1 of BAM B:
   a. Set BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR in (BAM A) to (BAM_B_BASE_ADDRESS + BAM BAM_P_EVNT_REG1)
   b. Set BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR (in BAM B) to (BAM_A_BASE_ADDRESS + BAM_P_EVNT_REG7).
10. Set BAM_P_EVNT_GEN_TRSHLDn [P_TRSHLD] field to define read/write event generation threshold.
    a. For a producer BAM, this field reflects the number of bytes pushed to the pipe after which BAM creates a write event to the peer BAM.
    b. For a consumer BAM, this reflects the number of bytes successfully acknowledged by the consumer after which BAM creates a read event to the peer BAM.

    > [!NOTE]
    > Make sure that the BAM_P_EVNT_GEN_TRSHLDn wouldn't cause the BAM to generate an event that fills the whole descriptor FIFO at once.

11. In BAM_PIPE_CONTROL register:
    a. Set PIPE_SYSTEM_MODE bit to 0.
    b. Set PIPE_DIRECTION bit to 1 if the BAM is a producer; otherwise, set to 0 for consumer BAM.
    c. Set BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT] bit to 1, which prevents BAM from producing write or read events to the peer BAM.
    d. Set the P_EN bit to 1.
12. After both the producer and the consumer have been configured and enabled, release both the BAM_P_HALTn [P_HALT] bits.
<!-- page 3194 -->

##### Hardware transactions data flow (BAM-to-BAM mode)

Figure 8-41 shows the BAM to BAM transaction data flow.

#### Figure 8-41: Hardware transactions data flow
*Description:* A block diagram showing the data and control flow between a BAM Producer (left) and a BAM Consumer (right) in BAM-to-BAM mode.
- At the top, a shared "Data FIFO" receives "Writes data" from the BAM Producer and provides "Reads data" to the BAM Consumer.
- At the bottom, a shared "Descriptor FIFO" receives "Writes descriptor" from the BAM Producer and provides "Reads descriptor" to the BAM Consumer.
- The BAM Producer maintains a `BAM_P_BYTES_FREE` register, and the BAM Consumer maintains a `BAM_P_BYTES_AVAIL` register.
- When the BAM Producer writes data, it "Creates write event" to update the BAM Consumer.
- When the BAM Consumer reads data, it "Sends read event" to update the BAM Producer's `BAM_P_BYTES_FREE`.
- Both BAM Producer and BAM Consumer perform "Update" operations locally.

Hardware transactions are as follows:
1. Producer BAM notifies producer that space is available in the data FIFO. Producer BAM updates BAM_P_PRDCR_SDBNDn [BAM_P_BYTES_FREE] to the producer, which can now write to the associated pipe's data FIFO.

   > [!NOTE]
   > At first, once the producer BAM (and pipe) is enabled, BAM would indicate that the whole data-FIFO is free.

2. Producer writes data to data FIFO
   a. Producer initiates write transactions to the data FIFO as the peripheral device generates the data.
   b. Producer BAM tracks the amount of space in the data FIFO of the associated pipe. When the pipe is full, the producer stops pushing data into the pipe, applying backpressure on the peripheral module. This ripples into the peripheral and flow controls the link. BAM buffers the data written from the peripheral to the data FIFO and its address adjusts to the address of the data FIFO. Even data not yet been verified to be error-free (for example, CRC-checked), and which the peripheral device could transmit, is written to the data FIFO.
3. Producer writes descriptor to the descriptor FIFO.
   a. Once the producer has written a block of data to the data FIFO, it writes a descriptor describing the block of data to the descriptor FIFO.
   b. Then, producer commits the data and cannot modify it again.
   c. Data has passed the integrity check by the peripheral (verified).
<!-- page 3195 -->

   The data block size is configurable per producer (and per pipe), and is determined in one of two ways:
   * The smallest unit of data that the producer can determine to be error free.
   * If the consumer protocol is set for a specific packet size (such as 512 B for USB bulk endpoints), the producer can optimize data transfer by using blocks of this size.

4. Producer informs consumer that data and descriptor FIFOs have been updated.
   a. Producer generates a write event notifying the consumer how many new descriptors and data has been committed to the FIFOs.
   b. A write event is generated under one of these conditions:
      * A full packet terminated by an EOT (see Figure 8-39) has been written to the data and descriptor FIFOs. (A packet comprises data with a series of descriptors).
      * Each individual descriptor written to the descriptor FIFO is reported to the consumer immediately (as a separate write event per descriptor). However, for pipes in which the consumer relates to data in units of packets, this option is used.
      * A threshold number of bytes was written to the data FIFO and committed by producer in the descriptor FIFO (this threshold is configurable per pipe).
      * Typically, this option is for pipes in which the consumer processes data without regard for packet division, such as the USB mass storage pipe. Here, the threshold is set to the size of a block of data.
5. Consumer reads descriptors from descriptor FIFO for the descriptors committed by the producer.
   Consumer BAM processes the descriptor and notifies the peripheral how much data is available in the pipe and if the pipe contains a full packet (EOT indication).
6. Consumer BAM notifies the consumer peripheral that data is available for reading from the pipe's data FIFO.
   Consumer BAM updates BYTES_AVAILABLE to the consumer peripheral, indicating the consumer can read data from pipe memory.
7. Consumer reads data from data FIFO based on the information received from the BAM.
8. Consumer informs producer that it consumed the data.
   * Consumer module acknowledges to consumer BAM that data transmitted successfully.
   * Consumer BAM generates a read event to producer BAM once a configurable number of bytes are acknowledged, indicating that number of bytes and the number of descriptors used from the descriptor FIFO.
     The consumer module cannot access acknowledged data (the data and descriptor entries are erased from the respective FIFOs).
   * Once producer BAM receives a read event from the consumer, it frees up the available space in the data FIFO and notifies producer peripheral that memory is available (updates BYTES_FREE).
<!-- page 3196 -->

#### 8.7.3.4.4 System transactions (system mode)

Data transaction process that occurs between a producer and consumer, one of which is system process, is referred as system mode. There are two options for this use case: system producer and system consumer.

##### System mode pipe configuration

To allocate a pipe in a BAM that works with a system producer or consumer (meaning with a set of I/O vectors and not with a peer BAM). Do the following for each pipe:
1. Perform pipe software reset. If the pipe is allocated immediately after a BAM universal reset, this step can be skipped.
2. Mask or unmask the interrupts for this pipe in the corresponding PIPE_IRQ_MASK bit in BAM_INTERRUPT_SOURCES_MASK register. The pipe must have its interrupts enabled.
3. Enable the interrupts for the pipe by enabling the relevant bits in the BAM_P_IRQ_ENn register. BAM_P_IRQ_ENn [P_PRCSD_DESC_IRQ] and/or BAM_P_IRQ_ENn [P_TRNSFR_END_IRQ] must be set.
4. Set the pipe descriptor FIFO address in BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_LSB and BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_MSB registers.
5. Set the size of the pipe descriptor buffer in BAM_P_FIFO_SIZESn [P_DESC_FIFO_SIZE] field.

   > [!NOTE]
   > Descriptor FIFO size must be at least 16 bytes, aligned at 8 bytes.

6. Allocate one or more system memory buffers to store the data.
7. Fill the descriptor FIFO with the needed descriptors: data descriptor, command descriptor, or immediate descriptor.
   * Prepare a list of descriptors for BAM according to the format in Section [missing].
   * Each descriptor is written to pipe descriptor FIFO address plus descriptor FIFO offset (see item 4 above). Descriptor FIFO offset is a software-maintained variable that points to the next location for a descriptor to be written.
   * The maximum number of descriptors provided to BAM at once should be at least 16 bytes (two descriptors) lower than the buffer's capacity. That is, there should be no more than descriptor-FIFO capacity minus two descriptors, outstanding for the BAM to process.
   * For each descriptor written, BAM_P_EVNT_REGn [P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST] is incremented by 8 bytes.
   * Software can set the INT bit in the descriptor to force BAM to issue an interrupt when it completes its processing. This signals the software of the progress and, if needed, to add descriptors.
     Software can get satisfied with the transfer-end interrupt that will be fired once a descriptor with EOT indication process finishes.
   * Software must wrap the writes in the descriptor circular buffer. When (DESCRIPTOR_FIFO_OFFSET = BAM_P_FIFO_SIZESn), DESCRIPTOR_FIFO_OFFSET is set to 0.
<!-- page 3197 -->

   * Update PIPE_DESCRIPTOR_FIFO_PEER_OFFSET field in BAM_P_EVNT_REGn with the new offset, according to the number of written descriptors.
     For example, if two descriptors were added, add 2 * size of(SPS_DESCRIPTOR) to DESCRIPTOR_FIFO_OFFSET and write the new value.
   * Wait for an interrupt from pipe:
     * PIPE_PROCESSED_DESCRIPTOR_INT indicates that a peripheral module processed a descriptor with a set INT bit (software may want to add more descriptors).
     * PIPE_OUT_OF_DESCRIPTORS_INT indicates BAM processed all descriptors in the descriptor FIFO (software may want to add more descriptors).
     * PIPE_TRANSFER_END_INTERRUPT (if BAM is a producer) indicates that an EOT was received from the peripheral; (if BAM is a consumer) indicates that a descriptor with the EOT bit set was processed.
   * Read the SW_FIFO_OFFSET field of the BAM_PIPE_DESCRIPTOR_FIFO_OFFSET register to get updates of the number of BAM-processed registers.

   > [!NOTE]
   > In system producer pipes, BAM increments the BAM_P_SW_OFSTS_REG once it finishes data-consuming (write data). If a messaging-only-EOT indication is received from the peripheral, BAM will temporarily decrement the BAM_P_SW_OFSTS_REG, write-back the EOT indication on the last descriptor, then re-increment the BAM_P_SW_OFSTS_REG. In order not to confuse such behavior, with a full release of the descriptor-FIFO, the software recommendation is updated to never allocate more than descriptor-FIFO minus two descriptors.

8. In the BAM_P_CTRLn register:
   * Set P_SYS_MODE bit to 1.
   * Set P_DIRECTION bit to:
     * 1 for BAM producer
     * 0 for BAM consumer
   * Set the P_EN bit to 1

##### System transactions data flow

When the producer or the consumer is a software process, the data flow is similar to the hardware transaction, but not identical.

There are two variations of system transaction data flow, depending on the use case.
<!-- page 3198 -->

##### System producer data flow

Figure 8-42 shows system producer data flow.

#### Figure 8-42: System producer transactions data flow
*Description:* A block diagram showing the data and control flow between a System Producer (software, left) and a BAM Consumer (hardware, right).
- "System memory" (top) contains the "Data buffer".
- The System Producer "Writes data" to the Data buffer, and the BAM Consumer "Reads data" from the Data buffer.
- A "Descriptor FIFO" (bottom) receives "Writes descriptor" from the System Producer and provides "Reads descriptor" to the BAM Consumer.
- The System Producer notifies the BAM Consumer of new descriptors by writing to `BAM_P_EVNT_REGn` ("Creates write event").
- The BAM Consumer performs "Update" and "Reads descriptor" / "Reads data".
- The BAM Consumer "Sends IRQ event" to update `BAM_P_IRQ_STTSn` on the System Producer side.

System producer transactions are as follows:
1. System allocates one or more system memory buffers to store the data.
2. System writes a set of descriptors to the descriptor FIFO.
   a. System notifies the BAM for location of the buffers by writing a series of descriptors to the descriptor FIFO (see Figure 8-39) describing the allocated buffers.
   b. The data start address field provides the start address of the system memory buffer. The BAM will assert an interrupt for each descriptor with INT indication or EOT indication (if the interrupt is enabled).
   c. Software notifies the BAM about the location of the descriptor FIFO via BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_LSBn and BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_MSBn.
   In this way, the software can scatter I/O vectors to the different locations in memory to which the descriptors point. Conversely, for a system producer, the consumer gathers I/O vectors.

   > [!NOTE]
   > The descriptor FIFO may remain in local memory space.

3. Software informs BAM of new descriptors available.
   a. Software notifies the BAM about how many descriptors in the descriptor FIFO were allocated, by writing to the BAM_P_EVNT_REGn [P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST]. Each time new descriptors are allocated, software should increment the BAM_P_EVNT_REGn by 8 per descriptor. Software also should take good care about the descriptor FIFO wrap-around case.
<!-- page 3199 -->

   The BAM interacts with the peripheral module as if the software was another BAM module (the peripheral module is unaware if the interaction is with another peripheral module or with software).
4. Using the descriptors from the system, the BAM transfers data directly from system memory. (In case of BAM-NDP, the actual transfer is done by the peripheral, instead of the BAM)
5. Consumer BAM notifies the consumer peripheral that data is available for reading from the pipe's data FIFO.
6. BAM generates interrupt. When processing a descriptor that has a set INT bit or EOT bit, BAM generates an interrupt that reaches the CPU.
   Now, the system knows that the data was fully transferred, from/to system memory and introduce new descriptors to the BAM, as needed.

   > [!NOTE]
   > In system mode, descriptor FIFO should never be full, because then, software cannot differentiate between FIFO full and FIFO empty.

   > [!NOTE]
   > BAM_P_SW_OFSTSn progress means that the descriptors data was fully transferred from/to the peripheral. There are some cases in which the last descriptors data transfer, from/to the peripheral, could be finished, but BAM didn't finish working on that descriptor. For example, descriptor with NWD, peripheral could acknowledge the NWD after data transfer has finished, or descriptor that after finishing its data transfer, peripheral initiates a MESSAGING_ONLY EOT indicating that the descriptor was the last descriptor in the transfer, in that case BAM would update the descriptor the last descriptor in the FIFO.
   >
   > For descriptors with NWD, the interrupt indicating that the descriptor was finished would not get asserted until the peripheral acknowledges the NWD.

##### System consumer data flow

Software reads (from the descriptor buffer) the descriptors that were processed by BAM (BAM updates the size and EOT fields of the descriptors processed with the actual data received from the peripheral module).

Figure 8-43 shows the system consumer data flow.
<!-- page 3200 -->

##### System consumer data flow

Figure 8-43 shows the system consumer data flow.

#### Figure 8-43: System consumer transactions data flow
*Description:* A block diagram showing the data and control flow between a BAM Producer (hardware, left) and a System Consumer (software, right).
- "System memory" (top) contains the "Data buffer" (allocated by the system).
- The BAM Producer "Writes data" to the Data buffer, and the System Consumer "Reads data" from the Data buffer.
- A "Descriptor FIFO" (bottom) receives "Writes descriptors" from the System Consumer.
- The BAM Producer "Reads and updates descriptors" in the Descriptor FIFO, and the System Consumer "Reads updated descriptors" from it.
- The BAM Producer maintains a `BAM_P_BYTES_FREE` register.
- The System Consumer notifies the BAM Producer of new descriptors (or reads) by writing to `BAM_P_EVNT_REGn` ("Sends read event").
- The BAM Producer "Creates IRQ event" to update `BAM_P_IRQ_STTSn` on the System Consumer side.
- The BAM Producer performs "Update" operations locally.

System consumer transactions are as follows:
1. System allocates one or more system memory buffers to store the data.
2. System writes a set of descriptors to the descriptor FIFO.
   a. System notifies the BAM for location of the buffers by writing a series of descriptors to the descriptor FIFO (see Figure 8-39) describing the allocated buffers.
   b. The data start address field provides the start address of the system memory buffer. The BAM will assert an interrupt for each descriptor with INT indication or EOT indication (if the interrupt is enabled).
   c. Software notifies the BAM about the location of the descriptor FIFO via BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_LSBn and BAM_P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR_MSBn.
   In this way, the software can scatter I/O vectors to the different locations in memory to which the descriptors point. Conversely, for a system producer, the consumer gathers I/O vectors.

   > [!NOTE]
   > The descriptor FIFO may remain in local memory space.

3. Software informs BAM of new descriptors available.
   a. Software notifies the BAM about how many descriptors in the descriptor FIFO were allocated, by writing to the BAM_P_EVNT_REGn [P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST]. Each time new descriptors are allocated, software should increment the BAM_P_EVNT_REGn by 8 per descriptor. Software also should take good care about the descriptor-FIFO wrap-around case.
   The BAM interacts with the peripheral module as if the software was another BAM module (the peripheral module is unaware if the interaction is with another peripheral module or with software).




<!-- page 3201 -->

4. Once producer BAM receives a read event from the consumer, it frees up the available space in the data FIFO and notifies producer peripheral that memory is available (updates BYTES_FREE).
5. Using the descriptors from the system, the BAM transfers data directly to system memory. (In case of BAM-NDP, the actual transfer is done by the peripheral, instead of the BAM)
6. BAM updates the size and EOT fields of the descriptors processed with the actual data received from the peripheral.
7. BAM generates interrupt. When processing a descriptor that has a set INT bit, or EOT bit. Now, the system knows that the data was fully transferred to system memory and introduce new descriptors to the BAM, as needed.

> [!NOTE]
> In system mode, descriptor FIFO should never be full, because then, software cannot differentiate between FIFO full and FIFO empty.

> [!NOTE]
> BAM_P_SW_OFSTSn progress means that the descriptors data was fully transferred from/to the peripheral. There're some cases in which the last descriptors data transfer, from/to the peripheral, could be finished, but BAM didn't finish working on that descriptor. For example, descriptor with NWD, peripheral could "acknowledge" the NWD after data transfer has finished, or descriptor that after finishing its data transfer, peripheral initiates a MESSAGING_ONLY EOT indicating that the descriptor was the last descriptor in the transfer, in that case BAM would update the descriptor the last descriptor in the FIFO.

> [!NOTE]
> For descriptors with NWD, the interrupt indicating that the descriptor was finished would not get asserted until the peripheral acknowledges the NWD.

### Command elements

Command descriptor (CD) start address points to a location in the memory in which the matching command elements lay. Each command element is structured by 4 DWORDS.

> [!NOTE]
> Using the command descriptor feature requires setting in BAM configuration to support it. See Section 8.7.3.4.2.
<!-- page 3202 -->

Figure 8-44 presents the command element structure.

#### Figure 8-44: Command element structure
*Description:* The command element structure consists of four 32-bit double words (DWORD0 to DWORD3). The structure varies depending on whether it is a Write or Read command:
- **DWORD 0**:
  - **Write**: Bits 31:24 contain the Command opcode (must be 0). Bits 23:0 contain the Target address in the peripheral.
  - **Read**: Bits 31:24 contain the Command opcode (must be 1). Bits 23:0 contain the Target address in the peripheral.
- **DWORD 1**:
  - **Write**: Data to be written.
  - **Read**: LSB destination address (lower 32 bits of the 36-bit destination memory address).
- **DWORD 2**:
  - **Write**: Write Mask (defines which bits of the target DWORD should be modified).
  - **Read**: Bits 31:4 are Reserved; Bits 3:0 contain the 4 MSBs of the 36-bit destination memory address.
- **DWORD 3**:
  - **Write**: Reserved.
  - **Read**: Reserved.

**Write command elements field:**
*   **Address** (bits 23:0 of the first DWORD): the target address in the peripheral of the write operation, that is the address in the peripheral at which the write-data will be written
*   **Command** (bits: 31:24 of the first DWORD): type of the command to be operated, in case of write-command-element it must be 0
*   **Data** (second DWORD): The data that should be written
*   **Mask** (third DWORD): 32 bits mask that defines which bit of the target DWORD should be modified
*   **Reserved** (fourth DWORD): Reserved for future enhancements

**Read command elements field:**
*   **Address** (bits 23:0 of the first DWORD): the target address in the peripheral of the read operation, i.e. the address in the peripheral from which the read-data will be read
*   **Command** (bits: 31:24 of the first DWORD): type of the command to be operated, in case of read-command-element it must be 1
*   **Destination** (second DWORD): The address in the memory to which the read-data will be written, it holds the 32 LSBs (from 36 bits) of the destination address
*   **Reserved (third DWORD) Destination Address 4 MSBs** (bits 3:0): The third in the command-element-descriptor holds the 4 MSBs (of the 36 bits) of the read-data memory destination address
*   **Reserved** (fourth DWORD): Reserved for future enhancements

> [!NOTE]
> It is recommended to use command descriptors on consumer pipes. Usage of command descriptors in producer pipes should be done in cases where no consumer pipe is available to transfer the command through.
<!-- page 3203 -->

> [!NOTE]
> Each command descriptor can point to either only write-command-elements, or only read-command-elements. That is, 1 command descriptor must not mix write-command-elements with read-command-elements.

> [!NOTE]
> Software can choose to work in one transaction - one data descriptor manner while it keeps the data descriptor big enough for the maximum possible transfer.

> [!NOTE]
> When BAM executes a command descriptor with NWD, it stalls all other command descriptors, even from other pipes, until the DONE_TOGGLE is updated by the peripheral.

> [!NOTE]
> For BAM-lite (only), in case this results in performance overhead that the peripheral cannot stand, software may implement similar functionality by pushing a command descriptor followed by a ZLT (i.e., a zero-sized descriptor) with NWD. To enable support of a ZLT followed by a command descriptor software should assert the BAM_CNFG_REG [BAM_ZLT_W_CD_SUPPORT] bit.

### Command data flow

The following sections define the sequence for queuing command transactions in addition to data transactions:

1. Software receives service request from application API.
2. Software writes the required command elements, containing the required peripheral configurations to be done for this command descriptors, in a specific continuous memory location.
3. Software writes the command descriptor containing the start address of the command elements (from step 2), to the Descriptor FIFO.
4. After queueing BAM data & command descriptors, Software then writes BAM_P_EVNT_REGn register(s) of associated pipe(s), to notify the BAM of the new added command descriptor.
5. Software waits for transaction complete interrupt from BAM.
6. Software receives additional service requests and queues appropriate command and data descriptors.
7. BAM interrupt asserts but starts next transaction immediately while software experiences interrupt overhead latency.
8. Software processes interrupt and informs application that transaction is complete. Then go to step 5 above.

Command descriptors may be pushed to either consumer pipe or producer pipe.

#### Command descriptor in consumer pipe (system to BAM pipe)

1. On consumer pipes, software can mix data & command descriptors as needed.
2. On the data descriptor preceding command descriptor, NWD bit must be asserted in order to assure that all the data has been transferred and the peripheral is ready to be re-configured.
<!-- page 3204 -->

3. Once the BAM detects data descriptor with NWD bit set, it will transfer the indication to the peripheral, stops publish pipe_bytes, and will not read new descriptors (of this pipe) until the DONE_TOGGLE is received.
4. The above statement is correct to each pipe independently.
5. Once the DONE_TOGGLE is received, the BAM will read and execute the command descriptor. When finished, it will restart sideband publishing (and new descriptors reading) so new data transfers can start.

#### Command descriptor in producer pipe (BAM to system)

1. On producer pipe software can mix data & command descriptor as needed.
2. Since the BAM has less information on transaction boundary in this mode, software must assure the following requirements:
   a. All data descriptors before a command descriptor must be used and closed by the transaction/transactions prior the new configuration cycle.
   b. The space published by data descriptors precede the command descriptor must be sufficient for all the transfers prior new configuration cycle.

### Security considerations when using Command Descriptor

When executing CD and accessing the peripheral, the transaction is going through the same path like regular configuration accesses do, that is, the access go through the configuration bridge for address decoding and security check (in secured flavors of BAM). The VMID/HPROTNS and MSA values for the CD configuration access is taken from the VMIDMT mapping block. The VMID value is the same value given for the BAM's master accesses (data/descriptors/events) related for the same pipe (where the CD came from).

### Locking mechanism

Command descriptor may have the lock bit set. Upon encountering a descriptor with lock bit set, the BAM will lock all other pipes not related to the current pipe group and keep handling the current pipe only until it sees the unlock set (then it will release all locked pipes). The actual locking is done on the new descriptor fetching for publishing, i.e. locked pipe will not fetch new descriptors even if it got event/events adding more descriptors for this pipe.

There are two options for defining lock groups, controlled by software bit `LOCK_EE_CTRL`:
- **a.** Each pipe CTRL register contains 5-bit field to define the pipe lock group. All pipes not within this group will be locked by this pipe upon lock event. (Default option)
- **b.** In addition to the lock group above, the Environment Execution (EE) associated to the pipe (in `BAM_P_TRUST_REGn`) is taking into consideration for the locking evaluation as well: ONLY pipes which are in the same group and relate to the same EE will not be locked by a certain pipe.

> [!NOTE]
> Pipe locking and unlocking should appear only in command-descriptor. In case a lock is required on a data descriptor this can be implemented by a dummy command-descriptor with lock/unlock bit asserted preceding/following the data descriptor.
<!-- page 3205 -->

> [!NOTE]
> Pipe locking does not affect previous descriptor publishment. i.e. there can be a case when locked pipe will still transfer data from prior published descriptors.

> [!NOTE]
> Prior the lock event, BAM does not guarantee ordering between pipes execution, hence, software needs to use the lock mechanism with care under this fact.

#### Lock super group

> [!NOTE]
> Valid for BAM-NDP and BAM-lite only.

Lock super group mechanism is one more virtualization level of the locking mechanism. A locking pipe will lock all pipes that are not in its lock group, and also in the same lock super group. Pipe lock super group is configured via `BAM_P_TRUST_REGn`.

### 8.7.3.5 BAM security

Security features that can be added to a BAM instance are of two types: master data interface security and slave configuration interface security.

#### 8.7.3.5.1 AHB master security

AHB master (data) security relies on virtual master IDs. Every secure slave validates access based on which virtual bus master is attempting to access it. BAM supports both of the following methods.

BAM and the peripheral wrapper receive their virtual master ID by:
- The fabric issues a master ID to each of its connected bus masters with an MID2VMID index table in the bus infrastructure (requires no BAM actions).
- The master can be set to output a software configurable VMID. A different VMID can be set for each pipe.

> [!NOTE]
> The VMID is provided by a VMIDMT module instantiated in the BAM.

#### 8.7.3.5.2 AHB slave security

The AHB slave (configuration) security is based on an APU instance in BAM.

Configuration security ensures:
- Only the trust group can perform actions that may cause errors to BAM functions, such as BAM disable and BAM software reset
- Controls configurations that change security settings
- The control group configures the general BAM configuration
- A specific security group is only allowed to read and write from its own registers. One group cannot access another group's registers for read or write
- All non-approved access:
<!-- page 3206 -->

- All non-approved access:
  - Write accesses write to a bit bucket.
  - Read accesses read 0x0.
  - From the AHB bus, the master performing the access does not know whether the transfer has failed the security check.
- When the APU is not configured to protect security, access is as if security is not present at all (the BAM and peripheral still work).

#### Setting up APU for access validation

To set up APU for access validation:
- Read and write accesses to a specific address should be either both allowed, or both restricted.
- Multi-VMID support: registers can be accessed by more than one VMID.
- APU determines a valid access by checking the VMID and the security group decoded by BAM or the peripheral.

#### BAM security groups

In addition to the standard address decoding, BAM decodes the AHB access, so a security group can access BAM. Table 8-174 lists the BAM security groups.

##### Table 8-174 BAM security groups

| Group | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| APU group | The security group of the APU's registers |
| Trust group | BAM and pipe trust registers for selecting the EE to which the BAM/pipe belongs |
| Debug group | Pipe internal state registers for debug |
| Control group | Overall operations, global interrupt management, and global errors |
| EE groups | Eight EE groups: Designate access to the new `BAM_IRQ_SRCS_EEi` and `BAM_IRQ_SRCS_UNMASKED_EEi` registers |
| Pipe groups | As many as the `MAX_PIPES` of BAM managing each pipe:<br>• Mode and direction<br>• Interrupt management<br>• Timer control<br>Configuring each pipe:<br>• Event address<br>• Event register<br>• Descriptor FIFO address and size<br>• Data FIFO address and size |
| Peripheral non-pipe groups | When accessing the peripherals address space, it's upon the peripheral to define which security group this access is accessing. Those security groups maybe one of the pipe. |

APU is given one-hot decode of these; the APU output is a signal that is ANDed with the HSEL AHB signal to block or allow AHB access.
<!-- page 3207 -->

### 8.7.3.6 BAM modules

There are four BAM modules integrated in the device:
- Secure BAM-Lite in BLSP subsystem
- BAM in USB2.0 subsystem
- BAM-NDP in QDSS
- Secure BAM-NDP in Crypto5 subsystem

#### 8.7.3.6.1 BLSP BAM-lite

The BAM low speed peripherals (BLSP) module gathers slow peripheral instances, specifically QUP and UART, and provides them with BAM capability.

BLSP sub-modules require low bandwidth and include only AHB slave functionality. The eDML design allows AHB slave modules to be connected to the Secure BAM-Lite module instantiated in BLSP. The security is handled by APU and VMIDMT located inside the BAM.

Figure 8-45 shows the block diagram of BLSP with the secure BAM-lite.

#### Figure 8-45: BLSP block diagram
*Description:* The diagram shows the BLSP (BAM Low Speed Peripherals) subsystem. It connects to the "Peripheral and system configuration NoC". Inside the BLSP:
- There is a **Secure BAM-lite** module, which includes **eDML** (enhanced Descriptor Manager Lite).
- The Secure BAM-lite connects to a **Configuration AHB bus**.
- Multiple **QUP** (Qualcomm Universal Peripheral) and **UART** instances are connected to the Configuration AHB bus and also have direct connections (likely data paths) to the Secure BAM-lite.
- The QUP and UART instances also interface with the **TLMM** (Top Level Multiplexing Manager).

Table 8-175 presents the integration details of BAM-lite inside BLSP.

| Module | BAM pipe | Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| UART0 | 0 | Producer |
| | 1 | Consumer |
| UART1 | 2 | Producer |

| QUP1 | 4 | Producer |
