The two main use cases of BLSP are BAM and non-BAM traffic. BAM traffic may contain data payload or commands.

#### Non-BAM use case

In the non-BAM use case the peripheral data and configuration is performed exclusively by software. This use case should be compliant to the pre-BLSP usage model and should use the exact same software.

This mode, however, creates a high load on software as the internal peripheral module buffering is low and this causes a high interrupt rate.

This use case should be used for short transactions where BAM configuration overhead may be considerable or in legacy software designs (where we want to minimize the software modifications).

> [!NOTE]
> In the non-BAM use case, periodic interrupts from the peripheral modules and the software maintain the data flow.

#### BAM use case

In the BAM use case, some of the peripheral data and configuration may be performed by the BAM hardware.
<!-- page 3209 -->

The BAM module is able to:
- Read descriptors and allow the peripheral module to read descriptor content.
- Receive data from the peripheral module and pack it in descriptors.

The BAM design assumes the peripheral module has an AHB master. The eDML allows modules without an AHB master to connect to the BAM. In addition, because peripherals without masters are usually low bandwidth, the eDML allows multiple peripherals to connect to the same BAM.

> [!NOTE]
> In the BAM use case, BAM hardware maintains the data flow, assisted by the BAM and BASI-side band between the peripheral module and eDML.

#### Data flows

Data flows between the peripheral NOC and the QUP/UART peripherals. Data is stored in small internal RAMs in the peripheral modules and can be read by BAM_eDML or directly by software.

In the BAM use case, BAM hardware maintains the data flow, assisted by the BAM and BASI-side band between the peripheral module and BAM_eDML.

In the non-BAM use case, periodic interrupts from the peripheral module and the software maintain the data flow.

#### Control modes

For UART, there are direct software access controls by the appropriate registers in the UART module.

The QUP module allows two control modes:
- Direct software access (same as in UART).
- BAM command descriptor.

Using command descriptors allows commands to be embedded in the peripheral between the BAM data descriptors. The command descriptor must be supported by the peripheral module to use the mask field. Only the QUP supports full command descriptors.

#### 8.7.3.6.3 QDSS BAM-NDP

Trace data may be moved to on-chip USB via BAM-BAM configuration, and transported to a host debugger PC. For this use case, the ETR is charged with moving data to a region of on-chip memory located close (in terms of cycles of latency) to the USB. The ETR is configured with a start address of this region of memory and a size. It then treats this region of memory as a circular buffer and continuously moves data to that region with no software intervention.

The associated BAM descriptors for this trace data are generated by the BAM-NDP within the QDSS that monitors the stream of data from the QDSS ETR to the USB data pipe memory. BAM-NDP is responsible for creating BAM descriptors for the stream of AXI1.0 transactions targeting the USB data pipe memory. This descriptor stream will target a descriptor FIFO closely coupled (latency) to the USB2.0.

To switch to BAM-NDP (from the processor interface):
* Configure and enable BAM-NDP.
* Set the `HIGH_SPD_DATA_EN_N` bit in the `CRYPTO_CONFIG` register to 0.

BAM does not transfer data from internal register settings only. It relies on descriptors stored in memory to direct the type of transfer. This scheme allows a processor to set up multiple descriptors at the time-zero beginning of the operation out of reset. The processor points BAM to the head of the descriptor FIFO in memory. Then, the data transfer launches.

#### 8.7.5.1.1 0x00000 BAM_CTRL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `BAM_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00020000`

BAM control register allows global controls for the BAM.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 | BAM_MESS_ONLY_CANCEL_WB | When active (1): BAM will DROP former descriptor write-backing and CANCEL_WB interrupt firing when former descriptor has been closed (accumulated=acknowledged) and ack_on_success with EOT and size 0 arrived (messaging only).<br>When legacy mode is used (0): In this case the former descriptor is closed (accumulated=acknowledged) and ack_on_success with EOT and size 0 arrived (messaging only). In this case the FIFO-pointer has been already advanced before the ack_on_success arrives and therefore we do write-back to former descriptor and fire interrupt.<br>1'b1 - Drop WB and Interrupt 1'b0 - legacy. |
| 19 | CACHE_MISS_ERR_RESP_EN | When set to '1', upon local ahb access results with cache miss, the bam_ndp will not stall the bus, and finish the access with error response.<br>This bit is relevant for BAM_NDP only. |
| 18:17 | LOCAL_CLK_GATING | These bits enable power saving by using a local clock gating cell. Bit 17:<br>1'b1: CGC is on, so that the clock is controlled by the HW and this is the reset value.<br>1'b0: CGC is off so that the clock is free running. Bit 18: reserved bit for future improvements. |

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | IBC_DISABLE | This bit enables power saving by disabling the inactivity clock timer/counter. This is useful when:<br>• The BAM is enabled but idling for long periods.<br>• The BAM is enabled and running but the inactivity timers/counters are not required by the software for operating the BAM. When the BAM is disabled, it automatically shuts down those timers to save power.<br>1'b1: Enable power saving mode<br>1'b0: Disable power saving mode |
| 15 | BAM_CACHED_DESC_STORE | This bit enables storage of a cached descriptor into RAM when doing context switch and loading it back when returning to this pipe. This is relevant for system modes only.<br>BAM to BAM consumer mode doesn't have this option.<br>Enabling this makes the context switch process slightly longer but reduces AHB descriptor fetch time later on. It also reduces the number of descriptor fetches done by the BAM if BAM is treating more than two pipes.<br>1'b1: Enabled<br>1'b0: Disabled<br>Available in BAM only |
| 14:13 | BAM_DESC_CACHE_SEL | This selector chooses the descriptor caching mode that will be used. This is relevant for system producer or consumer modes only.<br>2'b00: Cache when current descriptor has less than 64 bytes left.<br>2'b01: Cache when current descriptor has less than 128 bytes left.<br>2'b10: Immediate Auto cache: cache will happen whenever there are no descriptors cached. This might cause unnecessary descriptors reads when switching between more than two pipes. It is the most effective when each pipe processes more bytes than there are in an average descriptor (small descriptors, big block size), or when working with 2 or less pipes.<br>2'b11: Cache when descriptor is needed only. #### 8.7.5.1.2 0x00044 BAM_TIMER_CTRL

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `BAM_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00000000`

This register sets various controls and the threshold of the inactivity for interrupt triggering after long idle time.

The register can be written and read only when `INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED` generic equals to 1.

#### 8.7.5.1.3 0x00008 BAM_DESC_CNT_TRSHLD

* **Type:** RW
* **Clock:** `BAM_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00000001`

This register holds a threshold value for the counter summing the size of the descriptors provided. This value is global for all pipes but it is relevant for system producer BAM mode and both consumer modes, where descriptors summing takes place in order to provide the information to the peripheral via pipe bytes free (producer) or pipe bytes available interfaces. The register can be written and read only when `INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED` generic equals to 1.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 15:0 | CNT_TRSHLD | Threshold value.<br>The maximum allowed value is 32 kB.<br>The minimum allowed value is 1 (value 0 is not allowed).<br>Available in BAM only. |

* **Type:** R
* **Clock:** `BAM_CLK`
* **Reset state:** `0x00000000`

Interrupt status register describing the reason for the ongoing interrupt. This is an informative only register and therefore read only.

Clearing the interrupt bits is done by writing to `BAM_IRQ_CLR` register.

| 2 | BAM_ERROR_IRQ | This indicates a fatal error has happened in the BAM. Currently this might happen due to an unsuccessful pipe reset operation. |
| 1 | BAM_HRESP_ERR_IRQ | This interrupt indicates that an erroneous response has been received by the AHB master.<br>Additional information about the error may be read at `BAM_AHB_MASTER_ERR_*` registers.<br>Clearing this interrupt also clears the `BAM_AHB_MASTER_ERR_*` registers. Available in BAM only. |

##### 8.7.5.1.8 0x0007C BAM_CNFG_REG

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register holds the BAM configuration bits for bug fixes. It is highly recommended to follow the directions for each bit and set it accordingly.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | AOS_OVERFLOW_PRVNT | This bit enables overflow prevention when sideband block accumulates ack_on_success updates from peripherals to values higher than 0x7fff.<br>'1': enable ack-on_success overflow prevention. If current ack_on_success update causes overflow accept_ack_on_success_toggle will not approve the update until SB accumulator is cleared.<br>'0': disable ack-on_success overflow prevention. Available in BAM-NDP only.<br>Default value is '0' (Legacy). Recommended value is '1'. |
| 30 | MULTIPLE_EVENTS_DESC_AVAIL_EN | This is an enable bit for supporting multiple events received by a producer BAM2BAM and makes BAM-NDP to notify a correct desc_cache_avail bus. It fixed CR: QCTDD00209370. |
| 29 | MULTIPLE_EVENTS_SIZE_EN | This is an enable bit for supporting multiple events received by a producer BAM2BAM and makes BAM-NDP delivering correct descriptor sizes on local_ahb bit. It fixed CR: QCTDD00209379. |
<!-- page 3222 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 28 | BAM_ZLT_W_CD_SUPPORT | Recommended value: 1<br>Enables support of ZLT (i.e. a zero-sized descriptor) before a command-descriptor.<br>Specifically it supports a case on a pipe without any data-descriptors but with ZLT descriptors and command-descriptors only.<br>This allows putting NWD bit in the ZLT descriptor (instead of in the CMD) which results in better performance than using the NWD in the command-descriptor.<br>Available in BAM-lite only. |
| 27 | BAM_CD_ENABLE | Recommended value: 1<br>Enables the command descriptor feature. |
| 26 | BAM_AU_ACCUMED | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit fixes a bug in the ack update state machine, where an overflow happened while counting descriptors and reaching more than 64kB of calculated sizes.<br>1'b1: Enable fix<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM/BAM-NDP only |
| 25 | BAM_PSM_P_HD_DATA | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows pipe state machine to ignore retransmission requests if a pipe has just been initialized and process those as a regular fetch request. (consumer modes only).<br>When this bit disabled, BAM could fetch descriptors for a pipe which was reset and no descriptors were added yet, if a retransmission request followed after the reset.<br>1'b1: Enable fix<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |
| 24 | BAM_REG_P_EN | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit fixes the pipe configuration signals mux for the current active pipe in 2 pipes BAM.<br>When disabled, internal state machines might get into enabled states while the pipe is disabled. This would typically happen after pipe reset.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM/BAM-NDP only |
| 23 | BAM_WB_DSC_AVL_P_RST | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows the writeback state machine to reset the vector indicating there are available descriptors when a pipe reset occurs. If disabled, BAM might fetch descriptors after resetting and reconfiguring a pipe, even though no event (descriptors) was provided.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 22 | BAM_WB_RETR_SVPNT | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit fixes a bug where a pipe which was reset, still stored its retransmission savepoint, but into the illegal's pipe address space, thus hurting the last pipe of the BAM if the BAM had a total 4, 8 or 16 pipes.<br>This is relevant for producer to system modes only. (CR-0000151585)<br>1'b1: Enabled<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM/BAM-NDP only |
| 21 | BAM_WB_CSW_ACK_IDL | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows the writeback state machine to switch into idle state prior to visiting disabled state. This is needed when context switching from mode X to another pipe of mode X is well. This is required to fix a bug in the 2 pipes BAM.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM/BAM-NDP only |
| 20 | BAM_WB_BLK_CSW | Recommended value: 1<br>When enabled, this bit does not allow context switch to happen in the writeback state machine until it has created a descriptor. This might result in the descriptor not to be created ever, if it was the last one for that pipe.<br>Relevant for producer BAM-to-BAM mode only.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable available in BAM only |
| 19 | BAM_WB_P_RES | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows to reset all internal registers of the writeback state machine when performing pipe reset.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable available in BAM only |
| 18 | BAM_SI_P_RES | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows to reset all internal registers of the sideband inform state machine when performing pipe reset.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |
| 17 | BAM_AU_P_RES | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows to reset all internal registers of the ack update state machine when performing pipe reset.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |
<!-- page 3224 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 16 | BAM_PSM_P_RES | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows to reset all internal registers of the pipe state machine when performing pipe reset.<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |
| 15 | BAM_PSM_CSW_REQ | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit forces the context switch request from pipe state machine to RAM controller not to last longer than the slave requested. (2 Pipes BAM bug fix).<br>1'b1: Enable<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |
| 14 | BAM_SB_CLK_REQ | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows the clock request from the sideband block to propagate into the BAM's common clock request.<br>1'b1: Propagate sideband clock request<br>1'b0: Disable<br>Available in BAM only |

| 12 | BAM_NO_EXT_P_RST | Recommended value: 1<br>This bit allows the BAM / BAM Lite to ignore the externally connected blocks (eDML) when doing pipe reset.<br>The BAM, once instructed to pipe reset, first thing lets the externally connected block know a reset is needed. ##### 8.7.5.1.9 0x01000 BAM_REVISION

**Type:** R

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** Undefined

This register holds a hard coded revision number of the BAM RTL. This corresponds to the BAM target number in the IMS. Also additional BAM settings are reflected here.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:24 | INACTIV_TMR_BASE | This indicates the width of the inactivity timers base counter. |
| 23 | CMD_DESC_EN | This indicates BAM has command descriptor feature enabled in HW. |
| 22:21 | DESC_CACHE_DEPTH | This field indicates the per-pipe-descriptor-cache, could be 1-4:<br>2'b00: Descriptor cache depth of 1<br>2'b01: Descriptor cache depth of 2<br>2'b10: Descriptor cache depth of 3<br>2'b11: Descriptor cache depth of 4<br>Valid only for BAM_NDP. |
| 20 | NUM_INACTIV_TMRS | This bit is checked only if INACTIV_TMRS_EXST = 1.<br>This bit indicates how many inactivity timers are implemented according to value of INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED generic:<br>1'b1: One timer for global BAM activity (INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED = 1)<br>1'b0: MAX_PIPES timers for each pipe activity (INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED = 2) |
| 19 | INACTIV_TMRS_EXST | This indicates BAM has inactivity timers.<br>1'b1: Timers available (INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED = 1 or 2)<br>1'b0: No timers available (INACTIVITY_TIMERS_SUPPORTED = 0) |
| 18 | HIGH_FREQUENCY_BAM | This indicates BAM has double sampling on the ack on success interface.<br>1'b1: Ack on success double sampled<br>1'b0: No double sampling of ack on success |
| 17 | BAM_HAS_NO_BYPASS | This field indicates BAM has no bypass on the AHB data bus, from the peripheral AHB master to the fabric. When bypass is available, it is the default routing when BAM is disabled.<br>1'b1: No bypass<br>1'b0: Bypass exists |
| 16 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 15 | RESERVED | Reserved |
| 14 | AXI_ACTIVE | This field indicates BAM_NDP uses internal AXI bridge on the master port. |
<!-- page 3227 -->
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 13:12 | CE_BUFFER_SIZE | This field indicates the size (in data words) of the buffer which stores the command elements.<br>Each command element includes 4 words.<br>2'b00: 4 words (one command element).<br>2'b10: 8 words (2 command elements).<br>2'b11: 16 words (4 command elements).<br>Valid if CMD_DESC_EN = 1'b1. |
| 11:8 | NUM_EES | This indicates the number of interrupt lines (execution environments) supported by the BAM.<br>When 1 EE is supported, only the BAM_IRQ_SRCS_EE0 register exist.<br>When 4 EEs are supported, all BAM_IRQ_SRCS_EEi registers exist for i= [0..3]. |
| 7:0 | RESERVED | Reserved |

**Type:** RW

#### 8.7.5.1.18 0x03000+4096*i BAM_IRQ_SRCS_EEi

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

This interrupt status register provides a single interrupt bit per each pipe in the BAM and a single bit for the BAM (not pipe related) interrupt. This register is read only and provides fast indication for the software to decide which pipe triggered the interrupt. After checking this register, software BAM_IRQ_STTS reads the BAM_P_IRQ_STTSn register for the pipe interrupt reason and BAM_IRQ_STTS for the BAM interrupt reason.

This register has an alias BAM_IRQ_SRCS register.
<!-- page 3232 -->
Registers with i= [1..7] exist only when the BAM supports multiple EEs (NUM_EES field in the BAM_REVISION register).

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | BAM_IRQ | BAM global interrupt |
| 30:0 | P_IRQ | An interrupt bit per each pipe in the BAM. |

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

| 30:0 | P_IRQ_MSK | An interrupt mask bit per each pipe in the BAM.<br>0x1: ENABLE_PIPE_INTERRUPT (Enable Pipe interrupt)<br>0x0: DISABLE_PIPE_INTERRUPT (Disable Pipe interrupt) |

The register shows the pipes attributed to a specific EE, and an indication if BAM is enabled.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 11 | P_WRITE_NWD | BAM-lite feature.<br>Applicable to BAM2BAM producer pipes only.<br>When this bit is set for producer B2B pipe, NWD bit (bit number 28 in the second word of descriptor) will be written with EOT into the generated descriptor for the consumer usage.<br>This bit is not applicable in pipes belong to a Peripheral which uses MESSAGING_ONLY (e.g. USB2). |
| 10:9 | P_PREFETCH_LIMIT | BAM-lite feature<br>Selects the number of bytes to be prefetched by the BAM-lite, once a peripheral requests to read data from a pipe.<br>This feature is relevant for consumer modes only.<br>2'b00: 32 bytes at most (INCR8)<br>2'b01: 16 bytes at most (INCR4)<br>2'b10: 4 bytes at most (SINGLE)<br>Available in BAM-Lite only |

**Type:** W

<!-- page 3240 -->
#### 8.7.5.1.32 0x13020+4096*n BAM_P_TIMER_CTRLn

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register sets various controls and the threshold of the inactivity for interrupt triggering after long idle time.

The resolution of the pipe inactivity timers are in units set by a common counter. This common counter is controlled by a PARAMETER value of the BAM, and uses a separate clock, the inactivity_timers_clk. This clock can be slower than the BAM_CLK. The intent of the design is to use the sleep_clk, which is an always on 32kHz clock. This allows the BAM_CLK to be turned-off, while the base counter keeps counting. The width of this counter, as well of the rollover value are set using BAM PARAMETER. These values, taking the inactivity_timers_clk frequency define the pulse frequency that the base counter gives, and the threshold value can be calculated and set to interrupt after a specific time, regardless of the BAM_CLK frequency, and independent of clock power save features of the BAM_CLK. The timers continue counting even if the clock is turned off due to BAM dynamic hardware clock request voting.

The timer configuration is based on the inactivity_timers_clk period and the INACTIVITY_TIMER_WIDTH parameter constant. These parameters should be taken into account when setting this register. For example: for inactivity_timer_clk period of 1us and parameter is 3 and P_TIMER_THRSHLD is 10 will indicate the 2^3*1us*10 which is 80us of inactivity in a pipe before sending an interrupt.

The general formula is: 2^INACTIVITY_TIMER_WIDTH * clock_period * P_TIMER_TRSHLD.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31 | P_TIMER_RST | To begin using the inactivity timer the software should write the threshold and write 1 to this bit. writing the value 0 will hold the timer reset until value 1 is written again. Then the timer will start down counting from the P_TIMER_THRESOLD value<br>1'b1 - Active<br>1'b0 - Reset |
| 30 | P_TIMER_RUN | Will be used along with P_TIMER_MODE Not implemented at this time. Set to zero (0). |
| 29 | P_TIMER_MODE | Not implemented at this time. Set to zero (0). |
| 15:0 | P_TIMER_TRSHLD | Inactivity timer threshold for interrupt generation. |

### 8.7.5.1.35 BAM_P_SW_OFSTSn (0x13800 + 4096 * n)

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: BAM_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register denotes the pointer offset of the first not acknowledged descriptor. Meaning all descriptors prior to this one have been processed by the BAM. This register is only used by the software. After receiving an interrupt, software reads this register in order to know what descriptors has been processed.

When the BAM works as producer, software will usually read this value after descriptor processed interrupt or after the end of transfer interrupt.

When the BAM works as consumer, software will usually read this value after descriptor processed interrupt.

> [!NOTE]
> This is non relevant in BAM to BAM modes.

> [!NOTE]
> Although being writable, software should never write to this register. When using 2 pipes BAM, REVISION 0x03, this registers is read only.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:16 | SW_OFST_IN_DESC | Offset inside the descriptor. This value is used by the software only when a BAM is working as system producer. Then the SW can read this value to know how many bytes were written to the current descriptor if it was not closed down. This is useful for streaming mode. This field is NOT available in BAM-NDP. |
| 15:0 | SW_DESC_OFST | Descriptor FIFO offset. |

This register is where read/write events are sent to. If current BAM works as producer, it will receive read events into this register from the consumer. If the consumer is another BAM, it will write read events to this register. If the consumer is the software, it will prepare descriptors in the descriptor FIFO and update the DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST value in this register.

If current BAM works as consumer, opposite behavior is assumed.

Consumer sends this value to the producer as a part of a read event, for the producer to know how many bytes were consumed. When working in system mode, this value should be set to zero. BAM to BAM producer writes zero in this value. |
| 15:0 | P_DESC_FIFO_PEER_OFST | This field indicates the descriptor fifo offset pointer of the peer BAM (The BAM or the software which creates descriptors). For example when current BAM works as consumer for the current pipe, Producer BAM (or the software) updates this value to let the current pipe know about the new descriptors added in the descriptor fifo. |

Events are also issued after end of transfer received from the peripheral (Producer case), non regarding whether the pushed bytes count has reached the threshold or not.

* **Clock**: BAM_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register stores the MSB of address of the descriptor fifo beginning. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM.

> [!NOTE]
> This register is used by all modes.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR | 4 MSB of address (bits 35 to 32) of address of the descriptors fifo. This address must be 8 bytes aligned. |

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: BAM_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register stores the beginning of the data address space. This register is non relevant in system modes. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | P_DESC_FIFO_ADDR | 32 LSB of data address space beginning. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM. |

* **Type**: RW
* **Clock**: BAM_CLK
* **Reset state**: 0x00000000

This register stores the beginning of the data address space. This register is non relevant in system modes. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM.

### BAM_P_DATA_FIFO_ADDR_MSBn

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3:0 | P_DATA_FIFO_ADDR | 4 MSB of address (bits 35 to 32) of data address space beginning. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM. |

### 8.7.5.1.56 0x13930 + 4096 * n BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR_LSBn

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register stores the event destination address which is the address of `BAM_P_EVNT_REGn` in the BAM on the other side of the pipe.

Producer BAM will send write events to this address. Consumer BAM will send read events to this address. This is relevant only for BAM to BAM modes. In system modes, BAM doesn't issue write/read events. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 31:0 | P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR | 32 LSB of address of the event register in the peer BAM (second end of the pipe). Driver will configure this when initializing the pipe. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM. |

### 8.7.5.1.57 0x13934 + 4096 * n BAM_P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR_MSBn

**Type:** RW

**Clock:** BAM_CLK

**Reset state:** 0x00000000

This register stores the event destination address which is the address of `BAM_P_EVNT_REG` in the BAM on the other side of the pipe. Producer BAM will send write events to this address. Consumer BAM will send read events to this address.

This is relevant only for BAM to BAM modes. In system modes, BAM doesn't issue write/read events. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM.

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3:0 | P_EVNT_DEST_ADDR | 4 MSB of address (bits 35 to 32) of the event register in the peer BAM (second end of the pipe). Driver will configure this when initializing the pipe. Relevant only on 36 bit address BAM. |

## 8.8 Memory Management Units (MMU)

This section describes the system memory management unit.

### 8.8.1 SMMU overview

The SMMU is a hardware subsystem, which performs the translation of virtual memory addresses (VA) used by the processors to physical memory addresses (PA) in the physical memory system. The SMMU subsystem also effectively handles memory protection, cache control, and bus arbitration. The core of the SMMU subsystem is ARM CoreLink MMU-500 System Memory Management Unit (for more information, see Table 8-183).

Figure 8-49 shows a high-level overview of the SMMU subsystem.

#### Figure 8-49: SMMU overview

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph VM ["Virtual Memory"]
        VA["Virtual Addresses"]
    end
    
    subgraph SMMU_Sub ["SMMU"]
        SMMU["ARM CoreLink MMU-500"]
        AT["Address Translation"]
        SMMU -.-> AT
    end
    
    subgraph PM ["Physical Memory"]
        PA["Physical Addresses"]
    end
    
    VA -->|Virtual Address| SMMU
    AT -->|Physical Address| BUS[BUS]
    BUS --> PA
```

*Description:* High-level overview of the SMMU subsystem showing the transition from Virtual Memory space (Virtual Addresses) to Physical Memory space (Physical Addresses) via the SMMU (ARM CoreLink MMU-500 which performs address translation) and the BUS.
<!-- page 3253 -->

Table 8-182 lists the SMMU supported features.

#### Table 8-182: SMMU features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| **SMMU** | **Features of the ARM MMU-500 core:**<br>• Address virtualization to processors and other masters in the SoC<br>• Supports stage 1, 2 and nested address translations<br>• Supports translation table walks, compliant with ARM v7 and v8<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;– Single translation table walk may require multiple translation table lookups<br>• Supports 4 KB, 64 KB, 2 MB page sizes<br>• Provides multiple page table walk caches for storing intermediate page table walk data (IPA)<br>• Mapping of read/write transactions to contexts by using the associated “Stream ID” (see Section 8.8.3.6.1) and “Security state indication” attributes<br>• Supports Translation Lookaside Buffer Hit Under Miss (TLB HUM)<br><br>**Features of the SMMU subsystem:**<br>• SMMU subsystem includes two SMMU instances:<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;– APPS SMMU (consists of nine TBU and one TCU)<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;– GPU SMMU (consists of one TBU and one TCU)<br>• Supports 32-bit VA and 32-bit PA<br>• Supports 32 configurable contexts<br>• Generation of VMID values for each TBU master interface, derived from the Stream ID value associated with the read/write transaction<br>• TCU snooping the APPS CPU L2 caches (through the ACP port) for cached page table entries, using the BIMC redirect feature<br>• MPU for protecting the SMMU CSR space and the local CSR space<br>• MPU for protecting MSA = 1 access from DSP clients, as SMMU is bypassed for MSA = 1 clients<br>• Interrupt aggregation logic for APPS TCU context bank interrupts<br>• Clock gating |

### 8.8.1.1 SMMU key use cases

The SMMU subsystem is used for address virtualization of non-CPU masters.

The SMMU subsystem has the following two major benefits:
* **Memory defragmentation:** fragmented physical memory can be translated into contiguous virtual memory without moving data.
* **Memory protection:** nonallowed accesses to memory locations can be detected and prevented.

It also allows seamless expanding of DRAMs.
<!-- page 3254 -->

Figure 8-50 shows a typical SMMU example use case.

#### Figure 8-50: SMMU example usecase

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph VM ["Virtual Memory (Contiguous/Isolated)"]
        subgraph MR ["Contiguous Memory Region"]
            VM_MR1["Memory Region 1"]
            VM_MR2["Memory Region 2"]
        end
        VM_T1["Task 1"]
        VM_T2["Task 2"]
    end

    subgraph PM ["Physical Memory (Fragmented/Adjacent)"]
        PM_MR1["Memory Region 1"]
        PM_T1["Task 1"]
        PM_T2["Task 2"]
        PM_MR2["Memory Region 2"]
    end

    VM_MR1 --> PM_MR1
    VM_MR2 --> PM_MR2
    VM_T1 --> PM_T1
    VM_T2 --> PM_T2
```

*Description:* SMMU example usecase showing how physical memory fragmentation is resolved (Memory region 1 and 2 are contiguous in virtual memory but fragmented in physical memory) and how memory protection is enforced (Task 1 and 2 are adjacent in physical memory but separated in virtual memory, preventing accidental cross-writes).

The memory regions 1 and 2 are fragmented in the physical memory, but they appear as one contiguous memory region in the virtual memory space.

The tasks 1 and 2 are located next to each other in the physical memory, but nonadjacent in the virtual memory. This removes the risk of task 1 writing accidentally into task 2 area and vice versa.

### 8.8.3 SMMU functional description
The SMMU subsystem is composed of local page table caches (TBUs) distributed at each client master interface and central page table caches (TCUs) interconnected to BIMC through PTW AXI3 interface.

There are two TCUs - APSS and GPU (application and graphics). The APSS TCU has nine associated TBUs while the GPU TCU has one TBU. Each TBU is sync with its upstream master and each TCU is sync with the BIMC. The APSS TCU arbitrates transactions from different TBU based on programmable QoS.

Figure 8-52 and Figure 8-53 show a high-level overview of the SMMU functional blocks.

#### Figure 8-52 SMMU functional block diagram (1)
*Description:* A block diagram showing the SMMU subsystem components and their connections:
- **GFX TCU (Graphics TCU)**:
  - Connected to the **Graphics** master via a **TBU**.
  - Interfaced with **BIMC** via a **PTW AXI3 arbiter**.
- **APPS TCU**:
  - Interfaced with **BIMC** via a **PTW AXI3 arbiter**.
  - Connected to various system masters through individual **TBUs**:
    - **QDSP** (via TBU, connected through System NOC)
    - **MDP** (via TBU)
    - **VFE0** (via TBU)
    - **VFE1** (via TBU)
    - **CPP** (via TBU)
    - **JPEG** (via TBU)
    - **VENUS** (via TBU)
    - **LPASS** (via TBU)
    - **GPS** (via TBU)
    - **PRONTO** (via TBU)
    - **Peripheral and system configuration NoC** (via TBU)
    - **IPA** (via TBU)
<!-- page 3262 -->
#### Figure 8-53 SMMU functional block diagram (2)
*Description:* A detailed block diagram illustrating the SMMU subsystem's internal architecture, bus interfaces, and control flow:
- **Master Interface**:
  - Connects to the SMMU subsystem, passing through **QSB2.1 slave** and **QSB2.1 master** blocks.
  - Includes **SID2VMID** and **MPU** components.
  - Leads to **TBU-0 bus bridge** and **TBU-N bus bridge**.
  - Interfaced via **AXI3 master** and **AXI3 slave**.
- **Control and Interconnect**:
  - Contains **CLKON logic** (with CLKON in, CLKON out, and CLKON lines).
  - Contains **Interrupt aggregator logic** that outputs SMMU interrupts.
  - The core is **ARM CoreLink MMU-500**, which includes:
    - **APPS TCU** and **GFX TCU** with PTW masters and AXI3 programming interfaces.
    - A **PTW arbiter** leading to BIMC.
    - Bus adapters: **QSB2AXI**, **QSB2QSB**, and **AXI2QSB (Async)**.
    - Default and Local registers.
    - An **AHB decoder**, **MPU**, and **GFX 4K aperture registers**.
    - Interfacing to **PCNOC AHB**, **PCNOC AXI3**, and **GFX AXI3** for MMU configuration.

SMMU functional blocks:
* **ARM CoreLink MMU-500** – This is the core of the SMMU subsystem. The MMU-500 is a system-level MMU that translates an input address to an output address, based on address mapping and memory attribute information available in the MMU-500 internal registers and translation tables.
  > [!NOTE]
  > For more information about the ARM CoreLink MMU-500, see Table 8-183.
* **Translation buffer unit (TBU)** – The TBU contains a translation lookaside buffer (TLB) that caches page tables. There is a local TBU for each connected master.
  Software programs registers in the TCU to trigger invalidation of TLB caches when global page tables are updated. The TCU does invalidation of its local caches and also sends broadcast message to all connected TBUs. On receiving this invalidation message, each TBU invalidates its local TLB cache and responds to TCU with acknowledgment.
* **TCU (translation control unit)** – The TCU controls and manages the address translations. The TBU and TCU are the major functional blocks of the SMMU subsystem. The TBU caches
<!-- page 3263 -->
Frequently used address ranges and the TCU perform the page table walk.
* **Interrupt aggregator logic** – This logic aggregates all interrupts to one output interrupt. There are global, contexts, performance, secure, and nonsecure interrupts.
  The interrupts from the 32 Context Bank are aggregated (steered) into a single interrupt line.
  There are three sets of registers to select one of 32 interrupts:
  * `SMMU_ATCU_CXT_IRPT_0` is aggregated/steered using `SMMU_INTR_SEL_NS` (for nonsecure driver)
  * `SMMU_ATCU_CXT_IRPT_1` is aggregated or steered using `SMMU_INTR_SEL_NSHYP` (for Hypervisor driver)
  * `SMMU_ATCU_CXT_IRPT_2` is aggregated or steered using `SMMU_INTR_SEL_SEC` (for secure driver)
* For more information about the available SMMU interrupts, see Table 8-188 and Section 8.8.3.2.
* **Masters**: Hexagon DSP, MDP, VFE0, VFE1, CPP, JPEG, VENCDEC, LPASS, GPS, WCSS, Peripheral and system configuration NoC (PNOC/PERIPH), and GRAPHICS.
* **Clock ON logic** – This logic controls Turn ON/OFF of the SMMU clocks.
  For more information about the available SMMU clocks, see Table 8-186 and Section 8.8.3.1.2.
* **PTW arbiter** – This block arbitrates which TCU to be connected to the BIMC and provides access to the memory for page table walks (PTW).
* **APPS TCU PTW master** – Provides connection of APPS TCU to PTW arbiter.
* **GPU TCU PTW master** – Provides connection of APPS TCU to PTW arbiter.
* **BIMC (Bus interface memory controller)** – This block provides connection to the memory (LPDDR).
* **APPS TCU AXI3 programming I/F** – Interface for configuration of the APPS TCU.
* **GPU TCU AXI3 programming I/F** – Interface for configuration of the GPU TCU.

The SMMU uses inputs from the requesting master (Stream IDs (SID)) to identify a context. This context tells the SMMU what resources to use for the translation (including which translation tables to use).

For example (see Figure 8-52), transactions sent by the VFE0 master are received by the TBU on its slave interface to search for a TLB hit. On a miss, the TBU interacts with the TCU through its master interface, and initiates a page table walk. On receiving the page table entry or a TLB hit, the TBU then forwards the transaction to its master interface after the pending translation based on the page entry.

> [!NOTE]
> For more detailed description of the SMMU functionality, see Section, *About the functions and Operations* in ARM CoreLink MMU-500 System Memory Management Unit TRM (Table 8-183).
<!-- page 3264 -->
#### 8.8.3.1 SMMU power and clock management

##### 8.8.3.1.1 Initialization, configuration, and control sequence
To power up SMMU subsystem, first TCU universal asynchronous reset (UAR) is de-asserted and subsequently all TBUs UARs are deasserted. ARM MMU-500 design has power up FSMs internally within TBUs and TCUs, which start automatically once subsequent reset is deasserted. Also until ARM initialization sequence is complete, while low power FSM in ARM TBU is in low power state, it drops ready to upstream client bus interface.

##### 8.8.3.1.2 Clock gating
> [!NOTE]
> For more information, see Section *MMU clocking* in Chapter *Clock Management (GCC)*.

The SMMU subsystem supports software and hardware clock gating for all TCUs and TBUs using hardware signals:
* `i_tbun_clkon`/`o_tbun_clkon` for TBUn
* `i_tcun_clkon`/`o_tcun_clkon` for TCUn

There are no software registers within the SMMU subsystem to control clock gating. The control of the clock gating for each TCU and TBU resides within the SoC clock controller block.

Example:

`<clock_name>_CBCR`:
* **Clock Enable bit == 0**: Hardware Clock gating mode
  * Clock is turned ON/OFF depending on hardware vote
* **Clock Enable bit == 1**: Software Clock gating mode
  * Clock is turned ON irrespective of hardware vote

**Clock gating programming guide**

* **For APPS TCU/TBU** (TBU to TCU interface is asynchronous):
  * Software should turn ON clock to APPS TCU during APPS TCU register programming sequence.
* **For GPU TCU/TBU** (TBU to TCU interface is synchronous):
  * Software should turn ON clock to GPU TBU during GPU TLB invalidation sequence.
  * Software should turn ON clock to GPU TCU during GPU TCU register programming sequence while GPU master clock is Active.
<!-- page 3265 -->

#### 8.8.3.4 Error detection and handling
See the ARM MMU-500 technical reference manual and architecture document for details about error detection features supported by ARM (see the documents in Table 8-183).

The SMMU subsystem detects three kinds of errors:
* **MPU permission errors for SMMU configuration space**: The SMMU subsystem returns bus error response in this case for the configuration transaction failing MPU permission checks.
* **VA-PA mismatch error for DSP TBUs**: VA-PA match check is done for DSP TBUs to ensure that PA translated by the SMMU subsystem is the same as input VA and software has not enabled any translation for MSA = 1 accesses by accident.
  By default, the VA-PA match checker is enabled for all DSP TBUs. On a VA-PA mismatch, an ORed interrupt is sent to the APPS processor. The following registers are used to control VA-PA match interrupt:
  * `SMMU_MSA_BYPASS_INTR_EN_NSHYP`
* **MPU permission errors for DSP TBU clients**: The SMMU subsystem sends the transaction coming from the DSP client to the software configurable bus address in case of MSA = 1 transaction failing MPU permission checks for DSP TBUs.
<!-- page 3268 -->
For details of the software configurable bus address, see the following register:
* `SMMU_MSA_BYPASS_ERR_ADDR_NSHYP`

#### 8.8.3.5 Debug features

##### 8.8.3.5.1 CATS (Client-side address translation)
* There are two modes of generating SID for CATS:
  * CATS can use `AxAddr[25:23]` as SID, which allows each CB to have as little as 8 MB aperture. With the total 64 MB address range for CATS, test up to 8 CBs is possible.
  * SID can also be generated from the SMMU local registers (see Section 8.8.3.3.2).
* `SSD_Index` for PERIPH (peripheral and system configuration NoC) TBU CATS port is same as SID.
  * `SSD_Index` for other TBU CATS port is tied to `0x1`.
* 64 MB of CATS space is remapped by using upper 6 bits from SMMU local register.
* Two sets of registers:
  * One for 64-bit CATS and other for 128-bit CATS.
  * Both registers in secure space.
* For more information see the following registers:
  * `SMMU_CATS_64_BIT_CTL_SEC`
  * `SMMU_CATS_128_BIT_CTL_SEC`

#### 8.8.3.6 Security

##### 8.8.3.6.1 VMID for TBU client ports
The VMID for each TBU client port is generated using SID (StreamID) coming from the respective client. Details of the logic and associated registers are mentioned here:
* Generates VMID based on incoming SID from each TBU master:
  * `SID2VMID` instance per TBU.
  * Stream Mapping Registers (`SMR`) to mask/match incoming StreamID for generating VMID.
  * Number of SMRs for each TBU is decided based on “possible stream ID values” in Table 8-192.
  * Default VMID register for no match.
  * Fault interrupt generation if there is no-match and multimatch.
  * Fault interrupt enable/clear and status registers.
* Following is the list of supported SIDs and required VMIDs for each TBU master.

## 8.9 Pseudo-Random Number Generator (PRNG)

This section describes the Pseudo Random Number Generator (PRNG). It is used to generate cryptographic random numbers. The PRNG module has two primary uses:

- Cryptographic key exchange algorithms, such as Internet Key Exchange (IKE) and Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange.
- Gaming applications.

### 8.9.1 PRNG overview

There is one PRNG module integrated within the device.

Figure 8-54 shows a high level overview of the PRNG instance integrated in the SoC.

#### Figure 8-54: PRNG overview
*Description:* A block diagram showing the PRNG instance and its external connections. The "GCC" (Global Clock Controller) block is on the left, sending "Clocks" and "Resets" to the "PRNG" block on the right. The "PRNG" block has a bidirectional connection to the "Peripheral and System Configuration NoC" at the bottom, represented by separate input and output arrows.

The PRNG generates cryptographic random numbers. The two primary use cases are:

- The PRNG generates the primary hardware key, which is programmed into fuses (QFPROM) for each device.
- The Transport Layer Security (TLS) and its predecessor, the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL), are cryptographic protocols that provide communication security over the Internet. TLS and SSL encrypt the segments of network connections above the Transport Layer, using asymmetric cryptography for privacy and a keyed message authentication code for message reliability. To generate the session keys used for the secure connection, the client encrypts a random number with the server public key and sends the result to the server. Only the server must be able to decrypt it with its private key. From the random number, both parties generate key material for encryption and decryption.
<!-- page 3277 -->

### 8.9.4 PRNG functional description

Figure 8-56 shows high-level overview of PRNG module functional blocks:

- AHB slave interface with Register Interface (RIF) module.
- 16x32 synchronous RNG FIFO for entropy reading.
- Clock domain crossing exists in the entropy collector, where ring oscillator output is sampled by CC_PRNG_CLK.

#### Figure 8-56: PRNG functional block diagram
*Description:* A functional block diagram of the PRNG module.
At the top, there are four independent "Entropy Collector" blocks. Each block contains:
- a "CRC32 LFSR"
- a "Ring Oscillator"
- a "Health Monitoring" sub-block.
These collectors feed into the "PRNG_CORE" via a combined bus to the "ENTROPY FIFO(2X32)" block. An "Entropy shutdown" signal is sent back to the collectors from the "ENTROPY CONTROLLER" block within the PRNG_CORE.

The "PRNG_CORE" contains:
- "RNG Counters" which interface bidirectionally with the "RNG State machine".
- "RNG State machine" which also interfaces bidirectionally with "RIF registers" and outputs to the "SHA 256" block. It also receives feedback from the "RNG STATE COLLECTOR".
- "RIF registers" which interface bidirectionally with the external "Peripheral and System Configuration NoC".
- "ENTROPY FIFO(2X32)" which receives entropy data and is controlled by the "ENTROPY CONTROLLER". It outputs to the "SHA 256" block.
- "SHA 256" block which outputs to the "RNG STATE COLLECTOR" and the "RNG FIFO(16X32)".
- "RNG STATE COLLECTOR" which feeds back into the "RNG State machine".
- "RNG FIFO(16X32)" which outputs random numbers to the external "Peripheral and System Configuration NoC".

The external "Peripheral and System Configuration NoC" sits at the bottom, interfacing bidirectionally with "RIF registers" and receiving output from "RNG FIFO(16X32)".
<!-- page 3280 -->

### 8.9.5 PRNG theory of operation

The functional operation of the PRNG is based on the principals of Deterministic Random Bit Generator (DRBG).

Figure 8-57 shows DRBG mechanism functions.

#### Figure 8-57: Random bit generator block diagram
*Description:* A block diagram showing the DRBG (Deterministic Random Bit Generator) mechanism functions. The diagram consists of a central "Internal State" oval and several functions that interact with it:
- **Instantiate Function:** Receives "Personalization String", "Nonce", and "Entropy Input" from the "Consuming Application" and sets the initial "Internal State".
- **Reseed Function:** Receives "Entropy Input" and "Additional Input" from the "Consuming Application", and interacts bidirectionally with the "Internal State" to update it.
- **Uninstantiate Function:** Interacts with the "Internal State" (presumably to clear it).
- **Generate Function:** Receives "Additional Input" from the "Consuming Application", interacts bidirectionally with the "Internal State", and outputs "Pseudorandom Output" back to the "Consuming Application".
- **Tests & Error State:** A "Tests" block outputs to an "Error State" oval.

The PRNG module is composed of the following functions:

- **INSTANTIATE:** The instantiate function acquires entropy input and could combine it with a nonce and a personalization string to create a seed from which the initial internal state is created.
- **RESEED:** The reseed function acquires new entropy input and combines it with the current internal state, and any additional input that is provided, to create a new seed and a new internal state.
- **GENERATE:** The generate function generates pseudo-random bits upon request, using the current internal state, and generates a new internal state for the next request.
- **UN-INSTANTIATE:** The un-instantiate function erases the internal state.
- **HEALTH:** The health function determines that the DRBG mechanism continues to function correctly.


<!-- page 3281 -->
### 8.9.6 PRNG Initialization/configuration/control sequence(s)

The following configuration steps should be completed before PRNG module configuration.

1. Enable `CC_PRNG_CLK`; `PRNG_AHB_RESET` shall be asserted after `CC_PRNG_CLK` is enabled. The PRNG configuration can be as simple as two AHB write transactions, because default settings are applicable to most use cases. Software can choose to take optional configuration procedures, depending on the application.
2. Write to `PRNG_LFSR_CFG [RING_OSCn_CFG]` bit field (where n = 0 to 3) configures ring oscillators. The LFSR circuit in entropy collectors can be enabled through `PRNG_LFSR_CFG [LFSRn_EN]`, where n = 0 to 3.
3. (optional) Write to `PRNG_PERSONALIZATION_STRING` register can be obtained from other sources, such as key presses, searcher noise, or other system events, to increase entropy.
4. (optional) Write to `PRNG_RESEED_FREQ` register, which default value is 0x10000.
5. The default value can be used. There is no requirement to change this value unless there is evidence that the PRNG outputs are being attacked. The minimum number of GENERATE operations before RESEED is 2.
6. (optional) Write to `PRNG_INSTANTIATE_FREQ` register, which default value is 0x10000.
7. The default value can be used. There is no requirement to change this value unless there is evidence that the PRNG outputs are being attacked.
8. (optional) Write to `PRNG_GEN_WORDS` register, which default value is 0x8 words (or 256 bits).
9. Security strength is 128 bits, so default value is valid for most cases.
10. (optional) The default value of the `PRNG_SAMPLE_FREQ` register is 0x400. It is recommended not to sample the ring oscillator output on every clock to increase backtracking resistance.
11. (optional) The default value of the `PRNG_NUM_ENTROPY` register is 0x400 (or 1 KByte). This is the number of entropy bytes to be used in the INSTANTIATE and RESEED processes. Minimum value is 16 bytes, and maximum value is 235 bits per NIST.SP.800-90Ar1 standard.
12. Set `PRNG_CONFIG[PRNG_EN]` bit. If `PRNG_CONFIG [PRNG_EN]` is cleared, all FSMs reach and remain in the IDLE state upon completion of current operations. If the current operation requires dumping random numbers into the RNG FIFO, the RNG FIFO must be cleared. If the RNG FIFO is empty, reading `PRNG_DATA_OUT` register will return 0x0. In addition, `PRNG_CONFIG [PRNG_EN]` bit has no effect on entropy collectors.
<!-- page 3282 -->
### 8.9.7 PRNG input/output buffers and formats

* Random numbers generated from the PRNG module are stored in the RNG FIFO. This is a 16x32 FIFO and stores up to two random numbers of 256 bits each. The FIFO empty flag is tied to `PRNG_STATUS [DATA_AVAIL]`.
  * `PRNG_STATUS [DATA_AVAIL]` = 1h - Random numbers can be read out of `PRNG_DATA_OUT` register
  * `PRNG_STATUS [DATA_AVAIL]` = 0h - Zeroes read out of `PRNG_DATA_OUT` register.
* Eight reads are required to fetch a 256 bits random number.
* Data formats in memory (if any).
  * Endian of data.
  * Memory format: tile, linear.

### 8.9.8 PRNG module reset

The PRNG takes a single `PRNG_AHB_RESET` from the global clock controller (GCC). This asynchronous reset is coupled from `CC_PRNG_CLK`. This clock is present during a `PRNG_AHB_RESET` event. `PRNG_AHB_RESET` event resets the AHB slave module, RIF module, and PRNG core asynchronously.

In addition to `PRNG_AHB_RESET`, there is also a software reset, which is triggered by setting `PRNG_CONFIG [SW_RESET]` bit. This is a self-clearing reset. After being asserted through the AHB write transaction, `SW_RESET` resets RIF module contents after one cycle delay and remains high for two cycles to reset the PRNG core. Reading from `PRNG_CONFIG [SW_RESET]` always returns 0x0. Software reset does not reset the AHB slave module.

### 8.9.9 Reset state

When the PRNG module is in reset state:
* The FSMs are in IDLE state.
* The AHB slave is in IDLE state, waiting for AHB transactions to take place.
* The RIF module is in reset state. All registers take default value.
* The PRNG core is disabled.
* The LFSR and ring oscillator are held low in entropy collectors.

> [!NOTE]
> There are no software-controlled ring oscillator disables at the system level.
<!-- page 3283 -->
### 8.9.10 PRNG clocks

PRNG relies on `CC_PRNG_CLK` provided by the global clock controller (GCC). `CC_PRNG_CLK` clocks all registers in the PRNG module, including the CRC32 LFSR circuits, ring oscillator sampling circuits in entropy collectors, counters, SHA, RNG FIFO, etc. This clock can be turned off when no random numbers are required. However, by turning off the clock, internal states are considered corrupted. The next clock-on event shall be coupled with a `PRNG_AHB_RESET` assertion event to clear internal states.

`CC_PRNG_CLK` is synchronous to the host bus and is assumed to have the same frequency as the host bus clock. There is no minimum clock frequency requirement, while the maximum clock frequency is determined by the synthesis target frequency.

### 8.9.11 PRNG performance

#### 8.9.11.1 Block level features

The PRNG performance depends on the number of RESEED and INSTANTIATE operations inserted among GENERATE operations. Adding RESEED and INSTANTIATE operations enhances backtrack resistance of the core and prevents it from revealing internal states to the external world.

#### 8.9.11.2 System level performance

The performance requirement for the PRNG is that random data must be available to software at a total output rate of 10 Mbps, with a latency of 10 ms. Performance data is summarized in Table 8-199.

##### Table 8-199 PRNG System level performance data

| MBps | Mbps | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3.47 | 27.6 | Default register settings |
| 2.48 | 19.8 | Reduced Entropy Settings. See the register settings below. |

The PRNG is able to provide 27.6 Mbps or 3.47 MBps at the default settings.
<!-- page 3284 -->
#### 8.9.11.3 PRNG module security

The APU (external to this design) is configured so that only the secure root of trust (SROT) can write to the configuration registers. The software interface is specifically formulated to only require writes from the SROT, but reads can be allowed from any master that requires access to random numbers. To ensure that an attacker cannot determine the internal state of the PRNG, the software interface does not contain registers that explicitly read the V and C registers.

The software interface also provides for not using every output of the entropy collectors. Using less outputs from the entropy collectors minimizes the possibility of an attacker being able to guess the next output of the PRNG, because the number of possible states of the entropy collector exponentially increases with the number of clocks between samples. Therefore, a relatively large number of clocks between samples is recommended.

#### 8.9.11.4 PRNG module debug features

Turn on each ring oscillator independently of each other and observe the sample output as well as the divided-down frequency to correlate with expected outputs.

Debugging features incorporated in the design can aid debugging:
* Current operation status (IDLE, GENERATE, INSTANTIATE, RESEED) can be observed through `PRNG_STATUS [CURRENT_OPERATION]` field.
* Next operation status is indicated with the following fields:
  * `PRNG_STATUS [GENERATE_REQUIRED]`
  * `PRNG_STATUS [RESEED_REQUIRED]`
  * `PRNG_STATUS [INSTANTIATE_REQUIRED]`
* The ring oscillator health state can be observed through `PRNG_STATUS [RING_OSCn_HEALTHY]`, where n = 0 to 3.
* `PRNG_ENTROPY_CNTR [ENTROPY_CNTR]` field returns number of entropy collected in RESEED or INSTANTIATE operation.
* `PRNG_SAMPLE_CNTR [SAMPLE_CNTR]` field returns clock cycles count from last LFSR sample.
* `PRNG_GEN_CNTR` field returns GENERATE counter value.
* `PRNG_RESEED_CNTR [RESEED_CNTR]` field returns RESEED counter value.
* `PRNG_INSTANTIATE_CNTR [INSTANTIATE_CNTR]` field returns number of RESEED operations.

## 8.10 Temperature Sensors (TSENS)

This section describes the temperature sensor module. TSENS monitors the die temperature.

### 8.10.1 TSENS overview

The TSENS module is a digital controller, which provides software interface and control to key functionalities. It also includes periodic temperature measurement, interrupt generation, and hardware shutdown at extreme temperatures, to avoid permanent damage due to thermal run away or catastrophic timing failure at low temperatures.

Figure 8-58 shows a high-level overview of the TSENS instance integrated within the SoC master power manager (MPM2) block in the SoC.

#### Figure 8-58 TSENS overview
*Description:* Block diagram showing the TSENS module integrated within the MPM2 (SoC Master Power Manager) block. The TSENS contains a Comparator, Control logic, oscillator (osc), and Analog ADC block.
- Clocks and Resets are provided by the GCC (Global Clock Controller).
- Interrupts from TSENS are routed to the RPM (Resource Power Manager), APSS (Application Processor Subsystem), and QGIC (Qualcomm Generic Interrupt Controller).
- Five remote sensors connect to the Analog ADC block.
- An AHB slave bus connects TSENS to the Peripheral and system configuration NoC.
<!-- page 3292 -->
Table 8-209 lists the TSENS supported features.

#### Table 8-209 TSENS features

| Module name | Features |
| :--- | :--- |
| **TSENS** | <ul><li>Software reset capability</li><li>Programmable periodic measurement timer</li><li>Run-once capability</li><li>Support up to 11 (1 main and 10 remote) temperature sensors</li><li>Dedicated programmable temperature thresholds and a control for each individual sensor</li><li>Two programmable temperature limits:<ul><li>Upper temperature: to initiate a software system degradation or software shutdown</li><li>Lower temperature: to initiate a software system restore or software shutdown</li></ul></li><li>No high-speed clock required for temperature measurement and monitoring</li><li>Internal oscillator for ADC</li><li>Low-power operation during continuous mode (turning off the clocks and sensors between measurements)</li><li>Support of aggregated interrupt for thermal mitigation management</li><li>Maskable hardware interrupts per individual CPU core, with overwrite features for debug</li><li>Maskable hardware critical shutdown signal and its equivalent interrupt for debug during silicon bring-up</li></ul> |

### 8.10.3 TSENS functional description

#### 8.10.3.1 TSENS internal architecture

Figure 8-60 shows a high-level overview of TSENS functional blocks.

#### Figure 8-60 TSENS functional block diagram
*Description:* High-level functional block diagram of the TSENS module showing its internal blocks and interfaces.
- **Internal Blocks:**
  - **Control Logic:** Manages the overall operation.
  - **Measure Timer:** Triggers periodic measurements.
  - **Comparator:** Compares the measured temperature against defined threshold levels: MIN, LOWER, UPPER, and MAX. It generates the interrupts `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR` and `TSENS_MAX_MIN_INT`.
  - **TSENS Register Block:** Provides registers interface connected to the Peripheral and system configuration NoC via the AHB bus.
  - **ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter):** Digitizes the analog temperature measurements.
  - **OSC (Oscillator):** Clocked by `MPM_CLK` (32.768 kHz).
  - **Multiplexer:** Selects one of the 5 remote sensor inputs.
- **External Interfaces:**
  - **Resets:** `MPM_TSENSE_ARES` and `MPM_PS_HOLD_ARES`.
  - **Registers Clock/Reset:** `GCC_MPM_AHB_CLK` and `GCC_MPM_AHB_ARES`.
  - **Analog Inputs:** 5 Remote Sensors supplying Analog output to the Multiplexer.
  - **Power:** vdd, vss.

The TSENS consists of the following main blocks:
* **Measurement period timer:** periodically initiates a temperature measurement, so that the TSENS module can autonomously monitor the temperature of the system. The period timer is programmable to allow a range of delays for temperature monitoring. The minimum interval is 62.5 ms (0x01).
* **Remote temperature sensors:** each temperature sensor is implemented as a temperature-sensitive diode whose threshold voltage VTH changes with the temperature. A constant current is passed through the diode to provide a reference voltage to the ADC. Five external temperature sensors are supported.
* **ADC:** The analog-to-digital converter (ADC) converts the diode voltage to a digital value that can be compared to the preprogrammed limit values. The ADC creates an 10-bit digital output.
* **Oscillator:** The internal TSENS oscillator is a simple ring oscillator, used to clock the ADC for temperature measurements. The internal oscillator also provides the internal clock for values comparing and interrupts generation. When the interrupts are issued (if needed), the oscillator is disabled to conserve power. It cannot turn back on until the next temperature measurement.
<!-- page 3296 -->
* **Comparator logic:** compares the measured temperature value from the ADC with the preprogrammed temperature values for MAX, UPPER, LOWER, and MIN limits.
* **TSENS register block:** contains the configuration registers of TSENS module for software control.
* **Bus interface:** The TSENS is connected to the AHB bus through the SoC bus interface. The SoC bus interface operates on the `GCC_MPM_AHB_CLK` frequency. The register accesses must be synchronized to the SoC bus interface.

#### 8.10.3.2 TSENS power and clock management

The TSENS controller is sourced by the always-on (VDD_AO) LDO-regulated MPM2 power rail. The TSENS controller operation can be left on throughout the vddcx minimization cycle.

The TSENS module is clocked by the following clocks:
* **TSENS_REFCLK_DIV2:** Low-speed clock (32.768 kHz). This clock is sourced by the internal `mpm_clock` block from the MPM module.
* **GCC_MPM_AHB_CLK:** High-speed clock accessing TSENS registers. This clock is synchronous to the peripheral and system configuration NoC clock. It is managed by the NoC FSM. The `GCC_MPM_AHB_CLK` is configured to be on waiting state by default until the slave clock become active. When the NoC FSM is enabled, the GCC will handshake with the configuration NoC prior to turning off this clock. This clock is also votable. For more information see section Clock voting scheme in the chapter Clock Management (GCC).

#### 8.10.3.3 TSENS reset options

* **MPM_TSENSE_ARES:** Temperature sensor reset from MPM.
* **MPM_PS_HOLD_ARES:** Temperature sensor reset from GCC.
* **GCC_MPM_AHB_ARES:** Matching async reset for `GCC_MPM_AHB_CLK`.

#### 8.10.3.4 TSENS interrupts

* **TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR:** Indicates that the temperature is outside a certain set range.
* **TSENS_MAX_MIN_INT:** Maximum or minimum threshold interrupt.

#### 8.10.3.5 TSENS theory of operation

The TSENS module operates autonomously to measure the temperature periodically and reports back to the system when the temperature is out of the normal range of operation.

There are two parallel operations:
* Periodic temperature measurement and comparison
* Interrupt service by software

The periodic temperature measurement and comparison is performed to monitor the system temperature even if the software does not service the interrupt. This action prevents the system
<!-- page 3297 -->
from overheating or getting too cold if one or more processor cores are stuck and cannot service the temperature interrupt.

When the MIN or MAX temperature limit is reached, the TSENS module drives `TSENS_PSHOLD_ARES` low to the GCC to power down the system.

Figure 8-61 shows the flow diagram of the temperature control system.

#### Figure 8-61 Temperature control flow
*Description:* Flowchart of the temperature control system implemented in TSENS.
1. **Setup:**
   - Software sets up temperature limits and delays.
   - Software enables temperature sensing.
2. **Measurement Cycle Initialization:**
   - TSENS clears interrupts and starts the measurement period timer.
3. **Sampling Loop:**
   - TSENS samples and saves the last temperature for sensors 0 through 4 (temp0, temp1, temp2, temp3, temp4).
   - *Note:* The interrupt signal is generated only if all the temperature measurements are taken.
4. **Interrupt Generation:**
   - TSENS sends out interrupt signals.
5. **Threshold Checks (Evaluation):**
   - **Check 1: Over MAX temp or under MIN temp?**
     - **YES:** TSENS sets the MAX or MIN status flag -> TSENS drives the `PS_HOLD` signal low -> GCC moves to the OFF state.
     - **NO:** Proceed to Check 2.
   - **Check 2: Over UPPER or under LOWER temp?**
     - **YES:** TSENS sets the UPPER or LOWER status flag and generates an interrupt -> TSENS wakes up the core (if needed) -> Software services the interrupt.
     - **NO:** TSENS does nothing.
6. **Cycle Wait:**
   - TSENS waits for the measurement period before initiating the next sampling cycle.

##### 8.10.3.5.1 Temperature limits

There are four temperature level limits in the TSENS module.
* The MAX temperature limit indicates the system is near the absolute highest possible operation temperature. If the temperature reaches the MAX limit, an interrupt is generated, and the system is shut down.
* The UPPER and LOWER temperature limits are soft limits the software can program to monitor the temperature of the system. When the UPPER and LOWER temperature limits are
<!-- page 3298 -->
exceeded, the software can enable, disable, or degrade hardware resources to control the temperature.
* **The MIN temperature limit:** indicates the system temperature is too low and could cause functional failures. If the temperature comes down to the MIN limit, the hardware shuts down the system.

Figure 8-62 shows the four temperature limits defined in the TSENS module.

#### Figure 8-62 TSENS temperature limits
*Description:* Diagram showing the relationship between operational ranges and shutdown thresholds:
- **Abs MAX / Shutdown:** Highest limit.
- **MAX temperature limit:** Triggers shutdown.
- **UPPER temperature limit:** Soft threshold (limits the "Operational range" from above).
- **LOWER temperature limit:** Soft threshold (limits the "Operational range" from below).
- **MIN temperature limit:** Triggers shutdown.
- **Abs MIN / Shutdown:** Lowest limit.
- **Design range:** Encompasses the range between MIN temperature and MAX temperature.

#### 8.10.3.5.2 ADC temperature value calculation

ADC provides a quantized digital code to represent the input signal. The digital codes get post-processed and results are reported to a TSENS, which will use this information to make decisions and take actions. Therefore, it is important to correctly relate the digital codes back to the analog signals they represent.

The following bits should be read from the fuse block (QFPROM) to determine the calibration data:
* `TSENSn_BASE0`, n = 0 to num_controllers – 1
* `TSENSn_BASE1`, n = 0 to num_controllers – 1
* `TSENSn_OFFSET`, n = 0 to num_sensors – 1
* `TSENS_CAL_SEL` – used to determine offset and gain.

The ADC code at 30°C and 120°C would be respectively:

$$CODEn\_30C = (TSENS\_BASE0 \ll 3) - (TSENSn\_POINT1 \ll 3), \text{[code]}$$
<!-- page 3299 -->
$$CODEn\_120C = (TSENS\_BASE1 \ll 3) - (TSENSn\_POINT2 \ll 3), \text{[code]}$$

The absolute temperature is calculated from the measured ADC code of $CODEn$, n = sensor index (0, 1, 2, 4 or 5), using the following equation:

$$Temperature = 30 + \frac{90 \times (CODEn - CODEn\_30C)}{CODEn\_120C - CODEn\_30C}, [^\circ C]$$

The equation above could be rewritten to include offset and slope for calibration data. Therefore, the temperature is calculated as follows:

$$Temperature = 30 + SLOPEn \times (CODEn - OFFSETn), [^\circ C]$$

where

$$OFFSETn = CODEn\_30C, \text{[code]}$$

$$SLOPEn = \frac{90}{CODEn\_120C - CODEn\_30C}, [^\circ C/\text{code}]$$

Nevertheless, $SLOPEn$ has a decimal component and using integer math would result in truncation. As a result, the software multiplies slope by a factor before storing it and then removes the factor during the temperature calculation.

Example:

$$SLOPEn = \frac{90 \times FACTOR}{CODEn\_120C - CODEn\_30C}, [^\circ C/\text{code}]$$

$$Temperature = 30 + \frac{SLOPEn \times (CODEn - OFFSETn)}{FACTOR}, [^\circ C].$$
<!-- page 3300 -->
Figure 8-63 shows the ADC code (CODEn) as a function of the temperature (°C).

#### Figure 8-63 ADC temperature conversion plot
*Description:* A graph representing Temperature in °C (Y-axis, range -100 to 150) versus ADC code (CODEn, X-axis, range 200 to 1200). The plot illustrates a linear relationship where the ADC code increases as temperature rises.
