##### 8.10.3.5.4 Sequence and timing

When a module is enabled, the internal oscillator is started up and the TSENS clears the following register bits:
* TSENS_TRDY [TRDY]
* TSENS_Sn_STATUS [MIN_STATUS]
* TSENS_Sn_STATUS [LOWER_STATUS]
* TSENS_Sn_STATUS [UPPER_STATUS]
* TSENS_Sn_STATUS [MAX_STATUS]

The TSENS module takes an initial temperature measurement for each of the enabled temperature sensors. When a temperature measurement is taken, the measured value is stored to the LAST_TEMP[9:0] of the TSENS_Sn_STATUS registers.

After all remote temperature sensors are measured, the control logic generates interrupts. The TRDY signal can be generated only if all the temperature measurements are taken.

After the measurement, the control logic compares the stored temperature values to the temperature limits programmed in the THRESHOLD registers. The status register (TSENS_Sn_STATUS) bits are updated according to the following equations:
* MIN_STATUS set (logic 1) if any measured temperature is less than or equal to MIN_THRESHOLD
* LOWER_STATUS set (logic 1) if any measured temperature is less than LOWER_THRESHOLD and higher than MIN_THRESHOLD
* UPPER_STATUS set (logic 1) if any measured temperature is greater than UPPER_THRESHOLD and lower than MAX_THRESHOLD
* MAX_STATUS set (logic 1) if any measured temperature is greater than or equal to MAX_THRESHOLD

After the measured temperatures are compared with the limits and the appropriate STATUS values are stored to the TSENS_Sn_STATUS register, the internal oscillator is disabled and the TSENS module is put into a low-power state until the MEASURE_PERIOD expiration time. This time period is pre-defined to 0x01 and is not user controlled.

When the software performs its tasks, it can clear the status bits to the TSENS_Sn_STATUS registers by setting (to logic 1) either or both the UPPER_STATUS_CLR and LOWER_STATUS_CLR bits to the TSENS_Sn_UPPER_LOWER_STATUS_CTRL register. These bits must be cleared (set to logic 0) to return the TSENS module back to normal operation.
<!-- page 3302 -->

Figure 8-65 shows the timing sequence diagram for TSENS module.

#### Figure 8-65: Timing diagram for TSENS module
*Description:* A timing diagram showing the relationship between various signals in the TSENS module during temperature measurement.
The signals shown from top to bottom are:
*   `MPM_CLK`: A continuous, periodic clock signal. Note 1 indicates "Program limits and delay" is related to this clock.
*   `OSC`: The internal oscillator clock. It only oscillates (shows high frequency bursts) during the measurement phases. Note 2 indicates that the OSC generates frequency only when measurement operation occurs.
*   `Temperature & Thresholds`: A line representing the actual temperature is shown relative to four horizontal threshold lines: `MAX_THRESHOLD`, `UPPER_THRESHOLD`, `LOWER_THRESHOLD`, and `MIN_THRESHOLD`. The temperature starts below `LOWER_THRESHOLD`, rises above `UPPER_THRESHOLD` (crossing it between the first and second measurements), then falls below `LOWER_THRESHOLD` (crossing it before the third measurement), and finally stabilizes.
*   `TSENS_EN`: TSENS enable signal, which is high throughout the operation.
*   `INT_TIMER_CLR`: Internal timer clear signal. It pulses high at the start of each measurement cycle, initiating the measurement after a "Periodic measurement delay".
*   `INT_ADC_MEASURE[4:0]`: Active high signal during the actual ADC measurement. It aligns with the bursts of the `OSC` clock.
*   `TSENS_LAST_TEMP[9:0]`: Represents the stored last temperature value. It updates and stabilizes during the `INT_ADC_MEASURE` pulse.
*   `TSENS_TRDY_INT`: TSENS ready interrupt. It goes low at the start of the measurement cycle (when `INT_TIMER_CLR` pulses) and goes high when the measurement is complete and `TSENS_LAST_TEMP` is updated.
*   `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR`: The upper/lower threshold interrupt signal.
    *   It starts in an "Unknown" state (shaded block).
    *   It transitions to low.
    *   It transitions to high (Note 3) after the second measurement because the temperature crossed the `UPPER_THRESHOLD`.
    *   It is cleared (goes low) by software ("SW clear status bits").
    *   It transitions to high again (Note 4) after the third measurement because the temperature fell below the `LOWER_THRESHOLD` (crossing it).
    *   Note 5 shows it remaining low when no thresholds are crossed in subsequent measurements.

*   The internal oscillator (OSC) generates frequency only when measurement operation occurs
*   Program limits and delay
*   Limit crossed
*   Valid only if status bit not cleared by software request
*   Limit not crossed

##### 8.10.3.5.5 Programmable temperature limits

The UPPER and LOWER temperature limits (`UPPER_THRESHOLD` and `LOWER_THRESHOLD`) are programmable for software to define different temperature ranges.

For example, the software can set the `LOWER_THRESHOLD` to 0°C and the `UPPER_THRESHOLD` to 100°C. If the temperature rises above 100°C, the software could perform some task. Then it could reprogram the `LOWER_THRESHOLD` to 100°C, and the `UPPER_THRESHOLD` to 120°C.

The software then reprograms the temperature limits and can add hysteresis by programming the limits to provide some overlap. Using the previous example, the `LOWER_THRESHOLD` could be programmed to 90°C rather than 100°C to allow for a 10°C hysteresis in the temperature.

The MIN and MAX temperature limits (`MIN_THRESHOLD` and `MAX_THRESHOLD`) are programmed once upon boot up and are not user controlled.
<!-- page 3303 -->

###### Case: Software does not service an UPPER or LOWER interrupt

Depending upon the status of the system, the software might not service the interrupt in a timely fashion. When the software does not service the UPPER or LOWER interrupt (`TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR`), the interrupt is cleared at the next temperature measurement cycle. If the temperature still exceeds a limit, the interrupt is regenerated. However, if the temperature has fallen to within the limits, the interrupt will not be regenerated.

###### Case: PSHOLD-generated system reset – set to reboot

If the temperature reaches the MIN or MAX limit, `PS_HOLD` is de-asserted and the PMIC shuts down the system.

##### 8.10.3.5.6 Software interrupt routine

The hardware is defined to accommodate a variety of software control solutions. The software interrupt service routine can be created in phases to allow the software to develop over time.

###### UPPER/LOWER temperature limits interrupt routine

On an UPPER or LOWER interrupt, the software can negotiate with the appropriate software applications to modify the performance of the system to control the temperature.

Figure 8-66 shows the flow diagram for the negotiated control of system resources.

#### Figure 8-66: UPPER/LOWER temperature limit interrupt routine flow
*Description:* A flowchart showing the software interrupt routine when temperature limits (UPPER/LOWER) are crossed.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Figure 1-4"] --> Dec1{"TSENS: Over UPPER or under LOWER temp?"}
    Dec1 -- NO --> DoNothing["TSENS: Do nothing"]
    Dec1 -- YES --> SetFlag["TSENS: Set status flag UPPER and interrupt"]
    SetFlag --> WakeCore["TSENS: Wakeup selected core (if needed)"]
    WakeCore --> CheckRegs["CORE SW: Check interrupt status registers"]
    CheckRegs --> Dec2{"SW: UPPER or LOWER temp interrupt?"}
    Dec2 -- NO --> CheckOther["SW: Check for other levels"]
    Dec2 -- YES --> SignalApps["CORE SW: Signal the apps core to send GUI warning"]
    SignalApps --> SendWarning["SW: Send GUI warning"]
    SignalApps --> DetLoad["CORE SW: Determine how to modify system load (optional)"]
    DetLoad --> ClearFlags["CORE SW: Clear interrupt and status flags"]
```
<!-- page 3304 -->

The software uses the UPPER and LOWER limit interrupts to monitor the temperature of the system. As the temperature crosses the UPPER or LOWER limits, the software can re-program the limits. Once the UPPER and LOWER limits are sufficiently close to the MIN or MAX limits, the software can program the UPPER/LOWER interrupt to be a high priority interrupt, and the software routine can be changed to gracefully shut down of the system.

##### 8.10.3.6 Programming model

###### 8.10.3.6.1 Reading temperature measurement values

The last temperature measurement values are stored in separate registers corresponding to the remote temperature sensor. The temperature measurement values can be read at any time. The validity of the temperature measurement is dictated by how quickly the temperature is changing and the time since the last temperature measurement.

The sequence to read a temperature measurement value is:
1.  **SW:** Determine which sensor measurement values to read. TSENS registers
2.  **SW:** Read the `LAST_TEMP` value of the appropriate temperature sensors (`LAST_TEMP4`, `LAST_TEMP3`, `LAST_TEMP2`, `LAST_TEMP1`, `LAST_TEMP0`).
3.  **SW:** End

###### 8.10.3.6.2 UPPER/LOWER limit interrupt

When the temperature reaches above the UPPER temperature limit value or below the LOWER temperature limit value, the `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR` interrupt is sent to the system.

The UPPER or LOWER interrupt sequence is:
1.  **HW:** The temperature rises above `UPPER_THRESHOLD` or below `LOWER_THRESHOLD`.
2.  **HW:** The TSENS module clears the interrupts and takes a single temperature measurement of all enabled sensors.
3.  **HW:** The TSENS module determines that at least one of the measurements is above the `UPPER_THRESHOLD` or below the `LOWER_THRESHOLD`. The component generates the `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR` interrupt.
4.  **HW:** The TSENS module resets and starts the `MEASURE_PERIOD` timer = 0x01.
5.  **SW:** The software detects the interrupt and initiates an interrupt routine to address the `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR`.
6.  **SW:** The `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR` routine can do the following:
    *   Read the `LAST_TEMP` value of all enabled temperature sensors.
    *   Read the `UPPER_THRESHOLD` and `LOWER_THRESHOLD` (if not already stored by software).
    *   Compare the `LAST_TEMP` values to the UPPER and LOWER limits to determine which temperature sensor caused the interrupt and whether it is an UPPER or LOWER limit interrupt.
<!-- page 3305 -->

*   (Continuation of step 6 from page 3304) Initiate the software to determine its course of action, which can include:
    *   Do nothing
    *   Notify the user of the temperature condition (preferred)
    *   Reprogram the UPPER and LOWER limits
    *   Turn off/on the resources
    *   Degrade the performance or resources
    *   All the above, some of the above, or a completely different solution
7.  **SW:** Clear the interrupt status register by writing a 1 to either or both the `UPPER_STATUS_CLR` and `LOWER_STATUS_CLR` bits of the `TSENS_Sn_UPPER_LOWER_STATUS_CTRL` register. Then write a 0 to these registers to return to normal operation.
8.  **HW:** When the `MEASURE_PERIOD` timer expires, go to step 2.
9.  **SW:** End.

###### 8.10.3.6.3 Enabling the UPPER or LOWER interrupt

The thermal management algorithm requires the thermal application processor write-only registers. The thermal application processor performs the following sequence:
1.  Disable the upper or lower interrupt by clearing the `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTERRUPT_CTRL` register.
2.  Configure the upper or lower thresholds of the `TSENS_Sn_UPPER_LOWER_STATUS_CTRL` register.
3.  Enable the upper or lower interrupt by asserting the `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTERRUPT_CTRL` register, which defaults to 0 (disabled) at power-on reset.

###### 8.10.3.6.4 Clearing the UPPER or LOWER interrupt

If a sensor violates the corresponding upper or lower threshold, a combined `TSENS_UPPER_LOWER_INTR` interrupt (level sensitive) sends a trigger to the thermal application processor. The thermal management software responds to the interrupt as follows:
1.  Read `UPPER_STATUS` and `LOWER_STATUS` bits of the `TSENS_Sn_STATUS` register to determine if the sensor is violating the upper or lower threshold.
2.  Execute a thermal mitigation task accordingly.
3.  Clear the violating status bits by asserting and then de-asserting corresponding `UPPER_STATUS_CLR` or `LOWER_STATUS_CLR` bits of the `TSENS_Sn_UPPER_LOWER_STATUS_CTRL`.
<!-- page 3306 -->

### 8.11 Core Top Control and Status Registers (TCSR)

This section describes the core top CSR (TCSR) available in the SoC.

##### 8.11.1 TCSR overview

The TCSR consists of various control and status registers. TCSR provides mutex registers for the software to pass control among different execution environments (EE). Access control to a few TCSR registers is protected by one xPU that is configured as APU.

Certain sets of interrupts from subsystems come to TCSR to provide central locations for the software to quickly identify the interrupt sources. The interrupts are grouped together and then a summary interrupt is routed to the required processors.

Figure 8-67 shows a high-level overview of TCSR.

#### Figure 8-67: TCSR overview
*Description:* A block diagram illustrating the Core Top Control and Status Registers (TCSR) connections.

- **Summary Interrupts (Right):** The `Core top CSR` connects bi-directionally to the `Summary interrupts` block, which then routes summary interrupts (shown as bi-directional arrows) to subsystems: `RPM`, `APSS`, `Q6SS`, and `WCSS`.

### 8.11.3 TCSR functional description

Figure 8-69 illustrates the TCSR top-level diagram.

#### Figure 8-69: TCSR top-level diagram
*Description:* A block diagram showing the internal components of the TCSR module:
*   The **TCSR** block contains three sub-blocks: `TCSR_MUTEX`, `APU`, and `TCSR_REG`.
*   The AHB clock `GCC_TCSR_AHB_CLK` feeds into the **TCSR** block and is distributed to all three sub-blocks.

The TCSR consist of the following major blocks:
*   **TCSR_MUTEX** accommodates MUTEX registers (`TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n`).
*   **APU** is an xPU that is configured as an APU with 16 resource groups. APU is used to protect control and status registers.
*   **TCSR_REG** accommodates control and status registers.

> [!NOTE]
> Most of the TCSR registers are configured in boot or TZ and they are not software accessible.

#### 8.11.3.1 TCSR_MUTEX

TCSR_MUTEX block houses the MUTEX registers (`TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n`). They are used by the software for interprocessor spinlocking. Each MUTEX register occupies 4 KB of space and is not protected by xPU. These registers are required as not every processor supports exclusive access with bus locking.

The 32 hardware MUTEXES support the following features:
*   Each HW-MUTEX has a separate read/write MUTEX register.
*   Each MUTEX register can hold an integer value. Depending on that register value, the HW-MUTEX is either free, unlocked, or locked (see Table 8-223).
<!-- page 3314 -->

#### Table 8-223: State of the hardware MUTEX
| Integer value | Hardware MUTEX state |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | Free/unlocked |
| Nonzero | Locked |

#### 8.11.3.1.1 TCSR_MUTEX write and read from processor

The process to write to a MUTEX register from any processor depends on the value to be written and the stored value in the MUTEX register. Table 8-224 and Figure 8-70 explain the process of writing to a MUTEX register.

#### Table 8-224: Write to a MUTEX register
| Value to be written | Stored value | New value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | X (1) | 0 |
| X (1) | 0 | X (1) |
| X (1) | Y (1) | Y (1) |

1. X and Y are nonzero values. X may or may not equal to Y.

#### Figure 8-70: Write to a MUTEX n register
*Description:* A flowchart outlining the logic when writing to `TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n`:
1.  **Start**
2.  Check if **Value to be written = 0?**
    *   **Yes**: **Set TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n = 0 (MUTEX is unlocked)** -> **End**.
    *   **No**: Proceed to the next check.
3.  Check if the currently stored value **TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n = 0?**
    *   **Yes**: **Update TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n (MUTEX is locked)** -> **End**.
    *   **No**: **Don't update TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n (MUTEX is locked)** -> **End**.

A read from any processor of a MUTEX register returns the value stored in this register.
<!-- page 3315 -->

#### 8.11.3.1.2 Acquirement and release a MUTEX by SMEM driver

Figure 8-71 shows the process when the SMEM driver on a processor wants to acquire a MUTEX. Each processor has spinlock ID. It is a nonzero integer value assigned by the SMEM driver.

#### Figure 8-71: Acquiring of a MUTEX by SMEM driver
*Description:* A flowchart detailing how the SMEM driver acquires a MUTEX:
1.  **Start**
2.  **Write processor spinlock ID to MUTEX register**.
3.  **Read MUTEX register value**.
4.  Check: **Write is succeeded?** (Does the read value match the written spinlock ID?)
    *   **Yes**: Process complete, go to **End**.
    *   **No**: Loop back and retry:
        *   **Write processor spinlock ID to MUTEX register**.
        *   **Read MUTEX register value**.
        *   Check: **Write is succeeded?**
            *   **Yes** -> **End**.
            *   **No** -> Repeat the loop.

When the SMEM driver on a particular processor wants to release a MUTEX, it just writes 0 on the MUTEX register, and releases the MUTEX.

> [!NOTE]
> Writing 0 always succeeds irrespective of the current value on the MUTEX register.
<!-- page 3316 -->

#### 8.11.3.2 TCSR_REG

Timeout slave interrupt mask and status registers are combined under group TCSR_REG. These registers are used by the ABT module of the Interconnects. For more information, see chapter *Interconnects*.

#### 8.11.3.3 Interrupts

There are several interrupt sources routed to TCSR to provide central interrupt status so the software can quickly identify the interrupt sources. After the source is identified, interrupt needs to be cleared at subsystem level. To allow interrupt routed to destination when TCSR clock is disabled, all interrupt inputs to TCSR are level-interrupt.

#### 8.11.4.3 TCSR register definitions

##### 8.11.4.3.1 0x00005000+0x1000*n TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n, n=[0..31]

*   **Type:** RW
*   **Clock:** GCC_TCSR_AHB_CLK
*   **Reset state:** 0x00000000

The `MUTEX_REGn` register specifies the information regarding the access status of each of the 32 sections of memory, which is denoted by n. Register contents of 0 imply that the respective section of memory is free to use, and therefore unlocked. Nonzero contents would imply that the respective section of memory is in use, and therefore locked.

###### TCSR_MUTEX_REG_n
| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

## 8.12 Qualcomm fuse programmable read-only memory (QFPROM)

This section describes the Qualcomm fuse programmable read-only memory (QFPROM) available in the SoC.

### 8.12.1 QFPROM overview

The QFPROM is a set of eFuses programmed with particular values at the factory that identifies the device.

The SoC has 4 KB of QFPROM. The QFPROM is divided into functional regions. For more information about QFPROM regions on the SoC, see the Regions of QFPROM section. Most of the QFPROM regions are write-disabled to prevent any further changes post-programming. The only regions that are not write-disabled are the antirollback version regions that are changed with each antirollback feature update.

The eFuse burn results define a number of parameters within the device, including the device ID, family feature enabling, disabling, and speed bin classification. For detailed information about these parameters, see the Section 8.12.3.

#### 8.12.1.1 QFPROM acronyms and terms

Table 8-227 lists the common acronyms and terms used throughout this section.

##### Table 8-227 QFPROM acronyms and terms

| Acronym or term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| AP | Access port |
| eMMC | Embedded multimedia card |
| EN | Enable |
| FEC | Forward error correction |
| GPIO | General-purpose input/output |

### 8.12.2 Regions of QFPROM

Table 8-228 explains the three types of register regions of QFPROM in the chip.

##### Table 8-228 Types of regions

| Region type | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| QFPROM Raw Region | This region is used for programming fuses and verifying that the correct values were blown. Hardware supports only 32-bit accesses from the QFPROM. |
| Software/JTAG Registers (sense) | This region contains registers that are accessible by both Software and JTAG. This includes the QFPROM configuration registers. |
| QFPROM Corrected Region | This is a mirror of the QFPROM raw region. The only exception is that FEC is applied to this region to correct any failures and the FEC bits are parsed out of the read data. Therefore, only the true data bits are read from the QFPROM. This region is intended for functional use of the QFPROM stored data by software. |

Raw registers are used only for writing into QFPROM. Software uses the sense and corrected registers to read the register values. Table 8-229 lists the regions of the QFPROM with their start chip address of the corrected registers.

### 8.12.4 Read QFPROM values

Taking the information fused in QFPROM for a particular fuse name requires reading of the memory location (chip address). For example, to identify the serial number, a read has to be done of the Serial Num [31:0] chip address that starts at 0x0005C008. Power collapse is not possible on QFPROM.
<!-- page 3343 -->

## 8.13 Qualcomm Debug Subsystem (QDSS)

This section provides a feature overview of the Qualcomm Debug Subsystem (QDSS)

### 8.13.1 QDSS overview

QDSS provides the central control functionality for debugging and developing code. A debugger attaches to the QDSS DAP to establish and coordinate debug process. Via this connection to the DAP, the QDSS may be used to:

*   Coordinate debug process through:
    *   Primary debug interface – IEEE1149.1 (JTAG)
        *   For debugger connection
        *   Debugging via JTAG protocol
    *   Narrow Interface for Debug and Test (NIDnT) using:
        *   Serial Wire Debug and UART
        *   Serial Wire Debug and Trace modes with both software, and hardware methods
*   Determine the clock/power state of the debug system and request that the state be changed to initiate a debug session
*   Perform all varieties of invasive and noninvasive debug across system CPUs and DSPs
    *   ARMv8 External and Self-hosted Debuggers
    *   Watchdog Reset Debug
    *   PMIC Debug
    *   Abnormal Reset Debug
    *   Logging on un-tethered device
        *   LogKit Integration with QDSS Data
        *   Storing trace data into non-volatile memory for a longer trace history
        *   Support Byte Counter in QDSS to partition DDR into ping-pong buffers
*   Configure complex system cross triggering scenarios
*   Route system ATB trace data to one of the QDSS trace sinks
    *   Trace port interface unit (TPIU)
    *   Trace data to system memory
    *   Trace data over USB
    *   Dynamic reading via Embedded Trace FIFO
*   Use the STM to route stimulus port and hardware events trace to a given QDSS trace sink
*   Make AHB read or write transactions to the system (via the DAP directly) for memory watching, fast code download, peek/poke debug, etc.
<!-- page 3344 -->

*   An on-chip CPU may host an OS debugger and can be afforded the same QDSS functions described above, through the QDSS system AHB slave port.

### 8.13.4 QDSS functional description

Qualcomm Debug Subsystem (QDSS) is a hardware designed to merge multiple trace sources into a common interleaved data format. QDSS also provides a common high frequency trace timestamp clock, debug access port, and a full matrix of trigger event connectivity.

Figure 8-75 shows a high-level overview of QDSS functional blocks

#### Figure 8-75 QDSS functional block diagram
*Description:* A functional block diagram of the QDSS, showing the flow of trace data and control interfaces.
*   **Trace Data Flow:**
    *   **Sources:** "STM HW Events" and "STM AXI Slave" connect to the **STM** block. A **Timestamp Subsystem** also provides input to the STM. Other "ATB Trace Sources" enter the system directly.
    *   **Merging:** The STM output and direct ATB Trace Sources are merged by a **Funnel**.
    *   **Buffering:** The merged stream flows from the Funnel to the **ETB/ETF** (Embedded Trace Buffer / Embedded Trace FIFO).
    *   **Replication & Routing:** From the ETB/ETF, the stream goes to a **Replicator**, which splits the trace data into two paths:
        *   To the **TPIU**, which outputs trace data "To TLMM".
        *   To the **ETR**, which routes data either directly to the "ETR AXI Master" or through the **BAM-NDP** to the "BAM AHB Master".
*   **Control & Debug:**
    *   An "External debugger" connects to the **DAP Subsystem** (containing DAP AXI Master and Configuration AHB Slave).
    *   The DAP Subsystem connects to the "Peripheral and System Configuration NoC" and bidirectionally to the **CSR** (Control and Status Registers).
    *   A **Cross Triggering Subsystem** connects bidirectionally to the external "Cross trigger interface".


<!-- page 3351 -->
#### 8.13.4.1 QDSS power and clock management
All of the QDSS clock domains are shut down in mission (non-debug) mode operation at a root cell within the chip level clock controller. No additional power conservation techniques are required.

#### 8.13.4.2 QDSS reset options
Each of the clock domains highlighted in has a corresponding asynchronous reset provided by the SoC level clock controller.

Given the QDSS central role in system level debug, there are several system resets that require special consideration with respect to the QDSS reset domains.

#### 8.13.4.2.1 CDBGRSTREQ
This reset is driven by the DAP into the system and have implications on system reset domains as described in the . The intent of this reset is for the debugger to unlock a potentially hung debug APB bus, but not the end components on said debug APB bus. It is essentially a debug bus software override bit.
<!-- page 3352 -->
#### 8.13.4.2.2 SRST_N
This is a debugger’s means of holding the system cores in reset without affecting associated system debug logic to facilitate break-on-reset type operations. There is an SRST_N pin on the device as well as an SRST_N bit in the DAP. Either of these SRST_N mechanisms has the same implications on system reset domains as described in .

#### 8.13.4.2.3 System watchdog expiry (bite event)
In order to facilitate debugging around watchdog bite events (e.g. to recover the sequence of instruction trace leading up to a watchdog event on the system apps CPU), watchdog bite events have same system reset implications as SRST_N does.

### 8.13.4.3 QDSS ATB trace sources
ATB is the primary trace data transport physical layer bus. All system CPUs and DSPs supporting instruction and/or data trace functionality output this data to QDSS via ATB and ultimately is sinked by any one of the supported QDSS trace sinks.

#### 8.13.4.3.1 Trace Funnel
CoreSight Trace Funnel (CTF) is enhanced mixing pipe that combines all traces into a common trace output. It supports 8 ATB input ports, each of which defaults to DISABLED and must be enabled via bits ENS7-ENS0 of the Funnel Control Register (QDSS_IN_FUN0_CTRL_REG). Once enabled, the priority of the funnel ATB slave ports may be configured. QDSS trace funnel priority is determined via the Priority Control Register (QDSS_IN_FUN0_PRIORITY_CTRL_REG). The priority control register defines the order in which inputs are selected. Each 3-bit field represents a priority for each particular slave interface. Location 0 has the priority value for the first slave port. Location 1 is the priority value for the second slave port; Location 2 is the third, down to location 7, which has the priority value of the eighth slave port. Values represent the priority value for each port number. If you want to give highest priority to a particular slave port, the corresponding port must be programmed with the lowest value. Typically this is likely to be a port that has more important data or that has a small FIFO and is therefore likely to overflow.

Table 8-237 presents the QDSS Trace funnel source mapping.

##### Table 8-237 Trace Funnel source mapping

| ATB source name | CPU type | Funnel port # |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| RPM ETM ATB | Cortex M3 | S0 |
| QDSP6 ATB | QDSP6 | S1 |
| LPASS Q6 ATB | Q6 | S2 |
| SNOC ATB | N/A | S3 |
| A4X (in MMSS) ATB | N/A | S4 |
| MNOC ATB | N/A | S5 |
<!-- page 3353 -->
##### Table 8-237 Trace Funnel source mapping (continued)

| ATB source name | CPU type | Funnel port # |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| PNOC ATB | N/A | S6 |
| STM ATB | N/A | S7 |

If multiple ports (or all ports) are assigned the same priority value, then the funnel reverts to a pure round robin arbitration scheme amongst the ports with equivalent priority values.

QDSS_IN_FUN0_CTRL_REG also allows the configuration of the hold time applied on the funnel slave ports. The hold time is a period of time for a slave port to retain ownership of the master port. This hold time setting allows one to minimize ATID switching to maximize funnel output trace data bandwidth. Specifically, the HT field of this register is used to define the hold time.

The ATB Funnel holds for the minimum hold time and one additional cycle. The maximum value that can be entered is 0xE and this equates to 15 cycles.

#### 8.13.4.3.2 QDSS STM
The CoreSight STM is instrumentation trace macrocell with software and hardware stimulus ports that generates trace according to MIPI STPv2 protocol.

STM supports slave stimulus port interface, that allows any system master (typically a CPU or DSP) to instrument stimulus port traffic to the STM in order to insert specific MIPI STPv2 trace packets into the QDSS trace stream path to any of the support QDSS trace sinks. This port also implements an STM stimulus port translator for translating incoming transactions matching a given set of programmable AWIDs (in QDSS) from INCR/WRAP type bursts to FIXED (address) bursts.

The STM also implements extended hardware events interface. QDSS extends this interface to a programmable number of input bits. There is a static mux tree implemented in QDSS for selecting a 32 bit subset of this >32 bit input bus to be presented to the STM’s 32-bit hardware event interface.

#### 8.13.4.3.3 QDSS Timestamp subsystem
QDSS generates a 64 bit binary code decimal timestamp for consumption by timestamp capable trace sources (like CPU, RPM, STM, etc.). The 64 bit binary value is compressed into 9 bits from QDSS to target timestamp consumers with a single ready bit back from target timestamp consumer to QDSS (10 bits all together). This prepares 64-bit timestamp for transport to timestamp consumers, where it is decoded back.

#### 8.13.4.3.4 ATB replicator
The programmable 64-bit ATB replicator sends the ATB trace stream from the ETB/ETF to the TPIU and ETR. When in ETR mode, the TPIU arm of the replicator should be disabled using the replicator’s QDSS_REPL64_IDFILTER1 register. All QDSS_REPL64_IDFILTER1 bit fields reset to ‘0’s hence all ATB transactions are transparent to the TPIU (transparent meaning passing through the replicator unimpeded). So to disable the flow of ATB data to the TPIU in USB or ETR trace sinking modes, one set all bit fields of the QDSS_REPL64_IDFILTER1 register to ‘1’.
<!-- page 3354 -->
### 8.13.4.4 QDSS Trace sinks
There are several sinks for trace generated into QDSS over ATB buses:
* Embedded Trace Buffer (ETB)
  * In traditional circular capture buffer mode (ETB)
  * In FIFO mode (ETF), where debugger can drain the ETF whilst the ETF is being written to by one or more ATB trace sources.
* Trace Port Interface Unit (TPIU) - traditional pins trace egress over GPIOs
* USB - QDSS routes data via the ETR and QDSS BAM-NDP to USB 2.0 BAM and out over USB
* ETR to System Memory - ETR routes ATB trace data to a system memory (for example, external DRAM) via an ETR descriptor table maintained by a driver on a system CPU

#### 8.13.4.4.1 QDSS ETB/ETF
Embedded Trace Buffer (ETB) has two operational modes: circular buffer (ETB) trace sink or configured into hardware FIFO mode (ETF) for one of the other supported trace sinks (USB, TPIU, ETR).

In ETF mode, the component functions as a FIFO, where data is read out over an APB interface, usually by an external debugger. This provides a low-speed off-chip communication channel for retrieving trace data, reusing the existing JTAG or Serial Wire Debug (SWD) connection. In this mode, the large FIFO serves to absorb peak bandwidth burst periods from the various trace sources.

In ETB (circular buffer) mode there is a way of retrieving trace after a reset has been applied and removed from either core. This could be in the form of preserving pointers through reset by using Coresight CSR slave registers.

#### 8.13.4.4.2 QDSS TPIU
The TPIU acts as a bridge between the on-chip trace data, with separate IDs, to a data stream, encapsulating IDs where required, that is then captured by a Trace Port Analyzer (TPA). The internal formatter inserts source ID signals into the data packet stream so that trace data can be re-associated with its trace source. It contains an Asynchronous FIFO that enables trace data to be driven out at a speed that is not dependent on the on-chip bus clock. The internal trace-out block serializes formatted data before it goes off-chip. The TPIU includes a pattern generator unit that provides a simple set of defined bit sequences or patterns that can be output over the Trace Port and be detected by the TPA or other associated Trace Capture Device (TCD). The TCD can use these patterns to indicate if it is possible to increase or to decrease the trace port clock speed.

The three supported TPIU modes are:
1. Bypass - IDs are not incorporated and raw trace data is emitted. It is assumed that the trace source is not changing. This requires the use of TRACECTL.
2. Normal - Typical operation with capture devices that require use of a TRACECTL pin.
<!-- page 3355 -->
3. Continuous - An extension of normal mode except when the control pin would normally indicate no data to be captured, there is data emitted that shows this fact. Also, triggers are embedded into the data stream because they cannot be indicated otherwise.

> [!NOTE]
> A debugger which does not support TRACECTL must use Continuous mode.

For concurrency reasons, there are two copies of the trace signals brought out on the GPIOs - set A and set B.

> [!NOTE]
> For the full list and configuration of QDSS TPIU signals mapping to GPIO pins, see table “TLMM signal multiplexing and attributes” in the TLMM chapter.

#### 8.13.4.4.3 QDSS ETR
The ETR may be used to route trace data to a system memory. The ETR supports the use of a scatter-gather table that indicates the physical address regions to use. In most operating systems, it is not possible to guarantee the availability of memory with contiguous physical addresses after boot. To overcome this problem, the ETR supports the use of a scatter-gather table that indicates the location of physical memory blocks.

QDSS ETR master port interface bridges ATB trace stream traffic to the system NOC and out to system memory (for example, on-chip RAM or DDR RAM). In this use case, bridging of trace data to system memory is the trace sink and is coordinated via ETR specific descriptors.

#### 8.13.4.4.4 QDSS BAM-NDP
Trace data may be moved to an on-chip USB via a BAM-BAM configuration. For this use case, where ETR data is being streamed to USB pipe memory for transport over USB to a host debugger PC, the NDP BAM is responsible for creating BAM descriptors for the stream of AXI1.0 transactions targeting the USB data pipe memory. This descriptor stream will target a descriptor FIFO closely couple (latency) to the USB2.0. The ETR is configured with a start address of this region of memory and a size. It then treats this region of memory as a circular buffer and continuously moves data to that region with no software intervention.

> [!NOTE]
> For more information about QDSS BAM-NDP functional description, see BAM Chapter.

### 8.13.4.5 QDSS cross triggering
The QDSS cross trigger subsystem consists of ARM CoreSight components and provides a simple, standard, and easily scalable cross triggering programming model across CPU/DSP subsystems on the Device. The QDSS cross trigger subsystem is an ECT (in ARM terminology) where a CoreSight ECT consists of a number of CTIs and CTMs connected together.

Cross triggering can generally be seen as a full matrix of connectivity (an ARM ECT implementation) between any number of trigger sources (inputs) and trigger sinks (outputs).
<!-- page 3356 -->
#### 8.13.4.5.1 QDSS CTI
The CTI allows mapping a trigger on the Trigger interface to a signal on the Channel interface and vice versa. The mapping is user-programmable. When the CTI receives a channel event it maps this onto a trigger output. This enables subsystems to cross trigger with each other. The receiving and transmitting of triggers is performed through the trigger interface.

There are two main ways for triggers to be sourced in the system:
1. A trigger input to a CTI creates a trigger pulse/level.
2. Software makes a write to a specific CTI register to create a pulse trigger event on a given channel. There is a register to do this for all channels within a CTI.

Method 2 could be used, for example, by a high level driver to create a trigger to the SPDM and BIMC performance monitors to facilitate a coordinated dump trigger of their gathered data over a given interval of time.

#### 8.13.4.5.2 External (Non CPU) cross trigger I/O interface
SoC blocks such as the SPDM, BIMC monitors, NOC (probe) monitors participate in the SoC level cross triggering functionality provided by QDSS via the external (non cpu) cross trigger interface. For non CPU entities participating in the SoC level cross triggering functionality (or ECT), the CTI to which the non CPU communicates via a trigger interface is instanced within the QDSS.

#### 8.13.4.5.3 External (CPU) cross trigger channel interface
System CPUs and DSPs participate in the SoC level cross triggering functionality provided by QDSS via the external (CPU) cross trigger channel interface.

### 8.13.4.6 Debugger connection

#### 8.13.4.6.1 QDSS DAP
External debugger interface connects the DAP to an external debugger via the SoC primary JTAG pins. This connection may use legacy 1149.1 JTAG or ARM’s serial wire debug protocol. This allows a connected debugger to:
* Access QDSS ROM tables (within the DAP and within QDSS)
* Access QDSS and CPU subsystem debug APB bus slaves
* Make JTAG transactions to DAP JTAG-AP connected CPUs
* Make debug bus APB transactions to system CPUs debug units
* Make CDBGPWRUPREQ, CDBGRSTREQ requests to the system

QDSS DAP JTAG-AP master port interface allows a debugger to directly create AXI read or write transactions anywhere in the SoC memory map with stuffing load/store instructions into a halted CPU (64 bit addressing provides for LPAE support). This may be used for any type of debug scenario or to instrument a memory watch window on a debugger.
<!-- page 3357 -->
QDSS has an AHB slave port that allows any system bus master (typically a CPU or DSP) to access QDSS address space. This path allows an OS hosted debugger, for example, to have full QDSS debug control plane access to set up and monitor debug scenarios in the same manner that an attached external debugger would, except DAP JTAG-AP ports are not accessible.

#### 8.13.4.6.2 NIDnT
The device supports Narrow Interface for Debug and Test (NIDnT) multiplexed behind the SDC2 SoC pins. This allows trace in a commercial end-user device through serial wire debug (SWD).

SWD pins are brought out to the SD Card connector using multiple muxes. The muxes are controlled by TLMM_ETM_MODE register. TLMM_ETM_MODE register supports the default SD Card mode, the QDSS Trace mode, SWD+Trace using the NX method (SW), and SWD+ UART.

Table 8-238 presents the supported modes on the device, using the PS method (HW).

##### Table 8-238 NIDnT modes mapping

| Pin / Description | SD Card Signal (Mode 0) | Trace Only (Mode 1) | SWD + Trace (Mode 2) | SWD + UART (Mode 3) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1 | CLK | TRACECLK | TRACECLK | --- |
| 2 | CMD | TRACECTL | SRST_N | SRST_N |
| 3 | DATA0 | TRACEDATA[0] | TRACEDATA[0] | UART_TX |
| 4 | DATA1 | TRACEDATA[1] | TRACEDATA[1] | UART_RX |
| 5 | DATA2 | TRACEDATA[2] | SWDIO | SWDIO |
| 6 | DATA3 | TRACEDATA[3] | SWCLK | SWCLK |

> [!NOTE]
> For information about configuration of NIDnT signals, see section ETM trace multiplexing in the TLMM chapter.

| 31:0 | IRQBYTECNTVAL | This 32 bit value defines the number of bytes that, when moved by the ETR AXI interface, causes an interrupt that may be used by an EE to know how much data is present in memory requiring copy to some other location. A zero setting disables the interrupt. A one setting means 8 bytes, two 16 bytes, etc. In other words, the value in this register is the interrupt threshold times 8 bytes. |

## 8.13.5.5 QDSS_CXSTM register definitions

The CoreSight CXSTM is instrumentation trace macrocell with software and hardware stimulus ports that generates trace according to MIPI STPv2 protocol.

If stimulus writes select timestamping, a timestamp is output according to STPv2.) |

### 8.13.5.6.37 0x10FA0+4096*n QDSS_CTIn_CLAIMSET

**Type:** RW

**Reset State:** 0x0000000F

This is used in conjunction with Claim Tag Clear Register, CLAIMCLR. This register forms one half of the Claim Tag value. This location allows individual bits to be set, write, and returns the number of bits that can be set, read.
<!-- page 3434 -->

#### Table 8-421 QDSS_CTIn_CLAIMSET (Continued)

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3:0 | CLAIMSET_W | W | Each bit is considered separately: 0 = no effect, 1 = set this bit in the claim tag. |
| 3:0 | CLAIMSET_R | R | This claim tag bit is implemented<br>0xF: CLAIM_TAG_IMPLEMENTED_BITS (These bits are present within the claim tag field) |

### 8.13.5.6.38 0x10FA4+4096*n QDSS_CTIn_CLAIMCLR

**Type:** RW

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

This register is used in conjunction with Claim Tag Set Register, CLAIMSET. This register forms one half of the Claim Tag value. This location enables individual bits to be cleared, write, and returns the current Claim Tag value, read.

#### Table 8-422 QDSS_CTIn_CLAIMCLR

| Bits | Name | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3:0 | CLAIMCLR_W | W | Each bit is considered separately: 0 = no effect, 1 = clear this bit in the claim tag. |
| 3:0 | CLAIMCLR_R | R | The value present reflects the current setting of the Claim Tag. |

## 8.13.5.8 QDSS_IN_FUN0 register definitions

### 8.13.5.8.1 0x21000 QDSS_IN_FUN0_CTRL_REG

**Type:** RW

**Reset State:** 0x00000300

The Funnel Control Register enables the slave ports and defines the hold time of the slave ports. Hold time refers to the number of transactions that are output on the funnel master port from the same slave while that slave port atvalidsx is HIGH.

Hold time does not refer to clock cycles in this context.

### 8.13.5.8.2 0x21004 QDSS_IN_FUN0_PRIORITY_CTRL_REG

**Type:** RW

**Reset State:** 0x00000000

The Priority Control Register defines the order in which inputs are selected. Each 3-bit field represents a priority for each particular slave interface. Location 0 has the priority value for the first slave port. Location 1 is the priority value for the second slave port, Location 2 is the third, down to location 7, which has the priority value of the eighth slave port. Values represent the priority value for each port number. If you want to give highest priority to a particular slave port, the corresponding port must be programmed with the lowest value.

Typically this is likely to be a port that has more important data or that has a small FIFO and is therefore likely to overflow. If you want to give lowest priority to a particular slave port, the corresponding slave port must be programmed with the highest value.

Typically this is likely to be a device that has a large FIFO that is less likely to overflow or a source that has information that is of lower importance.

### 8.13.5.8.3 0x21F00 QDSS_IN_FUN0_ITCTRL

**Type:** RW  
**Reset State:** 0x00000000  

This register is used to enable topology detection. This register enables the component to switch from a functional mode, the default behavior, to integration mode where the inputs and outputs of the component can be directly controlled for the purpose of integration testing and topology solving.

> [!NOTE]  
> When a device has been in integration mode, it might not function with the original behavior.

After performing integration or topology detection, you must reset the system to ensure correct behavior of CoreSight and other connected system components that are affected by the integration or topology detection.

#### Table 8-476 QDSS_IN_FUN0_ITCTRL

| Bits | Name | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | INTEGRATION_MODE | Allows the component to switch from functional mode to integration mode or back. If no integration functionality is implemented, this register must read as zero.<br>0x1: INTEGRATION_MODE (Enable integration mode)<br>0x0: FUNCTIONAL_MODE (Disable integration mode) |

This bit can only be changed when TMCReady=1 and TraceCaptEn=0. This bit takes effect only when the EnFt register bit in this register is set. If EnTI bit is set to 1 when EnFt is 0, it results in formatting being enabled. This bit is clear on reset.<br>0x1: TRIGGER_INSERTION_ENABLED (Embed triggers into formatted trace stream)<br>0x0: TRIGGER_INSERTION_DISABLED (Triggers are not embedded into the formatted strace stream) |

### 8.13.5.10.24 0x25FA0 QDSS_ETFETB_CLAIMSET

**Type:** RW

**Reset State:** 0x0000000F

This is used in conjunction with Claim Tag Clear Register, CLAIMCLR. This register forms one half of the Claim Tag value. This location allows individual bits to be set, write, and returns the number of bits that can be set, read.

#### Table 8-540 QDSS_ETFETB_CLAIMSET

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 3:0 | CLAIMSET_R | R | This claim tag bit is implemented<br>0xF: CLAIM_TAG_IMPLEMENTED_BITS (These bits are present within the claim tag field) |

The transaction at the final destination does not have to match the characteristics of the original transaction. For reads this means that a location can be pre-fetched or can be fetched just once for multiple read transactions. For writes this means that a number of different writes can be merged together.
